Crazy fun game with friends.
I first played the original "Browser" version of this game a long time ago.
It was insanely fun then, and even more so now that they have an updated version.
The concept is simple: You hit a ball back and forth, trying to knock out your opponent.
The catch? The ball picks up speed. BIG TIME.
There are 5 characters, and each have their own special abilities and characteristics.
Some can cling to walls, Double jump, Skate along the ceiling, Wall jump, etc.
They also have a special meter that builds up after 4 sucessful hits, allowing your
character of choice to unleash their own unique special move.
The animation is fluid and the environments are well done,
and each stage comes with a pretty sick sound track.
But back to the speed. The game picks up insanely quickly, and you can easily
lose focus and get frustrated amidst all the chaos. (I had one friend who was turned away from this
game just because it was way too fast paced for him)
It's not for the weak. Haha.
It's easy to master the timing, but I can also see how some people would
think the game lacks depth beyond just hitting a ball.
I personally find great satisfaction going up against another person who can keep up.
The matches are extremely exciting, and this is a GREAT party game to play locally.
Hours upon hours of fun if you're competitve, and love getting hyped up during intense moments.
Highly recommended... The price is debatable as far as content goes, but I'm the type of person who
doesn't care too much for that.

Typically, when a game comes across the ethereal surface of my existential wooden desk, I try to finish the game or at least get to the point where I can no longer continue before settling on a review. Unfortunately, Black Desert Online offered no such opportunity as it is broken to the point where you will be hard pressed to even get beyond the start menu, much less actually be able to log into a server.
This will also be an atypical review in that I will be eschewing our established review category format. Why you might ask? Well, since you can’t actually play this game presently, all categories receive a 0 out of 10 as a result. additionally, I don’t want to lull you into a false sense of security by offering you beautiful screenshots of what the game would look like if you WERE actually able to play it. That could potentially add you to the list of confidence casualties (you know….you have an impressive rig that can play anything, so you think you will be an exception and the game will run immaculately for you despite its myriad issues).
Instead, I will simply list the issues I experienced, and then both cite and provide links to the issues everybody else seems to be having.
Black Desert Online incorporates XIGNcode anti cheat into their game. This is an invasive program that automatically installs to your computer when you install the game. The issues with XIGN are so pervasive, I won’t even start getting into that here. However, it is enough to simply say that the use of this was a terrible decision. There are so many better and far less invasive anti cheats that the use of XIGN is unacceptable. It’s also worth noting that it is difficult to remove XIGN from your computer once it’s in there. For more on XIGN, here is a search link from which you can find plenty.
60+ gb’s folks. ESO is a bit smaller file size than this game as is far more expansive. This suggests optimization issues, and those do in fact exist.
Black Desert Online hijacks your screen resolution and kicks it down to like 720x whatever. IF you can get into the options menu, you can adjust it back, but in my experience, it reverted every time I tried to fire the game up
Related to screen resolution, the game doesn’t actually fit on your screen without work. That means you won’t be able to access everything right off the bat. IF you can get the resolution to change, then you will be alright. However, it also starts in bordered full screen, which presents its own issues with seeing everything on the game’s start screen
Once I finally ironed out the resolution issues, I sat in loading hell….until I finally alt/escaped out of there and killed the program
After that, after firing the game up, I was presented with amazing looking loading screens, but no clickable options to start the game. Oh….the options were there, they simply were no longer interactive. It’s not fun to stare at the options and start buttons but not be able to actually click on them
While sitting in loading hell, the game would freeze and die….but not before using up like 70% of my active memory.
So, typically, you go through a list of basics when faced with issues like this: drivers updated, game updated *even forcing an update*), etc….I was unwilling to kill my anti-virus due to XIGN though, and realistically, I shouldn’t have to anyway. I can play Rising Storm 2 without doing so and it has hefty anti cheat software. I uninstalled and reinstalled. Alas, it was all to no avail. This is simply a game I am not able to get to run. So….is the issue me? I think not.
Just go through this thread on BDO’s own Steam hub. You will find copious examples of my issues and plenty of others as well. In fact, look through all the discussions. Apparently the game worked for the first day or two, and there is obviously the lucky few who are able (or claim they are able) to run this game on Steam even now, but you likely won’t be one of those. Even on the BDO host client, you will encounter many of these same issues.
Pearl Abyss and Kakao Games aren’t completely oblivious to these issues, but they haven’t made any progress to fixing them at all, and actually seem like they are really waiting for fan fixes instead of legitimate official patches. Not very inspiring. Hopefully they DO actually sort out the myriad issues plaguing the game though. It looks like a beautiful and awesome game to play if it could actually be played.
Presently, in its broken state, Black Desert Online is absolutely a title to stay away from, and even if it does get patched up, you are still going to want to wait for XIGN’s removal first.

Do you like spending a ridiculous amount of time on inventory management? Do you like spending half a game running back and forth across a map? Do you like minimal combat and a tremendous amount of time speed clicking through text? No? Then don't buy this game.
For starters, this game has its' moments. Just not enough for me.
The camera is wonky and when you finally find an angle that works for you, it will simply be reset the next second.
During combat, there is nothing more satisfying than trying to click on an opponent only to have them sway back and forth out of the way and spend all your AP on moving around the enemy. That was great. And since the aforementioned camera sucks donkey genitals, that will happen a few times when you find yourself wedged in someplace having combat at an awkard location. The allotment of AP points & the rate at which your characters grow is uneven. Me with a giant broadsword will do less damage per round than a wolf and their three attacks (not to mention that you and your six ap points will move a few steps while that wolf can cover an entire screen of distance and still have enough AP to attack you twice). That's if you can even hit anything. Which you won't. Often. Get those buffs up and it won't make a difference. Your archer will still miss. When the thing is a half a foot away.
Now for the inventory managment which will account for roughly 1/3rd of the game. You will spend a ton of time on it and bartering. And it is almost as tedious as running back and forth around the map a billion times. Almost.
All in all, I want to like it, just don't.

It has a fantastic soundtrack and I love the pixel art, and although the enemy design is realtively simple it fits the theme and it just works. Admittedly some of the bosses shine brighter than others (particularly Medved) but I get the feeling that that's kind of the point. I really like that the game doesn't bog you down with excessive reminders of your controls and mechanics and it just lets you figure out your preferred build, which is obviously part of the fact that this game pays homage to the old style of game design.  I haven't yet gotten all of the achievements but will definitely putting in the time to do so, and for $10 I think you'd struggle to find a better playthrough on steam. If you ever enjoyed any kind of platformer back in the day, this one's for you.

Well colour me tickled pink! (or... chartreuse?) It's Mega Man as a GameBoy, with innovative new mechanics and homages to the 80s at every turn... what's not to like? You will need to think about how you use the battery upgrades, although one can kind of break it by, say, getting too many protective case upgrades early on, prematurely eliminating the danger from water/shock/lava hazards. That just comes with the territory, however. There are some scrolling issues in the flying stages, and Rad glitched out of the playable area on me a couple times -- but that, again, comes with the territory.
Kudos to you, TruFun. You thought of just about everything to make it feel like you're playing this on the ol' gray brick, and I *will* be playing through this again one day.

Super Rad Raygun is a 2-D Action Platform game with a unique system of obtaining, using and improving the special abilities at your disposal; you can put "points" into each of your seven abilities to power them up, enabling you to decide how Rad Raygun controls.  For example, you can put more points into your blaster, which powers up your attack at the expense of battery power (which is Rad Raygun's stamina).  Or you can put points into Agility to unlock new jumps, slides and dashes.  I really enjoyed using this system, and found it to work exceptionally well in this game.
This game's platforming was a joy to play as well; it made great use of Rad Raygun's abilities, and reminded me a lot of classic Mega Man titles, which is great!
As far as controls and visuals go, Super Rad Raygun is heavily inspired by the Game Boy era of video games, emphasized by the large sprites, pixel art and, of course, the "Four unique shades of off-green".  This inspiration even included naming one of the main NPC's "Dr. Y" after Gunpei Yokoi, who was the main man behind the developement of the Game Boy itself!  There's even a part later in the game, which I won't spoil here, that further emphasized some of Gunpei Yokoi's history and achievements; a nice little treat for people who know their video game history!
Finally, the story and dialogue of the game is witty and light-hearted, if not a little shallow.  Don't expect any in-depth character development or anything of that nature, but the narrative makes for a good laugh.
Overall, this game is very enjoyable.  For me, it was a trip down nostalgia lane while also being something new and interesting.  If you're looking for a new, fun Action-Platform game to keep you busy for a few hours, then this is definitely for you.

Half-Life 2 wastes little time on exposition or cutscenes; There are no slideshows with heavy-handed narration about The Seven Hour War; You won't find audio-logs scattered about where Dr. Breen has recorded himself monologuing about Nova Prospekt; You never get to read Codex-entries on Civil Protection or Striders; Gordon Freeman never utters a single word and remains a silent protagonist. The story does not suffer from the absence of these things, instead validating the adage of 'less is more.'
The gameplay is excellent and you will, among other things, drive an airboat while trying to evade an attack helicopter before mounting a pulse turret on it and turning the tables, play hoops against a robot, navigate a zombie-infested mining town, drive a desert buggy along the coastline while dodging pony-sized insects, and attempt to break a captured rebel leader out of prison.
There are a couple of frustrating moments; Such as when you're forced to place physics objects to use as platforms or walkways. Something as basic as righting a barrel that's been knocked over is hilareously frustrating sometimes; In sections where you have a squad of soldiers under your command, they can easily get in the way and block doorways; And, the ending can feel very abrupt, especially if you don't intend to play the follow-up Episode One.

Someone clearly loved this game. The setting is a direct inspiration from Dark Souls, where you wander across ruined stone castles perched on enormous trees, surrounded by gigantic ancient creatures. Like Dark Souls, you're charged with going to the top of the world and the bottom of the world to ring bells and collect a macguffin.
This beautiful game was doomed to failure as soon as it was decided it needed a tacked-on JRPG combat system. The abilities and skill trees are pretty bland but largely forgiveable if the combat didn't constantly interrupt the flow of exploration and wonder. Although combat is largely optional, the boss fights aren't and they're annoying if you haven't been grinding out your levels.

Well, here you have it folks; the achievement apocalypse, the end of the achievement world, the death of achievements and hunters alike. Although the developer says that Zen vs Zombie (Achievement Hunter) is a "real game" and meant for more than just mediocre, grotesque farming of meaningless internet points, it's obvious what the true intended purpose of this game is. It even boasts in the Steam store image, where the word "achievment" is misspelled by the way, "10000 achievment".
You may be asking yourself, how do you unlock these achievements exactly? Simple! Just open the game and let it sit there. Nevermind playing the 5 subpar levels that look and function like a Newgrounds Flash-styled game that would be Blammed immediately, there's nothing related to doing that because that would make sense. Zen vs Zombie itself is a generic, run-of-the-mill 2D sidescrolling shooter where you have unlimited ammo and a useless health bar. Why is it useless? Well, because even if you run out of health, you just restart from a checkpoint or the beginning of the level and none of your progress is deleted. So you just run to the right, collect useless coins, shoot useless zombies with useless infinite ammo, while unlocking 10,361 useless achievements.
If you're thinking about buying Zen vs Zombie (Achievement Hunter) to unlock achievements and then refund, think again. It's going to take well over 2 hours to unlock all of them, since roughly 3,000 unlock per hour. The game itself lasts about 10-15 minutes, depending on your luck with the last level. Did I mention it also doesn't have a rebind option for the controls? For some reason, the developer thought it was a good idea to have a combination of WSAD to move and R to shoot; given that you're mostly running to the right all the time, it makes as much sense as the Chewbacca defense.

If it isn't already obvious, this game is for people who love music AND Shoot Em' Ups.  In addition, the difficulty of a given track is mostly dependent on the density of notes and the length of the song.  If all of that sounds great to you, then you will probably like this game.
Feature-wise, the game has many different game modes, mostly to cater to casual and hardcore players alike.  The 'Ultra' DLC adds more game modes and a small amount of progression in unlocking perks, but these are unlocked fairly quickly and mostly serve to simply make the game easier.  That is to say, choosing particular perks won't completely change the way you play, just make living not as difficult.  The inclusion of Steam Workshop is a nice touch which allows you to change the look of your spacecraft.
The game design is solid, I've yet to run into any instability or poor implementation as far as I can tell.  The UI is rather basic, which is fine.  They give you plenty of options to tailor your visual and audio experience.  That said, if you really want to get into using your own music, you will want to create specific folder(s) for this game.  The file system navigation is rather clunky and the way information is displayed for each track can be problematic, depending on how the music file properties have been filled out.  Once you get in-game, you will notice that the way your music is implemented into the game experience manifests in the brilliant and colorful visualizer as well as the pace at which enemies move, attack, spawn and the rate of fire of your own ship.  I have to admit that with the right music, I can really get into it.  You can make the intensity of the visualizer greater or lesser to suit your tastes.
In the end, I firmly believe this game is not worth $9.99 plus more for the DLC.  I got Beat Hazard + Ultra as part of a Humble Bundle, so it cost me a grand total of like $1.00 of the $7.00 I spent on the whole bundle.  I've spent maybe five hours playing it since I got it almost a year ago and I thought it was basically a good game.  For a $14.99 price point, I expect to spend at least twenty hours on a game, being far more engaged than I have been.  This is more of something to install on your laptop or mobile device to distract you while you're on the metro or taking a break from your homework.  The included music certainly isn't worth the gap in reasonable price.  There's maybe a handful of songs in there that are legitimately good.  Some of them put me off straight away.  And it's not that I hate on electronic music, I just believe that most of the tracks range from boring to off-putting.

First, there are the humans who have an interesting way of base building where you are tied into building power grids to extend your base. It's an interesting take on base building while the other base building race, the Beta are set up like Halo Wars take on base building, you only have four points to build on from your HQ. After that you have to call in extra hubs to start new bases. There walls can also be mounted by various units for added defense! Next comes the 'revolutionary' Goo race that has no base building to speak of at all. As mentioned the Goo have no buildings at all, instead they have Goo Mothers which are essentially mobile HQ units that spit out goo units while they also have the ability to consume any hapless enemy units that get to close! Got the basics of what's going on here? Good.
Now this game is supposed to lure you in with the tantalizing idea of facing this Goo enemy that eats units and can cross over any terrain for the most part. Sounds exciting right? Well, not quite. I'll get to that later, first the good!
Pros
-High level of detail in maps
-Professional looking cinematics
-Good Voice acting (Always adds a nice touch in any game! Mostly. Eh)
-Sharp looking units
-Soundtrack (Very inspiring)
-The goo!
Cons
-Bad AI pathing
-Bad campaign AI
-Invisible walls
-The goo!(Who would of thought?)
-Campaign leaves you on a cliffhanger(Alright so its not a real con, *shrug*)
The campaing is something to be lauded, at first anyhow. The campaign consists of 15 missions in all, and interestingly enough you get to play as every race during the campaign! The first five missions you play as the Beta, the mid part of the game finds you playing as the Humans, and for the final five missions you are the insidious, ravenous Goo!(Ahhhhhhh!).
The Beta missions are fun and are a nice introduction to the game mechanics, the game shines in these early missions as you plod through lush rainforests in defense of your home planet from these mysterious invaders in shiny vehicles. (Hint: They are not the Goo). The game runs fine until you run into Goo, the goo do change the gameplay and that's interesting. Truly it is. But it turned out to be a bit of a let down in all honesty. (Heres looking at you 'The Trench' and 'Crash site') I expected the goo to come in waves, to come tearing into my base and just start munching everything. It didn't to my dissapointment. As it turns out the Goo is very much like the other races in terms of units. One thing I noticed, especially on the Crash Site is how annoying it is to hunt down the Goo for good cause you always seem to miss one of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Goo mothers somehow, and then you have to chase that one across the map, it's not really a challenge, it's a test of patience really. I had some fear for the rest of the campaign missions that this would be a recurring theme.
Mission: Crash site tips!
-If you initial base is shot to hell, rush to build a repair pad, when you get the second Hand of Ruk bring it to your base and begin a fun process. Have one of your hands of ruk hunting goo mothers whilet the other gaurds your base and heals from the repair pad. RInse and repeat.
-Drop refineries on any resource veins you uncover! You can actually wall off half the map and man the walls, thus funneling the goo out into the open where it is easily defeated. Unorthodox? Maybe, but it works!
From the Beta campaign the game throws you into the Human side of the conflict where you and your robot allies seek to protect yourselves on two front's as the war heats up. The human's way of base building where you are tied into this sort of expanding grid system is a bit weird. Worse, if the grid is destroyed any buildings tied into it at that particular spot and beyond it go dead. I enjoy how you can spam artillery and turrets and basically turn the game into a tower defense game in most missions.
The human missions are also where you run into some annoying and or game breaking moments. Theres a campaign mission called 'The Observatory' that finds you facing down three Beta commanders at once in what promises to be an epic battle where you face overwhelming odds to save one of your only other human friends who survived the crash. I discovered something that kinda made the whole mission a cake walk.......
Mission: The Observatory tips!
-Build your defenses up at the elft entrance to your base, put up walls, spam turrets and artillery.
-Rush for invisibility tech for 'Dagger' units.
-Spam Dagger units while building up right side of base with plenty of artillery and anti air.
-Send Daggers to every enemy base.
-WIn.
-(Sigh in dissapointment of how easy it was)
Theres a theme here with invisible units, I promise. For some reason the AI cannot or refuses to build detector units in this mission. I won by blasting each base to bits with twenty something invisible daggers as the AI units stood there and let themselves get shot up. I Blew up the air base the same way. I then rushed the last base and blew it up too....using invisible Daggers.
Note: This was on hard difficulty too.
The next mission that manages to be a bother is 'The Terminal'. You and an AI commander from the Beta team up to take down the Goo! Yeah! Kick♥♥♥♥♥ It actually turns into a pseudo tower defense game sprinkled with 'Defend your useless Ally as the Goo munches everything'.
True story ahead here folks, my Ally in this mission came under attack by the Goo and even though I helped them fend off the Goo attack my Ally AI never built another unit for the rest of the game. Even though they still had refineries and factories
...
...
The goo in this particular mission sends out it's epic unit, 'The purger' or as I like to call the 'deer in headlights'. The Goos purger ended up finding my allies base and started attacking it, I thought the mission was over since the Purger could wipe out his base as the hapless units he did have showed no sign of moving to engage this new threat. Luckily for us both the Purger stayed right beneath his base beside the cliff top and only attacked his outlying buildings. The purger actually destroyed his outlier buildings and then instead of pushing fowards it stayed right where it was and didn't move. Taking advantage of this stupified Purger, I preceded to bomb it to smitherenes with impunity. The purger never moved a muscle as I bombed it to death.
...
On the flipside you do get to build the Human's epic unit! It is as glorious as it is shown in the cinematic trailer if your wondering. Another interesting thing that happened is that the Goo's units got stuck in corners and on cliffs and even units out in the open suddenly stopped moving and stayed still for the rest of the game. Perhaps they knew I was coming for them eh? A scared Goo enemy is a dead Goo enemy, or a sign of something wrong with the AI.... For the rest of that mission I preceded to chase goo around the map and eventually ended up hitting my unit cap as I patrolled every resource point and cornered the Goo. After bombing it to death the day was one! But was I having fun? Eh.... GreyGoo promised epic battles with this new mysterous race called the GreyGoo, it was going to be terrifying, insidious, and oddly enough not very grey,(More blackish??? Further data needed.) But instead I found myself dissapointed by the Goo and only kept playing the Campaign to see how the epic struggle between the three races would end.
I'm not going to talk about the Goo campaing much because that's where the game falls apart.
Two words: Invisible walls. Take a look at my pics of the game if you don't believe me folks. You can beat all the hard missions with invisible walls of Radiants. You can beat the last mission by rushing from the start... GreyGoo, a revolution unrealized.  :(

Divinity: Original Sin is an isometric RPG (similar to Diablo and Baldur's Gate) with an equal emphasis between combat and role playing.  The story is interesting and the puzzles and mysteries did manage to keep me guessing.  I love the excellent combat system which kept battles fun even when I had to reload due to a poor outcome.  Although there are a few minor flaws, I am having a lot of fun with this game.  Recommended!
PROS
+ Having TWO main characters (each with their own dialogue choices) is cool
+ Excellent skill and ability system (with bonuses based on dialogue choices)
+ Skills and abilities affect combat, role-playing, and exploration equally
+ Detailed graphics, sound and music
+ Exceptional combat and elemental system allows for highly tactical battles
+ Replaying battles with different strategies will change outcomes dramatically
+ Lots of charming details in the world and its inhabitants
CONS
- Additional party members aren't very memorable or customizable
- Rock, Paper, Scissors mini-game to convince or charm others is ridiculous
- Very little voice acting requires lots of reading
- Lots of saving and reloading (but has excellent 5x Quick Save system)
- Inventory management can be complex if you're a hoarder (like me)
- Fairly linear (going where you shouldn't will get you killed)

I've been craving a good RTS that will make me sweat. I bought this today, managed to make it to the fourth mission on Normal mode so far. I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked.
Resources are running out fast, you have to expand and the AI are relentlessly harassing you. This isn't a game where you can turtle and build a massive army to attack. Each base is temporary (aside from your HQ), each force of unit counters are critical. When you finally get half the map locked off and defended your population cap is up and you have to start deterring defenses to form an offensive force.

In contrast to most recent games, this difficulty curve is a pleasure. I don't want it forgiving, I don't want it easy. I want to be forced to play the mission over and over until I figure it out. I want to have to walk away and take a breather because the last hour resulted in a crushing loss based on a timer and some information they didn't give you until the very last possible minute.

This game is a let down due to the same gameplay as the previous game and no real additional features to the game other than you, as a player, having super powers. Granted the powers are awesome to have at first but after having the powers in the game for awhile the use of vehicles and most weapons are useless. Also, the map layout is the same as the previous game just some tweaks with added alien activity.
Also, the game content felt rushed and what I mean by that is that the company that developed this game orignally made it as an additional content for Saints Row the Third but decided to make it as a sequel to the Third. The game had the same scenario of liberating each city areas from alien controls in order to gain access to certain things (what it is I will not say because it is a spoiler).
Now the super powers that players can use are great in terms of speed, gliding, telekinesis, etc. The animation and gameplay combat was fluid so if your one of those players that don't care about plot story but super power "prototype" like combat than this game is just right for you.
Overall: 4/10
Reason being is poor story, same content/gameplay to the previous game, and boring after completing the story. The powers are great but takes away the purpose of using weapons and vehicles later on in the game. Trust me, once your done with the story, there is no replayable content.

As much as I appriciate the efforts of all those involved, I play a game for the game and story line, in fact after the first go around I usually turn the music down so i can pick up on sounds I missed, birds chirping,background noises I didnt hear. Incredible. Simply incredible game. It really is best played co-op, though the mechanics for it are a little clunky. One player has to make both characters, then have their friend join mid-game. The combat, exploration and RPG mechanics are spectacular. The only limit really is your creativity. This is hands down one of the most in-depth, creative and unique game experiences I have had in a long time.
Replay value is extremely high, as you and your friend can play different styles and morality. My first playthrough was a Two-Handed Warrior turned Battlemage, with my friend rolling an Archer/Geomancer. Our companions (you can have up to 2 cohorts) were a dedicated Two Handed Fighter/Tank, and a stealthy dual-dagger rogue. There is no AI for your party members, so one or both of you need to take control of your cohorts (I controlled my main + the Tank, friend controlled his main + the rogue)
Rerolling the game, we played a Wizard + Wizard combo, with no cohorts. And we killed everybody. Every single NPC we came across, once we were done with their quests, they would die. There were times that the game punished us heavily for this, and more than a few times we had to roll back our saves. But you have the freedom to do what you want.
Combat needs to be seen to be believed. The environment is as much a help as a hindrance. Use it wisely.
Buy this game. It is simply next-level.

This is a neutral review which tend to be negative. Here are, in my opinion, the pros, neutral and cons of Grim Dawn:
Pros:
- So many ways to build your character.
- Good replay value.
- Good variety in ennemies.
- Music and sounds are good.
Neutral:
- Not noob friendly. It's hard to understand the different damage types and how to build your character at first.
- Don't play this game is you want to play a good RPG. The RPG aspect is very poor. You can't customize your character at start and you have no personality. The narration is done only for some NPCs.
Cons:
QUANTITY OVER QUALITY !
- So many areas in the game feels like they are just here to add content to the game. No originality, copy/paste environments, vaste and boring fields... I had no fun playing certain parts of the game, but I played it, motivated by the chance to get good loot and improving my character.
- Same goes for the quests. Most of the quests are not original and not interesting.
- The loot is not very good. On normal difficulty you have rarely epic loot and maybe 1 or 2 legendary late game. That's fine even if it means you play all game with almost no very nice gear. But then, on elite (you have to play normal to unlock elite), you get empowered epic, which happens to be the same ****** loot with higher stats. Not fun at all to get. And again, very rarely legendary loot... So much work for not that much.
- This game have a bad balance. The normal difficulty was too easy all game except for one area that you can unlock 1 time per play with a key that you have to build with rare materials and the ennemies are harder to let you have the chance to get better loot. Then at elite, it was not as hard as normal and I got nothing good in this area, even worst loot than my normal playthrought... so frustrating. The rest of the game at elite was sometimes hard and and sometimes too easy again.
Conclusion:
This game is not bad, but there are so many flaws that prevent this game to be good. I don't recommand this game full price. If you're a hack & slash fan and you're able to live with the cons I mentionned, it can be a good buy in sale.

This game is kind of like a preview for the developers upcoming game, Eastshade. I'd only heard of the main game a few months back, and decided to drop the couple of dollars on this.
Leaving Lyndow has you wandering several small contained environments, interacting with several objects and completing a small number of simple tasks. It's a good precursor to setting up the world of Eastshade, giving you a bit of backstory and context that will no doubt play into the main game.
This game is a small little contained experience, and I like small little contained experiences. Leaving Lyndow has me more intrigued for Eastshade than I was before, for sure.
Also, I took a lot of screenshots, which is always a good sign. Even on what I can only assume is a small budget, the devs manage to do a great job with the environments, and the character models are actually kinda cool. Sure, it's not going to match up to Uncharted 4 in production values, but you shouldn't expect it to.
Basically, Leaving Lyndow is to Eastshade what MGS V: Ground Zeroes is to Phantom Pain.
Definitely reccomend.

Some people say it copied Minecraft and/or Team Fortress 2. The correct term is "ispiration for something original".
Block N Load combines a full class-based team FPS experience with a blocky 5v5 MOBA game, where you can build and reinforce your base AND destroy the enemy's. Each class has its own perks, and each one of them brings their own weapons and special blocks to help their team. All roles can be fulfilled by anyone, but some are better than others at certain tasks. All classes are balanced and competitive. Heck, you can duel as any class with an opponent and you'll always have a hope to win! There are no instakills in this game, if you want to bring down your opponent you gotta earn it like a pro.
Use your preparation time wisely! Build a base, earn resources by destroying blocks and demolishing entire structures with gratuitous laws of gravity! You'll need a lot of resources to build and reinforce, especially the Defensive classes.
Attack the enemy from the sides, the underground and the sky. Dig trenches and secret passages. Demolish the enemy's base with bombs and artillery barrages to help your digging tools. Place special structures behind them to allow respawning directly in their base and spying their movements... or build an entire base in their base, complete with turrets and mines, to make their lives hell! Hard as hell, but worth it!
Defend your base with mines, radars, turrets and lethal traps. No enemy must infiltrate your base unseen. Invaders must die!
Camping in an isolated corner won't get anything accomplished. Your kill count doesn't count. What matters is that you either defend your base OR attack the enemy base.
Balance means victory! Avoid using classes of which your team already has 1 or 2. Only certain classes can place certain blocks.
So what are you waiting for? Block in and give those Blockheads what's coming to 'em! Block Block Block! Block'a'Block'a'Block!

HD Neptunia is a game about games that are people.
And if HD Neptunia was a person, it would be wearing an adult teddy-bear onesie, yelling shrilly about pudding, and trying to grope its little sister.
You would not invite it to parties.
To put all of that another way: HD Neptunia is really not a game that was made for me. It *is* a solid JRPG, one with a number of interesting (if obtuse) systems, but it's wearing a visual novel over its head like a Scooby Doo ghost costume.
Neptunia is, if nothing else, a game of contrasts. It has a deeply mechanically crunchy combat and loot system, but it then spends half of the time you're playing it locking you into watching girls sit around and talk about pudding. It has a neat concept for its plot and flashes of genuine pathos in the storytelling, but then it runs right over those in its bulldozer on its way to demolish the fourth wall. Even the overwhelming lesbian undertones of the game are confused. They can't seem to decide whether they want to be about girls perving at each other for the benefit of the audience - or an actual attempt at romance between members of the (pretty much all-female) cast.
If you don't have a lot of experience with JRPGs, aren't an anime nerd, and don't like visual novels, this is probably not going to be a good time for you.
However, if all the reverse are true, you're probably going to like it.
I ended up on the fence about this title, mostly because I'm such a dork about JRPG systems that I've been mostly ignoring the plot in favor of the gameplay, but I'm ultimately giving it a recommend in hopes that this brings more JRPGs onto steam.
Ideally those would be non-pervy ones, instead of this recent barrage of Aksys and Compile Heart projects, but I'll take what I can get.

This game has about a dozen serious flaws and countless minor ones. Being completely blasted by neon rainbows any time you do just about anything will probably make you want to rip your eyes out halfway through your first song. Even if it doesn't, there's basically no way to see any important information on the screen, like small ships and hazardous debris. More than half the time I die, it's not because I failed to dodge a bullet or enemy, but is instead because of something that I never saw at all.
Power-ups will appear for a short duration, but the warning that they are about to disappear might as well not have been bothered being added given it's lack of usefulness. By the time they start to blink, unless you're practically on top of them already, there is no way you could possibly make it to pick them up anyways. This happens extremely frequently given that they drop randomly from enemies, and the enemies will frequently appear in extremely long strings from off screen. As a result, the enemies you kill will drop power-ups you can't reach because they are obstructed by other enemies.
The stream of enemies from off screen is also frustrating, as like many top-down shooters in a box, enemies can appear from off screen right where you are without warning. As a result, you are really restricted to an even smaller play area unless you'd like to risk rage and frustration.
Song volume seems to be a cosmetic power-up with no tangible effect in game. Added to the lack of significant differences between enemy appearance (there are about 5 non-bosses, with 3 beings practically identical), the game feels like it suffers from a shocking shortage of creativity.
All in all, I highly recommend you avoid buying this game. Despite liking this style of game (both top-down arcade shooters and dynamic music driven games) I feel like I wasted my money even though I picked it up for just a few dollars during a sale.

Upsides/Overview
I played hours upon hours of this game years ago on my xbox original. Without this game, the genre of first person shooter would be very different indeed. Not only does this game offer some of the best team based strategic play I've seen to date, but this game also did it around a time when battles on a large scale were not something to be brushed off as ordinary. The game is very fun, even if you're not a hardcore star wars fan. Multiplayer was unfortunately taken down as Gamespy closed, but not to worry, gameranger has servers online as I'm typing this out, and gameranger is free. You will experience lag on gameranger servers, but if you have the proper bandwidth and hardware to support your own server, you will have the chance to play a game that becomes exponentially more fun the more people you play with.
+Awesome Space Battles, Land Battles, and Land Battles in Space
+Vehicle gameplay
+Class counter-gameplay/Vehicle counter-gameplay
+Capture the Point (Conquest) style
+Plenty of awesome mods
+Very solid gunplay
+Galactic Conquest, a long term war to rule the galaxy (Evil laughing)
+Choice between CIS (Droids), Republic (Clones), The Empire (Stormtroopers), and The Rebels (Watch the damn movie)
+Upgrade/Mastery system on guns/classes
+A.I. is pretty great for space battles
+Multiplayer is still a thing
+I could go on for a long time
Downsides/Conclusion

-This game is old, and looks old
-You will experience bugs if you play long enough
-A.I. are often easy even on the hardest difficulty for a person who has gotten used to the game (Doesn't take very long)
-Overpowered advanced classes on some factions, underpowered on other factions, (The Bothan Spy really doesn't compare to the Empirial Officer, Shock Trooper way better than Wookies. Jet pack trooper and Clone Commander are really bad in comparison to the MagnaGaurd and Droideka and I could go on.)
-Playing by yourself isn't very fun after a while
-Playing with friends can easily be laggy
-Steam doesn't always have this game on sale for 5 bucks (If it is on sale for 5 or really anything but ten, get it, it's worth way more than 5, but because of its age it really doesn't need to be priced at 10.)
-Upcoming Battlefront 3 game may sweep the floor with this one, not neccesarily a bad thing if Battlefront 3 is actually good, but it is a bad thing if it sweeps this game under the rug for no reason.
In conclusion, you really need to get this game, and get your friends to get this game. If you haven't played it yet you need to. If you have played it already but don't have it, get it. If you have played it and have it, get another copy for your friend. If you don't have any friends and have it, get another copy and make a friend today.

I played this game twice, once without Xcom: Enemy Within and then once again with it.  Either way the game is great.  It nails the turn based strategy genre perfectly.  However, Enemy Within as a huge new dimension and level of customization and variety that makes the base game feel empty once you played it.  For those interested in buying this game I highly recommend buying the game along with the dlc, it makes a huge differnce.  For those framiliar with Civ 5 playing Xcom without Enemy within is like playing Civ 5 without Gods & Kings and Brave New World.  It's fine as is, but once you try it with the addons you can't go back.
As far as the actual game goes, it's great.  Building, training and customizing squads to take out on missions is incredibly rewarding.  Watching team members rank up build a loyalty to your favorite units that makes it all the more tradgic when they get caught in the crossfire.  The game isn't just all battle's though, when not on a mission you can build additions onto your base, conduct research to unlock new weapons and build all manner of alien technologies.
Since each mission (with the exception of a few big story missions) takes about 15-30min the game is prefect for the casual gamer who wants something the pass the time while still being high quality and engaging, but it also offers a depth and level of replay ability that will keep more experienced players engaged as well.  A great game that's is worth the time and money.

At the time this was made, there was definitely a lack of deep, difficult cRPG's and I am willing to support developers who create worthwhile things that cater to an unaddressed need. Now, though, Pillars of Eternity stands as a game that *wants* it's narrative to be taken seriously. For that reason, I'd recommend that game instead.

This is a neutral review which tend to be negative. Here are, in my opinion, the pros, neutral and cons of Grim Dawn:
Pros:
- So many ways to build your character.
- Good replay value.
- Good variety in ennemies.
- Music and sounds are good.
Neutral:
- Not noob friendly. It's hard to understand the different damage types and how to build your character at first.
- Don't play this game is you want to play a good RPG. The RPG aspect is very poor. You can't customize your character at start and you have no personality. The narration is done only for some NPCs.
Cons:
QUANTITY OVER QUALITY !
- So many areas in the game feels like they are just here to add content to the game. No originality, copy/paste environments, vaste and boring fields... I had no fun playing certain parts of the game, but I played it, motivated by the chance to get good loot and improving my character.
- Same goes for the quests. Most of the quests are not original and not interesting.
- The loot is not very good. On normal difficulty you have rarely epic loot and maybe 1 or 2 legendary late game. That's fine even if it means you play all game with almost no very nice gear. But then, on elite (you have to play normal to unlock elite), you get empowered epic, which happens to be the same ****** loot with higher stats. Not fun at all to get. And again, very rarely legendary loot... So much work for not that much.
- This game have a bad balance. The normal difficulty was too easy all game except for one area that you can unlock 1 time per play with a key that you have to build with rare materials and the ennemies are harder to let you have the chance to get better loot. Then at elite, it was not as hard as normal and I got nothing good in this area, even worst loot than my normal playthrought... so frustrating. The rest of the game at elite was sometimes hard and and sometimes too easy again.
Conclusion:
This game is not bad, but there are so many flaws that prevent this game to be good. I don't recommand this game full price. If you're a hack & slash fan and you're able to live with the cons I mentionned, it can be a good buy in sale.

Grim Dawn is a good value. At the price, I can't think of a better Diablo 2-like game (that's not to say that you can't find better for less... PoE for free is pretty darn good).
The overall setting is, well, grim. And that is kind of cool. Almost a halloween type feel, perfect for this time of year anyway (this is being written in October). However, the story line and quests were not too compelling for me. I do think the game's creator truly did try to create compelling lore (tons and tons of books to pick up and read, as well as non-required conversations with NPCs). It just didn't pull me in. There are a handful of quests that allow for choice and consequence, but not enough for me to feel like a part of the story.
The gameplay is actually quite good. I could never get my controller working quite the way I wanted, but that is likely more on me than anything else. Mouse and keyboard work great, though there are some levels (with staircases specifically) that cause problems with navigation if you don't click in the perfect spot for your character to run up.
That leads me to my first real issue of the game, and that is the maps... there is almost zero variability. Once you have made it through the game once, you know the maps. The quest locations never change, so there is no real reason to do full clears after your first playthrough.
The loot... oh the loot. This is where the game truly takes me back. After playing Diablo 3 far too much, I longed for the days of actually having to grind for gear you want. Kind of weird, I know, like asking to be tortured. But there is some satisfaction that comes from finding an epic piece of gear that your character can actually use.
My second, and really last, complaint is the multiplayer. In normal mode, it is no big deal to have connection issues. But in hardcore mode... that can spell the end to your character. I generally speaking have good internet connectivity. So when a game with some frequency causes me to rubberband around, like this one, it makes me scratch my head. If you do plan on playing hardcore mode, I strongly suggest never playing online.
My two complaints included, I strongly recommend this game. The support for it has been pretty good, the DLC is not necessary to enjoy the game to its fullest, and really, who doesn't like rolling trains over undead and worse?

I am typically not one for writing reviews. However, this game is an obvious labor of love and deserves a few shiny words. While I haven’t finished it yet, there isn't anything I could imagine happening along that path that could change how I feel about the game. This is foremost a fun and funny game. Its heavy handed references to the Gameboy and the decade that spawned it have more than once startled the dog with my literal lol-ing. But it's not straight old school here; the feel is a great mix between more modern hyper-precise indie platformer controls and teeth-grinding Gameboy slop. The highlight of this games mechanic is no doubt the power-up system which lets you (or forces you to) prepare to tread slowly into battle with heavy artillery or dodge past the enemy with well-timed acrobatic maneuvers.  So if you lived in the 80’s or just wish you did. Or if you owned a Gameboy or just wish you did, then you can’t go wrong with Rad Raygun!

Pirates of the European Seas is a stand-alone expansion pack for The Guild 2 that focuses mostly on piracy, naval trade and combat creating many more options for those that does not want prestige but notoriety.
The expansion adds a lot in terms of dependency between cities and this helps, in some degree, to alleviate the problems the AI have with maintaining production chains by letting the player sail around with ships trading between cities much easier and quicker than before. The piracy features also allow you a lot of new options in the opposite direction as you can now corner markets by denying access to certain raw goods in a specific city.
The developers also took great note of the community feedback and while Pirates of the European Seas is hardly bug free it is a great step forwards from the main game.
Pirates of the European Seas is a good solid expansion to an already entertaining concept and definitely worth a purchase if you liked The Guild II. It does however still suffer from poor AI and a somewhat broken economy.
You really need more convincing? Just buy it already.

I really want to like this more and am on the fence between recommend and not recommend - I finished a complete playthrough of SRR getting all batteries. It's a brilliant premise and foundation with some flawed balance issues and in the later levels seemingly lazy execution. I was in love with it for the first half and felt a bit underwhelmed by the end. Overall I would highly recommend the game if it can address some of those issues, which seem manageable in updates.
PROS:
-Smart battery system, a limiting mechanic heartwarmingly motivated by multiple sclerosis as said in the credits
-Feels like games you love - wonderful setting.
-First retro game since Shovel Knight that I've genuinely loved.
-Music (FantomenK is an awesome artist and delivers a fantastic soundtrack)
-Humor is spot on and the plot is even historically relevant / educational
-Dialogue is phenomenal
-Great aesthetics (references galore, Gameboy colors, vision dimming, 80s pop-culture references)
-Difficulty of first level is great (in contrast to the other reviewer)
-Controls generally responsive
-You can tell the creators love retro games and put a lot of thought into the details.
CONS:
-Balance - if you try to get batteries, you become overpowered and the difficulty becomes completely trivial. The battery mechanic falls apart fairly quickly. At the beginning the brilliance of the mechanic lies in the tradeoffs it forces. But once you pick up a few batteries you don't need to make those choices anymore.
-Stats - the stat increases are extreme. A few points in HP or attack will double and triple both stats. That reinforces the difficulty because with no batteries, you will get destroyed, and with just a few, you will be unstoppable. A system where stat increases are incremental would be better balanced.
-Level design - the design of levels shifts from clever to relatively tedious in the end. Enemy placements are usually completely in one's path and don't require much strategy to address. Some of the later levels are very short. It appears there is a decrease in the thought and care put into later levels.
-Hand-holding - the game feels like it's being played with training wheels. The game's difficulty decreases by the sheer lack of confidence it places in the player. Every turn seems rife with tutorials or reminders to go and get batteries. The water level is laden with extra health tanks to offset damage taken from the water, after telling you to get batteries for your armor so you won't take damage.
-Battery locations - some of the early batteries are challenging and involve platforming (like the mountain level). The later batteries are mostly in your path or in plain view, making picking them up feel like a chore rather than accomplishment.
-Boss rush - the majority of it is trivial, and then the revision of the last form of the last boss feels cheap and luck-based.
-It's Delancey, not Delancy. References to locations should get spelling right.

There will be many first impression reviews here, so instead I'll provide an in-depth review of the game's core mechanics. After beating the story a couple dozen times, earning all of the achievements (including Naked Raygun several times--and even once without backlight or arcshot) and sinking countless late nights, early mornings, and lunch breaks into the Time Attack mode, I can say only this:
& here's why:
I love the tactical design of Rad's energy mechanic because it forces me to be a better player. Limited resources are often unsuccessful in platformers because they're either too punishing or just overlooked in normal gameplay. Rad's energy system is fully integrated and it powers everything from double jumps to weapon blasts. Energy will only begin to regenerate once a specific amount of time has passed since the last used ability (there is a chart in the room above Dr. Y in Cape Canaveral which details the exact energy requirements and recharge rates per battery).
Because it means you need to be aware of the abilities you're using.
Because it means you're not flying through the game on autopilot: you need to be accurate with your attacks and precise with your movements. There are very few instant-death pitfalls and there are zero situations with unavoidable damage. Every boss can be defeated without receiving damage, every stage beaten without so much as chipping Rad's plastic... the challenge isn't always from risk of dying--as is the case in many platformers--the true challenge of Super Rad Raygun is in managing your energy. If you know a boss is about to lunge at you then you'll need to consciously stop attacking to reserve enough energy to double jump or dash around them.
More power isn't always the best solution. Higher stages of weapons require exponentially more energy per use, and there are many situations where it's better to have continuous damage instead of burst damage. A level 6 arcshot deals 45 damage and requires 100% of your energy while a level 4 arcshot deals 22 damage but requires just 36% energy. You won't receive any bonus damage for releasing an arcshot below its energy requirement: at level 6, even if you're at 99% energy, the attack will essentially fizzle and deal 2 damage but will still drain your entire energy reserve. If you plan to hit a boss with a devastating arcshot then you need to give our titular hero enough time to charge.
Instead, you could step down to a lower weapon tier to attack more frequently and with more flexibility, but with substantially lower damage per hit. This strategy has its own drawback: You can only ever have one arcshot on-screen at a time, so you should make it count. Similarly, you can only have three blaster projectiles on screen at a time. These limitations are by intentional design and are accurate to the era of gaming which has inspired Super Rad Raygun and they heavily contribute to the combat system's balance. You could keep your weapons at level zero and still beat the game (trust me)... but you can be much more efficient by playing around with the energy mechanics to find the perfect amount of energy you can expend before backing yourself into a corner.
Inseparable from Rad's energy system is the player's ability to freely change Rad's active upgrades. While it is possible to acquire every spare battery without replaying a single stage, it's much more likely that you'll only discover a handful on your first play through the story. Some are quite well hidden. The brightside is that you don't need all of them... or even most of them! At any time you can open Rad's powerup menu and shift around your batteries to suit the current situation.
Doing some recreational swimming? You won't need any Agility batteries.
Frolicking in the sunlight? No need for Backlighting!
Cosplaying a pin cushion? Move batteries from Max Health to Protective Case.
Not in the mood for boss hugs? Increase your Agility and air backdash to safety.
There's no downside to moving your batteries around--the menu even pauses the rest of the game. Some players may find this procedure a little tedious, but a little exploration is the perfect remedy. Stages are marked with an X once all of their batteries have been found, otherwise they're a blank circle. You're free to go through previous stages to claim undiscovered batteries. This is also a fantastic way to earn bits for upgrades because the batteries that you have already found are replaced by bit crates. Washington DC is especially lucrative for so-called
because it has two normal crates, three battery-replacing crates, and a boss for at least 1400 bits for each full clear.
You can greatly improve Rad's potential with a little farming at any point in the story. Nothing is stopping you from purchasing all of the upgrades before even moving on to NYC. Sure, you won't have enough batteries to actually fill the slots until much later, but you could shift specializations on a whim! This would create a relatively tame, relaxed atmosphere while you cruise through the rest of the game. Other players may find more satisfaction in depriving themselves of upgrades as an additional challenge. There's an achievement called
which involves completely abstaining from the purchase of Dr. Y's upgrades and it's actually very fun (and hard). It completely changes your pacing and tactics and provides the brutal, unforgiving experience that is secretly craved by us closet masochists.
There are a lot of fancy maneuvers that are only possible once Rad has been fully upgraded, and luckily TRU FUN has developed an outlet to explore your full capabilities. Playing a stage a second time allows you to activate a special mode in which you are timed through the entire stage. After finishing the stage, your final time is sent to a leaderboard and you can see how you stack up to everyone else.
There is very little "luck" or "RNG" involved in this game. Enemies appear in fixed locations and behave in predictable patterns. Bosses, too, behave in patterns and can be manipulated with careful, deliberate movements. Aside from a few minor bugs, there's little to catch an experienced player off guard. If you get hit or die it's almost always because you messed up; not because the game is unfair.

I'm sorry for being blunt, but this game sucks.
Not because it's short - it did take me 38 minutes to beat it, but those minutes could have been filled with wonders and awe - they just aren't.
Not because it's pretty - and it is, immensely, and even the atrociously modelled npcs can't change that.
Not because it has a good concept - and it does, it's a prime material for a nice bittersweet slice of life thing.
But in the end it all falls flat because of its lazy uninspired writing. The few conversations there are are boring, the single conflict of the game is superficial, there's not enough backstory to justify even its meagre length, the dialogue choices are strange and make protagonist look slightly sociopathic, and there's nothing impressive in the wording overall.
It's really strange to release such a thing as a prelude to a bigger project, because it sort of says everything about the quaity these people can produce - and it by no means good.
So if you value the story or emotional involvement, street clear, this is hardly the droid you're looking for. But if you want some cheap screenshot material, then by all means, go for it. Except you probably already own at least ten games that can be used for the same purpose. And they most probably offer something fun in return, you know, like games really should.

It's bee a while since I've played an good old-school JRPG... oh, wait a minute, this comes from French Canada?

As I said, Child of Light very much feels and plays like an olden-days JRPG:
You play as a princess roaming the lands to save a kingdom from a looming darkness. And while you do so, you meet companions along the way, quirky folk from various races inherent to the lands, each on their own quest for gain, fame, family or honour.
Conveniently the henchmen of darkness fight on a turn-based schedule, so that leaves a lot of time to think through which crystals you're going to craft and equipt to max your companioins skillset based on their occupation.
Jokes aside, this game is one of my recent favourites.
The art style is lovely - one of the concept arts funktioning as my desktop wallpaper at the moment - the music's memorable and the story's decent. Keeping everything in rhyme also gave it a nice flair and humour. And you can't really do anything wrong with a turn-based menue system, though adding that little Light Companion you controll with a cursor was a nice addition.
All in all, it filled a little JRPG-sized whole I had in my heart and I'm greatful for that.
Check it out if you have the same condition!

Speaking as one who has no experience of the other Telltale games to compare this too, I find this very enjoyable and worth playing. The setting and plot feel very authentic and in line with Martin's world, it doesn't try to be overly adventurous, the Forresters parallel the Starks in many ways, but I like how they wrote this as an accompaniment to the main series, while still including key characters and locations (and voice actors) from the main story.
I love the art style, not sure why some complain about it in the negative reviews, it's rather reminiscent of the style and atmosphere of the Crusader Kings II art I find.
In terms of story telling and quick time events this is a thrill to play, and the characters are appealing. Where this falls down for me mainly is the script (even compared to the TV series which can go over the top at times this seems to use excessive swearing, which just feels like lazy writing to me), and how very limited this actually is in its "choice" level. I don't know how the other Telltale games compare, but this really is a case of influencing how others view you it seems and very little else, maybe choosing to save or kill very minor characters, this is about it really, unless in the last two episodes it does drastically affect the ending. It's a shame, as the way you deal with characters and conversations in this game feels like the central aspect of gameplay, and is a lot of fun and quite challenging, but you quickly realised how flawed it is and how for the most part the same things happen and the same people get annoyed regardless of what you say or what choices you make.
These games could learn a lot from the likes of Deus Ex and the social component of its gameplay, which really does produce distinct outcomes.
Also regarding the music, it's very good and fits perfectly, but you do get a bit tired of hearing the same limited tracks over and over throughout the series...
Overall though a good experience, absorbing and worth buying.

Sadly, despite wanting to support the developers and there being things I do really like about this game, I have sadly had to give it a thumbs-down from a 'recommend' perspective, because it doesn't feel like a full game amongst other things.
+  The graphics are lovely
+  I like the rpg elements of choice in conversations
+  The interaction for point-and-click were well-done
+  The 'dream' sequence was really interesting and I wanted to know more
- Never got to know more, because the game stopped just as you started to get a feel for the character.  I explored everyhing and the game was completed in 42 minutes.
-  The choice of having all the mouths covered felt like a cop-out from an animation perspective.  Likewise none of the people really had any facial changes to show mood which was disappointing and sort of broke the immersion.  Even basic mood animations would have been better than the blank looks that only added to the creepy feel of the people.
-  The music mini-game was annoying, and I would have liked to have been able to quit it and not lose out on the cutscene.  As it was, you had to complete it, there was no other option.
-  Likewise you are stopped from exiting an area until you had explored all or most of it.
I understand that this was meant to be a test-bed for their other game 'Eastshade', but for a game that is less than 45 minutes long and feels unfinished from a story perspective (with no word on whether there are other 'episodes' coming for it), I don't feel this is a complete game that I would be able to recommend to others.  If the game had been cheaper and this was only the first installment of the story, I could better appreciate it, but sadly it isnt.  I can only hope that the developers take the feedback from the various comments and use them to better make their main game.

Hearts:
💘 Great color palettes
💘 Calming background music
💘 Pretty enviroment
💘 Fun mini-games
Broken hearts:
💔 Monotonous dialogues. Every person has exactly one emotion about the protagonist. The mother is proud, the uncle is mad and so on. Thus, the dialogue is extremely meaningless after each character spoke his or her first sentence. Because you will know, where the dialogue is heading (because it is already there) and nothing will surprise you.
💔 While many parts of the world looked pretty, others did not. Not at all. Whenever you take a look out of a window or try to spy into the distance, the world around you is shallow and empty.

Leaving Lyndow is, as I stated in my video, pretty only when you don't look too closely. Using very basic graphical assets in they way that they were definitely denotes a hell of a lot of talent on the part of the Developers. It oozes charm from the amount of objects that make one think back to their own childhood. Unfortunately, there was little else good I could find about the game and the reason for the negatives is that they seemed to be just a hairs breadth off the mark.
The people in the game are creepy beyond belief. Some with penetrating demonic gazes that would send shivers down your spine, while some also would arch their necks at unbelievably weird angles. Also, there is no real voice acting in the game, instead it leaves you to read the surprisingly boring and basic dialogue between yourself and the other characters. An odd disonance from the comparatively charming and well written notes and letters that you find along the way.
There was also the music puzzle where you are locked in with no ability to escape or bypass unless you play the notes in the right order to duplicate a song from a memory. I was forced against my will into this unnecessary litle minigame that I felt completely ambivalent about. The reason being is the game tries very hard to put you into the emotional mindset of someone leaving home for a very dangerous journey, but we're not left with any character development or reqaly anything meaningful at all to accomplish this.
Much of the reason that there is no intellectual or emotional impact, in addition to the bland and completely forgettable dialogue, is the play length. The game is under an hour long even when you take your time. You're simply not given the opportunity to give a crap about the main character or any of her friends or family which ultimately left me feeling completely ambivalent towards the game. And I'm sorry, but $4 for under an hour? C'mon. I respect myself more than that. It is an unacceptable play length for the price point that it is at and, aside from the clever use of lower-end assets to make a world that actually is pretty, the game has literally nothing else going for it except for the music.
While I don't hate the game, I can't recommend it to my viewership.

I've long been searching for a rhythm game with more entertaining gameplay than audiosurf's mono mode, but that requires less focus than Audiosurf's other modes,  so that I can enjoy the music. Beat Hazard claims to provide a 2D shooter that uses the music to generate the enemies, their movement, and your attack power; and were this the case it would be exactly what I was looking for.
However the music element of this game is simply tacked onto a fairly generic 2D space shooter. The enemy spawning appears to have more to do with the amount of time you are into the level, and if the music has any affect on it, I have not noticed it. The only effect music appears to actively have on the gameplay is the speed of enemy craft, and the speed (and colourfulness) of your guns. The only other way that the music interacts with the game, are volume power-ups, which you pick up to increase the volume of the music – and that brings me to my next big complaint: The game doesn't let you enjoy the music. The music starts of almost inaudible, and only reaches acceptable volumes after 3-5 volume power-ups (which you will loose when destroyed.) Even then, the sounds of your guns, and the other craft exploding will completely drown out the music – whoever came up with the volume feature clearly didn't understand the appeal of music games.
The visual design also has its issues. The gun and explosion effects are bright and garish, filling large portions of the screen and yet don't synch with the music at all. This would be a fine design for a bullet hell game (although still heavily entrenched at the garish end of them), but the way it is executed detracts heavily from the musical aspects of the game; this is particularly true when the genre of music is more relaxed and serene. The truth is that the game as a whole does a very bad job of conveying the feel of the tracks used, caring only for the music's volume to determine enemy and bullet speeds. Say what you like about Audiosurf, but at least that game made the tracks you surfed on feel like the song that was playing – and didn't get in the way of you listening to them.
I would not recommend this game, there are better examples of the two genres it is trying the fuse, and a superior version of this game can be achieved by finding a good 2D space shooter, turning the music off, and playing your own in the background. I suppose my search for a better rhythm game continues.

Yes, this game does have a very "expected" story of surviving a zombie apocalypse, but look at what this game does get right. It's rank up system makes sense, combining multiple attributes such as Agility, Power, and Survival.
For the Agility segment, such as running and dodging, vaulting and zip-lining,  and dive-kicking and climbing, are all very smooth to execute gameplay wise, and offers a unique way of exploring the world around you. Roger Craig Smith, the voice behind Kyle Crane (and a few RAM commercials) , does really well in capturing the realism of sprinting, such as the huffing and puffing you do after a long period of it. You can even turn yourself in midair after performing a vault, and grab a ledge that's to the side of you. To summarize Agility, you can combine a wide variety of actions of movement, and string them together, as if they were a combo streak. Dying Light captures a realistic sounding and feeling experience of a true parkoursman (if that is a word people use) , especially when you are being chased by Volatiles.
Power is focused mainly on just your weapons, from your Short Boning Knives to your All-Mighty Swinging Hammers. If you kill a zombie, you gain 200-400 PP (Power Points) depending on the build of that zombie, and what it is equipped with. However, if you journey across the map at night, you have double the amount of PP with each action performed. The weapons are categorized in Damage Points according to the Tier of the weapon. There is a Common Tier, Green Tier, Blue Tier, Purple Tier, and Orange Tier. Common Tier weapons range from 15-100 Damage, being not as effective early on in the game. Green weapons are a step-up, ranging from 205-420 Damage. Blue Tier = 500-700, Purple Tier = 800-1300, and Orange being 1400-3100 damage. There are also the occasional Gold Tiers, which range from anywhere in the spectrum, but do not have many repairs.
Your Survival Rank is short and simple. You get them from completing missions and picking up air drops.
The Survival Point range only depends on the mission, or the contents inside the drop you pick up. To get an air drop, simply look for an airplane that drops a parachuted box, or just listen for the bleep and the icon for the drop on your Mini-Map.
This game is a definite must-buy for zombie and parkour enthusiasts, mixing in beautiful next-gen visuals and rough and messy zombie killing. Also, you will hear this phrase every time night approaches. So, GOOD NIGHT, AND GOOD LUCK.
(This game would be recommended on a higher-end graphics card, to maximize the experience of it. It is incredibly nice to play in 60 FPS, so make sure you adjust your settings so. Your computer will automatically adjust it for you. All you have to do is turn V-Sync off in the Graphics option.)

Super Rad Raygun is a retro sidescroller that will kick your♥♥♥♥♥  It is the year 198X. Mullets are hot, and the war with the Soviets is colder than a refreshing glass of Cherry Coke.  You play as a super hero robot named Rad working in defense of a desperate America to fend off Soviet forces during the Cold War.  It’s your job to fight those dirty soviet ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s back and save America from a certain doom.  So step aside whitehouse body gaurds because Rad is here to ♥♥♥♥ing play.
You jump into the game and immediately feel the ‘ode to Megaman.  The movement is similiar, you can slide, double jump, activate special abilities...it all feels like home for those of who grew up on all those no-name Gameboy sidescrolling asskickers.  While your killin’ soviet baddies you’ll need to manage a battery resource meter that depletes with not only your special abilities, but simple double jumps and slides as well.
Hit up the bosses at the end of the level, get treated to some cutscenes and then choose your next victim on a Mario 3 style overworld.
Super Rad Raygun is filled to the brim with throwback 80’s humor, from rad himself spiciously shaped like a Game Boy, for example, to enemy forces that bare a strong resemblance to Super Mario Goomba’s and references to the greatness that was New Coke.   The game also harkens back to the visual style of Classic Zelda games when traversing levels where the screen splits up into different frames.  And of course, just look at the game.  We can’t ignore the puke green Gameboy overlay.  It’s....just so nostalgic.
With an 8 bit vibe comes 8 bit problems.  There aren’t many, but sometimes the controls can feel a bit floaty when double jumping, enemy gunfire can sometimes travel with you into new screens and hit your♥♥♥♥♥on the way in and the game can often feel oddly paced.  Sometimes sections are way too easy, only to be proceeded by very difficult enemy encounters, and vice versa.  It needs some tender lovin care and polish, but the lack of refinement is also what made these kinds of games kind of special back in the day...so it doesn’t feel like that big of a deal in the end.
I gotta say I loved my time with Super Rad Raygun - played several hours of it, got deep into the game and I have a neck ache from head bobbin to the rockin tunes all night.  I give it the thumbs up, and if you like these kinds of games it’s an easy pass from me.  You’ll find a lot to like here.
