Oh boy, where do I start.
Black Desert Online is in short, a grindy korean MMO with awesome graphics and combat. However, while there are a lot of grindy korean MMOs out there, I feel like Black Desert Online is probably the best.... Kind of.
The Graphics are absolutely amazing (If your computer can handle it) but once you enter a town the FPS goes to complete crap because of how many players play the game.
Combat: The Combat system is extremely smooth and PvP is awesome in black desert online. Unlike most MMOs where you spam numbers, Black Desert Online actually has you memorize combos like Shift E, w+RMB LMB+Shift RMB+Shift, Shift+E+Space which makes combat a lot more interesting. This is by far my favorite part of the game and the main reason I got into it. PvP is a ton of fun too.
Chat/Community: The chat is absolutely terrible and I recommend turning it off once you enter the game. It's literally just people crying for a costume, or some type of item that you can only obtain through purchasing it with real money. Or something about alienwares, or something about traps, and sometimes even Alienware Traps (Yeah... I really don't even know lol) At first it's absolutely hillarious but after awhile.... it gets kinda old. This isn't mentioning that there are tons of arguments as to whether or not Black Desert Online is p2w or not, which I will get to shortly. The community itself though is usually fairly nice, unless you say something bad about BDO, in which case they will usually either make fun of you or flame on you really hard.
Group play: Group play is basically non-existent until you reach lvl 56, where you will proceed to enter guilds/groups to grind for hours just to get half way to your next level.
Story: Black Desert Online does extremely well with it's story telling at first, but near the middle/end of the main story everything becomes extremely complicated in my opinion and it was very hard to follow what was actually going on. My favorite part of the story was the Black Spirit, who slowly becomes stronger and stronger as you do more quests for him.
Harvesting resources/nodes/trading: Out of all the MMOs I've ever played, Black Desert Online does this the best out of all of them. You can hire workers to transport materials, you can use a wagon to transport items from town to town should you want to go the "trader/business man" route. You can also chop down pretty much any tree as soon as you see it, harvest grass/crops for weeds and other neat stuff, fish (which is a lot more interactive than other MMOs, unless you choose to AFK fish which some people do) farm, mine, and even hunting animals (which eventually leads to hunting whales which is super awesome).
P2W/Pay for convenience/Cash shop aspects: Basically the reason I left the game. Costumes give you stat bonuses and unless your really lucky, you usually have a super small chance to get one legit from buying it off the market. This is because lots of people camp the market and bid on the costumes as well, making your chances much lower as I said above. There are two specific costumes in BDO that make you look camoflauged (Sorry if i misspelled that) hide your nametag which makes it a lot harder for people to notice you coming to them to attack them and also makes it harder for people to hit you in combat, and still give you even more stat bonuses. These two costumes each cost 34.00, which is why not many people have them. There are also horse costumes that give your horse special new passives that can be purchased, wagon costumes that give your wagon special new passives that can be purchased, and even boat costumes that give your boat special new passives that can be purchased. You can also purchase pets for 9-11 usd each in the pearl store, and can have 4 pets equipped at a time. Pets can be bought from the market place as well, but just like the costumes, people camp and bid on them as well. Through all my hours even with putting notices on nearly all pearl items I haven't gotten a single one. Anywho, back to pets. They pick up items for you and have other special passives that really help you out endgame. This sounds good, until you figure out that when you get a pet, they're tier 1, and can only pick up an item every 10 seconds. You have to mate 2 pets (which destroys both of them) to get a higher tier pet. Over and Over until you get to T4 usually. It would cost a lot of money to have 4 tier 4 pets. Unfortunately, endgame these pets are almost essential to your grind, making it very hard to progress otherwise. There are also Value Packs, which are the equivalent of a subscription. You can buy these from the marketplace but like I said above with the costumes, the chances are really low and people usually don't put up pearl items (items paid for using real money) up in the marketplace much. These value packs give you unlimited use of certain things, more weight, more inventory space, more money from marketplace sales, etc etc. There are also items you can buy from the pearl store that can instantly revive you, increase your inventory space even more, or even increase your weight even more. There are maids that you can also pay money for, which allow you to open up the market even if you aren't at the market. There's also furniture that you can buy using Pearls (real money currency but in BDO, given when you pay real money) but unfortunately that's really expensive too. Furniture in BDO can also be found, but found furniture usually doesn't give you enough interior points to actually progress your houses' rank. Furniture can also be bought in the market place but the price of furniture in there is usually either really expensive, the item gets taken super soon (like the costumes), or the interior points the furniture gives is mediocre. There's a lot more I'd like to cover but I'm afraid that my text space will end soon.
EDIT: Support and Staff: I forgot to mention this in my review originally, but the Support and Staff behind Black Desert Online are always helpful and really nice. I've had to send two tickets to them, one concerning a glitch in my inventory and another concerning something about my old account i used for a free trial, and the responses and help was always really fast, respectful, and nice. Most MMOs responses send you to some page with info or the responses are like robot responses and sound like they were copied and pasted with a few changes.
Conclusion: Black Desert Online is a really cool grindy, korean MMO with one of the best gathering and combat systems in any MMO we've ever seen, along with an awesome story that starts out really cool, but begins to become worse and worse as you progress further into it. The graphics are absolutely stunning.... Until you get into a town. Unfortunately, The cash shop gives players too many advantages and hinders those who don't like to put a lot of money into the game. Can you get by in the game without spending a single cent besides purchasing the game itself? Yes! Will people who pay money be a lot better than you? Generally speaking unless your the number 1 gamer or they're one of the worst, definetely! And by a long shot.
Final Verdict: Mixed. But since there's no mixed option for reviews, I'll make it negative. The game is definetely worth trying out and it's a ton of fun. I can definetely see myself hopping onto it again every now and then for awhile. It's an awesome game. But I just can't support all the P2W/Pay for convenience items that give people such a large edge over players who don't want to pay an extra cent, and don't want to get too into a game like that.

Addictive gameplay. Yes I am actually coming back for the gameplay, not the art or story. The art is great but it takes more than graphics to make me love a game. I'm not a fan of the constant rhyming in the story but it is supposed to be a storybook game and the gameplay is fun enough to forgive this. The battles have a twist to them. They are turn based but you have influence on the turn order. With your mouse you can slow one opponent at a time, this allows you to attack before them and interrupt their attack. I like it better than the traditional formula.
The battle strategy and the compulsion to find all the Oculi to craft the highest possible upgrades keep me coming back and make me forgive the cons. The battles can get repetitive when you fight the same combination of enemies in a row, but in the end I still want to grind through to get all the stardust, oculi, and skills upgrades. And when I get bored I can mix it up by using a different strategy. By the second half of the game there are several extra characters that allow you multiple options to win and it only gets better as you upgrade their skills. For example you can slow your opponents, paralyze them, speed yourself up, buff your stats, focus on one enemy at a time, or try to time it just right so that all three get interrupted while casting and have to wait longer.
The game can be overly easy on normal (except for some boss fights) so if you've played RPG's or even RTS's before and want a challenge you should pick hard. You can always switch to normal in the menu. I just finished the game and I'm about to try new game+ on hard.
I would also love a mobile spinoff that focuses on battles, obviously the mouse functions would have to be given up.
EDIT: The first time I opened this game I had a lot of bugs like skipping dialog and disappearing items in the menu. I had played the game for 6 hours in one sitting and the bugs were still there so I figured they would always be there. After opening it for the second time all of the bugs seemed to go away so if you have similar problems you can try restarting the game and/or your pc.

Well, Telltale and GRRM: two writers who don't bend the rules to give you a happy ending. How could this not be an excellent game?
Watching GoT is great, but it's a passive experience. You sit and watch and cheer for the goodies, talk to your colleagues about what a total b-word Cersei is, but until you've actually had the real Cersei Lannister interrogating you, with bare seconds to choose an answer that won't♥♥♥♥♥♥her off too much, you've never felt quite so immersed or vulnerable watching GoT. It feels rather like a mouse might, being trapped under a cat's paw whilst the cat tries to decide if it's hungry today.
You care about the characters; you care about the setting, and you know that if you say the wrong word it could mean disaster for you and your family. There is enough time given to the characters we know from the books and show; they don't just feel like token cameos, but an integral part of the plot without stealing the spotlight from the main characters' story.
If I had to find any negatives, they'd be minor. I've noticed one or two flashes of an American (or even Australian) accent slip out now and then, but for the most part the voice acting is on point. Also, it's clear no one at Telltale has ever picked up a weapon in their life, but to be fair, the combat in the show is not exactly convincing either for the most part, so it doesn't distract too much.
In all, I strongly recommend this to anyone who's caught up with the show. If you've only started watching season 1 and 2, for God's sake don't play this yet. Mind you, if you've managed to avoid the spoilers for this long, you're probably smart enough not to be even looking at this page.

XCOM unusual gameplay decisions:
1 - To save the entire globe from alien invasion you are given the princely sum of $500 a month.
From this $500 you will need to excavate a volcano, build labs, satellites and power plants. You will also need to recruit scientists, engineers and soldiers, plus buy all their kit and consumables.
Half the time you end up battling your own meagre budget rather than the aliens, desperately flogging your scrap alloys to stay solvent. Whilst cities around the world are burning, your shadowy boss will grumble at you over a crackly skype channel but still refuse to increase your funding.
2 - If your team's sniper dies you can't just recruit another trained sniper from any one of the nations that finance XCOM with tens of dollars. Presumably you can't afford to - You must train a rookie up on a zero hours contract that means they only advance their training when 'on the job' of killing aliens. This could take....days. Due to XCOM employment law, the rookie may then decide that sniping is not for them, and become another class of soldier instead. You will still have to pay them.
3- XCOM zombies are hugely tough. Hiding on top of the Mall won't work here - They move loads of squares each turn and (unusually for zombies) they can climb drainpipes. Blasting zombies at point blank with a shotgun (100% hit chance) won't work either - zombies just collapse and spawn another Cryssalid. The Cryssalid then proceeds to turn your soldier into....another zombie.
4- Although you land in an aircraft, XCOM decides the best way for you to tackle the alien threat is to fight from the ground, in small teams with no air support. Aliens that have jetpacks think differently. As they are not restricted by the moving square-by-square system, they will use their move to immediately take to the skies and land in cover, on your flank, anywhere on the map. Nothing you can do will stop them.
5- Your troops can carry enormous great laser rifles and full body armor, but either one extra armor vest OR one hand grenade, never both.
6 - Thin men can teleport in behind you and poison you. Once you're poisoned you may as well be dead without a first aid kit. If you decided to pack a solitary hand grenade instead of a first aid kit - Too bad.
(So it's a pretty unforgiving game)

What can I say about BDO? Well, I tried it on a whim expecting nothing more than a generic Asian grindfest MMO with nice customisation. I am happy to say that this is not the case.
Youll probably see alot of reviews of BDO both positive and negative stating that the game has no particular focus. This is entirley the case. For me, they seem to have combined so many different games into a (nice looking) online world.
Did you enjoy stardew valley/harvest moon? DBO has farming to a reasonable depth. Set one up into any location in the vast world to run your little crop farm.
Do you enjoy games with fishing mini games? DBOs got em.
Prefer a nautical life on the seas? Trading from port to port? Yup DBO has you covered. Lots of Islands and sea space to keep you busy.
Liked elite or the X series? Great, you have a fantasy version of similar mechanics. Buy low at one town, sell high at another. Upgrade your trade carts and its the merchant life for you.
Prefer to manage rather than mule? DBO has you covered with an array of minions who will farm/mine/lumber/proccess for you (albiet at a slower rate). Set them up into a production network to roll off items to sell to the other players.
Dont fancy any of the above? Acutally enjoy mob bashing, looting? yeah go for it. Vids on the store show you the combat, its great.

EDIT: Now that those awful fake reviews are gone, I'll post an actual review of the game but I will leave my original statement at the bottom of the review as it is still relevant, XIGNCODE IS NOT A ROOTKIT AND DOES NOT SCAN YOUR FILES OUTSIDE OF BDO RELATED FOLDERS.
I am in love with the game. This is because it meets a lot of my personal tastes and I would fully understand why people might not like it. Here are some of the main reasons why I love the game but others might not.
+Stuff to do - I am concerned in the games global chat when I see people immediately grinding up to a high level and then complaining there is nothing to do. This would be akin to playing shooter, only playing one map and using one gun and then complaining about lack of variety in the game. This is a sandbox MMORPG, not a theme park MMORPG. The primary difference between the two is that in a themepark MMORPG, you do the content in the order that the developer intended it to be seen in. This usually means leveling to max and then doing large scale end game dungeons, aka Raids. You do that content until you finish it and then you either repeat it a bunch of times or you wait until the next batch of content is released and most other content is secondary or tertiary. A Sandbox MMORPG means that the end game is whatever you make of it, the developers put in mechanics and the players decide which of them is the most important. What this means to me, is that there is a place for players in BDO that do not wish to do the "end game" of themepark MMOs. In some sense, the overarching goal in BDO is to get the best gear, however the paths you can take to reach that goal are much more varied than a themepark MMO. If you wish to hang out with friends, ride a boat into the ocean and spend your time deep sea fishing or train horses or farm vegetables and fruits or trade manufactured goods across the continent, all of those will enable you to become a powerful character in all aspects of the game, rather than just simply running the end game raid until you get the best gear.
+ The Combat -  The combat in BDO is quality enough to find itself in a dedicated single player beat-em-up style game (think Dynasty Warriors). It is an action style combat, so there is no tab targeting and skills require you to aim with your cursor and many can be cast on the move. This makes combat very fluid and rewards players for landing combos and precise movement in both PvE and PvP. If you are used to traditional MMO style combat with a hotbar and tab targeting, then it may be difficult to adjust to this style of combat.
+ The Visuals - The game is gorgeous for an MMO. It might not stand up to the most visually stunning single player releases of the past year or two, but it has a quality to it that nearly every other MMO on the market cannot touch. The only major thing lacking in this department would be armor customization as there are very few default armors availble and a lot of visual customization for your character is locked behind the cash shop. It is unfortunate, but not really a deal breaker for me as I quite like the default armors for my classes.
+The Scale - Scale is something that a lot of modern MMOs do not  care about. It's the difference between World of Warcraft pre-flying mounts and post flying mounts. The inability to fast travel in this game makes it so this MASSIVELY multiplayer online game, feels truly massive. Riding a horse down the coast over a dirt path while the waves crash along the rocks, traveling a few kilometers to the nearest town is peaceful in my eyes and makes the game world feel expansive and interesting. I understand that people might not like the lack of convienence of just hopping on an eagle or taking a portal but it is something that I sorely missed from older MMORPGS. Actually travelling across the ocean instead of giving me a loading screen made me feel a sense of wonder that I had not gotten since I was a young teenager booting up World of Warcraft in 2005 and running across the Barrens into Ashenvale.
+ Grind - There is an immense amount of grinding later in the game (past level 56) to achieve good amounts of gear and extra levels. I love this because I believe it gives a clear indication of those who are dedicated and those who are not. I do not want to be on the same power level as people who have been playing for a year within one month of playing, but I understand that people do not like playing catch up. Gear is gated behind money

Con:
Slow, glacially slow.  Every fight takes forever, the long drawn out nature of pretty much every action makes a very short game into a long one.
The actual amount of content is very small for an RPG.  It takes a good while to finish because everything is so slow.  I would quite often save and quit after a few fights thinking, I really can't be bothered.
Lack of UI polish.  Absolute bare minimum of assistance given to you to set things up.  Constant little niggles of 'why do I have to do that, a simple menu option would have been so easy.
Targetting is appalling, utterly awful.  Quite frequently just as you click on a target it will move and you click the ground instead, and your character will waste precious turns running around often getting whacked with attacks of opportunity.
Awful party organisation.  The drag and drop idea is dreadful.  Just make some standard hotkeys please.  In general the options for hotkeys are quite limited.
Very average story and plot.  The voice acting is equally average.  Given the slow pace of the game, you would think they had spent more time coming up with an few ideas of their own instead of adopting every RPG cliche.  Overall, outside the environmental mechanics, not much imagination used.
Buffs and Potions, tiny durations makes them pretty much redundant.
Pro:
The environmental effects can be fun, throwing barrels of oil at people is midly diverting for a few combats.  But the grinding slowness of fights kinda of deflates the fun.
Looks ok! Some of the environments look great, but it's all generic stuff.  Here's a fiery lava place, here's an icy mountain place (wot no dwarves?!!!)
er...
Overall I think this game is over-rated.   If you love slow turn based games this is probably a good choice for you, if you haven't played Torment, go play that. It's better.

Child of Light is absolutely gorgeous to look at and truly feels like a fairy tale in motion with its mix of pencils and watercolors: the art is backed up by an equally good soundtrack that quietly follows your exploration and turns suitably epic when you enter a fight. The gameplay is a throwback to older JRPGs with an action timeline where being attacked during a cast can see you interrupted and thrown back: this means good planning and timing- not to mention a judicious use of your skills- will go a long way towards making combat easier.
The game suffers a bit in complexity though as the actual RPG elements are a bit shallow: each level up sees you getting a point to spend on a branching skill tree but most unlocks are just passive bonuses, loot and equipment are also very basic and are basically only gems to slow in one of your three equipment slots and a few potions. The story is failry interesting but most characters, villains included, feel a bit too two-dimensional to be memorable and this mars the narrative a bit: there's enough to move the plot and make you want to see the ending but that is all.
Despite its basic gameplay and somewhat forgettable story Child of Light is still a game to recommend due to its interesting combat mechanics and gorgeous art: if you somehow missed it or it's still part of your backlog then know it's a game worth your time.

It's been a long time since we've had a good old school sci-fi RTS, wasn't it?
Well, if you are even a tiny bit into RTS genre - Grey Goo is definitely worth checking out.
It feels and plays like C&C in its best days. It looks gorgeous. It runs relatively well (aside from that weird framerate I have in menus and occasional drops when there are too many units, but devs are already aware of the problem).
Pick one of three factions and destroy your enemy. Each of the factions has almost completely different playstyle.
Humans (or Alpha) are tied to their base. They have to build conduits that carry power to their buildings. But conduits are pretty fragile. That forces you to be very careful about extending your base - you'll need to guard every building and conduit you have. To do that, you can use a variety of turrets that work from conduit (that's a unique Human feature).
Beta (aliens) are slightly more mobile than humans. They construct all the buildings as attachments to either the HQ or hubs. The hubs can be built pretty much anywhere in the world, thus making it pretty easy to expand your influence. You still have to guard your satellite hubs, but it's pretty easy to do with units mounted on walls (that's a unique Beta feature).
And then there Goo. It does not have bases, it's not tied to anything. It's just a Mother Goo and her children. You only way to survive is to replicate and capture each and every resource pool on the map. And then replicate again, morph into an army and kill everyone.
Oh, and every faction has it's own unique Epic Unit, which is, well, pretty epic, but slow.
It's a bit sad that Humans and Beta have such a little number of differences. But they are different enough to keep the gameplay fun and varied.
There are as well a lot of modern age takes and improvements in the game.
There's quite much less micro than say in Starcraft 2 - the games wants to do a lot of things for you (of course, you can pick to do most of them yourself, but it's not necessary, AI does a pretty good job at it).
For example, there are no workers - buildings are constructed by either spaceships or they just warp in.
The harvesters are as well managed automatically by the refinery, you don't have to worry about building optimal number of them - just about defending them from enemy.
And QWERT-shortcuts that was most likely inspired by DOTA-like games allow you to quickly build new units or building even when you are away from you base. It's quite much easier than microing in SC2.
The AI in game is pretty good (or maybe it's me who's terrible) - I was able to play against it without terribly losing only on easy. So, if you are skirmisher - you will probably love to play against it.
Netcode seems to be working OK too - tried a couple of MP games (but lost terribly, once again :D).
And, really, aside from that framerate bug that my machine experiences for some reason, I don't really have anything else to complain about. Game is rock solid RTS.

An incredibly tense and stressful game created by Telltale Games. The choices you make feel tense, they make you feel like your choices could really make or break whatever happens next. The characters (At least the main ones) are great. They're likeable, smart, cocky, sometimes even funny and also badass. The antagonists (Whitehills) of the game really make you feel for the Forresters, you'll really want to stab them in the throat or fill them up with arrows.
Now onto the bad side. Visually, it's meant to simulate an oil painting but fails on that on multiple occassions. Certain parts like the backdrops or scenery sections are stunning. But most of the time you'll notice incredibly muddy textures. Some animations also look very awkward and goofy at times, that includes facial animation. I could care less about the graphics but the animations do sometimes take me out of the experience.
Overall, this game is absolutely fantastic. In terms of story and characters at least. A solid 8 out of 10 so far.

For a game that relies solely on a choice-driven story, how the plot unfolded felt very reliant on scenarios that forgot to factor in any choices made by the player, resulting in asinine plot twists and unresolved plot holes. Leaving Lyndow is a short, meditative introduction to the intriguing world of Eastshade.
I only learned about Eastshade a few weeks ago, but was instantly intrigued by an interesting concept and an imaginative world. Leaving Lyndow is a short preview that the small development team are using in place of a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the fully fledged Eastshade game, which will be an open world adventure game following the journey of a travelling painter.
Leaving Lyndow gives us a taste of what to expect from that game, a gorgeous tease of one of the most intriguingly unconventional game worlds since Morrowind. The game is, as mentioned, particularly short (my first playthrough clocked in at approximately 30 minutes, though I plan to play through it more than once) but for the price of a particularly cheap sandwich, you can't go wrong. Unlike most games in the first person exploration genre, the areas of Leaving Lyndow are populated with NPCs with which you can engage in short conversations, granting a glimpse into a world already filled with history - you're not joining the protagonist at the beginning of her story, but in the middle of it. Gameplay mostly consists of exploring a few areas of Nava/Lyndow (unlike Eastshade, Leaving Lyndow is not open world and is instead made up of several hub areas) and poking around lived in areas for tantalising plot points. In addition, it must be noted that the understated, pleasant score greatly enhances the sensory landscape of Leaving Lyndow.
The only negatives I could really think of are that the game is, as described, relatively short - I did expect the island of Lyndow to be fully explorable before I purchased the game, which I felt would have extended playtime as I like to explore and poke around game worlds, however this is not the case. It must be acknowledged that the short length of Leaving Lyndow is intentional and it tells a complete slice of a much larger story. In addition, the game is gorgeous, but there is a jankiness to some of the NPCs and assets - I feel this is a limitation of the Unity engine rather than a reflection of the developer's talent as he has created some wonderfully interesting areas to explore.
If you want to support the development of a truly intriguing game and to take your first few steps into an imaginative and beautiful world, you should definitely purchase Leaving Lyndow.

XCOM unusual gameplay decisions:
1 - To save the entire globe from alien invasion you are given the princely sum of $500 a month.
From this $500 you will need to excavate a volcano, build labs, satellites and power plants. You will also need to recruit scientists, engineers and soldiers, plus buy all their kit and consumables.
Half the time you end up battling your own meagre budget rather than the aliens, desperately flogging your scrap alloys to stay solvent. Whilst cities around the world are burning, your shadowy boss will grumble at you over a crackly skype channel but still refuse to increase your funding.
2 - If your team's sniper dies you can't just recruit another trained sniper from any one of the nations that finance XCOM with tens of dollars. Presumably you can't afford to - You must train a rookie up on a zero hours contract that means they only advance their training when 'on the job' of killing aliens. This could take....days. Due to XCOM employment law, the rookie may then decide that sniping is not for them, and become another class of soldier instead. You will still have to pay them.
3- XCOM zombies are hugely tough. Hiding on top of the Mall won't work here - They move loads of squares each turn and (unusually for zombies) they can climb drainpipes. Blasting zombies at point blank with a shotgun (100% hit chance) won't work either - zombies just collapse and spawn another Cryssalid. The Cryssalid then proceeds to turn your soldier into....another zombie.
4- Although you land in an aircraft, XCOM decides the best way for you to tackle the alien threat is to fight from the ground, in small teams with no air support. Aliens that have jetpacks think differently. As they are not restricted by the moving square-by-square system, they will use their move to immediately take to the skies and land in cover, on your flank, anywhere on the map. Nothing you can do will stop them.
5- Your troops can carry enormous great laser rifles and full body armor, but either one extra armor vest OR one hand grenade, never both.
6 - Thin men can teleport in behind you and poison you. Once you're poisoned you may as well be dead without a first aid kit. If you decided to pack a solitary hand grenade instead of a first aid kit - Too bad.
(So it's a pretty unforgiving game)

This game is so depressing I can't find the strength to finish it, but I really love it and will one day face the consequences of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ choices I took in my playthrough.
I'm crap at this kind of strategy game, it's frustrating, and I generally don't have any fun while playing them but it seems that in the Banner Saga the story still manages to keep me going and I find myself getting better and less frustrated about my lack of skills (for which the game makes me pay full price). The scenery is really beautiful, the lore interesting and the storyline heart-wrenching. Austin Wintory, the soundtrack composer, has truly done a great job on this game. We probably get too attached to the characters, which would be great if I didn't kill like half of them by taking the worst choices.
The Banner Saga has three phases in gameplay : - One is when advancing the caravans, having to handle numbers, morale, food.
- Two is the dialogues and taking decisions, meaning having to deal with consequences (losing morale, losing caravan members, having a party member dying/fleeing, etc...). Some decisions seem to be random spawned during travel times, others are scripted.
- Three are the combats, split between taking decisions on battlefield strategy which will affect your fighters and clan members in your caravans, and also on the number of ennemies you will face in the turn-based combat system.
Overall, it really is a great game, quite challenging in many ways but it serves in conveying the characters' stuggles, it's depressing as hell, but also really beautiful with a great atmosphere.

A good RPG that you should try, but be aware of the strength and weaknesses of this game.
Read all the other feedbacks for the good stuff, Ill just write down the bad stuff as everybody ells skips it and just writes the good stuff.
There is only 2 big weakness with this game, imo.
1, Questing. You will be relaying on Google as you will mess up quests if you do not do them in the right order, and you will end up with quests in your quest log that can not be removed or finished.
Some quests are even gamebreaking if you do not finish them in the right order. Ending up with having to go to an earlier save, if you have one that far back.
I am all for a bit harder quest system where you need to think a bit, but this game have taken it to a whole new level. Some quests will be almost impossible to do because there is zero information, just a few words. You have to talk to every person in the game to find any relation and information on quests and how to go on with them. You stuck? Well, go talk to all NPCs there is and read all the text they tell you. It becomes more annoying than fun. It is a mess of a questing system that will not stop you from braking the game.
2, part of the combat. Ill try to explain.
The figures (you, npc's, monsters etc) have an motion when standing still. They sway back and forwards etc to create an image if being alive. The hitbox of the target you want to attack is the frame around the body. If you now click the target and he sways a bit and you missclick, you end up walking there instead of attacking him. That gave me so much rage during the game. I don't know how many times my ranged users ended up walking next to the target instead of attacking him just because the target just swayed a bit and I missclicked...
When playing like this the hit box should be around their feet, not the body, to prevent this.
A few small things.
Inventory. The backpacks should have their own sorting buttons, as they are now they are totally useless.
Crafting is uninteresting. The only thing I ended up using trough the game was resistance boost on gear and damage boost on weapons.
Gear stats:.... boots, rings, bracers, amulets... Damne, rings and amulets are hard to get, so getting rings and amulets with stats for your character is close to impossible.
Bracers. Never seen a bracer that is for casters. Only ranged users. Think I found one for melee users ones. Same with boots. Drop rate for this type of gear is extreme low compared to armour and weapon.
The map is so horrible. It feels like it is thrown in there as an afterthought. Some stuff are marked on the map while other stuff are not. An example, two shops is standing close to each other in the town. One shop is marked on the map while the other one is not. They should have redone the whole map.
Yes, I recommend playing the game, but be prepared for some annoyance too.

First, let's get real:  It's hard to not recommend a free game that doesn't crash your computer.  So, yeah, on that basis alone I would say you should download it.
But beyond that, this game could easily be priced at $5-10 and be worthwhile.  While the first hour or so made me want to beat my head against a wall for all the "Woe is me, everyday is so hum drum." blah blah that is the general setup to sooooo many of these stories, the actual writing and art and music were all rather good so I stuck with it.  Once I got past the tropey introductions of the different characters and got to the meat of the storyline for some of the girls is where I got to the point where I could say the game is worth $5-$10.
One of the things I appreciated was that the "Bad" end I got on the path with my first girl was still really fulfilling since it involved a conflict between two of the girls that I felt reflected the choices I had made rather accurately, and made me want to play again and try to figure out the deeper layers of the overall story.  Then there's the novelty of the Russian setting, which I know I haven't experienced before from this sort of game, so it was fun getting little tidbits about Soviet ice cream and having Borsch served for meals.
So yeah, if you're a fan of this genre there is no reason to not pick up Everlasting Summer for free.

Armed with a party clad as a vampire (Verde) and other fantasy creatures, I made my way through the game upon theoretical completion. No I did not create EVERY item, at least not the clothes. This game has tons of them and most only give a slight optical change to your favorite character. Most don't even offer stats.
This game is just that, a casual RPG with a freaky tech savy parody setting and tons of slapstick humor a la Japan. Accept this and this ride can be your favorite shopping spree for new clothes of a virtual "waifu". Otherwise try to enjoy the story or make a half hearted completion run for the achievements. If you literally want to "finish" this game, you might better marry it as it will take ages and all you get are even more clothes and wild dresses for your eye candy. Luckily they are so overpowered in the end, you can just wear the statless accessories that you like to see.
But in the end, that is what this game is about, right? Having fun with the goddesses, their friends and their dress-ups. Since the one downside is the reuse of monster- and dungeongraphics, you better use the dresses to get some change of pace. This will be an at best ignorant grind sometimes.
If you like such a game you have my full recommendation, otherwise you have my general recommendation if you like freaky RPGs whenever it is 50% off. Get it and maybe achieve it, but remember to have fun.

Upsides/Overview
I played hours upon hours of this game years ago on my xbox original. Without this game, the genre of first person shooter would be very different indeed. Not only does this game offer some of the best team based strategic play I've seen to date, but this game also did it around a time when battles on a large scale were not something to be brushed off as ordinary. The game is very fun, even if you're not a hardcore star wars fan. Multiplayer was unfortunately taken down as Gamespy closed, but not to worry, gameranger has servers online as I'm typing this out, and gameranger is free. You will experience lag on gameranger servers, but if you have the proper bandwidth and hardware to support your own server, you will have the chance to play a game that becomes exponentially more fun the more people you play with.
+Awesome Space Battles, Land Battles, and Land Battles in Space
+Vehicle gameplay
+Class counter-gameplay/Vehicle counter-gameplay
+Capture the Point (Conquest) style
+Plenty of awesome mods
+Very solid gunplay
+Galactic Conquest, a long term war to rule the galaxy (Evil laughing)
+Choice between CIS (Droids), Republic (Clones), The Empire (Stormtroopers), and The Rebels (Watch the damn movie)
+Upgrade/Mastery system on guns/classes
+A.I. is pretty great for space battles
+Multiplayer is still a thing
+I could go on for a long time
Downsides/Conclusion

-This game is old, and looks old
-You will experience bugs if you play long enough
-A.I. are often easy even on the hardest difficulty for a person who has gotten used to the game (Doesn't take very long)
-Overpowered advanced classes on some factions, underpowered on other factions, (The Bothan Spy really doesn't compare to the Empirial Officer, Shock Trooper way better than Wookies. Jet pack trooper and Clone Commander are really bad in comparison to the MagnaGaurd and Droideka and I could go on.)
-Playing by yourself isn't very fun after a while
-Playing with friends can easily be laggy
-Steam doesn't always have this game on sale for 5 bucks (If it is on sale for 5 or really anything but ten, get it, it's worth way more than 5, but because of its age it really doesn't need to be priced at 10.)
-Upcoming Battlefront 3 game may sweep the floor with this one, not neccesarily a bad thing if Battlefront 3 is actually good, but it is a bad thing if it sweeps this game under the rug for no reason.
In conclusion, you really need to get this game, and get your friends to get this game. If you haven't played it yet you need to. If you have played it already but don't have it, get it. If you have played it and have it, get another copy for your friend. If you don't have any friends and have it, get another copy and make a friend today.

I approve the full prize and I am thankful for the slight reduction in the Euro price, it shows that some publisher actually care for the conversion rates. Everyone who thinks it is outrageous to demand a full prize for a full game, but still pays 100$ for an incomplete and buggy game (cough AC cough FC cough), is an idiot. - Maybe the reintroduction of a ranking system for units? I grew quite fond of the little rank markers on units and was always sad when an Elite-gunner died...

This is a wonderfully crafted game- from the story to the mechanics, and even the graphics (while a little outdated) fit well.
Story wise, the plot follows a physicist named Gordon freeman who is dropped off in post alien invasion City 17. He proceeds to meet up with some old associates and rebels against the Combine, an alien force that has captured earth. On the whole, the characters are deep, there are wonderful comedic moments, and the story is engaging. It leaves on a bit of a cliffhanger, resolved in later games.
Mechanics wise, the game flows pretty smoothly, although I do have some qualms. The good most definetly outweighs the bad here. When playing this game, the puzzle aspect fits smoothly with the movement from level to level, and the combat is engaging and difficult. There are some adrenaline pumping moments, like the gunboat speeding down the waterways of City 17, or the first time you fight a strider.
Graphics wise, this is an older game- up to date graphics aren't expected. The visuals still hold up, though. They fit the game you are playing, and the color pallet perfectly suits each situation. The graphics, (at least at the time of the review) have agreed surprisingly well. It has some wonderfully cinematic moments, as well as great atmosphere creation throughout due to the lighting. I'm sure that if you wanted a graphical upgrade, there are mods for it, but in it's vanilla state it's still amazing.
My qualms with the game are few, and somewhat nitpicky. In terms of mechanics, I felt the gameplay could get super repetetive at times, like with having to fight off wave after wave of enemy with the same strategy. The good thing about this is that these repetitive bits end quickly. Another thing is that sometimes parts of the map look exactly the same, and you get turned around and walk in circles (or that may just be me.)
The biggest qualm I have with the game is exemplified perfectly with the final boss fight.

This whole game, besides my few nitpicks, is a wonderful game that introduced a cool puzzle aspect with the gravity gun, and it has an engaging storyline, as well as mechanics. I totally wholeheartedly recommend this game if you enjoy puzzles, first person shooters, sci-fi, and good games. Besides, this is one of the classics, so why not give it a go?

This game is equal parts Geometry Wars, Guitar Hero, and visualization software. Similar to Asteroids, the perspective is top-down, and you have free reign to move your ship in any direction (however, you are limited by the borders of the screen). The ideal way to play this game is with an Xbox 360 controller, as it is a twin-stick shooter (similar to Smash TV).
The major selling point is that it is also a visualizer. So, your "stages" are actually music tracks. The game ships with several dance/house/edm tracks, however you can add to that listing with music saved onto your hard drive, and for $1.00, you can add iTunes and m&a support. Because it's a visualizer, everything pulsates with the beat of the music; shots, powerups, and your ships lights all thump with the beat. Because of this, certain genres resonate better with it than others (club/hip hop/dance/edm/dubstep/soul/funk/pop being the best, with metal/psychobilly/punk being the most spasmatic). Interestingly, the game will sync enemies and bosses with the music, so when a song gets to a really intense part, you may suddenly get hit with twin bosses and similarly when there's not much going on in the track, you may wind up staring at an empty screen. The game also takes more detail into the game from your music selection by making adjustments to things like enemy/bullet speed, how many of your guns fire during the quieter segments, and how fast time-based score multiplier meters fill up.
The ideal purchase to make for this game is the Mega Bundle Pack, as it contains all of the DLC (including the aforementioned iTunes/m&a licensing). These include online co-op/competitive play, new bosses, and perks that can be applied to your gameplay, and the Shadow Ops Unit DLC, which adds a rank progression system, ship-specific goals (like destroy 100 asteroids, reach 1,000,000 points in a track), leaderboards for each ship, and even opens up the ship creating system to you. The higher you rank in the Shadow Ops Unit, the more points you get in creating a ship. It also lets you select an image on your hard drive for the ship and upload your creation to the steam workshop for others to download and use. This also means that you can download ships that other users have created (I've seen quite a few Millennium Falcons, Starship Enterprises, X-Wing Fighters, and Tie Fighters, but have also seen the Planet Express Ship, ships from other shooters, and even the Tardis).
However, due to the nature of this game's fast moving, brightly colored flashing particle effects, this is not something for epileptics to play or be around, as it will made them seize faster than Axl Rose would find a reason to not play a show. For the rest of us, the $16.99 price point for the Mega Bundle pack is really cheap. While there's virtually no story, it is quite fun to see what the game makes of your favorite music as well as push for the oldschool arcade goals of getting a high score.

Definitely recommend this game for Yu-Gi-Oh! fans. Talk about nostalgia. Yu-Gi-Oh! Legacy of the Duelist features battles from the original anime as well as its spinoffs. The game includes over 6,000 cards, over 90 characters and over 230 duels. The game also allows you to build and use your own custom built decks to complete campaign mode. You start out with a few premade decks but you're rewarded with cards and DP (duelist points) as you continue winning duels. Eventually you'll unlock packs in the card shop that you can purchase with the DP you earned. It's literally almost the same feeling you get when you buy booster packs IRL; estatic when you pull a card you wanted but appalled by the amount of money (DP in this case) you spent just to get that one card.
Pros:
+ Campaign Nostalgia
+ Easy Deck Building
+ Tutorial for New Players
+ Automatic Mechanics
+ 3 Pot of Greed in Campaign
Cons:
- Bland Music
- Animations, while minimum, are very lacking graphic wise and you can't skip it
- Pacing. Slower than you would expect on YgoPro due to animations.
If you want a game where everything is already available, up-to-date, fast paced and competitive, maybe this isn't the game for you. But if you want a more casual session filled with nostalgia, go ahead and pick this game up. It's definitely worth it.

(Update 30. June 2017 - Addendum at the end of the review)
Actual review, not just whining about rootkits for a change, coming right up.
Black Desert Online is a visually stunning and complex MMO with incredible potential but falls completely short of realizing it due to the majority of gameplay elements being designed with microtransactions in mind.
Let's get the good things out of the way:
The game looks really damn great for an MMO, the character editor is easily among the strongest I've seen in any game.
Combat feels responsive, tactical, 'kinetic' for lack of a better word, it mixes a classic cooldown hotkey-sequence stereotypical MMO system with fast and fluid DMC-style action combat, and does so very well.
A huge, rich... partially immersive world, full of lore and happenings all around the player. It's a joy to explore it and there are many beautiful sights to take in, whether you want to, or not... which brings us to the automatic pathfinding:
Easily the most sophisticated system I've seen in any MMO, just place a marker on the world map and press a button, and your character will find the safest route there, with a 99% success rate.
But here's where we're already leaving the "nice things to say" territory...
While the game has some very nifty quality-of-life features, it's lacking entirely in others. There is no "effective" quick-travel system. If you want to get from one end of the map to the other, you will have to run, or ride a horse there. There's a method to get your character from one major city to another, but you'll have to log out of that character and wait regardless.
You can view your items in storage from any point in the world, nifty, but storage is separated for every village and town in the game, expanding that storage for cash is an option, but for each of the five gameworld regions separately.
Character inventory has been doubled down on, not only do you have a limited amount of slots for items, but you also have a weight capacity for each of your characters, a savvy design choice if you plan on selling very expensive inventory and weight limit expansions, for each character separately, of course.
Defeated enemies drop an impressive amount of loot, which is great, but the loot stays locked to you for a very short time, and disappears a short time later, manual looting is very slow, and depending on server load hugely influenced by lag, encouraging you to buy pets, all of which loot for you, and you can equip 4 at once. Incredible!
To cut this short: The game is meticulously designed to maximize the rppu (revenue per paying user), to a point where the community itself will react negatively to people questioning whether or not this game is p2w "pay-to-win".
It's not. It is however designed in a way that paying will increase your enjoyment of it exponentially.
You WILL hit a sort of paywall eventually, no matter which aspect of the game you try to focus on, because each and every aspect is fully built around a p2e, pay to enjoy system. And most paid elements are cleverly priced in such a way that a more expensive option will always feel like a more worthwhile one.
An example: You grew to dislike your characters looks, you can either
A. Buy a 1-time coupon to change it once for 8€
B. Buy a 30 day coupon to have the ability to change it more often for 10€ or
C. Just go for a 30 day premium subscirption for 15€ which offers you a wide range of other benefits, like enabling a dye function for all your gear which includes all the dyes available in the game, which would alternatively also cost 10€ by itself.
The marketing psychology is clearly at work here, trying to leverage as many fallacies as a human could potentially commit, in order to convince you to buy something which has no intrinsic value.
But that's enough of railing on the business model, I just wanted to give potential buyers an insight how far their entrance fee will get them, let's move on to the remaining cons:
One big issue I found is how the game offers close to no social elements. Some even go as far as to say it's a singleplayer game with always-online. And after over a week of play I'm inclined to agree. At no point between level 1 and 56+ will you find the need to join up with another player, that will start once you want to get into very endgame stuff, most guilds won't even let you in unless you're level 56+ and have maxed out your gear.
Only endgame boss hunting lends itself to cooperation, the party system is extremely barebones, and you have to go to extensive effort to synchronize questing together unless you start playing with a friend from level 1.
Which brings us to the last point, which also offers a bit of an explanation to the previous one: The community.
Unless you get accepted into a guild, which will then almost instantly treat you like family, which is nice, most of the players you'll get to interact with are on a level of "toxicity" that rivals overwatch and league of legends.
It gets worse once you get past level 50 and the open-PvP system kicks in. If you dare to as much as get near a popular grindspot you will be attacked and murdered on sight without warning. Sometimes you get a bit of a warning in the form of vigorous insults, and once you're killed by players of a much higher level, you will be further insulted and blamed for making them kill you. (To be fair, that happend only twice each, the rest of the time I had a lovely grind at sausans)
Generally: If you value your time, money and dignity, avoid this game. If you have too much of column A and B, and none of column C,  then feel free to make this the new thing that will distract you from commiting suicide for a while. Or just invest in a Traveler's Package, play for the 30 days you'll get the included premium service and then quit and never look back.
30 days is more than enough to see everything the game has to offer.
###
Addendum:
After receiving some valid criticism after writing the review I've now stuck 300 hours into the game to see if there's more, and I can safely say there isn't. The game essentially turns into an idle game if you consider focusing on any of the "life skills" on offer. And easily 150 of my 300 hours have been spent having the game do its own thing over night. The softcap to your exp makes it absolutely pointless to do any combat once you've hit level 56, unless the weekend double exp is active, the rest of the week you may as well just do the afk-portion of the game.
I've also been accused of playing WoW and I can assure you that this is not the case. I've only ever played one western MMORPG and many, many Korean ones.
Furthermore I have left out the fact that there's a "Loyalty" currency in the game, which lets you, in theory, buy a very limited selection of cash shop items with time instead of money, in my opinion this is irrelevant since the rate at which "Loyalty" is accured will never become useful to the average player and is entirely negligible to new players and should not be a factor in a purchase decision.
So again, if you can get this game on a sale, you can enjoy some of the fun combat(if the servers ever stop lagging), but if you're not into that kind of thing just keep in mind there are many free idle games and cookie clicker clones on steam.

tl;dr - this could be one of the best mmos if not for frustrating F2P design pierced through the core gameplay experience.
I do not recommend this game unless you just want to waste a lot of time doing some crafting or fighting. Because I really feel like I wasted this time.
I have a feeling this game was designed from the start as F2P. And by that I mean everything was made in certain way for the F2P experience and possibility of milking as much as possible from players by annoying them with a lot of unnecessery walls.
Although gameplay itself is fun for a while, and features and concepts are sometimes just awesome... it is painfull to play. Unless you don't mind all of these cons:
- weapon and armor upgrade system is chance based. There is no standard weapons like in other mmos. All weapons and armors in the game have similar power, they only differ slightly in different stats and bonuses. So you basically can wear one armor through whole playthrough. BUT - you need to upgrade it with items which you need to farm or buy from players. BUT upgrading decreases durability and you need more of this item to repair it. BUT if upgrading fails at higher lvls item goes back in lvls. It is just pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and waste of time/money for me.
- having PC on for long times. Everything takes long and requires you to be logged in to work efficiently. Crafting, workers, regeneration of energy etc. If you log off most things don't work and you only regenerate fraction of energy.
- the best way to advance certain skills is just do the same dailies from the first town every day
- very unconvinient storage and weight issues when you don't pay. You can farm to increase them but again - more grind
- and even more grind, because everything is based on grind in this game.
- no dungeons, no interesting combat challenges. A few dumb bosses and thats it.
But PvP is good I heard, but I'm not interested in that.
I really wanted to like this game. Workers and crafting system alone looked awesome as hell! But I soon run into a wall where I would need to grind Contribution points by doing stupid quests every day to expand. I did it a few days but I just can't anymore. It feels so mundane and boring.
So I went to do some fighting. I reached 51lvl and got stuck too, because experience curve spikes so much after that I just bounced off it. And there was no fun in finding better gear because of this dumb concept of upgrading instead of getting better ones - you just walk back and forth, killing tons of mobs and going back to town to sell useless junk drops because you ran out of carry limit. And it is just annoying to pick up everything, there is so much junk drops but who knows, maybe this one had very rare thing? And you need to buy premium pets to autopick for you.
Ehhhh, I hate games like this. Not because they are bad but because they are corrupted by the free 2 play model so much they are not fun anymore, even with amazing features.
PS: From my experience this game is not P2W in a PvP meaning. You can't directly buy power. But it is pretty damn bad to play without paying. For gods sake, even costumes have bonuses.
PS: I'm PvE player, so PvP player experience may be different.

After finishing both Saints Row 2,3,and 4, I do believe my journey with Dahlia (my Boss/President) is complete. I am giving this game a thumbs up with some caveats.
1. The Story DLCs feel malnourished. the Christmas one was fun. But Enter the Dominatrix feels like "an alternate ending" to Saints Row: The Third. Even though production was hampered while Volition/Saints Row was sold to DeepSilver, the ETD DLC feels like scribbly notes in the dev's notebooks, with voiceovers by the cast. It feels... unfinished.
2. Since SR:TT, Saints Row has shifted gears. Not a bad thing, I'm down with that. But The newer games don't seem to have the level of interaction that SR2 had. SR4 attempts to remedy this with new races and tons more activities, but I miss racing cars and buying a 40oz, hopping into a septic truck and lowering some property values. HOWEVER, they still maintain that they are fun. Which they ARE. Which is important, right?
3.Inexplicable things and untouched-upon past events. The crew tend to jabber about past events like they were yesterday but never mention specifics. What happened in Salt Lake City? What happened when the President and that reporter were caught in that room? None of it is explained/expanded upon, and it feels less like characters interacting and more like just a way to lead-in to the random task that the crew is asking you to do. Just a thought.
Overall, the game is, at it's core, fun. Which is the whole point of playing games, right?

The game is most definitely a lot more fun than I gave it credit for beforehand. Whilst I haven't played a massive amount of RPG esque games in my life, the most hard worked on game I ever did play was Dragon's Quest: The Journey of the Cursed King, a very big favourite of mine, so I was hoping this game would meet expectation.
It's a very basic, run of the mill, turn based, cutesy RPG with some interesting ways of gaming machanics. I have yet to finish the game but it's definitely enjoyable.
The basic plot is that you play as Neptune, in a very computer/gaming inspired journey with a story that revolves around something called the Console War. You get a fairly small party to band with, and you have events, shops, information, customizable characters and a ton of fighting, and I definitely wouldn't say the game is too complex, althought make sure you're the right age before playing since you get a half-naked scene at least 10 minutes into the game. Shocker.
Like mentioned above, the game has some pretty cool mechanics. You can use things called plans which help you gain access to more dungeons, or use them for different items, extra or stronger enemies, weaker enemies, and accessories and materials. You have quests, which helps you get more money or items, or make you go back to old dungeons for more materials.
The voice acting you may find annoying, but personally I find it no different from any other dubbed-sounding anime, although repetitious speech will probably be your biggest problem, and I swear that the pink-haired girl, Compa, is voiced by the same person as Amy Rose from the 4kids TV Show, Sonic X, and that the main protagonist has the same voice actress as Konata from Lucky Star, although I could very likely be wrong. One thing that you can change however is the language, which can either be English or Japanese, no surprise there.
Interestingly in fights, there's an "order of attack" mechanic that lets you see which character or enemy will be attacking next, which if you watch carefully, can really assist in getting rid of large parties of foes in a shorter amount of time by prioritizing your attacks. With the money you get, you can get better weapons or wearable items to help boost your party's abilities and you level up as you go along.
I'll give you all a fair warning though, because it's very important and very typical for RPG's, but *GRINDING IS A MUST TO HAVE A SMOOTH RIDE THROUGH THIS GAME*. You get 2 of your first dungeons which are simple enough at a lower level, but you have to get yourself new weapons from the shop and keep repeatedly grinding in those 2 first dungeons and re-collect items because you will not be strong enough else! Once you get to the 2nd city in the game, you get better weapons and you should have enough money by then to get stronger weapons. Even then, you have to stick to the 2 first dungeons until you're killing enemies in 2-3 hits or less, even, because your 3rd dungeon (Zeca ruins) will wreck you, and the 4th one (Mechtro Factory) will introduce stronger enemies and bosses. The amount of times I have died to a bunny rabbit just for not being strong enough doesn't come close to funny.
Also, don't forget to save whenever you can in the main hub of the game. Saving is your friend and it wants to help you win!
Overall, gorgeous game graphics, good controls, interesting fighting mechanics and a pretty good story, although the comedy leaves a lot to be desired. If you like RPGs or JRPG style games, this is very likely a must for you to play.

Don't be fooled by the name, Grey Goo may be the old-school RTS you've been waiting for. At its heart it's a bit of a mix of Starcraft and C&C3, with enough differences to have easily fought for a place in the crowded RTS market of a few years ago. The question is how much its novelty in 2015 is part of the reasons it's getting some very good reviews?
I don't think it's unfair to say that Grey Goo is a bit rough around the edges. The graphics aren't going to push a mid-range PC much, and I did find some bugs with loading and menu screens, however the cut sequences are impressive for a team on a smaller budget and the overall style is classic RTS (in a good way).
The three factions comprise humans, the humanoid Beta, and the eponymous Goo. Other reviewers have commented that the former two are quite similar and the latter not great fun to play, but I'm quite liking all three and the more you play the more the subtlties are starting to come out. Also, the Goo is about as different a race as you're likely to see in an RTS and could lead to some interesting tactics in a three-way scrap. The team deserve some real credit here and I'm looking forward to seeing how the factions will develop, but I'd also like a few more skirmish maps to play about with (presumably we'll see both in DLC).
So, to answer my question, only a bit. I love this game. It's just the right amount of simplicity and depth... It's a basic concept, take your music, have the music generate levels that dynamically react to that music and power your weapons in kind... This basic idea has then been continously refined and improved upon until you have a really well developed fun little game to get your adreniline pumping while listening you your favourite tunes and enjoying some eyecandy.
Just a heads up before we go any further, this is a very visually intense game... If you are photo sensitive this game is not for you... While it is possible the low visuals setting and monitor calibration might make the game playable for you, I wouldn't risk it. It's a great game but it is intensionally designed to explosion of flashing coloured lights... And while delightful it's not worth risking your health... For everyone else... The higher the visual intensity the higher your high score, so blow you eyes out. :-P
As you can see from the screenshots the visuals are a major selling point for the game. Remember those old console demo disks and media player plug ins we used to download so we could have pretty procedural visulaisers  for our music? Well this game provides that, dials it up to 11 and then includes a damn decent if simple SHMUP as well.
I've followed it since launch and it started out just simple and enjoyable. However, the developer was highly active here on the steam forums and receptive to feedback to fine tune the game and continued to develop it the right way... That is to take in that feedback and come up with their own inovative solutions to the shortcommings. For example when the community demanded the addition of powerups the developer opted to rather than shoehorn in the standard cliché powerups seen in every shmup, to creatively create some inovative unique powerups of their own, their own system for collecting and using them and tailored existing and new enemies specifically to them to make a more dynamic interesting play experience.
The developer even went so far as to fix problems by adding new features we didn't even no we needed, but now we have them we couldn't live without them... I highly recommend getting the full package. The DLC for this game came much later but rounded out the play experience more then I could have imagined. With the core game, ultra and the shadow missions DLC you'll have a great balanced progression through the ranks as you upgrade you ship and refine your skills so you will simentaniously hit your peak in all departments right as you reach the top of the rankings, fully unlocking all the customisable  features so you having mastered the game you can fully adjust everything to suit your play style before you shift to targeting the leader boards and competing with your friends.
At time of writing I have every achievment (some easy, some hard), unlocked every feature and have invested a solid amount of time playing and mastering all the different game modes and features... And I'm not done. As I find new gems and get new songs to add to my media library I shall return to play them out repeatedly in beat hazard to the pleasure of my eyes and reflexes as well as my ears. I wouldn't spend all day playing it (now that I've completed the progression to obtain all unlockables), but it is a game I happily come back to for a few hours again and again every other week for a bit of fun and challange... Not to mention dive in to compete with my friends with from time to time. I recommend it to pretty much everyone (except the photosensitive).

I've been playing the first UFO back in 1994 and loved the approach in mixing resource management strategy with a tactics game. What put me off were the frequent and rather long battles, coupled with an input system that drove you nuts, especially when you had to switch between levels. At some point I had to give up. because it wasn't fun to fight 20 battles without having any idea if the game is actually progressing or not.
The remake did adress all the aforementioned problems. You actually have a steady game progression wich is tied to the narration of the plot. Controls are intuitive and allow a flawless execution of your ideas.
There are a few things left wanting, though. The difficulty ranges between stupidly easy and deadlock situations, in which you save and load over and over to have the lucky roll you need to survive the first enemy initiatve attack. But most of the time it is sufficient to advance slowly in a coherent fire line to blow the enemies to pieces. But well, I could live with that, although I didn't really feel like having to worry about tactics too much.
Another  tings is the missed opportunity to add some personality to your squad members. They are just some exchangeable, generic action figures without any personal background, distinctive traits or anytihng else that would make you feel care about their fate. But then, I'm still waiting for a worthy successor for Jagged Alliance 2, so I  guess that's too much to wish for atm.

My mission parameters were simple, find out what had happened to a force of Canadian Soldiers, in addition to a Canadian Shoreside town and it's residents. Events took a tragic twist, as the residents and soldiers had been mutated into Zombies at the hands of Chrysallids.
My squad swept the town swiftly and without injury, until we stumbled on a barge that had run aground, and it turned out that the Chrysallids had been using a dead whale inside the ship as a birthing chamber.
Captain Artyom "The Bear" Petrova, my genetically modified soldier took action as to re-activate the barge's transponder, allowing XCOM forces in the air to launch a air strike in order to remove the infestation. As Chrysallids had been birthing by the dozen, it was clear that I had to get my men out of the area as soon as possible. Upon making it back to the Skyranger, something was wrong. Artyom was not in the evac zone, he was barely behind, but so was a horde of Chrysallids and Infested Civilians.  Quick to take action, I sent "V1K-70R", my highly powerful M.E.C. Soldier in to assist Artyom in his escape. Artyom made a quick break for the Zone and reached it in time. Viktor made a break for it too, having only one step to being in the zone when the Aliens made their move, they piled on Viktor, mangling his robotic body, as the Skyranger fled from the scene and XCOM bombarded the town, I could only feel as though I could have done something to save both of them. Major Artyom Petrova was awarded the "Viktor Zayvetsky Award" upon his promotion, and a bagpipe funeral was enacted in memorial of my fallen soldier, who paid the ultimate price to save his comrade.
10/10 would get emotional over a virtual death again.

I am fairly new to visual novels, but I am a big fan of story led games so I was quite excited about Everlasting Summer. Sadly, it didn't do it for me. I only played 30 min before giving up. Anime breasts popping up everywhere triggered my anime-breast-sensitive epilepsy I think. Wish they put a warning.
Ok, the story is fairly immersive from the start, the graphics are beautiful and atmospheric, and the concept interesting, but the text needs to be edited to the point where it is cut down by at least half. That being said, if you persevere you can get into the flow (and eventully encounter big friendly anime breasts)
My understanding of this game's storyline is: 'man feels his life is hopeless but something surreal happens and he can now meet all these stereotypical women whose sole purpose is to change his life and maybe shag him'.
Tear jerker.
After 20min, The poorly edited text is too draining, and my anime-breast-epilepsy too easily triggered; it is hard to keep my interest in the storyline, since the story line is 'how many hot girls can I fall in love with -and shag?'
It's a shame cause I don't mind sexual content in game, but the sexual content in Everlasting Summer feels sneaky and pointless. I read somewhere the game's explicit sexual content had to be removed to be on Steam, which probably messed with how the game should feel as a whole, and would explain why I was so confused and seizing while playing it. Maybe on a different platform this game would have been advertised as a ponographic or erotica game (with a good old 'all the interchangeable women who changed my life when they shagged me' story in it).
So, random anime girls whose sole, deep desire is to shag you, just because your sad self fell asleep on a bus? Yes.
Complex story about the meaning of life and love? Not sure, but I'm still seizing.
I know a lot of people got hooked on the story and alternative endings, and I respect that, I just know that's not going to be me. Looking forward to trying more visual novels, just not this one.

I don't recommend running in guns blazing, neither do I recommend camping like that one dude who throws urine at his opponents and slices them up with a Kukri. (seriously, that dude is insane!)

Points.

When I play games on steam I do it to relax, to escape everyday stress and to get a break before I have to face my real-life problems again.
Visual novels tend to not have the therapeutic effect I'm after. Indeed, I had my doubts about this game as soon as I read the disclaimer about suicide. Oh well, whatever, right!? Violence is often glorified these days... nothing out of the ordinary here, I thought.
On my first lap I got the 'Lena, bad end'.
On my second lap I started aiming for the 'Lena, good end', but got distracted and stumbled upon 'Semyon, good end' instead. That cleared up a few things.
If you can look past the naive and suggestive graphics, the completely different -extreme - outcomes possible from seemingly innocent choices make this visual novel interesting. Whether it's actually good or not, I can't make up my mind. At least, the music and background art is good.
