I recommend this title, only to true ARPG fans, with some very strong caveats. While I have had a lot of fun (and frustration) playing Grim Dawn, it's unforgivable weakness is in its late game balance.
Obviously GD draws a lot of comparisons to Diablo 2 and 3. While it is better in some regards, worse in others, as those titles, it simply does not have their longevity. I've clocked in just over 2,000 hours in Diablo 3. I have around 10% that time in GD, and I feel that I've taken it as far as I can go.
First, what is not as good as D2 and D3, as well as some other ARPGs: Loot and balancing.
I have ran 4 different builds to the point I simply couldn't get any further. The difficulty settings of D3 is what allows for endless gameplay. In GD you start on Normal (with an optional Veteran difficulty that I honestly could not tell the difference except that there was less loot), then unlock Epic after completing the campaign, then unlock Ultimate after completing it on Epic. That's it, 3 difficulties, 3 times through the campaign, done. With level cap at 85, and no further options to continue playing, the game basically stops itself. However, of my 4 different builds, only one made it to the bitter end. And this is what I'm talking about balance here. What makes Epic and Ultimate more difficult is primarily the reduction of your resistances. So basically, you just die more often, xp becomes a grind, common minions often one-hit you out of nowhere, and some bosses (the trapped-in-a-box, no-retreat bosses) are simply unbeatable without the right build and very specific resistances. All that wouldn't be so bad, IF the game's claim that more difficult = better loot. But in over 200 hours of playing, I can tell you that it's just not true. If anything, I consistently got less good loot, but lots more junk loot. In every case, I was using the same equipment for 20 or more levels at a time for lack of getting anything better. Obviously, this is untenable when the monsters level with you. And the best gear I had was purchased, not looted. Over the course of 4 builds to Ultimate, up to levels 65 and 75 on average, I accumulated a sum total of 9 Legendary items, mostly unusable because of high requirements, or simply not as good as the epic items I already had from 20 levels ago. What this means is that I got rich, with just over 3 million iron bits on my final character, but with nothing  worthwhile to spend it on. So yes, GD is miserly with the good loot. Not a good feature when we all know that ARPGs are all about the loot. Even after the latest patch, I did a test run from middle to late Ultimate, and only got one legendary; the same gun that the Warden drops every time. Well I already had 3, thanks anyway. One could put the loot, or lack thereof, down to bad luck, but after 4 playthroughs, I can reasonably claim it's the system.
Now, what makes GD better than D3: Character builds and skills.
In D3 you get what you get as far as skills, they will be the same skills every time, they unlock at certain levels and at higher levels you can choose between them. That's it. This is the weakest point of D3. It sucks. GD has taken a step back with skills, more in line with D2, and allowed you to choose skills, then build on those preferred skills. And the passive skill tree is actually a constellation of skills that unlock new abilities or new attributes that you can then attach to whatever skill you prefer. This system allows for a high level of customization and control in your build, and is where GD really shines. The innovation of dual-class hybridization exponentially expands on the possibilities. Other good qualities are the lore, which is enough to keep you reading the notes, and the faction system. Factions are probably the best innovation to set GD apart from others in the genre.

One other detractor worth mentioning: Performance.
Even on lower settings, with reduced resolution, I constantly got lags and hitches, little micro-freezes. The gameworld is graphically nice, nothing extreme, so I think the problem is with distant LODs. It's as if the engine is trying to render too much at full detail, even long distance views and off-screen terrain. And shadow rendering seems to be glitched. They only look normal on higher settings. At medium and lower settings, the shadows glitch in a frenzied flashing of black triangles. Also, the game almost always freezes on exit, requiring alt-tab-del and a system reboot. This is extremely irritating and almost unforgivable in modern games.
In summary, Grim Dawn is a ton of fun for the true ARPG fan. Just trying out the different builds and hybrid classes is what makes it worthwhile. However, the miserly loot system and terrible late game balance gives it a short shelf life. My hours in GD had many frustrating moments where I nearly quit for good. But the character options kept me coming back to try again... with the same results. Certainly, D3 had a much bigger budget and amounts to pure candy for the ARPG fan, while GD is grittier, tougher, less rewarding. D3 has longevity, you can literally play forever. But GD got the most crucial part right that D3 got wrong; the role-playing. And that has made it worth playing.
*12-20-16 Edit: With recent updates addressing some of the issues I originally wrote about in this review, namely late game balance, I felt it warranted an edit. They have increased resistance buffs almost across the board for epics, making late game progression much more balanced and viable for a variety of builds. There have been many other improvements, but I felt this was the most significant.
CrateGames has continued to update and improve this game, with more on the way, including two new classes, presumably in a free update. This kind of dedication to their game sets them apart and could very well make Grim Dawn my favorite ARPG of all time.

Half-Life 2 is a classic in the FPS genre, along with its predecessor, Half-Life.
With this game, Valve intertwines great level design and gameplay to create encounters that are memorable, spontaneous, and fun. The game is constantly changing up the formula, so just when you think you've mastered the game, it introduces new mechanics that change the way you play the game from that point onwards. Valve finds inventive ways to use mechanics that have already been learned and flip them on their head to create encounters that feel new yet familiar.
Half-Life 2 has a great atmosphere. From the music on the soundtrack, to the ambient sounds and environmental storytelling, to the design of the creatures and the design of the world you inhabit, this game creates a believable place for you to get immersed in.
My greatest qualm with this game is the narrative. Not only are the cutscenes are a chore to sit through on a second or third playthrough, but these cutscenes/setpieces feel very unnatural for one reason: Gordon Freeman, being a silent protagonist, makes the interactions with NPC characters feel awkward. It feels like people are talking at you, rather than with you. Him being a silent protagonist is rarely acknowledged, and is not worked into the story whatsoever. The characters are great, but your lack of interaction with them hurts the connection you are supposed to build with them.
Despite this, many of the elements in the story work very well. The Combine feel like a force to be reckoned with, and their alien and oppressive nature motivates you to try to defeat them. However, my favorite part of the narrative is the overarching story involving
The ending of the game is
Honestly, if Valve never released the Half-Life 2 episodes, this ending would feel quite unsatisfactory, almost being a cop out. It doesn't feel like you have fully accomplished your goal by the end of the game.
Despite my problems with the story, Half-Life 2 is one of the most innovative and fun FPS games I have ever played, and well deserves much of the praise it gets.

Beat Hazard (along with the DLC) is one of the few games that I fully appreciate. It's definitely up there as far as quality twin-stick shooters go. There are just so many things that make this game good.
Play your own music - This was the very first 'play your own music' game that I got on Steam. It's not the most special feature on Beat Hazard but it's the main reason I enjoyed it as a twin-stick shooter. I don't have a lot of experience in the genre so being able to play on my own pace depending on the song used was a major positive factor for me.
Difficulty Adjustment - The difficulty is easily adjustable in a multitude of ways. You have your conventional difficulty settings (easy, etc, etc). Then you have visual intensity which to me is somewhat of a visual handicap (with benefits of course). Two other ways to adjust difficulty would be by picking songs with varied intensities or by playing with the new DLC content which adds ship customization complete with stats. In a game with this many options, it won't matter what skill level you are within the genre. It's still very possible to feel a small sense of accomplishment even as a casual player.
Music Discovery - In this day and age, I no longer listen to the radio unless I'm really bored while driving from location A to B. Beat Hazard allows you to play while listening to various radio stations (custom or default added). In all honesty, I have discovered a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of music during the few months that I have been really into Beat Hazard.
There's a lot more things that make Beat Hazard a wonderful game. For the sake of simplicity, I merely listed 3 of my favorite reasons.

For any fans of other Telltale games, this game is a must play, and while I don't think it's as quite as good as the Walking Dead Season 1 (which is altogether as masterpiece) I think this game certainly does a lot right.
This review was written as of the release of episode 4, so I have not yet seen the conclusion of the story.
One thing I was worried about coming into the game was that we wouldn't be playing as Game of Throne's main characters, but rather as a smaller house made specifically for this game. I'm sure many people have been wondering whether or not playing as this previously unkown house can live up to the lofty expectations set up by the political intrigue and interesting storytelling the main GoT story has set up. I am happy to say, that the story is as rich as the books themselves (well, maybe not quite that good, but it's a game, and it can't quite fit in every detail that 5 books were able to give). You will quickly grow attached to the new characters you meet, who are all very well crafted, and fit perfectly into the GoT myhtos. And if you are looking to interact with some of the more famous characters, then worry not, becase you get to talk to, and even befriend, many famous characters such as Daenerys, Jon Snow, Cersei Lannister, Tyrion, and more. This game does a great job of weaving in a story that interacts with the main story, but doesn't effect it in any major ways. I also want to add on about the choices. Many people are saying that your choices don't have an impact, but I honestly haven't noticed that. Obviously not everything you say will come back to haunt you, but I've had people reference things I said as other characters two chapters ago, so I think there is at least some fidelity when it comes to making decisions. And let me tell you, there are some very hard decisions to make.
One thing that was a little dissapointing were the graphics, but I don't think anyone was expecting a visual masterpiece from telltale. It keeps the same enjoyable art style that most of their other games have, and it fits in pretty well. Textures, however, are very muddy and low resolution at sometimes, which is confusing, as it can sometimes look even worse than some of the games that came before it, such as TWD. However, when this game is not suffering from this issue, or when you are in a scene where this is not apparent, the game can look quite good.
If you are looking for a game that works sort as a companion to the main GoT experience, then this is exactly what you are looking for. For any fans of the series, this is a mustplay. However, for people not familiar with either the TV show or the books, this game might be confusing at times. Many things go unexplained, so if you are looking to play this without knowledge of the world, you might want to read up on it first online. Anyway, onto my final points. This game has an incredible story, with the tense decision making that we have come to expect from telltale, and it certainly lives up to the telltale name. While it may have muddy graphics at times, this game still looks (and sounds) great, which excellent voice acting, and a good OST. With all this in mind, my final score for this game is...
9/10 for anyone who has read the books or wathced the show
8/10 for anyone who has not (some things may be hard to understand, and I can see some parts being very confusing)

Beat Hazard is arguably the best rhythm game I've ever played. If you like being overstimulated and filled with adrenaline whilst playing your favourite music, this is the game for you. If you want more customizability and an additional challenge? Buy the Ultra DLC aswell!
That being said, this game does have a few problems anyone who wishes to buy this game should know about:
1: I know the Steam store says this game has local coop, but that is restricted for those among us with Xbox controllers.
2: I also know the Steam store says it has multiplayer, which it does, but not really. You see, in order for you to play with your friends (or random people for that matter) you both need to have the exact same copy of the song(s) you want to play. And to make things even worse, when you reach above a certain number of songs both of you have in common (say a few thousand) multiplayer becomes impossible alltogether because the game will crash.
So if you want to go head-to-head or do coop with your friends, be prepared to send everyone the exact same limited copy of the songs you want to play together.
3: The game is not exactly privacy friendly, everything you do will be posted on a public leaderboard.
4: The Shadow Operations DLC, whilst fun, is kind of a mess. It introduces so called "Shadow Challenges" which are goals you need to accomplish without dying. Now let me tell you this, dying is a natural part of the game, in every game you have a number of lives and there's even a perk to allow you to have more lives, essentially making perks like these useless. In addition it will also remove your challenge progress if you decide to switch songs because you find the current one boring.
5: With the Shadow Operations DLC we can now create our own custom ships. This however has one minor issue that for some is easy to overcome and for others a giant impossible herdle. Whenever you want to save a custom ship in order to use it you are REQUIRED to publish your ship design on the public Steam Workshop.

I've played so many card games... well computer card games, I never really had the time to play the real versions other than Yu-Gi-Oh when I was a kid. That doesn't matter though I've played Hearthstone, Might & Magic: Duel of Champions, Magic the Gathering multiple versions and Duelyst. To keep it simple and short this might not top any of these games but it's done well enough that you can enjoy this, what truly matters is how Yu-Gi-Oh plays and that's what makes it stand out from the rest!
The good keyboard and mouse work well, there's also full controller support too. There is a full story mode with story mode deck builds that you can use... feels just like the show/anime, if you don't like them you can always use your own custom deck for story mode as well. The story mode rewards you with cards, points etc! Which it should or else it would be pointless but they get pretty deep with the rewarding it's fun. The game has about 6000 something cards in the core game and 7000 with DLC, now that's alot of cards to play with which is great! The deck building is pretty damn fleshed out here too you'll spend hours testing and tinkering unless you already know what card does what. The soundtrack is alright there's 3 or 4 songs but it keeps the mood going. The art is awesome and it does bring back good old memories, also everything is flashy and colourful enough for a card game!
The bad well the controls are really off at first but you get use to them, they could have done a better job with it! Like I said before the rewards are fun but the grinding on the other hand is not some can live with it others can't. I'm kind of in the middle ground with it, somedays I can be bothered other days I can't. The multiplayer has some issuses private lobbies don't work at all and there is also no anti cheat, luckly you can still invite friends in a public match. The battlefields look cheap but I suppose every field in every card game I've played has a cheap feel to it except Duelyst but that game is a different beast.
In the end some pros and cons merge with each other but overall it's a great game for the price... it's time to D-D-D-D-DUEL!

I'm only an hour into this game, and as we all know the RTS community tends to look for games with a lot of staying power. Rather than try and talk through every single bit and piece of the game I'm going to give my first impressions, then later on I'll try and throw something more complete up.
First things first: it's gorgeous. The cutscenes, the units, the buildings, everything feels really solid. I will say that my computer chugged a bit on the menu and at the beginning of each cutscene, but my computer (while pretty nice) isn't top of the line. Specs at the bottom if anyone cares. Weirdly enough the actual gameplay doesn't seem to have any slowdowns at all, so I'm wondering if it's just some minor glitch that'll be patched out.
Next up: it's fun! Most of the gameplay is pretty intuitive, the units respond in fairly interesting ways, and in general the game feels like a competent studio worked on it. There’s an old game design proverb.
"Adjust a mechanic by doubling or halving it."
Doing so immediately shows it’s relation to the rest of the game.
Putting that concept in a competitive game is resonant. Call it “gut feeling game design.” Double/half is a mechanic (concept?) people immediately understand. It makes Lethal League easy to teach, usually laying out the groundwork with:
-Hit the other player with the ball.
-Every time you hit the ball it goes faster.
-Smash the ball to double the speed.
Doubling is the interesting part. It immediately gives strength and weakness. Combine this with bunting ((halvingish speed and giving possession (the ability to win) to all players)) super moves, (break the rules) and ball parry (prevent the ball from being taken) you got mechanics that curate multidimensional bouts.
If there’s anything off about Lethal League it’s the characters. Outside of Raptor, there isn’t unity in design.
Lethal League is a fantastic competitive game, and an amazing party starter.

While SC and its ilk continue to dominate the RTS genre, there's space for CnC style games which emphasise strategy over clicks per minute.
It's a very well produced game, and while 2 of the factions are a little similar the third adds a good deal of spice and gameplay dynamics we've not seen in RTS before. While Universe At War (Petroglyph's last RTS) was innovative and interesting, it suffered from GFWL and the baggage of a controller-based setup scheme (someone somehwere thought peasants should have an RTS). This isn't burdened by any such limitations, and is very obviously a PC game from the ground up.
So - this is more macro strategy than micro management, and I think it's better for it. Don't for a minute assume there's no build orders, counters or clever tactics to be had here - there are plenty - you just don't need to (in fact, you can't) micromanage your resource collectors etc. for a 5% advantage over the other player.

The Banner saga:
I Really enjoyed this game, in fact I would have played trough it in one sitting if it were not for the fact that I had to do someting else called living.
The game is about leading caravans with soldiers, Varls (Big humans with horn on their heads) and villagers around an viking/ middle earth inspired world, fleeing and fighting evil armies.
The game have two different gamemechanics, First you have the caravan/town parts were you mostly automoves through different terrains, shop and goes through alot of different dialogues were you have to do alot of hard decisions.
There are no black and white choices were the results are easy to guess in advance.
During the caravan/town/fight mode you earn renown for different decisions you make, which you can spend on items, levelling up characters or use for getting supplies to your caravan.
Food and rest affects the caravans morale, which can end in people/soldiers leaving your caravan aswell as bad things happen...
The other part of the game is a turnbased tactical isometrical fight mode were you use different warriors to fight all kind of enemies.
Your soldiers have different skills and are able to level up after they have killed enough enemies.
As mentioned before there will allways be hard decisions to make, since you never have enough renown points to do whatever you want and this can lead to some stressed out situations.
The fight mode took some time to get used to since it is built in a kind of weird way.
The way the turnbased system is built up, you are punished for killing the enemies too early in the fights.
It is allways best to damage all of the enemies before killing them off one by one.
This took some time getting used too, and may be the biggest drawback for me.
The game looks gorgeous and the animations as well. Everything seems to be drawed by some great artist and makes me want to come back to the universe time and time again.
The story is good, where your decissions seems to change it in different ways.
IT is kind of like a rollercoaster. For a period you feel like you can crush any foes you meet, but in the next time, you are chased and do everything you can just to survive.
There are definetly a build up to the end and who knows what will happen in The Banner Saga 2.
I spent about 18 hours on the game before I saw the end credits.
I did not rush it and played in a moderate pace.
All in all a great game which I will recommend!

Banner saga is one of the best tactical rpgs i have ever played, and i will recommend this to anyone who shows any interest in rpgs.
The plot of the game is epic and a tad complex. Every character in the game can die save for maybe 2, and you will have plenty of chances to watch them die because of the choices you and you alone make. The world is locked in an eternal state of gray, there is no sun, there are no stars, no moon, only a vast expanse of gray in the sky. The world has turned colder than a witches♥♥♥♥♥ with everyone struggling to survive. There are three races in the game, humans, giants (called varl) and Dredge (think walking statues with yellow eyes). The game begins with three plot threads, two following varl, and one following humans. The Dredge are causing problems for everyone in the world, but no one is entirely sure why. I wont spoil any more of the plot aside from that.
Gameplay is split in two, combat and traveling. While traveling you have to manage your food, your moral and your caravan size. Food is used to not die, and can be used to boost moral, which is important to keep high. Your caravan size is also best to keep as high as possible, lest you get screwed over in certain events. Speaking of, as you travel you will encounter a number of events, each one has a number of options which will effect gameplay, what you pick will impact the story and may lead to great reward, or cause death, either to some members of the caravan, or a party member. You don't pick the destinations, you are stuck on a set path, and the plot keeps on rolling.
Combat is a square grid based tactical style. each unit goes in turn according to one of their stats, during a units turn it can both move and take an action. you have three options really, attack health, attack armour, or use ability. Your health is how much damage you deal, your armour is subtracted from any damage an enemy will try to inflict on you. The less health you have, the less damage you do. Characters each have a unique ability, which costs stars to use. At the start of every combat you have a group pool of stars to use based on the moral of your caravan, these are used to activate abilities, move additional spaces, or add power to your attacks, you can regain them in combat in various ways such as killing an enemy, but it wont carry over into the next fight and will reset every new encounter. Its a tad basic, but its always tense and very satisfying. It gets more interesting once you get some equipment and levels on your various characters.
The pacing of the game is one of ts greatest strengths, along with the semi branching plot. You are always encountering new events, always marching on with the plot, always making progress and always on edge. Each encounter will matter, either right there and then, or way down the road, you don't know until after you've made your choices. Banner saga is a satisfying experience from start to finish, and is well worth your time.

Star Wars Battlefront 2 is an awesome game. I have played this game for countless hours on both both the PC and PS2 (mores so on the PS2). There are so many awesome things about this game, such as the campaign. The Campaign mode takes you through Episode 3 through Episode 6. Not only is the campaign awesome, so is everythign else about this game. One great aspect is the Instant Action mode, where you are able to choose to play your favorite maps in what order you want (and dependng on the map in particular) play which era (Clone Wars or Empire). There are many great qualities about this game that I recommend you play this game.

I recommend buying D:OS (especially if it goes on sale), but that recommendation comes with some pretty large caveats. It is a fun game, but another reviewer said something I fully agree with: I enjoyed it less the longer I played it. As I played I went from thinking of the other party types I want to replay the game with to doubting I'll ever play through it again. It suffers from some really large design flaws. Read on for details.
D:OS's shining gem is its combat system. The turn-based combat is fun, even after dozens of hours of it. Combat encounters feel balanced (with a few notable exceptions) and it's very polished. This is good, because you're basically going to wade through and kill everything that gets in your way. Graphics and sound effects are wonderful and appropriate without taxing your GPU at all. The writing and humor is charming, though eventually gets a little tired.
Here's one easy tip that would have improved my playthrough significantly: don't bother collecting everything. Like many RPGs you can take or steal everything that is not glued down. You'll find yourself tempted to distract a character so you can steal the ink pot off their desk.
Most items in the game are useless (food especially), and you will be absolutely swimming in gold by mid-game just by selling the items you loot in combat. There are occasional things worth buying from vendors but they aren't expensive. I finished the game with almost 1 million gold laying around. It's an enormous waste of time to grab everything. However, just to laugh about it once, do steal a painting off the wall then immediately sell it back to the owner. *sigh* Realism...
There are dozens of smaller issues I have, but these to me are the should-I-buy-this-game type problems.
1. The game's first major issue is the opening hours. At the start, you are led to an optional tutorial dungeon and have one minor combat encounter. Then you enter the first main town where you will spend the next 5–10 hours running around talking to everyone to open up the storyline and gaining enough experience to leave the town and not get your butt kicked by the enemies just outside. This is a game with a
of dialog, which is great, but it is a really poor design to not let a player test their combat mettle until they've invested 10+ hours. That's why you read so many reports of people abandoning their first party and starting over once they understand the game mechanics better. This happens in a lot of RPGs, but most will let you realize your errors within the first hour or so. Replaying 5 hours of dialog is not fun.
2. You control a party of four characters which you can outfit from head to toe in gear. Unfortunately, loot in this game is horribly bland. Here are the possible magical mods you can get:
That's it. Even the unique weapons roll with only those options. There are no interesting or hard-to-find mods. At the end of the game (level ~20) I found myself still using some level 5 armor that rolled with + to main stats because I'd not found more interesting replacements.
3. Crafting. Everything about crafting kinda sucks. The interface, or rather the complete lack thereof, is the main problem. There are many many crafting recipes in the game but you alone are responsible for remembering them. There is no in-game list of the recipes you know. Everything is just "discoverable." Which means you'll keep a wiki page bookmarked and go to it when you're trying to remember how to craft something. It's all drag-and-drop for an "interface": drag item A onto item B to make item C. And your crafting character better be the one holding the ingredients because it won't succeed if you're trying to manipulate items in another characters inventory.
4. For all the trouble it is to craft, almost none of the things you can craft are worthwhile. All of the weapons and armor you can craft are non-magical. They have higher base armor or damage than items you find, but without any magical mods they will almost never be better than what you've found. Food is utterly useless, and potions eventually drop from enemies like rain. All I found useful from crafting were special arrows, spellbooks and equipment boosters (rubies, bowstrings, metal scraps, etc.).
5. Inventory management is a disaster. Items that inexplicably don't stack (like bone dust, the most common crafting ingredient, which I ended the game with about 80 of). Quest items never disappear, even after they are no longer needed. And lots of them just have generic names like "dusty parchment" or "note." Want to repair that bow? Unequip and send it to your blacksmith, fix it, send it back to your archer and then re-equip (yes those last two are required separate steps, you cannot drag from one character's inventory to another character's equip slot). Using the inventory filtering tabs is absolutely essential.
6. There are a handful of areas in the game where you're suddenly and without warning insta-killed by some gigantic blast of damage. There are tons of discoverable dig-up spots throughout the game. Some of them will just wipe your party when you do it.
You can hear the developers laughing when this happens, but this kind of BS is why save-scumming exists.
7. This is a game that gives you some choice. Many quests are skippable, or can be tackled in various order. However, there's a large misguidance in this.
This alone almost made me just stop playing, and really ruined the end of the game for me.
8. If that weren't enough, the game's ending is
from both a storyline and mechanics point of view. After investing so many hours, the ending was a slap in the face.
This is the least graceful handling of a game ending I've ever seen. And the story wrap-up is basically "you did the thing you were trying to do. The end."
Basically, my reaction after it all was just frustration, which compelled me to come write this review. It's a game worth playing, but really could use some major improvements.

Почти идеальная CRPG.
От создателей классического Divine divinity и чуть менее классических Beyond divinity и прочих Divinity (любят они это слово -_-) пришла к нам в прошлом году прямо из кикстартера эта "олдскульная фэнтези РПГ". И всё при ней: боги, демоны, тролли, орки, элементали, гоблины, маги, культы, амнезия, дикие лучники и добродушные воры, пьяные вояки-легионеры и потерявшиеся жрецы. Как положено в изометрии, как положено с прокачкой пати, как положено с моральными дилеммами и  притворной "нелинейностью". Всё это дело сдобрено кучей книжек (хотя не такой уж и кучей на самом деле. Тем более, что все они короткие и часто повторяются. Даже если вы очень любите читать лор - слишком много времени это не займёт), большим количеством качественно проработанных диалогов и неплохим сюжетом. Между диалогами и решением простых пазлов (как обязательных, так и не очень) вы можете подраться в походовом режиме с участием 2-4 персонажей с вашей стороны и 10+ врагов. Классы неплохо сбалансированы, враги не дают совсем расслабиться, особенно, если вы залезаете в территории, в которые вам залезать "не положено" (это к вопросу о "нелинейности"). В самом начале драться откровенно тяжеловато. Ближе к концу, когда потенциал всех классов раскрывается - становится немного проще.
Вообще, игра впечатляет по всем параметрам. Любовно проработанный мир, достойный визуальный ряд, отличнейшая музыка (клянусь, я даже русский вокал расслышал в одном или двух треках!) и море текста для прочтения =)
Под конец немного надоедают "пазлы", но это и немудрено с учётом того, что игра заняла у меня больше сотни (!) часов.   Игра не очень заботится о том, чтобы ты не потерялся. Если ты не читаешь диалоги и недостаточно внимателен при изучении мира, вполне реальна возможность заблудиться и не знать, что делать дальше. Магическая стрелочка не приведёт тебя к следующему шагу по основному квесту (хотя какие-то подсказки иногда можно получить).
Единственным серьёзным минусом этой игры лично для меня стал её сеттинг. Я и так не особо фанат "классического" фэнтези, а тут оно уж совсем классическое (с небольшими вкраплениями путешествий во времени/пространстве, но с ними сталкиваешься настолько редко, что ими можно пренебречь). Можно даже сказать сухое. Но это очень субъективный минус, кому-то именно такой сеттинг может как раз понравиться.
Чуть менее весомым минусом я бы назвал систему предметов, экипировки и денег. Денег у любого мало-мальского "хордера" со стажем будет очень много уже на второй час игры. Тратить их абсолютно некуда. Под конец у меня было тысяч 500-600 золотых монет и ровно ноль путей их применить. Экипировка полностью лишена "души". Легендарные вещи почти не отличаются от таких же магических и уникальных, обычно это сухие цифры и приросты по 10% за "уровень". Не то чтобы раздражает, выполняет свою миссию вроде бы, но и не впечатляет. И это при очень крутой системе крафта, которой хотелось бы пользоваться. Но особого смысла и нет (кроме пары-тройки "улучшающих" рецептов)- вещей которые падают хватает.
В целом 9.5/10, рекомендую и жду следующую часть. Как раз года через три, когда я опять буду готов к оркам и гоблинам, пусть выходит =)

Really fun and addictive rugby league management game. Not exactly cutting edge but it achieves what it sets out to do. I'm going to assume people reading this review have some sort of understanding of the sport.
Pros:
- The match engine does a very good job of simulating how attacking sets would work. Early in the set your forwards create a 'platform' by how well they get up the field, The better your 'platform' the more successful your back moves will be. This is a simple and easy to understand method of simulating attacking sets.
- Has a good level of tactical control, allowing you to choose what plays to use in which sets and control how much freedom your playmakers can have when attacking. You can choose to let your team play a very simple structure with your playmakers having very little say, or incorporate more complex moves with your playmakers having more freedom.
- The team calls give you a stronger control of the game i.e. one such is Engineroom Overdrive, which for a set or so, once per game, makes your forwards much more potent and create a much better platform.
- Staff management and training is also fun, allowing you to retrain players to different positions.
- The transfer market is fun, if not overpowered, other teams do not partake in mid-season transfers between themselves, only from players you have personally transfer listed in your own side. Ignoring the transfer market and only signing players whose contracts come to an end is a much more challenging and rewarding experience, this also forces you to cap manage.
- In game A.I. is pretty good, each team has unique attacking and defensive structures.
Cons:
- A little buggy, major one is when a scrum happens with your starting hooker off, the ball gets constantly passed to them.
- Players attributes do not change from season to season, defeats the purpose of signing young players. Player developement is also strange, the games forces the few players that can increase in calibre to stay in your academy (reserves) until they reach their max calibre, even if they are good enough to be in your first team.
- The player 'calibre' system is strange, occasions occur that despite two players having similar attributes, the player that is 'professional' calibre will still be much stronger than the 'semi-pro' one.
- Attributes are more centered to positions than players, resulting in, for example, James Roberts having a speed of 63/100 because he's a centre, despite being arguably the fasted guy in Rugby league. I understand that this may be required to make the match engine work though.
A really good start to what can hopefully be a strong long term franchise, really fun and I'm still not bored of it. If you love rugby league you'll adore this game.

This takes a new approach to the formula established in the original xcom games. The result is turn based tactical squad combat that is streamlined, yet satisfying. It still allows for a myriad of tactical approaches and unit combinations, while keeping ocmbat fast paced (relatively speaking, as it is a turn based game after all).
There is a large amount of research available, or discoverable (sometimes requiring capturing live aliens) to keep your soldiers and air units competitive with alien forces. Being an XCom game, there is also a base construction aspect (excavating and building facilities) as well as a global "metagame" that involves you managing the panic levels of the Council countries, lest they withdraw from the XCom Project. This multifacated challenge (ground combat, research, world panic) makes for an extremely engaging and rewarding experience, as you turn back the tide of the alien aggressors.
The game features a cinematic camera that often triggers when a unit is killing another unit. Even at the end of the game, I still grin when it does a flyby view of my sniper lining up an across-the-map kill shot. It remind me of the VATS kill cam from Fallout 3, and adds a nice bit of cinematic flare to the combat.
My only real complaints are the sometimes frustrating elevation/movement controls (which sometimes insist on auto-selecting the elevation it *thinks* you want, as opposed to selecting form the elevation you manually toggled to) and the clunky door-opening controls, which can inadvertantly open up a door/forcefield when you are trying to select anoter unit, even if the unit you are clicking on is nowhere near the door (any left-click will open it). Users have also reported crashes and stability issues, which is a shame for such a feature filled game.
However, if you are looking for a solid futuristic/scific squad based tactics game, with the addition of a deep research tree and globla panic metagame, look no further. Also, you would be highly recommended to pick up the expansion, "Enemy Within" as well. It only adds upon the already feature-packed package with all new research, gene mods, Mechanized troops, new faction, and more.

I grew up on the old school RTS games - Warcraft, C&C, Total Annihilation.  I only found out about Grey Goo two weeks ago and decided to give it a try.
I have been pleasently surprised.  It does have a slight C&C feel to it (not generals, but C&C, Red Alert type feel).  It plays like those old RTS with some of the annoying features of the old RTS games out of the picture.  (No camp in your base for your super weapon)
Like many said it is not a Starcraft so if you expect it to play like that you will be disappointed - there is not as much micro as you would have in SC and the pace is slower.
It feels very well polished, so far the single player campaign in the best I've played in an RTS in years.  It is a bit short, but the cutscenes are plentiful and the story is great.
The three factions are very different as well.  There may be a lot of similar units between them in some regards, but the base strategies differ vastly.
If you like RTS games and you liked the old ones back in the late 90's early 2k's pick this game up.  You won't regret it!

Here's my first review, so please be gentle
First of al Child of Light is very pleasant to the eyes. it's artwork is made with love for fantasy and imagniation. Also the storyline is nice, with lots of characters with background stories.
The gamesystem consist of two types: RPG and Turn based battles. The RPG part takes you through a lot of beautiful area's. you're free to go where you want to in this nice platform gameworld. Mostly you collect stones that you can equip to boost up your stats or weapons.
The Turn based battles work like they should. with a nice timebar that shows who's turn it is to attack. nothing special here. The battles are nicely animated and tend to be very hard at the end of the game. When you win a battle you get XP to level up.
Here it gets a little quirky. after almost every battle you level up, at first you're happy about it. but later on it gets irritating because all the playable characters level up. this means that most of the time you're busy upgrading the stats of all the characters. the upgrade system is also a bit off. Because between the move-upgrades you must first upgrade stats. but you have to follow a certain path, so you have little influence in the forming of your characters. this makes it quite lineair.
I think the developers would have made a better job if they took the stats-upgrades and move-upgrades apart.
The stone system is quite nice, allthough it also gets wearsome. collecting gems is fun at first, but to get the ultimate gems you have to merge a lot (50+) tier1 gems.
The first 90 percent of the game is quite easy for a medium experienced gamer. the last 10 percent are some tough bosses that need some luck/skill.
i would say 7/10.

This game is refreshing. Not only does it have a greaa soundtrack and absolutley stunning cutscenes, but you  get to choose what songs you want to play with the Jukebox feature. But onto the meat of the game. Of the three factions, the Beta are fairly typical for RTS games. They are well balanced and spread their bases around the map. This in contrast to the other base building faction, the Humans, who unlike the Beta, build one expanisve well-defended base. Their strategy is typically to turtle and send out waves to wear down enemies and pick off enemy instalments. Now, on to the real pull of this game; the Goo. The Goo are a completely new type of faction that has never been done before in this type of game. Instead of building a base, you start off with one Mother Goo, who, depending on hoe much resources it has absorbed, can spilt into smaller blobs called Proteans. There are 2 types of Proteans, Large ones, which are about as slow as the Mother Goo, and split into heavier unit types, such as tanks. The other type, is the zippy small Protean, which  spawns light infantry. On top of this, Mother Goo and Protean blobs can traverse any terrain, and absorb building and units, making them something akin to melee-range siege weapons. Despite all this innovation, the game has a few setbacks. Despite the campaign telling a good story and having constant and wonderful cutscenes, some of the levels are absolute hell, like the 5th and last Beta level, where after holding out for 15 minutes, you spend an hour running around the map chasing down the last goo blobs. The interface also is very clunky and unresponsive, though a lot of that can be changed by toying with your hotkeys. All in all, this game is just the breath of fresh air the genre needed, from all the Total Wars and Starcraft. 8.5/10

This game really snuck up on me. I hadn't even heard of it until I saw it in the "New Releases" in the strategy section here on Steam. At first I thought it was an Indie game, but its not. Its a monumental game, with a long rich single player campaign.
This game harkens back to the glory days of RTS, when every other PC game was RTS, and before cross-platform console games became the fad... and virtually spelled the end of the RTS genre. You see: its very hard to play RTS with one of those archaic gamepads, but rather than establish better peripherals for console (like mouse and keyboard), game companies simply dropped titles that didn't play well on console, so that they could release on Xbox and Playstation and PC with one giant game and get the largest userbase. Greed trumped making good and interesting games, and so everybody started making FPS.
I've gone off on a tangent, and I apologize... but there is a reason. Before the consoles became a serious gaming platform, RTS got a AAA+ treatment from publishers and development studios. They were graphically amazing, with fully rendered cutscenes, long rich campaigns around interesting stories, great dialog presented by great voice actors, well-balanced but with challenging AI (etc). And then it all went away (except for Starcraft 2 and some Space RTS's), leaving the RTS genre primarily being advanced by nostalgic Indie developers.
... at least: until now. This game is amazing. Its basically the game that I would expect to see from all major publishers if the Console fad hadn't taken off. Here's a more detailed breakdown:
---- THE GOOD ----
* GRAPHICS : Beautiful game. Awesome scenery filled with lush alien forests and swamps interspersed with strange alien machinery. The architecture of the buildings is imaginative and interesting, including the base buildings. Unit design is also interesting, with the human drones looking more like works of art than military machines. And of course there's the goo creatures: which are amazing to look at and scary. Explosions and laser bolts are quite beautiful too.
* FULLY RENDERED CUTSCENES AND BRIEFINGS : I feel like I'm playing Starcraft! Only... Starcraft had mostly in-engine cutscenes, not full renders. So Grey-Goo takes it one step further! After each mission the player is rewarded with a 30-second (or so) cutscene made with love. Its film-quality (no exaggeration). Then the next level briefing is also fully rendered. It all looks like full-performance capture (with very good actors). The detail is such that you can see the pores in the alien's skin. The races have distinct looks and styles of dress, and even change their clothes from mission to mission. Really big kudos. It helps draw the player in big-time.
* AI : The AI is challenging. Some levels can be very difficult, but usually this means you're missing some trick to circumvent a defense. While the AI is not quite human-quality, that is mitigated by the AI starting the level with established bases. So its not really a factor. Additonally, a difficulty setting allows you, if you do get stuck, to drop down to an easier level AI and not punish you too much.
* ASYMMETRICAL STRATEGY : Especially around base-building, each race has a different build style and strategy, which adds variety between the races and gives some insight into their culture.
* STORY : The story is really great so-far (I haven't completed the game), with interesting sci-fi concepts that are very believable (in fact: based on real theories). The dialog is great, and the voice acting delivering that dialog is great. Its all very immersive. Such that I played 11 hours straight today.
* EPIC UNITS : Epic units are always fun. Its hard to get them (as it should be), but once you have them, they're very impressive and fun, soaking a lot of damage while independently targeting numerous enemies and blasting them away. In one mission you get to have 2 at once... twice the slaughter... twice the fun!
* OPTIONAL OBJECTIVES : It adds a lot of replayability, especially for us full-completionists.
* THE HUMANS ARE SUPER-ADVANCED : This is more of my personal preference, but the humans in this game are a bit like the Protoss in Starcraft. Lots of super-clean lines, strange alien architecture and glowy bits... and I like that. Its a nice departure from the old trope of "OMG advanced aliens coming to kick our butts". But also, for the humans to have a bit of an alien feel as we become super-advanced... is really quite an interesting idea.
---- THE BAD ----
* No VETERANCY SYSTEM : While I am sure the developers intended this as a throwback to old RTS, veterancy was eventually added to most games in that genre, and for good reason: otherwise the strategy tends to be to make waves of units and send them on suicide missions. Because there is no veterancy in this game, that tactic has been reborn (with some variation). It would be nice if there were a reason to keep your units alive, and perhaps make healing them easier.
* THE CONTROLS : The controls are generally pretty good, but there are some weirdnesses like... if you select a unit and then the repair wrench, the unit is still selected. So you think you're controlling the unit but you aren't. Also like... the aliens have these great big battleships that you can assign soldiers to hop into and man gun-turrets... which is awesome! The problem is: there are 6 turrets, so they mostly cover the entirety of the top of the ship. But clicking on them selects the _unit_, not the _ship_ that they are riding in. This makes selecting the ship frustrating because you need to make sure you're clicking the back of it, or else it will select one of your gunners. Generally I learned just to assign the dreadnaught ship to a hotkey. But it was a minor annoyance.
* THE SOUND : While the sound is really good, including the music, it fluctuates wildly. If I have the cutscenes at normal volume, ingame is very loud.
* NO "DO YOU WANT TO EXIT" : Minor annoyance, but in a level with optional objectives, if you complete the primary objective, uncompleted optional objectives come up as _failed_. I'd prefer that the game tell me something like "Primary objective complete: are you ready to exit?" Or at least a "Complete primary objective? (Some optional objectives are still active!)"
* UNITS AREN'T SUPER-INTERESTING : While this contradicts what I said above a bit, I do have one qualm... there's not a lot of variance in the units. There are quite a few that, at first glance, I can't really tell apart. Also there are LOT of hovertanks. I think they should have considered a little more variety.
* UNITS ARE FAIRLY SYMMETRICAL : What I mean by this is... the aliens have regular soldiers, artillery, anti-vehicle, anti-infantry, bombers, fighters (etc), and so do the humans. The unit types between human and alien are virtually identical. While their base-building strategies are quite different, after the base is up, they're almost the same... with some variation for unique units and epic units. Its not like Starcraft where one species has great guns, the other has great armor and spells, and the other has enormous numbers. I do understand somewhat, why they cose not to do this though; because balancing asymmetrical RTS units is hard, and prone to exploitable failure. So its a minor disappointment, but an understandable one.
---- IN CLOSING ----
All of the plusses are big plusses for me, and all the minuses are minor. I highly recommend this game 9/10 , and I hope they DLC and sequel the hell out of it. Its very interesting, and I want more!  :)

I hate it when I regret buying a game, but unfortunately, that is the case with Child of Light. The trailer looked *amazing* and the reviews looked positive too. I was hoping this would be a beautiful game I could lose myself in. Unfortunately that was not the case.
The story of the game is about a princess who falls into a dream-world which she must explore and escape. Accordingly, the movements of the character are very dream-like and slow...contrary to the trailer, which showed her moving at a "normal" video game pace. Thus, trying to play this game was almost painful...it's like one of those dreams where you're trying to run but your feet are bogged down like you're trying to swim in a pool full of syrup. Not a pleasant gameplay experience at all.
I still tried to stick it out though, until I got to the combat part. I guess I'm just not used to puzzle-related combat styles in games, but, it just wasn't very fun to try to figure out. If you're used to games like that, then this won't be a problem. But it wasn't enjoyable for me at all.
The good parts about this game are the music and the graphics. The music is haunting and beautiful, and the graphics are styled to look like a moving watercolor painting you can explore...which is an awesome concept that is stunningly executed in this game. So since that part of the game is so awesome, I really wish the gameplay for this game hadn't been so hard to use. Because if you can't play the game, it doesn't matter how pretty it is to look at and listen to. Unless you just watch playthroughs of it on YouTube. Which is a possibility I guess.

When I saw this game the first time in the store, I was like "Oh, another pure fan-service game" But for some reason I really wanted it, I just had an inch that this game will be great, and soon a friend gifted it to me along with all the DLC, and I was right. The game is just amazing.
First of all, the game manages to defeat a problem a lot of RPG's have - Being repetive and boring.
This game includes a remake system, allowing you to customize pretty much everything using plans. Want to have different enemies appear in Avenir Factory? Find the plan in one of the stages, obtain the required items, and activate the plan; you just got tougher and different enemies in that place~! Feel like the game is too easy? Get the plan to weaken the enemies, obtain the items, and activate it~ now the game is easier! There's a lot more to this too, but there's too much to write it all. Getting and activating the plans is a lot of fun.
So here's the main way of attacking, when you press "Attack" during a battle, you have 3 commands:
Rush - Doesn't deal a lot of damage, but fills the EXE Gauge a lot faster. If you have filled the EXE gauge by at least 1, you can unleash addition EXE attacks, which you can fully customize to what they do. The EXE Gauge also allows you to use special moves called "EXE Drive" they deal a lot of damage, and also have a really neat attacking animations.
Power - This type of attack deals the most damage.
Break - These attacks are best used in order to lower the Enemy's Defense. The lower their defense is, the easier it is to defeat it And if you break the defense completely, they will be really weak and can be very easily defeated.
Every characters turn, you can attack up to 4 times. The first attack is always pre-determined by the character, however.
All three types of attacking are fully customizable. Want the 2nd Power Attack have a chance of inflicting poison, and the 3rd Break attack have a chance of freezing the enemy? You can definitely do that~! As you progress further in the game, you unlock more moves for your attacks to customize, making the battles a lot different.
In other words, the battle system is pretty original, and really fun to play with. You won't feel bored during them.
Now for the artwork and models~ The artwork is drawn pretty nicely and looks beautiful. The Models for the game are also very good, and have a nice Anime'ish look on them. The animations for all of the things (Walking, EXE drive, jumping, etc.) Are pretty nice and varying too.
Now for the voice actors for the characters~ The game developers have taken very good choices. Both Japanese and English Vocals are adorable, and perfectly fitting for the personalities and looks of characters, which is a big plus.
The Japanese Voices are 100% Complete, however the English ones don't seem to be. They seem to be about 70% complete, however, the remaining 30% which isn't dubbed seems to be in the less important parts of the game, so it isn't a big problem either.
And now for the music~ It's just beautiful. Each lands music theme is fitting into that Land's looks. As an example, Lastation, which is full of machinery, has a energetic theme which sounds like it has machinery inside it. It's hard to explain it, but I can guarantee that it sounds great.
And now for the characters~ They're all different, and have great personalities. Almost all of them show character development. A lot of them seem to be pure fan-service (Especially the CPU Forms) but that's kind of the charm. Most of their personas change when they enter they CPU form, causing pretty funny and great (and creepy in the case of a certain character..) conversations.
And the final part~ the story. It's really neat, it might seem to be boring at first, but in reality, it's really good. Even though, this game is basically a mockery of the Gamindustry- I mean,  Gaming Industry, it still manages to give it a unique story and charm, I didn't get from games in a long time. The game has also two endings, which is pretty great, as it gives variety. After you beat Story Mode, you can start New Game+, allowing you to use all of your levels from characters/money/items and start Story Mode all over again. NG+ is best to obtain the CPU Candicates, and just have lots of fun~! And if you're a completionist like me, 100% the game.
The game has a lot of references to other games/Companies, and most of the side characters have names after them, Like Marvy (Marvelous AQL) Iffy (Idea Factory) Compa (Compile Heart) and so on. And the Fan-Service is basically a joke about how a lot of people think that Anime is basically all about breast size and so on.
In other words, this games makes a lot of funny jokes, mocks the gaming industry in a funny, subtle way, has a great story, amazing music and vocals, radical battle system, makes a lot of references to various games/anime, and lots of replayibility and fun.
I've spend 84 hours at the moment of writing this review, and I plan to spend a lot more, as this game is really addicting and good. And I think it has became my new favorite game.
I'd definitely recommend getting it, especially if you like jokes and/or Anime. You will love it.

I'll start off by getting the obvious out of the way: this game is lovely. The art style and animations were very enjoyable for me. You can pan around in combat, with the isometric view, and there will be little tree limbs and stuff close to the screen, which are blurred since they're supposed to be out of focus. Yes, technically, there is no floating person or camera in the sky, but it wasn't invasive or distracting, and was a nice touch. So yeah, graphically, kudos to the development team, and I cannot complain at all here.
The music seemed nice while I listened to it. Eventually I stopped listening, but that was more a case of the rest of the game leaving me too disinterested or annoyed to care that much about anything else in the game.
The gameplay consists of reading dialog, watching people walk in one direction without input from the player, moving slowly, until something happens, making random decisions that impact you sometimes without any way to know or have a fair guess at the outcome or what's the "safe" option, etc. It's like FTL in that respect, except that in FTL, here's typically a no-risk option that's very obvious. The combat is strange. Your damage decreases every time you take health damage. Is it realistic? Sure. Realism does not automatically mean it's good, though. If my HP drops to 1, I want it to be intense, with me expecting myself to die but still thinking I could win. However, in this game, you're already guaranteed to lose, so continuing to play through the fight is just a waste of time, because your chances of survival dwindle more by the turn, and it's less interesting every turn because it's not a fair fight with a sight disadvantage any more, but rather, a curb-stomping of your party.
Also, if a character dies in a battle, the character is straight up dead. It did not give me the ability to revive, and it was not a scripted death. I looked online and sometimes there are scripted deaths, apparently, but this was not supposed to happen at this time. Oh! And the game had just leveled that character up for me and gave me a big wink and a nudge that I ought to spend my points I'd earned on that character. So in a challenging game with random stuff that can negatively impact you out of battle in an instant, and they're adding character death in a game that's longer than a couple of hours, in which a full roster of characters in battle is kinda important to have.
I found nothing I liked, whatsoever, about the gameplay in The Banner Saga. Not one thing. If I hadn't played Shadowrun: Dragonfall, I may have simply thought that I hated the entire genre of squad turn-based strategy gams, but that's not true. I loved Shadowrun: Dragonfall, and despite me being awful at it, I persevered and the combat was very intuitive with a lot of nice strategies involved. In The Banner Saga, however, the dwindling damage every time each party member is hit, the single action per turn when not moving, the inability to hit enemies with a bow and arrow unless you are within walking distance of the enemy so the enemy still hits me, thus negating the intention of ranged weapons vs melee enemies. I even had one time I had two archers who were together, and the system wouldn't let me fire at an enemy because the other archer was in front of me. Realistic? Yeah, but throw me a dang bone! The gameplay simply annoyed me from start to finish, in all ways.
I can't remember the story, and I played for several hours today. I like Game of Thrones, so it's not like political medieval/fantasy stuff doesn't appeal to me, and like I said, the art during the story was great. That said, although a great story and make a game with "meh" gameplay pretty cool, this game's story just didn't stimulate me enough to get interested in it or want to keep playing the game. This could have been a cool 1980s-style animated film with focus solely on plot and real events, rather than random text events and interruptions of poor combat. Since I didn't care about the story, I can find screenshots and trailers online to showcase the art style and music of the game in a bite-sized and sufficient pakage, and the game was not fun for me to play, there is absolutely no reason for me to continue playing this game, and I cannot in good faith recommend it.

Passing turns multiple times, in hopes that the proper character is in range, or enough armor has be picked off, etc., is just stupid..
Add to that, that the Renown required to lvl up (+5 per lvl) 10 at 2, 15 at 3, etc.) is the same resource used to buy vital supplies (the most important thing in game) and Items.. Items are the only equippable gear in game, and i would strongly advise against EVER buying any...

A surprisingly well written, funny game.  The characters all have their own personalities, the story is enough to keep you going, there's a whole lot of side quests to do.  Overall, this is a really fun JPRG, but not without its flaws.
There's some typos, some errors with the text not wrapping properly.  It's disturbingly frequent, really.  I've run into a couple sound glitches as well, like an audible "pop" before and after silent parts of dialog.  There's also one skill where one of the characters seems to use the wrong style of voice depending on their form.  Minor stuff, but bugs that were never fixed none-the-less.  The game also makes references still to the fact that it's on Vita, so they didn't bother to update it for the PC port.  Another strike against it.
One of the most glaring things, though, is that the game seems to have been designed with the DLC's increased level cap etc. in mind.  Skills don't really go "all the way", a lot of characters seem to stop progressing at a certain point.  I don't know if they start getting more skills etc. again with the DLC, but it feels like there were gaps left in to be ready for it.  There's also the issue that one of the achievements seems solely designed for the DLC, as playing over 70 hours with three play-throughs only netted me 1/10th of what I needed for it.  Now, I have no problem with DLC that just adds a bit of extra content.  I do have a problem when the DLC feels mandatory for getting a "complete" game.
All that said though, this game is still well built and fun enough that I don't mind recommending it.  And I'll probably look up the sequels too.  The characters are really fun, and funny, there's lots of little references.  All in all, it was an entertaining experience.  So, yea, if you like JRPGs, pick this one up!
Edit:  As a note on the repeated play-throughs, it does not take long to get back to the end game using New Game+.  You can skip the dialog, and you don't need to do the extra missions, plus you're already high level and can overpower every story enemy in the game.  So I had no issues with having to do that to unlock everything.
Edit 2: I have now completed the game with DLC.  Some of my complaints above turned out false.  The obvious "gaps" were not filled in the DLC.  You never gain more points to put all your best skills on, only limited to the same 400, you never gain any new magic, or ultimate attacks.  Though the DLC stuff isn't scaled very well either.  Each one adds a new dungeon that's meant for being max level for that DLC.  And you pretty much need all the DLC, as bits and pieces leave problems (such as getting the DLC character's colosseum weapons requires all three of the level DLCs).  So, still not perfect in that regard.  And, leveling itself, you don't go out and fight to level.  The EXP pay outs are not balanced for that.  They are designed that you find the handful of "jackpot" payout fights and farm those.

A very fun game, with some flaws.
Fun:
Co-op CRPG--with mods the game works for up to 4 players, and it's a heck of a lot of fun working together to take tough enemies down.
Multiple ways to approach things--most quests have a variety of approaches that you can take to solving them.  Talk a dog into helping you sniff out clues?  Or knock a door down and ransack a house for incriminating evidence?  Or just pillage the countryside until you find who you're looking for.  I guess you could...talk to people too.  Like a "normal person."
Elemental surfaces--the game employs a really fun system that lets you take advantage of your environment.  Break open an oil barrel and set the oil slick it creates on fire to slow down enemies.  Electrify a puddle of water.  Or an enemy's own blood spatter...  Confound enemy archers by putting up a smokescreen and force them to engage you up close.
Arguments--as you might expect, your protagonists will have to make decisions frequently, and Divinity OS goes the extra mile in the role-playing department by letting you discuss in-game between the two main characters about what you should do.  You can agree on a single course of action, or you can argue over two different choices by way of a rock-paper-scissor system.  This system is a lot of fun when you're playing with another real human, but sadly boring when you're playing on your own.  You can set one of a limited number of "personalities" for the character you aren't controlling, but arguements will then be decided by a combination of luck and charisma statistics.  You'll probably want to just set the other character to agree with you all the time, which leaves them kind of as another lifeless shell controlled by you rather than a believable partner.
Writing--it can be laugh-out-loud funny at times.  The game never takes itself TOO seriously, and that's it's greatest strength, reveling in silliness.
Flaws:
First the nitty-gritty.
Pathing--it's a pain in the behind.  Characters frequently don't walk the paths you set for them, and even when you unlink them from the character you're controlling directly, they'll still stumble off of a button you deliberately set them on.
I'm not sure what you call this, spell pathing maybe?  So many invisible walls in the environment block shots that by all accounts ought to be able to hit the target just fine.  Not being able to just lob a spell into a smoke cloud is also incredibly frustrating when you work with fire surfaces in almost every fight.  It becomes a painful pixel hunt to find that one in-game inch that sticks out enough for you to get a target.  As you get further into the game, AoE spells will be your best friend because they won't have the obnoxious requirements to fire in those situations.
Writing--party members don't really seem to have much in the way of development or depth beyond some very basic conversations to establish who they are.  Most named NPCs have more development from what I've seen so far.  The dialogue in the game in general can range from incredibly sparse, to long flowery diatribes about nothing of substance.
If you're an RPG fan looking for a game you can play with a friend, D:OS is a great game to scratch that itch. It maybe isn't up to all-time classic standards, but it promises a lot of fun in both single and multiplayer.

So after
, I think I can make an informed opinion about this game. It's an MMO, so I don't see how others can play for 4 hours and then decide its a bad game? I wouldn't exactly call this a review, you can go read someone else's, yet I really want to address somethings that I feel hold people back from even trying this game.
So on that note, I'll start with
(and they're things I was worried about too).
This is something I see pop-up alot and many people for some reason flag it as a massive problem. For those of you that don't know, BDO installs a Anti-cheat rootkit which does exactly what it says on the tin. Many people complain that this is bad conduct as the game does not alert you that it does this, yet the majority of multiplayer games/platforms will do this too (Take Blizzard's 'Warden' or Valve's 'VAC' systems). This is just clutching at straws, especially since it doesn't affect you outside the game (or inside it for that matter), yet most portray it to be like a virus magnet or an intrusion of privacy. I'm sure that it's written in the terms and conditions that they do this, just most choose to ignore it, and even if it's not, someone please explain to me why installing an anti-cheat system is bad conduct? I mean let's say Valve gave you the choice of wether you wanted to use VAC or not? Exactly that's a ridiculous thought.
Long story short: No. To everyone, P2W is different. To me personally P2W is when you can purchase something that puts you well ahead of everyone else who doesn't pay to win. And this game doesn't do that. All the top players have got there through putting in the time and effort, not through dishing out dolla'. But there is a Micro-transaction shop. The majority is cosmetic, yet there are some convenience items such as inventory space upgrades. Even the items which seem pay to win on paper(I.E the Elions tear which insta-reses you), really aren't that helpful and don't really put anyone at a disadvantage. Not only that but with the market system, you can buy the majority of Micro-Trans items with in game money (If you can get to it before a long term player snipes it). Overall, no matter what you buy at most it gives you a very insignificant Temporary advantage. Especially since the majority of these items (if not all) can be earned in-game.
Yes. Put simply this is a grindy game, and if that's not for you, you probably wont enjoy that part of the game. You can only gain exp through killing mobs for example. It's very Korean-MMO-Esq and its not a surprise that its a grind fest. ESPECIALLY the gear grinding. You could spend days maybe even weeks grinding for the best gear in the game, and this is perhaps one of the biggest downfalls of the game. While end game is what you make of it, if you plan to get the best gear, prepare to spend potentially hundreds of hours grinding away at the same content, with the hope that maybe just maybe, you may get a piece of boss gear in your life time.
Yet, if that isn't your goal, It doesn't feel like you're just murderising' everything. If you wanted to, you could get to level 50 in a few hours (near enough level cap, which ranges between around 59-63 from server to server). But there's quests to do too, which are a nice way to fill the time, as you will grind as a benefactor of questing.
Well. Alot. There's a whole lot to do if you don't feel like monster crushing.
-You can try and harvest materials around the map and process them into other materials or use them for things such Alchemy and cooking. Yes it has all the standard proffesions such as fishing and cooking.
-You can start a farm. Farm simulator 2017, nah mate, you want BDO. Essentially, you place a fence somewhere in the world and can plant crops. The day and night cycle, aswell as the zone, ground type and weather all affect the crops. Different crops grow at different rates, and there are tonnes of possibilities out there.
-Node Empire. Throughout the world, you can find nodes, which essentially are any town, outpost, city ETC. There are several main cities throughout the world and every node connects to one of these cities somehow. You can hire workers and send them to these nodes to do different things, from mining ores to farming crops, It's like having a world wide corporation. The workers themselves only need lodging and beer. You can then use these materials or sell them on the market, and with alot of workers you can almost monopolise the whole world.
-Horse and pet breeding. Yup, you can go out, catch horses and breed them. Different horses have different tiers and you can essentially breed the perfect horse with the perfect skills (you heard, horse skills). The same goes for pets (once you dish out some cash that is).
-Naval exploration. Not much to say about this. Once you're done exploring the main land and the desert, then you can buy or make yourself a boat and explore the oceans. From pirate jungles, to blue whale hunting there's just as much content off land, than on land.
-Guilds. Prehaps one of my favourite parts of the game, guilds make up a large portion of PvP and social content. Me and a friend started a guild, and within three or four days, we already have a twenty-four man guild, most of which are active players. It's very immersive too. Members sign a contract for one to thirty days and are paid everyday. Then, the guild leader can choose to hand out pay raises based on a players contribution to the guild. Then there's guild quests, which involve subjugation (kill X monsters within X amount of time), trade quests (earn X amount of money using the trade system) and gathering quests (gather X amount of materials within X amount of time). Sounds simple, yet with a group of guildies, it can be very fun and is a cool social experience.
-PVP. I've dabled in this, but the PVP either requires a big guild, or a very high skill cap. There's standard world PVP and then there's node wars and sieges. Players can capture a castle and get benefits for holding it. Other players try to siege it by building siege camps and weapons. Similarly, Node wars involve guilds fighting it out to hold points on the map and gain benefits for them.
-Trading. You can become a trader, wooo! You can buy things from a trade manager and take them to other nodes and sell them. Different items have different worth that changes over time, and different nodes will have different results when it comes to trading. It's also its own skill!
-The combat. My favourite part of the game. Prehaps the reason grinding is actually fun is becuase the combat is fun. Each class is very unique with a pretty extensive skill tree. Its all action combat, with a large focus on combos, which I personally never experienced before. Take a fighting game, you may have an X-X-X combo, but here you can upgrade so it  becomes an X-X-X-Y-B-X sort of combo. There's alot of variety and each class is fun to learn and play, and since theres alot of classes, there's alot to experience. Not to mention it's insanely satisfying. Every hit shows through animations, the audio ques are great, and the shaking screen effects make it seem like there's recoil with every hit and it just builds on more and more immersion.
And there's so much more, yet the more  I write this, the more I want to just go play the game. I hope this can help some people, atleast those that are wanting to try the game. And if you're still skeptical, just go try the seven day free trial? If you don't enjoy it, you don't have to buy it, But if you do, the game is like £6 so you cant miss out. Just don't go in expecting it to be anything like WoW or GW2, this is a whole new can of worms.

Half-Life 2 is a classic in the FPS genre, along with its predecessor, Half-Life.
With this game, Valve intertwines great level design and gameplay to create encounters that are memorable, spontaneous, and fun. The game is constantly changing up the formula, so just when you think you've mastered the game, it introduces new mechanics that change the way you play the game from that point onwards. Valve finds inventive ways to use mechanics that have already been learned and flip them on their head to create encounters that feel new yet familiar.
Half-Life 2 has a great atmosphere. From the music on the soundtrack, to the ambient sounds and environmental storytelling, to the design of the creatures and the design of the world you inhabit, this game creates a believable place for you to get immersed in.
My greatest qualm with this game is the narrative. Not only are the cutscenes are a chore to sit through on a second or third playthrough, but these cutscenes/setpieces feel very unnatural for one reason: Gordon Freeman, being a silent protagonist, makes the interactions with NPC characters feel awkward. It feels like people are talking at you, rather than with you. Him being a silent protagonist is rarely acknowledged, and is not worked into the story whatsoever. The characters are great, but your lack of interaction with them hurts the connection you are supposed to build with them.
Despite this, many of the elements in the story work very well. The Combine feel like a force to be reckoned with, and their alien and oppressive nature motivates you to try to defeat them. However, my favorite part of the narrative is the overarching story involving

Honestly, if Valve never released the Half-Life 2 episodes, this ending would feel quite unsatisfactory, almost being a cop out. It doesn't feel like you have fully accomplished your goal by the end of the game.
Despite my problems with the story, Half-Life 2 is one of the most innovative and fun FPS games I have ever played, and well deserves much of the praise it gets.
