I already became a big fan of this game series because this hits the right spot for me. The things I list could also be the things some people may not like.
Pros
1. Oh yeah, it's anime! - No doubt this game is anime not with just the graphics, but with anime jokes. They even poke fun at it being anime such as calling out anime tropes.
2. Why be serious? Be funny! - This game doesn't take itself serious. Lots of 4th wall-breaking, funny characters and enemies that's a nod to other games or anime. The jokes are very likable.
3. This port is better. - This game is actually a port from PS3, to PSVita, to PC. So changes are made to make the game better. From what I heard, combat is way more better on here.
4. Fanservice <3 – Not going to lie. There are fanservice here and there. Such as pressing buttons on still images to see the girl's breast bounce, dressing them up in swimsuits, and love pairing jokes. Fun fact: Lily is a literally meaning to “Yuri” in Japan, which means Lesbian love. The game has a “Lily System” where you pair up the girls. Sooooo....
5. Challenging. - This game can be hard if you are not careful. Some enemies can catch you off guard and one hit you, others, you need to prepare yourself and attack at the right moment.
6. The Combat System – The combat system reminds me of Lunar Star Silver Complete & Xenosaga Episode 1 combined. It's hard to explain without getting too wordy, but it's smooth and fast.
7. 100% Everything - Not too hard to 100%, and I find it fun to try.
Con
1. It's Animu, ugh! - You don't like anime, you hate all things anime, you may hate this game as well.
2. It's not serious – Game is too goofy.
3. Graphics – It could be better, but it was a port.
4. Lazy reused map design – Most dungeons look the same and is the biggest disappointment to me in the game.
5. English voice ac--g a mi—ing. – Sadly, the English voice direction is lacking in emotion and character fitting. But the worst is, some of the part they are suppose to speak like in Japanese, are missing. So you won't hear them speak when you set it to English.
6. Fanservice - You just not into that. And that's fine.
7. Your GFX card, your CPU, yuck! - Game may not like your graphic card, which can lead to some odd graphical glitches. People say downgrading or upgrading can fix most problems. Also, if you getting high CPU usage, be careful, this game can actually SOFT LOCK you, forcing you to reset. For some reason, the game's enemies can't make up their minds if something else is running your CPU usage high, and would just stay on the enemies' turn, not moving. Making it a soft lock.

Banner Saga is a fairly basic tactics/strategy RPG with an equally basic
semi-random adventure filling in time between fights. You watch a cutscene where a bunch of surly-looking white people with consonant-heavy names like Hrthfalk or Vrmnyr glare at each other, then choose a dialogue option. Something will happen, then you'll be treated to a 15-60 second unskippable, unspeed-up-able clip of your caravan walking to the right. Then an event will happen, which will most likely lead to a fight. The combat is super simple and not really worth discussing; imagine Advance Wars with even less depth and breadth. Fighting and choosing dialogue options makes up 99% of your gameplay, and about 20% of your time spent on Banner Saga in total. Yes, there really is that much fluff.
Much like FTL, the events that happen to your characters and the choices you're given are often obscure. A made-up example for the sake of avoiding spoilers: someone is coming over the hill. Do you kill them, or welcome them with open arms? Kind of a dumb question; you don't really know enough to make a good decision. Choosing either is ridiculous, yet Banner Saga forces you to make these sort of choices all the time.
The advertising copy for Banner Saga touts its difficult choices, but the choices are "difficult" for all the wrong reasons.
Normally, that would be annoying enough to cause me to stop playing, but the outcomes of the events didn't bother me. I'd gain a few supplies, or lose a few dozen men in my army, or in the worst case, an actual hero would die. But I have lots of heroes, and as for the army...
The army you're given charge of does almost nothing in this game, and exists solely as a currency you can gain or lose via random events. Ditto with the supplies that they consume. They only effect they have on your actual fighting is a small increase or decrease to a single stat for your real characters during fights.
The RPG-standards, Experience and Gold, have been combined into a single resource, Renown, that you must divide up as you see fit. You won't have enough to do everything; you're going to have to balance levelling up your heroes with purchasing army supplies and equippable trinkets. I think this is actually really well-designed and I liked it a lot, but it has one glaring flaw.
Renown being so precious means that the Right Choice is almost always the one that leads to a fight. You get Renown not only for winning fights, but also for each individual kill. So the safest way to go through the game is to kill everything and everyone, every chance you get. This way you can keep a well-stocked army with lots of high-level heroes. It's pretty unintuitive, and also makes you fight a lot more times than the meager battle system can really be interesting for.
I played this game a lot longer than I was expecting to. None of the systems by themselves are very good, and they don't really form a cohesive experience. I kept expecting something interesting to happen, but I just go more and more of the same. If you really, really like the art and story, maybe you can get through this, but I personally found both pretty mediocre. I give this game a 5/10 - it's not *bad* bad, but it's not really worth the time.

After playing the extensively, i will not lie: The game is a hit and miss. However, i believe that in that regard, it either hits hard or misses hard.
Where it hits hard, is that the gameplay is entertaining for a turn based RPG, mixing free-roam controls and variety in AAs into RPGs for positionals and variety to your basic attacks. At no time did i find myself frustrated to spam moves, as i usually had a great amount of control in how i used them.
Your attacks tend to culminate to a super attack from one of your characters. Aside from being beautiful, they make fights much shorter once they're woven into your combat. And evert character gets their own unique one!
Spells are for the most part not needed, however buffs and debuffs are 'very' noticable when used. Gear can have wide effects, from changing stats, to protecting your character more, to even altering the grid of range the character can strike in the case of weapons. Every weapon, outfit, and headpiece will alter character looks. Thanks to how weapons work, you can AoE enemies even with basic attacks, making weak encounters much faster.
The characters are fairly cliche, but mostly in the same manner as Disgaea where it's sort of an inside joke. Many of the characters follow tropes to the point that they can personally recite them, and 4th wall breaking is very common. The fact that they can represent a console or company you loved when you were younger is also a plus, as almost the entire cast is based off of some company or console.
Even the grinding has a sort of depth, with a drop system used to unlock new items, and even battle powers to enhance (or detract, be warned) your combat experience. The overworld system is similar to Earthbound, where all enemies can be seen and you can choose whether or not to fight them, with a mix of items, hidden items, and 'super' hidden items scattered throughout the levels.
The music i found to be as hit and miss as the game, and although i loved much of the art, the game can get a bit 'too' fanservicy at times (Breasts Jiggle even in CGs )
Where the game falls short is that for all the depth in the combat system, many fights are answered simply by being at the correct level to face them, and typically if you are then 'no' strategy will be required. Most boss fights culminate to outhealing the boss or leveling more. At most, i found VIT (physical defense) up helpful, however there are very few times to use MEN (magic defense)
There is 'no' reward for defeating unbeatable encounters. There is no win script. No exp, no credits. The story continues as if you still lost the fight.
The AA system and Lily system are greatly hindered by what your main 3 characters are, as there are several 'best' options that are hard to ignore (Give Neptune an "Ignore enemy traits" partner ASAP!).It's hard to experiment with AAs early on, as you won't have enough to use many of them until very late in the game, though don't be fooled: Rush break and power are all good at something! However, i did find many times Rush was the best option.
The last glaring flaw is that the story at times doesn't seem to know what it wants to be. it is a 'very' lighthearted story, yet it forces several serious moments into it as well. The ending was decent, however the last boss fight is 'very' anti-climactic, not even standing out amongst 'risky' enemies you've likely faced before this point. There are many unbeatable encounters, followed almost immediately by painfully easy encounters...sometimes against the same enemy!
However, despite these flaws, if they do not harm your view of the game you may find yourself to enjoy it greatly. Personally it's been one of my favorite experiences on Steam thus far. Pick a favorite CPU Canidate and give them your shares! :D

Minimal is a straightforward, minimalist-designed puzzle game with tons of levels (seriously the achievements show 250+). The game touts itself as having "no story, no clutter," and this is precisely what it is. For a few bucks it may keep you entertained for 15 minutes or more at a time, but it's definitely a pick-up and put-down game, not something you'll likely be glued to screen for hours at time with.
The sound is, you guessed it, minimal. There's a quiet ambiance music in the background and this music be either turned off or on through a musical note icon at the top of the screen. The graphics seem to be crisp, and you can alternate between windowed and fullscreen mode with Alt+Enter.
It's a puzzle game with set puzzles, so it's obviously  linear. As you figure out the gist of the game, the levels get progressively harder but you get better at figuring how to light up certain blocks and not others to match the pattern at the top of the screen.
I didn't experience any glitches or crashes during gameplay. It's not a graphically intense game, either, so it could probably run on that old dinosaur PC you have lying around.
All in all, a pleasant experience. The game is a pleasant, $4 game that you pick up when you're in the mood for a challenging yet relaxing puzzle.

I waited nearly a year before playing this game in the hopes that it would be fully fleshed out by now. Instead im playing what feels like a day 1 release with issues that should have been addressed long ago. As such while id like to recommend this game for everything else it does right, the things it doesnt do right are so frustrating and annoying that I cannot recommend this game.
Combat seems right for the most part but has some serious deficiencies that one would think would have been patched by now. Youll see your ranged units moving towards an enemy rather than attacking plenty of times as while the enemies movement animation is constantly playing (even when standing still), one moment your cursor is over them and the next its not. So the game now thinks because youve clicked 1 pixel beyond the artwork of the enemy that you now want to move to that location instead. Other supreme annoyances are ice on the ground, which every member will repeatedly slip and fall on, sometimes without end, and even outside of combat. What is the point in watching every character fall on their face and be imobile for 10 seconds, only to have them stand up and fall again?
Questing is ladden with ridiculous amounts of text. While I prefer questing that has depth to it (rather than simplistic go to X to kill Y and get Z), Divinity takes it way over the top. Every character, even non essential ones, has a mile of text to say. It makes trying to notice important bits from useless fluff expoentially harder. The amount of minor quests is also so overwhelming that youll quickly stop caring about the details and just use the "kill everything, clear everything, and I should end up completing most of it" approach.
Bartering with an NPC but you started the conversation with a character that doesnt have the bartering skill? You have to close the conversation and start over, because even if you select the right character in the bartering window, because they didnt start the conversation their skill doesnt count. Who thought this was a sensible design decision? Pointless waste of time. And since the game just loves wasting your time, how about the whole repair system. Everything you can repair for free, in the field, at any time. So why even have it degrade?
Overall the game looks great and sounds great, but the gameplay feels very crude in some aspects which should have been patched and addressed long ago. Maybe with an expansion or sequel they will get things right, but as is the game feels like a late beta.

Now that this is complete, I think I would suggest not buying this game.  If you're a Game of Thrones fan, I would suggest a "play video", or actually skipping it altogether.
The story is extremely immersive and intriguing. I have to give props to their good writers and excellent voice acting.  This is also concretely set in the Game of Thrones world, and feels natural there, not in any way forced.
The major downwside of this is the game is a game of choices.  The problem is almost always the choice makes no difference at all.  Some times you get a line of dialog, sometimes its completely ignored, and a few times the plot makes no sense based on your choice.  This slightly (ok majorly) takes away from the gamplay and turns it into a movie you're forced to take action in.  This honestly is what brings me to recommend watching a "lets play" video versus buying it.   Since its all the same anyway. I'm ok with certain plot points being fixed, it should be about the road to getting there and the road should feel personal, which it doesn't at all.
From a plot prespective this takes place during the second to thrid seasons of the tv program.  While its does feel well set in the game of thrones world, it honestly didn't feel like enhanced the world, the tv show, or anything really.  The last episode I was hoping was going to bring at least part of the story to some sort of conclusion while leaving room for more.  Instead, nothing felt concluded, and I just had more questions.  It felt very shallow to me.
So this is completely out now.  However I think its worth noting.  I personally would suggest not paying for any tale tale game till the game is complete for two reasons.  One you get all the episodes and don't have to wait (that way theres no production issues you end up waiting longer for, and it should be noted that from the relase date of episode 1 to the release date of episode 6 was more than 11 months.   Thats quite a hefty wait for 2 hours of content per episode)  The second reason is its often at a discount price.

THE PROLOGUE
- Awesome game! But lets start from beginning...
- For past few years, MMORPG market was in deep crisis. It desperately needed something new, fresh and well forged. The crisis started with the downfall of WoW, as its reign, some-what naturaly, ended with the death of the Lich King (that never droped me the sword btw dayum lol). Through the years to follow, many candidates put a claim on that empty spot of MMO thron. Sadly all of them very quickly proved to be Pay2Win frauds (Archage) or simply cheap WoW clones (Eso, Gw...). So the waiting prolonged and it felt like ethernity as nothing decent showed up on a horizont.
- And a funny fact, at the end, it literaly came from the horizont. South Korean company Pearl Abyss developed, I dare to say, a new-gen MMORPG called Black Desert Online.
THE STORY IN BITS AND BYTES
- The game has astonishing and with no doubt the best graphics of this genre atm. Nothing on the market can match the colors and details of BDO World.
- Combat system is built around combos. This is where I was most reserved cause combos in RPGs usually suffer from delays when switching between them but here they r executed surprisingly smoothly, making the combat extremely interactive. In same time it is reducing the keybinds and hotbars nessesity, as every combo has its unique key combination. So against all the expectations, I can say now Im a believer. Amen.
- Crafting, Gathering and Economy is very in-deep and all together it makes sense. The amount of mats is impressive but Devs avoided to make overhelming by making all the manufacturing proccess to be executed by the workers that r active even when player goes AFK. Also the big portion of mats gathering is done by the workers. Still its on players to make right decisions cause for example growing plants depends on the actual weather and temperature on the specific region of the Map. Mentioning the Map, in BDO its interactive, which is a new thing to see in RPG genre. It allows a player not just to navigate around but also to give orders to his workers, connect and upgrade Nodes, check weather conditions etc. There r also Day/Night and Season changes that give a complete picture of a living, real-time growing BDO World. Fishing by the coast allowes catching smaller fish, while sailing on the open sea gives opportunity to meet face to face with whales and some unique sea monsters. Diversity, diversity everywhere. This is actualy the first MMO that I dont have that odd feeling how everything actualy lacks life and is obviously AI guided.
PAY2WIN DEBATE
- The game does have In-Game shop that will always lure u with some investing of cash, but considering that initial full content price is 9e, my oppinion about micro-transaction is that they r fair deal. I found very few Pay-2-Win elements so far. There is no gear that is cash only restricted as every end-gear piece is obtainable with casual play style. U might ask: Ok, if that is true then where is the catch? The catch is that ppl want to win ASAP, they want end-gear and end-crystals ASAP. So they sink tons of money to cut the effective play time as much as possible and reach end-game in 1 month. Instead of doing that, better option is to take easier and lil longer way around. It will get u to the endgame in 3-4 months delay but with less cash investment, less stress, less emo break downs and less cryings on the forums or in review page just cause yr ench failed. Also it will provide u better game understanding.
- On that thought - this is an Eastern MMO. Its concept and story is delivered in different pace than western MMOs often r. This game should be taken with focus on exploring and finding whats suits u the best and brings most fun. Some do life skilling, some Node wars, some run World Bosses.
- What I found negative tho, is an Open World PvP that offers no protection to new players. Yes, its an MMO, and ganking is part of MMOs but some PvP restrictions should exist. Putting a 200GearScore newb player in a fighting pit (grind spots) against a 400GS veteran cant be called a fair PvP ambient. With a last patch, Devs added a PvP-only server, to motivate PvP oriented players to migrate from PvE servers.
THE CONCLUSION
- The conclusion is pretty short and it goes something like this - BDO is too good to be missed and IMO if the things go well, we r witnessing the birth of the best MMORPG ever.
- Oh yeah, thanks to Dev for his answer. I will mention it in my CV. LoL... Cheers!

Then they released The Following... I was really, really sceptic about this one.. Cars and wide open areas - doesn't sound like something I would enjoy at all as a laid-back player. I suspected they had changed tune to accommodate the more impatient players, but I bought it just to be supportive.
Boy was I wrong.
They pulled it off.
This DLC seems like a natural development of the gameplay, and I absolutely love it!
Level design, voice acting, sound, gameplay, graphic, scripting - it's so good you almost forget someone actually made this. It's just how it's supposed to be.
It's not as scary when you have a car to drive around in, but they balanced that out by making you enter caves and large constructions on foot.
I have not found anything major negative about The Following, but my pulse hasn't been low enough for me to think clearly since I installed this game.
If I could put one addition to the game it would be some generic repetable missions - like in skyrim.
If you play solo, as I almost always do, the grind gets a little easier with some sense of purpose.
But it's still fun without the missions - I just jumped two levels in Driver by trashing zombies at night time, and going back in for two levels more now.
Absolutely recommended!!!

This game taught me many things about real life:
Episode 1: I was locked out of my house last week, and I realized I had a paper clip and pocket knife in my car. I figured, "this will be a cinch" I started to pick my lock: click, click. Sh%#. Paper clip broke. Yep, lock is ruined.
*Hops wall, grabs key from under mat, and enters through back door*
Wife: "Why the hell did you come in from the back?" Me: "I locked myself out" Wife: "Why didn't you just knock?" Me: "I've been trying to learn parkour." *parkour into back room* Pursuit evaded.
Episode 2: I have to take the trash out, but it's getting dark outside. Wife: "the trash is still overflowing" Me: "True, but its almost dark. I don't think I can risk it." Wife: "Risk what?" Me: *looks at couch; chooses to wait until morning*
I wake up. Wife: "now that it's light out, how about that trash?" Me: "HELL YEAH. DOING IT!" *Grabs machete out of closet; ties up trash bag* Wife: "what the hell is with the sword?" Me: *parkour into front yard* Trash delivered. I feel stronger.
Episode 3: It's night time. Wierd noise on roof. Feeling unusually brave, I grab my new teddy bear (aka my machete) from under my pillow. Using my parkour skills I climb up my aluminum rain gutter. Rain gutter buckles under my weight and I crash to the ground. Startled, the cat on my roof scampers away. Mission accomplished.
Episode 4: My wife and I make dinner. I am cutting vegetables with a Hardened Beef Cleaver. I go to the bedroom and grab my Machete. I lay the Machete and Beef Cleaver on the counter. Me: "Which of these is better?" Wife: "For what? Why have you been acting so wierd lately?" Me: "Agreed." *Chops carrots with machete*

Grim Dawn is a very fun ARPG. The quests and story are well-written, the enemies are diverse, and the game allows for various different builds that you can edit to your liking. As such, the replayability potential that this game has is massive. The graphics are very nice, and it's set in a rather dark Victorian-era setting, which I believe this game nails perfectly. There's various different factions as well that you can improve your standing with, and there are different choices that you'll have to make that will affect how other parties see you. Lastly, the music compliments the theme extremely well; it's nothing extreme, but it's just right for a game like this. Also, I just LOVE the art style.
Now, I haven't played any other top-down RPGs before such as Diablo, but I was able to get into this very easily. So, if you haven't gotten into any top-down RPGs before, this would be a great place to start. You won't regret it, even at full price. I know I didn't.

We finally got an official Yugioh release on PC that isn't Power of the Chaos! While this game doesn't come with those spiffy looking anti-spell fragrances, it does come packed with the most cards in any Yugioh game ever. All the way up to Shining Victories, this covers the TCG/OCG from the beginning to roughly Early 2016. It is missing stuff from TDIL and INOV unfortunately but it's a welcome update to the vanilla release on console.
This game has tons of content for a $20 release, there's a fairly long story mode with duels from the show, there's battle pack draft and sealed play, online multiplayer and single player v AI quickplay.  The booster pack aspect is something that I enjoyed, but the contents of the packs are completely random (Why are Infernoids in a Bakura pack for instance?)
It does take some grinding to get anywhere decent with a non-story deck, and the story decks are mostly trash. I mean AWFUL. The deck for Yugi from his very first duel against Kaiba is literally pot of greed, swords of revealing light, heart of the underdog and vanilla monsters. Honestly I would've rather the draws be hard scripted or something because I was being forced to surrender and unable to do anything for multiple turns in one of the very first matches. That's not a good thing.
The interface is pretty bad. There's really frustrating prompts to chain card effects constantly and unlike YGOpro you can't just skip them.
Speaking of, while I purchased this game to support further GOOD releases from Konami, there's no real reason to play this over YGOpro. Losing Duelingnetwork was a blow to testing online, but this doesn't really replace that. I really doubt people are going to grind to build meta decks for a format that we left almost a full year ago in an interface that is not very intuitive in comparison to  devpro or something. For a casual fan or a moderately competitive player there's not real glaring flaws here, The single player alone is worth picking up if you enjoy any of the classic GBA games or the tag force series. There's also a small amount of animations for some of the ace monsters, which was a nice touch.
tl;dr - if you're looking to test your zodiacs, metalfoes or ABC, you literally can't here. But if you're looking for a relatively inexpensive yugioh video game, this is the best thing we've gotten since the PS2 days.

Pros:
+ Tense tactical person-to-alien combat (even person-to-person combat for the Enemy Within expansion).
+ Great graphics, nice and moody sound effects.
+ Completely interactive (i.e., destructible) environment.
+ Nice RPG elements.
+ Very good strategic shell.
Cons:
- Sometimes quirky camera movement during tactical combat.
- Annoying "camping" aliens that do not move until discovered, but then given a free move to either find cover or (in the case of the horrible Chryssalids) put themselves in good position for melee attacks for the next turn.
- Limited number of tactical maps, resulting in repetitions and the feeling of been-there-done-that as the game progresses.
- Limited air-to-air (interception) action (unlike the mini-game provided by Xenonauts).
Bottomline:
This is an excellent re-imagining of the old X-COM series combining state-of-the-art graphics with the original's strategic and tactical challenges. Those growing up with the originals should approach this game with an open mind, though, as some elements are radically changed and this game is not a mere remake of the originals.
The future of gaming is here.

I highly recommend this game! I've always had lots of fun playing (J) RPG games, but I hadn't felt much interst in actually persuing one to a finish lately. I guess eventually some felt pretty repetitive. But Neptunia keeps the action fresh with its excellent humor, obscur refrences to gamers and game history, a wide range of creative monsters, and lots of character customization.
The exploration is done somewhat via a world map interface that reminds me of the towns from Etrain Oddesy, it's easy and simple to use, and it includes the option of selecting and watching events at various towns that will give you bonus items for watching them. It's a clever way to allow the player to experience more of the story while not feeling like it's just a waste of time.
The equips in this game all alter the apearance of your characters, with the exception of basic bracelet accessory items. Not all of which alter stats though, as some outfits are just that, outfits that are just for fun without altering your stats. At times it seems silly that there are not stat boosts for most of the full costume changing body equips, but it's actually somewhat nice because then you can use what you want without feeling forced to change to a look you don't like just to gain better stats.
At times because of the way that it affects the appearance of the characters, many items are restricted to one character only, thus preventing you from using "yesterday's" old equips on a new character who joins the party. Though this is a minor thing as new items readily become available.
The only cons of this game are minor. I can only think of two.
1. The difficulty seems to spike incredibly right before a big end of chapter boss, and sometimes you must fight 2-3 bosses in a row without a save point in between. This can prove challenging, but it's also frustrating at times. But all it takes is some grinding to level up rather easily on the monsters in the bosses own area.
2. Money seems rather hard to come by at first making every last bit count. But this is remedied the more you play as it becomes more abundant as you go. It just makes for a rough start.
Overall I'd give this game a 9/10.
It's not perfect but it's a definite must have for any gamer that likes RPGs.

This game is terrible. Easily one of the worst JRPGs out of the 200+ I've played.
Let's start off with the pros:
+The attack animations are elaborate and fairly well done.
+The music isn't grating.
Now to the cons:
-Terrible PC port with limited resolutions and graphics options in general to choose from.
-No likable characters whatsoever. To call any of them characters is actually a stretch.
-The writing is just bad all around. None of the "jokes" work. Xbox girl for example is just there to make fun of the other girls flat chests. Just terrible.
-Incredibly basic battle system that tries to trick the player into thinking it has any depth. E.g. having to build up the EXE Drive is a complete time-waster at the start of any dungeon and of no actual strategic or tactical concern. Break moves are worthless as just using your strongest moves does almost as much GP damage but quite a bit more HP damage.
-Difficulty comes down purely to your level compared to the enemy's. Boss too hard? Nothing you can do but grind, there's literally no strategy to ANY of the fights.
-Muddy textures and boring, REPEATING stages.
In conclusion this is a low-budget mess that no one should buy. Play Trails in the Sky or one of the dozens of decent indie JRPGs on Steam instead. Or even Akiba's Trip if you want the combination of wacky Visual Novel with combat, albeit real-time.

There's been a steady trickle of CRPGs into my library since I discovered the wonders of fair, honest download services like GoG and Steam and a litany of beloved JRPGs from designers learnéd in the hows and whys of CRPG possibility to their own heritage prior to that (tri-Ace, Ikahara, Megaten, Lord Miyazaki, Lord Matsuno), but this year that rivulet turned into a deluge and riding along with this wave of gaming goodness is the CRPG talk of 2014:
Divinity: Original Sin.
Larian's infamous forced march into gamestyles they had no business dabbling with and away from their strengths are gone here; the AP-utilizing combat is sublime, a beautiful toolbox of♥♥♥♥♥♥to play with, and constantly throws you nasty new curveballs to force your mastery of said toolbox. Excellent quest design that has you thinkin' and searchin' instead of the Honey Do list grind that most RPGs got whittled down to. Fun loot system that ain't afraid to toss you powerful but narrowing playthings to build a character towards. A classy, table-top looking art direction that is stylish and distinct, a magnificent dreamlike and daring OST by one Kirill Pokrovsky, and alot of neat dialogue between the two Guardians and major NPCs that doesn't get enough love due to its cheeky nature. Co-op play in a narrative-heavy game that pulls it off! There is so much STUFF in this game to see and do and earn.
There are a few problems with this gem, befitting a talented developer just now getting to stretch their legs; outside of that conversation listed above, some of it is drab and mechanical, almost as if the character themselves weren't speaking, but the writer themselves dropping that information via speaking thru them (if that makes any sense). There are bugs that crash to desktop months in. You can also tell the KS cash didn't go far enough and got stretched thin (noticable but not necessarily bad since it means more of that sweet sweet fightin').

I would absolutely recommend this.  While similar in mechanics to the Walking Dead, Telltale have changed tone dramatically, and the result is awesome and tense.  The game does a good job making you care about the characters, and when you screw up you really feel bad, which is an achievement.  The cameos from cast members from the show are all well done, and it's cool to interact with Jon Snow and Tyrion Lannister, without these interactions feeling forced or corny.  While it pales slightly in comparison to the series that was run at the same time (Tales From the Borderlands) this is a great experience for the first five episodes and most of the sixth.  The only major gripe I have with the series is the ending, which I won't spoil except to say it's not satisfying and is just a sequel plug for season 2.
However, all things considered if you like Game of Thrones, it's a must play.  If you like the other Telltale adventure games, but haven't been following the show or books you might be a bit lost, but still might have a good time with this.  But in the words of Ramsay Snow, 'If you think that this has a happy ending, you haven't been paying attention.'

Grim Dawn, the hidden gem. With all the hype of AAA games nowadays, it is easy to miss the release of smaller games. I am grateful I got recommended Grim Dawn, as this is an excellent ARPG. The game design is super impressive, with the subtle changes to the game world, to make it feel like you are making a difference, the intelligent and organised UI to the beauty of the world itself. This game is fantastic for its price. I give it 9.5/10. Well done Crate Entertainment, you have a new Fan.
- 6 Classes, you get to pick two which makes your actual sub-class. (Soldier + Nightblade = Blademaster etc.) 15 Total. + The Devotion Tree (almost like a third class).
- Massive Customization for Skills
- Playstyle is unrestricted from class. Play how you want to play. (Firebreathing Dagger Warrior? Duel Wielding Pistol Demonologist? No problem)
- You can see physical changes to game world after completing certain quests. (I love this one)
- NPC Voice acting feels real. (main quest only)
- Can be played online with up to 4 people. PvP is an option for servers. (Also works on Hardcore, although Permadeath still applies)
- Can trade between characters and other people online.
- Singleplayer / Multiplayer can use the same character.
- Massive amount of items & crafting.
- Armor & Weapons have different skins and effects depending on the item.
- Easy Weapon Switching + Hotbar Switching.
- UI has neat tricks. (Auto Show Loot Filters etc.)
- Account Shared Warehouse (for loot transfer) + Personal Stash
- Teleport system for quick travel and trading. (Can make a Personal Rift (Portal) from anywhere.
- Multiple difficulty levels. (Normal, Veteran, Elite, Ultimate) + Option of going Hardcore (Permadeath) aswell.
- Grim Dawn is Mod Friendly.
- The game is abundant with RNG. Items & Skills.
- NPC Voicing only in main quests and could be completed.
- No character customisation. Limited to Female or Male.
- Game sometimes crashes, (not often, three times in 40+ hrs + has auto report crash function)
If you are a fan of Diablo or Path of Exile or would like to get into the ARPG genre, this game is for you. For its current price, it is definitely worth it. All in all. Phenomenal game.

Pros:
+ Tense tactical person-to-alien combat (even person-to-person combat for the Enemy Within expansion).
+ Great graphics, nice and moody sound effects.
+ Completely interactive (i.e., destructible) environment.
+ Nice RPG elements.
+ Very good strategic shell.
Cons:
- Sometimes quirky camera movement during tactical combat.
- Annoying "camping" aliens that do not move until discovered, but then given a free move to either find cover or (in the case of the horrible Chryssalids) put themselves in good position for melee attacks for the next turn.
- Limited number of tactical maps, resulting in repetitions and the feeling of been-there-done-that as the game progresses.
- Limited air-to-air (interception) action (unlike the mini-game provided by Xenonauts).
Bottomline:
This is an excellent re-imagining of the old X-COM series combining state-of-the-art graphics with the original's strategic and tactical challenges. Those growing up with the originals should approach this game with an open mind, though, as some elements are radically changed and this game is not a mere remake of the originals.

Overall:
This is a solid RTS.  If they keep releasing content, it'll be an instant classic.
Mechanics:
Walls have made a return and with them come units that receive defensive bonuses for mounting them. The cutscenes and music are great. The unit trees are great and the tech attachments include upgrades for units you might not expect. Resources are acquired via refineries, extractors (1:1) and pools. There's an optimal spot to place the extractors on the pools where you get +25% minerals per second, but if there's no other pools close by you may want to forego that bonus in favor of building two refineries and offsetting two extractors on a single pool.
Difficulty:
I've had to walk away from some missions on the campaign and reapproach with a different strategy with the difficulty just set to 'Normal'. To echo what another reviewer said, it seems the AI will scout you and if you don't have at least two factories cranking out units from the time you establish your first refinery, they're going to hit you with everything they've got.
Video:
What you see is what you get. It's a great looking game.
Audio:
I don't keep up with who composed which game, etc. I'm usually the guy who gets annoyed by the background music and turns it off so I can hear other things while I'm playing the game. Not so with Grey Goo. Really well done.

My first ever experience of an arcade machine was a game called Pong, I was five-ish and my Dad wanted to give it a try while waiting for a lane to come free at the Ten pin bowling ally. Dad was a Ten pin and a pinball wizard, but Arcade games were beyond him so he left the game in my incapable five year old hands. To say, I was no wizard and the game ended faster than an exploding balloon. A year later Breakout hits the Arcade and I was hooked on games for the first ever time, mostly because I could last half an hour without dying.
Ark Box Unlimited tries to be a cross between Breakout and Space Invaders. An implementation that should have been given more thought. No that PolarityFlow have fail, but more to the point that the game concept got lost and it is still just a Breakout on steroids.
Game play itself. Basically it is Breackout, with more bells and whistles. You start with a ship/bumper and fire a ball from it to knock out the bricks. As the ball bounces around you need to keep it in play, all the while collecting credits for upgrades and avoid bullets from alien ships. The faster you clear the screen of bricks the higher you score will be. But there is a fair bit of sacrificing in the game, do you want credits and sacrifice the ball or save the ball and watch the credits fly by. This is mostly controlled by A & D for left and right movement, the LMB for shooting the ball. The ball will get captured by your ship but this is random and no clear key or button is know. Also your ship will start shooting missiles after a certain time, but again this is random and you seem to have no control over this.
You can upgrade you ship with mods bought with credits collected any of the play modes (Upgrades seem to have littl or no effect on game play at this moment). You also have an Achievements wall (which looks to be separate to the one on Steam). There are four play mode to choose from, free play, arcade, community and customise. Community and Customise are both connected and should be classed as a single mode.
Free Play:- Free play you play six lots of six levels giving you a total of 36 levels to get highest score and then share that score on the Hall of fame, to keep score with others around the world or to beat their score. 36 missions in free mode.
Arcade:- Just as it says it is Arcade, so it is the obligatory 3 lives and if you loose them all. game over red rover.
Community:-  Is where you can play others creations and/or share you own.
Customise:- Here you get to create your own costume maps and either play them yourself or upload them for others to play.
In main menu Options you have the standard music and sound volume controls, plus a good assortment of video options. Also some limited customisation of ball and blocks.
The game graphics are crisp and clean 2D, music is ok but it is the same track for the whole game, so I recommend some Pet Shop Boys or Talking Heads mellowing in the background. In all Ark Box Unlimited is a nice stroll down memory lane and makes a nice time waster arcade. But if PolarityFlow should pimp up the Space invaders side of the game, then this could become a classic.

Child of Light is a fairytale roleplaying game in the vein of many fondly remembered children's stories.  Aurora, first born princess of the Austrian King, falls to illness and is transported to the fantastical land of Lemuria--a kingdom of monsters and anthropomorphic animals alike.  It is in both the adequately written prose and beautiful illustrations that one feels they are interacting in a proper storybook.  The gameplay also draws from a long-line of classic influences; side-scrolling areas are subtle in their similarities to Metroid-vania games, while the battle system is turn-based and real-time with a smattering of Grandia's system of delaying and interrupting actions with carefully timed attacks.
The combination of beautiful illustrations, a lullaby-like soundtrack, and a nostalgic battle system enticed me to return each day to learn a little more about Aurora's newfound whereabouts.  While dialogue between characters is again illustrated with beautiful character profiles, the conversations themselves can feel a little contrived at times--granted, I would snicker here and there.  Each part of Lemuria is broken up by chapters and again highlight the range of beauty that the game's artists are capable of showing us.  Animations are smooth and the use of lighting for backgrounds and objects really adds to the fantasy.
In the end, I found myself enjoying Child of Light for what it was trying to be; an interactive storybook that subtly entices you to turn each page carefully and deliberately in the hopes that you'll get lost in it.  At the same time, I was disappointed by that very thing--a mostly pretty game with a fun story that doesn't demand that you invest in their characters beyond some archetypical quirks.

Winning REQUIRES at least some grinding, but it's not too bad. Combat can get a little repeatative, but has enough progression that it's also not too bad. Keyboard controls are annoying; bearable, but I would definitely recommand a controller. I didn't like how the story progression would bounce the people in your merry band of adventurers around (except main 3), so you'll have a bunch of people rotating in and out as usable characters for most of the game (don't give them things, or remember to take items back before they disappear for ~2 chapters). Then towards the end you just get everybody (many of which are weak/underleved/worthless and a few random pretty unneeded characters), resulting in way more people than your 3 person party will ever use.
Overall though, I really enjoyed the game. Would definitely recommend if you're into anime style humor and jrpgs.

FTL is a rogue-like game with more than a dash of scifi for the taste. This is a unique game that has founded its own niche as a cross between strategy/rpg/scifi/roguelike. And it's awesome. Each battle is dangerous, every choice can bring you to your knees, and each battle can destroy your game. There are multiple ways to handle battles, from blowing the ship to shreds, blowing out the enemy oxygen and watching the crew asphyxiate, or my personal favorite, setting everything on fire, and watching the terror of the enemy crew as they realize that its too late. (Note: This game will make you a sadist).
The enemy pursuit is annoying after a few games, but fortunately there is actually a fairly active modding community online, that can turn this off as well as update the graphics (if that is actually a turnoff for you).
Overall, its a lightweight game where you can jump a few sectors in a few minutes here or there, and then come back a couple days later and play again. It doesn't demand too much of your time, (But it may break your will to live when you see your beloved starship blown to pieces before your eyes because you couldn't afford to make repairs).

The look of the game is pretty and unique, but you get accustomed to it quickly and it fails to keep suprising you. The rhyming of every voiceover and dialogue is intereresting in the beginning, but you quickly grow tired of it. Its still fun exploring the well-crafted world and interacting with the childish, but fun characters. The controls feel a bit rough compared to real plattformers (like Ori and the Blind Forest), but it's fun and relaxing once you can fly around.
I stopped playing early because I realy don't like the combat system. The combination of plattformer and turn-based-combat doesn't work for me, it always roughs up my flow when the fighting starts. True, you can avoid most fights, but fighting is the only way to level up, and there are fights you HAVE to take, so you need the XP to stay competitive.
I'm not that enthusiastic about classic RPG combat without positioning anyway. But there are games who manage to still make it fun. This game doesn't. Even with a few minor innovations, its brutally repetitive after a few fights. The skill trees are strange and don't give you the feeling of realy being able to develop a character in the direction of your chosing. And no ability you ever use in a fight makes you feel the least bit awesome.
The game sure has it's qualities, particularly in the art department. There are so many background layers, and sometimes super interesting things are happening there, with giant creatures moving around in the distance (I realy cheered for that when I noticed it). The animations are super smooth, i just kept turning for while just to whirl the characters hair around her face.
But at the end, the gameplay does not deliver. Its neither a good platformer (not the smoothest controls, no real skill challenges), nor a good RPG (boring skilltrees, generic combats). The look and the few innovations can't sell it.

The approach of using the combination of elements is a great one. But after a very few levels you saw them all and they will not change until you see the end screen. It gets boring over time to cast rain to create puddles to shock enemies moving/standing in them with electricity. Not much difference to cast oil fields and have them explode to burn enemies and create smoke clouds so the enemy rangers do not have a line of sight and very often simply skip their turn.
It is so much about creating areas the enemies will not step through - even if it would be relatively harmless for them - and have no line of sight.
The AI is simply bad. Bad pathing, bad combat behaviour. It just repeats from battle to battle.
Even on the hardest level the game was not really a challenge with a proper group setup. On this level the hardest fight for me was the Spider Boss in the Cave. I was probably one level too low to battle it. I had to kill it within the first two rounds or have at least one dead due to the horrible damage it does from the 3rd round on.
Crafting is more or less useless. Potions and Buff Spells last only very few turn so using them is often not advisable as killing an enemy is often the better option.
The most annoying thing is the endless number of containers that need to be looted. Feels like a million in the end. 98% do not contain anything at all. 1,9% contain useless stuff and 0,1% is the reason why you need to loot them. Very rarely there are objects you need to continue with the story in these containers. Looting so many containers takes a significant amount of your play time.
In the end I finsihed it asking myself why I do it. Well, I guess, just to say I finished it ;-)

The tactical, grid-based combat mechanic is done well. You have to take the time to think through your moves and watch the opponent's turns closely if you want to complete the game on a harder difficulty, but defeating the enemies without losing any of your characters is rewarding enough to do that. I, however, was personally looking for a more chill experience, so I played the game on easy and massively enjoyed it that way.
The story was surprisingly deep and immersive, and I found myself really mulling over every decision the characters face. Also, the artwork in this game is beautiful. Overall, I enjoyed it a lot, but I don't have a strong urge to go back and play it again on a harder difficulty.

Why do I like this "game"?
From what I gather most the decisions have little to no lasting impact on the story, which to some people is bad. There is very little game play. You walk around in a very rigid fashion, looking at very obviously highlighted bits and pieces, while occassionally being forced to mash this button, or press this button to avoid being bludgeoned (I'm never ready for it).
So why is it good? Because, it's a story (and a good one). Like all recent Telltale titles, the narrative is king...and as a Game of Thrones (and ASOIAF) enthusiast, the game captures brilliantly the messed up world created in the other mediums, and tells a story not before told. With cameos from the fantastic actors from the television show, it brings it together nicely. And while I realise most of my choices won't have far long lasting impact in the context of the story, I always end up feeling guilty regardless...which leads me to believe the story has me highly invested in the outcome, which can only mean, at least in my eyes, it's a story well told.
This game won't be everyone's cup of tea...in fact, I would hazard a guess people without any background in the show or books, and with no interest in learning should flat out ignore this, but anyone who enjoys the content, and is willing to sink a couple of hours per episode into this...interactive story, should seriously consider this title.

To start off; This game is worth much more than $10.
I'd argue that this MMO is one of the very few you can say there's almost too much to do. From lifeskilling, grinding, playing the marketplace, crafting, etc.. You'll always have some sort of goal to attain. If you want to play this as a single player RPG, there's more content than most actual single player RPG games.
This game does not hold your hand whatsoever. Black Desert is a completely different experience walking into it if you've come from ESO and WoW like I have. From gearing to making money, you won't find an MMO similar to this. You're thrown into a world, you do a tutorial, and from then, so many different paths open up to you. There isn't a certain path the game makes you follow, what you do is up to you.
Character Creation is a treat, from the body in general, to hair and eyes. You can edit the tiniest of details and really make your character yours. Every bit can be changed and molded to the way you like it.
Black Desert in terms of land, is massive. This is amplified by the fact there is no fast travel. You'll start off with a donkey, eventually capturing your own horse, and breeding horses to get better ones, allowing you to travel land faster. Not only can you adventure through the mainland, Black Desert has sailing, and realistically long sailing times at that. Some NPC ferrys will take almost an hour to get you to continents that have been added in previous updates.
If you're a fan of player housing like me, you've found the right MMO. Black Desert pulls of player housing and executes it so well. My only bone to pick with their system is that if you dont dish out real money, you cannot purchase wallpaper and flooring for your house. Apart from that, you can buy furniture from the market, NPCs, or craft it yourself (which is easier, I almost never see furniture on the market).
So, about the whole "Pay to Win?" debate: No, this game is not that. However, don't expect to only pay 10 dollars and nothing more. I would define Black Desert Online as Pay for Extreme Convenience. Some things you'll want to consider spending money on is pets to collect loot, Artisan's Memory for gear durability and Inventory expansions. Also, in order to look different, a costume from the Pearl shop is needed, or you could attempt to snipe one off the marketplace when it's sold, but your chances are low.  Although, some people have not spent any more than the game's price and get inventory expansions and costumes without spending real money, it's just not as simple or easy.

The currently definitive yugioh game, I've played from PSX era, PS2 era, gba ds and psp era games, this trumps them all (though tag force had some nicer visuals, it had nowhere near the card pool)
As long as the keep updating this game, there's no reason not to get it if you're a yu-gi-oh fan, and I honestly can't necessarily fault them for the dlc design considering that for the price of a pack and a half you get an entire structure set, plus these are mostly all cards post release of the game(back when it first launched to now).
Onto the story, though, so, to begin, the singleplayer campaign is incredibly extensive, you have a plethora of duels, then you can play as either person once you beat it once, using your own deck or the deck that person used at that point in the story(with some slight modifications, which I see as no issue since you really need those to make the decks playable under normal conditions), then in addition to that each person unlocks a challenge duel using a stronger themed deck usually, each time you beat a person you get their signature card + 2 cards from their deck, if you lose, you get 1 card from their deck at random, and win or lose you'll get currency which you can exchange for card packs or booster drafts, as far as I know, this game contains pretty much all the cards in the game up to around last spring, with new ones coming in as dlc and game updates, (zuzu boyle packs for example include aquaactress cards which were released late last year, where muh graydles doe?)
deck editing is pretty intuitive, lots of commands, and I guess it flew over my head but this game is really optimized for PC, can use mouse for lots of stuff, which you should be able to, but nice that it's so well implemented + keyboard typing for stuff which seems lost on console ports nowadays XD.
There's online, of course, it works pretty well, only got into a few matches though and most were with a friend, doesn't seem to be too many people playing online right now (hopefully this game gets more popular as people realize it's on steam).
All in all, this is by far and large the best yu-gi-oh! title I've played to date, and if they keep it updated and keep bringing the new stuff in, even if it's at a 6 month-year delay, this game will easily stay the definitive yugioh title for me!
To the Uninitiated, this game is basically a simultaneous turn based strategy (you have plenty of input and have to keep an eye on what's going on even on the opponent's turn, often times cards they play can make you take actions as well.) with 6836 cards currently in the base game for the $20 price, you have A LOT of deck building options and the variety is insane with the number of effects and styles of archetypes in this game, there's a little something for everyone, I've been a player of this game since early 2002-2004 and haven't been able to give it up for too long, it's a game that you'll just keep coming back to in order to see all the new changes, new styles of cards and what not, if you're ever going to play a card game where you make a super gimmicky deck this is the one to do it in for sure; but for the competitive folk there's a lot at the top level as well, and this game includes all the cards neccessary for a cyber dragon infinity deck (or majespecter, d/d/d, zefra if you buy the dlc's) to stay competitive in multiplayer ranked once you've learned the game

This game taught me many things about real life:
Episode 1: I was locked out of my house last week, and I realized I had a paper clip and pocket knife in my car. I figured, "this will be a cinch" I started to pick my lock: click, click. Sh%#. Paper clip broke. Yep, lock is ruined.
*Hops wall, grabs key from under mat, and enters through back door*
Wife: "Why the hell did you come in from the back?" Me: "I locked myself out" Wife: "Why didn't you just knock?" Me: "I've been trying to learn parkour." *parkour into back room* Pursuit evaded.
Episode 2: I have to take the trash out, but it's getting dark outside. Wife: "the trash is still overflowing" Me: "True, but its almost dark. I don't think I can risk it." Wife: "Risk what?" Me: *looks at couch; chooses to wait until morning*
I wake up. Wife: "now that it's light out, how about that trash?" Me: "HELL YEAH. DOING IT!" *Grabs machete out of closet; ties up trash bag* Wife: "what the hell is with the sword?" Me: *parkour into front yard* Trash delivered. I feel stronger.
Episode 3: It's night time. Wierd noise on roof. Feeling unusually brave, I grab my new teddy bear (aka my machete) from under my pillow. Using my parkour skills I climb up my aluminum rain gutter. Rain gutter buckles under my weight and I crash to the ground. Startled, the cat on my roof scampers away. Mission accomplished.
Episode 4: My wife and I make dinner. I am cutting vegetables with a Hardened Beef Cleaver. I go to the bedroom and grab my Machete. I lay the Machete and Beef Cleaver on the counter. Me: "Which of these is better?" Wife: "For what? Why have you been acting so wierd lately?" Me: "Agreed." *Chops carrots with machete*

The Following taught me even more about real life:
Episode 5: Been training for awhile now with Teddy. Let’s just say we eat a lot of squirrel for dinner. Came across a Javelina unexpectedly while trying to fix our stupid water pump (living in SW USA) and realized my skills weren’t exactly “legendary.” Teddy failed. I failed. I ran. *Jumps through kitchen window; hoofs it to the tool shed* *Sets Teddy on the workbench, grabs tazer, duct tapes tazer to Teddy, wraps metal wiring from tazer around blade, activate tazer, Teddy lights up like a F’in Christmas tree*

This is the story of Jordan Walsch.
Jordan Walsch signed on with XCOM to fight the alien menace. His best friends, Grace and Matt, tagged along. Each of them were promoted to Squaddie during their first missions, and they were given their combat roles. Jordan became an Assault trooper, Matt Support, and Grace Heavy.
Matt gave his life to save Jordan in a botched mission. Grace spent weeks recovering from her wounds.
Jordan was given the nickname "Spitfire" after his next mission. The loss of his friend turned him into a hardened killing machine. The commander recognized that, and Jordan began receiving promotions and being given experimental weapons and armor.
Jordan picked up a few more friends on the battlefield. He swore not to let any more good men die. But it wasn't long before the aliens took another one of his companions. Beatriz, a Brazilian medic, was gunned down right in front of Jordan. He and Grace made the aliens pay with their lives.
After that Jordan was the spearhead of every operation. The commander sent him on every mission. And Jordan never failed. His fellow soldiers relied on and supported his unorthodox brute force tactics.
Eventually Jordan and his friends were promoted to the highest combat rank of XCOM: Colonel. They became a cohesive unit on the battlefield. The researchers made sure they were equipped with the most advanced tech available. Jordan was even hand picked by the commander for a special project. He was the only one in XCOM that completed the training.
*Spoilers censored*
When the time came to take the fight to the aliens, Jordan did not hesitate. He led his team to the enemy (spoiler). But in the end, the aliens' psionic powers turned half of the squad against itself. The cohesion was lost, and Jordan called for covering fire from the team sniper, Boone. Boone was a crackshot, perhaps a little too good. His bullet went straight through the (spoiler)'s skull, severing the link between it and the squad. Jordan's heart sank, however, when Grace slumped to the floor. The experience shattered her mind, killing her instantly. He called to the squad's medic, Miracle, but for nothing. Miracle had also died from the experience. Two more of his friends, dead in an instant. What if he could have disabled the alien, or somehow severed its link without harming his friends? He didn't know, and it didn't matter. As the rest of the squad began to evacuate, he turned toward the (spoiler). He knew what he had to do. Boone and Domingo were the only ones to make it home that day. They had won, but at what cost?
Rest in peace, my friends.
Mayara (Heavy)
Matt (Support - Medic)
Beatriz (Support -Medic)
Benjamin (Rookie)
Grace (Heavy)
Miracle (Support - Medic)
Jordan (Assault, Psionic Operative)
All of these characters, along with a few others, were named after my friends. I cared about them, I panicked when they were in danger and I was heartbroken to see them killed. Leaving the bodies behind to evac the surviving soldiers when things went south was not easy. This was the one of the most emotional experiences I've ever had in a game (Note: I haven't played Spec Ops: The Line.) and I loved it. The fact that it didn't have to come from scripted events and cutscenes made it even better.
I've only played through the game once at this point, but I certainly plan to run through it a few more times. This game is worth its current full price, but if you can catch it while it's on sale there is no reason to pass this up.

In this game you play as Semyon, an antisocial Russian man ostensibly in his late twenties or thirties who spends most of his time in his small apartment in front of his computer doing little of importance. However, things change for him when he travels to a school reunion one winter day and falls asleep on the bus ride there. When he wakes up, it is suddenly summer and he arrives at a youth pioneer camp in the 1980s Soviet Union. Obviously confused by this sudden change in his circumstances, he enters the camp as just another pioneer and is treated as such by the others. He becomes determined to seek out answers for why he has arrived in such an unusual location, but he also realizes that things might not be so bad there and might be able to make friends or find love.
For me, this was only the second visual novel I have played through in its entirety, the first being the legendary
(2012), so my review may be limited by a lack of knowledge of comparable games of the genre. To start off with, this game is not really a "game" per se, but a visual novel which, as the name implies, involves mostly reading with some visuals and little input from the player. In
, the player has to pick options along the way that dictates the main character's relationship with the other characters and will lead to different paths. In total, there are thirteen endings to achieve in this game.
As it is the main point of a visual novel, I thought the story was pretty good. Without going into spoilers, I was pleasantly surprised to see what kind of twists and turns the story takes as you go through the various routes and endings. There were many plot points that I did not see coming. It would have been easy to just come up with a basic romance plot for each girl, but the developers of this game went further. Not only are the relationships between characters explored, but the game adds in some philosophical musing and a sort-of science fiction element as Semyon tries to figure out the nature of his situation. This certainly made the game more interesting than I would have predicted beforehand. The nature of the game also forces the player to really play through every possible ending in order to fully comprehend the story. Although it is a good story overall, I still had the feeling after achieving 100% completion that not all answers were given, leaving me somewhat confused.
The characters in the game run the gamut from interesting to okay at best. Although it seems there was an attempt made to fully flesh out the characters, I still felt some of them came off as somewhat clichéd. You have Olga Dmitrievna, a typical domineering authority figure, Slavya, the upright model pioneer, Ulyana, the spunky younger pioneer, and so on. This is not to say that the characters are bad, and some of them do indeed get more depth later in the story, but some just felt like something I have seen before.
I thought that the artwork in the game was generally excellent. This is especially true of the background art which is all fantastic. I really appreciated the amount of work and detail that went into them in order to bring the environments to life. The character sprites were fine, nothing really exceptional in my opinion but they serve their purpose. The CGs were really hit and miss, though. That is where the game really shows its collaborative development as the art between them was very inconsistent and some of them could really have used some improvement and more attention to detail.
The music overall was very good and it did a great job of integrating itself into the story and help set the mood.
When it comes to the gameplay, well, it is a visual novel so there is not much to it. There is the ability to save and there is an option to skip text that you have already read (which you will definitely need unless you want to spend countless hours rereading text in order to get all the endings).
This game also includes a side story focusing on a relationship between Semyon and Zhenya.
As a final note, this Steam release by default has the adult content disabled. There is a patch floating around that can easily re-enable it, which is necessary if you want to unlock all the possible images in the collection.
To conclude, while not a perfect game by any means, this was a generally positive experience for me. If you do not like visual novels, this game is not likely to convert you. However, if you are open to playing the genre, this game has an interesting story and some excellent art. Of course, one of the big plusses is that the game is available for free so you do not have much to lose by giving it a try.

Having previously played Agarest 1 & Zero from the same developers, and having found those to be utter dross, I had low expectations when I started playing this game, expecting it to basically be the same, with a coating of gaming industry meta-commentary.
..What a nice improvement this one is compared to those two games.
Well, the fanservice is still there, and they tend to lay the meta-commentary (and related jokes) a bit too thick, but it's pretty tolerable, and the story even enjoyable as it generally doesn't take itself too seriously. The gameplay is also miles ahead of agarest, though still "ok" by most standards. It'll bore you if you're looking for intricate or interesting gameplay, but otherwise it does it's job pretty well.
Graphics wise, there's pretty much no options, aside from a resolution option of up to 1080p, though it does support at least 60fps. Baffling is the choice of API for this game, with it using OpenGL instead of the usual DirectX9/10/11 APIs, which is somewhat bad news for us AMD GPU users, as the drivers for it are known to be rubbish, with my FPS tending to hover around 50-60.
So,with all said.. Pretty good romp if you get it on a sale.

Background: It is in the realm of games like Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics.
Replayability: Some story changes can allow you to bypass or experience new things but overall the game shines in its Storyline.  Low Replayability.
Combat Mechanics:  Standard Grid based, range oriented, simplified stat mechanical battles. Each character has a specific set of abilities and death and failure are very easy to attain even on Easy Mode. Not much Class overlap as the cast of characters is Small but this makes them memorable as you progress through the 10-15 hour story.
Social Mechanics: Social interaction plays a big part in who you recruit, battles you fight, who dies...sorry for the minor spoiler, but look you're humans running from an unstoppable horde of shadow soldiers and its dead Winter.  People are gonna die from swords and starvation.
Notable Notes: Oh my gosh the Artwork in this game is RIDICULOUS. Like I got distracted by the look at feel of the paintings. Even the Combat Grid and atmosphere is just a thrill ride of pure unadulterated Artistic Expression.  It reminds me of the same feeling I had when I first picked up Okami back in the day.
Final Thoughts: Those of us old guys from the 90s who have fond memories on the GameBoy Advance slugging through the massive influx of Grid based JRPGs will find a ray of light in the Banner Saga. <3 Play well my friends.

I’ve now played it for 14 hours, tried getting into it and learning the mechanics and I still can’t think of anything nice to say about it. There is literally nothing about it that I like. No idea why my friends find it fun and keep playing it.
If you don’t mind reading a longer rant, let me elaborate:
I think it’s boring, grindy and repetitive. There isn’t much in the way of depth and variety. It doesn’t emphasize teamwork the way many other co-op games do. It seems like the best (or at least sufficiently good) tactic is to find one good position and camp there for 6­–9 waves shooting at enemies as they approach. You only need to move around the map during the boss fight or when a large part of your team dies. There’s little need for communication between the players once you’ve found the right spot. Mostly people just call out tougher enemies like Fleshpounds and Scrakes.
I don’t like the enemies or their AI: all they seem to do is walk towards the player by the shortest route and attack. Zombies aren’t supposed to be particularly smart, but in, say, Left 4 Dead their behavior is more believable and they’re more fun to fight. They also spawn really close to you and/or teleport around, so it feels like they pop into existence rather than come from somewhere.
I also didn’t enjoy the gunplay, although it’s hard to put a finger on why. It’s not that bad, maybe it comes down to sound design, fast animations, the fact that the enemies are pretty spongy and the way the screen is constantly covered with bright high contrast special effects that make it hard to tell what your weapon does to the zeds.

TL;DR: Buy this game, but prepare yourself as it is not easy when you first start out.

Divinity: Original Sin was one of the best surprises I've had in gaming in a long while.
I've played a couple of Larian Studios' previous games: Divine Divinity and Beyond Divinity.  I thought both games were okay, but they weren't so great that they made me a fan of Larian Studios.  So when I bought Divinity: Original Sin last month, thanks to a sale, I didn't have particularly high expectations.  I figured the game would be fun enough to tide me over until PIllars of Eternity came out in late March, 2015.
Boy was I wrong.  And I'm glad I was wrong.  D:OS turned out to be one of the very best computer roleplaying games I've ever played.  I think so highly of it for several reasons:
I did not know how long the first playthrough would take.  I figured I'd get at least 50 hours of gameplay out of it.  I ended up taking 216 hours to complete my first playthrough of the game.  This game was fun and fascinating throughout all of those 216 hours.
Before Divinity: Original Sin, I had NEVER spent over 120 hours on a single playthrough of a CRPG.  I'm guessing I completed Planescape: Torment - one of my all-time favorite video games - for the first time in under 100 hours.  Similarly, my first playthroughs of open-world RPGs like Elder Scrolls: Morrowind and Fallout 3 took me about 100 hours or so.  Out of nowhere I wind up buying this RPG from a relatively unknown studio, and I end up being engaged by it longer than most other games I've ever played.
I think a majority of gamers who play this game will like the amount of content it has to offer.  It has A LOT.  On top of that, it provides the user enough motivation to play it more than once.

Managing the itemization of a roleplaying game can be ridiculously challenging.  Take for example Fallout: New Vegas.  I enjoyed F:NV quite a bit.  I've clocked in maybe 300 hours of playtime in New Vegas across multiple (attempted) playthroughs.  One of my few complaints about that game was its itemization.  Specifically, it did not take long for me to acquire what I considered to be optimal gear in any of my playthroughs.  I preferred to play the game as a gunslinger who's friendly with the NCR, so for me the best firearms as well as the best armor were found in the Honest Hearts DLC. Once I completed Honest Hearts, I had the guns and the gear I knew I'd be using for the rest of the game.  Everything else I found was sold so I could accumulate a silly amount of caps that I would not spend on anything.
Divinity: Original Sin does not have this problem.  In fact, it has some of the best itemization I've ever seen in an RPG or any other video game.
The power of all equippable items in the game are influenced by item rarity (Common, Magical, Rare, Legendary, Unique).  At a certain point in the game, you'll want all of your items to be Legendary or Unique.  Item power is also determined by the level of the item.  So a level 15 Legendary item is going to be more powerful than a level 10 Legendary.
Because of the way Larian designed their loot, there is the possibility of finding upgrades all the way until the end of the game.  This made every single combat victory, every single hidden treasure chest, and even every single search-able crate a fun experience, because you never know when or where you'll find the weapon, armor, or magical goodie you'll use to beat the game.
I really can't rave enough about the desing of Divinity: Original Sin's loot.  Whenever I engage in a discussion about how itemization can be done right, I will use D:OS as one of my top examples.
**Too many good things to say, really**
This review has already become much longer than I intended.  The bottom line is that Divinity: Original Sin is an excellent game.  If you like RPGs influenced by classics like Planescape: Torment and Baldur's Gate, if you like fantasy games, or if you enjoy games that mix humor with quality storytelling, then you'll probably enjoy the hell out of this game.

The Banner Saga is an inventive stratgy RPG wrapped in a particularly dark fiction.
The Banner Saga sucked me in with its art direction and strategy elements that I found really interesting even if they didn't always work out for me 100% of the time.  Battles with the enemy in a more traditional strategy format are separated by sometimes lengthy stretches where you make difficult leadership decisions for your group as they grow weary or contested with each other.  These are all text-driven, as is most of the narrative as you travel from one village to the next pushing the story along.  I don't know that I always felt confident that the way I was leveling characters or assigning equipment was going to serve me best in battle, or that because of this confusion I was getting the most out of the strategy battle sections.
I think this is sometimes the point of The Banner Saga, though.  Nothing is for sure.  Nothing is easy.  What you and your band are going through is disastrous and the enemy is always looming, never a clear answer as to where you are going next or what you will encounter.  The Banner Saga is dark and utilizes left of center mechanics, but I really apprecaite what Stoic was going for here and overall really enjoyed this title.
Recommended.

Something I love about Telltale games is the fact that they continue a story I'm already interested in. I'll say now, I did not read the GoT books. I do enjoy the TV show a lot though. I think the story and character's flaws are brilliant, and as much as I hate it, I love knowing that I don't know what will happen. My favorite storyline so far is Mira's. I love the political aspect, and I've had trouble making some of the choices that were presented to me. That's how it should be.
Overall, we know that these type of games by Telltale tend to all lead down the same road, but I think the story-telling is what makes these games worth playing. Would it be better if your choices actually shaped the outcome? Of course. But I have zero complaints about an interactive story that will give me new insight into a world I've already grown fond of.

It's not a big deal ... Now... on to the game side.
The game is one if not the most beautiful games I have ever played! The lighting and shadows and animations are just great. When suset comes its fun to just watch how realistic it appears, The water is what I would expect to see, the rocks, mountains and valleys are beautiful!
One things that is starting to be apparent.... this is kind of a life sim as much as a game. Buying horses and wagons, and dealing and setting up buyers and such.
I play a Wizard caster and the spell choices are vast and its easy to  specialize in a certain area.

If you try to sell womething that is populr at the marker place the game will stop and tell you that you may be better off selling it there to make more money! This way you dont sell that staff of XXXX for 50 silver and find out later it was worth $5Million silver at the market place.
Which brings me to another important feature that I really like and it keeps the economy in check. If you go to sell an item it gives you what the min and max that item is worth out there in the world and you can NOT gouge for more than the economy will take... if you try to sell it for more than max market value it just puts it  back down to the max price at that time. Now, in all fairness I want to go over what some would consider a downside in the game.
