It is easy to rip on the Star Wars prequels. You can picket and cry foul that Lucas betrayed your childhood and that he turned a once revolutionary film series into a sameless Disney style toy template (Oh the irony). However, you should consider all the good it has brought as well. Cool music from John Williams, double lightsabers, awesome new spacecraft and Video Games.
Amongst the heaps of shovelware Lucasarts published during the prequel frenzy there were a bunch of amazing gems. Like Episode One Racer, Knights of the Old Republic, Battle for Naboo, Galactic Battlegrounds and eventually: Battlefront. Based off the Battlefield: 1942 concept, Battlefront allowed players to experience the battles of both the prequels and originals from the perspective of the ordinary stormtrooper or battledroid. It was amazing, but was not enough.
Enter Battlefront 2, the bigger, better and more amazing version of an already amazing game. Fear the day when stormtroopers suddenly learn how to shoot, because that is when you're really playing this game.
In general, the game is split in two different modes: Single and Mulitplayer. In singleplayer you play the tour of duty of the 501st Legion of the clone army, who after defeating the seperatist droid army become the elite troopers under the command of Darth Vader. The whole campaign is a short sequence with random objectives, but the whole is narrated by Temuera Morrison, the actor for Jango Fett and every Clone trooper ever. It adds some legitimacy to the whole romp. The other major single player mode is Galactic Conquest. It is a large scale turn based tactics game where you try to manouver your fleet with troops around the galaxy and subjugate (or liberate, if you're into that sort of thing; you tree sniffing hippie). You can employ bonusses, granted to you by owning certain planets.
On the other hand of the spectum is multiplayer; and this is the reason why we're here. Allowing 64 peeps to take to the field at the same time...that's real warfare. This game was at the frontline of modern FPS development. You'll see many mainstays of modern shooters make their debut here, such as endurance rewards, killstreak rewards and other unlockable perks. Most destructive of the lot are the Jedi units. The ultimate streak reward gives you access one of the saga's heroes and elevates your lowly soldier rank to harbinger of death with a lightsaber. The sheer terror, characters like Darth Maul and Mace Windu inspire is amazing as they cut through swathes of troops.
The real selling point though are the maps. The maps are open and wide to accomodate the massive amount of players. However, each map has a lot of secret passages and corridors that allow for exploration and experimentation. On top of that, the level of detail is amazing. Intricate care was taken to make all the maps look like they came right off the movie screen. You can run around the death star, from the hangar with the falcon, into the prison block, jump into the grabage shute, fight through the barracs, blow up the main laser, pace past the tractor beam generator, kick over the conference table where Vader expressed his opinion about a lack of faith and finally back to the hangar, all in one level.
Along side are the space battle stages. These battles are big, point based levels where you take to the stars in fighters, bombers and boarding craft. You either earn points by shooting down other fighters in dogfights or bomb their capital ships to bits, or you board them and start sabotaging their internal systems. It's a sweet change of pace, although it can be hassle to fly without a gamepad.
It's therefore a shame the game's description on the Steam store reads that all online functionality in dead as of this year's May. Which is pure bantha poodoo. You still get around with some trickery. Even better, at this pricepoint, you might just better off telling all your friends to just buy it and bring their laptop over (it's old enough to run on any potato at this point), and just host a massive LAN party to restore balance to Force once and for all.

I'm going to open this review with an important preface: I made it 51 hours into this title before I'm calling it quits. But, wait, isn't my review a recommendation?!
Right off the bat: this game is not for everyone. In fact, it's not for me either. This is a long game with turn-based battles and lots of dialogue and books/letters/notes to read. If that doesn't sound fun, this game probably won't change your mind. Trust your instincts. I don't usually enjoy that type of game but gave it a go because of the astounding reviews.
With that acknowledged, I respect that a very talented and very passionate team worked very hard on this game - and it shows. The characters have a good deal of story between them, the plot is intriguing, the world is well-realized, the graphics are quite attractive, and the performance is pretty consistent throughout.
I won't spoil anything of the plot. I know those that are drawn to this sort of game would be frustrated to have anything ruined for them - and rightfully so. This is a game that's all about the journey.
Performance-wise, there's only one thing I feel important to point out. This game was designed to be very scalable, and I believe that is likely the case. For better or worse, my only test platfrom is an i5 4690k with a GTX970. One thing that was ignored in coding the engine, however, is multicore performance. Without fiddling with some settings, the game almost entirely uses the first available core. This leads to a little frustration as you'll go from 120fps out in the woods or a cave to sub-60 in the middle of a city and no graphical tweaking will make much of a difference.
But such is life. If it really bugs you, there's an option to limit the framerate as you see fit. A game like this is very playable even at 30fps.
In summary, if time is precious and you really need to feel you made a lot of progress with the time you spare on video games, this title may frustrate you. I mentioned I'm about 51 hours into the title. By the walkthroughs I've looked at, that seems to put me at about 60% complete. In fact, I've more than once spent an entire hour organizing my inventory and distributing character stats and gear. However, if you were raised on Baldur's Gate or even Dungeons and Dragons and want a beautiful return to old-school RPG goodness, I believe you'll be elated with this title.
Hats off to a very talented team. Though I left the game without completing it, you've certainly earned my admiration!

Teams are composed of 6 people. The game is lost when all team members die, however if one or more survive a wave, then any dead teammates will respawn, but will need to find their weapon at their location of death. Any person can be one of 10 perks (Or classes, whatever you wanna call it), including, but not limited to,
. Each perk can level up individually as you play it, up to level 25. Every 5 levels, you get two choose one of two new skills (You can swap pretty much any time, though) as a bonus to a specific perk, such as extra reload time or damage.
There is also a wide variety of weapons for each and every class, each with their own cheap or expensive price tag. There's lots of fun in exploring the different weapons with different perks!
Another really fun mechanic is "Zed time", which occurs during many kills at once (Lotta headshots, first kills, explosion kills, etc). It's slow motion! It lasts a couple of seconds, but can be incredibly useful,
Each game lasts
rounds (16, 20, 30 minute games respectively), depending on what you search for.

Levelling up perks does not take too long for the first 20 levels, though the final 5 levels take much longer. All in all it's not gonna take forever to level up though.

being the easiest and
being the hardest.
The increase in difficulty comes from stuff like certain enemies having resistances to certain weapons (Bullets, explosions, fire, etc.), working together as a team and staying close to eachother, managing ammo and investing money, taking more damage in general, and keeping eachother healed.
The difficulty decreases as you level up the perk of your choice, as you get stat bonuses and skills along the way.
There are many interesting enemy types that are strong against some perks and weak to others.
Most of the time there are common
which simply grab you, but eventually you'll see more enemies, such as the
, who scream at any nearby player, or the
which is invisible until it attacks or is attack (Or is revealed by a
perk!)

, or the hulking
These will sometimes require teamwork to kill.
Yes, each boss is unique and has their own strengths and weaknesses. All of them require good teamwork in order to kill, but can be solo'd with enough skill!
Yes, healing is rewarding as you get medic experience and money from it, however it does take some time getting used to. You can either heal yourself or a teammate with your healing syringe, which recharges over time, or you could pick up an HMTech weapon, such as a shotgun or assault rifle. Block N Load Review
UPDATED REVIEW 12/27
TL;DR – Repetitive game, in using different classes and blocks to defend an objective. Also has microtransactions for loot crates.
RELEASE DATE: May 1, 2015
DEVELOPER: Jagex, Artplant
PUBLISHER: Jagex
Block N Load is a team based FPS with a unique twist in that you can build. There a several classes you can pick from which are:
Brawn being the tanks who soak up damage.
Skill being the damage dealers who deal with the enemy.
Brains being the support class who build blocks that help the team such as health and ammo blocks.
Gameplay wise, you use blocks to defend an objective. The maps vary in design and can either have one, two, or three objectives. Maps can be voted on before a match starts. Many of the maps have unique designs such as one where you could be fighting on a sandy beach to close-quarter combat in a bunker.
There are a variety of blocks to use such as health and ammo blocks that obviously provide health and ammo regen for heroes that need it, to mine blocks which act as traps and damage the enemy, to sandbag blocks which can be used to route the enemy to certain chokepoints or serve as a way to delay the enemy from damaging the objective.
The classes in the game also have different heroes as they are called.  Cogwheel is a brawn hero and uses a minigun and a cannon as weapons. Along with using his special block, mortars to bombard the enemy. He can also build radars to help his team detect the enemy along with respawn pads to help his team respawn closer to the enemy base. Sarge is another brawn and has the same blocks as Cogwheel but uses a machine gun and a bazooka to deal with the enemy. He also has a special block, C4 that can be used to blow up the enemies’ fortifications.
O.P Juan Shinobi is a skill hero and uses a katana and throwing stars as weapons. Along with his special block, ninja shrine to teleport himself out of danger. Some of the blocks he has are caltrops that damage the enemy and fake blocks which usually have low health but disguise themselves as a surrounding block, useful for making traps. Nigel is another skill hero and has the same blocks as O.P Juan Shinobi but uses a rifle and a revolver as weapons. His special block, is a tiki statue, which when placed can disorientate the enemy and expose them on the minimap.
Doc Eliza, is a brain hero and uses a gas launcher and gas grenades as weapons. Her special block is a gas trap, that can damage enemies upon approaching it. Some of the blocks she uses are health and ammo blocks, that can help a hero regenerate health and ammo for their weapons. Tony is another brain hero, and has the same blocks as Doc Eliza but uses a shotgun as a weapon and has a glue gun to repair damaged blocks. His special block is a turret that can
damage enemies.
All heroes usually have the same common blocks such brick, crate, and sandbag blocks but they do also have blocks unique to their role. Such as brawn heroes being the only ones to have radar and respawn pads, while brain heroes being the only ones to have health and ammo blocks.
Heroes also have different playstyles in terms of their role as well. Cogwheel and Sarge although both being brawn heroes can be used differently, for example Cogwheel could stay back and let the mortars do their job and then move into the damage the enemy’s objective block while Sarge could get right in their faces and use his C4 to destroy their wall.
Graphically the game is voxel based so it has that cartoonish look as some other games have. The world itself is semi-destructible except for steel blocks which are used for the spawn points. Blocks can also collapse and thus one could use rockets or explosives on the bottom of an enemy’s wall and it’ll collapse.
The in-game currency of the game are gold bars and the microtransaction currency are silver bars which can be bought with real world money. Microtransactions involve cosmetics and unfortunately, their form of a loot box called bounty box. Bounty boxes come in silver, gold, and diamond and these can contain block skins, hero skins, *heroes, gold bars, and dust that is used to upgrade blocks. Silver bounty box can only be bought with in-game currency at 2500 gold bars or 10x for 25,000 gold bars. Gold and diamond bounty boxes can only be bought via microtransaction currency. You can also obtain silver bounty boxes in-game by playing and claim a free one every 4 hours.
Now as to whether I would recommend the game? Originally the game came out for around $15 when first released and shortly there after within a month or two, Jagex decided to make it free-to-play. As of this review the game has a very small player base and you will usually end up facing the same players over and over. The gameplay itself is also repetitive seeing as the niche of the game is using blocks to defend an objective.
Now would I recommend this game?
YES, if you don’t mind that the game has a smaller player base and repetitive gameplay.
On a side note, when the game was first released it had a thriving community unfortunately due to Jagex’s incompetence, such as the game not being advertised to the wider gaming community it has thus ended up like other games that Jagex has created essentially becoming a vegetable. The game was UPDATED a few weeks ago and thus we’ll see if it can make a comeback.

Forewarning: this review assumes you will be buying the Enemy Within DLC along with the base Enemy Unknown game. While it isn't required, you'll be missing out on some of the content described in this recommendation if you only grab the base game.
XCOM, a game in which you lead a paramilitary extraterrestrial combat unit of the same name, is a hybrid of two different game types; on one hand, you have the tactical turn based combat pitting your squad of soldiers versus the invading alien force in various missions to counter their incursion onto Earth, with your troops often outnumbered and outgunned. On the other hand, you have the strategic research and development aspect that takes place at XCOM HQ in between missions, where you'll analyze and adapt alien technology for use by your soldiers, who will also gradually increase in combat effectiveness the more they're exposed to combat.
While your soldiers will begin with simple conventional body armor and ballistic firearms, as the war and your arsenal of adapted alien technology stretches on into the later months of the year, you'll be presented with various options to further improve their equipment and skills, with access to tools such as flight enabled power armor and camouflage suits that blend your soldiers in with the environment, genetic enhancements that allow soldiers to leap onto buildings from ground level and emit bioelectric waves that detect invisible enemies, or even augment them into mech troopers equipped with miniguns and flamethrowers.
All in all, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a very well crafted game that will test your skills and tactics in a variety of environments and situations, and can easily provide hundreds of hours of gameplay.

OK here is now my first review ever. I want to apologize if my english is not that great but I did not wanted to make review only in my language.
So here we go.
- The graphics and the attention to details are very good
- A weather system. Streets getting wet and reflecting in cities. Gras swinging in the wind. Beautiful sunsets...
- The entire world feels alive and not empty like some people say. A lot of different NPC's are running around in city’s and talking
to each other. Then there are horse wagons who are trading goods between cities. You can literally hear NPCs talking to each other in every corner of the cities
- The sound and especially the voice acting is phenomenal. Which surprised me really because you need to keep in mind that this is an MMORPG after all.
- I really like the design of the world and Monsters. It is not so colorful and exaggerated like other asia grinders (e.g. TERA).
- The character creation is average. I have seen ones that are more complex but this still stands out. And here is why: You are able to save your character in a file so you do not need to recreate them if you do not like any aspect of them after the creation. You can also choose from other player’s uploaded creations if you want.
- It has a very complex trading and crafting system. You can create trade routes on the world map that gives you bonus income if you do it correctly. You can even trade items by yourself between cities.
- The ability to auto run to checkpoints you can set by yourself anywhere on the world map.
- AFK Fishing
- You can actually dive underwater
- You can sailing your own boat
Doesn't sound that bad after all? Then brace yourself for the cons.
- The combat system is difficult with many hotkey-combos. This has been done far better in other action-mmmo’s.
- Unable to trade other players. You have to grind all your gear by yourself. This also reduces the social contact between players a lot.
- Selling items at the marketplace (ingame-ebay) feels incredible unfair. If you sell an item you only get 65% of that estimated value because of taxes.
This further encourage people to not trade anything if they do not really have to. But why...? Why not reducing the overall money income instead of creating such a massive money sink.
- The way the monsters are behaving. You can only hold 8 monsters agro at the same time. If you have 8 mobs agro and following you, then any other monster you attack is invulnerable and does not get aggressive at all. My lack of recommendation for this game really boils down to the core gameplay not being very fun.
During battles, your options aren't really that varied between different fights. You pretty much just build up your exe drive, heal, and unleash special attacks. And each battle seems to take way too long, in my opinion - you just keep doing that over and over and it's not fun at all. And if you mess up because you weren't strong enough, didn't pick the right abilities, didn't pick the right equipment, or something else involving customizing your loadout in menus, you die and have to start all the way back at the world map or one of the very sparsely placed save points. Sometimes, you'll even have to fight several difficult battles without a save, which is just an unforgivable waste of precious gaming time.
It seems a lot of the battle is decided in the abilitiy and equipment customization. So most of the critical decisions involves using menus and comparing numbers, which just isn't vey fun to me.
It's just not very fun if you really value your time. It really sucks when you die and have to start back at a save point. Compare this to a game like xenoblade chronicles where you don't lose any progress at all when you die. It feels like this game just re-uses old RPG conventions without seriously considering how fun they are. And games have come a long way since those conventions existed, so it's really easy to point to so many other games and say "you'll have lots more fun per minute playing that other game instead of hyperdimensional neptunia".
That would be forgivable if the other content was interesting like the visuals, writing, etc...Actually, the writing is kind of entertaining but it can't carry the game by itself. Also, they re-use lots of assets, lots of music gets played over and over again and is too short to get away with that, and it's just overall not worth suffering through the unpleasant gameplay.

If I had to describe this game with a single word, that word would be charming. Because nearly everything about this game charms me to no end, from the art style, to the music, to the characters you come across, to the general playstyle. I could go on and on about all of the things I love about this game... However, if I could use a second word to describe this game, it would be disappointing. Why? Because after all of the beautifully charming things this game has to offer, and despite all of the potential the story had to be GREAT, the story ended in a very cliche manner, which was a MUCH LARGER DISAPPOINTMENT to me than I thought it could be. The story, thoughout a large majority of the game, was just as charming as the rest of the game, yet as the end neared, it slowly came to be VERY cliche, which made the ending disappointingly predictable and boring. It's just... this game was SO UNIQUE in A LOT of ways, but then... I'm not sure if the developers wanted to rush to finish the game or not, but the ending was just SO DISSATISFYING, and I can't put my finger on why they'd decide to do such a thing to such a beautifully unique game.
Despite all that I say, though, I would still recommend this game to anyone who enjoys artistic games such as this one, mostly just for the experience. However, I also warn those that choose to play it that they'll probably be pretty disappointed by the end of it. I still love the game, but I also feel it's a good example of how cliches can ruin a game's story, and perhaps the game experience in its entirety.
(Also, to those who decide not to play it JUST because of the fact that this game is run through Uplay, shame on you. As long as Uplay isn't preventing you from playing the game somehow (which I personally had no issues with), this game deserves better.)

A particular JRPG that you will either come to hate or love. If you despise any of the following then do not grab this game
-Grinding
-Basic plot
-Only has two endings, both of which are positive, one being the "True" end.
-All playable characters are girls
-Backtracking (You basically end up revisiting areas you have already been through multiple times)
-Lolis
-Turn-based combat system
For the most part, this game isn't complex  in any shape or form. People looking for a game that has an extremely expanded story that can be manipulated or influenced differently through very minute actions, this is not one of them. This is a game that you just enjoy for the characters and endless playability. Once you beat the game once, you can restart with all your stats that you gained through leveling and thus your characters can constantly grow. However your enemies do NOT grow with them. You will find yourself one-shotting most of the story-based bosses at one point or another after your first play-through.
So what gives this the aformentioned "endless playability"? It's the monsters that you can fight on the side and new equips that become available through a seperate mode in-game that isn't related to the story. There are a TON of hidden things you can find in the dungeons and certain things that can only be found during specific chapters throughout the story. New challenging monsters can become available, new equipment to buff your characters to their max, and of course, the fun in trying to create the best team once you unlock all playable characters. If you're someone that loves to find everything and reach the absolute peak of what you can achieve in a game, then this will certainly eat up your time.
Now bluntly speaking, this is definitely a game where much of its charm is in the characters so you really need to have SOME kind of interest in anime/manga/otaku culture, call it what you will to really enjoy this game. Naturally, if that is all about you, then you'll probably love this game if not for anything else, you are playing as adorable overpowered girls. Of course, there is a fair share of minor fanservice as well if you're into that also.
Those looking for a bit more:
The combat system is encounter and then turn-based. If you have played any of the Final Fantasy games or Legend of Dragoon, this is pretty much identicle to those combat systems. Each character, you will notice has stats that gear them towards specific methods of combat. Melee/Magic/ or a mix of both is what you will pretty much be looking at. Certain characters have a wider range of attack while others are more confined. Anyone that has played their share of turn-based strategy games should really know what to expect from this game.
Overall, I personally love this game and am still playing it with a party that is roughly between levels 130-160 and I still have ways to go in terms of equipment and monsters to beat. I fully recommend this to anybody that enjoys turn-based strategy games and if you like playing as combat lolis.

I was reluctant to buy this game at first, as I hadn't heard a lot about it. It didn't really appeal to me, I thought it was just going to be another clickfest with no replayability. I couldn't have been more wrong.
First of all, the music. The music makes this game what it is. Ben Prunty did a brilliant job of this. You load the game up (which takes seconds), and you're instantly hearing this beautiful chiptune. This continues throughout the game, as there is never a moment without music. It changes depending on your situation, too, which is a nice feature that some games lack or do poorly. Seriously, the sound in this game is the best I've heard.
Secondly, the replayability. I've never actually completed a game yet, and find that each time I play I adopt a different tactic. The game does a great job of encouraging the player to spend as much time as possible earning scrap (the currency in the game) for upgrades, but in a non-grindy, intense, and diverse way. I'll get to combat later though. While encouraging a slow approach to the game, it also forces the player to advance to the next sector or suffer the wrath of the pursuing rebel fleet.
Combat. I've never enjoyed combat in a game quite so much as I do in this one. The enemies, while of a set number of races and morals, are all different in their combat. Some will aim to cripple your weapons systems as soon as possible, others will try to disable critical systems to distract you while they attack your defenses. There's also the type to teleport on-board and destroy you from the inside, breaking through your doors and destroying systems and crew. The best part about combat in this game is that anything the AI can do, you can do, and anything you can do, the AI can do.
The different races in the game add a level of complexity that is easy to understand, yet challenging to make decisions about. Some specialise in hand-to-hand combat, whereas others are there to improve and defend systems. Each have their own rivalries and alliances, as well as a personality that can actually affect your gameplay style. You will often find yourself chosing a decision that is morally right over one that benefits you, simply because you feel sympathy for the poor guys. Equally, you also feel anger towards certain groups, and find yourself vying to kill every last one of them.
There are so many aspects to this game that I can't cover them all in one review. Buy the game for yourself and see. You won't regret it.

I was too anxious to sleep since Santa Claus was on his way, so I opted to venture into the living room in the dead of the night while everyone else was asleep. Eventually, the computer crashed since it was a piece of junk, and I continued staring at the screen for several minutes. Just staring at the pitch black monitor. I finally came to and looked at the clock hanging on the wall. It was 5 o'clock. I had just experience what was perhaps the most intense, colourful and psychologically damaging ecstasy ride I might ever feel in my lifetime.
When you play this game, you don't blink, you don't breathe, you don't do anything but watch, play and think of nothing. Your soul is absorbed into the monitor as it displays the flashing lights of hypnotism that is Beat Hazard and just when you think it couldn't get any trippier than that, you realise the light intensity goes past 100%.

This was my first experience with XCOM. The Enemy Unknown game was pretty fun, I completed it twice; once attempting to maintain my force until the end with frequent saves. The second play through I used a bunch of custom functions to make everything more permanent (now that I had some insight into the capacities of choosing engineering or science, the important balance of income satellites, and the utility of base layout.)
+Pros
+ graphics are beautiful and simple. It won't overwhelm any computer but still has a distinctly well-designed look without looking cheap.
+ lots of choices and replay value, the full affect of the game can't be experienced in one go. Gotta play it twice and make different choices (won't be boring during round 2)
+ in 3 full play throughs, I only saw the same map generated once.
+ No matter how beefy my snipers got, certain aliens still posed enough threat to kill my players if I didn't plan really hard--and reload from a save when I took a super necessary and risky strategy in order to take them down without a death.
+Alien strength is related to your gear and progression, not your place in the story. If you hold back before progressing, the next story mission will be scaled well to your improved gear. (I have tried overpowering a mission once and ended up having aliens load that were definitely not supposed to appear that early in the game. Screwed up my research order. I deserved it.)
-cons
- camera has 4 directions, instead of 360' liberty
- alien behaviour is predictable.
- player models are a little contrived--not a lot of selection in faces/hair. Enemy Within adds more colour, new outfits, even languages. (LANGUAGES WAS AWESOME THOUGH--super unimportant detail by really fun to have only one of my players confirm an action in Polish.)
- The story is really really short, likely to encourage you to do multiple play throughs.
- The game is incomplete without the Enemy Within Expansion. I had no idea how disappointed I would be with Enemy Unknown with the retroactive additions of the expansion. For that price tag, XCOM shouldn't sell these games separately. Ever.
BUY ENEMY WITHIN. Find a good time when both are a reasonable price together. I expected "enemy within" to be an expansion, and it isn't. It's an identical playthrough of 'enemy unknown' but with additional side missions, two new fields of study "genetics/cybernetics" to compliment the "research lab/Workshop" dynamic in the first game. It made the entire game feel more well rounded and gave me much much greater flexibility in playstyle. I played a super genetically enhanced 3 snipers, 1 support, 1 assault, 1 heavy team. WAS AWESOME. Then I just ♥♥♥♥ed around and made everyone a mechwarrior for the last level (since I'd played it 3 times now)

OK here is now my first review ever. I want to apologize if my english is not that great but I did not wanted to make review only in my language.
So here we go.
- The graphics and the attention to details are very good
- A weather system. Streets getting wet and reflecting in cities. Gras swinging in the wind. Beautiful sunsets...
- The entire world feels alive and not empty like some people say. A lot of different NPC's are running around in city’s and talking
to each other. Then there are horse wagons who are trading goods between cities. You can literally hear NPCs talking to each other in every corner of the cities
- The sound and especially the voice acting is phenomenal. Which surprised me really because you need to keep in mind that this is an MMORPG after all.
- I really like the design of the world and Monsters. It is not so colorful and exaggerated like other asia grinders (e.g. TERA).
- The character creation is average. I have seen ones that are more complex but this still stands out. And here is why: You are able to save your character in a file so you do not need to recreate them if you do not like any aspect of them after the creation. You can also choose from other player’s uploaded creations if you want.
- It has a very complex trading and crafting system. You can create trade routes on the world map that gives you bonus income if you do it correctly. You can even trade items by yourself between cities.
- The ability to auto run to checkpoints you can set by yourself anywhere on the world map.
- AFK Fishing
- You can actually dive underwater
- You can sailing your own boat
Doesn't sound that bad after all? Then brace yourself for the cons.
- The combat system is difficult with many hotkey-combos. This has been done far better in other action-mmmo’s.
- Unable to trade other players. You have to grind all your gear by yourself. This also reduces the social contact between players a lot.
- Selling items at the marketplace (ingame-ebay) feels incredible unfair. If you sell an item you only get 65% of that estimated value because of taxes.
This further encourage people to not trade anything if they do not really have to. But why...? Why not reducing the overall money income instead of creating such a massive money sink.
- The way the monsters are behaving. You can only hold 8 monsters agro at the same time. If you have 8 mobs agro and following you, then any other monster you attack is invulnerable and does not get aggressive at all. This is the most unrealistic and weird thing you will ever encounter in a mmorpg. On top of that, you can't also loot more than 8 mobs at the same time. If you kill
9 Monsters then the loot from the first one will instantly disappear.
- Very few armor variation. You don’t feels much progression in grind new gear because it looks mostly the same. This is to encourage players to buy outfits for real money from the cash shop
- The cash-shop prices are insanely high. You can have up to 4 pets out. Each pet cost 9 Euro (Basically 10 because you can only buy currency for 10Euro minimal).A single outfit cost 29 Euro. And with the very few armor variation, you definitely want an outfit at some point. This price is too high even for a free-mmo. So here's the thing. Lethal League technically doesn't have a lot of content. I'm about 8 hours in and I've already maxed level and beaten the arcade mode once. But we have an old saying in the male community. "It's not the size, it's how you use it". This game is horrendously fun in multiplayer. The controls are tight and the netcode is top notch quality. The game relies on two things to make multiplayer fun: Satisfaction value and reaction time. Luckily, it nails both of them. First of all, I'll actually explain the game. It works in a small square room (One of five maps) and a ball spawns in the middle. Every time a player hits the ball, it becomes his color and it cannot hurt him, only his enemies. While hitting the ball he can also do two things: Aiming the ball up or down and activating his special ability. The special abilities add some depth due to learning how each should be used to the best effect. For example, one characters special allows the ball to travel through walls for a little while. At first I only tried to fake people out with it on the ground, and catch them unawares. But over time I learned that if I applied an aim to it I could cause it to go flying through the ground and the cieling at an angle, which is incredibly hard to perdict and dodge accordingly. Alright, on to the aforementioned satisfaction value. As the ball gets to higher and higher velocites, each smacking of the ball results in the player smacking the ball for not only about 5-6 seconds straight, but also the screen freaking out to high hell. So basically, every time you hit the ball, it feels like you just punched through the earth. Additionally, the music is some of the best I've ever heard in a video game. The tracks are nice and varied, with each track seemingly blending in with the endless sounds of the ball getting smacked into the fifth dimension. The one aspect which can devide people is the art style. It's a simplistic art style, no doubt, but some will find it attractive and some will find it boring. It's really just a matter of opinion. All in all, it's a blast with friends and the soundtrack is amazing, but if you just want to find a good solo experience, I don't know why you're looking at an arena fighting game.

It might seem simple, and it is, but sometimes simple fun is better than overly complicated things. In this game you fight your opponents by hitting a ball at them and that's it, on the surface. It's basically an easy to learn and hard to master game.
Each character of the 5 you (at least currently) have to choose from has their own abilities, for one they all have different jumps of varying height and I think their movement speed varies too but it might be the visuals tricking me. On top of that they all have different special attacks, one makes the ball warp through the arena wall and come out on the other side, one double swings at the ball to increase the speed by ridiculous amounts and so on. The visuals aren't amazing but for this kind of game they work quite well. Not all games has to be super flashy 3D and stuff, if the game works better with a simple 2D look then that's the better choise in my opinion.
The music for the game is great. I haven't heard a track in there that I wish wasn't playing, overall really good sound effects too.
I personally recommend playing on a controller but I'm sure it works fine on keyboard too, all keys are cusomizable for your comfort.
Scores for those who need them:

A gorgeous turn based strategy RPG that's equally a choose-your-own-adventure visual novel.
Honestly, the visual novel part sounds boring – I’m not a big fan of the genre. However, don't let that dissuade you; I was easily won over, because this really is a case where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
The story options available in the visual novel mode and the resources available in the turn based strategy mode are reciprocally affected by your choices in each. Some of the other RPG elements include character stat upgrades, shops, and loot for use in battle. There’s also some resource management mechanics with regard to time, caravan morale, and supplies.
It's all very well designed. You want to stare at these beautiful works of art. The story is extremely well paced and ramps up an atmosphere of desperate and hopeless dread that keeps you wanting to find out what happens next – think the walking dead, where people can only run, never rest, and main characters die for no good reason or cause *you* made a bad call.  Your decisions matter. Additionally, there's interesting and relevant lore sprinkled throughout.
My only complaint is that it’s too short, which is almost always the mark of a good book and sometimes that mark of a good game, as it is here. Also, the game may be a tad unforgiving: I really wanted to take back my bad choices, but saves are automatic and usually only occur after the consequences are revealed.
I give it an 85% overall goodness.

Through frustration and an actual threat to my sanity, I've managed to hammer through tens of hours of FTL: Faster Than Light. A game that will remind you, cruelly I might add, of the fact that you are infact - in this day and age - playing against a machine time and time again.
FTL will lull you to a (false) sense of security by giving you the chance to upgrade your ship and your crew to the ultimate fighting machine. Dozens of system and crew upgrades will give you a false sense of security once you come across the Big Bad of the game: the rebellion's flagship, a seemingly indestructible monolith of destruction. After 50 hours of gameplay, I still haven't been able to defeat this multi-layered monstrosity.
The story itself is simple, paralleling a generic movie trope: a single survivor of a disastrous event who'll have to forward the data on the assumed vulnerability of the enemy to the remains of the once-oh-so-grand fleet. Fighting and negotiating your way through multiple hostile areas will give you an array of upgrades, increasing your chances of taking on the Big Bad. However, a single mistake - or a stroke of bad luck - may and will end your voyage way too early.
One of the few complaints I have about this game is that the maximal amount of scrap - the currency of the game - can be gained through combat, foregoing the possible diplomatic/subversive/other-than-that tactics. Either that or I'm just bad at the game.

I love the Viking setting.  I enjoy the story, and it certainly kept my attention.  The combat has some interesting mechanics: armor break, the fact that strength is health, and some great special moves.
However, the turns and initiative are implemented in a really frustrating way that, in the end, has ruined this game for me.
First, each side gets to move one unit per turn, no matter how many units are remaining, in a fixed rotation.  As enemy units are injured and lose health, they also lose the ability to deal damage.  However, once they are killed, their spot in the initiative order is filled by another healthy unit.  If I have 4 units remaining, but the enemy has only 2 units, then those units will each act twice as frequently as my 4 units, and they will have a distinct advantage.  Sometimes I may have a couple of units across the map who have just killed their opponents, and while those two waste turns walking back to the other side, the fewer remaining enemy units that are engaged with the other half of my force will be attacking twice as often as those units near them.
Bottom line is that killing an enemy unit is generally a bad idea until the very end of the fight.
I have adjusted to this tactic, as unintuitive and frustrating as it sometimes is.  Now that I have advanced sufficiently, I was able to raise the Strength of one of my favorite units to 18.  Now, his key ability, the sweeping attack that hits 3 enemies, has been rendered much weaker.  Many weak enemy units can be killed by a single 18 STR attack.  When he had only 16 STR, he could severely injure 3 of these weak units in one blow, which was fantastic.  Now, he kills them outright, and what remains are 3 stronger units that now get to attack twice as frequently.
Killing an enemy unit is a bad idea?  Killing 3 of them even worse?  My favorite character is too strong, and that's a tactical disadvantage?
To me, this is just a bridge too far.
Is it novel?  Yes.  Can you work around it?  Sure.  But it draws out the combat as you avoid weakened enemies and chase down the healthy ones before you start delivering the killing blow.  And the longer I play this game, the less I enjoy it.

Jagex is back with another block shooter (First one being Ace of Spades), looking to squeeze more money out of the pockets of children horny for blocky construction games that involve guns.
My main issue with this game is that it can't decide who to target, kids who are to dumb to figure out something or actually somewhat compitent players. The reason for this thought is that this game requires ALOT of teamplay, the game requires you to fortify and protect your base and destroy the enemy base. There are a few side objects you need to destroy before you can attack the main one. The issue where the game can't decide wherther it's for incompitent players or kids lay much in the combat of the game. When i played the game i choose to play as sarge, who has a machine gun and rocket launcher. Your machinegun has a mag of 100 shots and you carry about 3 mags in total. I almost NEVER managed to kill anyone using less than a full magazine, as the damage on the gun was CRAZY low. That's where you go "But datz u who can't aim, stoopid." surprisingly, it isn't i once crawled into a hole an enemy had dug, the class being a sniper and i stood at point blank range at his back and it still took me about 80 shots to kill him.
What adds insult to this is that there aren't any ammo drops. Yeah, you can't resupply ammo, or health unless you have a Medic or Engineer in your team to place health and ammo blocks. This is where the big focus in teamplay plays in, and when 80% of your team haven't even reached puberty you're out of luck champ.
Characters:
The characters introduced have no personality or creativity put into them, it's your average Engineer, soldier, medic, heavy, spy(or if you prefer 'assassin' class.) and sniper. Spiced up with different generic looks to make them feel familiar and easy to remember even if it in the end make your team look like a bunch of cosplayers fresh from a convention.
Your characters also spout out random quotes from movies so that kids can giggle about knowing where the quote is from or whatever the hell. These quotes and lines get repetitive REALLY DAMN FAST, the game won't even give you 1 minute of peace and quiet without a quote being mentioned. And it doesn't help that many of the quotes make no sense for characters to say in the first place and are just forced.
And don't bother trying to sneak or dig under the enemy, your characters make alot of noise. The enemy can hear you coming under them or by them from a mile away, which ruins the whole thing. The thought of not actually knowing if the enemy is currently setting up bombs right at your feet  sounds like an interesting concept but its horribly executed in this game, especially since the maps are so tiny. You never need to worry about them sneaking under you because you'll hear their mining or their character spouting qutoes from underneath you. Letting you know that they're there undearneath you and probably setting  something up.
I there are so many flaws in this game and things that makes it an annoying experience, though i didn't experience any crashes or anything that breaks the game. So if you are 10 and don't want to install gun mods for your minecraft then fine, buy this junk. But if you have some bloody standard in games you should know in advance to not even bother with games like this.

I'm not a fan of Beat-em-ups myself, just because i haven't played any of them in my childhood, except for Fighting Force, but it was 3D and pretty different in gameplay than classic 2D Beat-em-ups. Plus, as a huge character action nut, i'm too used to fast and stylish combat.
So, i wasn't really dissapointed with this game not being a classic beat-em-up.
It's more like... a rhythm game. Without music base.
Let me explain.
The story is as simple as John Wick - some guys stole your pet (a very grumpy cat), it's time to get it back and kick♥♥♥♥♥
Gameplay consists of you endlesly running to the right, while zombies and other guys run towards you.
Your dude (who looks totally awesome imho) has 4 attacks according to 4 face buttons - upper attack, forward attack, down attack and backward attack. Though, your main ones are first three, because backward one only used to punch zombies running from the left. They can also be chained in combo.
But you don't just punch them as you want, you need to attack them right in time, you want to aim for a perfect strike. Not only because it gives you more points and multiplier, but also because its needed for more effective killing, like some of zombies can be killed in one perfect instead of two normal strikes and so one.
Also, some enemies require using specific attacks in order to defeat them or to dismember them in order two acquiring projectile that can be used to kill more zombies.
You see, this game has so much killing and styling potential, you just need to understand how everything works, which is not hard considering that this game has a nice "How to Play" that tells you everything you need.
And even if it IS repetetive, it's a fun game nonetheless, perfect in small doses.

The game is a MMORPG. People say it copied WoW, or some other game. But you can judge for yourself.
Positives:
* You have a lot of stuff to do, no matter what, you will most certainly never run out before you get bored. You have Life skills, which is crafting, fishing, hunting and all kinds of things.
* It has an advanced Guild feeling to it, you can even have your own Guild Boat, and so forth. It makes the game more united in a way that players can unite and play etc.
* It is complicated meaning it is fun to learn about it and develope your own feel on how to play the game. You can solely be an adventurer or you can be the best guild by going on missions. Hell you can become a billionare by doing node business.
* Advanced character developement
* Advanced character creation
* Balanced game DP/AP as of the basic skills your characters have.
Negatives:
* When downloading this game it brings you it's own version of an "anti-virus" it is called XingCode 3. XingCode3 scans your HDD each 48hours for activity.
After uninstalling BDO ( Black Desert Online ) it does not disappear you need to delete it via regedit manually.
* It is very complicated for new comers I would say. You need to learn about CP ( Contribution Points), how Nodes work. Fishing, Crafting, Working etc etc.
It takes time so be patient.
* You can level up very fast and it does not take much of a grinding aspect tho it gets "harder" by that I mean it takes longer to reach a new level. I am level 40 now in just 2 and a half day on my main.
* It is a huge debate whether this game is on the P2W ( Pay to win) side or not. Sure if you want you can become rich by paying and selling your Pearl items ( Premium Items ) on the user market for millions.
* The economy is well divided, you can become a millionare very fast in this game and therefor I believe the game's economy is unbalanced.

**SPOILERS**
In "Soul Searching," there is a main purpose that is NOT supported by the game itself. That unsupported purpose is that we as people have to tackle our problems, not run away from them. While the black-and-white cutscenes do have characters that reflect upon this concept, the main story diverts completely away from it. The main story is short and very uneventful. You seem to be soul searching only because your ancestors did so, not because you actually need to. What did soul searching have to do with mending the friendship between people and dragons again? The story is completely capable of completion WITHOUT awakening any souls and learning their ablities. When the dragon took me back to my home island and the game ended, I wondered if throughout the game I was either trying to save souls (from what?) or create peace with dragons and humans again. Would I reccomend this game for only seven dollars? Only if you're looking for something aesthetic and pleasing to the eye. But to those who are searching for a clear and sensible story, be warned.

I had heard pretty good things about Child of Light.  It looked pretty cool so I thought I'd give it a shot.  Well, the background artwork is quite nice, for sure, but the design and animation of the characters feels a bit sloppy (though I do like the flowing hair).  Besides that, I don't have much to complain about what it looks like.  The game itself, however, is not very interesting.  Even the puzzles are simple and somewhat repetitive, involving lighting up different objects in a pattern.  While flying around and collecting treasure and potions I forget to use can be mildly entertaining, the battles are a disappointment.  It works kind of like turn based strategy of sorts, where you can use your glowing firefly to slow down the opponents.  In other words, battles are about timing and luck.  Even though you get different characters and can work strategies out with the different styles, the main problem is that it is boring.  It is the same type of battle over and over and over again.  Fly around, fight new monsters, fly around, fight more monsters.  Also, I would have liked it if at least three characters could be placed in the battle at a time like the enemies are.  I want to like the game, but I really just can’t.  The fights are pretty long and simply a lot of repetition of trying to blast enemies with your most powerful spell while attempting to avoid becoming paralyzed.  It can take forever.  Lastly, this is more of a personal preference, but I did not like the dialog between characters that shows up quite often.  It does not add to the plot and the poetry feels hastily thrown together to find something, anything that rhymes.  It gets annoying, especially when a new character joins the team and then every single other character must introduce themselves to that one.  Overall, I think the game could have been much better if there were a few tweaks made to it, but as it stands, I’m not very impressed.  Also, Uplay is a hassle.

This game is in all seriousess a love letter to the art that is gaming.
pros:
-The game is long, main campaign takes around 25-30 hours id say, if you want the true ending then that adds a few more hours on and you will want to see it.
-combat system is highly addictive and satisfying, its simple turn based mixed with hack and slash, a perfect mix of both worlds id say, struggle to think of a way they could improve it apart from adding more attacks or skills at high levels.

-Animations and effects are extremely well done
-Very good port, no drops, no crashes. its capped at 1080p but modding tools are at hand to change that minor flaw
-Voice acting is some of the best, they really go with their various personalities, id go as far to say that its some of the best work ever done. Its in english or japanese, pick your poison.
-Each charecters has their own skill set with 90% unique abilties, mostly the low level stuff is given to multiple charecters but they all have various weapon types so how those attacks come out will vary.
-In depth lore based around consoles(mostly the older generation). Its a good send off to those consoles that have passed.
Cons
-People that havent played it will judge you(this bothers some people)
- dungeons cant complex pretty linear
- graphics dont blow your face off
- Once finishing the game you will 100% of the time wonder what you are going to do with the rest off your life.(unless you have the sequel)
All in all though, i cant recommend this enough, wheather you like anime or old games or funny stuff or lolis or consoles or lore maybe even general jrpgs this game is one of a kind. It gets overlooked a lot due to the fact that the way it presents itself isnt really the best style to go with in all honesty but when you look past it then its certainly in the top tier of games on the market.

ard turn-based strategy combat game. If you are exceedingly good at those

I keep wanting to like this genre. I keep being disappointed. And yes, fanboys: I suck. So what. If
suck too, you will come to hate this beautiful horror.

A great turn-based story-driven game that has vikings and norse mythology blended with original characters in a new setting.  Beautifully drawn and feels like playing your way through a fantastic movie.  The story picks up with a caravan that has to travel to all the corners of the world collecting taxes, you join the caravan on their home run and happen upon a soon to be king (varl) prince who is also travelling back to the capital, you join your caravan with their warriors, old friends; and thus begins your journey.
You manage the caravans supplies (a resource that keeps the caravan alive) upgrade heroes at camp, heal, and then move along through the large game world (viewable through a nicely annotated and decorated map).
You encounter problems along your path with multiple solutions, and the cool this is that the choices you make here actually affect your game, both immediately in the form of different rewards or punishments, and later on in parts of the story as relationships between your characters develop.
This is a great game, highly recommend it!

The Banner Saga is perhaps one of the most beautiful artistic games that I have ever played. Add onto that with beautiful music and amazing character development.
I won't spoil the story, but I do assure you that the story is amazing in it's own way, while the story does have some decision making, it's both impactful and unexpected. Some 'good' choices that you might've made might be bad choices later on, or vice versa. It's really hard to tell. So pay close attention to dialouge and situations that will leave characters either dead, your caravan short-handed on a few fighters and varls, or the worse part supplies.
The combat in this game takes notes from other combat sequences with this style. But makes it more 'simpler' and easy for the player to understand. Just keep an eye on your morale and survey the battlefield before charging head on. You can 'upgrade' the characters stats and do "trainning" scenarios to further your understanding of possible combat scenarios. However, what could've been useful is for the game to allow us to make this trainning combat scenarios ourselves rather than being pre-selected. What's more is that, nothing reallly comes out of trainning.
Lastly. And this might be a personal gripe. Or it could be something players had asked before. But there is no "save" feature in the options screen. The only way you can save is by making camp. While it might serve a purpose, or it's on players shoulders for paying close attention. Whatever the case maybe. It would be nice to have the actually ability to re-role some of our choices through manual saves.
And seeing how there is a sequel already and (to my belief) no further plans for updating the game. Hopefully, when or if a Banner Saga 3 comes along. I hope Stoic considers a "manual save" feature.
Other than that, The Banner Saga itself is a must have for anyone who likes artistic and visual effort. And a bit of simplistic but overall gripping edge with a game.

This is a visual novel with large number of endings and also an expansive and well written story.
The basics are very standard VN staples (i.e. your character gets dropped into a strange situation with a number of ‘interested’ parties to interact with) but it has been approached with a distinctly Russian (unsurprisingly) twist. The plot is carried through well but gets a little introspective and overly convoluted, the tongue in cheek poke at the rose tinted memory of the soviet era and its institutions is of note. The characters are all memorable and fleshed out well in their respective paths. Its good to have something different i.e. isn’t Japanese or the rubbish vn’s from the US.
+
Good story with multi-layered plot
A different take on the VN standards
Good characters
Long
-
The art is of variable quality – a strange chimera of Russian orthodoxy, Manga inspired and Western comic book(some of its good but other bits just look creepy)
Sound is basic (understandable on the budget)
Occasionally gets over convoluted
Definitely worth adding to your collection and far better than a large number of VN’s you have to pay for

I've been trying to play a consistent multiplayer game with a mate, multiple times now, and have had so many issues that we have given up in frustration, following the latest significant issue where we lost a save game for no reason, without warning. No crash or anything. We tried to load to a quicksave we'd made a minute previously and it ended up loading a save game from 3 hours back, with no record of any of our quicksaves or autosaves over that time. I agree, we probably should have saved properly over that length of time. However, this isn't the first time this has happened to us. This is not a linear game, however I will say you'll be limited at times as to where you can go due to enemy level difference, which you can sometimes circumvent.  As an example I snuck through a whole canyon of higher level orcs and goblins to access a mine with my rogue, then teleported the rest of the party inside to continue.  This can be problematic however if you can't find enemies you can level up on.
This is a LONG game, and you can really tell that they put effort in refining it.  There are a lot of events that had me laughing out loud too; the developers have quite a sense of humor.
If you're a fan of the genre I wouldn't pass it up.

This game is excellent.
I was at first put off by the turn based aspect having never played this genre at all before - but then remembered all those years playing Advanced Heroquest and D&D titles when i was a kid! Turn based never detracted from the fun then - and definitely does not now! In this case the battles are turn based but the movement is free roaming, meaning you just point and click your way around like an adventure title to explore.
The movement and squad based stuff reminds me a little of syndicate from my Amiga gaming days - and the RPG system is your Morrowind /  Two Worlds / Risen / fable style menus with stats a plenty to upgrade and items / spells to manage. It can be a bit fiddly when you open up too menu menus at once on screen, but generally navigation and finding what you need is pretty simple.
The quests are in my opinion pretty difficult and they are far from the usual "go fetch" quests that litter the watered down elder scrolls games now (damn i miss daggerfall......), and definitely take some getting used to especially the turn-based battles - not being told all the information is a regular part of D:OS, and sometimes you dont really even know what your quest is until later. You can find people related to a quest out of sequence to each other so until you have the whole story, you wouldn't know how to proceed. Its very clever and makes you THINK.... (no flashing arrows and lines pointing you between quest characters here). Some foes can destroy you in a matter of seconds early on, and you learn quickly that stocking up and preparing your spells / best weapons prior to an encounter is not optional.... its how you survive.
Characters are pretty well voice acted and there is some funny dialogue. Its not a game for someone who hates reading though - as there is (as in any decent RPG) a fair amount of text alongside the voice acting, and although you have a journal a lot relies on memory as to where items are and who gave you quests. Mostly your journal mostly serves you as it ticks off parts as you complete a quest.
It really fills you with a sense of accomplishment with each quest you complete - a little like when you finally defeat a boss on DARK SOULS - except this really relies on being more skillful than lucky (having the right team, and upgrading them according to your battle needs is essential - Dark Souls, i generally found most bosses were won by perseverance and luck. Roll, dodge, swipe.... roll dodge swipe... oops died again... repeat until complete... it never felt like i had much control or freedom to explore and completion was a grind more than an enjoyable experience). You also have very little XP jumps, so getting your character to the next level is pretty difficult, so you end up being very cautious about splashing out those earned ability points / perks.
Having multiple ways to get to each part of a quest really fleshes out the RPG style of this title and makes you feel as though you do really have choices and those choices do change the outcomes.
Cracking game - well worth a go!

While the Cons I have listed below seem long, and might give the impression that I dislike this game, I actually do like this game a lot even after 60 hours in. A lot of the Cons apply to a whole lot of games in the market, so they can be considered things that prevent this game from being truly awesome (which few games truly are). This is a game that does a lot right and competently, creating an overall fun game that is continually engaging and challenging.
CONS:
Initial accessibility
A lot of things are not explained, like needing specific tools for specific jobs. After the shovel was introduced at the start, the subsequent special tools like shears, repair hammer, identification magnifying glass, mortar and pestle, etc are not explained. Once you push through the initial stage and learn how the game works, it is fine.
Opaque crafting system
Crafting in this game is completely opaque with no record keeping. Yes, you find a bunch of skill books that teach you new recipes, but the exact things you can create with these new recipes are not recorded. So after "learning" recipes, you still have to trial and error to learn them yourself. Other than that, it is a simple and elegant crafting system. I think they could have done away with the crafting skill books completely, and just level locked the crafting by the availability of materials.
Quest clues
I think that finding the balance between hand holding and giving clues is a hard, but many quests have that "you have got to be kidding me" quality. Even after Googling the solution, you still might not know how you're supposed to figure it out yourself. Not a frequent thing, but it does exist, again, it is a hard balance and I have forgiven bigger studios of worst things in bigger titles.
Linear
The game is pretty much linear. There is a main questline and many secondary quests, but I feel that it is almost necessary to do all the secondary quests in order to level up enough to progress in the main quest. Levels make a big difference so higher level mobs in big groups will tear up your party. I guess that is a clear indication that you're at the wrong place. The only thing this affects is replayability, if you're playing through once, the linear quality of the game is not a big problem. Most quests are fun to play.
Slightly Repetitive combat
Combat can get slightly repetitive but they aren't very frequent (this is not an action RPG). They are usually broken up by challenging fights that break things up, so overall it is a small matter.
Progression
For spell casters, the feeling of progression does not feel as strong as they are for the physical damage dealers, where armour and weapon upgrades make a bigger difference to their damage. Spells a character learn at low levels are still relevant at high levels. Having said that, the feeling of progression for the physical damage dealers seem too tied with their gear. A weapon upgrade is the single biggest damage boost for them.
Some skills are quite pointless, like Bartering. There is plenty of money that it does not matter. I think it is pretty no brainer to keep boosting the damage stat, like Strength, Dexterity or Intelligence. Occasionally putting points into Constitution and Willpower when the team is suffering too much from control effects.
Deadend conversation result
At least once, choices during conversations lead to certain quests being unaccessible. There is a character which, if you refuse to help him with something, will no longer give you the option to pick up a quest, which leads to the inability to complete another quest. The result of not being able to pick up the quest is that the party does not gain access to the ability to use the best class weapons in the game. All caused by a casual reply. The only way back is to steal a skillbook that gives ONE character access to the skill book. All these remaining unknown to the players unless they Google the problem. Realistic, yes, but blocking access to content is generally a silly thing for developers to do. I had to unpack the savegame file and use a hex editor to change the NPC before I can receive the quest, forever getting a tampered savegame warning everytime I load in. This is what I would term as the only game breaking, gaming experience breaking problem. Not bad for a pretty ambitious game from a smaller developer.
I have not used a Hex Editor on a savegame since Ultima 5. So yes, in a way, this game gives the complete old school CRPG experience.

There are a lot of reviews, and perhaps one more isn't needed. But hopefully this will be a good one for those of you on the fence, since this game is not usually on sale. In summary, yes, this game is worth $39.99. No question!
First, the positives. For a game funded through Kickstarter and seemingly made under financial duress, the polish is that of a larger publisher's work. There are some aspects of it that do scream "needed more budget," but overall, this is a fine piece of work.
The gameplay itself is also fun, yet simple. Combat relies a lot on terrain, use of elements, distance, position... for such a seemingly simple setup, the combat can get really creative. You can sneak around and plant oil barrels in preparation for a fight with an invisible character, and then set off a giant explosion with fire. Of course, then fiery oil is everywhere and no one can see anything, and if you use a lot of barrels, you might get caught in the spreading flames. Combat in Divinity is often like this, with crazy sequences.
The story is also not just a placeholder. It's funny, self-aware, sometimes terrifying. The game doesn't take itself too seriously but it can get very dark. The campy, dark humor is very refreshing, and conversations with NCPs more entertaining than it should be.
The character creation is very flexible, and at a later point in the game you can even reset your character (!), at the cost of re-quiring all your skillbooks. I haven't got to play CO-OP, but I imagine the reset was for this kind of gameplay.
There are some negatives, not insignificant. The graphics can be extremely frustrating to target in combat, as the area to click on for enemies actually moves around with the opponent's outline. The UI, especially how items and the stash works, is absolutely cluttered and terrible. The bags you get don't make it any simpler. The other problem is the game likes to use puzzles, and these puzzles are often absolutely opaque. There's no way to figure them out, or the solution is so narrow and specific, you probably would have never thought of it.
The paper-rock-scissors event to solve disputes between characters is utterly irritating, especially in single play. I imagine in COOP it's probably hilarious. But I don't like that it occurs with NPCs, since it's really just a random chance to overcome your opponent.
These cons aside, Divinity is a really magical game. It's pretty, it's fun, you can play with a friend (which I will do very soon!) and you won't regret purchasing it, even at full price. Highly recommended!

Note that this review pertains only to the first Episode.
Telltale Games’ animated novel (for lack of a better descriptor) certainly feels like George R.R. Martin’s land of Westeros. Although the game’s official FAQ at Telltale Games’ website claims that one can enjoy the game without having watched any of the HBO series or read the books, there are way too many situations where it becomes a hindrance to understanding what’s happening. My best advice is that you can enjoy without having watched the show or read the books, but you’ll be missing a lot of story undercurrents if you haven’t. The game’s storyline starts at the Red Wedding (Season 3, Episode 9) and has its own story path, so it isn’t necessary to have watched beyond that point.
The story is presented in a comic-booky kind of style (much like other Telltale serials like
and
). Story events unfold through multiple points of view (much like the books), with each providing their piece of the whole. Gameplay consists of many quicktime events (QTEs) and conversational decisions made on a timer. Like previous games, player decisions don't have much of an effect on the overall story, but do affect the appearance (or not) and reactions of NPCs. The game is made without direct input from Mr. Martin (aside from story veto power), but with input from Mr. Martin’s personal assistant and with oversight from HBO, so it stays fairly true to the world and the existing storyline of the series.
The purpose of a review is to give players who are deciding whether to play the game a heads-up on the things they might like and dislike about the game, so here comes The Good, The Bad and The Ugly.
: as I said at the outset, the game certainly feels like the Westeros of the TV series and it stays true to that feel. The voice acting is superbly done and major players from the series lend their talents where appropriate. The graphics are excellent, although animation is very slightly stuttery at times, so major props to the art and animation teams. About the only nitpicky issue that I've seen is that the art team can't seem to decide whether the sword in the Forrester's sigil is point-up or point-down. The story moves along fairly quickly and is certainly engaging, especially so if you are a fan of either the books or the series. Just on those merits alone, fans needing a “Game of Thrones” fix should put this on should-get list. And those who have concerns should know that I've seen none of the gratuitous boobage for which the series is so (in)famous.
: I’ll start with the default settings. We’re talking about a game whose minimum requirements are a dual-core at 2.3 GHz, 4GB of RAM and a video card with at least a gig of VRAM. Why does this game default to windowed mode at 800x600 resolution? Your initial menu options are to Play and to create a Telltale Games account. After you get done Googling the question (or reading this), you’ll find that the “Settings” menu is way off-screen to the right (just click the little right-bracket to scroll the menu) and you can change those to something more to your liking. Once that’s done, you’ll be good to go. The rest of the defaults are pretty solidly matched to your current system specs, although you might want to tweak the sound volume a bit.
I am not a huge fan of QTEs. In my mind they serve little purpose other than as a means to create a contrived sense of urgency. In some games they are a break from the monotony of normal game mechanics, but in this game they pretty much are the normal game mechanics. In and of itself, this is not such a big deal. The reason why it’s under “The Bad” is because they artificially break the story flow. This is an animated novel, after all. Just when the player’s head is fairly immersed in following the story and characters, it’s time to grab the mouse or hunt for the proper key and should that be just a click or a click-and-hold or should it be a lot of fast tapping or do I need to fast-tap and move the mouse or… what do you mean I’m dead?!? So it’s either sit hunched over the keyboard waiting for the visual cues of the QTE or try to follow the story as it unfolds and die a lot.
: I know that I’m seriously biased against QTE’s, so they’re under “The Bad” rather than being down here where I’d love to put them (did I mention that I really don’t like QTEs?). They truly are a game-breaker for me. Fortunately they seem to only appear in action scenes and there aren't that many in this episode. Aside from QTEs, there isn’t any Ugly to be found.
The game is solidly designed, well-written, well-acted, and extremely engaging. You will definitely want to pass on this game if you’re seeking run-and-gun action. It’s just not there. But if you can live without it, you might want to pass on this game if you’re not big on the graphic style, although it does not detract from the game in the least. You might also want to pass on it if you’re not big on Martin’s world or the HBO series. If neither of those two are concerns, this game is definitely worth a look. And even if those two are important, you still might find yourself pleasantly surprised by how well done the game is.

TL:DR: This game isn't worth $15. Free alternatives are Stepmania, FFR, and osu! mania (to an extent).
Long answer:
Out of curiosity I thought I would try this game to see how much it differs from other VSRGs. $15 is a bit steep for these types of games but I thought they might've done something interesting that would make it worth it. Here are some pros and cons I have with the game:
*DISCLAIMER*: I will be comparing this game A LOT to Stepmania, another VSRG. The reason for this is that they are so similar to each other, it would be crazy not to compare the two.
PROS:
- The game seems to have a fairly professional feel and doesn't feel like it was made halfassed
- The customizability in the settings for the game is extensive (feels VERY similar to stepmania)
- Supports replays. This is especially good for this game because Stepmania, the game that is most similar to this game, does not have this feature at the moment
- There is no prep work to get this game running with an assortment of maps
CONS For rhythm game enthusiasts:
- If you are halfway decent at Stepmania, this game will be way too easy. I've gotten platinum scoring (99%) on practically all of the hardest difficulties with only one or two tries
- The timing is way too basic. At this point, there are only two timing windows: you hit the note, or you missed it. There is no other timing windows e.g. in stepmania there is Marvelous, Perfect, Great, Good, Bad, Boo and Miss
-  It's difficulty is based more on modifiers of the file rather than actual note density and patterns. Also a lot of the maps play like maps in Stepmania that are not supposed to be played with c-mod due to rapid bpm changes
CONS for caual players:
- It's just so expensive. 15 dollars for a game that could be played virtually the same and subjectively better for free is just not worth paying money for
Conclusion: This game would have been pretty good if it were the only option for this type of game genre. It's well-put together and has a good assortment of songs. Since this not the case, however, I cannot recommend it. There are other games that do this concept, in my opinion, better AND for free.
