Grim Dawn is kind of boring and repetitive, though I have no idea if it's the game's fault or problem with all ARPG "Diablo-likes" as I'm not familiar with the genre. Finished the game on Hardcore Veteran, with one additional early game dead character and here's my personal impressions:
The game is heavily dependent on only maxing certain skills out instead of spreading out, meaning the vast majority of your game time is spent doing nothing but spamming the same few moves over and over and over and over again on the samey mob groups, even bosses. This is made even worse by the fact that every class has the best few skills unlocked at 50 skill points (instead of say, class skill unlocks being tied to your character's actual level), meaning you have even less incentive to waste precious skill points dual classing early on despite it being one of the game's selling points. To give a concrete example; you're speccing into bleed damage, therefore you max out all bleed related skills, passives, procs etc. without paying much heed to other ones. My succesful character was a retaliation tank, therefore the only things worth picking up for my character were passive percentage or flat increases to survivability and retaliation damage, with few additional procs from gear that you have no guarantee of getting due to the random nature of loot, so good luck if your dream build relies on a specific set bonus or gear related ability.
You supposedly have two whole quickbars available, but the only things I needed on my succesful Soldier (specced very late into Commando for more passives) were number keys 1-3 and left and right mouse click, plus health potion hotkey. All the number keys and right mouse click were for refreshing temporary buffs, which could have been automatic for all I cared since it was good to have them constantly up. Most of the damage and important stuff is passive and random procs. My dead Conjurer wasn't much different; just ordering pets to attack and dancing the 1-2-3 button tango of bleed resist debuff, followed by bleed attack and another bleed attack ad infinitum.
Replay value with other class combinations is also near non-existent due to how linear and lacking in roleplaying the game is, despite imaginative character building itself being lucrative on paper. First you'll be imagining all sorts of fancy ideas, only to quickly realize that once you get the related skills you want you won't be doing anything apart from spamming them. This applies to nearly all situations and actually viable class combinations. The enemies themselves aren't varied enough to warrant respeccing or changing up your playstyle, as f.ex. you can cause heavy bleed damage even to bleed resistant enemies like skeletons simply by stacking more bleed damage and bleed resist reducing debuffs. Only properly challenging parts of the game are certain hero monsters or boss fights with harder hitting, often dodgeable AoE attacks (as in they require actual player input in order to not get hit), but they aren't very varied gameplay wise and you'll still be mostly facetanking as melee or kiting as usual as a ranged or caster character.
The general feel of Grim Dawn is honestly like playing a single player MMORPG with less involving gameplay, and no stuff that makes MMOs worthwhile like an active community, PvP or other things that keep you playing. Just NG+ and extra dungeons for grinding more purple gear, doing the exact same thing you did for the last 20 hours.
Story or setting aren't really spectacular either and the ending is really abrupt, feels outright unfinished in fact. I didn't even realize the game was over before noticing that the quest giver didn't give me the next step. Nothing in the story advanced anywhere or was solved. I'm not asking for "hero saves the day and everyone lives happily ever after" ending, but the original main villains of the game get suddenly shafted halfway through and nothing about them gets explained or solved anywhere, no big encounters or anything at all. Not even an ending cinematic or credits roll, just an achievement and announcement that you've unlocked harder difficulty NG+ after you turn the quest in. Also, there's only one boss music used in two boss fights, the final boss doesn't even have its own music, or any music at all for that matter, which made me assume the game bugged out or something. It feels really cheap.
Where Grim Dawn excels is giving the player lots of options in deciding their build, and repetitive fights for mindless loot can be somewhat mind-numbingly pleasureable time sink if you enjoy that sort of thing, but it's marred by the actual gameplay being too samey facetanking or constant kiting and spamming the same moves (as spending points on something else than upgrading your preferred damage type or skills is not something you ever want to do), with the only difference between early and late game gameplay being that late game gameplay is a lot more flashier and the mobs are visually bigger. The vast majority of your game time will be holding down the left mouse button.

Everlasting Summer. If only this novel was indeed 'everlasting' - because I personally didn't want it to end. A surreal world, a dreamlike artstyle, a nostalgiac feel (even though I had never heard of a Pioneer Camp in my life before playing/reading this). For a free game, it delivers that of which paid games often don't even come close to. It hosts a small but fairly deep range of characters with strange plot twists and unconventional story lines (Miku's route ohgoodlord). Although at times I was screaming at the monitor, begging to make a decision, when the chance came around to choose where to go next, or who to talk to, it was, in the end, satisfying. If only I knew Russian and could play the flurry of user-made mods that we find in the workshop, instead staring at their titles like we're squinting at a resteraunt menu through the lens of a sniper rifle scope.
When I first picked up this game, I honestly didn't think much, and I had no idea what the plot was, where we were going, and who I was going to meet. Personally, for any visual novel and especially Everlasting Summer, I think this is the best way to experience it. Anyway, as the days rolled by, I fell in love with the game and it's characters, settling upon one of them and almost crying myself to sleep when it was over and all 13 endings were done and my scrapbook was more full than the bags of sugar you need to carry (Damn Olga). Not only is the art well done, the music is gorgeous - the visual novel definitely wouldn't be the same without it. Sometimes I just sit at the menu screen and listen to the beautiful music by Sergey Eybog and 'Between August and December' (after your many runs through the game, you'll feel relaxed and almost heartbroken at the menu screen, trust me). I'm almost certain that you and Semyon (who is surprisingly relatable) will enjoy your time at Camp Совенок, and you will forge memories that will last with you for time to come!

This game has a dark-gore-Victorian ambience that, personally, I love. All the decoration, the colors, the houses, roads, each cave, the entire map makes you feel that ambience. About that, the scenarios are not randomly generated, each map is almost the same each time you start a game: rocks, bodies, some enemies will change their position, but the maps don't change. And "that" is something really GOOD. Why? If you have been playing to torchlight or diablo, each dungeon are random each time you enter. But it lacks of personality. Here, you will find secret areas, secret caves, which don't appear in the map, are hidden from the sight, sometimes you need to find a secret lever to open the entrance. There are hidden areas, which you will unlock with some explosive help, runes or... well, I won't tell you all the secrets. There are letters and books that will teach you the story of Cairn, or simply a love letter from a dead body to his loved and beside that, the ambience, because here you feel the love that their creators invested everywhere, with little details like a tree, a clock, a sewer, the office of a doctor, the lair of a thief...
You will think that you know a zone perfectly, but you will find secrets that you didn't notice that were there before, and THAT is surprising in this kind of games.
The isometric view is correct, much more better than others like path of exile. The shadows, textures, details etc... excellent (for a game like this, don't compare it with Doom)
Spells and attack effects? Really good. Fire and ice, venom, caos, guns, temblors... Just watch a gameplay and you will see it.

Inevitably, this game receives comparisons to the other two big names in the ARPG genre,
Diablo 3 and Path of Exile. I like both of those games in doses, but here's what gets me on both of them: top-end play is tedious as hell. You want to play through the hardest content without dying in two seconds? Sure, take the door on the left that says "thousands of hours of playtime".
Admittedly, I have a good deal of time played in this game, but even my ~350 hours in this game would make me a total noob in either of the other two games listed. In Grim Dawn, however, I have several very solid characters that can play through end game content (mostly!).
One thing that annoys me in many ARPGs is that you end up picking a single ability and building your entire character around it. No more! Well... unless you want to. Yes, you will likely have a primary damage skill/spell, but if you don't support it with several other active abilities, not including buffs, you're doing yourself a tremendous disservice. My strongest character, for example, has a combo five or six abilities long, not including on-hit effects that proc off of those.
A good bit of your damage in this game comes from procs, especially those from the novel Devotion system which provides a secondary form of advancement for your character. As a result, high level play ends up looking pretty badass. You'll have a million particle effects swarming the screen as you summon volcanos, meteors, poison clouds, lightning... you name it. And some careful planning goes a long way to making sure that it's not just pretty but effective.
People with epilepsy, bad graphics cards, or poor eyesight might want to treat this as a negative, mind you.
Oh, you screwed up and put too many points into a skill that isn't quite as useful as you thought?
There's an npc in the first town that will let you spend money (iron coins) to respec. Or if you're too busy even to bother with that (it can get a bit expensive), go download a trainer. Your character is stored on your computer! If you're the cheating sort, that means you can also download all kinds of files to try new builds, gear, and so forth.
This is both a plus and minus depending on who you are. If you want a highly competitive scene where everyone is trying to find the best builds, either of the other major games will be a better choice. What multiplayer exists may include cheaters for aforementioned reasons. But if you want to zone out and zap baddies by yourself, it gives you the tools to build a character who won't get totally shafted by RNG so as to be unable to play the highest difficulty. Not saying it's a cakewalk, but you're not going to hit a numbers wall that forces you to grind for hours and hours just to progress (coughDiablo3atreleasecough) -- at least, not until the very, very late game, post final boss on the hardest difficulty.
Lots of options, lots of content, lots of flexibility for people who don't care to dedicate their lives to it like other ARPGs. If this appeals to you, get this game! Get it yesterday!

Game is extremely tedious.* **
*Everything has durability - the axe you use to chop trees, a fishing pole, cooking stove (what ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stove only gets 100 uses?), butcher's knife, etc.
*The auction house (market place) has minimum and maximum prices for each item, so it is more like a lottery than truly bidding on the items you want.
*There is extremely limited trading between characters, so much of the economy runs off of cash shop items being sold on the auction house.
*Areas in the game are separated - you can link up resource nodes and send people to work. It is neat. However, they are restricted by region - so stuff made in one city can't be used in the next. You can transfer it... but yet again more tedium.
*Pets have actual uses, this is great! However, good luck getting one if you don't use the cash shop. Want the best pets? you can breed them... by buying more pets on the cash shop.
*Overlay gear, the kind which is normally only cosmetic, provides stat bonuses. Better get out your wallet.
*There are a lot of missing tooltips and explanations in game. Veterans of the game love it, because they can act accomplished for having already compensated for extremely poor in-game details.
*Game is disappointingly easy in early levels... am told this improves toward end levels, but what seems like an impressive combat system is ruined, imo, because of zero actual pve challenge early game. Combat is more of a "gets in the way while trying to use my frail axe on this tree."
**Game is probably great if you're willing to sink tons of cash into it. Be prepared to spend tons of hours doing boring things only to realize there is only more of the same ahead.

Too many times developers come along and remake an old classic with the mindset of keeping only the barebones of the original, while gutting the rest in favor of dumbed down, streamlined gameplay to appeal to a wide, diverse audience.
With XCom, they did it right. Here you have a remake that retains the soul of the original, along with most of the things that made it a masterpiece. While some things are streamined and 'dumbed down' just enough to appeal to a wider audience, it only succeeds in creating a slightly more accessable XCOM such that a wide variety of new players can get in on this unique, brilliant game without being off put by a huge learning curve.
Plus you have the bonuses of modern graphics, interesting, detailed battlefields, a variety of alien types, and so much more to breathe a new, modern feel into a game once dominated by static menus and charming, if primitive, pixel art.
And for veteran players(far more experienced than I am, I might add), you have the Long War mod, for extra game length and difficulty for those who want the full experience from '93.
Bottom line: buy this game. Seriously. It's worth the full $30 asking price, but it's often on sale for around $15, and it's some of the best cash you'll spend on Steam.

This game is about taking risks.
On the strategy layer the player manages the base building, research, soldiers and much more. There are a lot of things to keep track of and the game does a wonderful job by presenting the base in an ingenious “ant-farm” view. The complexity of the base and amount of things to manage increase each simulated month and the player is forced to make hard decisions what to prioritize. The game excellently builds up tension leading to a great finale.
Core of the game is the tactical layer. The turn-based ground combat has a superb presentation and feels just right. Here the game really shines. Every misstep can mean death for a soldier and the failure of the mission and in turn more death and failures in following missions. But time is of the essence to collect the resource “meld” or disarming bombs, etc.
The best way to play this game is with iron man mode enabled (= no reloads), which means all decisions are final.  Never did I experience so much tension, drama and relief in any other game.

Hey, a walking simulator that doesn't suck!
In many ways, Corpse of Discovery reminds me of Soma, yes, that Soma. The horror game from Frictional Games that involves lots of walking from A to B while ocassionally listening (and conversing with, in Soma anyway) with a female A.I. who is also the driving force behind your objectives. As you try to reach these objectives, you will encounter monsters (I'm not very comfortable calling them monsters in either game) that may hinder you in making immediate progress.
The dividing line between these two games is that Corpse of Discovery is made on a budget, while Soma has a triple-A polish fitting any effort by giants like EA or Ubisoft. When I say that Corpse of Discovery is made on a budget, I mean it looks like a decent 360 title circa 2008-2010 but with some added annoyances. Some of the flora you'll encounter in the game, as solid as they might seem, can be clipped through. Same goes for ankle/knee high-ish rocks. This is a bit frustrating as it gives the game an air of being unfinished, though not gamebreaking.
In terms of setting, story, and gameplay, the game excels in the two former and does precisely what it should do with the latter. Being a walking simulator, by default the game sports somewhat rudimentary mechanics; you walk, sprint, jump, and activate stuff and that is it. Setting is... everchanging and has some fantastical imagery to show you. Story is also very interesting and plays around with family as a theme, which is a direct contrast to what the game is. If you can ignore the graphical and technical shortcomings of the game, Corpse of Discovery is an engrossing sci-fi adventure that sucks you in and demands your attention. Being relatively cheap is also plus for the game, so that is worth keeping in mind. All in all, I cannot recommend Corpse of Discovery enough, even despite its budgetary limitations.

Overall: 8/10
What a fun, polished, classic-style RPG!
D:OS is hands down the best RPG of this sort since Dragon Age: Origins. Interesting combat system, good story line, and never a dull moment.
PROS
+ Not a single "fetch" quest. Seriously, about 100 quests and not a single one of them falls into the "go get me 10 pairs of smelly panties" category.
+ Excellent graphics with bright colors, excellent level of detail, atmospheric nuances, weather, terrain, all very beautiful to watch.
+ Interesting, innovative, detailed and hard to master combat system. When "fight" is on, solid tactics are essential.
+ Lots of content, areas to explores, NPCs. D:OS' world is very much alive and full of detail. A single, completist playthrough is well over 100 hours.
+ Humor galore. Easter eggs, puns, funny remarks everywhere. For the first time ever I even paid attention to "achievements", each one a nod to some more or less obscure rock track (Sleeping Village, Disciples of the Watch and No More Mr Nice Guy among my favs).
+ Appropriate sound track, not invasive, you won't feel the need to turn it off.
+ Game is very polished, in 150 hours i've encountered just one, quite minor, graphic glitch.
CONS
- Characters are devoid of any real personality: voice overs are sparse, character build doesn't help, you don't really get attached to your main character as you would have done with Origins, or ME's Shepard, or even with Baldur's Gate. You get stronger and stronger, but you don't "grow".
- The UI would need an overhaul, inventory management is tedious and a time waster.
- Some quests are too obscure and counter intuitive, if you really want to complete everything you will need to go check a walkthrough from time to time unless you enjoy pixel-hunting for a semi invisible knob or switch.

It's less of a game and more of a "fish tank". You have some tools with which to affect an environment, and you use them to help various organisms grow and thrive. Some organisms have different unchangeable rules than others (ex: trees can grow up or down, but never underground or sideways, while worms and bacteria can only grow in soil), but all can be tweaked in one way or another. There are various soil/environmental conditions and nutrients that affect everything on the screen.
Xenobloom has various modes that provide different game rules.
Normal mode is almost a clicker-genre game— you harvest plants for "power" (basic points with which to influence growth and organism environmental preferences), modify the environment by adding or removing soil, and slowly unlock more organisms. The goal is to grow as much stuff as possible all over your screen. Environment-wide tweaks are just something to spend points on to keep them turned on— random events will raise and lower them, among other things (such as adding/removing soil).
Experimental mode is normal mode, but without resource (power) restrictions.
Observation mode plays the game for you. It would make a great screensaver.
Ecology mode is the most realistic, though it's far from accurate to reality. Environmental settings (water, wind, phosphorus, nitrogen, oxygen, carbon, sunlight, etc.) can't be directly affected, and organisms are changed to produce an excess of one thing while consuming a smaller amount of something else (ex: tall grass produces oxygen while consuming nitrogen). The player no longer has power restrictions for changing plant variables and terrain; the objective is to balance the various organisms so that every environmental variable reaches its maximum. If an environmental variable gets low, organisms that depend on it will struggle to survive.
Xenobloom isn't for everyone, but it's cheap and well-designed. I haven't encountered any bugs, and I love seeing systems like these at work. I'd love to see more sandbox games focused around restricted manipulation of an environment and its inhabitants.

There are many games which have multiplayer mode and only a number of them ends up as global hits which are played by lots of players and in which connection issues are rarity or aren't issues at all. While this game isn't this kind of title yet, I need to say this game is a little gem which should shine really bright in near future. But let's start from the beginning.
Lethal League is a game where your main goal is to control ball and hit it as hard as possible to hurt your opponents and knock them down, while also using unique techniques limited to each of playable characters. Sounds simple, right ? But I assure you it's not that easy, especially when the movement with which ball move after few hits may reach RIDICULOUS speed and hitting the ball itself (or counter it by pressing X which is a kind of a block which stops the movement of it) may be a really tough challenge. This game will test your dexterity, reaction time and timing, which are really crucial here. So in other words I would call this title easy to learn (it's literally jump, hit and block buttons), but hard to fully master.
Graphics are as simple as in screenshots, but I need to say they are still estethic and look nice with bright colors mixed in (I also like in overall the style game brings with interesting characters). And I need to mention one more thing, which is really, REALLY crucial - music. My gosh, music in this one is one of the best things I heard in gaming history. Electronic climates created by really talented artists like Grillo, zeroSCAR or Klaus Veen fits the climate of the game perfectly, while being perfectly well made. I would say music alone in this game make this game worth to purchase, it's THAT good.
To sum it up game is really well made flash-like game with incredible competitive potential. Game basics are simple to learn, but this game has this crucial element, which make it fun, challenging and mostly work like some sort of a drug, which forces you to play it as much as you can. I give it 9,5/10 as I feel 5 characters is kind of a small numbers of possible options if you ask me. But I assure you - this one will become one of the best gaming hits ever. At least it has great potential to become one.

Lethal League is a truly hillarious, over the top take on pong and fighting games.
The general concept is to defeat your opponentt and reduce their stocks (think smash bros) by smashing them with the ball. The ball will deal damage to your opponents after you hit it, but can be hit by them, which can then cause it to deal damage to you. As in pong, you keep rallying the ball back and forth, with it getting faster and faster until one of you is hit, at which point you lose a life and the ball resets.
What sounds like a very simple concept rapidly becomes a hillarious series of "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥" moments in which the ball is going so incredibly fast that you'd think it impossible to hit, but then someone does, and it gets even faster.
Throw in a bunch of colourful and creative characters and stages, along with an incredible sound track, and some very fancy and flashy visual and sound effects that wouldn't feel out of place in an Anime or Manga, and you get an enjoyable and hillarious experience.
Would reccomend playing with friends (up to 4 player) for added hillarity and fun.

is an indie game that was born from the result of a school project that focuses on a 2D danmaku shooter similar to
, but without all the sci-fi action.  It instead takes a safer route by portraying itself as a casual game that's easy to pick up and play.  Though it doesn't seem that fascinating on the surface, I found myself intrigued by the "orbit" system implemented.
The gameplay is simply, yet enjoyable.  It focuses on your main character, an alien spaceship aiming to destroy all humans (tourists and natives), dinosaurs (with mounted guns to provide a bit of a challenge if you're aiming for those achievements), and an active volcano's boulders.  The more entertaining part of the gameplay was using the tractor beam to collect various objects as ammo and sending them into orbit...but watch out, your ammo might hit you if you're not careful!  Of course, the most quirky aspect of this game is the destruction of the targets, where villagers will explode into villager heads and dinosaurs will explode into several copies of their own heads.
The music is nothing special and is what you'd expect from a casual game and a class project, but the sound effects are quite fitting.  Sadly, the game's scope is limited by its own simplicity, without having room for growth.  You may find yourself getting bored after a while of playing as you'll essentially see more of the same from wave to wave.  At this point, you'll be grinding (or challenging yourself) to get those achievements.  Speaking of which, one of the developers of this project has been kind enough to reduce some of the kill caps on the kill achievements, making them a little more fair to get.  A friendly staff helps the game's image.
Frankly, despite the limited scope, I recommend
if you're an achievement hunter or if you're simply looking for a casual game to settle down with.  It should take you around 5-6 hours to get all achievements of this game.  Try not to take this game too seriously, it's a school project and a casual experience.
6/10  Though the Dinos are Derpy, this game isn't too Derpy at all.

Too many times developers come along and remake an old classic with the mindset of keeping only the barebones of the original, while gutting the rest in favor of dumbed down, streamlined gameplay to appeal to a wide, diverse audience.
With XCom, they did it right. Here you have a remake that retains the soul of the original, along with most of the things that made it a masterpiece. While some things are streamined and 'dumbed down' just enough to appeal to a wider audience, it only succeeds in creating a slightly more accessable XCOM such that a wide variety of new players can get in on this unique, brilliant game without being off put by a huge learning curve.
Plus you have the bonuses of modern graphics, interesting, detailed battlefields, a variety of alien types, and so much more to breathe a new, modern feel into a game once dominated by static menus and charming, if primitive, pixel art.
And for veteran players(far more experienced than I am, I might add), you have the Long War mod, for extra game length and difficulty for those who want the full experience from '93.
Bottom line: buy this game. Seriously. It's worth the full $30 asking price, but it's often on sale for around $15, and it's some of the best cash you'll spend on Steam.

This game is about taking risks.
On the strategy layer the player manages the base building, research, soldiers and much more. There are a lot of things to keep track of and the game does a wonderful job by presenting the base in an ingenious “ant-farm” view. The complexity of the base and amount of things to manage increase each simulated month and the player is forced to make hard decisions what to prioritize. The game excellently builds up tension leading to a great finale.
Core of the game is the tactical layer. The turn-based ground combat has a superb presentation and feels just right. Here the game really shines. Every misstep can mean death for a soldier and the failure of the mission and in turn more death and failures in following missions. But time is of the essence to collect the resource “meld” or disarming bombs, etc.
The best way to play this game is with iron man mode enabled (= no reloads), which means all decisions are final.  Never did I experience so much tension, drama and relief in any other game.

Child of Light is a somewhat short but still fun take on the RPG genre.  I played the game on the casual difficulty, there is also an option for hardcore difficulty but I'm not sure what that changes that makes to the gameplay.
You start off as a girl named Aurora who begins a journey in another land.  At the start of the game you are only limited to walking along the ground however you will soon be granted the gift of flight and the game takes off from there.  After learning to fly you'll begin exploring the world of Lemuria and gaining companions to explore the world with you and fight the evil your tasked to fight.
The combat in the game is active turn based combat with the ability to have your turn or the enemies turn interupted.  There is the waiting phase and the casting phase.  If you attack an enemy in the casting phase they will lose their attack, while if the enemy attacks you in that phase you lose your turn.  There are skills both passive and active (friendly or enemy) that can speed up or slow down your waiting/casting bar.  There are not to many complicated enemies in the game.  Most enemies are pretty easy to decipher what they are weak to (Water/Fire/Lightning/Light) and you are able to slot some gems into your weapons/armour to plan for them.  As well some characters have type specific damge.
And moving into Characters.  The game features a wide array of various side kicks to help Aurora in her quest.  The side characters have a unique look and feel to them.  Your elemental light companion will be your main companion through the whole game and does add some uniqueness to the game.  He has the ability to find hidden areas as well as aid in battle or heal Aurora outside of battle.  However when the battles begin is where the most of the characters begin to feel kind of generic.  Most of the characters have very similar abilities outside of a select few.  For the most part they have a single target attack, multi target attack and then a spell of some sort.  For my play through I only used 3 or 4 of I think the 8 avaiilable side characters.  You also gain levels fairly frequently which lets you keep adding to the skill tree.  The skill tree seems large at first, however the amount of levels gained, the tree fills quickly.  But progressing through the skill tree doesn't provide as big a reward as it should, most of it is just increasing damage for certain abilities.
The enemies do also fall into the generic sorts in battle.  There isn't the biggest diversity of enemy types and then some are reused for the different element types (Fire/Water/Lightning), but there's enough types you won't see the same ones over and over gain the whole game.
The story is good, nothing ground breaking or exremely memorable.  But it does have it's moments that keep you interested in it.
The art is probably the biggest thing that I enjoyed about the game.  The game has a very unique/interesting art style and while not everyone may like it, I felt it suits the game's story and overall feel of the game.  There are variety of unique locations in the game and the art does make them feel unique and makes the game enjoyable to explore.
The levels/areas in the game are fairly straight forward.  There are some puzzles and hidden areas to find, but for the most part each area is pretty simple and straight forward to go through.  There is a little bit of backtracking throughout the game but not enough that it gets frustratiing.
The game is a uPlay activated game and for some that's a big issue.  I've never really had any big issues with uPlay that haven't got resolved quickly.  The game does go on sale fairly frequently and I would suggest picking it up on sale as it is fairly short and not overly difficult.  Also the DLC is not realy required however I did enjoy the Golem so I feel that might be worth picking up with the game.
Overall if you are looking for a not to difficult active turn based RPG with unique visuals than this game should meet all those requirements.  If you are looking for a lengthy adventure, or a more challenging task, than this is something you may want to pass over.  I enjoyed the game for what it was and it was enjoyable to play through.

I love this game.  There, I said it... I really really love it.
I was instantly captivated by the visuals, which is what instantly drew me to it. For a 3rd person SRPG the graphics are prenominal, brightly coloured and crisp.  It's like playing a cartoon and exactly what you'd hope they be.  You can zoom in on almost anything to little detriment in quality (which you will do often to select certain items from a selection that are close together) and rotate the camera 90 degrees too, to see past scenery.  Both function as wanted.
The visuals also complement the general tone of the game, quests and dialogue.  They are cartoony without becoming juvenile, and the general tone is humorous and light hearted without losing sincerity.  This is refreshing after the usual misguided attempts at humour found in other games recently, or the very serious (but understandably so) demeanour of games like Baldurs Gate and Dragon Age.  Finding a giant talking clam moments after killing a necromancer whom was trying to kill me didn’t detract, and conversing with the many rats during a quest where you are investigating a murder doesn’t either.
The music is fantastic, and along with the other atmospheric noises, it doesn’t detract either.  No annoying distant crowd noises looping, or voices that don’t fit the bill.  Although, mentioning the voices, there is a metric ♥♥♥♥-tonne of dialogue in this game, and understandingly that means that most of it is text based.  Fear not… as before mentioned, the tone and humour lead to this being a delight, not a chore, and it’s fun to seek out the quirky odd characters to help you on your way.
The crafting/cooking system is amazingly detailed.  It all makes sense, and you will be seeking out those books (or sneakily reading them in people’s houses) to gain the recipes to finally find out what all your ingredients are for.  Superbly done; it doesn’t feel forced like in survival games, nor does it feel redundant like a lot of other RPGs (Elder Scrolls… I am looking at you! I have never once crafted a potion or poison that I didn’t have to in those games!)
The gameplay is split into the usual exploring/solving/questing, and combat.  The first lot I kind of mentioned above, how it feels less a chore and more an entertaining part of the game.  There is little in the way of guiding you, no markers appearing everywhere or items highlighting for your convenience, so it is up to you to listen to the hints and tips.  There is a journal to help you remember, but it only gets the salient points.  Characters are all willing to have the same conversations with you again if you forget, and dialogue saves in a log too so you can refer to it.  There are a lot of decisions to make too, with a system that doesn’t just split right/wrong or good/bad.  Each decision can give you points in one of 9 pairs of traits and you gain bonuses depending on which side of the scale you sit.  This works really well for things such as bold/cautious or independent/obedient and really makes the game feel a lot closer to a table top RPG than normal within the videogame world.  On top of that you can actually decide differently for your 2 characters (although not the 2 companions that you can use to make an overall team of 4).  This is an interesting concept where you can make your characters converse or argue and end up with different builds.  It comes into its own in multiplayer, however, when you can converse with the other player and disagree on decisions within the game world.
Combat is also fantastic and fresh.  Although initially it looks very much like Fallout 1 and 2 with the action points it comes into its own with the strategy involved.  Combat is heavily based around the elements, with water/ice/fire/poison/earth and electricity all having impact on the way the battles play out.  On top of that, the elements interact with each other. Combine water and electricity to stun multiple enemies, or flame a gas cloud to make a wide area explosion.  It leaves you planning ahead and trying to effect the enemy without leaving yourself exposed.
Overall I can’t recommend this game enough to any would-be adventurer or SRPG fan.  You can sink hours into it without realising, and without an ounce of boredom. Definitely one I will be returning to a lot!

A rogue-like space mission in which you must deliver the last hope of a dying Federation in a marathon trip through several varied sectors. Your journey is restricted both by your limited fuel and the approaching Rebel fleet, so grinding isn't really an option. Each game should take around a half hour to an hour and a half and there is a nearly endless combination of weapons and modules to experiment with. Everything is controlled by very simple resources and upgrade trees, keeping the learning curve short. All great things which make for a great game. What I couldn't get over, and what drains a good portion of the fun out of this game for me, is just how random a rogue-like. It is nearly impossible to set a goal beyond survival and success. Various weapon combinations might excite you, but there is no guarantee you'll ever get a shot at testing them. The trade off here is, of course, that each playthrough is unique and if that's what you're looking for, FTL is perfect for you. However, if you look to strategy games for intense planning and not the fun a constant wrench in the works makes for, this might not be the game for you.

Corpse of Discovery a weird sci fi fictional plat forming intense game. Playing in between 3-4 hours. The game, quality explodes my expectations, when first launching the game you get an eerie feeling that whatever happens  when you decide to hit the new game words, displayed on the menu. It's going to be a first person narrative story! Oh I wonder How I knew that?
When first entering the mind of an astronaut that had just momentarily awakened. The environment around you appears to be a base of some sort. I hadn't been certain whether I was on aboard a ship,  land base maybe? upon further expectation you discover in first person objects around your bedroom that relates to the time you had spent on earth, now in control of a character who is nameless as far as I can tell? You begin to walk around the exterior, doors will separate you from other rooms. I won’t go into detail as what is in each room, but I do suggest you re observe everything you’ve already interacted with as you progress this solemn tale.
Through the story you’l find your self traversing planets with epic environments that range from a desert, flora and fauna filled, and some with life forms of all kinds yet to be named, as well discovered. I never found myself being bored once I began to explore a planet.  A little circle bot will accompany you for every planet you are on, giving you reassurance of the terrific work your performing, that few humans will ever carry the likeliness that you will one day bring back to earth. The bot itself also records data of you and the planet you are on, eventually relaying the information back to the company you work for. I don’t want to get into details for the story, I will say it’s easily the strongest trait for this particular title.
Plat forming, a huge part in Corpse of Discovery, you’ll find yourself avoiding and planning routes ahead as some objectives require you to travel to high mountain areas that at first look impossible to explore till your actually at the base of the it. Your given a small jet pack like boost to help you plan your jumps accordingly. Again I don’t want to spoil anything for you, but there will be moments where your deciding how your going to go about this planet, just by looking ahead of you. I’ll argue that’s about as game play as it gets, some planets offer different resistances of gravity, allowing you to enjoy some higher jumps, which can be satisfying as you’ll notice for various reasons I can’t go into.
You find yourself accompanied by much dialog, as well many different types of “feeling” music, is the only way I can think of how to describe that right now. Some of it evokes feeling that make you feel like your an alien on another planet, horror, sadness, anger, so much is great with this sound track, if I had to complain about one factor I had noticed with my play through, that periodically the music would cut off without reason destroying some of the immersion I had settled in myself at that point. Now that im on that topic, you as a player of discovery, will notice some glitches. I found nothing game breaking, but they are there, I hope you don’t find anything, but be forewarned!
I wish I had more to say, but really you should just buy this game, it’s slow, plays with your emotions, and delivers a fantastic ending that will spin your head around for the next couple of hours. I hope these dev’s keep up the quality they delivered in this walking, jumping discovery game, which I always recommend to people around me. I paid $1.50 for this on a sale it had, but I would gladly fork over another $10.00.  Good day!

Get this game.
No really. If you need a fastpaced, short but addicting game that's playable with 4 of your buds, or some strangers online, this is for you.
Lethal League is comparable to a game of tennis or pong. Except totally insane and chaotic. And you aim to kill your opponent with the ball instead of passing them. While there's order in the chaos, nothing is more fun to get the ball speed up to insane heights and hope you survive.
The game rules and controls are simple and to the point; hit the ball, bunt the ball and jump to avoid the ball, while trying to hit other characters with it. Each of the 5 characters has their own specific special abilities.
There might be a learning curve when it comes to timing your shots and being able to track the ball the faster it goes, but with practice comes alot of fun, and when you master it, it gets EVEN BETTER. It's recommended to play with friends, locally or online, but randoms can be fun too if you find the right guy.
GGPO, this game's online component, is a little more tighter than done with Street FIghter 3: Online edition, altho sometimes you notice people dying yet not, but the game is so fast you don't care anyway and adjust accordingly.
If there's one slight I would give this game: Not too often, It can and will crash at a certain point, persumably one of the characters specials will hit the ball and might crash one of the players out of the game. It's a sad thing too, because other times it won't happen and gameplay flows fine. I'm expecting this to be fixed in an upcoming patch of some sort.
All in all, an excellent fun and simple game that gets deeper the more you get into it, and a great way for a bunch of buds to spend some time smacking each other in the face with high velocity balls.

When I read "A sandbox growing game where you shape the evolution of an alien ecosystem." I got excited thinking I could observe and influence evolution. This game has very little to do with evolution. It is more about intelligent design.
There are 3 tools available to you. Make life happen. Move some dirt. Kill a thing.
I wish I could say something on the gameplay but I had no idea what I was doing most of the time since there is no explanation and most of what I learned was by trial and error while farting out life clouds. It seemed like the yellow power meter allowed you to change conditions in the environment and the purple DNA meter which is filled by killing mature lifeforms which when filled unlocks or "evolves" a new lifeform.
You have no direct control over what you unlock or the specific lifeforms you are seeding so it is difficult to create isolated environments.
None of it matters though. Which "plants" are in the area don't matter except in ecosystem mode. How does sunlight affect each individual organism? I can't tell you and the game won't say much other than unfavourable, tolerable and favourable. Those are the 3 levels of the 9 environmental variables. One of which being love. What does that even mean? What does it influence?
The fact that the game refers to all of the lifeforms as plants inlcuding bacteria and fungi and the lack of understanding of the mechanics of evolution suggests the dev or devs know absolutely nothing of biology.
I don't get it. I don't understand the point of the game. I don't get what I am supposed to do.
If this were being sold as an interactive screensaver as many have described it I could recommend it but it isn't and I can't.

If you like top-down hack'n'slash type games such as the original Zelda games or random maze generated gameplay like in the Binding of Isaac, then this may tickle your fancy.  The Story Goes on [Although Currently in Early Access] is a fun-fast paced game with hidden secrets and unique items.
The gameplay goes very quickly and dying is something I may call a feature to the game: it works like losing lives, but as a throwback to old retro Atari/NES era games, you start from the beginning upon game over.  This however doesn't depreciate gameplay in the slightest since the levels only get progressively harder and getting back to where you died takes mere minutes.
Regardless of that apparent length, purchasing the game will have you playing it for countless hours (I've already racked up a dozen myself in the last week)!  Bugs do come up from time to time, but as an early access game this comes to be expected and I can't really say any have made the game unplayable.  The few bugs there are have come and gone very quickly since the team provides updates almost daily.
Perhaps one of my favorite features about this game is that it's community-driven and community-made.  No, an entire community is not coding the game, but there are forum threads based in game discussion and Google Docs for players to post bug reports, recommendations, suggestions and sometimes supply their own art assets for the game.  The team creating The Story Goes On isn't working alone, and this is one of few Early Access games I feel I actual contribute to in the development process.  In fact, a few achievements, graphical changes and items I suggested have already made it in the game!
This game is certainly worth the minor change you need to shell out for it and it's one that you can pick up whenever you want; no save points, no getting stuck on a hard boss(bosses that spawn are completely random).
You'll never experience the same maze/dungeon twice!

While this was a good game, I don't believe it was a great game.  The combat style, while very cool and fun in the beginning, quickly plays itself out.  The main problem is the lack of variety of enemies.  When you are fighting a robot hoarde, it quickly becomes grindy and difficult when the variety of attacks is so limited and their vulnerabilities are nil.  That is not to say I think they should have gone the route of weaknesses-to-elementals approach, but something at least to switch it up a little.  The other problem I found was the difficulty curve.  It goes from easy fights to nearly impossible fairly quickly.  Some of the characters with the nicer special attacks come in later in the game, resulting in you having to "game" the fights to get those characters to make the final "kill-shot" to get the options for promotions.  Probably, an old RPG cumulative "XP" would have been better than one character getting full credit for getting the parting killing shot off.
The final battle is especially difficult unless you have your characters really leveled up by that point.  Letting you take Rook or Alette out of the mix for the whole game and then requiring that both be in your posse for the toughest battle felt rather short-sighted by the developer.  That being said, since Alette had such horrible specials and was overall mediocre in combat (as well as being whiny, uninteresting, and seemed to have her mouth perpetually open like some gormless mouthbreather), I didn't use her or level her at all, and therefore, was unable to choose her as the one to use the silver arrow at the final battle.  I did like that they did the widowed-father/daughter main characters, as you don't see that much in games or media in general.
Overall, it was a good game with an interesting story, but it may have been a bit too difficult and played out too long for a game that uses the same basic combat against the same basic enemies against the same basic backdrops.

A little history lesson.
A couple years back there was a free game called Ace of Spades. Think of it as a mix of minecraft and old shooters, it was more of a trench warfare type game. Then Jagex came alone, and purchased Ace of Spades. They shut the entire thing down and made a worse paid version, which died rather quickly.
Now we come to this game, it's Ace of Spades again but with a different name and a few new features, even the font is the same! Everyone who bought AoS has been abandoned and now they're cashing in with an entirely new product that could have just been an update to the original.
As soon as the player numbers for this game dwindle they'll end all support and probably work on something else they get make money off of. If this game was free, I would be alright with it. But abandoning a game and a paid update is not something we should be supporting. If you want to play a game like this, play the original at

Grim Dawn is a case of "quantity over quality". This holds true for all of its game mechanics, items, characters and monsters. It plucks ideas from most isometric action RPGs that came before it, munges them together and expects the result to be deep and compelling by virtue of its complexity while doing nothing particularly new or innovative. The game is unbalanced and bland, especially since the RNG is all over the place. It's a heavy grid with a flimsy non-story in an uninspired realisation of the otherwise rich and compelling Warhammer universe.
It sucked me in nonetheless, as these types of games do, but it's just boring and I felt I had done and seen everything before in better, earlier games.

This game is amazing. In my top 5 of all time.
Pros:
-Best part of the game is the character development. If you are interested in theorycrafting, playing through this game will be absolutely delightful for you. It is rewarding and fun to see your build come to life and work! The game also encourages tweaking your build by making it easy to respec (within certain limits). I have beat the game (first difficulty) with 3 different characters, and working on a fourth now. Each build more fun and interesting (and better) than the last.
-IMO my other favorite part of this game is the lore. Seems sort of cliche to say that a game is influenced by Dark Souls, but the way the lore is delivered is definitely influenced by DS (which is one of the best parts of the souls series). You get most of the lore from skill descriptions, which have a way of introducing certain characters that echo throughout the entire game, from skills, items, dialogue options, and more.
-Above point helps the world feel quite full. Tons and tons of secret areas that play interestingly with your mini map. The world building is quite good and synthesis crisp mechanics, character development, and lore for an increasingly rewarding experience. I am a fan.
-The community is fantastic.
Cons
For me the only real flaw is the lack of multiplayer. I actually co-op a lot with friends, specially in the new crucible mode. However the game is clearly not designed for multiplayer, which hopefully will be improved in a DLC.
There also seems to be virtually no PVP, which in some part is the fault of the community, as technically PVP is possible, it just doesn't really happen and isn't a part of the community (from my casual perusal of various forums). However if Crate incentivized pvp it might take off. Would almost definitely not be balanced but would still be interesting to watch a meta develop, and would be fun!
That being said I don't think Crate will add much PVP support because they listen to their community, which isn't really calling for PVP. So I am in the minority here.
I am fine with this because I love the new free content released by crate (new quests, dungeons and loot). Now that the core is down, expect a lot from the new content. I should also add here (so far) the DLC is fantastic and reasonably priced.
TLDR; I love this game and in a few years, after some DLC, I think it will be widely considered a classic. Most importantly it is FUN, which is surprisingly rare in this modern gaming age.
EDIT: DLC was damn good, one of the best ARPG ever.

Beat Hazard is a fantastic little music game that takes music files you have and creates a twin-sticks shooter out of them.
The base Beat Hazard game contains three mode: Normal play, Survival, and Chill Out. Normal play has you selecting a single song, acting as one stage; this includes five different difficulties of play. You have until the end of the song to survive and score as many points as possible. Survival takes a list of your songs and plays them all in succession, the aim being to survive as long as possible while scoring points, ending when you have no lives left. Chill Out mode allows you to casually play along to songs without limited lives, enjoying the game without stress. Chill Out mode also employs the difficulty options of normal play. On top of all of this is an addictive little rank progression system.
With the addition of the Ultra DLC, however, this game becomes a completely different beast. New enemies, new weapons, the addition of perks and an upgrade system, and new multiplayer and Boss Rush modes all amount to being well worth the $5. There are also some smaller changes as well, such as your ship no longer moving with momentum à la Asteroids, which makes the game much more playable, and seemingly some changes to hitboxes.
All in all, I certainly recommend buying the base game, and cannot recommend buying the Ultra DLC along with it. Note that there is seperate DLC for the support of iTunes files, as well. I would also highly recommend a controller.
Edit: I'm back years later, with tons of new music. It's amazing to see a game grow so much without any input from the developer needed. Now I have hours and hours of new content to go through!

edit: This review is old and no longer reflects the game. Changes were made (e.g the addition of ecological elements).
Note that much of this review will involve comparisons with EarthTongue since both have very similar concepts.
The tldr version of this review: Xenobloom’s ecosystem is fun to experiment with, without being burdened by frustrating mechanics found in other ecosystem games (& I’m not just referring to Earthtongue), but Xenobloom lacks interactions (both between creatures & their environment) and behaviors which are one of the things make ecosystems interesting. Xenoblooms ability to modify species is cool but could use more options.
I also would have liked the climate/nutrient-availability to influence what flora grew. Whether or not the lack of explanation for a lot of things is good or bad will likely vary between people (I didn’t mind too much).
Pro-
The currency system for using tools in Xenobloom is better than EarthTongue’s (and other ecosystem games for that matter). In EarthTongue it was “interventions” that the player had to pay a certain amount of each time the player used a tool. The player’s only means of gaining interventions was for them to slowly generate over time. But using tools were so expensive, and gaining interventions took so long, that ecosystems could collapsed before you could even afford to use the tools to maintain the ecosystem; not to mention it made experimenting for fun challenging (which often killed the fun for me).
Xenobloom utilizes a similar system of needing “Power” to use tools, power which also slowly generate over time. Yet, unlike EarthTongue, the player can also obtain “power” from removing soil & flora from the ecosystem or altering the environment to be “less favorable”. This system is much less frustrating, yet at the same time without make it too easy since not waiting means taking away from the ecosystem (at least if your not playing “Experimental mode”).
Xenobloom also allows you to modify the species, something one can’t do in EarthTongue. (However there are only 4 options…)
Con-
Probably the main thing which Earthtoungue has much of which Xenobloom is lacking in is species behaviors and interactions. In Earthtongue species, including flora, had many different behaviors and interact with each other and their environment. In Xenobloom they seem to just spawn in areas that are favorable and die when they’re unfavorable, and the only interactions that I could notice was an implied relationship between all flora & microbes, as all flora die without them.
I don’t think the lack of fauna justifies lack of interactions because in real life flora-like-organisms do interact with each other. Certain plants can utilize their roots and surround fungi networks to share nutrients with other plants. Certain plants, that produce toxins to defend against herbivores, can also release chemicals to alert other plants to the herbivores so that they can release their toxins before herbivores feed on them.  On a more negative side some plants produce herbicides to kill competing plants and there’s also a plants (such as Indian Pipe and Mistletoe) that steal nutrients from other plants. I could go on about many other examples, including flora that’s not “plants” (e.g Vascular-plant/fungi, Legume/Nitrogen-Fixating-Bacteria, Lichen/Algae & Coral/Zooxanthellae) but back to the review. 	Then of course there’s how plants impact their environment (e.g producing oxygen, taking in Carbon dioxide and other gases, recycling nutrients from the soil and etc.)
I think Xenoblooms lack of interactions is a negative thing because ecosystems are “interactions between organisms and their environment.’ Lacking interactions doesn’t really make it much of an ecosystem.
Mixed
I think it’s odd that there’s an ability to alter nutrient availability and climate, yet it directly doesn’t impact what grows but rather the amount and location of microbes that the plants need. I would have liked nutrient needs & climate tolerances were factors in what could grow (and perhaps even be an option in the plant editor).
I also imagine some people might be put off by how a lot of things aren’t explained. But for others it might add to the charm of exploration.

One of the remains of a human village whose mayor was killed in an attack by the evil Dredge (a race of stone people who returned after having thought been vanquished) and a much larger party of giants who originally were tax collectors for the giant king (at least my understanding of the story please correct me if I am incorrect) but then sent on a quest to protect the giant prince who is killed by the dredge.
I'm sure these two parties will meet in the future of the story or entangle each others actions in some way. I am personally excited to find out!

Played through this game today.
It was a beautiful game with a fairly interesting story, although presented in a somewhat bizarre fashion. Sort of similar to Lifeless Planet in this regard. However, unlike Lifeless Planet, this game just kind of droned on. It took me a little less than three hours to complete, and I really wish it had taken about half that. It became a very boring affair going out to basically do the same things over and over with minor changes to your base in between. That actually kind of killed the immersion for me.
As far as the actual gameplay, it was pretty smooth. It's an exploration game, so you really just move about, jumping and when available, using your jetpack to navigate alien planets. You will interact with your objectives, but mostly you just take in the visuals and listen to what also seemed like overly long dialogue.
Now, I dont want to pan this too hard because it is evident that this game was a labor of love, and it definitely had its positives, but overall, I just ended up finding myself bored. The pacing never changes throughout. Just sort of you wandering at what amounts to a casual pace with, as mentioned before, somewhat droning dialogue.
I'd say it is worth checking out when you dont have anything else you'd like to play or simply want an interlude between other games, but I'd also bet you will end up feeling bored like I did.
5 out of 10 for me personally. I'm giving it a no as a recommendation because, like I say, it ends up just being boring.

While I am recommending Corpse, it's with quite a few caveats. So treat this as a"it's good, but wait for a sale" kind of recommendation.
I'm not a fan of writing long reviews, so here are the essentials.
=====In most places, the writing is decent, but a little on the nose now and then.
=====The procedural generation the team used allows them to create a bunch of massive maps that they wouldn't have been able to make traditionally with the same time and budget constraints, but the terrain itself is messy and noticeably inorganic. However, if you allow yourself to play along, then it shouldn't bother you too much, and you'll get to see some cool set-pieces as well.
=====As of writing this, optimization still isn't quite up to snuff, and you'll most likely run into some stuttering issues every now and then, but it's noticeably improved since release.
=====The story itself is pretty interesting throughout, but takes a bit of a predictable route towards the end. Not that there's anything wrong with that, but I personally felt like the ending could have been much more than what it was.
=====Controls were easy to use and understand, and the jet-pack you get three levels in makes traversal of the map a high point of the game. Which is good, since you'll be spending a lot of time going from point A to point B.
Overall, Corpse of Discovery is an interesting game, and I'm glad I played it, but I'm pretty easy to please. It's a decent story, written in a messy hand.

FIrst of all I can only recommend this game if it's extremely on sale. I got this for two dollars, and having played it I think it's a fair price for at least five.
My favorite part of this game is just the exploration, travelling through unknown planets that look awesome yet have very real dangers. It was super immersive......that is when it worked. I had a handful of frustrating moments when I would clip through the floor to my death or get caught in a graphics hole. When I play these games though I understand how difficult it is for a small team to program a 3D game like this, and that you just have to accept glitches like that.
The story was interesting enough to keep me going to find out what happens nexts but it was just underwhelming. The game beats you over the the head with the "REMEMBER YOUR FAMILY!?!?!" shtick in a very ham-fisted fashion. The voice acting from all the family members was poor and unbelievable. Also I'm ninety percent sure that the plot of this game was doing that " I'm purposely vague and abstract so I can pretend I'm being profound and meaningful" sort of thing. I realized halfway that all these weird plot points I was finding were just pointless BS, and it was pretty disappointing. Was the astronaut dead the whole time? Was he picked up and died in a hospital later? Was he just stranded on the planet? Is this all just a dream or a coma fantasy? Who knows, I don't even think the devs did tbh.
A.V.A., your robot companion, was a fantastic character though. Watching her slowly change over each sequence was really awesome. Her dialogue, while not really having a point a lot of the time, was meaninful in characterizing her as a sentient being going through an existential crisis.
So if you like jumping around weird abstract planets in low gravity with  jetpack, you should buy this game. Just don't go into it expecting a deep plot or any sort of clarification or closure on what's going on.

Discloser I got this copy of the game from a promotion from Phosphor Games at PAX 2015.
With that out of the way, Corpse of Discovery is game in vane of Dear Ester but with platforming and exploration thrown in the mix as the game progress.
The story seems simple, you are and Astronaut on your final mission for Discover Corps. You can’t return home to your family till you complete this mission. Your only companion is a Mobile AI that aids you in your mission. From the start your mission is in trouble. Your shuttle crashes and you’re injured. You awake in your sleeping bunk and start piecing who you are and the status of your mission from points of interest within your vessel. You seeming complete your mission only to wake and have the day begin again. With new points of interest, tool/gadgets to use, and different mission parameters on the same planet which is completely altered from the previous day.
I didn’t have any hardware or software problems running settings on the highest level. This isn’t a graphically intense game but very good looking.
This is isn’t going to appeal to everyone. If you ignore all the points of interest other than mission required ones the game is very short.
For me this was a good adventure to play; worlds to explore and mystery that unravels its self as you play.

When 'Lifeless Planet' was anounced about a year ago I was very excited. Exploring an alien planet in a realistic setting sounded like a great premise. Unfortunately the game turned out to be a platformer with a largely empty environments. I also experienced a game breaking bug about 90% through which meant I couldn't finish it.
Corpse of Discovery delivers where Lifeless Planet failed. Its environments are much larger and more interesting and the exploring is about discovery and not about quick, carefully timed jumps from platform to platform. It's story is completely different and for a long time I was left wondering in which direction it would go. The graphics aren't perfect (many tufts of grass hovering in mid air in some levels) but I haven't experienced any significant slow downs and the game never crashed.
The premise of the game is that you are an astronaut who wakes up in a research lab on an alien planet. Your shuttle has crashed and the chances of you surviving are slim. After watching a message from your family you get your assignment and head out of the airlock. After completing your objective everything turns to black and you awake in the same room. This happens again and again. Is it all a dream, is this a virtual experience, is it a psychological test of the CoD or is there something else going on entirely? Much is left up to you, the player, to figure out which might not be everyones cup of tea. But at about three hours of play time it never drags on and I quite enjoyed it. If you can get it on a discount you won't be disappointed.

Always been a fan of PC action RPGs, there's definitely no shortage of them on PC nowadays, some have been great and others not so much.  I'd say Grim Dawn falls more towards the great ones.
Easiest game for me to compare this to would be Diablo 3 since I've played that game the most recently and its freshest in my head.  The loot in this game seems a lot more varied and you need to study it more to see if it'll be a better fit for your character than you would in Diablo.   Also when doing quests Grim Dawn doesn't hold your hand like Diablo does, meaning in Grim Dawn if you're told to go help or find someone, there's not going to be a map marker that you go run off to over and over.  YOu need to listen to the details, figure out where on the map that person/item might be and go find it.  Now yeah when you get really close there'll be a quest marker on your minimap but thats it.
My first criticism of this game would be its difficulty...or lack there of.  I'm no whiz when it comes to ARPGS but I've played quite a few.  I started this game at the max difficulty it allows you to select when you start a game which is Veteran.  I played the main storyline for a few hours, leveled my character all the way up to level 22 and at that point never even needed to stress or use a single health potion while fighting.  Character always seemed rather overpowered.  Past that level I started to get a little bit of a challenge and had to use a few health potions and micromanage my skills a little bit, but the combat definitely isn't as compelling as it is in Diablo 3.
If i could change anything about this game the first thing I would do is to make it harder, or at least unlock the next difficulty tier earlier.
I had received this game as part of the Humble Monthly bundle so I didn't get it for free, but I was really happy with the game and wanted to support the devs some more so I bought their DLC Crucible and it is a great add on for this game.  Gives the game sort of a "rift" feel like the end game content of Diablo 3.  Best part about the DLC for me is it gives a lot more of the challenge that's missing in the main game, but my only gripe is when you go back to your main game the enemies are even easier since you usually come back with much better gear and higher level.  That's okay though because the story missions are fun even if the combat is easy and I know once I unlock the harder difficuties things should hopefully be better.
If you're looking for a fun Action RPG then I'd say this game is right up there with the likes of Titan Quest, Torchlight, and Diablo.  Its fun, loot is great, I like the different classes and skills and I'm sure I'll get many more hours of enjoyment out of this.

It's easy to heap praise on the combat because it's so engaging, and it's certainly a high point in this adventure. That's not what makes Child of Light stand out, though. Rather, it's how confident it is in its own feelings of woe. There are so few games willing to explore that dull ache that I became mesmerized by Aurora's journey, even when I needed to step away from her plight while I regained my composure. Child of Light is a wonderfully realized, somber adventure, and I couldn't be happier that such a game exists.

You control an astronaut waking up on a space station as a recorded voice wishes you good luck with your mission, after listening to a message from your family and your mission briefing you set on the planet while an hovering robot blurts out mission parameters and HR slogans.
The aforementioned story doesn't have to be taken at face value though as Corpse of Discovery wants to use it as a metaphor: while the game has an interesting premise and some good moments its dull gameplay and ham-fisted narrative hold it back.
-the art style is pretty nice
-good soundtrack and voice acting
-the first levels are interesting
-there's a good amount of dark and vitriolic humor that makes you both smile and think
-some dialogues are pretty good and function as high points in the game
-graphics are a bit of a mixed bag, while the levels look from decent to nice the draw distance is bad and there's some noticeable graphical glitches, the framerate can also be dodgy at times
-repetitiveness sets in after a couple levels, this is made worse by the amount of ground you have to cover between points of interest and some instadeath threats that'll see you go back to the previous checkpoint
-the narrative as a whole is pretty awkward, most of the time it's content to just be obscure but when it's time to make a point it comes out as too obvious and cliched
Corpse of Discovery is off to a strong start with its mistery story and weird locations to explore, sadly its attempt at a more active take on walking simulators doesn't always work well: jumping and jetpacking around is quite fun but it eventually grows dull when you realize there's quite alot of space between objectives, even more so if you want to explore optional stuff, and that getting there is for the most part a boring affair.
The story also takes a dive once you realize it's used as a metaphor about something else, sadly it's done in an unoriginal way for the most part: without spoiling anything the point the game tries to make also explains it being deadset on giving you task after task to grind through, too bad this intentional repetitiveness helps the point as much as it hurts the gameplay.
All things considered I can't recommend Corpse of Discovery, a few good points notwithstanding its story and ending were ultimately not good enough to make its dull gameplay worth slogging through over and over.

So, I'm not really a big review writer, but this game is just so, so good that I feel like it deserves the review.
FTL is a rogue-like spaceship game set in a universe during a rebellion. Yeah, sounds pretty much like Star Wars, but in FTL, the rebels are the "bad guys" and you play as a federation cruiser. There are also many other races in the universe besides humans. There are the "Engi" who are naturally great repairmen, due to being made up of nano-bots, but as such are pretty gentle and are not good fighters. The "Zoltan" are allies of the Engi. They are made up of energy, so they can power systems just by being in the room! However, they are pretty fragile. The "Mantis" are a warrior race, made for combat. However, they really suck at reparing (hey, you try to repair a ship with spikes instead of hands!). The "Rockmen" have skin that is textured like rock, and just as hard. They are super tanky, and can stand in and fight fires without being damaged. However, they are pretty slow. The "Slug" are exactly what they sound like, but aren't as slow as a real slug. They are very cunning and shady, and have telepathic powers. The "Lanius" are scavengers that consume metal. They drain the oxygen from the room they are in, but don't take damage from not having oxygen. They also are pretty sluggish. There is also a secret race, but I won't spoil what it is ;)
In FTL, you have to manage a ship, which means commanding crew, firing weapons, and allocating power. You also can upgrade your ship with scrap, or buy things from stores. Some events will force you to make some hard decisions, so be ready!
In FTL, your ultimate goal is to deliver information to the front lines of the war. Of course, that means you have to stay in one piece. Once you make it, you have to defeat the rebel flagship, a monstrosity twice as big as other ships. In order to defeat this flagship, your ship really needs to be upgraded, and that means you need money. Which means you have to fight people.
Of course! There are:
-10 ships to unlock and use, with 2 or 3 unlockable layouts for each ship.
-Very well done aesthetics
-A nice soundtrack
-Infinite replayability
-Easy to learn but very hard to win
-No bugs (that I've noticed)
-A great modding community that has unfortunatley died, but the mods still work and are easy to install
10/10 worth the money!

Always been a fan of PC action RPGs, there's definitely no shortage of them on PC nowadays, some have been great and others not so much.  I'd say Grim Dawn falls more towards the great ones.
Easiest game for me to compare this to would be Diablo 3 since I've played that game the most recently and its freshest in my head.  The loot in this game seems a lot more varied and you need to study it more to see if it'll be a better fit for your character than you would in Diablo.   Also when doing quests Grim Dawn doesn't hold your hand like Diablo does, meaning in Grim Dawn if you're told to go help or find someone, there's not going to be a map marker that you go run off to over and over.  YOu need to listen to the details, figure out where on the map that person/item might be and go find it.  Now yeah when you get really close there'll be a quest marker on your minimap but thats it.
My first criticism of this game would be its difficulty...or lack there of.  I'm no whiz when it comes to ARPGS but I've played quite a few.  I started this game at the max difficulty it allows you to select when you start a game which is Veteran.  I played the main storyline for a few hours, leveled my character all the way up to level 22 and at that point never even needed to stress or use a single health potion while fighting.  Character always seemed rather overpowered.  Past that level I started to get a little bit of a challenge and had to use a few health potions and micromanage my skills a little bit, but the combat definitely isn't as compelling as it is in Diablo 3.
If i could change anything about this game the first thing I would do is to make it harder, or at least unlock the next difficulty tier earlier.
I had received this game as part of the Humble Monthly bundle so I didn't get it for free, but I was really happy with the game and wanted to support the devs some more so I bought their DLC Crucible and it is a great add on for this game.  Gives the game sort of a "rift" feel like the end game content of Diablo 3.  Best part about the DLC for me is it gives a lot more of the challenge that's missing in the main game, but my only gripe is when you go back to your main game the enemies are even easier since you usually come back with much better gear and higher level.  That's okay though because the story missions are fun even if the combat is easy and I know once I unlock the harder difficuties things should hopefully be better.
If you're looking for a fun Action RPG then I'd say this game is right up there with the likes of Titan Quest, Torchlight, and Diablo.  Its fun, loot is great, I like the different classes and skills and I'm sure I'll get many more hours of enjoyment out of this.
