Your (voiced) companion AI and the music were easily the best part of this game, both are fantastic and make the journey worth taking. Another great addition was the gradual platforming that found it's way into the gameplay, making it less of a 'walking simulator' and more of an actual game. The jetpack physics are well designed and an enjoyable way to get around.
With such a strong start, I was hoping for a really great ending or a good twist. Something like Moon with Sam Rockwell or Oblivion with Tom Cruise. Unfortunately, what we get is a family message and a childish lullaby. Despite requiring only 4 hours to complete (some side objectives), I felt it dragged on for the last two missions and could have been summed up sooner. Had the story been stronger, this wouldn't have been a problem.
My personal taste in storytelling is responsible for what I primarily didn't like about the game and despite that I can easily recommend it. The $15 price tag is too much for what you get here, but a sale makes it an easy buy.

This game has significant problems, but has many great ideas and if you can get past the problematic aspects (see later) is could be well worth your time.
It is one of the few Visual Novels where I've wanted to see all of the endings, both good and bad.
The variety in endings is a big part of this game. They are not just carbon copy endings with a different girl (or not), a significant portion of the content of this comes from 9 very different endings (plus 4 more good/bad variants), and very different approaches to get to those endings, but to say more would be a big spoiler, even though there is plenty of "all is not what it seems" signposting.
In interface terms, it's one of the best Visual Novel experiences I've had. The skip mechanism is excellent, only skipping text you've seen before and pausing at the first line of unseen text. Plus you can also rewind, allowing you to go back to just before a decision point to save.
The music is fantastic, evocative and appropriate - it really helps set the scene just as much as the (generally) excellent artwork.
While the earlier endings are really well done, the later endings really do take the game to another level, even the unbuquitous harem ending was an interesting take on the trope.
If heteronormativity annoys you, this game probably isn't for you, it is deeply engrained in it's structure. Having said that, there was one surprisingly 'gay' moment.
There are quite a lot of misogynistic "just a girl" & "girls can't do that" type comments from our protagonist, and lots of "carry my heavy bag" and "act like a man" crap in this game, but I'm willing to give the game a pass given the setting.
The Lena bad ending needs to come with a trigger warning for suicide. The disclaimer at the start implies that there may be triggering content, but doesn't say how to avoid it.
Unless you are using a walk-though, please avoid the Lena route if this might affect you.
The panty shots are annoyingly gratuitous however, especially the sexualisation of the 14 year old Ulyana. Many of them are unavoidable too, so you get flashes of panty every time you fast forward through large parts of the game.

Lethal League is a projectile fighting game that plays like nothing else I know of. To make immediate comparisons, it's like Smash Bros meets Pong meets Divekick, with a lot of emphasis on the Divekick part. The goal of the game is incredibly simple: hit the ball to gain control of it, try to smack it into everybody else. If someone else hits the ball, don't get hit and try to return the ball.
This game is deceptively simple, and I say this because even though the mechanics are limited, the ways in which you use those mechanics are actually fairly deep. You have two main actions you can take, you can hit the ball or you can bunt the ball. When you hit the ball, you can either send it flying straight, or angle it up or down. Bunting the ball will slow it down to its lowest possible speed and pop it in the air, giving you time to place your next hit strategically. Every hit will cause the ball to gain more speed, making it harder to keep track of, dodge, and hit.
But it turns out that there's WAY MORE STUFF YOU CAN DO THAN THAT. There are six ways of hitting the ball: on the ground, you can angle it up, down, or straight forward, in the air you can angle it up, forward, or spike it to the ground. Spiking the ball automatically doubles the speed, so you can cause the ball to get faster multiplicatively by spiking it over and over again. You can also bunt the ball up, forward, backward, or straight down, giving you options on where you place the ball. Hitting a ball at the same time as your opponent causes you guys to clash and bounce off each other. And with the five characters, each one has their own super move, swing speeds, swing arcs, and hitting angles. This game hits every fighting game requirement in respect to its depth, but at the same time it has that appeal that Divekick has of being super easy to pick up.
The music is amazing in this game, all the tracks are taken from independent music creators, and it sets the entire tone of the game really well. Tracks are intense and fun, matching the frantic gameplay. The sound design isn't shabby either, as the ball increases in speed you hear sonic booms, the hit sounds are really nice and snappy, this game loves to bombard you with its really solid sound design.
The art style is really great, too. Well drawn backgrounds that aren't too busy, but are still dynamic and change as the ball moves faster and faster. The characters are really interesting looking and are animated well, and your moves feel like they have weight behind them.
As for the online, it works beautifully. Lag is completely unnoticable, when it works it works well. I did have occasional disconnection problems, but it was pretty negligable as me and my friends could jump back into the game really easily if anything went wrong and pick up with a fresh round.
The only possible complaint you can levy against this game really is that the content is slightly lacking. With only five characters to choose from and six stages, it might leave you wishing for a little more to play with. But all in all, this game is an incredibly solid mechanical marvel that is great fun with friends. I give this a solid recommendation; there's no reason not to have this in your library.

Child of Light is a 2D side scroller with stunning visuals,creative puzzles and simple RPG elements . This game will require Uplay account to start . I personally never had any problems with Uplay but some people do . If you not getting CD key , delet Uplay and install latest version (it should let you in without cd key)
Please note that this game will not run well on integrated graphics unless you have at least low end card build into your computer . Requirments for this game are very low but not low enough to run it on Labtops that are build for internet browsing .
The Story in this game is very generic as some people pointed out in negative reviews . All the plot twists are predictable but my eyes were tearing more than once. It is a same story about princess and stepmother you herd a million times but it does a good job of conveying emotions and setting the atmosphere . Granted you have to like kid stories to fully enjoy this game .
Gameplay is a turn-based combat . It is like old over the top RPG games only in 2D side scroller. You have to run into enemies to start combat so its not in real time . If you played many RPGs I would recommend starting the game on expert mode or it might be too easy . Few boss fights kicked my booty so I had to grind few levels which reminds good old times .
I spotted 2 big flawed design mistakes with gameplay . You will notice that enemies do not have any information regarding their resitances (some are color coded and the other are not ) I made a guide for that if you run into that problem .Also if you use AOE buffs they will only apply to 2 party members that are in the combat ( which is wird because after using a Buffing character you would want to switch to damage character so it defeats the purpose of AOE buff)
There are 7 to 8 characters ( 9 with DLC ) that will be in your party . They all have their own skill trees with passive and active skills . You will need to strategically use each one to beat the game .
Beside gameplay this game is very pretty  . You don't see many big companies do these kind of games and I have to say that Ubi deservs some praise on this one . I mean it looks like you playing inside the painting entire time .
You can play this game with 2 players in a HotSeat . One will control Aurora and the other will control a little flying thing that can pick items , slow down enemies and heal party members .
I don't have kids but if  you have 7-10 year olds maybe it will be a fun activity . This game is pretty much kid friendly .
Overall I would give this game 9/10 for what it is . If you like RPGs,pretty side scrollers and kid's stories then it should be a fun experience .

The Banner Saga tells a truly epic story.  It's not pretentious.  Every person who rises to a challenge sounds like a real person rising to a challenge whose scope should be simply beyond them.  The flaws in the characters feel truly heart wrenching, and the world they dwell in feesl so rich.
The art style reminds me of cartoons from when I was a child, especially obscure ones like David the Gnome.  It feels refreshing to see a game made in this classic style.  Nothing was done to look flashy.  No stupid looking spin moves (there is a spin move for one class, but it looks solid, grounded in the reality of the world), no ridiculous demonstrations of accuracy or .  The art makes the combat feel visceral, and the character's pain feels so much more real because of it.
The game play has a surprising amount of depth to it, especially in hard mode.  What characters you choose changes the way you have to play with them, and there are enough characters of different varieties to have a really different experience each time you play through.
One of my favorite games from the PS2.

First of all, I love this game.  The elemental interactions and the freedom of how to tackle fights and most missions is glorious.  The game's description will tell you more about what's in store.  In the vast majority of situations, I feel very rewarded and have a strong sense of player agency over what I do.
However, this game has a LOT of bugs.  Most of them fairly minor, but there are a lot of them.  Audio that sometimes doesn't play, resurrections that seem to resurrect only the target's armor (which looks absurd), AI enemies that get stuck on occasion, skills that don't work properly on occasion; there are many more than I just mentioned, but the overall experience is so good that they're merely a nuisance and not game-breaking...
...and then (*POTENTIAL SPOILER*):
I tried to Bairdotr's quest.  A major bug still, after the game being out since June, is not fixed.  If I chose to complete the quest one way, the way I wanted, the game decided that I and my co-op player could only have 3 total characters (2 players plus 1 NPC companion).  Since this is unacceptable, we reloaded the save to before the quest was completed, and we completed it in a different way, not the way I wished.  I enjoyed the story behind the quest; finishing it the way I was forced to finish it completed the quest officially but rendered Bairdotr's story utterly moot.  Bairdotr didn't even have anything to say about how I completed it, the quest that was so important to her.
So, to sum, the game is wonderful, but I'm EXTREMELY disappointed that after at least 5 months (the first instance I can see of this bug being reported was in September 2014) this bug has not been fixed.  It feels all the more disappointing because I was enjoying the game so much--I simply had to see what Divinity would throw at us next, and I haven't felt this invested in a game in a long time.  Which is why this bug feels like a cold slap to the face or a punch to the gut.  Simply inexcusable that something this major hasn't been patched.

So I got this as a gift from my friend but this game is a blast to play and here's why.
You have 10 perks to choose which are (Beserker, Commando, Support, Field Medic, Demolitionist, Firebug, Gunslinger, Sharpshooter, SWAT and Survivalist) which each perks have their own benefits. This makes the game have it's own leveling system. As you level up (no matter what perk you using) you will have passive stats as you level up. These vary from Increased Damage to Increased Body Armor. Depending on what perk you're using.
There's a gameplay element called Zed Time which makes the game go slow motion. This will proc if you did enough headshots in a row or did something amazing like having a killing spree without reloading. This can feel overpowered but most likely on newer players, they will never get the full benefits of Zed Time until they've reached Level 25 on a Perk.
Zed Times are practically used for lining up easy headshots or think of a escape time for a short period of time.
Map wise, the maps are great but some aren't. Some are huge, some that aren't. So the maps are meh but you can download community maps so that's great.
Coop Gameplay is the core focused on this game. This game is meant to be played with friends. Playing Solo can be a bit boring as this game relies on repetitive gameplay but seemingly satisfying leveling up system and difficulty scaling.
More players means more Zeds to kill and their health will be beefed up depending how many people are on one server. (Yes, it's not always 6 man, you can find servers that are on 16 man or even better.. 32 man server.)
The optimization to this game is good. As a matter of fact a GTX 750ti with i5 3470 (can be found cheaply on used market) can simply run this game at High Details @ 1080p60 no problem. Nvidia FLEX does require a good GPU (GTX 970 should be enough) to run with Nvidia FLEX.
Keep in mind that in PS4/Xbox One version, they suffer from FPS drops (due to their underpowered CPU) so I highly suggest you buying it on Steam unless your computer can't really run it.
The weapons are also amazing and the animations are fantastic.
But it can't come out good without cons now don't it?
The cons -
The game is super duper repetitive. If you don't like repetitive content then I highly suggest don't buy this game.
This game relies on super grind in terms of XP. So the same as the first con.
The game uses the similar AI Director in Left 4 Dead 2, leaving you with RNG based spawns.
(If you don't know what I mean, a Hard Difficulty and wave 3 can somewhat spawn with Quarter Pounds in that early wave.)
This game relies on "AIMING", so for the love of god don't hate on the game because you can't aim♥♥♥♥♥♥
There are few cons but they are just minors so I didn't really bother putting them here.

So, I'm not really a big review writer, but this game is just so, so good that I feel like it deserves the review.
FTL is a rogue-like spaceship game set in a universe during a rebellion. Yeah, sounds pretty much like Star Wars, but in FTL, the rebels are the "bad guys" and you play as a federation cruiser. There are also many other races in the universe besides humans. There are the "Engi" who are naturally great repairmen, due to being made up of nano-bots, but as such are pretty gentle and are not good fighters. The "Zoltan" are allies of the Engi. They are made up of energy, so they can power systems just by being in the room! However, they are pretty fragile. The "Mantis" are a warrior race, made for combat. However, they really suck at reparing (hey, you try to repair a ship with spikes instead of hands!). The "Rockmen" have skin that is textured like rock, and just as hard. They are super tanky, and can stand in and fight fires without being damaged. However, they are pretty slow. The "Slug" are exactly what they sound like, but aren't as slow as a real slug. They are very cunning and shady, and have telepathic powers. The "Lanius" are scavengers that consume metal. They drain the oxygen from the room they are in, but don't take damage from not having oxygen. They also are pretty sluggish. There is also a secret race, but I won't spoil what it is ;)
In FTL, you have to manage a ship, which means commanding crew, firing weapons, and allocating power. You also can upgrade your ship with scrap, or buy things from stores. Some events will force you to make some hard decisions, so be ready!
In FTL, your ultimate goal is to deliver information to the front lines of the war. Of course, that means you have to stay in one piece. Once you make it, you have to defeat the rebel flagship, a monstrosity twice as big as other ships. In order to defeat this flagship, your ship really needs to be upgraded, and that means you need money. Which means you have to fight people.
Of course! There are:
-10 ships to unlock and use, with 2 or 3 unlockable layouts for each ship.
-Very well done aesthetics
-A nice soundtrack
-Infinite replayability
-Easy to learn but very hard to win
-No bugs (that I've noticed)
-A great modding community that has unfortunatley died, but the mods still work and are easy to install
10/10 worth the money!

The following is copied from my review on
[Disclosure: Game copy supplied by Developer/Publisher]
Corpse of Discovery is a first-person surreal exploration game published and developed by Phosphor Games Studio, Phosphor games have previously worked on the following titles Horn, The Dark Meadow,The path to Luma, WWE Immortals, Man of Steel and World War Z as well as developing console release Heroes Reborn.
“You wake up on a base in a new, unexplored planet. Your landing craft is torn to pieces and your gear is scattered. Why are you here? What is your mission? How will you ever get back home to your family?
Corpse of Discovery is a thought-provoking first-person planetary exploration game located on 6 unexplored planets. As the player, all you know is that to return home, you must complete the mission at-hand for the Corps of Discovery. However, with each mission completed, you’re left with unresolved questions and zero answers.
The game plays very much like a first person platformer of sorts, but as mentioned has heavy exploration elements. The developer has listed the game as a “walking simulator” whilst there is a lot more to the game, that definition is a harsh but fair one. As you journey through six planets you are required to use various tools such as the jet pack to avoid deadly obstacles and/or contend with a hazardous environment as well as avoiding the mysterious shadow wraith-like creatures that kill you on-sight.
On your first day once you wake up you’re surrounded by various items such as photos and drawings, many of the items can be interacted with and give you back story to your character or in some cases your character will also make a comment regarding the object in question. The first order of business is to see if there is a message from home, after that you can explore the various rooms before entering the “main computer” module (command centre) where you are told about your mission. From there you exit the base and are greeted by the friendly A.V.A unit who will accompany you on your mission.
A.V.A gives you a quick recap on the mission as well as any relevant additional information regarding the planet and its environment. As the various objectives are completed she will record the findings usually making some kind of observation while marking the next objective for you. However whilst on your journey additional markers start to appear, which upon investigation A.V.A doesn’t seem to be able to see what you can see. You initially shrug this off as despite her intelligence she is just an AI unit.
The game is deliberately light on length and mechanics. However as mentioned earlier plays a lot like a first person platformer, it should be noted that the jet pack takes a little getting used to. That being said after a while you’ll find yourself reaching various areas and platforms that you wouldn’t have thought that you could have done. In addition, the radiation shielding is used to make the player think their way around the various different obstacles in order to not get burnt to a crisp by the solar radiation is well implemented.
The game does suffer from some pretty bad “pop in” with regards to the graphical assets, there is also some clipping though objects, The only other issues I experienced were two crashes, the first while pausing the game whilst jumping and the second was right before the end sequence, however a quick reload got me right back to where I was. The game is also let down ever so slightly by not having the main character voice acted.
Graphically, the worlds are breath-taking and suitably “alien-looking”. The addition of a restricted view “as though you’re wearing an actual helmet” shows nice attention to detail.  It should also be noted that most of the objectives that the player interacts with are unusual in the way in which they are presented, however by the end of the game it (kind of) becomes clear (deliberately vague to not spoil the game). The soundtrack is full of haunting piano melodies which caused a few goose-bumps. I would like to point out that the pre-menu loading screens (ie where developer/publisher is listed) is one of the funkiest soundtracks I have heard in a long while and made me smile every time I heard it.
Overall, Corpse Of Discovery is highly artistic while rather abstract in many areas, so the game itself as a whole can take a little to wrap your head around, and has a very Interstellar (the movie) feel to it. This game is a little bit special, I don’t do “titles” for my reviews but if I did it would be somewhere along the lines of “games like this are why I wanted to be a games reviewer”. I have no shame in admitting Corpse of Discovery took me through a rollercoaster of emotions from goose-bumps and shivers down my spine to full on laugh out loud moments and all way back to near tears. It should be noted that this game is designed towards a more mature audience, due to its themes. I could write forever about this game, but you really should experience it for yourself as the game truly is beautiful, but as the score indicates it may not be for everyone.
7/10

SPOILER FREE
I picked this up based on Jesse Cox's video on it - it was an intriguing premise and I was very curious to see what was going on within the game's story.
As it states in the game's News/Updates, this isn't a game for everyone. It's an interactive story, a narrative museum or, as the common term these days is, a "walking simulator," in that its focus is on story and creating a certain atmosphere to create a narrative experience with limited gameplay mechanics. That said, the game has a few (easy) jumping puzzles, and a few times I had to spend some time figuring out the path to my next objective. If this isn't something you like, then skip it.
If you enjoy games of this type and a sci-fi plot and alien worlds, then you may want to give this a look.
As said, the gameplay mechanics are relatively simple. Walking, sprinting, interacting. Later on you will also make use of a jetpack. The controls were absolutely fine. I'm not a twitch gamer and I managed fine.
The game's design is very neat, with lots of detail in your little home base (most of it not interactive). The alien worlds are also each unique in their own way and offer a variety of different environments. Each planet seems very large, though I'm uncertain if there's much point to deviating from your objectives too much.
The graphics quality was good on my GTX770Ti. On planets you will find that there's many decorative objects through which you can clip, and some through which you don't - you will learn which is which. Occasionally walls glitch a bit. Unfortunately, there's a fair amount of environmental pop in and even at maximum the view distance seemed a bit short, and on a few occasions I was left wondering if a certain direction would be navigable because I couldn't see if there would be solid ground, a cliff, a ramp etc. I think I would have preferred some fog to obscure the pop in, and perhaps low res models for far off environments to make navigation easier.
The game sets up an intriguing mystery within the first half hour that drew me in rather effectively and provided the motivation to continue playing. While progressing I spun several theories in my head as to where the story was leading. However, I found that by mid-game it was pretty clear, despite a few doubts in the back of my brain.
Most of the gameplay has you chasing objectives on the planet surface, having to figure out how to get there and avoiding obstacles. You can die, but the consequences aren't severe. When you get a new objective, always check if there's a "secondary" in your HUD and check that one, too, to get the full story. Unfortunately, after the original WTF-factor of some of the things you encounter, some of the things you see will become a bit mundane.
The voice acting was a very nice touch, and in the last chapter I had quite a few laughs. The main character is silent except for on screen text. Some of the text disappears quickly, and sometimes it's so long it obscures a fair part of the screen. I wish there had been a different solution for this. Your little companion drone AVA is fairly fleshed out and undergoes her own little character arc.
The game is fairly introspective and in a few ways hit close to home for me. The resolution was IMHO slightly weak. I obviously don't want to spoilt it, but I was more left wondering, how the end would be presented and not what would happen. In hindsight the game functions as a parabel on ... a few topics; again no spoilers.
I finished the game in 5 hours. As with most games in its genre there's little replay value, unless you want to see if you missed any secondary objectives. €15.- may seem a bit steep for that. I don't regret the purchase (it's cheaper than going to the movies), but I can see why people interested in this game may want to wait for a sale.

Very very pretty, but extremely obtuse and unegaging. Play experience best summed up thusly: Frustrated... bored... frustrated... bored.
Maybe a more focused introductory tutorial with more challenging combat? The game kept throwing new things at me, but in the ~5 hours I played, I'm not sure I ever got hit, or even aggroed. The low levels mobs are so easy and the introductory area so chaotic there was never a reason to learn what the skills do.  I joked with my friends, "My ranger can throw a spinkick, but I have no idea why." It didn't feel like I was engaged in combat. It felt like I was waving a damage hose around and things died. I also got lots of "immune" notices all the time, so whatever secondary effects my skills had were not doing anything. What were those effects? Why were the enemies immune? How would I know?
Maybe brand new players don't need to be hearing about things like node investment, building ownership and knowledges. Maybe they don't need to have high level players charging through their midst on carriages. Maybe they don't need to have all chat channels on by default. It clutters an already confusing new player experience, and adds another layer of obfuscation keeping me from getting invested.
I also found grouping with friends to be both difficult and fruitless. It felt like we had to stay very close together or we would quickly and irrevecably lose track of each other. And when we were together, there was no point. There was no discernable difference between fighting enemies together or separately. Our multiplayer experience quickly devolved into one player "driving" through the fetch quests while the rest of us autofollowed.

The graphics performance needs to be drastically improved before I could recommend anyone purchasing this game. I experienced some bad framerate drops, poor texture loading, and I thought there could have been more refinement. The audio is hit and miss with some sounds popping in and out when they should be consistant. The "glitched screen" actually kind of gives you a headache - annoyingly. Epileptics beware.
I'll be getting my refund.
On a good note, the game is VERY promising. If they can clean it up, it will be a great experience. That's just it though, this is an experience game. It's not about fighting. A 'walking sim' if you will. The story however is catchy and I do want to complete this game, just not in it's current state.

A very simple game; yet tons of fun that can last you for ages.

It has a ranking system, which mostly serves it's purpose for showing off especially when you get to the elite rank, from there it's just Elite 1, Elite 2 and so on.
There are plenty of perks to go about. More lives, an extra percentage to all points gained from an enemy, more missiles and superbombs.
It would be nice to have a campaign of sorts with it; but the other modes make up for that with Boss Rush and Survival both which can get very hectic quite fast.
And above all; it plays by your music which is something I thoroughly enjoy. Be it fast paced, blaring rock/metal or something more relaxed and gentle, whatever song you pick, the game changes in what enemies will spawn, how fast they shoot, how powerful your shots are etc.
Worth giving a go if you want to just waste a few hours...or weeks.

This game is trying to combine a 'bullet-hell' arcade shooter with a game that reacts to and changes with a chosen music file, and honestly, it is mediocre at both.
A few specific examples of things I don't like about the game:
- When you die, your ship drops a number of powerups.  There have been many times where I've died early in a level, and ended up better off for it because of the drops (I've even had my score multiplier increase after dying).
- The levels are randomly generated, even with the same song, so high scores per song are basically meaningless.
- As far as I can tell, the only way the game 'reacts' to your music is by slowing down the enemies and your fire-rate (and weakening your weapons it seems) during slow or quiet parts of songs.  A major downside of this, is that for songs that are slow and/or quiet by nature, it is nearly impossible to kill anything because your bullets are so weak and shoot so slowly.
- A side note, if you don't like games with excessively bright and flashing lights, do NOT buy this game.  I have the visual intensity set to 25% and it is still a seizure on the screen.
All that said, if you want an arcade shooter whose soundtrack is your own music library, then this is the game for you.  Although you'd be better off buying a real bullet-hell game, muting the game's music, and playing your own.  If you want a game that generates levels based off of your music tracks, then check out Audiosurf.

First off the art and music in this game are wonderfully done.  It's just a beautiful game to experience from an aethetics standpoint.  On top of that the story is pretty good as well and I'm left looking forward to playing the sequel purely to see how things turn out after the final events of the game.
The parts of the game I'm left feeling more mixed about are the combat and decision making portions.  On one hand I did enjoy the combat...I just felt it got a bit...samey after the up-teenth time doing it.  You get to upgrade your characters, but even at that point there are some characters whose abilities just seem better than others because they're less prone to RNG or whatever.  I might have just been bad at strategizing, which is a fair amount of the combat - some characters are bigger than others or have abilities that affect allies, so there's definitely some thought that needs to go into where you place your pieces on the board during each battle.
I felt like the decisions you make really carried weight - letting people join your group could make your renown  increase at the cost of your supplies not going as far.  Or maybe the people you let join end up causing trouble and you lose stuff as a result.  Those are more minor examples, but overall I felt like the decisions did impact how I played the game a fair amount because I had to decide between buying items to make my fighters stronger or buying more supplies so my caravan didn't starve during our journey.  How your decisions end up playing out definitely does add a sense of unpredictability throughout the game, especially for those few choices that don't end up yielding results until a bit after you've made them - sometimes everything seems like it's just fine until you're getting screwed over yet again...maybe I just didn't learn my lesson the first couple times I got burned.
Regardless of the couple shortcomings of the game, overall it was a pleasant experience.  While the gameplay is solid, it can feel lackluster at times, but the artistry of this game alone should be reason enough to dedicate some of your time to it.

Divinity Original Sin made me believe in video games again.
It may not be perfect, but no game really is. I was not prepared to like a game that is just so.. retro. Not in this day and age. Every other game just rushes you through.. everything has to be on the nose and obvious. Not this one. It wants you to take your time with it. And it will reward you. It even made me want to play the old Bioware games again.
The combat system has to be one of the most entertaining things around. I liked it even better than Xcom's system and didn't even mind a couple of retries on the harder battles. You will die a couple of times, but here it's part of the fun.
Other than the combat, this game delivers a lot. Cool little moments, a very good story that evolves from a murder mystery to much more and of course, the weird, trademark Larian-humor. It's all there.
My personal game of 2014. I hope these devs get to make many more games.

Without getting into specific spoilers, there's a pretty solid analogy being made in this narrative that hit home with me. It's not subtle, which is... perhaps just the roughness of a quick indie-type dev cycle (even if this isn't really an indie title). That doesn't bother me much. It lacks polish, but the core of the thing works.
It's surreal narrative arc with a cycle of progression not unlike Groundhog's Day (the movie), a floating drone assistant that goes through several personality shifts. And it drops existentialist bombs on the regular. The game tells you from the beginning that you will succeed, that your mission is nearly complete, and that you will be reward upon your return home. As one might guess from the cover art, all does not go well.
Also, I'm pretty sure I'm smack dab in the middle of the target audience for this narrative. There are a bunch of details in there that describe things in my life almost eerily accurately, so that's fascinating. The whole tone of the thing is weird and sad, and at the end I felt weird and sad, even though it didn't explicitly tell me to feel that way, so I think the design is working.
It's rough experiment, through and through, but I was compelled to finish. It leaves me wanting to see a new game about this organization and to be able to do more hands-on science in this universe. Also- the LAVA planet is awesome. Just sayin'.

As of 9/2/2015, there's a horrific memory leak in the game (to the tune of ~100KB per second), and the Unity engine starts struggling once the process passes the 3GB memory mark.  Even the beefiest of gaming PCs drop to <15fps after ten minutes of playing the game.  The only way to actually make progress in the game without headaches is to exit and restart the game after every checkpoint... which jars you out of any immersion being offered.
But even if the performance issues weren't present, I still feel like I got beaten upside the head with the story, to the extent that I simply couldn't relate to the main character anymore.  Sorry, but I prefer my Aesops to be a little more subtle.

This game is trying to combine a 'bullet-hell' arcade shooter with a game that reacts to and changes with a chosen music file, and honestly, it is mediocre at both.
A few specific examples of things I don't like about the game:
- When you die, your ship drops a number of powerups.  There have been many times where I've died early in a level, and ended up better off for it because of the drops (I've even had my score multiplier increase after dying).
- The levels are randomly generated, even with the same song, so high scores per song are basically meaningless.
- As far as I can tell, the only way the game 'reacts' to your music is by slowing down the enemies and your fire-rate (and weakening your weapons it seems) during slow or quiet parts of songs.  A major downside of this, is that for songs that are slow and/or quiet by nature, it is nearly impossible to kill anything because your bullets are so weak and shoot so slowly.
- A side note, if you don't like games with excessively bright and flashing lights, do NOT buy this game.  I have the visual intensity set to 25% and it is still a seizure on the screen.
All that said, if you want an arcade shooter whose soundtrack is your own music library, then this is the game for you.  Although you'd be better off buying a real bullet-hell game, muting the game's music, and playing your own.  If you want a game that generates levels based off of your music tracks, then check out Audiosurf.

This game is simply beautiful - from the hand-drawn graphics to the soothing background music. The battle music is epic and reminiscent of Final Fantasy VII. The turn-based combat is nicely unique with the option of using your little glow-worm friend to slow down opponents and heal allies, giving you the chance to get that all important potion or cast in before you're anhilated. Combat is not your usual one-shot-as-you-go, and I admit a couple of the boss fights have taken me a couple of attempts. There is also a nice option to switch out your allies mid-fight to give you the upper edge. Game is not quick to play - the story unwinds slowly as you meet new characters. I've been playing for about 2.5 hours and have only just reached chapter 4/10. The skill/talent tree is also reminiscent of the Final Fantasy games. The puzzles are interesting to complete.
As a bonus, if you're playing this single-player, you also get to control your little friend too, which can be a bit tricky to manage both to begin with, but you soon get the hang of it.
The only downfall I found was the jumping - until you recieve the ability to fly, the jumps are very tight and can be difficult to make with a controller as I couldn't quite get the right diagonal key-press. I found myself putting down the controller and using the directional arrows on my keyboard to complete the jumps - much easier. This, obviously, is no longer an issue once you gain flying.
Overall I give this game 10/10. It's fun, quirky, engaging, and not over-simplified. And guys - don't dismiss this game as being girly. Give it a try, you never know you might like it!

Game: Beat Hazard Ultra
Genre: Music Shooter
Developer: Cold Beam Games
System: Steam (PC)
Total Score: 88/100
Value Score: 8.8/10
• Story: */10
o The game has no storyline whatsoever.
• Characters: 8/10
o There are no actual characters in the game but the objects within the game feature themselves as a type of character. You have several types of enemies with all sorts of appearances and attacks that come in many forms and shapes. There are about 3-4 different type of bosses each with unique form and attack. There are also mini boss versions of the bosses. There's also the player character or player characters if you go multiplayer. UPDATE - There are more ships now to play as than before and now the option to play as community created ships makes the selection quite appealing.
• GamePlay: 10/10
o The game is like a Japanese side scroller shooter which you play as a vehicle and destroy objects that come towards you in the form of meteors, debris, enemy ships, or just giant creatures. You must destroy them to get points and power ups which can do a multitude of things such as a multipler which can increase your score, a P power up which increases your attack power, a VOL power up which increases the volume of the music (in which affects your basic shooting attack pattern and burst shot). You can pretty much use the built in music collection or import your own tracks to play in the background of the game. The music affects your shot attacks, affects the enemy presence and how some power ups are distributed or appear - it is all based on Rhythm or the beat of the game. You have the choice to play single player, multiplayer, boss mode (which you fight bosses non-stop), or even the ability to play the classic Beat Hazard game upon start up for a different visual appearance and different UI. There are ranks which you can achieve based on raking up points from each game you do along with the fact you can unlock/use bonuses in the form of perks you can equip to make things interesting such as increased difficulty or giving you a boost of power in the beginning of a game.
• Graphics: 7/10
o Although the game isnt as graphic intense as most other recent games the game shines at its own creativity. The music itself develops the intensity of the lighting and special effects - depending on the rhythm different colors and splashes may occur which adds variety to the game and gives you a adrenaline rush feeling. However its best to stay back otherwise you'll have a high chance of getting a Seizure (as the game warns you as well when you start it).
• Sound: 7/10
o The game has basic sound effects for explosions, attacks and going through the menu. It feels and sounds like you are literally in a early 1990s or a late 1980s game which is quite nostalgic. There are no voice overs or anything unless you count what you hear in the music or the built in radio.
• Music: 10/10
o The game features a set of tracks already built in along with some radio stations for players who have no music on their computer. The reason why this aspect receives a perfect score is the ability to add your own music to the game which is the ultimate option for this aspect.
• Length: 6/10
o Because the game consists of a side scroller shooter with limited music (and you can add more music) with no direction or storyline the game's length is quite minimal. There are ranks and bonuses in the form of perks you can unlock however should only take you no more than 3 hours to get everything unlocked. UPDATE - Due to the inclusion of the Shadow Operations DLC - there's more to unlock in terms of content (ships) and ranks.
• Replay Value: 10/10
o Although the game has no direction, it allows you to pave your own direction with the ability to put your own music you can play this game and get a different result each time you play. Every game is absolutely different. If single player isnt enough to satisfy your hunger you can do multiplayer co-op or even competitive. There's also boss mode and of course you add music tracks of your own to change up the pace of the game. You can also unlock additional difficulties through perks.
• Player Value: 10/10
o This game is absolutely recommended especially for fans of the music genre, love music and loves shooters. The game is also a great multiplayer experience as you can play all the modes in competitive or co-op (this includes the boss rush mode). You can import your own music or use the built in music or radio stations to give you a different experience each time you play. This is a great game for both hardcore fanatics who want to brag about points or compete with each other and super casuals who just want something to spend time on even if it is for just one game.

***Contains Spoilers for the TV show for the penultimate episodes of Season 3 onwards***
Game of Thrones - A Telltale Game Series is a point & click adventure games from the legendary Telltale game studios. In GoT - ATGS you follow the story of the House Forrester, a relatively small Northern house who reside in Ironrath. The lord of House Forrester was killed on the night of the Red Wedding and as you play through this game you will see how House Forrester struggles to survive in Westeros' new political climate brought on by the death of the King in the North.
Do not expect this game to be an introduction to the world of Westeros, the game begins on the night of the Red Wedding (Season 3 Episode 9) and there is no explanation of events that have taken place. This game is meant only for those who have seen the show and/or read the books.
This review has been written based only on the first three episodes which are currently the only ones available
+Telltale have stepped away from their usual cel-shaded graphics and have opted for a watercolour art style which looks nice but doesn't come without issues (more on that later)
+As is expected from Telltale the voice acting is fantastic and they even have some of the actors from the show in the game
+Despite the game focusing on a relatively unimportant house we still get to see some of the show's main characters such as Tyrion Lannister, Jon Snow and Danaerys Targaryen
+Relatively interesting plot
+As is expected from Game of Thrones there is more than one protagonist followed by the narrative though they are all members of the House Forrester
+It's easy to relate to the main playable characters and they're very likeable
+Some nice fight sequences which I really enjoyed playing
+Some shocking deaths and it capture the brutality of GoT well
+Decisions have to be made in a matter of seconds, puts a lot of pressure on the player
+Provides more content to enjoy for Game of Thrones fans which can never be a bad thing
+Good atmosphere and the first episode specifically has a lot of tension
+Nice music which fits the game very well
+Six planned episodes instead of Telltale's usal five
+/-You follow a small and, in the grand scheme of things, a unimportant house. Don't get me wrong the story is interesting and it's nice to follow a lesser known house but personally I feel like the politics of Game of Thrones between the larger houses which is what makes GoT so great (in my opionion) is completely lost as House Forrester only interacts properly with one other house which is again quite small
-Your choices have very little to no impact on what happens in the game
-For some reason there's a lot of blurring with the new art style which is not only distracting but also makes it hard to see at some points
-
(Season 4 spoiler)
-Controls feel pretty clunky
Verdict:
8
Game of Thrones - A Telltale Game Series provides a good story in an excellent universe and manages to, for the most part, capture the spirit of GoT. This is in no way TellTale's best game but it's still a must buy for fans of the TV show and/or the books.

Astounding game thus far. An amazing piece of the Divinity series. I highly enjoy this game, for several reasons.
*IMPORTANT NOTE: THIS REVIEW COVERS SINGLE PLAYER ONLY, I haven't gotten to the multiplayer yet*
*TL;DR at bottom*
Pros:
Characters, by you:
The game prompts you to create two characters when you start the game. This seems odd at first but soon makes sense. The game's options of customization are somewhat limited, but even if you don't like how they look now, you don't have to start a whole new game. Later in the game you get access to a special place where you can change your appearance for free, as many times as you want, forever.
Skills abound:
The game has several skill trees, and you can freely chose what skills you want to use from them providing you have the level to do so. The game has several pre-made classes, but these are really in title only. You can make anything you could imagine. Want to be a necromancer who can heal his allies? Invest in Witchcraft and Hydrophist and you're off to a good start. Want to be a powerful warrior with range weapon capabilities? You can do that. You want to be a spellcaster who can summon powerful beings of all shapes and sizes, and blow up his foes? Yup, that one too. Use your imagination.
The best part? You don't have to be very skilled in a spelltree to learn a high level spell, just a certain level. This is offset by the increase in cost of the spell, but that can be managed to a point.
Explore, divide, and counquer:
Explore multiple parts of the map at the same time! Divide your party and take them different places. This can sometimes even be neccessary, as some puzzles require you to be in two places at once. And early game, you get an item set (I won't say what) that allows instant teleportation from one to the other, so if one person in your two groups is carrying one, you can quickly and easily teleport to the other, either to help in combat or to escape from it.
The game is a real puzzle grinder. Your journal starts pretty empty, but start talking to people and it fills up quick. Your map is also great, you can place markers on it that you can give custom descriptions of an area if you need to come back or is of some importance.
Got a chest you can't open? Mark it.
Enemy you can't kill yet? Mark it.
Puzzle got you stumped? Mark it.
Like a certain shop? Mar... you get the idea.
Oh did I mention waypoint gates? They are everywhere and you can teleport to them freely. Forever.
Combat, the good stuff:
The part you love, the part that you live for. Combat is a turnbased RTS hybrid. You have action points, and everything you do costs some points. Moving, attacking, using items, and casting spells all take points. There are a plethora of things you can do, and you have all the time in the world to think about it. Choose your actions with care, as there is no undo button.
Even the terrain can be used to your advantage. Cover an area with oil, and it slows enemies. Light that oil on fire, and watch em burn. Then, use a poison based spell on the burning ground and it creates a poison cloud, which also explodes when exposed to fire. And that's just one combo. You can do more. So much more. Coat them in water, shock them with electricity. Be creative, it can be rewarding.
Just watch out for lava. Touch it and die. No, seriously, don't do it.
As with all games, there are some downsides (hey you find a perfect game, let me know. I'll contact the hospital for you)
So, here we are.
Cons:
Characters, just not quite there:
The (current) options for how your characters look is somewhat limited. Mods obviously will increase these, and the developers may also release more over time. Some people aren't huge fans of mods, so those who aren't, this is a downside. The characters have voices you can pick, but they, too, are limited. Again, mods may help, but here it would be less so.
Shopping (Highway robbery):
You might think this extreme, but it isn't. The game provides you with the ability to trade with anyone (and I mean anyone). Of course, most people don't have much, aside from shopkeeps of course. Don't neglect to barter with people tho, you never know....
The shops are priced VERY high. The most basic stuff is easily over 100 gold at the start of the game. The ressurection scrolls, for example (a staple item), costs anywhere from 200-300 gold. Potions aren't much better, the lowest health pots selling around 130 gold apeice. Now I'm on normal difficulty, so maybe the prices are jacked up somewhat, but even then, I'm still skeptical.
Levels and Skills (where are you?):
Leveling in this game is challenging. The monsters don't respawn, so no grinding. Much more realistic IMO, but does make getting EXP difficult. Granted you get EXP doing almost everything, but only once. Oh, and dead characters don't get EXP when an enemy is killed, so if someone dies, you'll want to try to revive them ASAP. Levels are pretty far apart, but make a huge difference per level. This goes for your enemies as well; if they are 2-3 levels higher than you, expect a hard fight.
Skills are also hard to get. Most are found in shops, and you do find skill books lying around or dropped by enemies. However you often don't get a skillbook you can use, as it's random and doesn't skew towards your selected expertise. While there are many skills in game, you can only know a few at a time. One level in a skillset lets you learn any skill, but only 3, and high tier skills cost more action points due to low skill. Skill books are consumed on use, and if all your slots are full, you have to forget a skill to learn a new one. But that forgotten skill is lost forever.
Yeah not how I would have done it. Also, since all skills are cooldown based rather than mana (which has it's own pros/cons) you can find yourself in a bit of a jam. This is alleviated somewhat by scrolls, but only to an extent.
Combat, the cruel mistriss:
Combat is unforgiving. You have to be carful how you click your mouse as you can accidently fire a skill on the wrong place/target. Magic is friendly fire, so if you fire a spell at an enemy and you hit an ally, they get his the same way. Enemies too, as you can try to heal an ally but, opps, you clicked the enemy and now they are healing.
Sorry, my bad. Didn't mean to make your job harder warrior.
Enemies can mess up as well. A few times I've seen the AI attack me and the arrow strike hits an obstacle. This doesn't happen often, but does happen. Don't count on it tho, cuz they correct their errors quickly.
TL;DR version:
The good:

As a huge fan of George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice And Fire book series and Telltale's other titles The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, I was really looking forward to this title. However, I've found myself more and more disappointed with each episode I've played. I wanted to reserve judgment until the first season was complete, but playing the game seems more like a chore that I have to force myself to complete.
The first, and perhaps the most obvious negative, are the graphical capabilities. Telltale's games were never very impressive in the graphical department, but the Walking Dead was at least adequate, and The Wolf Among Us had some great art direction and used a bright, attractive set of colors. This game, however, fails to reach even a mediocre level. It has a similar style to The Walking Dead, but the textures are far muddier and at a lower resolution. The colors are unattractive; the artists seemed to rely on only a mixture of earth tones. It's not inspired artistically, and it's inadequate technically. Perhaps the artists felt too constrained by being forced to live up to the style of the HBO series. Whatever the reason, the game looks very poor, and it strongly affects the experience in a way that I didn't expect it to.
This leads me into the bigger problem with the series: Everything in the game seems grating and unpleasant. I play video games for entertainment and escapism, and playing this game is simply not an enjoyable experience. The beauty of A Song Of Ice And Fire is that things feel real despite it being set in a fantastical world. People are human and make choices that often best serve their own interests. It's somewhat cynical, but events occur that feel believable, which is an incredible accomplishment when you're reading about people living through decade-long winters and dragons. Terrible things sometimes happen to good people in the real world, and A Song Of Ice And Fire reflects that. The good guys don't always win, but when they do, it's special. The tragedies make the heroic moments all the more enjoyable. You find yourself grinning from ear to ear and pumping your first when a character you love finds good fortune or acts heroically and things go well. It's all about the payoff.
The problem with this game is that so far, throughout the three episodes of this series, only torturously terrible things have happened. There has not been a single moment of triumph. It actually damages any feeling of suspense or tension the designers are trying for, because I've so far been taught by the game that no matter what decisions I make, something awful is sure to happen because of them. Im fact, I'm not even positive that you can avoid any of the terrible occurences from taking place, as I've replayed some sections and made different choices and had nothing change. The same people still die, the same people get angry with me.
About halfway through the third episode I found myself deliberately making the most aggressive choices possible despite their likelihood of leading to poor situations for the characters, and when I stopped to consider why, I realized that the game had trained my thought process to expect the worst, and thus attempt to get it over as quickly as possible. This is a very bad thing for a game, and playing through these episodes feels utterly masochistic. Literally nothing good has happened to any of these characters through three episodes. They die, they become grievously wounded, they're insulted constantly, etc. It's all absolutely punishing with zero payoff, and my desire to continue playing wanes with each chapter Telltale releases.
In conclusion: What makes A Song Of Ice And Fire so enjoyable despite its bleakness are the monumental triumphs of characters you've grown to love in the face of so much violence and despair. The writers of this game series simply do not seem to understand this, and as a result playing this game is an incredibly unpleasant experience. Everything about it is unremarkable at best, and ugly and unattractive at worst, from its graphics, to its characters, to its plot.
As the first season of this series is yet to be completely released, I will edit this review upon my completion of it. If I can manage to force myself to complete it, that is.

In my opinion Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is a great RPG with good combat mechanics, a great story, an interesting crafting system and a lot of references to anime and games. It doesn't take itself seriously and breaks the fourth wall more than once and makes you smile a lot. It can get a bit grindy in the mid game but it didn't bother me because I focused on crafting and questing in that rather short segment. It offers a good replayability because of new dungeons you might have missed or skipped due to a lack of ingredients to craft it, stronger enemies to fight which you couldn't bring down in your first playthrough and therefore new Ingredients to craft better gear and more dungeons. It also includes plans in the crafting system which adat the difficulty. You are able to begin another cycle on your completed playthrough with the same levels, ingredients, plans and unlocks you finished the game with, and the story doesn't get in the way on your second playthrough because you can skip the dialogue/visual novel parts and cutscenes.
In the end you always find something to do: farming, grinding, questing or crafting. It is well worth your money if you like to be entertained, to struggle, and to explore.

After playing this game for over 100 hours, I can definitely say without a doubt that this game is worth trying out.
The story was very enjoyable to play through. It does not take itself seriously and that is what I love so much about it. It dives into a topic that all gamer can relate to, The Console War. It's both stupid and fun at the same time and the game capture that feeling almost perfectly with its hilarious story line and sometimes literally laugh out loud moment. Storywise, this is the strongest part of the game without a shadow of a doubt.
The game is a tactical strategy turn-based game where each character takes turn positioning themselves in the best way possible to deal out maximum power to as many enemies as possible. Dealing damages to enemies will fill up your "EXE gauge". After it is filled you are allowed to unleash some really powerful attack that will decimate your enemies in very stylistic ways. You can also create something called a "Game Disk" where you can burn multiple chips with various perks to help you in combat. It's very useful to get the hang of this system early on as it can help you from anywhere as increasing your EXP gained from battles to healing and replenishing your HP and SP. You can also mix and match different characters as each have their own passive abilities that will boost and help their teammates in battles. This is very important because not only are you gaining passive abilities but by putting certain characters together, you can unlock certain moves that are almost twice as powerful and effective. This leads to multiple ways to play the games. Gameplay wise, it is also solid.
Graphically, this is the weakest part of the game. It was ported from the PS Vita and it really shows. The textures look terrible and there is very little customization that you can do in the game when it comes to the video setting. The details are bland and are very unsatisfying to look at. Not to mention this game reuses A LOT of enemies and dungeon making it worse as you are constantly looking at the same five or six design being stretch out to over thirty areas of the game. The enemies have very littles varieties from each others that are within their own species. It is very littles changes that just scream laziness. This is the one department that you need to really worry about and take into consideration when deciding to purchase this game.
It was very hard for me to write that last part because I really love this game. And anytime there is a big flaw that is in the game you love it just really suck. But, if you are willing to look over the graphics and the disappointing varieties of dungeons and enemies in the game I think you can honestly have a great time with this game. My recommendation is to buy the game on sale if you are still unsure. That is what I did. I bought it for $8.99 and I don't regret a single thing. I think this game warrants a chance to be play. Even if you don't like it, you can just refund it and get your money back. So, what are you waiting for? Give the game a chance!

This world feels alive. There's so much to do (and so much money to earn!). BDO started out feeling like a typical MMO with some unique combat elements, but it's more unique than it lets on. You're not just building a character, you're building an empire.  You level primarily from killing mobs, quests instead are more useful for their Contribution Points which allow you to unlock Nodes along the world map. In towns you can rent lodging and hire workers to work in town, or outside it in one of your nodes if that node supplies something. As you gain points you'll find yourself creating a vast network of nodes that allow you to earn money and trade at greater prices with farther reach. You'll also setup workers to generate items that you can turn into money, essentially creating a passive income network.
The gear system is not for you if you're into endless drops in a Diablo-esque gear party, BDO is instead focused on taking a piece of gear and upgrading it. You invest resources and at higher levels have a chance of losing progress/harming items as you attempt to upgrade them. You can also just buy already upgraded items off the market. It can be frustrating, but honestly it makes upgrades feel super special and the simplicity has an elegance to it that I find charming.
The game can be kept running in tray while you AFK fish or process items in crafting. You can also auto-loop a path on the map for leveling up your horse or carrying weight.
Yes, there's weight in this game! You can be carrying too much. It adds depth to cost/profit prediction and logic. You'll value storage space, and suddenly packs on your mount are a god send. Ever wondered how in RPGs people transport millions of heavy gold/silver pieces? Well in BDO that's a factor. If it sounds annoying, it's not, as suddenly the storage in each town/hub becomes an asset cache to be put to work. You can also convert cash to gold bars and invest them.
PvP Is a big part of BDO. Guilds war over nodes which they can control. Nodes generate tax revenue. The longer a guild runs a node the more stable/happy it is the better it is at generating revenue.  Much of the endgame focus is on building your fortune and PvP.
The combo system in BDO is what makes the combat feel unique. Abilities can be triggered using key/mouse combos like shift+lmb and certain moves combo with other moves creating a symphony of pain and death for your enemies. A well executed string of moves is pretty to look at and savage in damage.
I'm really enjoying BDO. You might say I'm hooked - and unexpectedly. It has a lot of depth and it's still revealing new things to me every day, and I have heard from players playing longer than me it's still revealing new things to them. There's a lot to explore and the exploration is part of the fun.  If you're looking for a new MMO experience, you enjoy resource management, and don't mind a bit of a grind - please try BDO. Take your time and don't let it scare you away, it's fun and not as overwhelming as it first seems.

I played with the expansion Enemy Within, which is well worth it, it add lots of contents.
Overall i like the game, it's a very good tactical turn strategy game.
What i like about XCOM:
>Diversity: good amount of customization of your soldiers, class and squad composition
>Gameplay: the game took me some time to beat in normal, and is really hard in classic difficulty, i lost more than once. they added a reasonabile variety on the type of mission you can undertake, and some side objective have randomized position. This combined with the large selection of maps mean that you cannot spam the same strategy over and over, and have to think before you move your soldiers. A single mission take from 30m to 1h to complete.
I also liked the strategic decisions involved in the research and base management.
>Campaign: i like how the campaign is handled overall, it will take you probably about 30h to complete the first time you manage not to lose
>Difficulty: This game is hard. It's made harder the first few playtrough by the lack of knoweldge on what you should research first and how the finer points of combat are handled. The difficulty still does not feel unfair, when i lost, it was because i made some wrong decisions along the line, and once you lose some missions, some of your veterans and some supporting nations, thing start to snowball until you lose.
What i didn't like about XCOM:
>Bugs: There are several bugs here and there that make the experience worse. Especially on multiplayer. Example: If you play on classic ironman with tutorial on, about 1h into the games, the tutorial ask you to click on a prompt instead of clicking on a building. If you do that, the screen bug out. If you quit and load, the ironman saved an action you did, but the tutorial expect you to do it again. long story short you lose the save file, with no recovery aviabile.
Example2: in the map fury, the audio is bugged, and the music will ignore your audio settings, again very anoying.
Example3: sometime in multiplayers, one of your soldiers will bug out, preventing you from taking action that turn.
>Camera: i find the camera fiddly to use, it happened more than once that i clicked expecting a soldier to move somewhere and instead he moved in a place in the background, leading to said soldier horrible death. The camera force me to always carefully check the path of the soldiers, which is annoying.
>Enemy spawn: The enemy in the maps spawn in pack in random position and start moving once you spot them, it doesn't seem bad, but if you play you'll find out that sometimes on pack will activate 2 or 3 nearby packs at once. Using ghost equipement you can abuse the artificial stupidity to have a much safer and trivial mission, because they wont start shooting until you see them AND they see you.

In the game industry of our world we have seen countless companies come and go, bringing us amazing consoles, epic games, and so much enjoyment and innovation. From the simple joysticks and clunky cartridges of the past, to the sleek disc-based consoles of today, videogaming over the ages has told a rich and and storied saga. Now imagine if you will, a world where people live and die based on the market shares of their respective game comnpanies. A world where software pirates and modchip makers are the scourge of the seas. A world ruled by digitally deified divas who symbolize the hopes and dreams of their console nations. Welcome to the digital frontier of Gamindustri!
Released last year on the Playstation Vita, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 has now been ported onto the PC, and is offered for sale exclusively on Steam. The entire experience is here, with all the trimmings (including plenty of DLC to buy!). Sadly it's been a little clunky so far, with many issues popping up here and there, but Idea Factory has been fast to listen to fan feedback and fix everything up! Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 marks the fourth outing for the series, and though it may be a reboot it is also the longest, most hilariously off the wall and over the top game to grace the series yet. If Hyperdimension Neptunia mk2 was considered a reboot of the original, then perhaps that makes Hyperdimension Neptuinia Re:Birth1 a reboot of a reboot! This literal rebirth of the original game takes the original story, polishes it up a few notches, and sticks it on top of the gameplay system that made Hyperdimension Neptunia: Victory so great.
To be brutally honest, the original Hyperdimension Neptunia for PS3 was an absolute soul-breaking slog, with hours of grinding and frankly boring combat dragging the experience on. The only saving grace was its story, which made the most of things with its masterful console war allegory. Thankfully having been moved over to the gameplay stylings of Victory, Re:Birth1 is propelled high and above its clunky progenitor. With the far more exciting battle system on offer in this entry, traveling through the games myriad dungeons and leveling up no longer feels like such a chore. Unrestrained by the formerly boring gameplay, the story is now free to take center stage.
When it comes right down to it, Re;Birth1 is STILL a shining example of that the series can offer. The PC library could definitely use more JRPG experiences like these, as it's mainly been a bland morass of western RPGS until now. I for one would gladly go for every Neptunia adventure again if they were to be ported to the PC. Now get on Steam and buy this awesome game, or I'll send Iris Heart after you!

You'll often find yourself haphazardly sprinting about when you get to a slower part of a song and your screen becomes approximately eighty percent space junk and asteroids (which are extremely annoying and often not worth shooting due to the chaos it causes), and a faster ship without the slipperiness of the original would have been perfect.

I don't remember how I was introduced to the prototype, but I shared it with my housemates and we've played hours worth of games over the course of the last six months. The simplicity, the visceral feedback, and the mindgames are what really make this game special. You can learn all the mechanics there is to learn in about 2 minutes, but what really takes a long time is learning how to read your opponent, what they're going to do and how to prepare for you. TotalBiscuit criticised the art style, but I have to disagree with him - The Boombox culture of south central los Angeles personified in cartoon form is a really fresh direction for a game to take. Maybe the palette has been exaggerated and might be a bit noisy, but I'll be damned if every single hit, every single return of the ball with the little flash particle animations isn't an instant dopamine hit.
TL;Dr - simple game with a lot of strategic depth, great music, fresh art, solid mechanics. Recommend to everybody, I hope the guys at Reptile make millions of dollars.

I'll list my complaints first because that's usually what people look for in reviews.
1. The crafting system is pretty unintuitive and not very creative. All you do is drag one item over the other and it creates a product, so literally all you need is 2 items to make something.
2. If you misclick because the enemy was moving around too much in his idle animation and issued a move command instead of attack, you can't cancel your move command.
3. The god damned NPCs keep repeating the same phrases over and over... you can't exactly mute dialogue either because you'd still hear their echoes even though their voice is silent.
4. Stealing makes the game way too easy early on; you can get 20k+ gold before you even hit level 4
5. Some skills/traits/talents are completely obsolete, such as choosing between altruistic and egotistical. All reputation does is give you better prices when bartering with someone, so that +2 reputation is garbage compared to +1 bartering.
6. There are 4 characters you can have in your party, but max players for co-op is 2, unless you get the mod that unlocks the 3rd and 4th slots for others to join.
Now, for the positives
1. There is no class system; you can literally build your character in however way you want it.
2. The game doesn't hold your hand; you simply pick up quests and figure out how to do them. It's not like "go to this location pinpointed exactly on your map and do this for me." I mean♥♥♥♥♥♥ if they knew exactly how to do the thing they requested you to do, why the ♥♥♥♥ would they send you on that quest to begin with?
3. I usually hate turn based combat, but this game actually makes it really fun with the variety of abilities your characters have.
4. Everything is RNG like a true old school RPG. Loot has random stats, henchmen have random talents, etc.
5. Lots of references, riddles, and secrets, which makes exploration feel like it's worth your time.

I thoroughly enjoyed playing this game - it has strong appeal to those of us who love a true turn-based combat system that makes every combat a strategic endeavor. The use of the various elements in context was a ton of fun, and every battle seemed to feature a few different ways to win. The storyline is fun and engaging, with plenty of sidequests to go alongside the main plot. This game was a throwback to some old school RPG days where certain puzzles gave you very minimal hints and you certainly never were led by the hand to easy completion in some spots (and the trusty internet can always bail you out if you're really stuck). I also enjoyed the crafting elements of the game, though fair warning, the game really requires you to experiment here - there are very little in-game guides on this (there are a ton of craftable materials and options, but only a limited few are described in-game). My only mild complaint (and this is a minimal one) was that there seems to be a lot of "junk" items that really are not needed and only serve as clutter (gear, weapons, books, ingrediants), especially after you cross roughly the mid-point of the game. I strongly recommend this game to those who enjoy a good RPG challenge and engaging, entertaining, strategic combat. Hack-N-Slash and lead-you-by-the-hand quest lovers, this one may be quite different than what you're used to.
Also, one side note: I played my two main characters as a mage and rogue. I don't typically go for rogue-types (most RPGs make this role far too weak compared to other options), but Divinity:OS realy nailed it on the rogue in this one. He was a ton of fun to play, brought a very real, huge benefit on the battle field (sneak/backstab is incredibly effective), and could shoplift a lot of useful stuff early on when gold is short. Highly recommend fitting a rogue in your party if you play this one....

Good VN, bad JRPG.
I like having the VN style cutscenes mixed in with an actual game, but the actual game part isn't very good. It is maybe 10% actual content and 90% grinding out items and XP. As long as you do all the side content, you will be leveled enough for the story missions, but if you skip out on the grinding you will be incredibly underleveled when you get to the next boss.
Most of the side content involves grinding out items for the crafting system. There are also repeatable missions, all of which are generic collect X items or kill Y monsters. When grinding out the items you need for you plans it is a total pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to keep track of what you need since nearly every reskinned enemy drops a unique item, so there are hundreds of possible items to use. You can look up monters to see what they drop, but that just means scrolling through dozens of enemies looking for the item you want. Then just do that a hundred times for all the plans you get.
The enviroments are not very good looking and there are maybe 10 different enviroments, with most zones just being some slight remixes. The enemies too are just a lot of reskins as well as just straight up reusing previous enemies.
It took be over 40 hours to do most of the content, but it feels like there was less than 10 hours of game on there. I like it for all the reasons that other people list, but I can't overlook all the bad qualities. If you cut out most of the crap it would be a good 10-20 hour game, but as it is it is mostly wasted time.

I like it because It's a game that rewards clever tactics, and adaptability. It's my first rougelike game, so I'm not really sure how the rougelike aspects hold up to others in the genre, but the randomization forces you to adapt your tactics to whats on hand, which keeps the game fresh, and allows you to get creative without having to worry about the optimal loadout. Which is not to say it's rut free, your average battle involves alpha striking the opponents shields, taking out their weapons, and then pounding the defenseless ship into scrap. However that's not all fights, and it's the fights where your back is to the wall that the game really shines. Failure is always an option, one lucky or unlucky hit, can send you back to the start screen, your never to big or bad to get crushed.
I remember one game where I hit a mantis (aliens that excel in boarding actions) cruiser, and the battle is going pretty well, I'm picking their ship apart with relative easy with a couple of Mk II burst lasers. The Mantis start boarding and before I know it I have six mantis on my ship eating my crew. I loose half my crew trying to fight them, then round my remaining crew memebers up in the medbay for a last stand, and vac the ship to kill as many of them as I can before they come and get me. They suprise me by going for a death or glory run on my shields, and suddenly the fight I couldn't loose becomes one I can't win. between the vaccum in the ship and the mantis onboard I can't get my shield repaired before the two previously innefective beam weapons carve my ship up like a chirtmas turkey.
