So, after using Han Solo to slide tackle my way into a CP, while dropping a bomb behind me that I blew up to kill three stormtroopers moments later, I realized I should probably review this game (if only to add to the avalanche of good reviews).  For those who did used to play and are on the fence about buying:
- "Is it still as good as I remember?"  Yes, yes it is.
- "Is the PC port functional?" Nearly flawless, next question.
- "I've spent years playing brown-grey corridor MMS games. Will that long treahcerous slo-" Yes, you'll be lost in pleasant nostalgia at a REAL shooter, and it won't stop.
Now, for those who haven't played: do. This game may be an older game, but it harkens back to a day where games just gave you a gun, patted you fondly on the bum and said: "Go nuts stormtrooper/rebel/Han Solo".None of these scripted walks/vehicle sections, pressing F to pay respects or watching dumb NPCs prattle on in front of you, You can play as differing classes (or heroes) in maps where the objective is to take the enemy command points and hold them until either you or they run out of reinforcements. As good as the game is, though, I do have to point out a couple flaws that may frustrate newcomers (though these are not reasons to skip buying the game):
- The enemy NPCs have that unpleasant quality where they automatically KNOW you're the player character, so any attempt to storm a room with ten of your fellow soldiers will end with you being the first one targeted by everybody right out of the gate.
- Your own NPCs are almost endearingly inept at everything, whether it be holding cps or taking them. They also have a tendency to toss grenades in your direction in an attempt to take out the enemy you're fighting, leaving you to kinda work your way out of that situation.
- I should mention that if you're gonna play the campaigns, there are no checkpoints. If you fail within a second of the end of the mission, you get to startt over from scratch.
Still, at the end of the day, if you like shooters, get it.

5/10 Beautiful RTS; weak GUI; bad AI units (your own)
So, this is F2P for multiplayer; pay for the solo single player campaign.  I do not see any other DLC temptations or microtransactions.  Play MP for free--why not?  I played the solo campaign only.
Spawn camps happen automatically after you capture for your team.  Then, the gathering location can easily be set on the class converter: Ranged, strong-Slow Melee, weaker-Fast Melee, Bombs, Healers.  Units can be converted at any time by sending them to the appropriate converter.
Look at the screenshots; the graphics are nice.  However, the melee unit has curved pincers like a crab, the ranged unit has flat beetle wings.  So, when zoomed out a bit as you must, the two units are almost indisguishable.  Not good.
The basic mechanical balance of the fighting is somewhat Rock Paper Scissors.  RANGED units beat SLOW MELEE; SLOW MELEE beats FAST MELEE; FAST MELEE beats RANGED.  There are quick select icons to the right to select ALL of a certain class in your army--5 or hundreds.  However, this is often completely useless.  Because of the RPS fighting mechanic, you must mostly create a mixed fighting unit.  Singularly focused groups can be quickly decimated.  Like any RTS, you may window select a group and ctrl-5 to set a groups hotkey to 5.
Unfortunately, when directing groups they will go to where you indicate, grouping up like morons, ready for 1 bomb unit to kill most all of them.  So, I spent much time trying to individually spread out a group to patrol and defend an area.  Unfortunately, units are created and killed at such a pace, that you will have difficulty trying to keep pace with any sort of assigned patrol (spinning in tight circles.)  And, on many occassions, I watched as my assigned units would spin in idiotic circles as enemies moved slowly by, refusing to fight.  There is no feature to specify Hold ground; Attack only when Attecked VERSES Attack anything within AGRO range.  Ranged units seemed to agro and fire on anything in range, but would get swarmed and killed as friendly allies would spin in circles close by, doing nothing.  Idiotic AI quickly ruins a game as it did BOID.
I finished the campaign on the easiest of the 3 difficulties (Normal).  The unreasonable execution of the GUI and AI made this quite challenging and a chore, desperately trying to seperate and locate 100 units.  The Enemy has an unfair advantage at first as you set up a base and defend.  Once a successful defense is formed, the speedy spawning precipitates an easy steamrolling victory.
But it is free for MP--you cannot be dissapointed too much in a free game.  Dont like it?  Junk it.  It is not a P2W teaser.
5/10  Do not pay more than $1 for the Solo, Single player experience. If your units will not behave in Solo play, they will not work any better in MP.

There is one word that best descibes Dying Light:  density.  Dying Light takes everything great from Dead Island and massively improves on it.
At first glance, upon being let loose in the sandbox that is Dying Light, you may think the map is small.  I know that was my first impression.  As you explore the city and further the story, you find out just how large the map truly is.  About halfway through the main story line, you will open up another large city area.  The word density truly takes on meaning when you begin exploring this location.  The game opens up more and more locations, including challenge areas (sort of like dungeons in Skyrim) as the game progresses.  Interior locations are numerous, almost mind boggling at times, especially in Old Town.  There are sewers to explore as well.  Transition areas and hidden caverns also help to increase exploration time.  Old Town is really 3 maps stacked on top of each other as there are layers and layers of places to explore.  The Following expansion provides another area to explore, even larger than the main game.
And explore you shall.  If you played Dead Island you remember how many times you had to loot that hard shell suitcase, which came in different colors to "spice things up." This became incredibly stale as your eyes became used to scanning for that same container, among just a few others.  With Dying Light, looting shouldn't get too stale as the game presents more and more "containers" for you to loot, such as cupboards, trash cans, crates, locked boxes, medicine cabinets, dressers, and of course the bodies of those you slay.  The game will despawn bodies after a while but will drop a "loot package" on the ground for you to loot when you feel safe enough to do so.
Loot is numerous and the amount of melee weapons you can wield is staggering.  Just like Dead Island you can modify your weapons by attaching enhancements which increase power, stability, and or durability, as well as, elemental effects.  Speaking of durability, at first you will be annoyed with this.  I know I was.  But after a while, as you find a greater variety of weapons such as rifles and pistols, you won't have to repair nearly as many times as you did at first as your arsenal will grow.  Each melee weapon has a limited amount of durability, then it breaks.  But again, you won't grow too attached to weapons as you'll have an infinite supply of them waiting to be looted or crafted.  Yes, you can craft weapons and some of the best ones are hidden throughout the world as blueprints.  Dying Light has quite a few easter eggs and hidden locations for you to find, adding even more density to an already deep game.
Gunplay is also great in Dying Light, a big improvement over Dead Island.  The rifles sound "meaty." I highly recommend completing Bozak's Horde though.  It's a challenge where, once completed, you receive blueprints to Bozak's Bow.  This bow is great and is better than the ones added in The Following expansion.   You can craft or buy arrows for it and you can retrieve your arrows most of the time after firing them.  Any game with bows as a weapon has my interest right off.
The best way to describe what you can do in Dying Light is to compare it to GTA V.  There are so many things to do you will often get distracted and forget what you started out for.  Air drops add another layer of fun as they seem to entice you to put on hold your current task to get to them first.  I remember that at one point I was trying to sneak into an area at night, attempting to avoid nightstalkers, and an air drop was initiated not too far from me.  But in Dying Light, nights are dark, and I kept arguing with myself over whether or not going for the air drop was smart.  I decided to take off running for it and alerted the nightstalkers around me by accident.  I was almost there, I could see the airdrop.  Almost there...I popped flairs around the air drop and the nightstalkers paused for a moment, screaming and clawing at the air.  I hastily popped open the drop and looted it.  The flair went out and the nightstalkers closed in and ripped me to shreds.  Ah well.  Maybe next time.  These are the kinds of moments Dying Light can provide.  Tense, rewarding, and at times dangerous.
I won't spend much time discussing the parkour element of the game as that's well known to everyone thinking about buying it.  Let's just say that the parkour/player movement in this game is leaps and bounds (pun intended) better than ANY game in its genre.  Movement is fluid once you get used to it.  Add a grappling hook, which you get later on, and I'm sold...the movement and freedom in this game is liberating and will make it hard to go back to any open world game that restricts your movement.
I found the characters to be as interesting as they could be, considering the "zombie apocolypse character archetype" has been used to death (pun intended) with the vast amount of zombie games out there.  But, I remember all the main characters as they are engaging and sometimes funny enough to be remembered.  Many other reviwers have commented that the characters and story are boring.  I haven't found them to be so at all.  The voice acting is well done and varied enough to keep you engaged.  As you explore the city, you'll encounter survivors that are there saveable but some that are just waiting to tell you their story, adding to the lore of the game.  It's touches like this that make a world feel as engaging as this one does.
I have yet to finish the story as I am having so much fun playing in this sandbox.  Perhaps I never will finish the story.  If that becomes the case, I won't feel cheated at all because it will have been my choice to just roam, kill zeds, loot, and explore to my heart's content.
Zombies are not difficult by themeselves.  But, Dying Light's dense environments provide so many spots for zombies to hide that you can't ever get too comfortable.  Loot that extra box at your peril.  Killing zeds is extremely satisfying.  Sometimes I find myself snapping out of a 30 minute 'kill fest" where I swear I was in a Kill Bill scene.  Speaking of Kill Bill, you can use a katana in Dying Light!
Overall, I can truthfully say that Dying Light, plus its recent expansion called The Following, has and will continue to provide more return for my money than the last 5 games I've bought on Steam.  The possibilities with this game are endless and when you add seamless multiplayer/coop to this discussion, you can see why Dying Light is worth the asking price if you like zombie or open world, "do whatever you want" type games.  If you're a gamer that likes to take your time, explore, loot, get distracted, etc. then I wouldn't be surprised if it provides you with 500+ hours of play time.  I highly recommend this game and the season pass which includes all DLC.

Summary of the full review:
The Banner Saga is an immensely unique, and, by no coincidence, immensely good game that combines great artistic design and robust C&C mechanics with a highly entertaining and deceptively complex battle system. The Banner Saga has only a few outright flaws; the shoddy dialogues and the constant need to click-click-click through them line by line are a blemish on an otherwise engaging narrative. Moreover, the startling lack of enemy variety and the relatively dumb AI keep the battle system from realizing its potential for true tactical greatness. The game's system of choices and consequences also has far less of an impact on the story than Stoic's PR department has been trying to claim; nonetheless, it still offers an engaging and immersive range of decisions that will directly influence your battle performance and can occasionally result in major character deaths.
I suspect that The Banner Saga will always be the subject of great controversy; it has a kind of self-assured swagger, flaunting all of its little weirdnesses and weaknesses without making much of an effort to look like a typical tactical cRPG or a typical casual story game. The game features heaps upon heaps of idiosyncratic gameplay systems, like the strange combination of a broad C&C system with a fully pre-determined linear story, the fact that you will rarely if ever be able to see a "game over" screen, the "sit back and immerse yourself" approach to map travel, and a whole slew of novel and deeply unrealistic combat mechanics. You may choose to accept or reject these mechanics according to your personal preferences; all I can tell you is that all of these elements stand in the service of a fully coherent and extremely tightly designed gameplay experience that I deeply enjoyed playing through.

The idea of a competetive sports game isn't that uncommon. In the early days there was Windjammers. A discthrowing 1v1 pong-like game in a form of a fightinggame with different specialmoves and characters.
This game on the other hand takes those Ideas and give them a new look and feel and resembles one of the most unique games of this decade.
#### What are we doing exactly? #####
The goal of the game is getting a ball to hit your opponents. You can hit the ball in many directions and the ball is bouncing of the walls. There are different attacks and specials you can do to speed up the ball or causing it to change directions.
####### Gameplay ######
Smooth as butter. Easy to learn, hard to master. You can get relatively far with just playing with feel and a little bit random button presses. But if you learn how to combo, parry and reducing your hitlag, you can get constant wins.
####### Graphics #######
The graphics are completely 2D. It looks like it was done by MS Paint, but it has its own funky style. The graphics are snappy and look good. Especially the effects when you hit the ball as it reaches the speeds of  max 1000000pixel/s (I think thats the speedindex)
####### Balance ########
The game seems to be well balanced. Every character is different and has a specialattack and peculiarities like walljump, doublejump, wallclinging and driving across the ceiling with a skateboard. Also the angles, in which the ball flies after a hit, are different aswell. Because it is more about how you handle the ball, i don't think there will be overpowered characters.
####### Network ########
The netcode is powered by ggpo. You can feel how good the netcode is.. even with 4 players it's smooth as hell. There are some hickups, witch result in disconnects, but considering the age of the game, I wouldn't be surprised if the game got some updates to fix this. After all it's just a little annoyance, which is forgotten after you desperately try to reconnect to the massive fun. (which is fast anyway)
###### Conclusion ######
The game is a must-have. The fun we had in just 6 hours was tremendous. The game is best played with 4 players, in a 2v2 teammatch.

If you have played ace of spades or other similar games that introduces voxel base building and first person shooter but was disappointed, then you might avoid it with this game, Block N Load. BnL is trying to have a fine balance between letting a player enjoy base building such as placing blocks, traps, turrets and other gadgets around within a certain time limit, before all hell breaks loose and the big wall is removed. At the same time it is allowing first person shooter fans to have fun just shooting anything and everything, blocks, traps, turrets, players and so on.
Whether you want to focus on building defense, traps and buildings using blocks then you can contribute that way. If you want to go in gunning, then you can do that. If you want to stay behind and snipe, you can do that too. Maybe you want to sneak around and climb up the walls, you can do that too. Perhaps you want to mix it all up, you can do that too.
All in all, it offers a great variety and strategy when playing. If you don't care much for team play you can still have fun just playing lone wolf, gathering resources by breaking bricks and using them to put out lots of firepower in turrets or just traps, even intel such as radar.
If you are terrible at FPS but always wanted to have fun playing an FPS this is your chance to still be a team player, contribute and even end up first in your team...even if you lost the match. As you rack up points also by destroying bricks and placements while building new things. So killing alone might not be sufficient anymore.
So if you enjoy building, placing out things, sneaking, sniping, gunning, running, climbing, jumping, digging, healing, being random, trying to be creative or figure out new ways to combine the different classes you all play as a team who have access to different equipment, to create a new way to attack, defend or just be crazy creative while bombs and gunshot is flying around...then so be it. Do that...
It's a great game. Play it...
Classes - Standard equipment + unique equipment for the class you choose. Level them up, get bonus and more powerful buffs...
Come on, go on....I know you want to play it...

Grim Dawn is an action RPG set in a world that has been invaded by a race of demons. The player controls a single character from an overhead camera perspective as they engage in real time combat against endless hordes of enemies. The gameplay is what you'd expect from an action RPG. There isn't much focus on the story, and the core gameplay loop is pretty much "kill stuff - get better loot - kill stronger stuff - gain stronger abilities - repeat".
I have to admit I'm not usually a big fan of action RPGs, but I'm glad I took a chance on Grim Dawn, because I actually quite enjoyed playing this game. I found the combat in games like Torchlight and Path of Exile to be a bit repetitive and boring, but although Grim Dawn has that same style of never letting you walk for more than 30 seconds in any direction without throwing another horde of 15-20 enemies at you (seriously, I killed more than 29 thousand enemies over the course of the game), the combat felt interesting and tactical, mainly thanks to the massive variety of abilities you can use.
The good
•	6 classes to choose from, and you can multi-class.
•	Lots of abilities on each class skill tree including melee and ranged attacks, sustained auras, passive buffs and radial attacks, many of which can be upgraded with added status effects such as stun, bleed or knockdown.
•	Adding components to weapons and armour can give extra abilities such as poison grenades, shield bash, or a percentage chance to deal elemental damage to nearby enemies when they hit you.
•	Exploring the world to find and activate hidden shrines gives special upgrade points that can further increase your character's stats, and grant access to even more powerful abilities - my favourite creates an energy shield when my health is low, which absorbs all damage taken for a short time.
•	Decent variety of enemies including demons, animals and Human bandits. Some have special abilities such as healing allies, summoning allies, freezing or stunning the player, and flame auras.
•	You'll often see different types of enemies attacking each other, which makes the world feel alive. Its not like everything is just standing around waiting to attack the player.
•	You have a personal portal which allows you to fast travel to a town at any time. This is really useful for someone like me who is obsessive about collecting and selling every piece of loot.
•	There's a ton of content. The maps are huge, and it took me 50 hours to finish the main quest and most side quests. The way that shrines, side quests and loot chests are hidden away in far corners of the world encourages thorough exploration.
•	Music is pretty good and I could maintain 60 fps on max graphics settings on a PC that is a few years old.
•	I only suffered 1 full crash, and didn't notice any other bugs.
The bad
•	Story is quite generic and lacks depth. None of the NPCs say or do anything remotely interesting, and I never cared about them at all.
•	AI can be a bit dumb at times. Often in underground dungeons, ranged enemies would try to shoot me through brick walls. Bosses seem to have a specific zone where they'll attack you, so if you retreat far enough they'll disengage and let you heal instead of finishing you off.
•	You can make some basic decisions on a few quests, for example choosing which of two factions to side with. But this system doesn't seem to impact the world state as much as the store page suggests. Its nowhere near Mass Effect or Witcher level of choice and consequence.
•	You can't save in the middle of a dungeon, and all enemies respawn when you reload the game. This doesn't combine well with the massive maps, and on a couple of occasions it forced me to continue playing long after I'd planned to stop, in order to finish a dungeon or find and activate the next fast travel portal. You basically have to allow 2 hours for every playing session to be certain of making any real progress. (XP and loot are constantly saved). I'm not sure if this is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you die because I haven't actually died yet (normal difficulty).
The recommendation
I'd rank Grim Dawn as the best action RPG I've played, and I'm sure true fans of the genre will absolutely love it. Its definitely value for money at full price.

Lethal League is pretty unique in the world of fighting games. The focus on a single projectile livens up an old genre with pong-like battle mechanics.
Lethal League is also quite easy to pick up. The controls are simple, though there are a number of little tricks to learn, as well as ball trajectories. It will make a great party game, and it's a lot of fun for 2-4 players (the more the merrier IMO, though a good 1 on 1 can be intense).
The solo 'challenge' mode is sufficiently challenging, and if that's not enough, you can also hone your skills against hard bots in versus play. As a solo player, you'll likely spend most of your time in online matches. My experience with online play has been good so far, often feeling as good as the local game.
The art style is a matter of personal preference. I love it. I also love the way visual effects are tied in with the game's core mechanics, with distortion animations playing when the ball breaks certain speeds.
The game's starting roster is small - just 5 characters - but they play quite differently. Some of the differences are obvious, like special attacks, jumps and special movement (like clinging to walls or skateboarding on the ceiling), while other differences are more subtle (like the angles of upwards and downwards strokes). There are rumours of more in the works, and it has been said that new characters will be added to the game in free updates.
With all this in mind, Lethal League is a wonderful gem of a game, perfect for people who want something to play with friends, locally and online, and also great for competitive fighting game players looking for new ways to test their skills and reflexes without memorizing long combos.

Dying Light.
A perfect sequel to Dead Island without the awkward name and numeral deal.
But really, Techland outdid themselves in gameplay improvements between these otherwise unrelated zombie combat simulators.
The only thing is, how much exactly did they change? I could just say everything is extremely similar, besides what isn’t. But that wouldn’t be much of a review.
What we have here is Dead Island, with some added features. Don't get me wrong, I really enjoyed playing this game. Let me put it this way; I tried on three separate occasions to play Dead Island, but every time I tried I would get really bored halfway through. Three goddamn tries.
But I beat Dying Light.
I’m one of those strange people who thought Mirror’s Edge was a fantastic game, so naturally upon hearing parkour was a large part of the new Techland zombie killer game, I was friggin excited. But I had my reserves, and as it turns out I had good reason. Besides the midnight flights from Mr. Volatile and his friends, the parkour, and the graphics, this is a Dead Island game. It has the same weapon crafting system, which ranges from “Okay, cool” to “Holy crap thats badass” to “Why?”. It doesn't have the imagination of the Dead Rising series, where some weapons are way over the top, but it only added to the fun. In Dying Light, crafting a weapon doesn’t really come down to what is best for your situation, instead it quickly boiled down to what didn't injure me when I stepped over the burning or electrocuted bodies. Even so, I stuck with bleeding and electricity (the mod I used most was called Exorcist and it was super fun) because if it rained the electricity arced out and made a thunderous bang whenever I got a critical hit, which was very satisfying. But having to wait ages for a body to stop having electricity-based seizures, or burning before I could loot it or moved past got old extremely fast. And bleeding did not seem to do anything, but I used it just in case. Also because it didn't hurt me.
The game also has the same constant fetch quest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as its predecessor. ALMOST. EVERY. QUEST. I understand your options are limited, but Jesus.
Zombie combat remained pretty dang good, but again, it got very old. Personally I hated guns in Dead Island, and while they had their uses against Rais’s thugs I hated them in this game too. It sucks when you only use a game feature not because you want to, but because you have little choice.
The music was good. Nothing to write home about.
The story was good. I felt for the characters, I felt they were relatable, and every encounter with Rais was pulse pounding and memorable. Again, wasn’t groundbreaking, but it was interesting.
I played one night of multiplayer, and found it stacked against the human player. The hives are really tough to kill, and the night hunter’s Left-4-Dead-esque pounce is a little overpowered. Then again, multiplayer isn’t my forte, so maybe I was just awful.
All in all. More of the same AAA zombie game from Techland. The new features felt like gimmicks at times. Fun gimmicks, don't get me wrong, but I really hope this developer leaves its comfort zone in the future. Play it. It’s fun, it’s action packed, and it’s a good game.
But don't expect a complete original.
P.s. I'll update when I play some dlc.

Your decisions have consequences. We see this a lot in video games. While many games bring this to life through its story (so that you get multiple different endings), Banner Saga does most of this *minor spoiler alert* through your party (people you invested resources and time to grow are going to die, and it's going to kill you - either emotionally or gameplay wise).
Graphics: I enjoy the art style and visuals in the Banner Saga. Even without amazing high definition graphics or epic 3D models, it does well to convey how frightening and bleak the world can be, or how beautiful the world could be in nature. You find your jaw dropping at beautiful designs of God Stones and other amazing backdrops. Like Transistor, the style is timeless and would not need any HD remake in the future - even if you pick this up in 2020.
Combat: I'm no pro at turn-based combat games, so I won't comment much. Thankfully, there's all sorts of difficulty settings and would allow someone like me to enjoy the story without bashing my head over gameplay blockers.
The story: While it may be a fantasy world, the story is about love, honor, justice, war, and invokes philosophical questions regarding doing good and doing evil, right and wrong. It is beautifully woven - ha ha pun intended - through the story of Rook and Iver (two different tales that eventually meet). It will surprise you, it will anger you (in the good way because you care about these characters), and it will make you cry (or sad, at least).
After finishing this game, I immediately bought its sequel The Banner Saga 2. Honestly, even if you don't intend to play its sequel, The Banner Saga (1) is worth playing through just on its own merit.

I own pretty much all of the TellTale games library, and all in all the Game of Thrones is a good game.  Their new company idea is to give you a movie type feel.  Yes your decsions have very little over-all impact upon the game as a whole and the story plotline can NOT be changed, but truthfully that has always been the way with TT Games.  Yes I think TT Games should not false advertise about how their game "choices" has impact.  Seeing how the only impact it shows usually is just dialog with characters.  Yes as stated prior, it is an illisionary choice.  For TTG to make a game be a true choice game would be an incredible undertaking of time & money - easily making their games cost allot more.  But I'd love to see them make a game this way one day.
The acting from their characters are TOP NOTCH, but that isn't new or special, they always do great in this area.  Ever play their Borderlands game?  It'll crack you up with laughter allot.
The graphics are good too, I'm not sure why some are complaining about that.  Always TTG uses a cartoon type look for their games.  I doubt that ever changes.  It looks a bit grainy to give you that dark/harsh world feeling.
TellTale Game of Thrones does do well to show you the harsh, brutal and darkness that envelops Westeros after the king dies.  And TTG does really a great job to fit in pieces of back story AND add new stories to this fantasy world.   YES you must have prior knowledge of the show (watch up to season 3) or books before playing this game or you'll be very confused.
I do miss puzzles - yes TTG doesn't do puzzles anymore.  Not for a while now, "Back to the Future & Jurrasic Park" games I think were their last ones.  I am not totally sure why they don't anymore - but my best guess is that they wanted to open up their games to a larger market.  You can't deny their success in company growth since.  In the end, they are in business to make money.
So all-in-all, I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the show or books so long as you don't get to stuck on wanting to effect the game as a whole.   Because that isn't going to happen and as I said.  And if you can handle a game that is played in a harsh reality and is humorless, then you won't be disappointed with this game.
Thank you for reading.

Just so you guys know, I was one of the people who was horribly let down by Jagex's fantastic butchering of Ace Of Spades which left me unsatisfied and . So When I first heard of this game, I was FURIOUS. How dare Jagex make another game using the same font layout for the title using the same concept?
So I started playing it recently, and I'm amazed with how far they've come and how much they've improved. With no dedicated fanbase of origin like Ace Of Spades, they took some neat creative freedom, making a MOBA-styled shooter with building integrated into the gameplay. Gameplay can have a lot of variety, as one can shift between offense and defense pretty quickly! using the same character! Destructive items are limited by the fact that they cost a lot of "blocks" to build and take awhile to do so, discouraging griefers from just spamming bombs as they would have to gather the resources  to break blocks by digging a ton first.
Only nitpick I have right now is the time it takes to find a match, but that's presumably due to the game being in beta and weekend-long windows that the devs have been leaving for public testing. It's also a bit difficult to use the weapons in combat as there are no bots one can train against to help track moving targets, so it's reccomended you bring your 1337 tracking skillz to this game from other games.
Overall, a very enjoyable and chaotic game!

After 80 hours, I finished the game.  I enjoyed my experience, though I'm slightly conflicted in my recommendation.  It's not for everyone, or even everyone who has only played recent RPG's.  It is, however, a worthwhile experience.
Does this game have heart?  Yes.  Is the story and combat engaging?  Yes.  Is it challenging?  Yes.
But is it good?  Well, mostly.
Make no mistake.  This is influenced by traditional RPG from the days of old, where you cut your teeth doing seemingly very difficult things until you've figured out their trick (much like real life).  There are rarely quest map markers to show you your next objective ala Skyrim, and no fairy hanging around telling you what to do.  It's just a world where there are lots of problems, and lots of possible solutions.
In a way, this game reminds me of the Stalker series and The Witcher.  You can do anything you want, but a lot of it will end in a quick demise.  Of course I can refuse the troll bridge toll, but doing so will get me pounded.  I can, and did, murder some town NPCs I disliked, and I did so when I knew I would come out on top.  That was satisfying.
Enough abstracts.  Here's my in game experience.
Hours 1 - 5 (WTF am I doing?):
I landed on a beach with little clue how to proceed in the world.  I did some random things, was generally lost.  There are so many deathtraps around town and enemies harder than me, that I didn't want to venture anywhere and contemplated uninstalling the game.
Hours 5 - 20 (Oh hey, this is cool):
My friend who played the game 10 more hours than me told me about the crucial "Minor Heal" spell and free bed at the inn.  That, combined with teleporting pyramid abuse (infinite town portals, group teleport anywhere, anytime), injected whole new life into exploration and combat.
Hours 20 - 30 (Money, money money!):
I've discovered that sneaking and invis lets me liberate the entire wealth of my town.  I am now swimming in gold, and fights are enjoyable.  I love my rogue Wolgraff, but he dies so quickly.  At least I have an infinite supply of minions to summon to be fodder for me.
I've defeated several awesome bosses through ingenuously manipulating weather effects and feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥  This is fun!
Hours 30 - 40 (2nd town: keeping things fresh):
Yeah, being badass is relative.  There are many things more dangerous than I.  Things are challenging, but I'm getting along.
Hours 40 - 60 (Yeah!!!!):
I've had a blast!  I've been to exotic locations of legend.  Slew tyrants and monsters alike.  Made major plot points and am fighting a crazy, ridiculous cult.  I sparred my wits against many enemies that would have crossed swords with me, and then killed them anyway for the XP.  It's totally justified, since they were the evil ones, not me.
Hours 60 - 70 (still good, but getting stale):
I now own the collective wealth of many nations.  I can't even sell my gear because no trader has any money left (despite restocking when I level). Only the legendary (and previously invulnerable) death knights give me pause. Most enemies have too many HP and do too little damage, making fights unnecessarily long.  This feels like a grind.
Hours 70 - 80 (OCD kept me going):
Game is over! Whew.  The final stretch was interesting, but combat posed no challenge. There were some ludicrous puzzles that would've been frustrating if I didn't consult a wiki guide every hour.  The last boss could never damage any character below 90% hp due to my gear, shields, and healing.  He did, however, take 30 minutes of solid whacking to kill.
My friend has also reviewed this game and pointed out the following:
1) This game feels like an inventory management chore at times.
Me: CORRECT.  There are many quest items and I didn't want to throw anything away.  Therefore, I hoarded stuff like I did in Skyrim.
2) Early game, enemies poison and burn you way too much; the AI can be unforgivingly brutal.
Me: YEP.  But I exploited the AI as I would Dark Souls -- nothing is a cheap shot.  If I have to run away 10 times to kill some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and then cast smoke screen and do cheap lightning bolts from areas they can't see, I'd do it in a heart beat. The world is unforgiving, and so am I.
Protip: Zombies bleed poison.  Poison + fire = explosion.  Throw an infinite use, indestructible, lit candle into their "blood" and yell YIPEE KIYAY as you send them into their fiery un-deaths.
3) It's hard to click on enemies in combat.
Me: FALSE.  Press "B" to have an overhead view.  Now you can click on everyone, every time.  To be fair, I didn't discover this button until hour 70, which by then is too late.
In conclusion, D:OS has been a fun but at times tedious ride.  I enjoyed the openness and challenges that its combat and puzzles gave me early game, and disliked their tedium and obtrusiveness later on near the end.  I would recommend this to anyone who misses Icewind Dale, Baldur's Gate, and enjoys a challenge.  For those who can't live without quest markers, exploiting enemy AI, and sometimes reading a wiki to get ahead, this game may not be for you.  And nothing is wrong with that.
P.S. The "Pet Pal" perk was good to have.  Animals say VERY useful and interesting things (not to mention give quests and XP).  I thought it worthless and shunned it for half the game, but in hindsight, it dramatically enhances the flavor of the game.

Divinity Original Sin is an excellent title - especially from an indie studio. This is easily the best rpg of this style I have played in over a decade.
The community's reviews are spot on for the most part (about the awesomeness of this game), but I just want to point out a few things that I felt the game could improve on:
- The game has a steep learning curve (I actually enjoyed this and it was my favorite part about the game). But here was the issue. Once I figured out the learning curve and learned the mechanics, the game suddenly felt too easy and exploitable. Some of the mechanics are far too overpowered once you understand how they interact. In this sense, it was extremely gratifying to get to this point, but once this point of understanding was achieved, I became incredibly bored. Even on the hardest difficulty you can simply "out-mechanic" the game by using cheese tactics. Some skills need to be rebalanced.
- The inventory system is awkwardly tedious. I won't go in depth but the way the loot is split between your characters and split gold and all that nonsense... it just adds more micromanagement. I understand this is more realistic, but it doesn't add anything interesting and only takes up your time.
- This is much more personal opinion I suppose, but I felt like some of the story arcs were far too drawn out. One of the driving factors in a game is the feeling like you are making progress - progress is good. But some of the lengths of the main quests in this game are sooooo long and I started to lose interest. I just wanted to know what happened next, but it took so long to get to it. There's a fine line between creating suspense/interest and the time it requires to build it. If you build it for too long, interest will be lost.
Minus the points mentioned above, Divinity OS is a great title, and I highly recommend it.
P.S. - As a quick side note, this game does not hold your hand. If you are not willing to spend about 5-7 hours just figuring out the basic mechanics of the game, you will not enjoy this title.

It's a fever dream.
Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball is just as complex and unintuitive as the name makes it sound. That's not a bad thing though.
Story: Who needs a story when you have robots?
Gameplay: Oh boy. As you may be able to tell by the name, you play dodgeball on rollerskates, meaning momentum-cancelling and precision aiming is difficult. You pick up a dodgeball by riding over it, and hold and release l-click to throw it. You can catch opponent's dodgeballs by clicking them in the air at the right range, and insane ricochet shots are common. There's a myriad of different game modes. From Team Death Match, to Capture the Flag, to freaking Baseketball Races, you'll find plenty to keep yourself occupied.
Trick shots are the bread and butter of this game. There are so many different ways to kill your enemies, your kills will begin to have names like "Long Range Godlike Helicopter Ricochet Multikill". Pure insanity.
Once you add in power-ups, you have no clue what's happening at all. Just have fun.
The look and music of the game goes perfectly with the chaos of the gameplay. You're a glowing robot, in a disco arena, throwing discoballs at other glowing robots, all the while dubstep pumps into your poor fragile ears. The whole experience is chaos, which is exactly what its' supposed to be.
If you wanna have some pure, unadultered fun, this is a great way to do it. Combined with the price, I would recommend this game to anyone and everyone. 7.5/10

thoughts --

I really feel like the game hit the genre out of the park (much like Torchlight 2) in the way that it has enough depth to support many, many end-game builds. All to often ARPGs restrict you to a set of best practices that don't allow for a ton of creativity. Virtually every boss on the hardest difficulty is killable with any reasonable class-combo/gear setup, which is a very nice breath of fresh air.
Pros:
- Writing is on point
- combat is fun and easy to map out
- builds are diverse and enable you to actually tackle the game in different ways (like PoE)
- faction & crafting systems make sense. They are not too dense.
- design is great; environments to enemies, everything is visually appealing.
- Single-player economy is completely balanced. Its fantastic.
Cons:
- no mod tools yet (i dont know if they are coming)
- The end-game story is lackluster. It felt like the end boss was really the beginning of another area as the fight had no major climax.
- Music was somewhat weak throughout the game.
- More voiced sections would do wonders to make the story more engaging.

So, after using Han Solo to slide tackle my way into a CP, while dropping a bomb behind me that I blew up to kill three stormtroopers moments later, I realized I should probably review this game (if only to add to the avalanche of good reviews).  For those who did used to play and are on the fence about buying:
- "Is it still as good as I remember?"  Yes, yes it is.
- "Is the PC port functional?" Nearly flawless, next question.
- "I've spent years playing brown-grey corridor MMS games. Will that long treahcerous slo-" Yes, you'll be lost in pleasant nostalgia at a REAL shooter, and it won't stop.
Now, for those who haven't played: do. This game may be an older game, but it harkens back to a day where games just gave you a gun, patted you fondly on the bum and said: "Go nuts stormtrooper/rebel/Han Solo".None of these scripted walks/vehicle sections, pressing F to pay respects or watching dumb NPCs prattle on in front of you, You can play as differing classes (or heroes) in maps where the objective is to take the enemy command points and hold them until either you or they run out of reinforcements. As good as the game is, though, I do have to point out a couple flaws that may frustrate newcomers (though these are not reasons to skip buying the game):
- The enemy NPCs have that unpleasant quality where they automatically KNOW you're the player character, so any attempt to storm a room with ten of your fellow soldiers will end with you being the first one targeted by everybody right out of the gate.
- Your own NPCs are almost endearingly inept at everything, whether it be holding cps or taking them. They also have a tendency to toss grenades in your direction in an attempt to take out the enemy you're fighting, leaving you to kinda work your way out of that situation.
- I should mention that if you're gonna play the campaigns, there are no checkpoints. If you fail within a second of the end of the mission, you get to startt over from scratch.
Still, at the end of the day, if you like shooters, get it.

I love this game quite a bit. It's probably my third favorite Hack and Slash RPG ever after Diablo 2 and PoE. Why? Because it understands what makes the genre so great and so beloved by so many people, and it delivers on all that.
Like most ARPGs, the story is nothing special, and isn't really the main focus here. However, the world that the game is set in is very unique and intriguing. It's sort of like the old west mixed with fantasy and the post apocalypse. It really reminded me of the world of Stephen King's Dark Tower series, and that in no way is a bad thing. Grim Dawn's world is, as you might imagine, dark and grim and desperate, and that desperation comes through in the world design and in the people you talk to.
I also think that this game nails something that most ARPGs forget about, and that is the actual role playing. While only a few NPCs are fully voiced (this is clearly a budget game, and is priced as such) most NPCs have interesting things to tell the player about the world and their place in it. Furthermore, there are several points in the game where you have to make choices, for instance, whether to trust a certain person, whether to hire this blacksmith or that one, etc. Some of these choices are minor and others are more serious, but they all feel important and weighty when you are making them.
But the gameplay is really the star of the show here, and the reason why you are buying Grim Dawn. And it's great. Your hits feel meaty and visceral. Your enemies are fiercesome and unrelenting. Your skills feel useful and powerful, and there's a real sense of progress as you level up. You are given tremendous freedom in leveling up your character; you choose two classes to specialize in as you level up, and then can choose freely from both of those classes' skill trees. The great thing is that all of these classes feel interesting and fleshed-out on their own, but when you have the ability to combine any two, you get some truly unique combinations. You can be a powerful warrior who swings a two-handed weapon and throws molotov cocktails. You can be a gunman with dual pistols and a pet raven. You can be a battlemage with a sword in one hand and a spelltome in the other. Pretty much any combination of classes and/or playstyles is viable here. I don't think I've played any other game that offers so much freedom in how you build your character.
You might worry that because this is a budget game that the loot system might be bare-bones, but that isn't the case. There's tons of different weapons and armors that can have tons of magical properties, and that's not even counting the game's rare and legendary items. Whatever type of weapon your character uses - pistols, rifles, one or two handed melee weapons, magic off-hands, you name it - the game has tons of variations on it. This is game is a spiritual successor to Titan Quest, and like that game Grim Dawn also has crafting materials that you can combine and add to your gear to give you new skills or better attributes.
I could go on and on about all of the various things that this game does right but I'll just say this: Grim Dawn is fantastic and if you like Hack and Slash RPGs, you must own this game. Even if you've never played a Diablo clone before, I think that you would enjoy this game if you give yourself some time to learn the gameplay systems. Grim Dawn is, in short, a masterpiece of the genre.

In celebration of Grimm Dawns Birthday I am giving it a proper review.
Grimm Dawn is an ARPG that does quite a bit to distinguish itself in the genre. It is challenging, rewards intelligent play, and allows a considerable amount of flexibility.  It's best to discuss it piece by piece.
Dual Classing:
This was something the developers introduced with Titan Quest and have brought into Grimm Dawn. Each class is solid on its own and dual classing is optional, but dual classing allows a much broader variety of build options and a lot of room for experimentation. This also adds a lot of replayability to the game. In addition to dual classing there are also a devotion points acquired by shrines that allow players to further customize their builds with specialized bonus's.
Difficulty:
Not every build is viable, not all class combinations are equal, but make no mistake, the game is tightly balanced. When leveling up placing points into class level (not the skills) increases all the stats on a character, in addition there is one stat point per level which gives 3 points to a specific stat. While progressing through the game, if you put too many points into the class level you won't have any powerful skills to employ and that can make progress more difficult in spite of being generally stronger. Conversely, putting too many points in skills and very few into class levels will leave the character having difficulty equipping gear and lower health and energy pools and regeneration leaving the character frail and easily killed. The best part about this is that players can tailor their experience with this balance. One of my favorite builds was a glass cannon saboteur that killed fast and died fast resulting in a very fast paced play style that was as difficult as it was rewarding.
TL/DR: The game is challenging and won't hold your hand, it is well balanced and flexible.
Combat:
The combat can be slow or quick depending on your build, and if in multiplayer, your team. The enemy AI is good but doesn't do anything particularly impressive, most of the challenge comes from mob composition. Some builds will reward strategic thinking more than others, but assessing a situation quickly and prioritizing targets is more often than not strongly encouraged and rewarded.
Crafting:
The crafting and upgrading mechanics are extensive and are only hampered by a very limited inventory system. Weapons, armor, accessories, set items, and top gear can all be crafted if you are lucky enough to find the recipe for them. Almost all of the crafting materials can be used to upgrade equipment, and many have other uses like unlocking shrines. There are no crafting levels so no grind beyond acquiring materials and recipes. The crafting mechanics are quick, easy, and extensive.
Player Choice:
Throughout the game there are tons of choices to be made that have mostly minor consequences. These choices are not on par with CRPG's like the original Fallout 1&2 or BG but it is a lot more than is standard for ARPGs. You can align yourself with most factions, each with its own rewards, in some cases choices determine who lives or dies, but you won't alter the overarching story. The choices become most obvious, and amusing, half way in while playing multiplayer and you discover that your teammates are divided between two major factions in the middle of a war and have to fight both sides separately.
Loot:
The loot system is also extensive with monster infrequents, material collection, and certain gear only dropping from certain enemies or bosses. Loot drops are frequent, good loot is not. There is no magic find stat, which means all players can focus on being good in combat instead of trying to be lucky charms. The loot can be exclusive to each player or shared depending on the hosts settings in multiplayer and players can filter game searches by loot mechanics, either way, players can still trade amongst themselves.
Open World:
The open world is vast with a lot of optional and interesting content. It is not randomly generated but it is large enough to keep things interesting. Some areas are blocked off until players have progressed far enough in the story, but there are also huge sections hidden away. A lot of the map exploration will occur for bounty hunts and shrines, but simply wandering around to explore is itself rewarding.
Setting:
The setting is lovecraftian post apocalyptic with victorian aesthetics. Guns and crossbows are the primary ranged weapons, alchemy is science, and insane cultists perform dark rituals. It is grimdark with blood and death everywhere and humanity struggling on the brink of extinction. There are no rainbows or unicorns.
Ultimately the game is awesome and an excellent value for the price. If you enjoyed Diablo 1&2 back in the day but felt Diablo 3 was too much 4kids or too much WoW then look no further.

Talk about a beautiful and engaging game. Child of Light is an RPG from Ubisoft Montreal. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Firstly, the thing that struck me the most about this game is the art. The artwork is beautiful in every sense of the word. It has a distinctive, watercolor style and it works splendidly with the premise of the game. You’ll really feel like you’re playing through a storybook and it is a wonderful experience.
The story of the game is pretty good and it is filled with interesting characters (and enemies). The game world itself is a great canvas on which the story is able to unfold. It’s imaginative, original, and refreshing.
There’s a good variety of enemy types for you to take on during the course of the game. There’s more than enough to keep you interested in combat.
The combat system itself is very old school. It’s set on a timer, and you’ll need to time your character’s attacks if you don’t want to get interrupted and have to take a penalty on your timer.
The Bad
As far as RPGs go, I typically go in expecting to have at least a good handful of items to equip my character/party with. While CoL does have some items, it is quite lacking on the changeable weapons front.
The Meh
Even if you get this one through Steam, you’ll be having to play it through Uplay.
Verdict: Yea
Child of Light is a solid RPG and a worthwhile addition to any collection (and that is just for the artwork alone). You can find it in the Steam Store and with the Halloween Sale (most likely) just around the corner, you should keep an eye out for this one. As always, thanks for reading.

Killing Floor 2 is my first into the series.  First person shooters have been a favorite of mine since the original Wolfenstein and Doom from back in the day.  Killing Floor has a lot to bring people if you are looking for a cooperative style zombie killing game.  I feel like this game competes with Left 4 Dead in certain aspects while in others is completely different.  For instance, Killing Floor has no campaign, its just waves of "Zeds" aka zombies that all have different aspects to them.  The bigger zombies have better defenses, are more resistant to certain things while weaker to others, and the boss is the ultimate bullet sponge.
Killing Floor 2 looks fantastic on 25560x1440p with everything cranked up and getting 75 frames a second.  My monitor is 75 hertz so any more frames wouldn't be worth the while so I locked it with vSync.  Anyways, all the fluids, physics, and detail on the levels are great.  Nothing here to complain about as nothing looks like its pixelated, even up close.  The music and sound effects are all great and everything seems to flow with the battle pace as you go further into the waves.  If it's one thing I think they could have done better though is that some of the objects that you could seemingly jump on are blocked.  This is strange as other objects of similar size or type you can jump on.  For instance, the cars in Paris you can stand on while the car on the barn level you cannot.  Just a minor gripe if anything though.
The gun play in this game feels so much more superior to other games like Left 4 Dead.  Everything feels right and there are tons of weapons to mess with.  It's best to pick some from the class you chose but it doesn't heart to cross-train.  For instance, I'd frequently pick up a medical gun that doubles as a pistol as support even though my role is shotguns and ammo resupply.  It always helps to have someone that can double up in the event of a Zed overrun.  Speaking of classes, there are a crap ton to pick from.  Classes like the Beserker for melee, commando, medic, support, demolitionist, sniper, gunslinger, SWAT, survivalist, and so on.
When looking for multiplayer matches, please for the love of god, do not use matchmaking.  It's terrible, also, don't pick hard,suicidal, hell on earth.  Pick normal until you get the feel of the game.  Get to level 5 or 10 on a few classes before you go up to hard.  All you do is make everyone else's life harder when you join harder difficulties with no experience and no perks due to the lack of levels.  Stick with normal, learn the game, get a perk or two per class you like and then move up in difficulty.  I'm at 10 hours or so and I am still playing on normal getting a few classes to level 10 so I can fill a role that needs filled on a team as necessary.  Additionally, ignore the community, I'd say half of them are brain dead and toxic, a quarter of them are nice and know how to play, and the other quarter don't say anything and do a normal job on the team.  Use the server browser and apply filters to find servers that meet your difficulty needs.
Overall Killing Floor 2 has plenty of levels, a few bosses in which it desperately needs more, good gunplay, and a fantastic set of options to choose from when picking classes.  Lootboxes are 100% cosmetic and can be gotten through normal means and nothing seems too imbalanced that makes the game unplayable or unfair.  There is a "Versus" mode where you can play the Zeds but I haven't went there yet.  I don't really care to play against people anymore as I get older and slower than the younger generation.  I'm looking for a good experience to fill the time between my job and family life.

So,I've got a "gold" xbox membership which means I pay a yearly fee and get free or discounted games each month.  This month, Banner 2 game up with a deal I couldn't resist.
Within minutes I had purchase Banner 1 and started the plot from the beginning.  The game completely sucker-punched my childhood D&D sessions right in the baby-maker.  I'm hooked.
Gee, I thought... wouldn't it be great if it ran on Linux so I could play it onmy laptop while I'm away....
And here we are.
To me, this game balances nicely between plot-driven narrative and strategic table-top wargaming of old.  The graphics are spot on and the story is both rich and yet simple to grasp.  The initial tutorial can become a bit cumbersome on replay, as there seems to be no way to skip through,... and a few of the conversations seem a bit overly-segmented (do i always have to click through every sentence individually?) however the final result is well worth the small detractions.
I'm curious to see just how far the plot arcs can swing based upon alternate choices.  If it is possible to make Mass Effect scales of changes, this game could easily get a 9 out of 10 from me.
I'm really looking forward to importing my Banner 1 savegame into Banner 2.  Let's see where this goes....

Dying Light.
A perfect sequel to Dead Island without the awkward name and numeral deal.
But really, Techland outdid themselves in gameplay improvements between these otherwise unrelated zombie combat simulators.
The only thing is, how much exactly did they change? I could just say everything is extremely similar, besides what isn’t. But that wouldn’t be much of a review.
What we have here is Dead Island, with some added features. Don't get me wrong, I really enjoyed playing this game. Let me put it this way; I tried on three separate occasions to play Dead Island, but every time I tried I would get really bored halfway through. Three goddamn tries.
But I beat Dying Light.
I’m one of those strange people who thought Mirror’s Edge was a fantastic game, so naturally upon hearing parkour was a large part of the new Techland zombie killer game, I was friggin excited. But I had my reserves, and as it turns out I had good reason. Besides the midnight flights from Mr. Volatile and his friends, the parkour, and the graphics, this is a Dead Island game. It has the same weapon crafting system, which ranges from “Okay, cool” to “Holy crap thats badass” to “Why?”. It doesn't have the imagination of the Dead Rising series, where some weapons are way over the top, but it only added to the fun. In Dying Light, crafting a weapon doesn’t really come down to what is best for your situation, instead it quickly boiled down to what didn't injure me when I stepped over the burning or electrocuted bodies. Even so, I stuck with bleeding and electricity (the mod I used most was called Exorcist and it was super fun) because if it rained the electricity arced out and made a thunderous bang whenever I got a critical hit, which was very satisfying. But having to wait ages for a body to stop having electricity-based seizures, or burning before I could loot it or moved past got old extremely fast. And bleeding did not seem to do anything, but I used it just in case. Also because it didn't hurt me.
The game also has the same constant fetch quest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as its predecessor. ALMOST. EVERY. QUEST. I understand your options are limited, but Jesus.
Zombie combat remained pretty dang good, but again, it got very old. Personally I hated guns in Dead Island, and while they had their uses against Rais’s thugs I hated them in this game too. It sucks when you only use a game feature not because you want to, but because you have little choice.
The music was good. Nothing to write home about.
The story was good. I felt for the characters, I felt they were relatable, and every encounter with Rais was pulse pounding and memorable. Again, wasn’t groundbreaking, but it was interesting.
I played one night of multiplayer, and found it stacked against the human player. The hives are really tough to kill, and the night hunter’s Left-4-Dead-esque pounce is a little overpowered. Then again, multiplayer isn’t my forte, so maybe I was just awful.
All in all. More of the same AAA zombie game from Techland. The new features felt like gimmicks at times. Fun gimmicks, don't get me wrong, but I really hope this developer leaves its comfort zone in the future. Play it. It’s fun, it’s action packed, and it’s a good game.
But don't expect a complete original.
P.s. I'll update when I play some dlc.

COMBAT:
Mechanically, combat is pretty straightforward in TBS. Each unit has armor and strength; armor reduces incoming damage, while strength is both health and damage. Most of the time you'll be sundering armor first to let other characters do more damage, but combat still feels interesting since you have to carefully decide where to place everyone, when to spend willpower to boost your attacks or use abilities, and who to include in your party to combine the most useful character abilities and stats. I did not buy this game for the fighting, but if you like tactical turn-based combat, this gets the job done in a fairly simple manner. My biggest grudge would be the lack of clarity in some ability descriptions, and a lack of detail in the tutorial regarding some of the interface. There were several instances of "Oh, if I had known that earlier..."
STORY:
I was mostly interested in the game for its theme and its focus on choice and consequences, and I was not disappointed. The story was interesting, and the characters varied, although I wish a few things about the lore had been explained more. Where the game truly shined for me was in the choice department. You won't just be deciding who to be friends with, or be given false choices that send you to the same game state. It doesn't take long until the game gives you the burden of decisions with no clear outcomes, with several lives hanging in the balance. Who to save, who to side with, who to trust, whether to let people starve or risk them dying in battle, when to uphold your principles and when to do anything to survive... It soon felt like every other choice had me think "I don't know enough to make the right decision!" or "No! I'll lose someone either way!"... which is exactly the position the characters were in. I may not have seen a game before where my choices had so much impact, nor have I spent so long looking at a screen wondering what to pick. The game really makes you feel like you are sharing the characters' struggle and responsible for getting people out of it alive.
Because of this, I also expect to have a decent level of replayability as you can drastically influence the smaller events of the story and determine who lives and who dies. Combined to the large amount of recruitable NPCs and their varied classes that let you experience combat in different ways, I can easily imagine doing 2 or 3 playthroughs even without achievement hunting.
ART & SOUND:
While I appreciate the overall aesthetic of the game, I can't say either the visuals or music stood out for me in the end. The travelling caravan looks nice enough at first, but gets stale after a few hours of scenery changing very slightly as it scrolls past slowly. The animation is minimal, which I think is fine as I see it more as a step above a visual novel rather than a step down from fully animated cinematics. The rest is up to one's taste. The music fits the game well, moody during travel and adequately bombastic or tense during battle, but isn't the kind of soundtrack I would buy on its own.
Overall, a great purchase and a memorable game and story. I'd buy the sequels if they were on Linux.

Short and sweet:
I did not play the other Divinity titles, and I'm not one to play Dungeons and Dragons in real life, though I can understand the appeal. That being said Divinity: Original Sin (DOS) is hands down the best RPG I've played in recent years from a gameplay perspective. I'd recommend this game to anybody who enjoys the RPG genre, as it will not let you down. I've taken my first taste of a Divinity title and now all I want is more; with more multiplayer components and systems that support 4-player (or even 6-8 players) out of the box.
The turn-based gameplay is absolutely perfect; the classes (that you can completely customize yourself) are diverse and fun to play, leaving a lot of replay value in the game although the campaign itself is massive enough alone. Graphically the game looks great and after a quick graphic-streaming fix in the game files it ran seamlessly at 144FPS 2560x1440 resolution.
I'd heavily recommend a decent 4-player mod or 4-player edit as with 4 people the game is even more fun; though by itself it would still offer people a good experience. Even with the massive content rich evnironment myself and all those I know who love this game are left craving more; different campaigns from the communities and DLC from the developers bringing us new campaigns!

If you like RPGs and turn-based combat, you can't go wrong.  Great story, plenty of content, and I loved the elemental aspect of the magic in combat and never tired of blowing things up, electrocuting them or freezing them solid.  Seeing enemies turned into ash and blowing away in the wind was especially satisfying.  I enjoyed this game so much that I feel it deserves a thorough and nit-picky review about its flaws.  Overall they are relatively minor complaints but worth wading through in some detail.
1) Crafting - I picked up about a zillion different ingredients, read every single receipe book I came across, hoarded items that gave me Crafting bonuses, got excited when I found the Forge in the Shelter Plane and then... I never made anything except arrows (special arrowhead + arrowshaft).  Hm, lame.  Perhaps it was intended as a purely optional element, but it would've been nice to have some more in-game motivation to use crafting.  There are tons of potions, I barely needed to use any of them even on the hardest difficulty (my only use for Intellegence potions was to equip Sarongs that had an Int bonus and a high Int requirement).  In fact, if you have even one spellcaster I think it's safe to say you never need to use any potions at all except for healing at the very beginning of the game.  Perhaps some Large or Huge resistance potions later on in the game but still... not really.  There's also no shortage of great Legendary and Unique gear in the game, and while I wondered if I was ever going to craft some amazing sword or bow or armor on the Shelter Plane Forge, nothing came of it.  In fact the weresheep armor is the only thing that tempted me to dig into it, but I followed the storyline to its conclusion and I never found the weresheep or finished that subplot.  I think this aspect could use a major reworking for the next game.  I heard complaints it was clunky, I never even found out.  The only thing I really "crafted" was the Whisky to get the Orcs drunk.
2) Combat balance - this is always tricky but a few combat abilities stood out as quite overpowered.  Knockdown, in particular, is just way way way too good (and used much too little against you).  Between Boulder Bash which is just so amazing and the Man-at-Arms knockdown ability and the Scoundrel trips... by the time you are level twelve or so everyone you fight just gets knocked down ASAP and for the most part stays there.  That combined with Charm abilites, from Rapture and the Scoundrels up-close Charm ability, and Charm arrows (which frankly you almost never need to use) is just so broken and no enemy had any strategy to counter it.  By the time you really start to fight the terrifying Death Knights you just de-invulnerable them and Charm one and blah... not so scary after all.  Even the great Leandra, who was quite well built up in the story, when you finally encounter her, just goes straight onto her♥♥♥♥♥when a boulder lands on her head and she stays down the whole battle.  Our arch-enemy arch-mage didn't even get a spell off on the hardest difficulty setting in multiple plays through of that fight... not so great.  By the end my elemental mage plus Jahan were just wrecking everything so thoroughly that I'm tempted to try another playthrough without a pure mage at all.
3) The utility of melee - I liked Madora, I enjoyed her storyline, and she was the only melee character in my party.  She did her fair share of work early on, but as the party grew in power she turned into a door stop.  I developed her in a very straightforward way, going straight up in Strength and then tweaking up Con/Speed/Percep to improve Action Points, getting Man-at-Arms up to 5 right away and then just pumping into Two-handed and Armor-specialist and Body-building.  Maybe that was a mistake but it seemed like the way to go and even fit her in-game personality.  By level twelve or so she didn't need to do much at all.  She'd stand out in front to take a little abuse although that wasn't that much of an issue, she'd chop someone in the face sometimes, but mostly she just stood around Inspiring and very ocassionally Helping someone up or patting them out if they were burning or healing them.  Her utility was diminished to the point of being bothersome while my two elemental mages and archer, all with Glass-cannon (which might just be broken also) lit everything up from afar.  It wasn't really fun to just spacebar through Madoras turn so many times after level fifteen, and I didn't really need her again until the very final fight of the game where she was a champ.
4) Spell "book" balance - I don't want to get into much detail here, but I think more time could be spent balancing out the variety and power of the different elemental spells.  There were a lot of spells, which was great, but it would've been nice to need to use a wider variety of them in combat and in puzzle solving.  There might have been a little too much pounding on Boulder Bash, Piercing Ice Shard, Lightning Bolt, Fireball, Deadly Spores, Burning Blaze, and then obv the awesome higher level spells (Meteor Strike in particular just incinerated anything not immune to fire too easily).  Again, tricky but worth tweaking.
5) Immersion - one of the most difficult things to capture in any good RPG is a sense that the world is alive and that schemes are unfolding outside and around the player in a way that feels more dynamic than it really even could be.  While the writing of D:OS is excellent, they didn't really nail this aspect of it.  There were way too many clueless un-updated dialogs with major and minor NPCs, particularly as you got deeper into the game.  There were too many looping conversations and stand-around NPCs that could've at least been updated from chapter to chapter as the major plot lines unfolded.  I found the human bartender in the Orc building still walking around and offering up the primo whiskey I'd made him to the Orcs who'd already been slaughtered in an epic battle that happened right in front of him particularly grating.  They could've spent a lot more time on this.  Perhaps its something they can keep cleaning up as the game is patched.  There were too many immersion breaking moments.
6)  Perception (I mean YOUR perception player) - this was perhaps the most annoying nitpick I had.  There were simply too many times when I (not my PCs) was expected to see some tiny button or lever somewhere that wasn't highlighted or pointed out in any way (like what happens when a PC passes a perception-test and you get that shimmery silver animation plus some kind of dialog notice).  I mean, yeah this super♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off a few times.  Really, I was supposed to just see that tiny♥♥♥♥♥button in the middle of the spiderweb?  Give me a break guys.  Ar'quilla has a perception of 15, I have a perception of 4.  Please don't make me push my face six inches away from my laptop screen so I can figure out how to get to the next area.
Anyway, don't get me wrong... a great game and I loved the time I spent playing it.  I'm looking forward to another playthrough with different character types and of course to Larian's next game.

Their are eight races, including the Humans (Basic people who level up in skills a little faster), Zoltan (Beings made of almost pure energy, able to power parts of the ship by themselves,, 40 less health),  Rockmen (Large rock creatures, impervious to fire, and have 50 extra health), Engi (Possibly robot/android cratures with halved attack damage, but repair systems by two times the regular speed), Mantis (Bug like creatures with 1.50 times walking speed, double attack damage, but halved repair speed), Slugs (They can see people in parts of the ship if the sensors are out, aswell as in enemy ships) Lanius (Metalic-Like beings with 125 health, dont require oxygen, but they suck oxygen out of any room they're in), and *SPOILERS* Crystalmen (A secret race, basically a sister race to rockmen, made of crystal, they have 125 health, suffocate 2 times as slow, and can lockdown a room with they're special ability). Robot Rollerderby Disco Dodgeball... I must admit, I bought this on a whim in a Steam sale as the absurdity of the name just sounded strangely compelling. What began as an impulse buy ended up being a purchase that I have very much enjoyed and so I am recommending it in the hope that more people will buy and play this underrated game.
So what is this game all about? Essentially it is a first person shooter with each player controlling a wheeled robot, working together as a team or individually by throwing dodgeballs at each other. While doing so, you can score trick shots in different ways such as hitting an opponent from distance, hitting an opponent with a ricochet or hitting an opponent while you're in the air.
To help you in this, there are a number of different power-ups you can obtain such as making your ball bigger, giving you  homing ball, and many others.
In addition, this game has a wide range of game modes, from the traditional death match (both team based and ffa) and a capture  the flag variant (called capture the cube), to less traditional game modes such as hoops (where teams try to score points by shooting a golden ball through their opponent's hoops), kingping (the kingping is a player who gets points for kills with more points for trick kills, if he or she gets killed, the player who killed them becomes the kingping and can begin accumulating points, the first player to reach a certain number of points wins). One of the strengths of this game is the huge range of game modes so you're bound to find a game mode which you particularly enjoy, while some servers rotate through the different game modes randomly, others are dedicated to a particular game mode.
The actual arenas in which the battles take place are crazy colourful places with lots of ramps, bridges and tunnels, as well as open spaces depeding on the map. With a name including the word disco, you can guess the maps and the aesthetic of the game is very colourful, with 'techno' music, flashing lights  and changing colours aplenty, combined with the colourful explosions when someone gets hit by a dodgeball.
Another strength of the game is the huge amount of customisation options, many of which are available for free if you're patient, as with games like TF2, you will randomly find items (either customisation items or crafting items) just during game play, while you also get something when you level up. In terms of customisation, you can customise the look of your robot including its wheel, giving it a hat, it's face. You can also set the logo of a group you're in to appear on the back of your robot (nice free advertising for them!).
The battles themselves are fun and thrilling, and depending on how many players are in the game can be a bit manic and crazy, the battles are fast paced as well. You can easily play for just a few minutes or hours quite easily, often I've been in a case of saying to myself "Just one more round" and still be playing five or more rounds later.
Overall I strongly recommend this game to everyone. It's not too expensive, get it on sale if you like but I don't think that is necessary to get a game that is good value for money.
Pros:
- Fun, frantic, fast-paced battles
- Lots of customisation options which you don't need to pay extra for
- Many diferent game modes, both FFA and team-based
- Lots of diferent power ups keep battles interesting
Cons
- Not many players on all the time, so you might be playing bots (part of the reason why I'm writing this review!)
- Avoid if  you suffer from epilipsy
- Can't think of many more tbh...

This game is a definite 8 out of 10 only because of a few minor things that may or may not bug you. As a hack'n'slash type RPG, it offers everything you might expect from the genre. If you have played Titan Quest before, then Grim Dawn will feel like a sequel in terms of gameplay mechanics. Like in Titan Quest's Epic and Legendary game modes, Grim Dawn allows you to play the game again while maintaining your equipment, level and skills. This mode is split into two parts, elite and ultimate, respectively. The game gets a lot harder each time, but the loot gets better too. The game's top-tier legendary items are only available from elite onwards.
So why 8? Because I didn't find the maps particulary interesting. While they certainly convey feelings of dread, war and destruction, I kinda expected more variations. There are caves, grasslands, dungeons, caves, grasslands, and more dungeons. That is not to say there is no unique landscapes, but the variety is fairly limited. Although there are nice little secret areas, it's a bit tiresome to grind through the game with little change in environment. Other than that, Grim Dawn is spectacular game with great graphics.
