Are you a fan of the ol' days on Diablo 1 and 2? Then read this:
---
Okay, well I'm not going to say it's a bad game, but it's far from good. I'm a HUGE ARPG fan, and of course like most of you, started in the Diablo days. After getting bored of the grind in Diablo 3, I went to PoE and that was great for 1 month, but then that started to wear down and thus lead me to Grim Dawn.
Here's what I like and dislike about Grim Dawn:
+++Positives:
+Great artwork & design
+Runs very well even on low-spec PC's
---Negatives:
-No community (Yeah I know you can find players to play with, but no global chats, no trade chats, nothing)
-Skill system and stat system is not exciting (I normally get excited leveling up to use new skills. Grim Dawn just doesn't seem to do that for me. Skill tree feels quite bland)
-AI isn't on point (The mobs don't offer much of a challenge. Bosses seem a little too easy)
-PVP Disappointing (As a huge fan of the crazy havoc Diablo 2 offered in terms of PVP and the toxic community that came with it, I am disappointed to see no effort made for PVP on Grim Dawn as well as the other top ARPG's)
-Pathing and movement (I found the pathing of the characters was not as smooth as the other ARPG games. Especially when going up and down narrow sets of stairs)
-Story line is flat (I found myself mostly skipping all dialogue interaction with NPC's just to hurry up and progress forward. What happened to those amazing cinematic days like in Diablo 2 and the amazing voice overs?)
-Just feels like a single player game (I want to be emersed in an online world, especially when it's the type of game which requires grinding for gear pieces and so fourth. Playing with 1-3 other players is just not much of a multiplayer game).
----
So I guess with more negative's than positives, I'd have to say I don't recommend this game for those who have the same types of expectations and needs in a type of game like this. They need to put in a lot more work before I can actually even casually play this.

Short, sweet and deliciously twisted. "Little Nightmares" offers incredible ambience and many puzzles to solve; some simple, some tedious, but all rather satisfying. Delightfully creepy, the game seems to have two underlying messages. First, that eating meat is bad and makes otherwise decent people turn bad. Second, children can be creepy even when they are actively trying to do good.
Music, art and animation drive the story. There's actually no dialogue at all; most of the narrative is implied, inferred and otherwise observed. This approach is very welcome, quite refreshing and does a great service to the tale being told. If I've grasped that tale correctly, of course. ;-)
The only gripe to be levelled at this lovely game are in the controls department. Specifically, how loose, inaccurate and unresponsive the controls can be. The innate charm of the game more than makes up for many of the frustrations a player may encounter due to the oft poorly-executed controls. In fact, it seems as though the game relies too heavily on the idea that sloppy controls are a forgiveable offence given how enamoured the player may be with the game world, atmosphere and desire to press on. Fingers crossed that the issue has been (or will be) addressed in the DLC.
8/10, two thumbs up. For sheer entertainment, "Little Nightmares" is worth the price of admission, ESPECIALLY on sale. For those who enjoy puzzles and twisted stories told in dark worlds, look no further.

You will need to reverse engineer your own new armor and laser weapons, and eventually plasma weapons which are for some reason twice as effective as the alien's own weapons. Soldiers gain experience when they actually manage to kill anything, which isn't too hard since the aliens send out their most puny little aliens armed with plasma pistols to fight you. As they rank up they gain new abilities and begin to gain improbable aiming skills and can headshot an alien while pointing in the wrong direction through 3 walls. Or gain the ability to magically make all reaction fire completely miss. Eventually you'll gain psionics and end up mind controlling all those aliens to fight for you for a couple of turns.

This game is great!
+ Graphically, it’s impressive.
+ The world is dense and full of life, all while being large and interesting. Even in areas where enemy mobs don’t necessarily spawn, you can find wildlife like weasels, bears, and hogs along with numerous plants to collect.
+ Combat is fun, interesting, and interactive. The classes feel different for the most part too. Just remember, things like the witch and wizard are basically carbon copies with different genders.
<THEY DO HAVE SOME DIFFERECNES THOUGH, SO KEEP THAT IN MIND>
+ There are a ton of areas to explore and numerous enemies to fight.
+ You level up to 50 very fast, making progression to that point feel smooth and interesting.
- The game can be hard to run for some due to its graphics. There is also a lot of UI clutter and tons of pop up notifications regarding various things at first. I recommend that anyone who downloads this game immediately toys with the UI to get it the way you want along with turning off some of the notifications. (New players really don’t need notifications regarding things sold on the auction house for four bajillion dollars, right?)
- There is no fast travel to accompany the immense world. Instead, the game has an auto-path built in. You select a destination, hit default ‘T’, and you character will automatically run to that area. This can be somewhat tedious and can get a little boring, but at the same time you sometimes come across cool things on the trip to your selected location. This travel time can also be mitigated with horses.
- Combat can be really confusing at first. Things aren’t really explained well, and a lot of learning your abilities and combos consist of sitting in a field of weak enemies and taking pot shots and doing target practice.
- While there may be a TON of different enemies, combat overall doesn’t change much. It’s a whole lot of hack and slash.
- You level up to 50 quickly. Like, there are guides on how to do it in a matter of hours. But after that! Whew, that’s something. That is where the true game comes in to play. Leveling past that can be one heck of a wall, so heads up.
For the price you pay for the base game, it's totally worth it!
A lot of people say it's pay to win, but it really isn't. It's pay for convenience. You pay for cosmetics, pets that pick-up loot for you, and things like that. Nothing that you 100% need or that will really aid you in things like PVP. This game also has no monthly subscription, which is cool.
About the only thing that is somewhat irritating is inventory/weight/character slots. These are somewhat limited, and can be bought for real money.
But!
Keep in mind that inventory and weight limit can be increased in game for free, it just requires a little effort. As far as I know though, the only way to increase the character limit is through using loyalty points, which are rewarded for playing. This could actually take a LONG time. Though, the game gives you two slots right off the bat, and that should hold you off for a while.
All in all, the game is really solid for $10. I spent some money on some things because I like to support the developers, but it really isn't NEEDED. I would for sure recommend this to anyone who is into large scale MMORPG's.
~~NOTE~~
My one really big complaint is that after level 50, the game becomes open PVP, which can be a problem when you start attempting to farm popular spots. Most guys seem nice in the sence of "don't ♥♥♥♥ with me and I won't ♥♥♥♥ with you."
However, some purposely go out of their way to kill lower level/new people. But, hey, all games have their jerks, right?

An incredibly enjoyable experience, the Banner Saga manages to achieve the hugely satisfying feeling of actually having control over the events in the game, with enough twists, turns, and hard decisions to allow for at least two full playthroughs - it does feel like the games ends a couple of hours too soon, but there's a reasonable amount of replayability, and your save file can be ported across to this game's sequel, allowing you to live with the consequences of your previous choices.
With combat elements from many isometric turn-based RPGs, the game's easy to pick up and play, whilst having a higher skill ceiling than I expected, whilst the out-of-combat experience feels incredibly similar to Faster Than Light, whilst adding in conversations that will more often than not tend to fill you in when it comes to lore. The game's visuals and soundtrack are something memorable - its grand sweeping landscapes, and tense music bring the atmosphere of the game together. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the first of The Banner Sagas, even if it felt like it could have been a more fully fleshed out experience, and I can't wait to sink my teeth into its sequel.

Long wall of text here of my nitpicking opinion mostly from playing
(because giving a review based on a group of us playing each other without a clue of what's going on isnt really a review xD):
Pros:
Gameplay wise is really fun to prepare your base and see how well it fares against one another. Thinking of creative ways to build a defend from turrents and tikis flanking the cube to underground mines that will leave a nice surprise for tunnelers is really satisfying when you see it working.
Attacking is also really fun with multiple revenues of assault. Ive seen various creative ways people attempt to siege ranging from backdoor spawn point assaults to overhead bombing using a bridge which all ends in a beautiful carnage. The reaction on the opponents face when you successfully destroyed half their defenses with a giant bomb from down under is really satisfying.
The characters are really unique with each character bringing something different to the lineup (other than Sarge and Cogwheel whom I feel both are more or less the same in terms of weapons and playstyle).
The maps are also unique with each map having a different building style to ensure its fortitude.
Cons:
I would hope there would be more effective long range sieging/front up assault methods. In most cases long range attacks via rocket launchers and etc would just get patched up too easily by new blocks or the turret guy's repair gun.  Playing cogwheel for example, I felt that its fairly pointless to attempt to break the enemy walls up front with my cannon considering the damage will be patched up when I respawn and return to it.
Upfront assaults will rarely work too with most of the defense mechanisms shredding you within seconds unless your team have 3 "Sweet Sciences" rushing your base which is pretty scary if you're the defense. I would debate that using bombs  are considered to be upfront but as long as the opponents are somewhat decent they would easily spot your attempts and foil it before you could even plant the bomb. I feel you guys should work on improving  long range sieging/upfront method since it's the most generic approach most people would think of and it should be at least somewhat viable rather than relying on sneaky tricks or incompetent defense players.
There were also a few moments of server lag which causes everyone to freeze and we had to leave the game prematurely. Hopefully you guys found the source of this issue.
Also the number of times I have died from shift climbing a wall into oblivion is countless. Not sure if its just me but I feel there should be a slight pause for whenever you climb using that method rather than continuing to sprint after you reached the top.

So far the best I've gotten is chapter 6. I'm really not sure if I'm going to tough it out and finish this game, because there are just so many glaring problems with it.
The combat is fun, don't get me wrong. It's easily the best part of the game, but the problems come in outside of the combat. Most games like this, for example, Fire Emblem, have you gain characters that can die in battle. In Banner Saga however, your units only get injured in battle and need to rest. This means that they instead die (or leave your party some other way) from scripted events outside of the combat. That is just so wrong. It completely prevents you from crafting the team you really want, not to mention any items equipped to a unit that dies or leaves the party is lost forever. This could be saved if these didn't happen often, but they happen TOO often. Hell, there's an achievement for keeping one character alive that has at least 4 scripted events in which he can die throughout the story.
This gets worse because of one event in chapter 6 that essentially sums up to "Rocks fall, everyone dies." An unavoidable (by that point) scripted event that makes you lose 3 characters, just like that. From what I can tell, it starts in chapter 2-3, and based on very minute decisions you make then, 3 chapters later your characters will just die no matter what. That is seriously not okay.
I want to like this game, I really do. But I am just being constantly frustrated by the complete lack of personal team building. It's really hard to get attached to your characters when you have no stable way of keeping them in your party.

After playing (only) over a 100 hours and having the true ending and normal ending, I thought it might be about time for me to write a review for this great game. I'll put a pro and con tl;dr below with some additional points included.
First off, I've gotta say that the story is pretty good, albeit very basic for most parts. The premise is what's special, with the world being Gamindustri and the 4 countries representing Sega(Planetune/Planeptune), Sony(Lastation), Microsoft(Leanbox) and Big N(Luwee/Lowee). Each of them has a goddess(called CPU in the often more than just purely stupid localization, more on it below), which represent the consoles of the seventh generation of their respective nation, them being: Neptune(the cancelled Sega Neptune), Noire(PS3), Vert(Xbox360) and Blanc(Wii). Then their are also some backgrounds to the world of course which'll be part of the story, but barely anything but basic stuff.
The Main-Antagonist Arfoire actually represents the R4-Module in the localised version and all kinds of similiar stuff in the original(read: Japanese version/spoken text) with her name being Majekonnu there.
The most special part of the story is the constant 4th wall-breaking, especially by our MC, Neptune.
Next up I'll talk about the gameplay. Although it's called a JRPG by almost everybody, I'd rather call the fighting system a TBS, most reminiscent of Super Robot Taisen/Wars NEO for Wii, but wether you know it or not, I'll elaborate: Just like in classic JRPG-fighting-systems you and your opponent take turns dependent on AGI, and have multiple Attack-Options. Here comes the difference through. On the characters turn you actually walk around with them depending on their corresponding stat and depending on the weapon you've got a range for attacking. When an opponent is in range and you attack, you actually start a kind of simplistic Combo with 3 types of attacks where you can set different ones in the menu and of course learn more through leveling up. You can chain up to 4, with the first 3 being of the basic-types and the 4th being a special Combo-Finisher, for which you've gotta increase the so called EXE-Gauge by attacking the opponnents. And then there's also 2 special attack-menus, one being for normal special attacks and spells, while the other is a type of finishing move and also includes Team-Moves. You can use these instead of starting a combo and the range of effect of them is undependent on your weapon, and differs per Skill.
You can take up to 3 girls into battle, and each of them can have 1 support, with whom they can tag out during battle, receive support from them and (in certain cases) do special Team-Moves.
Now I'll come down to the fanservice: Panty-Shots sometimes appear during the fights(if you change your camera-height accordingly), and that's it for them mostly, if not completely. Dialouge-wise there are some small things and then there's the rather cute flirting of
, but since it's more cute, I won't even really call it fanservice. The biggest part of fanservice might be the jiggling breats(even almost flat Blanc-samas ^^") during the CGs. That's about it, maybe a few things here and there in the dialogue, but not neraly as much as is often exaggerated here.
And then there's the design of everything: The characters are all distinct, and albeit most of them being rather equipped with tropes, none of them are empty characters. Remember folks, tropes are NOT inherently a bad thing, it's more like the opposite unless handeled poorly. After all, a character that fits NO tropes will ALWAYS be completely without any distinct features.(in case you think otherwise, prove it to me and I'll add an "ALMOST")
The design of the dungeons is done really good, optically. NOT A SINGLE MAP IS IN EXISTENCE TWICE. However, most of the same type are very similiar to each other.  Take note, that "same type" means the same textures and stuff.
Now for the worst part of the design through: The Monsters. While each of the base-types is designed really well and almost - if not absolutely - all are references to the one or other thing, the annoying part is the over-using of the same model. Now, that would be absolutely fine imho if they were always recolored. But there are only a few recolors of them all, making for way too few models. The first dragon you can encounter actually uses the same model as the one in the last dungeon, not even recolored, but the names differ, and only them sadly. But, over time you'll get used to that. Actually, it's not really annoying at all, just a minus point I had to mention.
Lastly I'll go over the localization briefly. Most of the time it's done quite well. Only a few things are omitted here and there in comparison to the spoken japanese text, and a few times completely senseless or useless stuff is added in the sentence. The worst thing is, when the added things are making a character appear ooc(out of character). This actually frequently happens with Neptune in the localization. While she's kidding around most of the time, the localization has her ooc quite often. Everytime she uses slang except at the start of the meeting Falcom in Planetune. But that's still on a bearable level in this one. A bit worse is the handling of Compa's "Monster-san". Whenever she says it, they just omit the "-san", which in itself is absolutely ok. BUT one time during a scene where she actually tries to call the seriousness back they made "Mr. Monster" out of it. Now, if she would've used it from the beginning, it wouldn't do anything to that scene, but like this, it seems as through she doesn't even try to get the seriousness back. That's only 1 example, there are more, but overally the localization is - as I said already - ok. Some references are changed out to make more sense to a western audience, absolutely ok for a localization. Although I almost forgot the worst point of the localization, which are the jokes. Often you can be sure the joke you're reading is absolutely out of place AND context, or just completely added. This mostly gets done to NORMAL sentences, and for example Neptune's "take nep"-thingy and the "Pika" were NOT existent in the original, she said normal stuff in place of these. The only other really bad thing is the changing of terminology. Here's a list of the top of my head:
"Basilicom" actually was "church", nothing else.
"CPU" was ALWAYS "goddess", NOT "CPU", NEVER and actually is quite senseless...
"HDD" is completely senseless as well, if not even more than "CPU". The original said "Megamika", which roughly would translate to "Goddessfication", or for the sake of making it flow better in english sentences, "goddess-form".
These are the most prominent things, there likely where some more senseless changes.
I'll give it a solid 8.5/10, if not for the localization it'd be a solid 9/10. I loved this game and will call it a must-have for fans of JRPGs.

I found this game disappointing at best.
Little Nightmares is a LIMBO/INSIDE clone that decides its innovation to the genre would be to add 3D platforming and hide and seek to what is essentially a side-scroller. The controls, combined with the aforementioned 3D platforming can make for an awkward experience as very often you will find yourself repeating sections. This is not due to a lack of understanding of what needs to be done, but simply an inability to translate the movements you want to make into the actual game.
Just like the games that Little Nightmares has found itself imitating, it has oodles of atmosphere, but frustratingly it has the exact inverse in story. The game tries to do the 'indie' thing and not directly communicate a story, instead hoping you will do the work for it. What this often means is that you are creating the story in your own mind and attributing it to the game. In reality though, everyone will have a different idea of what exactly the game is about. For me that means the game has failed to communicate its message, if no-one can agree on what that message actually was.
The fun factor often gets looked-down upon by those who think that games don't have to be 'fun', they can be a form of art. This is true. However, a game has to justify this through being something more than 'just a game'. Little Nightmares does not do this for me. I do not think it is fun, I do not think it is meaningful. I do think, sadly, that it is a disappointment.

Princess maker is basically a game about raising numbers to get certain endings based on those numbers.  If you're the type who likes playing with numbers to see how it changes the character, combat, and the endings, this series is probably your cup of tea.  Unfortunately Princess Maker Refine 1 has very, very little to offer in one of the most crucial parts of this kind of game, story.  There are no events or changes to the story for doing anything in any order so long as you end the game with certain numbers.
+The art is cute
- But it has a few NSFW scenes (Maybe a + if you're into girl hentai?)
+ The overall story is interesting.  A national hero who became crippled after fighting off the demon king decides to help raise the next generation.  I really liked the true queen ending.
- There is almost no story between the beginning intro and the ending.
-Combat is extremely frustrating and -very- reliant on RNG.  No matter how skilled your daughter is, she will always have a % chance every turn to panic and flee from battle against even the weakest opponents, and critical strikes will end almost all battles instantly.
? This game has no guides or instructions to it, staying true to children having no instruction manual.  Be sure to read a guide if you want to succeed.
? This game was worth 2 serious playthroughs and a fast, joke playthrough for me.  The last one still felt like a chore even though I tried to keep it quick.
Overall I do not recommend this game simply because Princess Maker Refine 2 does everything better for a slightly higher price tag.

First Try on Lethal League!
The video can be found here:
Lethal League is an interesting take on a projectile based fighting game.
The controls are reduced to their bare minimum, giving you the option to jump, hit and punt, but the timing of these commands is what divides the good from the best. Since the ball can be hit in any angle you want there are a lot of factors to consider on how and when to hit it or if you want to slow the ball down with a punt to smash it more acurrately.
Currently there are 5 playable characters available, which for a launch line-up is okay, but I hope that more characters will be added soon. Each character has its own special ability which you can use when your power meter(I haven't heard an official name for that yet) is full. You can fill your power meter by hitting the ball and when it's full you can release your special ability by pressing the hit button again while you are hitting the ball. What is quite notable as well is that each character has special movment and jumping capabilities. For example, Candyman cannot walljump, therefore he is able to jump higher.
There are also 6 levels, but here are some weakpoints the game has in my opinion. The levels are just backgrounds, there is no real interaction with what is going on in the front. For example there is a level where you are on a street. In the background you see a tank(at least it looks like one to me) and buildings. Wouldn't it be awesome, if these elements would come into play, for example the tank shoots one of the buildings and rubble is coming down and affects the ball or makes you go away from certain areas? At least I would like that.
Another thing is that the graphical fidelity leaves a lot to be desired. While I dig the artstyle that looks like jet-set radio in 2D, the backgrounds just don't really look that good.
What is great though is the animations quality which give you a nice feel of the velocity of the ball and let the controlls feel really good. It also has to be noted that the stop motion moments when hitting a very fast ball are extremely funny and change depending on what level you are currently at.
The game also features a progression system which lets you unlock new colouring for the playable characters.
Last, but not least, let's talk about the soundeffects and the soundtrack. The soundeffects are quite nice and there is a nice variety on sound cues available. The soundtrack itself features different artists. To be honest, it is not my style of music, but I found it really fitting and enjoyable at times.
Having not tried the multiplayer yet, there is one big component missing, but from what I've heard, the netcode is working fine, only disconnects seem to make big trouble.
Now to the conclusion: Is the game worth it? In my opinion there is a lot of fun and enjoyment to be had in this game, especially when you have 3 other to people to play and talk with in Skype or Teamspeak. It is easy to learn, but hard to master(I normally hate these sayings, but when it's true I can't help it). So even if you are not that good at the game, you might be able to get your enjoyment out of it.
The only thing, people might be turned off by is the graphics, but in my opinion this game is a case of gameplay beating graphics in terms of making a joyful experience.
The price is 12€ or your regional equivalent. Buying a 4 or a 2 pack is even more recommended, because of the reasons that are stated above.

As a fan of the Princess Maker series and it's western spiritual successors (Cute Knight, Long Live the Queen), I largely bought this as a curiosity to kill time and hopefully encourage the translation of PM 3-5. That's where the series gets really interesting. As a piece of gaming history, it is amusing enough but hasn't aged overly well. If you're interested in the PM series, Princess Maker 2 is hands down the better place to start.
Gameplay consists of scheduling three classes/work placements for you daughter each month between the ages of 10 - 18. These placements then increase or decrease a selection of stats, with the goal of balancing these and developing your daughter into a successful adult (or not, as the case may be). For example, if you send your daughter off to work as a Hunter expect her Dexterity to rise, but her Glamour to crash. There is also the chance to send your daughter off adventuring in the wilderness, complete with simplistic RPG combat. Unlike PM2 your general success in the various ending seem to be tied to her Reputation as opposed to individual stats.
Pros compared to Princess Maker 2
+ Prettier and more varied artwork. While Maria's dresses don't come with stat changes she does get 4 free dresses everytime she ages. I also enjoyed seeing the shifting village landscape through the window behind her to depict the season changes.
+ Larger adventuring area. Though this is just one single large area as opposed to four distinct biomes, but presented an interesting challenge the first few times through.
+ Less moody daughter. PM2 expanded a number of the daughter's stats, some of which affected her temperament causing her to be unresponsive. For new players Princess Maker offers a slightly easier introduction to the stat raising genre as some of these additional triggers are absent.
Cons compared to Princess Maker 2
- Disappointing lack of 'mysteries'. One of my favourite aspects of PM2 was discovering things like the fairy at the oasis or fighting the ghost in the graveyard. This aspect is completely absent.
- Combat is HARD. Like I'm sitting at 400 stamina, 280 strength and 250 dex and pretty good equipment. I'm having almost as much trouble adventuring then I did when I had half those. There seems to be a high element of luck involved.
- There's quite a lot of nudity in the CGs. This normally doesn't really bother me (hey, I'm european) but it seems a bit excessive. It's not even the vacation images, but the random topless rivals in the Harvest Tournament that seem completely gratutious.
- Text weirdly disjoints itself inside the text box creating distracting broken typos.
- No Cube or rival girls. The game feels a bit lonely in comparison.

This game is great!
+ Graphically, it’s impressive.
+ The world is dense and full of life, all while being large and interesting. Even in areas where enemy mobs don’t necessarily spawn, you can find wildlife like weasels, bears, and hogs along with numerous plants to collect.
+ Combat is fun, interesting, and interactive. The classes feel different for the most part too. Just remember, things like the witch and wizard are basically carbon copies with different genders.
<THEY DO HAVE SOME DIFFERECNES THOUGH, SO KEEP THAT IN MIND>
+ There are a ton of areas to explore and numerous enemies to fight.
+ You level up to 50 very fast, making progression to that point feel smooth and interesting.
- The game can be hard to run for some due to its graphics. There is also a lot of UI clutter and tons of pop up notifications regarding various things at first. I recommend that anyone who downloads this game immediately toys with the UI to get it the way you want along with turning off some of the notifications. (New players really don’t need notifications regarding things sold on the auction house for four bajillion dollars, right?)
- There is no fast travel to accompany the immense world. Instead, the game has an auto-path built in. You select a destination, hit default ‘T’, and you character will automatically run to that area. This can be somewhat tedious and can get a little boring, but at the same time you sometimes come across cool things on the trip to your selected location. This travel time can also be mitigated with horses.
- Combat can be really confusing at first. Things aren’t really explained well, and a lot of learning your abilities and combos consist of sitting in a field of weak enemies and taking pot shots and doing target practice.
- While there may be a TON of different enemies, combat overall doesn’t change much. It’s a whole lot of hack and slash.
- You level up to 50 quickly. Like, there are guides on how to do it in a matter of hours. But after that! Whew, that’s something. That is where the true game comes in to play. Leveling past that can be one heck of a wall, so heads up.
For the price you pay for the base game, it's totally worth it!
A lot of people say it's pay to win, but it really isn't. It's pay for convenience. You pay for cosmetics, pets that pick-up loot for you, and things like that. Nothing that you 100% need or that will really aid you in things like PVP. This game also has no monthly subscription, which is cool.
About the only thing that is somewhat irritating is inventory/weight/character slots. These are somewhat limited, and can be bought for real money.
But!
Keep in mind that inventory and weight limit can be increased in game for free, it just requires a little effort. As far as I know though, the only way to increase the character limit is through using loyalty points, which are rewarded for playing. This could actually take a LONG time. Though, the game gives you two slots right off the bat, and that should hold you off for a while.
All in all, the game is really solid for $10. I spent some money on some things because I like to support the developers, but it really isn't NEEDED. I would for sure recommend this to anyone who is into large scale MMORPG's.
~~NOTE~~
My one really big complaint is that after level 50, the game becomes open PVP, which can be a problem when you start attempting to farm popular spots. Most guys seem nice in the sence of "don't ♥♥♥♥ with me and I won't ♥♥♥♥ with you."
However, some purposely go out of their way to kill lower level/new people. But, hey, all games have their jerks, right?
The combats fun in a different sort of way, takes a min. to get use to. Overall a very pretty game, with a decent story.

As a projectile fighting game Lethal Leagues core is simple: hit your opponent with a ball to score and ultimately win a match.
You can try a bare bones prototype on reptile games' website to see if you like that concept.
Like many other recent small competitive games this one challenges the player with high risk&reward as a single hit from the ball is a knock out. Although if you or your team hit the ball last it won't harm you.
The intense fun of this game starts to kick in once you've hit the ball back and forth a few times, ever increasing its speed to ridiculously high levels (speedometer at the bottom on the boombox). Normal hits only increase the ball speed by 1, charged hits and smashes however
the speed. With more speed the hit lag will increase, the screen will shake, the background will change, intense visual effects will ripple across the screen and the characters will throw catchy phrases at each other as they hit the ball. Next to jumping and swinging you can also bunt the ball to slightly decrease the speed and carefuly set up your next attack.
The movement mechanics are very solid. You can move right and left as you jump, you can tap for a short hop or hold to jump higher and stay in the air longer as well as press down to fall faster.
The selectable characters two major mechanic differences are their method of gaining height (high jump, wall jump, double jump, wall ride, ...) and their special move, which can be activated with a full special bar (builds up by hitting the ball).
Next to online and local multiplayer with up to 4 people there is also a single player challenge with 10 increasingly difficult stages to beat in sequence and in local multiplayer there are 7 levels of AI difficulty with the highest one still being a challenge even if you are already very good at the game - although not as engaging as a good human player will probably be.
And it's a damn lot of fun.

The graphics are wonderful to look at but you have to turn around to see all nooks and crannys. Normally, in an isometric (or near-isometric) view you don't need to rotate the camera. Here, you have to, because oterhwise you miss a barrel or crate in a corner of a dungeon. And that crate may contain an item you need to progress. So you have to check out painstakingly every corner from every angle. And hover with the mouse because you may not recognize an interactable item. Pressing ALT (or whatever) you get labels of items (much like in Diablo) but then what? Hold it all time long and just interact with labels? Why then the graphics. You could do without that WONDERFUL barrel perfectly textured and everything, because all you notice is the label "Barrel". So that makes somehow no sense, it is self-defeating.
I love old-school RPGs and sandboxes, look at my games, most are of that kind (I don't have Baldur's Gate, Fallout, Icewind Dale + 20 or + 30 other games along those lines in steam but just on the desktop installed without DRM, so count those in, too). That said, I don't think this game is an oldschool RPG. It is pretty modern under many aspects, but lacks some necessary mechanics to make it work. Oldschool does not mean that you don't get pointers on what to do. It means that those pointers aren't just icons on a map, but the map is already pretty well designed without those pointers. Here, the map is useless. I can't zoom in enough to see BOUNDARIES. It looks like a satellite photo of the world, which is VERY COOL and pretty and it is colorful and everything... technically perfect... but useless. An abstaction (the true meaning of "map") would have been better, with a clear representation of what I've seen and where to continue exploring. Instead you see just right at the beginning from the beach a portal but that portal is unreachable (above the cliff). Similarly, it might be beyond a wall. So to get there you shouldn't use the map because it is misleading. You wan't see the impediment and think that proximity is enough. Just walk there and when you are close you'll get there. But NO! The way to get there might be all around the level (e.G. through Cyseal) and not directly from the beach. But you can't tell walls and cliffs on the map. So that's not oldschool. Ultima Underworld or Baldur's Gate have excellent maps in contrast.
I try to read but I don't enjoy it. In Icewind Dale I read EVERY SINGLE F**** LINE in every dialog and every book. Here, you speak to an unseamingly unimportant guy and he tells you his lifelong story. In the end you wonder "so what is the quest?" and totally unrelated he says something along the lines of "kill 10 rats" without any feeling of "WOW, FOR LORE, YOU KNOW!" You feel utterly unimpressed by remarkably uninteresting storytelling without any epicness. Mundane stuff you would be do without. Put that in contrast to, say, Planescape Torment, and you'll see the huge difference. Quantity over quality? Please, it's like reading <your modern fantasy title here> after having read the Illiad or the Odyssey. I thought we were beyond that fast-food logic. How should I call it? Junk-text. Gets pretty tiresome after 1 hour of tedious reading.
Music. I won't comment on that. I switched it off after the very first game menu cacofony. I makes my ears bleed. Soundtracks in movies or many AAA games are not comparable.
Frustration, that's what this game is about. I'll leave it at that and turn to real old-school and sandbox titles. Pitty I was a backers on KS and my name is hard-coded into it.

heres my full written review
Lethal league is a game where the hype never stops  and neither does the ball. the core game is like combat pong  or dodge ball but there is a lot of nuance moves and tricks the make this game competitive and really fun.play with your friends. even if you don't have any, GO ONLINE and play against some other online warriors, don't want to get rekt. the challenge mode will keep you busy the fun never stops with a myriad of different stages and retro music that will remind you of jet set radio- always a good thing. the game is by team reptile the same people behind megabyte punch which came out august of 2013.after making megabyte punch the games developers were showing off a new kind of fighting game at major competitions the game was praised and so lethal league was born.
the gameplay of lethal league is simple you can't really do much you can jump strike and punt. only 3 buttons but the maneuvers you can string together using these 3 buttons are essential to mastering the game. each one of your moves jump, strike, and  punt all have a different functionality depending on the situation and character.each character has a unique jump mechanic such as wall jump double jump ect. all characters have a downward strike will jumping. and all characters have a special move after hitting something 4 times.there are 5 characters so far. switch,raptor,sonata,candyman and latch. learning your characters move set, mobility, and strengths is key to knowing what to do in each situation and really adds depth to the game. my 2 favorite character so far are switch and sonta, switch  can ride on the walls and has a pretty horizontal swing. on the other hand sonata has a double jump and had a pretty vertical swing . each character differences do add some subtly to the game and doesn't change the core gameplay. unlike other fighting game where u have to know each character's inputs and timing this game is all about timing so u can hope on any character pretty much and still be competent. the moment to moment gameplay can look a little daunting to new players but the simple mechanics make it easy to hop in the game and just play and once you start to learn how to predict the ball then thats when you'll really get into the deep nuance  of this game. the developers did a good job of showing you the basic of the gameplay in their tutorial while still giving you the opportunity to discover new game mechanics on your own. overall the gameplay is simple yet hard to master and thats what u want ina competitive game
getting into a game online is really easy its been a good number of people playing everytime i how on must i had to wait for a game was 1-2 minutes but most happen withen 30 secs. im on the west coast so your milage may vary
the gameplay is great and all but what i think really deserves praise is the music and art tim and dion did a great job with a game art the style of the art really fits the game a sorta pixel art of future streetscapes and urban environments really adds to the feel of the games atmosphere
the music gets me pumped to play so lethal league. i can listen to the music without the game. thats the sign of good music. a sorta mix sounds like the music for the jet set series with a modern twist
im having fun with lethal league and even though it won't be my go to competitive game i'm glad i have it in my library and i can hop in anytime and play the best version of pong there is :D

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a tile turn based stragety game much like Final Fantasy Tactics. This franchise has a long history, but Enemy Unknown is my introduction to the franchise. Pros:
Gamplay Mechanics are easy to get used to
Difficulty isn't too bad. Especially for those who have a extensive backround with turn based RPG games
Stroy was original (I don't have expereince with turn based RPG games that have enemy aliens. So this is true mainly for me)
Camera work and graphics add to the entertainment value

guys alike.

For thrity dollars XCOM: Enemy Uknown is worth it. Especially if you're looking for something refreshing and have a turn
based RPG backround. The replayability is subjective as I've seen folks with over 100 hours into this game, but I don't
see any point in playing again once it has been beaten. It runs the perfect amount of time and offers bonus options for a
replay through for those looking for a one time play through game. And who knows, maybe it will surprise you and pull
you in for another run through. Howver I can't comment on a second paythrough because I won't be replaying this
game.

If you love South Park you will love this game. The visuals are not earth-shattering but neither were visuals in the series. Obsidian did a very good job presenting the game as an interactive film.
Before playing the game itself you should start binge watching South Park since all items you will find are references to certain episodes. The humor relates to men's early puberty laughs... and that is exactly why you should play it.
The main plot and side quests are funny and predictable (but enough WTF twists mixed into it) while the combat system is simple enough but very enjoyable. Most of the quests are focuessed on the town of South Park but all the small details make it genuine. The replay value of the game is low since once you completed it... it's done.
The combat system allows for enough variation but don't expect a strategic dog fight - the boss fights are fun to do - and you'll manage to acquire all skills along the way. You can spend time on customizing your character, wearables and weapons (quite fun to combine some!).
My only points of attention are:
- The game should be played while using a controller since it works overall well
- DLC's are limited and they do not offer additional quests, which is a shame considering all ingredients are there
- The game should include multiplayer (like the Lego series)
Summarizing:
- Fun if you love South Park, if not this might not be the game for you
- Main quest and side missions are fun al be it a bit limited in scope and linear
- DLC's only offer additional weapons and clothes but you don't need any of that to succeed
- Plays like an interactive movie an thats ok!
- Happy farting!

I'm more than happy to pay for The Banner Saga 2 - I love the game, and I'm attached to the characters and world and want to know what happens - but when the credits rolled I was a little shocked that the game was already over. I felt like I was just getting started, that the story was beginning to pick up and that I'd just hit the first major milestone in the game. But the first major milestone was the end, and now I'm forced to spend more money to play on (which, again, I'm happy to do, but I'm not a fan of this model).
Overall I'd highly recommend this - just be aware that there are only a few hours of gameplay here.

I'm going to go against the grain here and object. I'm sure it's a *great* game for those interested in this sort of thing, but apparently it just doesn't suit me. Why? (If you want the long story short, skip to the last paragraph. If you want the short story long, read anything by Dickens.)
I have spent 12 minutes in this game. That's it. You start out reading the diary of some boring-life boy who really has nothing to say of importance except he has weird dreams and ends up on a bus that seems to take him the place in his dreams. I mean, I understand most folks these days have no meaning to life, spend more time on the computer than with people, and may not even have real-life friends. But I don't relate to that sort of thing. My life is monotonous as he states, but, I still enjoy most aspects.
Ultimately, I spent about 11 minutes reading what I thought was the intro. I am guessing that's how the whole game is though, since I found a way to skip all the conversations to the points where you make decisions. It seems like a "Choose Your Own Adventure" sort of book (those who grew up in the 80s/90s in the US should know what I'm talking about)... but there are a LOT of pages between each choice. In those 11 minutes, I got one. After I started skipping conversation, I got really lost and encountered some "cute" anime girls and another choice, at which point I had no clue what was going on and I was realising this is a novel with a choice interspersed here and there. And as I stated, I have books to read, where I can read more than a sentence or two at a time without clicking, and games that actually let me walk through and interact the story going on (despite how railroaded they may be).
Basically: this game seems to be a novel where you have to click to read the next sentence. Occasionally you get to make a one-out-of-two-options choice. If you want to get into a game by reading, I'm sure it's great. If you're a weasely little twerp who is "woe is me, my life sucks because I don't know how to meet girls and don't bother trying and can't work at McDonalds" (okay, so that's being a bit sarcastic but that's the vibe the protagonist gave me), you might be able to relate Otherwise, meh.

- Occassional stuttering after a loading screen - small graphical glitch, only flaw I noticed.

A really fun game. I honestly cannot remember the last time I had so much fun playing a shooter.
Graphics:
The graphics look much more like TF2 than Minecraft, but are unique to themselves. Though there are blocks, many of them are not cubes. There are all shapes and sizes.  It looks sleek and modern, not retro at all. There are also nice shadow and lighting effects. The style works for the type of game it is. In the heat of battles, blocks fly everywhere from explosions going off all around you, which adds to the experience drasticly.
Gameplay:
First and foremost is the unique ability to break or build anything. It adds a layer of strategy not found in most shooters. Defenses do not have to be complicated to be effective, though complicated desings can work if applied correctly. It takes a lot of time to develop good strategies for building on each map.
Once the match begins, after the build stage, you can do just about anything. Digging under a base is as viable as building over one. As others have said, unlike in Minecraft, there is gravity, so you will not be able to build floating bridges.
Each character feels really unique, and you really need one from each of the 3 categories to be successful (usually).  The weapons in this game are SOOO satisfying. A combination of good sound effects and visual effects makes each one pop, and landing a shot, no matter the weapon, always feels good. Each character also has a special ability, which, for most characters, offers support for yourself and all surrounding teamates.
Teamwork is key in this game. You need to use text or voice chat to tell eachother what you are doing, and make sure to plan attacks ahead of time. Running in wildly is not an option in this game, even for the tank class Cog.
Right now there is only one gamemode: Destroy the Base, but the developers are going to have more ready for launch in less than a month. I am hoping for a Payload type mode, where players place the tracks for the bomb train to follow.
Despite just one gamemode, I have yet to become bored, thanks to well designed maps that offer good variety. Player map creation is another planned feature to be looking forward to.
Overall I would HIGHLY recommend this game. It has something for everybody, even those who don't usually like shooters. I hope that this game will continue to expand and grow a healthy community once it is released in a few weeks!

Yet another Princess Maker has come back alive for Steam!
This game was originally released as PC-9801 back in the early 90's. The refine version was then released in 2003, and now has arrived to Steam!
You are a hero who saved a country from the Demons. One day, you decide to adopt a child from an orphanage. Your next eight years of journey with this girl now begins. Will her dream become true to be a Princess? Or will she take a different path in her future? Her future is in your hands!
Game Features:
Adventure Mode - Send her out to the fields! Get treasures and defeat those monsters on the way!
Once a year events - Chose from Combat / Beauty contents. Demonstrate your power! Show off your beauty and capture someone's heart!
Vacations - Boost your skills. Make memories with cute illustrations.
Meet the NPCs - Become a lady to meet those important NPCs in the castle!
Hear the citizens impressions of your daughter (full voiced too)!
Many endings - Endless game play with multiple endings.
Pros:
Opening skip available / Another great game to come play repeatedly as it has many different endings. Can you collect them all? / Fun adventure mode / Challenge once a year event to show off your hard work! / Full voiced in Japanese, even those onlookers! / Nostalgic MIDI or PCM sounds and musics / Supports Win 10 - 64 bit / High resolution even on full screen mode (800x600 window) / No pixalated hair, clothes and rooms. All smooth colors on screen / 40 save slots. You don't need to erase those hard work you made in the past! Re-visit your ending(s)!
Cons:
Eight years will past fast / Cube is not in this game / Screen size is 800x600 / If you are playing on Japanese setting, names can only be given in English alphabets (NO Hiragana/Katakana/Kanji) / Alphabets are layed out funny when deciding name. Full caps letters on left side. Starting from the top left, A then goes downwards to E. Next letter on the right side of the first row of alphabets on left and repeats until Z. Then continues to small letters starting from a. Takes a bit to get used to finding letters / UI uses similar colors. Bars are a bit hard to see in the status window.

I was forewarned by a friend not to expect much. That the story told in the game would not live up to the series.
I must say, after having played it, I must beg him to differ. The story is as close as it gets to a GRRM-level plot, without having the man directly involved himself in the writing.
There are surprises aplenty, and characterisations, that get you really involved.
Story-wise, my only complaint is that the Forrester family feels like a palette-swap of the Starks at times. They are still their own personalities, but you still have the southron widowed Lady who was married to a honorable, strong northern Lord, etc.
The graphics are admittedly bad, which at times can be distracting, but overall, a very enjoyable experience that I would recommend playing if you are a fan of the Song of Ice and Fire universe.

The gameplay is very repetitive, and grindy. If you enjoy cute anime girls and a cute parody like story, it can be entertaining and fun for a few play throughs. The equipment system is oversimplified to the point where you're basically just dressing up anime girls and building up an unreasonable amount of random mob trash and credits to craft and increase your wardrobe because the stat differentials on outfits is basically non existant. The weapon choices follow a fairly linear scaling path, and almost always has a clear winner, so you're kind of stuck using the one the game wants you to use instead of picking the cosmetic weapon of choice, contrary to the wardrobe path.
One redeeming factor is the difficulty of the game, as you can scale the mobs in a menu to basically easy or hard, if either would make the game more enjoyable with no penalties or bonuses for either. It allows you to kind of move through the story at your own pace without getting punished. Also the game runs very smoothly and the battle skill animation scenes for specials are kind of fun to watch for each character for the first few times.
I felt like you didn't get to use a lot of the extra characters for very long in a play through which was a bummer as there are quite a few fun side characters. After you finish a playthrough and move onto ng+ your character list is wiped out until you reaquire them through the story. Also due to skill distribution and character balancing, certain characters are just simply going to be better than others. Rip Compa.
All in all the game was pretty fun for what it was if you know what you're getting going into it. It's just a light hearted rpg that doesn't take itself seriously, with a cute storyline, cute characters, and a little fan service on the side, but hardly any depth on the combat/equipment/crafting side of things.

This is my first forray into a Telltale Game and I bought it thinking it was a glorified dating sim-style text adventure set in the GoT storyverse and would be a game where I could sit back, dictate the fate of the characters, all while sipping scotch on the rocks. Nope. Fingers were glued to the mouse and keyboard, and I ended up with watered down scotch by the end of the first chapter because I didn't want to miss a chance to steer the dialogue the I would want, so the time limit to respond is a nice touch that streamlines the storytelling and makes it feel more natural. Suffice it to say, that it's thoroughly engaging and really captures the 'don't become emotionally invested' spirit of its source material (even though you will because it's natural and inevitable given the amount of time that you spend with House Forrester). It's pretty clever how they only let you have four different save files. I can see the potential for replayability, even though I haven't started a second one. I've messed up on more than one occasion and I'm going to see them through. It's also pretty cool to see characters from the series making appearances in a parallel storyline. My only gripe about the game so far has to do with input from the mouse. I don't know if it's intentional or not, but the speed at which I move the mouse in real life is slowed down significantly in game. It's made for some real frustrating moments where I'd have to move the cursor to a point on screen and not get there in time, forcing me to relive the same death scene over and over again. Real annoying, but that's probably more on me than the game because I could always just get better at using a mouse.
Edit: I worked out an issue where it finally registered my controller and am having an overall better go at it. Would recommend playing with a controlling over mouse and keyboard.

I really loved this game. The gameplay was intense, the story was intriguing, and I really loved the music. However, I did have a few issues.
When I first downloaded the game, the game refused to launch. I continuously got a loading screen for downloading Direct X (which I already had), and never even made it to the title screen. Ironically, I had this same issue with another game recently. Finally I got the idea to download a different game to my computer, hoping that whatever my computer thought this game was missing, it would be included in the second game's download. Not sure if that's what fixed it, but after that the game finally loaded.
Every time I exited the game and tried to load it again later, I got the same Direct X downloading screen. To circumvent that, I tried loading from Steam and from my desktop icon at the same time, and eventually the title screen loaded. But I had to do this every single time.
Also, when I got to the final area (The Lady's Quarters), after I got captured the first time the game crashed in the same place about four or five times. I noticed it typically happened if I paused for a moment, so I tried not pausing at all and finally made it all the way through.
I also played through the DLC content, and every time I was captured by the Granny in The Depths, the game crashed. This caused me to have to reload, going through the same rigmarole I mentioned above to get the game to re-launch. I finally made it through that area and was happy to note that I didn't have that issue in The Hideaway.
Despite those technical issues, I loved the game, and would absolutely play it again.

To tell the truth, I'm not a big fan of "reviving" old titles (namely, failures like Bionic Commando, Dragon Age 2, Resident Evil 6, and of course Duke Nukem Forever), and I'm a strong believer that even the greatest predecessor doesn't always make a good successor. Also, being a huge fan of the original XCom series, I was worried that this game would fail a lot -- especially in comparison to the legendary predecessor. Well, good thing that this isn't the case.
I'll say this straight up: XCom made me ecstatic. When this game was released, it has basically re-launched the trend on tactical squad turn-based strategies in the industry. Does that ring any bells? If not, keep on reading.
Visually, I can't call Enemy Unknown a state-of-the-art project -- it does, however look
good. Marines, aliens, explosions and SFX do look as stylish as it gets. Animations are smooth, dying marines (and aliens as well) cough out blood and fall... pretty dramatically, I must say.
What also adds to the drama is the camera angles -- now that's some great work right there! Lining up a good sniper shot shows you sniper's perspective, a bullet and the falling enemy. Let's just say, there are few things that Michael Bay could've picked up for his movies.
The battles are really great too, even with no directed camera angles: turn-based fights require a lot of teamwork between your troops -- AI isn't stupid, he'll flank, use cover and try to corner your soldiers, which would lead to you losing them permanently (oh yeah, death is permanent in here). If you're not playing on Easy difficulty, of course -- which I strongly
recommend.
Both squad- and base management are really great. However, squad management shines the most when you're playing on a Iron Man option -- the one with no saves (except for when you actually quit the game). There's nothing more painful than seeing your favorite sniper, that you've grown fond of and practically bonded to, dying to an alien fire. But I definitely recommend playing with that option on -- it adds to your game experience significantly.
As of the storyline, I won't spoil anything, I'll just leave you with the fact that it's well-written and not as obvious as you might think (for a UFO-flick).
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

My favorite game of all time.
-For me, the best part of The Banner Saga is the balance between battle and narrative. Never once did I feel antsy to fight or starving for story; the pacing is impeccable and keeps the player engaged.
-In battle, the Banner Saga has a few refreshing reforms to isometric tactical RPGs that completely set it apart from games like Final Fantasy Tactics or Fire Emblem. The armor-strength system, turn order, variation in the number of spaces a unit takes up as a giant or human, and inability to heal gave me an entirely unique experience. Simple, but immensely effective, and fueling the gritty environment.
-The story is dark, desperate, but full of hope. While there is relatively limited dialogue between characters, this makes each interaction all the more special. I do, however, recommend immediately playing The Banner Saga 2, as it completes certain character arcs with a little more satisfaction.
-Decision making is stressful and exciting, I often stared at the screen agonizing about the repercussions simple choices could have on my supplies, morale, and wellbeing of characters. Initially, I had no idea permadeath occurred outside of battle, and my first introduction to it in Chapter 2 was so shocking, abrupt, and ruthless (Again, furthering the gritty environment). Because this is outside of battle, character death can be addressed in aa more impactful way, as a part of the story and your decisions, (in comparison to fire emblem where it is solely a strategy mistake, and you get maybe one or two lines of generic death dialogue). Characters will die, without last words, but you will witness their actions and feel like crap because it wasn't because you moved one unit square too close to the enemy, but in order to save your supplies/their loved ones/ambush/pride/etc.
-Its downright visually stunning. Rather than be overwhelmed by the dark tones, you will be enchanted by the bright visuals. The art direction in this game is focused on a realistic fantasy- these are the axes and clothing vikings would wear, feeding the realistic grit. Gorgeously animated, designed, colored. Just so freaking gorgeous. SO PRETTY.
I recommend this to every single person I know that enjoys tactical RPGs.

People who think games like Dark Souls is hard have probably never played FTL before. This strategy game where you control a space-ship that is running away from the Rebel fleet in an attempt to save the galaxy is honestly one of the most difficult rouge-like's that I've ever played. There were so many times when I'd reach the final boss of the game with max health and soon find my ship completely destroyed in mere moments simply because they'd breach my defenses before I could even graze their ship. This unforgiving game only lets you have one life throughout the whole game, and finding that the game runs on the weirdest random number generator doesn't exactly make things a lot easier on the player. The different weapons and ships make this game a hell of a lot more interesting, as you constantly have to make changes to your every move throughout the entire game. One moment, you may be dominating a supply ship to the point where they try to flee; but they can't because you shot down their engines. The next, the exact same thing is happening to you. With the new Advanced Edition, the entire game pretty much was changed and rebalanced (Flak is the most OP weapon. Get as much as you can). This game deserves a 9/10, for it's only problem being that unlocking new ships is too vague for most people to get, and with it's weird random number generator it makes it nearly impossible to determine if "this gameplay will get me a new ship to use".

As a game it's extremely grind heavy and there's hardly any skill variation when it comes to combat. Each character has around 5-9 "spells" that you can use with mana, but generally speaking all the damage spells are lackluster and mostly pointless. The game revolves around spamming your EXE megamoves and finding ways to maximize the growth of the EXE gauge. There's really no any variation how the fights play out.
Also the games dmg/resistance algorithms are kinda scewed. You'll need to reach a certain treshold to do dmg to an enemy, if its migitation stat exceed your attack stat by far, you'll be basically doing 0 dmg with every move. Most high level monsters also have autoheal in the beginning of their turn so it's not even possible to kill them without spamming EXE skills because they outheal normal spells and attacks.
There's also element system with 4 elements, but there's really no info available what is weak against what making the whole system pointless. Figuring it out and writing the stuff on a notepad really isn't something you want to do, considering 99% of JRPGs with elemental system offers abilites to figure out enemy weaknesses. Sometimes you'll notice a zero popping out and go "oh yeah, elemental things in this game."
The turn indicator thingie is also kinda weird. I didn't bother googling why it does the things it does, but especially bosses can pull turns out of their asses and with the autoheal mechanic it's kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. This makes EXE spamming even more important.
The music isn't all that great to be honest. Compared to games like Persona 4 the soundtrack is lacking bad. Voice acting is superb though, at least with Japanese audio.
Art is decent but heavily recycled and so are the dungeons. There's dozens of dungeons with the same layout and tens of monsters with the same model.
Also the game heavily relies on the plan system which is all about the grinding. You'll be running same dungeons over and over and over and over again and again and again. You'll grow tired of using the system very fast, turning the dungeon modifications on and off repeatedly. The UI for this is lacking and should've been improved.
It's a decent game to kill time in anime settings, but can't really recommend it for anyone. I'm playing it because I have no life, but I'm in no way blind to its faults. First thing you'll notice is the fact that the game makers LOVE HUGE DIGITS. Apparently someone in marketing came up with the notion that BIG NUMBERS ARE BETTER.

If you enjoy other Telltale games, and/or GoT, don't ruin those things for yourself by playing this game.
There is an enormous volume of positive reviews for this game so if you want pros, go read those, I’m just gonna list cons.
-The first and most immediately noticeable problem with this game is that, despite being quite literally inundated with masturbatory references to the show upon which it’s based (right down to the same exact f*cking intro), it feels nothing like Game of Thrones.
- Kinda similar to first con: the storyline itself is a rather significant tonal shift and drop in writing quality compared to the source material, almost like what you’d expect if you were going to read a moderately-intelligent 14 year-old’s GoT fanfic or something.
-The constant cameos by major characters from the show are, without exception, out-of-place and really seem like they were put in just to say, “We paid through the f*cking nose to get these guys to come voice their show characters in our game and you had better like it because there’s more where this came from!”
-Frequent, pointless QTEs.
-The “hand-painted”  visuals probably sounded good in theory, in practice however, they look like less of a style choice, more like some way to skimp on the art asset budget.
-Voice acting from non-show characters is dodgy at best.
-Decisions have no impact on the story at all.
Tl;dr: Roommate and I barely slogged through first episode and alt+f4’d the second one 10 minutes in.

As far as art style and concept goes, this is one of the most beautiful games I have ever come across. Character and level design feel like a Studio Ghibli movie, that was directed by Tim Burton, with creative input from Sylvain Chomet.
But the gameplay unfortunately is lacking in some aspects, especially:
- Lack of consistency. Things that work in level A, will not work in level B.
- Movement. Due to the design of the game and the placement of the cameras, you'll miss that jump or that corner more often than not. Quite frustrating when things are going fast.
- Quite a lot of hand holding. "Puzzles" are always too obvious, as is your way to traverse levels. I would have loved a bit more challenge.
All in all, I'd still recommend it. It's short and the atmosphere you get out of it is brilliant. But gameplay wise I was quite often a bit frustrated to say the least.

The general art style is lovely. The music is lovely. The controls are not my favorite, but are just fine. The puzzles are fun. The environments are lovingly crafted. And the Nomes are freaking adorable.

It's saying a lot of really interesting stuff about childhood and abuse and the way children perceive the world around them, but I honestly never connected with that on an emotional level. I can sit and think, "Oh yes, that's significant and meaningful symbolism right there," but I never really FELT it, and that's important when dealing with such powerful topics. I dunno, maybe I'm just a goober who can't connect with things on an emotional level anymore, but I there were a few really key points I felt the story didn't earn, beats that came out of time.
If you really like Inside, Limbo, and stuff like that and need a fix, then yeah, give this a shot. But you can also just, you know, play those games... Again, I really want to like Little Nightmares more because it's right up my alley and I think you can honestly make a case for it, but I feel like the story took too many missteps for me to honestly recommend it.
That's just my opinion, though; feel free to disagree. I'd love to have a more in-depth discussion about it, so maybe I should recommend it after all... I'm torn.
Oh well.

If you want to know what this game is think asteroids on steroids to your favourite music tracks. This is my go-to game whenever I just want to zone out and kill some time playing something while listening to music, but don't feel like starting a new game or concentrating on a story, etc. This is my Tetris.
This perhaps isn't the best game if you only want to kill a *little* time, since it plays your music collection (and therefore has the best sound track ever), everytime you say "I'll quit after this round!" it goes and picks yet another great track and you end up saying "Well... maybe after this one!"
What I love about this game is that can be customised to suit your mood - harder difficulties are *HARD*, easier difficulties are easy. The intensity of the game depends on the intensity of the music track you play. You can unlock perks and assign them to help in different ways. After a high score? Put your perks into score multipliers and sacrifice the extra weapons. Feel like a challenge? Assign your perks to weapons and bump the difficulty up (I'm actually pretty good at Suicidal difficulty now ;). Want to just take it easy? Lower the difficulty and put on some relaxing music.
The game actually comes with a decent selection of music from a range of genres, which I discovered while unlocking the Music Tour achievement. Of course it has a fair bit of electronic music, which you would expect from a game like this, but I very happy to see it actually has some decent alternative rock & metal tracks as well. It can also stream music from a number of Internet radio stations (no idea if it's possible to add more), but of course you will really want to bring your own music collection to enjoy this game the most. For me, that's European style Symphonic Power Metal \m/
The perks can be a bit of a grind to unlock, and even more so to fully upgrade them. Unlocking them just takes score, but upgrading them can only be done by picking up in game money - and that only drops $10 at a time. That's not really a problem as the low-mid levels are fairly cheap and is all you need as long as you aren't trying to play on Suicidal difficulty, but maxing them out does take a fair while.
Let's talk weapons. Like most asteroids type games you have a generic laser that can be upgraded by picking up POWer ups. This one is actually pretty good - it has a decent spread and can take out a large number of enemies pretty quickly. The unique thing about this game is the intensity of your weapons also depends on the intensity of the music - picking up VOL+ powerups increases the volume, making your weapons more powerful, but at the same time it also spawns more enemies and makes them faster.
Your second weapon is of course some kind of super bomb, also known as the "OH GOD TOO MANY ENEMIES!!!" panic button to take out most of the nearby enemies and give you a few seconds of invaulnerability. Then you have the reflective shield, homing micro missiles and the Ultra Beam to quickly eradicate a large group of enemies in a given direction. I love that none of these weapons feel like duplicates and they all have their place - knowing which one to use when becomes very important in the higher difficulties.
You remember back in the nineties how games used to have warnings on the box & the first page of the manual not to play them if you suffer from epilepsy? Well, I do. Anyway - I think this game actually means it, it uses a lot of very intense strobing visuals which (other than causing epilectic siezures) can make it pretty hard to see incoming projectiles - when I first started playing half the time I couldn't see what had killed me. The visuals can be toned down (or increased to epic proportions!!!), but personally I kept them on 100% and just got used to them.
If you are going to buy this, get the Beat Hazard Ultra DLC - some of the stuff I mentioned here is specific to that DLC and the base game does not have a huge amount of variety in terms of enemies, weapons, etc. The only reason not to get the Ultra DLC is to try it out a bit and see if you like it. As soon as you are convinced, buy the Ultra DLC.

Having a hard time getting into this game. I know most people are complaining about the grinding, or pay-to-win aspects, but honestly I haven't gotten far enough in the game to care about those things yet.
Character creation is awesome, and shows off the graphics amazingly.
Combat is interesting, though I personally have a hard time with combo/reflex oriented combat. I end up just button-mashing and hoping combos happen because I can't remember the moves. I was expecting a more wow-oriented interface, where I could use numbers to trigger abilities instead of key/mouse combinations.
The problem I'm having is the world... it doesn't seem engaging. It's just misc fantasy world number 5542. I don't feel like the world has an engaging story to make it feel special and unique. I'm moving from misc quest to misc quest, not caring who gave them to me or why they want the quest done. If you used the same map in another game, nobody would notice. The NPCs seem bland and have no personalities other than their outfits. I know it's all translated from Korean, but I personally have a hard time with the language. I know this is typical of eastern-language translations, but I still find it disorientating and hard to read.
I'm having a very hard time getting into it, and it's not giving me any indication that it will be worth it.

Online multiplayer and skirmish games are both free; purchasing the game grants access to the fairly standard campaign mode. There is a map editor, but no randomized maps (there are plenty of maps included, though). The interface could be improved: tool-tips appear entirely too slowly, counters are not indicated on the aforementioned tool-tips, the minimap is useless, and you can’t zoom in or out. Units are unique in appearance, although they fall into general categories (fast, ranged, healer). There are hard counters in the game for the basic units (guns beat crabs beat scouts beat guns) and turrets that can be captured to freeze, fight, or revert enemy units to their basic form. Units auto-attack while moving, but do not move as a group, resulting in a lot of micromanagement. Difficulty in managing units is compounded by the fast pace of the game; typically, one wrong move (such as losing a large battle, or losing units to a neutral location) is enough to do you in, as the AI is adept at the mechanics. While the campaign isn’t really worth the cost, those who can handle simplified, fast-paced real-time strategy games have nothing to lose in downloading the free skirmish and multiplayer modes.
