Steam hours played: 101
Rating: 9.5 out of 10
This game features the strongest AI that I have seen since, "Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares" ( MOO 2 was released in 1996. I read that a M.I.T. coder created the Artificial Intelligence for MOO 2 ). When I play "XCOM: Enemy Unknown", it is like playing against a Grandmaster chess player.
X-COM is turn based, in 3 dimensions and multiple horizontal planes ( think multi-storey housing ). The ruleset is simple to learn. Factoring in the sum of simple rules, your human error, tiredness and sometimes unpredictable, alien behaviour and the tactical combat scales up to something epic ( especially when you miss your shots ). Featuring a destructible environment: thin walls will melt; trees will scorch; fuel-laden vehicles will explode.
Visually, the art direction is very high ( I love Unreal Engine 3's wisps of random smoke from smudge sticks, flames, burning cars and scorched earth ). The game was immersive ( voice overs and cut scenes ) and scary, to the point that I filled my diapers several times. Michael McCann wrote the music ( he composed the award-winning sound track for "Deus Ex: Human Revolution" ). My favourite tracks are:
6:33 "Ready for Battle (Choose Squad)"
11:41 "Vigilo Confido"
34:36 "Snap Shot"
"XCOM: Enemy Unknown Soundtrack (Full)"
The game is very addictive. The first time that I loaded it up, I played for 27 hours straight and was awake for maybe 36 hours. Take with a grain of salt, reviews with less than 30 hours played because that is ( laughable and ) only half of one game!
Although Steam shows that I have 101 hours played, I have only played the game 3 times. The first was on classic ( =hard difficulty ) and I got face-rolled; failing the Zhang mission 5 times. I then switched to "Normal" difficulty - Ironman Mode. I finally succeeded on game three ( even though I lost my support healer prior to the base invasion ( double miss on 99% to hit, combined with poor decision making and underestimating the enemy ) and never replaced him ( and my heavy weapons expert died during the actual base invasion - later replaced with some new recruit ).
The negative reviews, with people crying like babies ( regarding game mechanics ) irk me because I finished the game with no healer and zero battles lost ( World Stats Comparison ). Yes, it hurts to lose a squad member ( like it hurts to lose a hero in role playing games ) since levelling up each squad member is time consuming. 99% of the rules that the AI is using against you, can be used against it ( there are no-brainer technological counters to the slight mobility bonus given to the AI ). You get two actions per turn and I love the fact that you are committed to your decisions ( for better or for worse ). There are no cheese mechanics ( like inching forward a centimetre at a time ). Cover mechanics are used ( similar to Shadowrun: Dragonfall - half or full shield ).
I deducted 0.5 from the final score, due to relatively minor issues regarding the interface design and gameplay mechanics.
Rating: 9.5 out of 10

Faster than Light is a 'Space Rogue-Like' game that came into being by virtue of a Kickstarter project by Indie Developer Subset Games. It promises a starship captain experience where the player can manage both crew and ship in relative detail.
The player takes the role of a Starship Captain with vital information that will help turn the tide of war in the on going conflict between the Rebels and the Federation. The player is allowed to select and manage a variety of ships, each having their own set of crew and abilities which can expand as you progress. Once again, upgrade your ship, expand your crew and try to stay alive till the very end.
+
- The game sports simple pixel art graphics that invokes a retro feel, and, in my opinion, suits it very well. The gameplay is what makes this game shine however and as stated in the INTRODUCTION, this game attempts to simulate a Starship captain by letting the player assign crew to man the ships internal systems, order power to be diverted to different parts of the ship, focus fire on an enemy ship's weapon systems and many many more.
+
- Easy, Normal or Hard, all extremley unforgiving. This is a game where you need to bite down hard and take the consequences of your actions and choices like an adult, much like all 'Rogue-Like' games. You die, then you start all-over again. Learning from your mistake is part of the game's charm.
+
- Good varriety of ships, weapons, and crew all of which unlocks as you progress. The unlocking system was set up to ensure that every new game will be different and provide unique experiences.
+
- Great soundtrack from a small indie game. Bigger game developers should learn that not every game needs orchestral pieces to make a game's music pleasing.
-
- Aside from purchasing weapon system and ship components, you won't be able to customize the ship's looks or the layout since said layout is on a preset. I would have liked to construct my own ship.
-
- The only available game mode is the default escape scenario. It would be nice if they would add new campaigns or scenarios like, escort mission, defense campaign etc. It would definitely spice things up. A much more expansive map would also be welcome.
-
- Being able to talk and may be train your crew outside combat (specially if you find an empty system) would be a welcome addition. More interaction is needed like basic dialogues between the people on your ship to give it more life. It would be a statisfying feeling if you have resolved a conflict between two crew members.
for a great price. It's definitely not for everyone, specially people who has no patience for Rogue-Like games.
This games requires 25% skill, 25% planning and 50% luck. Everytime you start a new campaign it would be a different experience from the last. The game allows most sci-fi fans to totally immerse themselves in the shoes of a Starship captain much like the heroes from the great Space Travel franchises such as Star Trek, Firefly, Babylon 5 & Battlestar Galactica.

This game is so good, that I've decided to make a review of it, because it has only 92% of the reviews are positive, and that is not enough! :) So let's get started, I try to be less biased and more informative. I am going to make a short interview with myself :)
-What kind of game is this?
D:OS is a classic RPG with isometric point-of-view and turned based combat. The game can be played in solo, but should be played in coop, to have additional gaming experience!
- Does it have an open world, and/or a non-linear flow of events?
Yes and no. The game itself uses gateway bosses to prevent you from getting into high level areas. You may defeat these mobs anyway, but the game gets considerably hard when fighting against enemies with more than 1-2 levels higher than yours. Also, the quests are plentlyful but linear, though it is up to you when would you like to take care of them.
- What about character-generation, skills, classes?
The game features two main characters, either by made the one solo player, or made by you and your coop partner (in that case, you bring only 1 character with you). There are a total number of 11 pre-defined classes, but leveling is totally non-linear and you may vary your characters the way you please. There are 9 skill-trees, 6 main attributes, plenty of abilities and a load of talents as well, so leveling is extremely fun, deep, and...well...complicated. At least on first glance.
- What about combat and interaction?
As I said, combat is turn-based. It is really easy to handle, and I love to fight in this game. Very rewarding and fun! Each of your party-members and opposition have action points, and each action requires a specific amount of it. When attacking with weapons, there is a chance of a successful hit shown is percentage (for example: 78% to hit). Also, there are a lot of different feats, like resistances, blocking ability, evading, etc. During combat, the game rolls for your characters and the enemies as well to see if a specific status/effect became active or not. For example contacting with fire can cause a burning but high level bodybuilding or protection against fire can negate/reduce that effect. There is a rolling: 100(chance on default)-70(your modifier)=30(the number you need to avoid). You roll 48, it's OK, you roll 22, you'll burn for a few rounds.
Social interactions are well made, although the game lacks voice-over, as most conversations are read-only. You may choose between several dialogue-options to move things forward. This is easy to use and to understand. The game features dual-dialogues between the two main characters (either by made the solo player or by your and your coop-partner's character). During these conversations you can either make an agreement about some important matters about quests, or can argue about it. If there's a debate between you and your partner, or between the players and the AI, the game uses a Rock-paper-scissors minigame to decide the winner of the debate. This might seem off-genre, but didn't bother me.
- How difficult is this game, and how long is it?
The game is pretty difficult on hard mode. You have to make careful choices during combat, must use your brain and should save often. The number of quicksave slots can be varied by the player, so you may have more than 15 different slots just for F5, so you can avoid accidents. The game has an autosave system as well. You may save whenever you want, there are no checkpoints. You can't save during conversations though, but if you play coop and your partner is the host, than he/she can.
The game must be pretty long. After 91hrs, I am on level 14, and level 20 is the soft cap. I figure that 100-120 hrs is required to finish, considering that you do most quests, want to understand the plot, play on higher difficulty, and dig into crafting and other things.
- What can you tell about the technical stuff of this game?
Graphics are functional. The game can look fairly good, but today's standards are pretty high, and so I have to say that the visual section is not that good in this game. It didn't bother me at all, and I wouldn't say it's ugly or anything. But is far from gorgeus. The audio section is much better though! You'll love the soundtrack, it has a lot of memorable tracks. Voice acting is well-made, but once again: many of the dialogues are read-only. Sound effects are averge.
- Does this game has any cons?
Yes, but minor ones only. First of all, it uses a pretty ornate English, and it can be really hard to understand every single word even for fairly good english-speakers (considering that you are not a native speaker, just like me). What makes this even worse is that the game has an awkward journal system. Though there are notes on every single quest, your objective is not always that clear. The game won't hold your hand while you're struggling to save the world. This is a whole new experience in these days of casual gaming, so while it's fun and rewarding, it makes things difficult. Also there are no objective markers on the map, just a few ones occasionally. The RPS-system is quite dull, and it is not perfectly protected from the cheating AI to say the least. During combat some effects are hard to understand as sometimes they won't apply even when they should. Also, some markers during combat, for example backstab are pretty hectic and sometimes 'hard to catch' if you know what I mean. Even if you zoom in, the enemy does different animations during your turn, and if you fail to click on the hitbox, you may move instead of firing an arrow. The hitbox system could be better, with larger hitboxes. Puzzles are awkward in this game: the game fails to confirm that you've just solved them, and sometimes you keep looking for additional pieces while it is already done. This is hardly rewarding, and can take a lot of time, and again it is because of the aforementioned journal-system, with all its faults.
- What is you conclusion and closing words?
This game is pure awesomeness. It has everything I've ever wanted from a game: it has 2 player coop, difficult, long, interesting, has a nice level-system, demands some brainwork, and features some meaningful choices. I mean during these days of AAA RPGs, it is a new experience that you can actually screw things up and people can die because you've made mistakes.
I would recommend this game to anybody who wants to have a lifetime gaming experience, is older than 13 and understands english pretty good (although there are other languages available so this might not be a problem after all). If you have a friend with a similar taste in computer games, you are in for a treat.
You don't want to miss this game, trust me! :)

I suggest googling the units they don't teach you about in the tutorial, then practicing with them for awhile in bots mode. No where in the free part do they give you a guide on the units, maybe in the $10 single player campaign idk. Also, if you use the site I looked at, they don't talk about the turrets or special control points, or the robot unit thing (which is beast). There are two turrets, one looks like a spartan sword from Halo, that, once destroyed, stays destroyed. The second turret, has 5 cells, each needs to be filled with a unit to acheive the maximum rate of fire, they can also be destroyed, captured, and rebuilt under your team (or your opponents)! Then there are three special control points that give you an ability that can decide the game. The first one has a picture of a snowflake, and when ready it will freeze ALL units within its radius, and the best part is you choose where it hits! The second, which is a very useful tool, is the warp station, pretty straight foward, you can use it to teleport units from point A, to point B, it is used by first setting down the warp radius circle around what you want sent, and then a second radius circle around where you want it warped to. The third, which can turn the game, is the reset station, like the snowflake, when charged it gives you the option to set a radius, anything within will be changed back into the basic unit you get from spawners, and doesn't affect basics, im not sure if it affects your units, but it probably does. Then there are two spawner types, one is big, and spawns basics at a faster rate, and the default which spawns basics at an average rate. The robot unit is a special unit, you can only have one at a time, or at all if the map doesn't have the spawn station for it, and if it does, it is automatically under your control and spawns a robot after a cooldown once the previous has died, it is both ranged and melee, can't be poisoned, or leeched im sure, and has alot of health, note that the spawners can't be captured or destroyed so don't send units to sit on the enemies, it wont stop them, and might just damage or kill a couple. The multiplayer runs smooth, its just the users that have bad connection sometimes and there is no penalty or reward for winning and losing in quick fights, so its a good place to relax and practice.

I don't really want to give this Game a negative Review, but there are no grey areas in the reviewsystem and if I ask myself "would you recommend this game to others" I simply can't get myself to say yes.
Let me try to explain my reasoning:
The game has an interesting artstyle and some elements of norse-mythology, and works with a mixture of oregan-trail style  traveling(where you make decisions along the way) and turn based combat on a grid.
So far so good, a solid concept.
My problems with the game:
None of the characters, were all that memorable to me, they all felt kind of bland and those that I rememberd were rather annoying(mostly the humans, the Varl, a race of horned giants, were mostly bland warriors).
The oregan-trail elements of the game actually felt kind of fun to me, but I found the combat to be so utterly dull and repetetative... You fight a bunch of really tough(tough in the sense of, they are able to take a ton of damage, not that they are difficult to beat) enemys that repeat over and over again, with little variety. Maybe there will be more interesting enemys later, but that still doesn't change my second problem with the game:
The characters don't all that many abilitys, in fact, they have one per character and their base attacks. And Most of the time you just move a character, hit a thing and thats it, as long as you don't let your groupsize shrink to much during the out-of-combat-events and just gather all your characters in one place, you should be able to defeat most encounters with ease.
Most of the time the combat just felt like it was getting in the way of the storyprogression though...
So yeah, since I am someone who rather likes really complex turn based combat, I sadly can't recommend this game.

As a pure audiovisual experience the Banner Saga is superb, both the artwork and the soundtrack are amazing.
Unfortunately as a game it has several major issues. The turn-based battles are not that good and get repetitive really quickly. The caravan management side of things doesn't fare much better. There's plenty of choices to be made, but often the consequences feel very unpredictable and unfair. Furthermore, the main path through the game is fairly fixed anyway and in the long run your choices don't really matter much. Even running out of supplies for days on end doesn't seem like a big deal, you just lose a few people from your caravan.
I backed the Banner Saga on Kickstarter and really wanted to like the game. Unfortunately the gameplay is just too weak and the game has too many bad design decisions for me to truly enjoy. I played through the game on normal difficulty.
The good:
- Gorgeous visuals
- Amazing soundtrack
- The Norse mythology inspired world is quite interesting
The bad:
- There's lots of choices, but the consequences often seem very unpredictable and most of the time don't seem to matter much in the long run
- The turn-based combat is pretty weak with some questionable design choices, especially the way turn order is determined and how remaining hit points and attack strength are combined into one stat
- There's very little variety in battles, in pretty much every battle you'll be fighting the same few enemies
- Using renown for both leveling up and for supplies & items was a very annoying design decision
- Ending is very abrupt

I bought this game several months after its release, heard a lot of positive reviews and decided to try it on my own.
Banner Saga is a fantastic game in my opinion. I finished it three times, taking different decisions during the playthroughs just to see all the consequences they could have (and had!).
I liked the setting very much, the epic viking saga of last stand of both humans and giants against a merciless invader horde. Heroes and their personalities are quite memorable, I enjoyed every bit of dialogue. The system of somewhat random events in-between your main battles is not new, we could see the same in Fasterthanlight, but it does surprisingly good here.
Tactical battles mechanic is interesting, exploring various character options while advancing their level and unlocking new abilities gives some hidden depth to the game.
The visual part is awesome, plain awesome. The same could be said of 100% fitting soundtrack, the melodies create just the right mood for the game events flow.
I cannot say this is a game for everyone, but if you enjoy tactical battles and storytelling you'll likely fall in love with this game. To me it's nothing but a masterpiece.
Looking forward to the sequel.

This game is all about picking one of various ships and making it from the start to the end area and beating up the boss. Sound easy? You'd be gravely mistaken. This game lives up to the "Rogue-like" genre which it's claimed to be. Most of the game is down to sheer luck and split second choices which can result in completing the objective or having your ship become a new debris field. Customisation in this game is highly extensive as well. Depending on what you buy or salvage you can outfit your ship with a huge variety of weapons and modules to ultimatly destory any pesky rebel or pirate that gets in your way. You can also customise your crew by using the various races from the standard humans, the fire-proof and tanky rockmen or the flesh-tearing mantises which will make any boarding crew have a really bad day. Be warned this is a "rouge-like" so you can and WILL fail often which will result in a full restart but that's just part of the charm. One build may work one time but the game maybe cruel and not give you what you wish the second time. Overall this game is easily worth the £7 it is priced at and is easily one of my favourite steam games now.   9.5/10

PROS:
For around the first half of the game, combat and customization get increasingly deep and engaging.
Combat move animations are skippable.
Good background music.
The anthropomorphized-game-console premise is used with a fairly light touch and not belabored.
There are some amusing joke enemies and attacks.
CONS:
Some dialogue makes very little sense, either because of lazy translation or because it's making overly obscure references.
Past a certain point, only one kind of special attack is doing any meaningful damage to hard enemies, so combat towards the end of the game is just a matter of figuring out how to apply those attacks as often as possible, and other mechanics stop mattering.
Enemies generally don't have anything to make them different from other enemies, besides stats. That means any two combats will probably play out the same way, other than how long they are, how often you need to heal, and how long you spend doing normal attacks before you use special ones.
There are many quests that involve nothing but repetitively fighting the same type of enemy over and over.
Dungeon design is almost nonexistent; each dungeon is almost just one big room to walk up to enemies in, and some dungeon maps are recycled completely for more than one dungeon.
???:
Most playable characters have clothing customization items and large, painstakingly animated breasts.
Overall, there is far too much shallow grinding in the later parts of this game for me to recommend it, despite a promising early start.

I am also not a fan of games that require players to "roll the dice." Each time you reach a fork in the road, you choose what to do next. The problem is, both of them can hurt you, and both of them can be beneficial. I understand that for some, this creates depth and makes you act quickly (it makes the game seem more realistic, and you make decisions without knowing their consequences). I would rather use my best judgment and play a game "correctly," after trial-and-error and learning. You cannot truly become "skilled" at FTL; you can only hope for the best.
This is a great game, but it's not for me.

Crawl is a really good asymmetrical multiplayer game. Probably one of the best concepts for a game in recent memory, and the execution is generally quite good. The combat & level interactions are a bit janky but it's certainly not terrible, just not as good as it could be. The most fun is in sabotaging your friend as often as possible. I only played with one friend and two bots but I feel like it would shine with 4 players as it's more of a chaotic mess of fighting for the lead.
I'm not the biggest fan of how the game is so focused on levelling up monsters but then the actual endgame is just a pre-determined boss that has no bearing on anything the dead have achieved while not being the human player. But in general, Crawl is a great game with lots of tense battles for power that make it fun with a friend. I don't think single player has much appeal tbh but there is a decent amount of unlockables which is cool. I wish there was more games like this, would be even better with working online play. I definitely plan to give Crawl another chance, hopefully with a full crowd. Still an easy recommendation.

Really great game. The dialogue is really well written, funny, and filled with references to anime / video games (even to the point where the characters you play as are references themselves). Storywise this game never takes itself too seriously, and it takes every oppurtunity it gets to either throw a punch at the fourth wall, or deal out fanservice. The characters are adorable and have unique personalities that makes each of them interesting.
This game is really pretty to look at. The graphics are very basic, but that still works for a game like this. The special + super attacks are still very pretty to look at. One thing that irks me is that dungeon designs are recycled throughout the game. Not a dealbreaker by any means, but I still would've loved to see more creativity than using ctrl+c and ctrl+v for a couple of dungeon designs.
Music is alright. The songs fit the situations they are playing in, but none of them are really memorable. The sound effects are really great, especially during attacks they're really satisfying to listen to. The japanese voice acting, atleast, is really good. (Except Compa's voice is kinda annoying in my opinion.)
The combat system in this game is pretty good and the combo system works well. You can customize which attacks you want attach. You get 4 attacks for each combo, the first one is a staple attack and then you can use Rush attacks (for increasing a super attack meter), Power attacks (for dealing the most damage), and Break attacks (for wrecking armor). You also get special and super attacks. Pretty simple system, but still really compelling.
The game is very grindy, not only for levelling for preparing against bosses (especially during the endgame, and if you want the max level achievements for each characters), but also for materials, which are used for crafting many different items, like healing potions, weapons, armor, etc., making them available in the shop. In most cases, this means tracking down several monsters, slaying them, and hope you get the item you're looking for. Needless to say, this can get really tedious.
Another gripe I have with this game is that the New Game+ mode doesn't increase the level of the enemies. Slaying early-game monsters while you're pretty much godmode really isn't fun to me. You'll probably want to play NG+ once or twice for the extra memory. (trust me, you'll need it, especially if you want all the achievements) Other than that, NG+ doesn't bring any benefits as opposed to just continuing playing the endgame save file.
Overall, while there are clear flaws with this game, they are easily outweighted by the hilarious writing, the lovable characters, and the satisfactory combat. This is definitely not a game for everyone, but if you can look past the heavy grinding and the sheer amount of fanservice, I'd recommend giving this game a chance.

Little Nightmares, for me, was an entertaining adventure from start to finish. Though the story is not revealed at once (or truly, fully, ever), I was able to piece together the journey that the protagonist, Six, takes to escape the clutches of her captors. This horror-puzzle-platformer is in the same vein as Limbo; a stark, often violent end, when caught or killed.
PROS:
+ The atmosphere is stellar. I was sold on being inside of a tankard at sea.
+ Along with the atomsphere, the sound design was great. Hearing the muffled sounds of stomping to foreshadowing enemy movement, or the shrieks the Chefs made when they spotted you all played nicely into the game's fear factor.
+ Character design. This is my favorite aspect of Little Nightmares. There are only four distinguishable characters in the game: the janitor, the two chefs, and the lady. In the second-to-last level there is a plethora of obese characters, but they are often indistinguishable, and rightfully so. BUT -- the four main antagonists are creepily created (another props to the sound design is the wheezing noises the characters make to distinguish themselves from one another). I would love to see a sequel to the game if only to see what new characters could be introduced to the world.
+ The cinematic strength of the game. Although at times the camera angle would be bothersome (see below), certain cinematic shots- ones wherein the purpose was to hint at an upcoming enemy or level- worked masterfully in the game's favor. It was the little things like this that made Little Nightmares a game to remember.
CONS:
- The game's length is short, but at a sale price of $9.99, I found it was worth it. I take much longer than the normal gamer to complete a game and I still beat it over the course of two days.
- The camera angle was the antagonist at a few points in the game. Rather than adjust to where Six was positioned, the camera decided to do it's own thang and stay positioned in some obscure spot.
- Unclear achievements. This may just be a "me thing" - but I didn't discover until nearly 1/3 of the way through that lighting the lamps, breaking the china dolls, and hugging the gnomes all where necessary to achieve certain Steam achievements. It would have been nice to see some on-screen text that corresponded from the start.
OVERALL: 9/10

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1, I bought this game yesterday and already have accumulated almost 30 hours.
This means one of two things:
1. This game is f**king amazing and everyone who likes anime stuff should buy it
or
2. I need friends
.....It's probably both now that I think about it.....
But in all seriousness, this game is spectacular.
There will be a tl;dr at the end.
The gameplay is your typical turn-based J-RPG that people have come to love, myself included, but also serves as a Visual Novel as well. The content gets really grindy after a while, like, really really grindy. Like, Shao Hao dailies grindy (props if you got that reference). It's great if you can stomach grinds and like the gameplay, but boring and seemingly a waste of time if you don't.
My crappy computer which can't run CS:GO on all low settings at 30fps ran this game at 60fps on the highest settings, so this game has almost no system requirements other than memory. The only significant problem I've had is with the game crashing at what seems like random times. So be careful about that if that happens to you, and, most importantly, SAVE EVERY CHANCE YOU GET!!!!.
The combat flows so smoothly for a J-RPG that it's almost hard to get used to. You use strategy and the right usage of abilities to take down enemies (for example you wouldn't want to use your hard hitting attacks when the dragon has all of his guard points up, so you would want to widdle that down first). It all feels so fresh from what seems like a genre of game that's/on the verge of being over-saturated.
The world of Gamindustri is split into four regions (worlds? sectors? cities? countries? I have no idea), Lastation, Leanbox, Lowee and Planeptune, of which a goddess watches each. These regions' goddesses battle for control over this world, this is the Console War.
As you can tell just from those two sentences, this game is a parody of all things game related. It also loves to break the fourth wall, just in the first five minutes of the game it does that twice. Some of the jokes you can see from a mile away though, and, as rare as they may be, somes jokes can completely fly over your head un-noticed.
The characters are what make this game what it is though, the only way I can describe them is just "Lovable". The main characters consist of the trio of Neptune, Compa and IF. Neptune is the lovable main character who's unknowingly the Goddess of Planeptune because she has lost her memory after falling down to Planeptune due to a fight between goddesses. Compa is the aspiring doctor that finds Neptune after she falls, she's also my least favorite character and, in the Japanese dub, has the most annoying voice I've heard in any game yet (yes, it beats "Hey! Listen!"). And finally there is IF, a travelling adventurer that happens to stumble upon Neptune and Compa in a dungeon and decides to tag along with them.
IF is my favorite character in this game, not only is she voiced (in the Japanese dub) by Ueda Kana, who also voices Tousaka Rin from Fate/Stay Night, but she has a very sarcastic sense of humor for someone who seems so serious, which I love.
The story isn't going to win any awards, but it's exactly the kind of story that fits a game like HyperNeptune, light-hearted, fun and quirky.
Instead of having seperate translations for both the English and Japanese dubs, they decided to have the same translation for both versions. This is extremely annoying when reading the Japanese dubbed version, since the translation box on screen doesn't match what the characters are saying at all sometimes.
For example, one line that was translated bad early on was: "師匠...師匠....師匠....もしかして, 師匠?!?!?"(Shishou...shishou...shishou....moshikashite, shishou?!?!?). Their translation: "A t-t-t-t-tome?!?". The actual translation: "A tome... a tome.... a tome... Wait, it can't possibly be, a tome?!?!?".
Translation errors like these are spewed across HyperNeptune, it all fits with what the English voice actors are saying but if you're reading the Japanese dubbed version and know just common phrases and grammar, it really seems off.
Hyperdimension Neptunia is a remarkably charming and funny game that can appeal to any gamer that loves/can tolerate anime themes and characters. While it does have it's flaws, especially in the translation field *grummle grummle*, it's nothing that completely ruins the foundation that the game is built upon.
This has become one of my favorite games I've played in the past 10 years, and I'm glad to call myself one of the fandom.
I rate this game an 8/10 with a recommendation to buy it when it goes on sale, because they make this game dirt cheap sometimes (I love you summer sale), I picked this game up for $9 and it was a $9 well spent.

BDO is a game where you have freedom to do anything you want. Be it fishing, farming, cooking, fighting etc. This is one of those games where you are not restricted to quests to gain levels, rather, they are for you to do at your own leisure (Very much like Runescape). Whilst there are story related quests, they are not necessary to enjoy the game.
Other than the variety of activities you can do in this game, the map is also huge. It will without a doubt take you a long time to fully explore it. There is also no means of fast travelling, meaning you will actually have to travel the distance (Using mounts or ships). Whilst this aspect may be tedious at times, it's this realism that makes this game feel much more alive.
In terms of wether this game is P2W, i'd say no it depends. It can be for aethetic reasons and for convienience such as more inventory space or pets. Pet's in particular are essentail for efficient grinding.
This game isn't expensive, rather, it's dirt cheap if you consider the number of hours you'll potentially put into it. I highly recommend you get this game.

I finally picked this up on a sale because it's been popping up in my recommendations view nearly every single day, as well as being critically acclaimed and recommended by so many others.
What I expected going into it was a fairly linear adventure with tactical combat and story where your choices on how to proceed was of outmost importance.
And now that I've completed it....
Ehh...
Alright, ok, I guess in a sense I got pretty much exactly what I expected, but at the same time.... not really.
But, before we go any further.....
----SPOILER WARNING!----
The following alludes to events in the game without going into specifics. If you want to go into the game knowing absolutely nothing about what will happen, do NOT continue reading.
You have been warned.
The game is excellently made, with wonderful graphics and engaging characters you grow to care about. You emphasize with their dilemmas, and are torn whenever you have to resolve them.
However, this only lasts for about one third of the game before you start to see a pattern, and upon passing the half-point you realize the truth.
This game is unhappy. That's the best word I can use to describe it. It is unhappy in the extreme. You will feel that everything you do is wrong, and that there really is no way out that is even slightly hopeful. By the time I reached the finale I just wanted the game to END already so I could get it all over with and do something else, because each and every choice I was presented with was hollow... the world tempted me with hope I knew by this point I could not have, because everything was going to suck no matter what anyway. It was a frustrating feeling, knowing that choice was more or less an illusion, and one that actively punished you arbitrarily by killing off characters you spent points levelling up due to a plot decision you made much earlier in the game, and deleting the items they wore in the process.
I managed to scrape by, but I find it absolutely feasable that you could hopelessly screw yourself to the point where the game would be more or less unbeatable simply by investing in the wrong characters. Perhaps this too was an illusion, and if so, good job in making me think my choces mattered in at least one thing.
Honestly, I wish I could give this game a neutral rating, because I cannot really recommend it, and yet it's not really a bad game at all.
This game absolutely achives what it sets out to do, and in a very engaging and beautiful manner. The graphics are nothing short of gorgeous at times, and the music sets the desired tone perfectly. The tactical combat is a little weak, but does its job despite being hampered by the story choice system.
All that said, I have absolutely no desire whatsoever to play the sequel. I don't even care what happens to the characters anymore, because I'm sure many of them will just die horribly in some engaging and tragic manner I cannot look away from, thinking I could've saved them when In reality I could not.
If you're a sucker for punishment dressed up in one of the most engaging and pretty dresses ever, play this game. If not, look for something else.
I'm erring on the side of positivity and giving the game the thumbs up, but this is the kind of game I'm both glad I played and regretting it at the same time.

A solid realtime roguelike where every action offers progress, but every mistake is punished severely, and just enough randomness to keep things interesting. Lots of weapon and equipment variety, to the point that most 'builds' are viable. Paths branch, but it's not immeadiately obvious which path you get beyond the first choice
. Item descriptions fill in the more you use them, essentially eliminating the need to remember every item's purpose, or to keep a guide bookmarked. Enemies are interesting, balanced, and distinct from each other.
Completed Run 1: After 12.5 hours total play (and many deaths), I finished my first run. The game continues to evolve in complexity.  Persistance between runs fills in slowly. So far I've unlocked 4 characters, 1 weapon schematic
and three book pages. Still a long way to go.
Completed Run 2: Second run done after just under 20 hours. Gameplay remains balanced and fair, but I've gotten to the point that I can usually reach the last or second-to-last bosses before I die. Both my sucessful runs have involved focus, good choices, and a bit of luck. 7 characters and lots of schematics and book pages found so far.
Final thoughts: I won't spoil anything else, but the game continues to surprise me even after 30+ hours, most especially in regards to how mementos interact with each other.
5/5; would recommend.

The Banner Saga is a turn based RPG set in an apocalyptic fantasy world being invaded by a host of armored giants dubbed "The Dredge". Stoic, the developers of The Banner Saga have recently released a sequel and have even released on mobile platforms due to its success on steam. The Banner saga is a singleplayer-only game with a story mode that has the interesting main mechanic of switching between two different points of view for the first half of the game. The Banner Saga contains 7 chapters and each thrilling chapter will keep you on edge for the entire time. Chapters are fairly lengthy, each ranging from an hour to two at most and for me I ended up finishing the game in about 10-11 hours on my first run through.
In the Banner saga there is two different phases in the game: Caravan phase and combat phase. When you're in your caravan phase you oversee your caravan as you try to head to your next destination. This is where you make almost all your choices and also where you will see the various resting points in the game. As the game progresses you find various different resting points where your caravan can take a break in places such as towns and villages or sometimes even near one of the holy godstones. While you're camped out at a resting point you can access your hero screen, your map, and you can even have chats with some of the characters in the caravan. In this phase your caravan slowly consumes supplies which can be bought at markets in some villages or even acquired through some choices. There are also different items for sale in the markets although most of them are very basic passives that don't really add that much to gameplay. The items really could benefit by giving you new skills or maybe skill point boosts but instead they're just rather bland passives. In order to buy anything though you need renown, the games currency. You acquire renown from killing people in combat, although I do believe there are some major decisions that grant renown. Renown can also be used to level up your characters for combat however I feel that most of the time these upgrades are too expensive and you end up being unable to buy items and supplies because of it. The caravan also has a morale system where, depending on the current morale level your characters may suffer a penalty in combat.
The combat phase is a pretty refreshing take on turn-based combat due to the willpower system. Willpower is a stat on your characters that, in combat, they can use to increase the damage of their attacks or allow them to use special abilities. In The Banner Saga there's two types of damage you can deal to enemies: Strength and Armor. Strength is the stat that determines how much damage you can do to an enemy, so if you attack an enemies strength then they'll do less damage. If you decide to attack the enemies armor however, then that will open them up and make them take extra strength damage from future attacks. It is absolutely critical to make sure you don't only attack health or armor but instead mix them up. I really dislike how the more damage dealt to your strength the less damage you deal because then the combat can devolve into who gets the first hit. Every character that you have can be upgraded, up to level five, for increasing amounts of renown and this is where, as I said, you end up sinking most of your renown. Every character has a class but they mean very little and the characters all follow the same archetype and some characters literally use the same model with a slight recolor. I wish that instead of having loads of characters that you could equip for combat you could have fewer combatants with more unique models and stories. Even with these flaws The Banner Saga still has a very unique take on a combat system that, in my opinion, has begun to get stale.
The story of the Banner Saga is also one of its strong points as it is both unique and easy to follow without letting the two detract from the plot. The story, without spoiling much, is essentially divided into two parts until about halfway through the game. The first part you play as Hakon, one of the co-commanders of a group of giant-like beings called varl. You're goal is to essentially escort a human prince to the varl capital of Grofheim so that you can seal an alliance between the two races. The other side of the campaign you play as Rook, a human father who is out hunting with his daughter, Alette, when they run into a dredge footsoldier and have to retreat back to their village. The chieftain of their village ends up being killed so Rook has to take command of the caravan and help them reach safety. With the counsel of the chieftains wife and some old friends, Rook sets out with the caravan in tow in the hopes of making it to the nearby city of Frostvellr. The story features a strong mechanic of choice, similar to Telltale's "The Walking Dead" series and this takes an already intriguing story and gives it all the emotional twists and turns that come with choice based storytelling. Most of the time the choices you make result in effects like getting or losing supplies or having morale changes but in some cases you can gain or lose characters. However, you can never really alter the story that much from a set line of main events for it to make a significant difference in the end but it's nice to have choices that actually feel like they effect gameplay. The story has so many mysterious elements that you cannot help but to keep playing just so you can find out the next little bit of character development or lore.
An intriguing story of camaraderie in the face of ahnihilation that revives turn based combat and shows how important choice can be.

Faster than Light is a 'Space Rogue-Like' game that came into being by virtue of a Kickstarter project by Indie Developer Subset Games. It promises a starship captain experience where the player can manage both crew and ship in relative detail.
The player takes the role of a Starship Captain with vital information that will help turn the tide of war in the on going conflict between the Rebels and the Federation. The player is allowed to select and manage a variety of ships, each having their own set of crew and abilities which can expand as you progress. Once again, upgrade your ship, expand your crew and try to stay alive till the very end.
+
- The game sports simple pixel art graphics that invokes a retro feel, and, in my opinion, suits it very well. The gameplay is what makes this game shine however and as stated in the INTRODUCTION, this game attempts to simulate a Starship captain by letting the player assign crew to man the ships internal systems, order power to be diverted to different parts of the ship, focus fire on an enemy ship's weapon systems and many many more.
+
- Easy, Normal or Hard, all extremley unforgiving. This is a game where you need to bite down hard and take the consequences of your actions and choices like an adult, much like all 'Rogue-Like' games. You die, then you start all-over again. Learning from your mistake is part of the game's charm.
+
- Good varriety of ships, weapons, and crew all of which unlocks as you progress. The unlocking system was set up to ensure that every new game will be different and provide unique experiences.
+
- Great soundtrack from a small indie game. Bigger game developers should learn that not every game needs orchestral pieces to make a game's music pleasing.
-
- Aside from purchasing weapon system and ship components, you won't be able to customize the ship's looks or the layout since said layout is on a preset. I would have liked to construct my own ship.
-
- The only available game mode is the default escape scenario. It would be nice if they would add new campaigns or scenarios like, escort mission, defense campaign etc. It would definitely spice things up. A much more expansive map would also be welcome.
-
- Being able to talk and may be train your crew outside combat (specially if you find an empty system) would be a welcome addition. More interaction is needed like basic dialogues between the people on your ship to give it more life. It would be a statisfying feeling if you have resolved a conflict between two crew members.
for a great price. It's definitely not for everyone, specially people who has no patience for Rogue-Like games.

You've probably heard about this one a bunch but it's certainly worth mentioning. The Banner Saga is a narrative-driven strategy game derived largely from historically accurate Norse mythology. You take on the the part of two different main characters whose stories eventually collide in a well written and visually stunning manner.
The visuals are stunningly well-drawn and feel like a Disney tale made for adults as you traipse through scenic and meticulously hand drawn landscapes that are immersive and hypnotic all at once. I often found myself content to simply watch the world slowly roll by as monumental structures and sacked hamlets highlight a very real kind of struggle among scared people on the run from a tireless enemy.
The soundtrack is an authentic mix of calming and rousing Northern European musicianship; the thunderous clash of drums hammer away as your steel clashes with that of Nordic mythology in a way that is completely and utterly engrossing.
A surprisingly non-linear series of character choices lead to development and plot twists I constantly found myself pleasantly surprised by while the combat was approachable but not so complicated as to be esoteric.
Aside from some gripes I have with the menu when fiddling with your characters stats, I found this game to be a great representation of what alternative style strategy games can look like when reduced to the core elements of storytelling and immersion. If you're at all a fan of action point based RPG's, let The Banner Saga carry you away on a wayward journey through chaotic hordes of a mysterious enemy while the nerd within you gets off on resource management of your caravan as it threatens to tear itself apart.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1, I bought this game yesterday and already have accumulated almost 30 hours.
This means one of two things:
1. This game is f**king amazing and everyone who likes anime stuff should buy it
or
2. I need friends
.....It's probably both now that I think about it.....
But in all seriousness, this game is spectacular.
There will be a tl;dr at the end.
The gameplay is your typical turn-based J-RPG that people have come to love, myself included, but also serves as a Visual Novel as well. The content gets really grindy after a while, like, really really grindy. Like, Shao Hao dailies grindy (props if you got that reference). It's great if you can stomach grinds and like the gameplay, but boring and seemingly a waste of time if you don't.
My crappy computer which can't run CS:GO on all low settings at 30fps ran this game at 60fps on the highest settings, so this game has almost no system requirements other than memory. The only significant problem I've had is with the game crashing at what seems like random times. So be careful about that if that happens to you, and, most importantly, SAVE EVERY CHANCE YOU GET!!!!.
The combat flows so smoothly for a J-RPG that it's almost hard to get used to. You use strategy and the right usage of abilities to take down enemies (for example you wouldn't want to use your hard hitting attacks when the dragon has all of his guard points up, so you would want to widdle that down first). It all feels so fresh from what seems like a genre of game that's/on the verge of being over-saturated.
The world of Gamindustri is split into four regions (worlds? sectors? cities? countries? I have no idea), Lastation, Leanbox, Lowee and Planeptune, of which a goddess watches each. These regions' goddesses battle for control over this world, this is the Console War.
As you can tell just from those two sentences, this game is a parody of all things game related. It also loves to break the fourth wall, just in the first five minutes of the game it does that twice. Some of the jokes you can see from a mile away though, and, as rare as they may be, somes jokes can completely fly over your head un-noticed.
The characters are what make this game what it is though, the only way I can describe them is just "Lovable". The main characters consist of the trio of Neptune, Compa and IF. Neptune is the lovable main character who's unknowingly the Goddess of Planeptune because she has lost her memory after falling down to Planeptune due to a fight between goddesses. Compa is the aspiring doctor that finds Neptune after she falls, she's also my least favorite character and, in the Japanese dub, has the most annoying voice I've heard in any game yet (yes, it beats "Hey! Listen!"). And finally there is IF, a travelling adventurer that happens to stumble upon Neptune and Compa in a dungeon and decides to tag along with them.
IF is my favorite character in this game, not only is she voiced (in the Japanese dub) by Ueda Kana, who also voices Tousaka Rin from Fate/Stay Night, but she has a very sarcastic sense of humor for someone who seems so serious, which I love.
The story isn't going to win any awards, but it's exactly the kind of story that fits a game like HyperNeptune, light-hearted, fun and quirky.
Instead of having seperate translations for both the English and Japanese dubs, they decided to have the same translation for both versions. This is extremely annoying when reading the Japanese dubbed version, since the translation box on screen doesn't match what the characters are saying at all sometimes.
For example, one line that was translated bad early on was: "師匠...師匠....師匠....もしかして, 師匠?!?!?"(Shishou...shishou...shishou....moshikashite, shishou?!?!?). Their translation: "A t-t-t-t-tome?!?". The actual translation: "A tome... a tome.... a tome... Wait, it can't possibly be, a tome?!?!?".
Translation errors like these are spewed across HyperNeptune, it all fits with what the English voice actors are saying but if you're reading the Japanese dubbed version and know just common phrases and grammar, it really seems off.
Hyperdimension Neptunia is a remarkably charming and funny game that can appeal to any gamer that loves/can tolerate anime themes and characters. While it does have it's flaws, especially in the translation field *grummle grummle*, it's nothing that completely ruins the foundation that the game is built upon.
This has become one of my favorite games I've played in the past 10 years, and I'm glad to call myself one of the fandom.
I rate this game an 8/10 with a recommendation to buy it when it goes on sale, because they make this game dirt cheap sometimes (I love you summer sale), I picked this game up for $9 and it was a $9 well spent.

Innumerable times before have I entered into that antediluvian pit. How one gazes in those brief, fleeting moments of respite at cracks in the wall only to find broken brick the only barrier between themselves and the infinite abyss. And when that mind is stilled in cosmic fear, I strike them down. As their blood flows from their body, I feast. As their humanity spills from their very being it is I who steals it away. There can be no rest then, however. There is no rest here. Only madness, suffering, and domination. There can be only one who can wrest away their humanity from this accursed death trap. Fools were they who came to this place to find glory. And those same fools will damn us all down here in their misguided failures. Only the most corrupted here will find redemption. Only the most damned will have the pleasure of salvation. Back biters and scheming liars will find their momentary victories, but they will fall slain in the face of the momumental power which stands between them and sunlight. It is only the most vile, twisted, and damnable who can find escape. He with both intent and method to brutalize his fellow brother for one more gasp of fresh air is he who will leave... But he will return. The allure is too great. The pain, a pleasure. Inumerable times before have I entered. Inumerable times more will I leave.

Oh man. Where do I begin with this game? There's so much done right about this game that it's very quickly becoming one of my favourite rougelikes. Let's just dive right into the dungeon and start chopping off the pros and cons of this insanely unique and fast-paced competitive Gauntlet-inspired roguelike.
Pros:
+Fast paced couch competition. The game is super quick to pick up and just as wasy to learn, utilizing only the movement directions and two buttons.
+Most unique idea for a rogulike in a long time. The fact that AI or other friends control your ENTIRE JOURNEY is so fresh and innovative that I honestly can't think of a game to compare it to.
+Amazing art direction and fluent animation. You can tell there was so much heart and soul poured into this game, I completely understand it taking 4 years of hard work and devotion to reach what we see today.
+Brilliant soundtrack.
+Unfair. Why is that a good thing? Because this game *prides* itself on being unfair in one way or another. It feels so amazing to be the big, bad monster that tears through the Hero or vice versa, and when you manage to wittle down or kill as like, a tiny fish while everyone else are hulking behemoths, everyone goes freaking bananas. It's such a fun concept, even when you're losing.
+Cheap pricetag, sitting at only $15.
+Amazing two "bonus" bosses which can be found and posessed by any player.
All that said, this is not a perfect game. It's close, and I've definitely got to mark it down as my favourite roguelike yet, but let's get into the downsides of this passion project.
Cons:
-Lacks diversity. This is the game's biggest downfall. There's only one type of floor design, three total bosses, and the monsters themselves become a tad bit repetitive once you've been around the block. Don't get me wrong, it's still a good start, but I'd absolutely LOVE to see more variation in the future such as an ice temple or lava corridor in the later floors.
-Little to no way to make the Hero actually do stuff; i.e, you can't stop them from stalling at all. If you're friends with some real dickbags, they can decide to troll you by finding a safe spot while being the Hero and just not do anything. The only area this really applies is the Shops due to slimes and ectoplasm, but it can still be an issue.
-No online multiplayer.
-Slimes have so much untapped potential.
-Lackluster AI. It's either too easy and brainless or too ridiculously difficult. No inbetween.
All those things said, all-in-all I'd have to give this game a 9.5/10. Powerhoof spent YEARS working on this amazing game, and it truly shows. It's a wonderful title and I would heavily reccomend getting it if you have friends to play it with.

In all honestly the price of this game is a bit to low for the surprisingly good visuals and combat system. Mind anyone reading this, i'm comming from the perspective a small group of friends playing casualy (our goal was to build a boat so we could sail the sea.)
+ Game looks good the areas are vibrant and varied.
+ Towns feel pretty alive with constant player travel and npc population.
+++ Combat system is fluid and reasonably deep (ie not just number mashing on a hotbar...though you could just do that if you really wanted to) and just plain fun.
++ Exploration feels good even if just to see the new locations.
+ Interaction with enviroment and others is a nice touch.
+ Classes are varried
But the game beyond that is where that price feels justified.
--- No player trading beyond basic healing items making sharing of resources impossable
- Players can not do most of the crafting in game, you hire NPC workers to do a large portion of it for you (such as tools and equipment)
-- You need to "befriend" npc merchants before they will sell you most of their wares (done by finding conversation topics they like via exploration, and/or talking to every npc you ever see just to talk to the arms dealer who will only talk about farmers from the nearby farm) Just seems like a very odd way to force people to explore
-Menus are obtuse and hard to understand at first glance
-- Game is slow to get rolling, consider lv1-50 the tutorial
Overall the game is nice to look at, and the combat is suprisingly good for an mmo but the rest of the game only serves to drag it down, and the over protective restraints on trading serve to ruin any chance the game had and has at a real community of players.
I will not recomend anyone buy this game for anything other than to mess around with friends, to beat up local wildlife of varying danger, and to enjoy the scenery, so for that a price tag of $10 seems fair, just try not to take the rest of game all that seriously or (atleast in my case) it will only get frustrating and disapoint on the whole.

My only complaint would be the sometimes buggy combat and the durability mechanics. I don’t think certain weapons should break as quick as they do, or should cost so much to recreate. Otherwise I’d certainly give Dying Light a 9/10.

Divinity: Original Sin has become one of my new favorites. Starting with the simple, it's a turn-based "tactical" RPG. You can control up to a party of 4, and you cycle through your characters in an order based on their (and their enemies') initiative stat. In combat, you fire off spells and hack away at enemies in this turn-based fashion. It may sound dull to some, but every choice counts in a battle, especially if you are facing a boss or a group that is a higher level than you are.
If you play any other RPG. you would probably not think twice about taking on a level 6 enemy when you're level 5, it would just take a bit longer, right? In DIvinity, although it is possible with the right strategy, taking on a group that is one level higher than yours can result in your enemies to steamroll over your group. It can be quite hard, especially before you get a hang of the combat system.
The combat is very satisfying; it looks good, sounds good, and your characters deal a significant amount of damage whenever you get an attack off. The difficulty doesn't come from the enemies being arrow-sponges, it comes from your own mistakes. While shooting a fire arrow into a oil surface sounds great at first, you soon realize that your archers and mages cannot see through the smoke, forcing you to wait for the black clouds to disperse. I've personally accidentally gotten many party members killed by shooting a fire arrow into a barrel, only to have them be killed in the resulting explosions from a gas cloud that emerged from the barrel. There are many fun and unique ways to die, as well as kill enemies. Some fights can be over before your close-quarters guys can even reach the enemies, just by taking advantage of different material surfaces (Oil, water, gas, etc.).
When you're out of combat, you're probably running around trying to solve a puzzle or interrogate someone for clues, which is all fairly enjoyable. The writing is brilliant, and pulls me right into the universe. Fortunetely, the game doesn't take itself too seriously, and will crack a joke every now and then. Sometimes the main characters will poke fun at ech other, or you'll read a silly book. The crafting system is deviously simple, and many recipies can be solved just by thinking about them for a bit. How do you make pizza sauce? Smash a tomato.
My only observation about the game that could turn some people away from the game is the exteremely slow progression. I've put about 30 hours into one party at the time of this review, and they are all level 9. Compared to other RPG's, Divinity runs at a snail's pace. It doesn't bother me though. As a result of the leveling being so slow, you have to seriously consider how to allocate your skill points, instead of just throwing them in whatever sounds the best at first glance. Do I want to talk to animals, or be able to heal when I stand in blood? Do I want to be able to cast fireballs, or wield that awesome crossbow I found? You get the idea.
Overall, this is easily my GOTY 2014. If you are a fan of turn-based combat and RPG's, I would highly recommend this game. Even if you aren't so keen on turn-based, the Divinity system feels oddly...Satisfying, and might just change your mind.
If you're ready for an adventure, I couldn't think of a better choice.

You've probably heard about this one a bunch but it's certainly worth mentioning. The Banner Saga is a narrative-driven strategy game derived largely from historically accurate Norse mythology. You take on the the part of two different main characters whose stories eventually collide in a well written and visually stunning manner.
The visuals are stunningly well-drawn and feel like a Disney tale made for adults as you traipse through scenic and meticulously hand drawn landscapes that are immersive and hypnotic all at once. I often found myself content to simply watch the world slowly roll by as monumental structures and sacked hamlets highlight a very real kind of struggle among scared people on the run from a tireless enemy.
The soundtrack is an authentic mix of calming and rousing Northern European musicianship; the thunderous clash of drums hammer away as your steel clashes with that of Nordic mythology in a way that is completely and utterly engrossing.
A surprisingly non-linear series of character choices lead to development and plot twists I constantly found myself pleasantly surprised by while the combat was approachable but not so complicated as to be esoteric.
Aside from some gripes I have with the menu when fiddling with your characters stats, I found this game to be a great representation of what alternative style strategy games can look like when reduced to the core elements of storytelling and immersion. If you're at all a fan of action point based RPG's, let The Banner Saga carry you away on a wayward journey through chaotic hordes of a mysterious enemy while the nerd within you gets off on resource management of your caravan as it threatens to tear itself apart.

The Banner Saga: a very ambitious game that delivers.... more or less.
Before I get to discuss the problems I have to say that the graphics/artworks are beautiful and  the soundtrack is gorgeous .
Now let's get to the meat of the game:
-The game is advertised as a game based on every decision that you take....and that is more or less true. Some of your choices affect the game that is true but not by very much except from like 2 of them. Also the game is not afraid to take decisions without asking you. For example: in the beginning I chose to level up a character because I liked his stats and skills and I said "well if I level up this guy I will crush my enemies in no time" . Well quess what: THE GAME DECIDES THAT THEY HAVE TO LEAVE AND RIGHT AFTER I SPENT MY LEVEL POINTS ON THEM. You don't get to see them until the final  battle and you don't get a character with similar attributes anywhere in the game . So in the final battle you get them right, but they are already low level by the  standard of that time.  What the hell?
-For a game praised for the importance of your choices the game is quite linear. The game will switch most of the time between 2 groups of people whenever the story wants. Which makes it a bit harder to follow the plot.
-The gameplay consists of a turn based combat strategy game. It's refreshing and unique but is also  so basic and you will get bored in a few battles. It is also sometimes punishing and unforgiving.
Overall the game is good but not what people make it out to be . I give it a 6-7/10 . It's enjoyable but gets tedious by the end of the game.

I'll have to rewrite this review at some stage as when you start the game is really unfair and too punishing, but once you start to achieve mastery it's actually too easy, but amazing fun uncovering all of the mysteries!!
What really makes a difference is:
-understanding the combat
-having the ability to cut trees and smash rocks on the first level
-having a bow to kill bosses (or a lot of hp/stamina/dex/str/agr with a good +6 katana)
-understanding how to unlock the blue doors in dungeons
-knowing how to cook raw meat
-knowing that you start with 4 estus flasks (left ctrl) (less with other characters)
-knowing that you can inspect items before choosing (radial menu then magnifying glass)
-having enough perception to spot breakable walls, traps and hidden switches
-knowing that death first cuts you xp in half then reduces the REMAINING amount based upon your violence % eg. 100% violence means you keep 50% of your TOTAL xp gained
(this could be shown to the player with Veil (Death) taking 50% and perhaps the thousandfold god taking the next portion based upon violence%)
-knowing that you can dig up xp gems but also that the hunger cost is too high so it's only worth it if you need 1-2 more to buy an upgrade
-knowing that maximum hunger slowly drains your max hp, reduces your defence & increases stamina cost
-knowing that the estus flask is instant cast, can be used in combat, also causes knockback, damage, heals allies, can break wood/stone/crystal (but not steel/magic)
-knowing that trees should not be cut from the side
-knowing what the numbers on weapons mean
-slowly learning what each of the mementos and sub-equipment do
(Risk of Rain did this much better - telling you the name and brief effect text when picked up with the item log giving more detailed info like specific stats and flavor text - some things are fun to discover but some things you like to know early - balance is key here)
Nookrium is a small youtuber (sub count not physical proportions.. I assume), but he played this on 6th Sep and it looked really cool and obsucre. Plus I really like the art style and was making a game that also stole Teleglitch's LOS effect (unlit geometry extending towards the camera), so thought I'd give it a shot. When watching videos it's hard not to see the LOS effect as black towers, but when playing you're so focused that you only see it as a LOS effect!
In the beginning it feels impossible to make any meaningful progression.
Then you discover the Estus Flask (named "Surge" & bound to left control).
From there the game really opens up before you!!
Some NPC's giving hints in the beginning would be nice (for those that take the time to listen) but I do like the way that item descriptions are unlocked slowly.
However I would like a way to get permanent progression earlier even if it is only a +1 str increase - it's better than nothing
(edit: you can get permanent progression but you need to have a fairly decent run before this to happen - it isn't like Dead Cells where you can make small progression on EVERY run - most of your progression in the early days will be learning the mechanics and mastering the combat which can be frustrating when the game seems to treat you unfairly at every turn).
Still it's a fun game with a very Dark Souls combat system (long wind up times for yourself and enemies, but high damage, with dodging and parrying necessary to progress). I can't wait to finally get 1 bit of permanent progression though (once you get a few decent runs in the game really opens up with achievements unlocking new characters, more starting equipment/resources, and collecting currency to give your next run a boost)
[EDIT: Finally got some progression with 2 classes unlocked and some stats gained and can now progress through multiple bosses. However I find that enemies scale much faster than I do with each level completed and soon have too much hp for the amount of damage I can deal out and there's no way I can respec all my points into weapon damage]

You definitely don't have that problem with this game. There are so many different options and paths you can choose to make your character truly unique, similar to perhaps Path of Exile. The only real complaint I have is that it takes a fairly decent amount of time to get more than a few abilities to make the game more interesting. For the first 40 levels or so I had 1-2 abilities that I would just spam over and over. Once I reached level 65 I was able to get 4 abilities and have a nice cooldown rotation I could go to. To put that into perspective level 40 (Which was about a single playthrough of the game) took around 25 hours. Another small complaint I have is while the gear has a lot of different stats, the higher tier gear doesn't drop too often and it doesn't feel very powerful. Other than that I loved the lore and story in the game and had a fantastic time playing through the story.
TL;DR: More complex than Diablo 3, less complex than Path of Exile. It's worth a buy, if you like either game or similar games.

It's not perfect by any means, but I enjoyed the game greatly.  The story is engaging and the artwork is beautiful.  The game is punishingly difficult and pretty much no matter what you do, you're going to regret doing it.
My biggest gripe is the combat itself though...  The turn order just switches back and forth between your characters and enemies until there's only 1 enemy left in which case, this stops and your characters can go right after each other.  What this means is that, when you get down to two to three enemies, is that they get to keep going after each of your characters, forcing your characters to take multiple hits in quick succession.  This basically forced me to weaken enemies rather than killing them outright.  And once weakening all the enemies, then killing them...
I would give the game 7/10.

+ I am of two minds about this game. First, I really enjoyed most of it (without having beat it yet -- more on that later). There's a charming quality about Divinity: OS with its oldschool gameplay and humorous writing. The combat is very solid and has clever mechanics with mixing damage types and environmental hazards. Play your cards just right and the results can be devastating. The story was fairly interesting, and I thought the writing was in general very well done. Some of the humor genuinely had me laughing. Act 1 in particular was fantastic.
- Now, the not so good. First, D:OS is long. Really, really long. I put about 100 hours into the game before eventually losing interest. The way it's designed sucks up way more time than it should. One reason why is poor item management. Keeping track and selling/buying items is a huge pain in the rear. Town trips are frequent and long.
- Second, the game takes the oldschool approach to the extreme, to a fault IMO. D:OS seems to pride itself on not holding your hand, or being very helpful at all. There's no compass, no quest or location markers. Your only information on quests are short journal entries. It's very easy to feel lost in D:OS. The number of quests you get are daunting, with no indication of what order they should be approached or even where to begin. Events in the game just seem to unfold randomly based on where you aimlessly roam around the maps. It's possible to get stuck doing difficult missions without realizing there was an easier quest line you could have done instead. And then when you do go back to the easier quests, then they're too easy.
- Act 2 seemed to be a slight dropoff in quality compared to Act 1. For instance, I noticed several typos in NPC text that I don't remember noticing in Act 1. Like it was a bit rushed by comparison.
Ultimately, I recommend it for anyone looking for a hardcore, oldschool experience who is willing to spend many, many hours managing items in town or being frustrated by the obscure quest logs, not knowing where to find some random scroll or amulet needed to progress. For anyone else who is used to modern game mechanics...you will probably lose interest early.

In Celebration of Violence is a clearly Dark Souls inspired action roguelike...
What? Wait, where are you going? It's actually good!
The main thrust of the game is that you are an amnesiac killer undertaking a quest to kill the gods. You do so at the start with nothing but your wits, a training sword, pitchfork, and torch, with a good helping of other classes unlockable via achievements.
The combat has a definite learning curve, but once I understood it, it felt like how an action roguelike should feel. Timing is everything, and a well timed parry or dodge can be the difference between life and death. That is, until you learn how to properly abuse the game and get a massive halberd, ghost blade, and a swarm of fireballs, spiders and flies backing you up and you can wade through hordes of enemies like a god of violence itself.
Additional abilities are unlocked in play by finding and buying momentos. These range from the practical, like stat boosts, to bonkers, like the aforementioned spiders. One of the game's minor annoyances, though, is the length of time it takes to unlock the description of each momento. The developer (literally one guy doing all of this) added a pop up message when picking up an momento that just gves a stat bonus to indicate which stat is getting it, but while some other effects are obvious, like the saw blade giving you a circular saw blade friend, others are opaque enough that I have no clue what they do, even after 20+ hours of game time.
\
UPDATE:
Another good thing about this game is that the developer is adding new QoL stuff with almost every patch, and releases a patch almost every week. The last few patches increased the default walk speed and reduced the amount of times of picking up a momento before fully ID'ing it. That;s pretty awesome!
/
There is permanent progression in the game, too. Experience points can be saved at the end of each boss, and if you die, you save a percentage based on your level of violence. How that is calculated, however, is beyond me. These points can be used to buy permanent stat upgrades, percentage point by percentage point. The good thing is that these bonuses carry between classes, so raising your speed on your lowly peasant will also give you a bump if you are playing the sneaky misanthrope.
While there are minor faults and annoyances, there is only one big ugly mark against this game. The only way to save a game is to beat a level, beat its boss, then shatter the mirror to the next level and use the shard.
Listen, I get the thematic weight of that. I also have work in the morning. Having to get through a level, a boss, and possibly an optional dungeon to reach a save point can take over an hour. It is incredibly impractical. Being able to save and quit anywhere is a roguelike staple mechanic for good reason. Limiting it to "save and quit when no enemies are aware of you" would be perfectly fine.
With that said, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. It is fun, addicting, and has equal parts "OH GOD I'M GONNA DIE" and "OH YEAH YOU YOU'RE GONNA DIE!" moments to keep it fresh and entertaining. It's well worth the $8!

A Song of Fire and Ice (Game of Thrones) = Love it.
Telltale Games = Love them.
Put them together and I was thinking how amazing it would be.
YET, it just isn't.
+ I do recommend this game as it is interesting for GOT/Telltale fans, yet it just feels slower and less intense than the other Telltale games.
+Real character voices (HOWEVER QUITE RARE) and real Game of Thrones families and story.
-The plot feels it moves really slowly, 3 episodes completed yet I could probably tell a friend all that has happened within a minute.
-There seems to be more plot holes (I.E. why would this person do that/say that) and character flaws. Some chracters seem happy and friendly then the next line crazy, then angry, then happy and then whatever you told your characater to do became completely irrelevant or someone took what you said the wrong way for no reason.
- Most of the characters I don't feel anything for. In other Telltale games or in Game of Thrones you feel for the people in it, but if basically anyone in this game dies I don't really care, which means I am more wreckless with decisions which I should be toying with in my mind.
