Got the game with all it's DLC on a steam sale, played through it once (3 days->30 hours), got the true ending and am now playing the next of the series.
The story:
The story is pretty lighthearted and forgettable. I read most of the dialouge, but I could've done without it.
The Characters:
The Characters can all be put into a certain stereotype, but they're all quite enjoyable. They didn't go overbored with the stereotypes, so no character (other than Compa, ♥♥♥♥ Compa) is annoying or frustrating to read from/about.
The sound/graphics:
The game has a 3D-anime look, if that's your thing. The animations look quite nice, there are three attacks that have problems, Vert's Exe-Drive has some camera issues and Historie's (DLC character) spells make the game lag. (For me anyways, but I have a TITAN and i7)
The sound is quite good, the voice actors did a good job, but I must say I enjoyed the japanese voices more because the fit the characters looks better, in my opinion.
The Gameplay:
Pretty much what you expect from a JRPG, a very interesting in-battle movement and "placement" system is being used, giving the almost boring turnbased system a new feel. Each character has nine possible attacks (27 possible combinations of a combo) if s/he chooses to use the normal attack. Each character has at least three skills, most of them have 4 and there are 12 (I think) characters total. But only 4 of them are viable for he end-game, or so I've been told.
After you've completed the game there's very little reasonm to play through it at all if you're not a completionist.
EDIT: Be warned, a lot of the dungeons and enemies get reused, 15 hours into the game I've seen the exactly same dungeon with a new name six seperate times. Enemies have the same problem, you get a lot of recolours and renames.
After chapter five or when your characters reach level 25 the normal combos become pretty useless, the only way to dent a bosses health is by spamming rush-combos to fill the exe-bar and then spamming your exe-drives.
Concolusion:
The game is quite a nice looker and does give you a lot to do.
I don't think it's a viable purchase at full-price, but maybe I'm just cheap. Anything from 50% and onwards in price reduction and I recommend it heartily.

I’m going to start this review with something that sounds like a slam, though it isn't: I really wanted to love Child of Light. But I didn’t. The reason that I wanted to love it is that from the very first trailer I saw I was enchanted with the graphical styles of the game. This enchantment lasted well into my first playthrough; well past the point where I tired of some game elements I was still excited just to look at each new part of the world Child of Light laid out for me. Every bit of scenery and every sprite looks hand crafted. Winsome characters and sumptuous backgrounds have the look of ink and watercolor art from some gorgeous, moody storybook.
Woods give way to craggy rocks give way to villages revealing one stunning tableau after another. Broken statues stare poignantly. Light shines through stained glass and down from treetops. Giants are visible in the hazy distance… There is beauty, often mixed with melancholy, everywhere—even the fights are suffused with it. The animation of Aurora, the protagonist, is also arresting. The attention paid to the movement of her long hair alone is worthy of mention, as are the animations of her wielding a sword clearly too heavy for her tiny body.
All this is true, but my reaction to the game as a whole is more measured. As mentioned, you play as Aurora, an Austrian princess snatched into a fantasy land where she must lead a struggle against the Queen of Dark whose aim is to steal all natural light in the kingdom. You must recruit allies to your party and complete quests to defeat the Queen. Gameply is a mix of metroidvania, side-scroller environments with puzzles, and quasi-turn-based RPG battles. The integration of these two is interesting: encounters are not random. Monsters are visible in the over-world, and how you interact with them there determines who has the initiative at the beginning of a fight. Another interesting mechanic is that your cursor is a character, a glowing sprite, which moves independently of Aurora and interacts with the environment aiding her progress. Mousing over objects is often counted as the sprite interacting with them, so to some degree you are controlling two characters at once. In general, the over world elements of play are quite easy, though.
Battles involve two party members squaring off against a squad of monsters. The action is driven by a timeline, with each character receiving actions at intervals. This differs from a turn-based system in that the intervals vary significantly between combatants, and can be further manipulated by player actions. Character progression, via a branching maze of unlockable nodes ala FF X, unlock new combat abilities. This simple mechanic generates a variety of interesting fights, though by the end of the game I felt the battles were becoming somewhat monotonous, as often happens with turn-based battle mechanics in simple games.
The game is linier and story-driven. It is here that I had my major complaints. The game creators aimed for a moving coming of age story. (If you have seen it, the Neil Gaiman movie Mirrormask seems to be very much the sort of thing they were aiming for.) But this falls short in a number of ways. One reason is that story scenes are done in a kind of storybook mode with largely static images of the characters acompanied by text. Compared to the rest of the game these sequences are oddly uncharismatic. But a much more major shortcoming is the dialogue itself. The game sets all dialogue in verse. But it seems the writers did not have the skill to make this device actually work for them resulting in bad rhymes and perpetually stilted wording. This verbal lack of poise is oddly at odds with the stunning visual beauty of the game. Perhaps these factors alone are enough to explain my mixed feelings towards the story.
In the final count Child of light still offers a wondrous world to explore and marvel at, it still casts a spell. It just didn’t quite live up to its potential. I was left feeling that if every aspect of the game showed the beauty and polish that the graphics do then Child of Light would be one of the greats. The gorgeous, well-built, casual RPG Child of Light actually is makes me badly wish I could play that game.

I'm a big fan of twinstick shooters and am always on a quest to find one that can match the king of them all, Smash TV.  In recent times I've gone through Renegade Ops, Splatter, UBERMOSH, Nuclear Throne and Serious Sam: The Bogus Detour.
It's a real shame this one has mostly negative reviews- I thought it was great!  I didn't try multiplayer, only solo, and with the girl character it wasn't too hard to beat- the game is very short.
I think some people didn't quite get what they were looking for, because quite often you have to play defensively and run away to avoid being overwhelmed by the hordes of enemy scum- I rather like that! Adding to this tactical element, It's also been made so there's a movement penalty when you fire- a slight delay- which adds to the tension as you have to make each shot count or the swarm will get you.
For players who are finding the game too hard, I recommend choosing the female character.  In effect she provides an "easy" mode, since her superpower generates a generous collection of health pickups.
Each level is short - about a couple of minutes long- but you have to complete 6 in a row to hit a checkpoint.  I was happy with the amount of variety in the levels- there are different challenges which are hinted at in the text intros.
The graphics speak for themselves- I really liked 'em.  It's refreshing to see bright polygonal cartoons again in a market saturated with retro pixel art, or moody textured stuff. Most of the characters are very small, but the larger bosses really show off the artistic talent here. Picking out CONS, I'd say the music is rather generic, but it doesn't harm the game.  On rare occasions overhanging scenery obscures the action- which is a really silly mistake.  If you paid full whack for the game I can see how you'd be disappointed by its short length, but having only paid pennies I didn't mind at all.
I might well play it through again in "Hardcore" mode with the male character, to see if I can unlock the next character, whoever he or she might be!

But the most important element in a fantasy world is its ability to immerse you in it. And that is where this game fails completely.
This game is filled with stupid jokes and real-world references that constantly remind you that you're playing a video game. Ex., you walk on a pier, separated from a chest by a rope. Your character says something like, "The greatest source hunters in the world and we can't get past a rope." Ex., I looted a unique sword -- "Peter Lee's Sword", with the flavor text "For Peter Lee. This is far from a AAA title. No day/night/weather cycles. NPC's stand in the same spot forever, repeating the same canned phrases. Mediocre graphics. Campy battle music that sounds like the intro the Munsters.

Dying Light is fantastic. I'm on my second playthrough of the vanilla game and just into the new content and it's easily one of my favorite games in the last few years. If it had a weak point I think it'd be the story and sometimes how it's presented, and I found the story's ending a little bit...dissatisfying. But EVERYTHING else about it is nonstop fun. Parkouring across the city or country from building to building, running and jumping and grappling is so much fun the game could just be that and I think I'd love it, but then you have awesome fighting mechanics that make the decapitation, dismemberment and immolation of enemies so fun you'll giggle like a maniac.
Now with the Following, they've given us cars that we can customize and run over zombies with. I'm cooping with my SO and his brother and it is seriously one of my favorite things we've ever played.  The melee weapons are fantastic and the DLC has brought us way better guns (though I still love slashing things with machetes, personally). I love the blueprints and collectables and exploring.
There's some times the game really gets my heart pounding too. Being chased by a healthy grouping of Volatiles at night and you accidentally have molotovs keyed up instead of the grappling hook? Or there's just nowhere to run? Better pray you have a backup plan.  There's some genuinely creepy and disturbing parts too.
Overall, it's a blast. It's a gory, drivey, parkoury blast.

Played it in two marathon sittings, completed in just over 12 hours. There's a admirable fatalism to aspects of the choices you make. This isn't one where the prudent or moral choice is obvious. The consequences of your decisions are permanent and influenced by the game's thematic fatalism, which is fitting for a game about the end of the world. You make decisions, and these decisions have important impacts, but you aren't ever really in control.
The combat mechanics are interesting and in some ways unorthodox. Damage output is linked to health, and vulnerability is linked to armor. Since turn order is always alternating (unless there is only one enemy left), it often makes more sense to weaken many enemies than to gang up and kill one at time. Classes and skills combine in interesting ways, almost like a card-based board game with a spatial element.
As the characters are hand-drawn, the camera is fixed. This can cause some crowding which can make it hard to select the enemy you intend to attack. Minor gripe aside, Banner Saga is a great game and certainly worth the price.

After over 100 hours of gameplay, I finally managed to slog through this game to the end, if only just to say that I completed it. Don't get me wrong, I don't absolutely hate the game; it's just that it more than overstayed its welcome in addition to having significant flaws.
First of all, the crafting system is just horrendous. It's extremely unintuitive and tedious. Let's say you want to create a magic scroll. You must first acquire yourself an ink pot and a quill. Good luck with that, because no vendors sell them. I ended up having to steal them from a friendly NPC. You must then combine them by dragging the icon for the quill over the icon for the ink pot, then stand by and watch a progress bar fill, in order to create an "Ink Pot & Quill". Now you have to get some pixie dust. Find a bone and grind it to dust using a mortar and pestle; oh yeah, you need one of those as well. Now find a stardust plant and throw it in the mortar and pestle to create stardust. Now combine the bonemeal and stardust to make pixie dust. Now sprinkle some pixie dust on the ink pot and quill to make "Magic Ink Pot and Quill"! Now find an axe and a log of wood. Hack up the log with the axe to get a few wood chips. Now find a bucket and search all over town for a well. Draw water from the well into the bucket. Combine the water and one pile of wood chips to make one "Mush of Wood". Now search all over town for a furnace. Throw the wood mush on the furnace; lo and behold: One sheet of paper! Now kill a dangerous Water Elemental and take its essence. Rub the water essence on the sheet of paper to make a "Blank Water Scroll". Now is the moment we've all been waiting for! Use the magic ink pot and quill on the blank water scroll to create... oh, no sorry, your crafting skill is too low. Now go kill dozens of insane demons and level up in order to increase your crafting. Great, can we craft the scroll now? As I was saying, use the magic ink pot and quill on the blank water scroll to create... wait for it... a random, low-level, one-time-use water magic scroll! You managed to do all of this without any indication in game of what you needed to do! Wasn't that worth it guys?
The loot in this game sucks. Mainly you will find more ingredients for crafting and lots and lots of vendor trash. It's hard to afford anything in the beginning, but keep picking up those garbage items and dozens of hours later you'll be swimming in gold! Which goes back to my previous point: why would you craft anything when the items you craft are inferior to the gear you will inevitably have already found by the time you figure out how to craft anything?
I like that this game avoids the "follow the pointer" trend in modern video games. However, the game world is quite large and it would be nice if there was some—any—indication of where you need to go without exploring every square inch of the map. Want to know where some place is in town? Too bad you can't just ask an NPC, because they don't have that interaction programmed in. Want to delve further into your current quest objective in order to understand what it is you're trying to accomplish? Too bad, because the one relevant NPC can only tell you some generic, fluff dialogue.
I could go on, but the final criticism that I want to raise is that the writing is just not compelling. It's one of the most ham-fisted and saccharine takes on the "world is ending" trope I've ever seen. It would have been nice if I could just go on adventures with some nuance and intrigue, rather than having to prevent existence from coming to an end by a contrived plot device.
Not recommended.

Pros:
- Addictive as all hell. This game is so interesting and enthralling that you can't put it down. The variety of enemies and challenges, along with random events always keep you on your toes and clicking that Scan for Activity button just one more time. And then again.
- Wide variety of character designs that never get boring. Sectoids, Mutons, Elites, Tall Men, Commander Sectoids, Chrysallis', Floaters, Heavy Floates, Berserkers. I'm probably leaving out a few, but those are a good sampling of the enemies in this game. No two even look similar, (Even the Floaters/Heavy Floaters which are the same alien. They are designed very independently) and it makes introducing a new class of alien exciting because you know you can take them dead/alive back to the base for an interrogation/autopsy that will unlock new things.
- Turn based combat that I didn't know I missed. Turned based combat always seemed a little stiff and unengaging to me before XCOM, but they've really managed to bring a little color to the cheeks of this game play with it. Despite having all the time in the world to react, there's still this tight tension in the air that helps make this game so addicting.
- Variety of classes and abilities. Just as the enemies are varied, your soldiers are no less. You don't choose which class your Rookies get, instead they earn them by how you utilize them, which I found interesting. Each class has its own unique abilities/handicaps, and they all really balance each other once you put them all on a team together. [SPOILERS] Once you get the PSI abilities, it really takes off. It's rare to find a soldier with the Gift, but when you do, you charish them.
- Balanced side characters. While I don't care much for the Commander or the head of the XCOM project, I really adore the scientist and engineer. They're so full of life and play off of each other so well. Even the soldiers, which, honestly don't have a lot of personality, can sort of grow one after they've reached a high enough rank.
- A story that gradually raises the stakes in a way that doesn't seem luticrous, which is hard to do considering the plot is aliens. That's kind of a good summary of the game. Tough but fair.
-Balancing base management/global stability with turn based combat. This may seem like it'd be quite tenuous and strain to try and balance all of these things at once, but I think that's the point. To feel the true strain you're under as the commander. YOU are in charge of making sure everything stays afloat, and you really feel every failure.
Cons:
- Impossible hard at times. I've had to just quit out of missions and lose a countries allegiance because some levels are unrealistically hard. I had a team of six Colonel's (two being Psychic), and when they walked into the first room there were eighteen enemies packed together, each with over four lines of HP. Discouraged, I immediately aborted the mission and lost Argentina.
-Sattelites. I will never look at them the same way again. While the concept is good, they become a horrible pain. They're a short term easy way of lowering a countries panic rating, but after some countries already have one, you can't give them another one, so you just have to pray a UFO will invade their country so you can try to lower their panic rating.
- Honestly, I'm not really a fan of the panic rating scale in general. I have enough to worry about with research, engineering, soldiers, power, etc. without worrying about what Nigeria feels.
- Glitchy at times. The game has never outright crashed on me, but it has frozen on the Alien Activity screen when an enemy clipped through a wall and it wouldn't move forward. I've also had soldiers with a 98% chance of hitting an enemy miss the shot because they, for some reason, spun around and fired in the opposite direction. I currently have an invisible soldier not because of equipment, but because his skin glitched and he is now only a floating gun.
- Abductions. I hate having to deal with them, not because they're hard (though they are), but because you can only respond to one of three, forcing two other countries to raise their panic rating. And when you have to choose between three countries with equal panic ratings, you basically just have to choose which country gives you the most money and say goodbye to the other two, because they sure as hell won't forgive you not responding.
Overall, it's addictive, fun, and intense. A must buy.

Brief Summary: Despite a few flaws, the game is beautiful and well-constructed. Recommended.
Details:
Storyline - The story is subtly moving, building an excellent sense of doom and foreboding that escalates as the game goes on. The choices and consequences capture the loneliness of leadership well. The choices make a big difference, keeping the game tense.
Art and Soundtrack - The game looks stunning and the soundtrack is beautiful and haunting.
Combat - The combat works reasonably well. The system is unique insofar as it has a fixed you-them-you-them... initiative structure, which means having greater numbers is not necessarily an advantage. Rather than focusing damage on specific targets (the norm of SRPGs) The game encourages weakening as many targets as possible, before moving in for kills.
Niggles:
The game can be punishing in places. You have one pool of xp to level all your characters and if a character you focussed on dies from a story event. Tough. That xp is gone.
Also the game could do with an undo or extend move feature, to make the occasional attack of "Fat Fingers" less disastrous.
Overall, really enjoyed it and look forward to seeing where they go with the 2nd one.

Awesome game. Extremely underrated and well worth the asking price despite being in early access.
Basically, this game is a roguelite with emphasis on weighty and deliberate combat. The roguelite aspects pertain to features like permadeath, unidentified potions, shrines (which kind of work like simplified god/religion systems prevalent in some roguelikes like DC:SS). There are also some niche minor aspects of the game like ritual sites and elemental buffs that are roguelike-y in nature.
As for the actual combat, pretty much every movement in the game carries some momentum. This means combat tends to be dynamic and deliberate. For example, for some enemies you might want to play defensively, walk backwards and use a strong attack with a high strength value to stun them and kill them quickly. Alternatively, if you're fighting a bunch of weaker enemies as well as ranged units you can ready an attack and have it swing immediately after you dodge into a group of enemies and wreak havoc.  My only real complaint here is that you can roflstomp the entire game without any real strategy or coordination if you figure out how to abuse shrines for massive amounts of stats and items.
Another thing I'd like to mention is that the developer really cares about the game. For instance, in the discussion thread I made a post concerning the game's difficulty, and he responded pretty much immediately, discussing plans of what he might do in the future with certain aspects of the game.
But yeah. This game is highly underrated, and shows promise to improve further with pretty frequent significant content updates.

I've only played this game a few times with friends, but I've found the spirit and idea of this game wonderfully fun!  Its execution is generally very solid, though I will quibble a bit and say there's a distinct lack of visual contrast between specters and background.  This is especially true in a busy, high-action room, and it is additionally true in cases when jumping as a specter between different traps or world items.  The aiming also takes a bit to get used to, since most items only allow you to aim on the cardinal directions (N/S/E/W), and the delay between possession of a trap, engagement of it, and the actual doing/shooting of whatever it does/shoots I've found hard to nail down.
This game, like so many games that rely on precision timing, plays much better locally than it does streamed through a Steam Link or other machine - the added network and transcode latency makes controlls noticably more sluggish than when playing locally with a locally attached controller or kb/mouse.
OVerall, a very cool, fun romp.  The OST's awesome, and the voice work of the narrator is on-point.  It's a bit rough around the edges as noted, but I feel like those are fairly minor points compared to its success as a high-action local coop PVP dungeon crawler (basically). :)

tl;dr A fun co-op game for you and up to three other friends (or the AI, but that's not as fun).
Pretty fun and hectic local co-op game. Key word being local - make sure you have friends to play with. Each playthrough centers around trying to stop whichever boss/Elder God is about to be resurrected. There are three different bosses. You get three attempts per boss - if the Hero fails, it's game over and the God is summoned for the end of the world. Matches are short, 30-60 minutes. You level up both are the Hero and the monster-summoning Wraiths. Each player levels up the monsters they can summon once the Hero reaches the floor exit staircase (which also heals everyone). Once someone reaches level 10, they have to get to the Boss Portal while the Wraiths try to kill him with traps and monsters that they can summon/possess. Once you get to the Boss, the Wraiths possess parts of the boss and try to kill the Hero.
Each successful playthrough unlocks new monsters, weapons, deities to worship (affects stats and which monsters you can summon/upgrade), etc. Wraiths can collect ectoplasm to summon low-level slimes. The Hero has to kill all enemies to escape the room he's in.
Game looks gorgeous. Haven't encountered any technical problems so far. I wonder if the devs plan to implement online play, because local-only really limits the potential. Maybe Hamachi/Tunngle/some other virtual LAN program will work, but latency is probably the concern the devs had since you have to immediately start moving once you resurrect as the Hero or turn into a Wraith.

I purchased this game last year to play it with my daughter, who, at the time, was only 6.  I never would have played this game, if not for her.  She loved the game dearly, including the artwork, music, and characters.  I ended up liking it myself, as well.  She was a little nervous about the battles, so I would help her with that aspect of the game.  Otherwise she was the one who controlled Aurora, and it was easy enough for her using a controller.  I enjoyed reading the story to her, and she enjoyed all the different voices I made up for each character.
Now we are on our second play through, and she is now 7.  Since she only remembers bits and pieces from playing last year, it's like playing the game all over again.  Like visiting an old friend you haven't seen in a long time.  Now she can actually read what the characters are saying, while I voice them.  She even offers to voice Aurora herself.   She even plays through most of the battles now, herself.  I didn't expect this game to have any replay value when I purchased it last year, but here we are playing it again.
I'm often looking for things to share and do with my daughter, and games like this and Ori and the Blind Forest, are rare gems.  I highly recomend this game for parents looking for a little something extra to share with their children.  It is an excellent and endearing game, and well worth the price.

Brief Summary: Despite a few flaws, the game is beautiful and well-constructed. Recommended.
Details:
Storyline - The story is subtly moving, building an excellent sense of doom and foreboding that escalates as the game goes on. The choices and consequences capture the loneliness of leadership well. The choices make a big difference, keeping the game tense.
Art and Soundtrack - The game looks stunning and the soundtrack is beautiful and haunting.
Combat - The combat works reasonably well. The system is unique insofar as it has a fixed you-them-you-them... initiative structure, which means having greater numbers is not necessarily an advantage. Rather than focusing damage on specific targets (the norm of SRPGs) The game encourages weakening as many targets as possible, before moving in for kills.
Niggles:
The game can be punishing in places. You have one pool of xp to level all your characters and if a character you focussed on dies from a story event. Tough. That xp is gone.
Also the game could do with an undo or extend move feature, to make the occasional attack of "Fat Fingers" less disastrous.
Overall, really enjoyed it and look forward to seeing where they go with the 2nd one.

The plot and universe are a bit wishy washy, but it makes up for it with humour, ridiculous situations and some bizzare stories, it this is your sort of thing. Nothing epic like the LOTR trilogy, but you'll get to choose between

Overall it's a solid recommendation if you like crpgs, being one of the best games to come out of Kickstarter and getting top places on charts of 2014.

As usual for TellTale, a very well done choose-your-own-adventure-ish game with various actors from the show playing their characters.  In their usual fashion, they mix in (barely) choice-based story-telling with action sequences that fit perfectly in the Song of Fire and Ice / Game of Thrones world.  Plus you get to visit many of the more famous areas of Westeros throughout the game.
However, there are some negative points.  TellTale still does not support Linux / Steam OS despite saying they want to support all platforms (a fact will prevent me from purchasing any further TellTale games).  The game does not seem to care about any choices you make, it just kind of pushing you along the story with little consequence but this isn't new or a huge deal considering it is pretty well designed.  Lastly, there is no Steam Cloud support as of yet so whatever machine you play it on you will have to keep playign it on to progress.  That or move your save files.
Overall a pretty solid game with some minor issues that can be easily fixed... well, except for the choices thing, but they always seem to do that.

This game is a  great J-RPG. If you've played any of the "Mario & Luigi" or "Paper Mario" (excluding Super Paper Mario) games, then you are already used to the overworld where you can roam around and then initiate turn-based battles upon hitting or being hit by an enemy-- however you cannot manually dodge attacks in this game.
This is a game in which you can only save at save points in-dungeon or from the menu in the map, the latter of which is not always the best option, as you will lose whatever of your "EXE drive" which you have filled in the dungeon. This limited saving is a challenging element, as you cannot just save right in front of a boss.
This game requires a lot of grinding at several points, but the character's different combos can make what may sound like a boring, tedious task something much more diverse and fun, allowing you to experiment more and build your strategy.
This is not a game you can get and then easily beat in a day, nor can you just plow through without strategy unless you have grinded to be substantially more powerful than the enemies.
Oh, and of course, big anime tiddies and boob jiggle physics are present.

It has truly never been a better time for gamers, who love space sims. With the emergence of games like Strike Suit Zero and X Rebirth, to remind us of our childhood fantasies of being Han Solo (while forcing our younger brothers to ware bear-suits and act like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥), the indie-game market has successfully jumped on the bandwagon as well. Sci Fi styled games have been hitting the Steam-Store faster than my face hits the pavement after a night out on the town. But instead of playing one of the many early access (AKA: not yet finished) games, currently littering my “Recommended-By-Steam” inbox, I have decided to recommend a game I have played on to completion and can honestly praise like the godsend it is, namely FTL (Faster Than Light).
FTL is a spaceship management game from 2012, which was the resolute of a successful Kick-Starter campaign. This review is coming at a rather convenient time, seeing as a massive content update and iPad version have recently been released. But it can’t beat the PC version, if you ask me (PC=Master gaming race and all that).
The story goes: You (the player) take command of an imperial ship and its crew in order to warn the Empire’s HQ form the impending rebel invasion. You must trek the stars, in a turn-based-strategy from solar-system to solar-system, destroying, saving and always looting other spaceships and/or random encounters in order to stay on the run and upgrade your ship for the “Last Stand”.
The game’s aesthetics take the form of a charming 8-bit look, giving everything just enough distinction to make out what you’re looking at, but not enough to break that nostalgic feeling of early hand-held Nintendo games. The music is fittingly retro as well, with just enough diversity as not to get on your nerves. The story itself and the encounters are conveyed through textboxes with predetermined answers that vary depending on the ship’s current outfit and crew. All in all, the game seems to consciously drop the modern empty spectacle for a more thoughtful kind of gameplay.
What makes FTL stand out so much is that it uses its relatively simple gameplay elements, like the Native Americans used the buffalo (every single part). At the beginning of each game, every ship is outfitted with a few upgrades, that determines your imitate play stile and reaction-choices to random encounters. But soon after, you will have your pick of upgrades to enhance or diversify your battle strategies. The combat is not turn-based, but with the pause function it might as well be. It’s the kind of game that rewards crafty thinking. You could obliterate your opponents head on with a barrage of missiles, or beam your crew members over for a boarding attack. Or, if you’re the passive-aggressive civil servant type like me, you could clock your ship and take pot-shots at the enemy’s oxygen tanks and gleefully watch as their crew suffocate. Every ship model has natural strengths with certain strategies and even the crewmen come in various flavours of alien, who too have various strengths completing certain tasks like putting out fires or repairing damage.
To top it all off, like the pretty girl at the end of the bar who gives you just enough attention for you to mess up, FTL has a permadeath function: meaning when your ship is destroyed, you’ll have to start again from the very beginning. All crew members and ship upgrades are lost to the endless void of space, with no reloads or saved games to retrieve them from. This puts many gamers off, feeling that that investing hours in to a game, only to have it blow up in ones face, is a total waste of time. But with every game the player has the chance to unlock new ships and layouts for their unlocked ones. The game achieves a nigh endless replay value this way.
For all FTL’s weaknesses in the graphics and sound department, one can’t help one’s self but get increasingly engrossed in the game when the thought off permanently losing a crucial crewmate, as the enemy sets the dammed medical-bay on fire for the umpteenth time, crosses one’s mind. But that’s just what permadeath does to a game. The only way to make it more engrossing is to have someone else play the game, while you sit on a tall chair behind them and bark out orders.
“As if all those orders meant something, Captain Kirk!”

I tend to recommend most games that are free unless they are horrible.  Boid is an interesting little game.  I do not, however, think it is currently classified correctly.  Boid is more like a MOBA that had a baby with an RTS.  It does not have levelable heroes like most MOBA but it autogenerates little troops that go along little pathways and the maps are very MOBA like with lanes and what not.  The RTS elements are that rather than having predefined lanes that these autogenerated troops go down, you manipulate the pathways to convert standard units to more specialized forms and then to take over enemy nodes.  That's it.  It's a MOBA with no heroes where you change the pathways of the grunt troops and watch it all unfold.
It doesn't have a lot of the standard aspects of an RTS:
1. No resources to collect and manage other than the capture points
2. No technology tree to customize your loadouts and skills for your units.
3. No building, base creation or deployable defense structures of any kind.
4. No assignable squad numbers to manage your units - this is as basic as RTS mechanics get.
4. No patroling mechanisms, attack toggling, etc. - I had enemy units go right past mine and they did nothing - there is no way to set units with certain behavioral macros.
5. No special units with unique skills that must be proc'ed by the player.
6. Absolutely no terrain differences that require specialized units (IE land, air, water, etc.)
Does it take strategy?  Yeah.  I imagine if I play a little longer, layers of complexity will be revealed in terms of what troops you want to produce to counteract what the other players are doing.    In the end, Boid is elegant and simple.  I can imagine some people would get really into things like this, I just prefer something with more substance.  Give it a spin.  You'll know if it is something you're into or not in about 5-10 minutes.

There are a few games out there let you 'play' you music collection. The most notable examples on Steam being Audiosurf and this.
At its core this a simple twin-stick shooter but the joy of it is how the game reacts to music. The more intense the music the more enemies appear but the stronger your ship's firepower. There are plenty of tracks included with the game, mostly dance 'choons' but the real fun comes when you start using your own music. I couldn't resist trying to break it by using Irish folk tunes, but surprisingly the stages that got created were amongst the hardest I played.
After a twin-stick shooter that isn't Geometry Wars? After a new and exciting way to experience your music collection that isn't Audiosurf? This game is the answer to both those wants and more.
It is worth noting that this is best played with a controller, something with at least two control sticks, otherwise your experience may be a lot less fun.

Grim Dawn is the spiritual successor to Titan Quest, an ARPG set in Greek Mythology, only this time it is an original setting with an original story.  The game begins as you awaken from a hanging.  Your crime: being corrupted by Aetherial energy.  Coming under the influence of this energy gives the gift of superhuman abilities (aka the skill tree), but can also turn you into a shambling undead.  You are sent to investigate this Aetherial energy in a nearby cave to win the influence of the town that tried to hang you, and the story carries on from there.
There are 6 different classes in the game: Soldier, focusing on physical, bleed, and internal trauma damages with a focus on defensive shield-use; Shaman, a two-handed weapon focused character that deals a combination of lightning, bleed, and retaliation damage with defensive life leech and regeneration abilities, and can also summon a briarthorn beast; Nightblade, a very offensively minded melee dual wield character with a cold, pierce, and poison/acid damage focus, and can also benefit from guns or crossbows; Arcanist, the spell-caster with a bevy of elemental skills but is very strong with fire and aether damage, and uses damage reflection and damage mitigation sphere skills for defense; Occultist, a summoner focused caster strong with chaos, vitality, fire and poison/acid damage that uses a combination of acid retaliation and life leech for defense; and finally Demolitionist, a bomb tossing, trap throwing gun toting pyromaniac using mostly fire and lightning damage and uses a variety of stuns, blinds and fumbling attacks for defense.
You pick your first class on your first level up, with the ability to pick a second class at level 10. It is highly recommended to do so as each class has multiple synergies with another and leveling up two skill trees instead of one provides you with more character stats: PHYSIQUE, CUNNING, and SPIRIT. Physique regulates your hit points and ability to wear heavy armor. Cunning regulates your pierce and bleed damage as well as chance to hit and critical chance. Spirit regulates your mana pool, and elemental damage.
Another important part of your character is the Devotion map.  Throughout the game there are shrines that require certain craftable materials in order to restore them. Restoring a shrine gives you a devotion point.  On the devotion screen are many constellations, each a cluster of connected devotion points that provide themed skills and abilities.  Some of the skills gained from the completion of a constellation can be attached to a skill on your skill tree, making it more powerful.  It adds another satisfying layer of complexity to your character, and is absolutely necessary to master in order to tackle the harder difficulties.
Crafting is very deep and involved.  At around character level 15 you recieve a quest to recruit a blacksmith. There are two different blacksmiths to pick from, one is stronger for magic based characters, the other for physical damage characters.  This blacksmith can make either a random magic weapon armor for you or you can find rare and unique recipes dropped by monsters.  The ingredients for these recipies are also dropped by monsters. The ingredients can also be infused into weapons to give them different stats and abilities.
There is also a faction system.  Defeating certain types of enemies raises your influence with the 5 or 6 different factions in the game. Different levels of influence allow you to buy different tiers of equipment from faction vendors. It should also be noted that defeating enemies also lowers their standing with you, and you can even become so hated that special super unique enemies can spawn from that group of enemies, and hunt you down.
Combat is very visceral and satisfying.  Critical attacks shake the screen and send send your enemies flying.  All skills have a unique animation and are very fun to use.  There are 4 Acts and 3 difficulties.  The max character level is 85.

It's tough not to recommend this game, but ultimately there are too many things dragging it down for me to want to continue playing.
At base, this game is great. Wonderful character customization, interesting battles, cool abilities. What more could you want from an RPG?
-How about an interface that doesn't feel like it came from 1999? Managing your inventory is a nightmare; you'll have to constantly shuffle gear from one character to another if you want to sell/repair anything, and many vendors don't carry much money, so if you want to sell your items to them, you'll need to buy a roughly equally valued pile of goods from them during the exchange or you won't get your money's worth.
-Acquiring new skills from skillbooks is slow and boring, really taking the fun out of gaining levels. Woohoo! I gained a level and get a point to put into a stat which affects a number, but in no way affects how I play the game. Yay. Why not just let us acquire skills naturally as we level up instead of making us unlock the ability to learn certain skills and THEN force us to find the requisite skillbooks, too?
-Combat takes too long. Enemies move too slowly on their turn, and while it may not bother you at first, after so many turns of combat you'll feel like you're wasting your life watching enemies do their thing.
-Trying to find where to go/what to do for most quests is a miasma of confusion; again, it feels like 1999 all over again.
Divinity: Original Sin has a lot to like about it, and if you're really into '90s-era PC RPGs, you'll probably have a blast, but if you've become accustomed to the kind of quality-of-life improvements in modern RPGs like X-Com: Enemy Unknown, you may grow tired of Divinity: Original Sin's obstinately old-school mentality.

Did you enjoy the creepy atmosphere, intuitive puzzles, and platforming of Limbo and Inside? Well I'm guessing the creators of Little Nightmares did too.
But when it comes to video games, imitation is often a lot more tolerable. I like that style of atmosphere and gameplay, and there isn't that much of it getting made most of the time.
Little Nightmares adds its own contributions into the mix. It has its own style and atmosphere, and I love the environments and enemy designs. It all looks like a sort of nightmare stop motion animation.
It also doesn't waste a lot of time. It rarely felt like any type of challenge or enemy outstayed its welcome, and each section felt distinct and effective. By the end I felt I'd had a well-rounded experience without a whole lot of filler.
I've reviewed the DLC individually, but here's the takeaway:
The Depths: Mostly just a water level. Short and kind of one-note.
The Hideaway: Satisyfing, adds some new ideas and goals that make it more substantial.

Of all the games I play, my favorites are shooters and action role playing games (ARPGs). To me, the gold standard of ARPGs is the Diablo series (specifically Diablo 2 and Diablo 3). I love Diablo 3 and the attention Blizzard has given this game. I've spent hundereds of hours playing this game and building some hugely powerful characters that I'm very invested in. I've played other ARPGs, but few hold a candle to Diablo 3 (though many are compared to this standard). Then, along comes Grim Dawn, and I've got to say, this game is every bit as good and enjoyable to me as Diablo 3. It is different in many ways, but has some awesome elements that I wished Diablo 3 had. The graphics and story are great, and the character builds and possibilities are massive. Though, like Diablo 3, Grim Dawn is a hack and slash loot collector at it's core; it never becomes tiring, as you strive to blast wave after wave of baddies in the interests of leveling up and collecting better loot, so that your character is the baddest dude (or gal) in town. If you like ARPGs, i think next to Diablo 3, Grim Dawn is the best one out there.

A great game, but definitely not for everybody. If you aren't a fan of anime-style games, esspecially ones that put an emphasis on the waifus (Seriously, there's an item called the "Waifu Ribbon"), you might want ot look at a different game.
A few things I liked.
Without the DLC, max level is 99. With all the DLC, that raises to 999. If you want to reach level 999, be prepared for A LOT of grinding. Fortunately, once you can beat some of the tougher enemies, you can gain anywhere from 2 to 8 levels from a single battle, so it doesn't feel as if you aren't getting anywhere in the process. At around level 400 it took me about 30 minutes to gain roughly 50 levels or so. Or you can visit the Colosseum, with no penalty for losing and some of the higher end battles giving over 30 million exp, it cuts down on grinding by a lot.
Getting materials can also be a pretty grindy process. Between the Guild missions (if you do them, most are optional) and creating the plans, you need a ton of certain materials. Finding which monster drops a certain material and where it lives can be a pain, even with the Nepedia. So I ended up finding a chart online and using it quite a bit.
The dungeons do repeat quite a bit. There are a variety of different environments, but almost every dungeon of the same environment is a copy+paste of a previous dungeon, and only sometimes is there any change at all. Occasionally one will have a small area across a wooden bridge or something that a previous dungeon didn't have, but the maps are still almost the exact same.
One of the biggest problems I had was a huge jump in what level you had to be for the final 3 dungeons. I unlocked the first of them probably around level 200, but I couldn't even damage the enemies until almost level 750 and couldn't consistantly defeat them for almost another 100 levels after that.
Finally, a heads-up. If you're considering buyingthere was a plethora of problems when it first launched and I'm not sure how much progress IFI has made fixing them. It took me some time to figure out how to get the game to even start, but after that I didn't have any issues. If you want to see what people are/were having problems with and some of the fixes people found, visit the discussion page and browse through a little bit. It probably wouldn't hurt to look at some of those before you actually buy either HDNR;B1 or HDNR;B2.

It's been a while since I've played any Telltale games. I'd previously played
and a few of the
games, but those were more similar to classic point and click adventure games while
focuses primarily on dialogue choices instead of item manipulation and puzzle solving.
I enjoyed the story, and I do feel it fit in well in the world of
. Just to be clear about my familiarity with the series, I have read all the released books and up through Season 3 Episode 7 of the television series.
I do hope to get caught up on the rest of the show soon.
For most dialogue choices, there is a meter that counts down so you have to make a decision in time, otherwise you will remain silent (with it's own consequences). This added some interesting tension and I may have made some different choices than if I had more time to think things over. I tended to play the middle ground too often, I think, veering in one direction, then bringing it back in as I reconsidered. This tended to make people more upset than anything. Whether my choices had any real long-standing consequences in the end remains to be seen throughout the rest of the series.
The quicktime events where I had to tap a key repeatedly or dodge just in time were kind of annoying, especially since I didn't want to make too much noise and wake up my son who was sleeping upstairs. Maybe I need to get a quieter keyboard.
The graphics engine used in
definitely feels a bit dated. I don't mind the "oil paint" filter, but there seemed to be a weird flickering as well. At first I thought this was only above flames, but then I also saw it in random places. Not a deal breaker, but a bit odd. Some of the character models were a bit ugly, but really only felt jarring for the characters who have real-life actor counterparts that I'm used to seeing.
Overall, I'm satisfied with this first episode even if I felt it had a few issues. I look forward to Episode 2 and hope to play through the series in its entirety.

Little Nightmare sets only one goal: escape. Delivering a great story and stunning ambiance, this title impresses until the very end and, to date,  is probably the best of its genre. Sadly, the game mechanics aren't par with the art direction, and nothing will really motivate players to invest more time than needed for its short initial play through. As a narrative experience, though, it won't disappoint and leave you begging for more.
Recommended on sales, or for any fan of ambient platformers (Limbo, Inside, Spate...)
Not recommended if you get your kicks by solving hard puzzles (The Room) or jumping into action.
+ Impeccable art direction
+ Most of the time, great physics
+ Beautiful wordless narrative
= The game's pacing isn't for everyone
= A couple of gameplay incoherence
= Puzzles could have been more elaborate
- The perspective will mess you up
-----------
Full review
-----------
You literally start at Six. Six, a little yellow running hooded girl spawning from a suitcase, and fated to escape The Maw, a facility which goal is best left uncovered for now. The first impression the game gives is awe for its fantastic polish and esthetic, reminding the player of a Tim Burton stop motion movie. Six has to hide, run and solve a number of puzzles in order to get out, and does so thanks to her strong little legs and arms, equipped with nothing else than a lighter (which, really is only there to add to the ambiance).
Here, no jumping on enemy heads to flatten them, no bullets, and generally more escape than confrontation. Little Nightmares is all about finding the right timing, remaining silent, and not getting noticed by the grotesque and deformed hosts of The Maw. Although wordless, Little Nightmares was developped as an interactive story, apparently based around the feelings of inadequacy one can feel when transing from childhood to early adulthood. Everything is exaggerated, disproportionate, and, of course, nightmarish.
As with all games of its kind (Limbo, Intside, Spate, etc...) the ambiance is the major selling point of this title, and it actually manages to take its proposition to the next level: everything, from sounds to physics, is here to make players feel ill at ease and, as a result, the fear of the unknown might very well crawl inside their brains, especially when starting a new area. The visuals are absolutely in tune as well, as the Unreal Engine 4 is put to excellent use. Delivery wise, I would definitely consider this game as the best of its kind.
Are fear and ambiance enough to make this game an absolute masterpiece though? I do not think so. To begin with, the major problem with its gameplay comes from the same daring camera angles that make its visuals so engrossing: Six will rather often err in an unwanted direction, or fall to her death, beacause of skewed perspective to which the controls aren't always adapted.
Past this technical observation, I personally feel that this game bears a lot of unexploited potential. Why, for instance, give Six a lighter which she will never use to advance the plot? Why give an action button which will trigger everything in the game save one specific switch? And what about throwing items only used in a couple of cases? These under exploited mechanics, combined with the slow pace of the hide-and-seek phases, made me feel more relieved to be able to move to the next challenge rather than feel content as the result of having solved a well thought puzzle.
All in all, I feel that the only real challenge of the game is the intermittent struggle against the camera's perspective, and that, with these fantastic physics and ambiance, play time could have been considerably lenghtened by the use more-than-just-simplistic puzzles. As it is, the game is as good as its story, and there is no motivation to return to it once the final chapter has been closed.
Even with its low replayability level and strong 'ambiance over action' concept, it remains that Little Nightmares successfully reaches its goals by delivering an interesting methaphorical story, great immersion and overal gameplay which will most likely trigger real emotions (mostly disgust, but the fun kind).
I would recomend it to ambient platformer fans as a must play game, and for all others I would definitely suggest to grab it on sales as it is a definite milestone in the genre.

There is something innately satisfying about playing your favourite music in a videogame, and that satisfaction is magnified tenfold when you're blasting the bejeesus out of the music in question! Beat Hazard has musical mayhem unlike anything I've quite experienced before ...think top-down, twin-stick shooter ala the excellent Geometry Wars, but even more chaotic!
Beat Hazard can quite literally take any track you throw at it and turn it into a challenging, borderline insane experience as asteroids, multi-segment worms, scores of fighters and advanced ships with attracting and repelling magnets aim to lay a beat down on you. Thankfully you're not even close to undefended, and the game has a satisfying level up hook that sees you gaining ranks and experience that allow you to equip powerful boosts like homing missiles and shields, or simply give yourself an edge with extra lives and bonus damage.
It all combines into a delightfully frenetic on-screen experience, whether it's in one-off songs or in the survival mode that plays entire albums of your choosing if you so wish (my personal favourite mode!) Combined with some internet radio options, the potential of this game is virtually unlimited.
Easily worth the price at full cost, and for the frequent 50-75% off sales it's really a no brainer. Pick your favourite tunes then pick up this game and get blasting!

Was really interested in this game. Who hasn't wanted to pilot a starship into combat while managing the energy of ship systems a la Star Trek? "Weapons are down!" "Reroute primary systems through the secondary relay!" "Target their engines!" Unfortunately after about 30 hours in I can not recommend this game.
Resources, rewards, events, maps, enemy encounters, shop location, shop items for sale are all determined by the RNG. Very little is left up to player control.
You may have a run where you get tons of resources are plentiful, or where you're left a pauper scrounging for scrap, can't find the shop, or the the shop has nothing decent for sale. Standard fair if you've played Binding of Isaac. Unlike Binding of Isaac, FTL is hampered by...
Unlike other Rogue-likes/lites like Binding of Isaac and Rogue Legacy where you take direct control of your character; FTL gives the chance for "random encounters" every system jump similar to a JRPG.
Combat in FTL is largely turn-based where you wait for your weapon cooldowns to end, and many of them are extremely long making combat tedious. This is further exacerbated as anytime your weapons are disabled your cooldowns start over.
Attacking an enemy ship is simple. Target a system on the enemy ship and fire. Attack their weapons to disable their ability to attack, or shields to lower their defensive capabilities. Aiming is left completely up to the RNG which determines whether your shot hits or misses. There is zero player skill involved.
This is the biggest area of frustration when half or all of your salvo hits empty space and the computer's attack cripples every vital system on your vessel. All thanks to dumb luck.
Evasion (chance to dodge) is controlled by the "Engines" so the more your enemy's engines are upgraded, the higher the chance for you to miss. The same applies to your chance to dodge the enemies shots. Taking out the engines or cockpit means a guarenteed hit, but there is no way to increase the accuracy of your weapons when you initially target them. You just have to
enough of your shots will connect to disable the system, and
they aren't repaired before your next attack.
FTL has some of the worst enemy AI I have ever seen.
This is shown consistently by the computer's use of transporters, bombs, and beam based weapons.
Often times they will port teams into your docking bay or empty rooms when transporters can port to ANY location and never miss, teleport bombs to systemless rooms (bombs can only damage systems) and firing beam weapons while your shields are up (most beams can't damage while shields are up)
Imagine if you played a game where the enemy randomly started attacking a wall. Or a racing game where the other car randomly threw itself into a ditch. Would you find that acceptable?
Of course not, but in FTL?  "GAME OF THE YEAR!"
The strategy guides online even mention utilizing the horrid AI to achieve victory. Targeting certain ship systems near the cockpit will cause the pilot to leave his post to repair them. Meaning while he's gone you get free hits. That's just bad programming.
The reason for this terrible AI is because if the enemy ships knew how to play, you'd lose every single time.
In most video games the enemy is an obstacle. In FTL the enemy is a resource.
The foundation of FTL is grinding just like World of Warcraft.
You kill ships (mobs) to get scrap (gold/exp) and sometimes get weapons/new crewmen (loot).
Unlike WoW, in FTL your EXP and gold are the same thing. Scrap is used for buying, upgrading and repairing. Meaning that taking too much damage will result in you spending EXP to heal instead of upgrading. Meanwhile the enemy only gets stronger.
The game also has the "rebel fleet" a few jumps behind the player making it impossible to search every system for ships to grind. You just have to pick the longest path and
for enough encounters and
you don't get hit too many times.
This is the reason I call it backwards.
In Rogue Legacy your objective is chests as they contain the most gold. Enemies are an obstacle and often times it's better to avoid them entirely because you can't just heal your character whenever. That's good strategy. Similarily with Binding of Isaac. Once you've found and entered the special rooms you can just forget exploring the rest of the dungeon and go to the boss or exploring other rooms to try for key/bomb drops for future levels. Again good strategy.
Both instances in RL and BOI are the players choice. In FTL you MUST take the longest path to each sector exit to increase your odds of resources as EVERY encounter could potentially gift you with  weapons or crew.  This is then hampered by the fact that you can't guarantee a hit or avoid taking damage in combat, meaning a percentage of your EXP will eventually have to go to repairs (unless you're super lucky), again by what your reward type/amount is, again by the fact that you can't search every system for enemies to grind, again while searching for a shop, and again depending on what the shop has for sale. All of these elements are controlled by the RNG making everything in FTL nothing but coin flip after coin flip.
FTL's most impressive accomplishment is the psychology based around it.
The gameplay is tedious and repetive, but addictive. This is accomplished by juxtaposing an artificially inflated difficulty curve against randomly rewarding the player with scrap and loot drops. Sometimes just for jumping into a system.
By bestowing these rewards upon the player, it encourages them to continue pumping in hours of their life into the game. If you're having a good run you're motivated by greed and a sense of empowerment. "I want more weapons more scrap, give me MOAR!! I am invincible! HAHAHA!"
If you're having a bad run you're motivated by hope and desperation. "Just have to make it to a shop to repair. I can do it. Maybe this system...no...maybe the next system."
Regardless of whether you're having the most amazing run ever, the final boss can still curb-stomp you into the dirt with just a few well placed shots.
This is due to the fact that the fight is hard, but has no sense of fair play as the rebel flag ship's "Power Surge" ability cannot be prevented even by disabling the weapons, and killing the crew results in an AI taking control of the ship. I'm no stranger to having bosses with special abilities, and multiple forms, but boss fights are supposed to be a test of what the player has learned up to this point. FTL's boss fight goes completely against established gameplay mechanics that were taught to the player in every encounter up to this point. ie: disabling weapon systems disables weapons, and killing crew disables ship.
It's not just the final boss. Enemy ships often have weapons that don't exist for purchase in game that have cooldowns lower than the player to ensure the computer gets the first shot.
The computer can also target multiple systems with multishot weapons like the Burst Laser Mk 3 (5 shots) while the player must spend all shots on a single system. Clearly the player is playing one game while the computer is playing another.
While some games use RNG's to add a sense of uniqueness to each playthrough, FTL goes much further and attempts to turn the RNG into a genre.  FTL is a game built on luck based difficulty and skinner box mechanics.
It's not skill to defeat an opponent who spent the fight porting bombs into empty rooms, and it's not a lack of skill if you lost because your entire salvo missed thanks to the RNG. It's luck, plain and simple.
FTL is more slot machine than space simulator. Avoid.

I have been playing this game for about some time now and this is what I can say about it...
Pros:
-Excellent gameplay
-Awesome graphics
-Huge open world map
-Large amount of NPCs that make the world feel alive
-Fun to form guilds with friends
-Tons of activities to fall back to if you get tired of fighting
But here is where the game got really ugly for me...
Cons:
-Quirky and awkward character creation
-Overcrowded servers where getting by without someone stealing your kills is difficult at best
-Random PvP zones all over the map which you never know when you're about to step into
-You can join guilds but there aren't any real group missions
-Ridiculously convoluted standard UI that can get irritating quickly
-If you don't want your character to look like a farmer, then you must spend real money
-You also need to spend real money to change something the quirky creation tool messed up
-Connection issues which apparently the developers have made not attempt at fixing
-The character outfits are only teases for the most part
-Combat can feel repetitive at times
-Grinding starts to feel like a chore real soon
-There is no clear indication on how to take on how crafting works
-A very toxic fan community
Over all, this game comes out as a mixed bag... A nasty bag who had a really bad day.
P.S:
Don't come to me replying with "Oh, you expect things handed to you on a silver plater, hurr durr." Or "You just don't understand how the game works and you suck" Or even "The game developers need to make money from somewhere" I'm not going to buy into that BS!! This is not a free to play game. this is a purchased game, and damn right I expect something out of a game I paid for.

"Battlefront 2 isn't a good looking game, but its pretty damn fun. The combat is epic although guns lack weight and the animations look like♥♥♥♥♥in first person. The game is very similar to the first but honestly, why would you want it to be a completely different game as a sequel? It is not like it didn't add things. It has also many of the maps from battlefront 1, but whats wrong with that? Its like L4D 2 is now adays, it eventually got all L4D1 maps. Sure it makes the original feel more worthless, but it makes the sequel so much better. Star ship battles have been introduced, which are sort of a simplified combat space sim where you must beat the enemy by killing them or destroying systems on the enemy main battle ship. This is very fun to do and looks pretty epic, although I wish you could actually blow up the enemy ship (although this would have to take a very large amount of hits). Heros have been introduced, which are overpowered units awarded after a certain amount of time to the best player on each team (different in campaign and galactic conquest mode). There is galactic conquest mode where you have a simple map with planets, where you and the opponent take turns moving ships around, buying new unit types and buying special bonuses which give an powerful passive (or hero unit) to use once before a battle. If you move onto an enemy planet, you start a conquest gametype battle type which you win by depleting enemy reinforcements or capturing all spawn points. These battles give you more credits to buy bonuses, units and ships. If you move to an enemy ship, to begin a star ship battle, ending with the losers ship destroyed. This is a fun gamemode if your playing against a friend, but the AI seems pretty incompetent at stopping you (although I have not tried it on elite difficulty, and Felucia in the empire conquest is almost impossible to win). Some maps have a unique idea that gives variety. Kasheek for example has a constant spawn of free wookies who don't count to the reinforcements (but cannot be controlled by a player) on the good side. Hoth has two insta respawning giant AT ATs on the empire side that take huge damage or a successful snowspeeder ship wire hook kill (yes, just like in the movie) and those AT ATs act as slow mobile spawn points for the empire. Sadly many of the maps simply don't have these things which is disapointing, as it gives a great deal of variety. Some maps have heros which are completely useless, mainly the Fett's and Princess Leia. Space combat is also hurt due to bad PC controls which while bareable, are completely useless against anyone even using a gamepad. Still it is essentially a simple space sim, so that is to be expected. Hit detection on thrown lightsabers, and blocking in general seems to also be a bit inconsistant. AI also is hit and miss, most of the time they work 'ok' but there is times where for example when they control a jedi, they will stun you take you to near death, then run past you and stand still while you gun them down from behind. The hero assault mode is fun where you play heroes vs villians, but it is sadly only on one map. Hunt mode however is on a small number of maps where you can play as the aliens or animals from the planet in a death match mode. (Things like Wumpas vs Rebels and Ewoks vs Empire). A big problem is they did not bring the maps from Battlefront 1 that had aircraft for support on ground battles, aside from Hoth, which only have dog fighting (for some reason) weapons on the snow speeders and the hooks they use to take out AT ATs. Sound and music quality is good, but it just uses sounds directly from the movies, even the music is all from the movies, which is good in some ways, bad in others.
Overall its a good game with some problems, but still very enjoyable game. Also since its old, its pretty cheap on steam, however I have heard there is problems with sound on some computers which causes incompatability and crashs when entering battle. However I have not had any of these problems on my Windows 7 laptop (which albiet is pretty awful) and headphones apparently prevent the crashs as headphone drivers seem to not cause problems. This is likely just a problem with a few sound cards but due to the amount of people annoyed at it, it could be a more common one. Recommend pirating first so you can quickly test if the sound card problem affects you. Unless there is a demo (I have not bothered to check if there is one). "

Easily one of the most underappreciated Steam games I've ever seen
Basically you create a basic character, you go around what I can only assume is some kind of manor to check out some of the stuff you collected, and then you go outside and find mirrors. The mirrors function as portals to areas where enemies, unlockables, and loot and thrown about in a labyrinth fashion. You die and you have to restart. If you saved your items (which i have not even figured out how to do yet) they can be used in future playthroughs along with xp for character upgrades based on your violence % (kinda).
Binding of Isaac

- Rooms (of sorts)
- Item collecting
- Angled display
- Hordes of enemies that can be fought by learning their patterns
- Boxes and other destructables that break in almost the exact same way as BoI

Dark Souls
- Tough enemies
- Slow, methodical, difficult fights
- Exploration in large, intricate landscapes
- Dying over and over and over
- Large focus on dodging
Rogue Legacy
- Lineage mechanic (somewhat)
- Knight aesthetic
- Kill enemy/box -> currency -> stuff
Pros:
- Well polished
- Nice visuals
- Not too hard
- Pretty cheap
- Exciting fights
- Upgrades m8
- Focus on strategy
Cons:
- Extreme lack of mechanic explaination (even with the manual)

- Somewhat lack of a linear focus
- Levels are just filled with random stuff all over the place
- Game is pretty unknown (sadly) = not much help from guides (only a few) or websites
Overall:
8/10 Worth a go

Bad gameplay, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pixel graphics, and about 8 genders, all of which do nothing.
Seriously though, this might be a good game, but it's too much of a ♥♥♥♥ing grind for me to find out. The game basically has no set up behind it. It just throws you into a poorly drawn world with no explaination beyond a single page that explains the controls and how to buy weapons. Important gameplay mechanics go completely unexplained.
What determines how much XP I keep on death? Is it how much I have on me when I die? How much I spend on random items in purple crystals in the woods? The ♥♥♥♥ are these items and what do they do?
What determines the character I start as next time? Because I usually start as a peasant but then one time it randomly gives me a "Monster", a blood soaked naked guy with a knife. Why? And why does this not seem to stay unlocked? Imagine playing a roguelike as a wizard and then having the game suddenly say "ok, this run you have to play barbarian." and then when you die quickly because you have no clue what any of this♥♥♥♥♥♥is it just takes that class away from you like a kid taking his ball and going home.
What the hell are all these random statues at the start? I have to pay XP to use them but there are no enemies around here that I can see so whats the point? Why are there like 8 ♥♥♥♥ing genders to choose from? I don't even recognize most of these; there's male, female, intersex, attack helicopter and ♥♥♥♥ing omni-queer. And fine, whatever, pander to the gender snakes, but none of these choices actually change anything. The player model is the same little chicken nugget on pixel limbs regardless of what you choose, so what is the ♥♥♥♥ing point?
The combat, which the game seems to be trying to sell itself on, is just budget dark souls, like so many games these days. You have your light attack, your strong attack, your dodge move that is packed with i-frames, your stamina bar that you have to manage, and your limited number of heal items.  And like most of these rip offs, it's inferior in basically every way. The game seems to love spamming you with somewhere between 3 and 7 enemies at every encounter, the dodge roll doesn't feel as effective or satisfying as a DS one- partially because the animations of the crappy little pixel people aren't as easy to read as a 3d character, and the entire experience just lacks any viscera feeling. Oh look, I hit a pixel blob and it fell down. Oh, the bloodlust pulses through me. Truely I feel the berserker joy of battle.
I can see from the trailers that the game might get more exciting later on but here's the thing: I'm not gonna get to the fun parts because I have no desire to ♥♥♥♥ing grind my way to them. You can level up in this game, and the levels stay between lives, but the process is the most grind heavy thing I've seen since a korean MMO. You retain a certain amount of experience when you die. How the game determines what that amount is, I don't ♥♥♥♥ing know. But if you have enough you can level up your stats. Each level up brings that stat up by 1%. Yes, 1 whole ♥♥♥♥ing percent. And it's not like there's just a few stats, there's like 8 or 10 of them. And it takes more and more experience each time. I cannot fathom the number of times you'd have to grind through this game before your stats reached any reasonable level, and I have no desire to do so. Mostly because the gameplay was so goddamn boring.
So yes, I fully admit that maybe, after 20 hours of grinding up stats and getting stuff, this game might be fun. And if you're insane enough to want to waste 20 hours of your life as payment for a lack luster 2d pixel dark souls, than be my guest.  But I'm not gonna bust my♥♥♥♥♥and waste my time to git gud and advance in a game that I already have no interest in continuing.

'In Celebration Of Violence' was an interesting game for me to review. I was drawn by its title and all the killing I saw in its steam page videos. Sadly the first impressions were disappointing, given the name and what I saw I expected something with more action and mindless shooting, slashing, smashing, etc. Some alternative to Hero Siege type of games. After overcoming all the disappointment, I gave it a try and I was overwhelmed by all this seemingly shallow game has to offer. It was like, walking into a park and suddenly falling into a hole so deep that you couldn't see the sky above you and the catch is that you need to learn to climb by yourself. Essentially trying to describe 'In Celebration Of Violence' with a few words, I would say it's a roguelike top town hack n slash, that uses elements from the titles such as 'Dark Souls'.
PROS
>The combat, you'll need to be precise, time your moves, mistakes are punishable and you need to be careful. The game is mostly revolved around combat, and for that, it uses many rules, most commonly found in games like 'Dark Souls'. Some of these rules are, successful parry can stun your opponent, your attacks have a 'wind up' animation that essentially is your character preparing to strike, you can dodge and with a shield equipped you can block. Your attacks can vary depending on the weapon you use, some have long reach others wide arc and some are almost point blank but they hit almost instantly. Roguelike plus all these, means you have lots of combinations that will change your playstyle.
>Killing and breaking stuff awards experience, that must be picked up, either by you or your enemies. Don't worry, if an enemy picks up experience and dies it drops it as well. However, this does not apply to health drops, which are lost and probably heal the enemy! With experience points, you can buy items in your playthrough, use them to cast spells that are on cooldown, or, most importantly save it, so future characters can use them to improve base stats, for all heroes, and purchase items at the starting area. These items become available once you find their corresponding blueprint and there are tens of them in total!
>Given the game's roguelike nature, it has tons of stuff for the player to figure out. From basic stuff like how currency works, how you break stuff, what each spell do, what each potion do, what are the weapon buffs, what each item do, to more important stuff as how you unlock characters or who, why and what are you doing. In each playthrough, or even better, attempt you will try something new, find something new and hopefully make some progress! Expect to die A LOT!
>Achievements! Lots of them and most have a direct impact on your game! From making you a bit faster to unlocking new characters! You might as well look at them for hints!
>Details! Lots of them! You can starve, you can bleed to your demise, you can be cold or hot! And most will affect your effectiveness, e.g. while starving your stamina will drain considerably faster than normal!
>Various maps, enemies, and environment. Each with its pros, cons, and visual differences so it's easy to recognize and act accordingly.
CONS
>It has a harsh learning curve, you will start by dying quite many times and as you start leveling some skills and using your experience to get items.
>It feels very slow and sluggish at first. Until you understand how and when to move, and investing some points into the mobility related attributes, the character movement, and even attack animations will look that they need quite some time.
>The music is simply lackluster. I cannot tell if it is a placeholder or not, but my gameplay got considerably improved when I muted it. The sounds on the other hand, while not something special, are ok.
>The levels boundaries, while black walls that sometimes can provide a clever way to limit players field of view making it more realistic, can become tiresome. This gets amplified to the narrow areas that are randomly generated for each map.
>No customization for controls. Be keyboard and mouse or gamepad, you must go with the preset. However, these are not terrible.
Overall, 'In Celebration Of Violence' is a good game, and most importantly, being in early access and having so many features, makes its full release even more promising!
