A restaurant/prison/ship/island/ holocaust dungeon that seems to cater children to grotesque and oversized adults in a world seemingly designed to pull those threads of previously overcome or forgotten fears out of your deepest childhood memories. This is a world that idealizes the ugly, gluttonous, perversions of the world and shuns the beautiful, moral and unsullied - But that is only what it seems. Whether it was intentional or not, my estimation of the intention and deeper meaning behind the story is more a metaphor depicting the vivid imagination of a child who is unable to rationalize a disgusting world and an unloving mother. From her vantage point the world is as you, the player, view it. As you move though just the first few rooms you will encounter items that appear to indicate that she has been there before. The suitcase you awake in has pictures in it and the room appears lived in; the hanging man (apparent father) on the way to the blanket rope leading to the playroom protected by electrified bars which leads to the nursery and children’s cafeteria… I won’t mention every little detail but it appears as if our protagonist escaped to our starting point which is where she turns and decides to go back. As you progress through the levels she develops out of the docile and sweet, spindly little girl into a monster in her own right. More and more she seems bent on revenging the perceived injustices of the world she is trapped in rather than mearly escaping it. You feel the loss of innocence in this development as you make the decision to eat the gnome instead of the sausage… but then… wasn’t the sausage made of children?
By the end you assume control of your world and denounce the parent who’s apparent vanity stood between you and the warmth of a mothers love and security of a happy home as well as all those who indulged or ignored her negligence. The ending leaves just leaves you feeling justified and victorious; shutting the door on that world and stepping into the light of a new one.

This is the type of game perfect for a lazy afternoon.  If I want something that is short and quick, casual enough to be relaxing, yet also long enough to the point where I still gain some sense of accomplishment -- this game can really fit the bill.  Its short length can make me more forgiving of its issues, yet long enough where I can appreciate the unique atmosphere and character throughout the duration of the game.
Playing as Six, you traverse across several levels comprising of either platforming puzzles or stealth, while trying to escape the giant ship known as the Maw.  These puzzles aren't particularly tough, and only lend to it being that nice one-sit-down-playthrough game this serves to be.  The levels are nicely varied, mixing up rooms where you can take it at your pace and think about the solution, to the rooms dealing with various enemies in the game.  The levels, overall, do a good job marrying gameplay with atmosphere, creating an engrossing experience at times.
These times, though, can be interrupted by moments of frustration.  The controls are clunky, and combined with the 2D nature of the camera, can lead to accidental deaths.  Especially in situations where precision jumping is required, it can take a couple tries to succeed -- simply because the camera and controls combine to frustrate.  In other situations where you must evade certain enemies, the hitboxes can be very wonky -- you'll be seemingly out of literal arms' reach, only to rubber band into their grasp for a death.  Other areas are very trial-and-error, which require multiple deaths to learn pathing and patterns to complete the level.  And, in one or two instances in the DLC, key objects in rooms needed to progress would literally glitch out and disappear, rendering me to restart and do everything over again.  These things happen sparingly, but they do break the atmosphere of the game when they do happen.
However, when the game works as intended, it allows Little Nightmares to shine with its undoubted strong point -- its atmosphere.  Every area is as engaging and interesting as the last, and it always kept me wanting to see more.  The story is told without any dialogue, which is a really interesting way to let the player interpret the nuances of the story and motivations.  It allows the imagination to run a bit, too, which only immerses more to when key events in the game happen.  It's a really clever way to keep the player engaged throughout, and it's interesting to hear how different people interpret the story.  The graphics help with this, as it's every bit as moody as the environments themselves.  The short length is a plus, in my eyes, because it doesn't overstay its welcome, allowing the player to see the game as it is -- a game for a lazy afternoon or evening, with a rewarding experience.
In essence, it's an average platformer that gets major brownie points for its atmosphere and character.  This game took me a shade over 3 hours to complete the main story, and an extra 2 hours to complete the DLC.  If this is too short of a game for you, consider picking everything up on sale.  Regardless, despite its minor flaws, it is worth checking out.

The game is perhaps too short, but good gametime value for the price. What slightly lets it down is a resource system that seems either tacked on or conceptualised from the beginning but underdeveloped. It does not serve any real purpose in the interest of gameplay.

I tried getting into this game 3 times now so I thought I'd write a review on my experience. I've never played the BG series that a lot of people seem to compare this game to so I might just not be a fan of this game style.
I could never bring myself to go pass the 2nd town in the 12.6 hours I've played. Most of the time I just ran around talking to npcs and completing quests/side quests that were pretty boring to me as some of them just involved running around town talking to people. Controlling 2 people in single player also breaks the immersion of roleplay. Arguing with myself (because we have 2 main characters for some reason in singleplayer) turned it into a what-I-wanted-for-characteristics grind using this system.
The combat and exploration is pretty much the same throughout the entire first zone. I don't see it hinting that the combat is gonna get more strategic or synergetic between characters outside of what I started with (aka tank and spank with CC's thrown in there that you start out with). The exploration involved opening a bunch of containers...many many containers and the occasional locked container hoping to find something worth wasting your time over because of RNG making the box empty or containing worthless items... and talking to a bunch of npcs for many hours...
Overall pretty bland and stale due to the pacing and the lack of sense of progression, and fighting being a minor and also very bland part of the game. The free exploration and being able to pick/steal anything seemed cool at first because it seemed to make the game have a lot of choices of what to do, but that is not true. Maybe if I can bring myself to continue playing this it'll get better, but as of pretty much completing the first town, I wouldn't recommend this game.
Main points of the game:
- Picking items up or stealing them (gets pretty boring).
- Opening a lot of containers in this game is a waste of time but is necessary (without mods) to have items to use/sell.
- Talk to a bunch of npcs.
- When you kill something, it doesnt come back (without mods). After you kill mobs in an area once, you basically cannot play with the combat system as there is nothing to fight.
- The respawning mobs in the mod also make originally friendly npcs not do anything while you kill them over and over and over for items and experience. They also respawn as generic npcs with no functionality other than dying from you breaking your weapon on them over and over.
- Leveling is slow and very bland (damage and defense bonuses seem to be the strong point over getting new skills to improve strategy and synergy).
- Seemingly random instant death events if you go to free explore. The only purpose of which is to make you restart the game at the last point you saved and anger you (mine fields, more mine fields, mine field in that grave you're digging, mob that's 7 levels higher than you in that grave that kills your guys in 1 hit, suicidal bomber skeleton in that grave you're digging).
The game is really good. But the translation into French seems mecanistic to me and completely dries the natural poetry of the artworks and in fact the natural poetry of French Language....

One of the most fun shooter games out there. I may only have a little bit of hours into the game, but on the PS2? Psh, only game I played!
It's fairly balanced, has plenty of different and unique planets to fight on, and it has lasers! Sadly, no cats though...
You can fight as the Galactic Empire, Rebel Alliance, Confederacy of Independant Systems (C.I.S) or the Galactic Republic. Each team is composed of 7 classes: Infantry, Rocket, Sniper, Engineer, and 2 specials. Each faction has about 3 or 4 heros available, with the likes of Yoda, Darth Vader, Anakin Skywalker, and more. Mods can also add to this list.
The game has 16 different land battle maps, and 5 different layouts for space battles. The modes include Instant Action (Jump straight into a battle), Campaign (Fight through the later years of the Clone Wars, and partway through the Galactic Civil War in a set of objectives), and Galactic Conquest (Battle against the opposing faction in a full on war for control of the galaxy).
If you get bored with the content of the game, you can find mods to add plenty of content to the game. They're easy to install, and can truly add the bang to your buck. If you want some starters, the Ultimate Conversion Pack is a great start. I also have a few guides favorited on my profile that have plenty of new maps for you to try.

Do you like shooting stuff? You do? Good, because Gunnheim is a no-frills twin-stick shooter that dispenses with everything that doesn't involve blowing things to smithereens. Forget long tutorials, meandering stories and character setups, you'll be dropped straight into the action.
A hub splits the game into 4 zones, each containing 7 short levels (played in random order) + a final boss area. The goal is to shoot your way through to the finish line and defeat the game's 4 bosses blocking your way to the final encounter. Progress mid-zone is not saved, which I didn't mind at all because the gameplay is a lot of fun once you get the hang of it.
Zone 1 is quite the standard affair but things get a lot more interesting after that, not only in terms of environments but in the enemies and the way that they attack and what's required of you to complete the levels. Difficulty is not selectable and the challenge is fairly standard. I had quite a bit of trouble geting past "Are We Lost?" the first time around, but afterwards I finished the game in 1 sitting without too much trouble, after getting the knack of dodging (and not falling into holes). The other thing you may need a few minutes to familiarize yourself with is the aiming. Your character will first turn to face the direction you push the right stick to instead of instantly shooting in that line.
Gunnheim mixes cartoony graphics with gorey action into a beautiful blend of pure carnage. For a family-friendly experience, you can turn the blood off. Environments and enemies are fairly low in detail but this contrasts with surprisingly nice light and shadow effects. Blue lasers rebounding everywhere while campfires cast light and shadow onto the rocks is a pretty cool sight to behold!
Speaking of the weapons, this is my favourite element of Gunnheim. At almost 4 hours in I was still finding new weapons from the random drops. Miniguns, grenade launchers, laser cannons, acid shotguns (!!!) and the others are a real joy to wield and when I picked up what I can only describe as a
BFG, my jaw dropped when I pulled that trigger. That was an A+ moment :)
2 characters are unlocked from the beginning with 2 more as unlockables. I didn't like the male character's default weapon because it slows your movement when you fire, making it harder to dodge bullets. I learned to love the shotgun-packing female character pretty quickly and found her first aid skill to be indespensible in single-player.
I haven't tried the co-op mode, but I can only imagine it would amplify the fun. Most people should find a good deal of replayability here with the addiont of Hardcore and online/local co-op modes.
If you're looking for a straight-to-the-point twin-stick shooter thats fun to play and has some nice surprises in store, I highly recommend you give Gunnheim a try.

I have just spent several hours with Boid,  a simplistic 2D RTS that has you take control of several amoeba like organisms in underwater cavernous environments and pits you against an equal foe located on the other side of the map. Brought to us by indie developer tinyBuild Games, also known for the satrical "No Time To Explain".
The idea is simple, take over all control points on the map before your opponent can. Control points are broken into two basic categories,  spawn points that slowly spawn new troops up to a maximum of five at a time, and evolution points which allow you to morph your creatures into various upgraded forms, like a strong crab like creature, a long range laser canon, and speedy scouts among other variations.  You are tasked with controlling your flow of new units while strategically choosing which path to take and which upgrades to use and balance everything accordingly. All actions are controlled by a simple click of the mouse, and a side panel gives you a brief summary of units available, and selected, and you can use waypoints to help automate some of your troops to specific defense points or upgrades to capture.
Both offline and online modes are already included in the most recent build. The offline version features a fairly good A.I. which can challenge new comers to the game and is a good way of getting acquainted with most of the unit types, and general gameplay. Multiplayer of course is where a game like this shines, as adapting to a human player's differing strategies and changes of pace are where the real challenge and fun is. With the recent addition of leagues, and ranked play, you can easily lose hours to Boid.
Graphically Boid's 2D graphics are simple, yet colourful and make it easy to identify unit types by their shape, as well as identify enemies. Winning and losing spawn points is shown graphically by quick flashes of light on the screen to give you a quick clue that you may need to investigate elsewhere. The submerged aquatic setting is full of life, and the lighting effects give great depth on what is otherwise a flat world.
Available now on the Steam Early Access program at a measly $3.29 CAD, Boid is a steal for anyone looking for an easy to pick up, but competitive RTS. One that is being well supported by the developer with regular updates and improvements.

This is the makings of a cult classic but there's some things holding it back. Its good fun with a friend and a couple of controllers.
Gunnheim plays a little different than you would expect, basically you have a primary weapon that is generally not good enough to really beat things down with. It'll get you by but you need the special weapon drops. Those special weapon drops tend to have very low ammo so it adds a surprisingly strategic element to the game when you have to decide when is the best time to pull the trigger - because getting it wrong probably means death.
Enemies are distinctly different and you have to deal with them all a little bit differently which adds a lot to the strategy element. Feedback is pretty good too, response from the gameplay is very readable. The 'arcade'-y feel and old school menu art is awesome.
It's super simple yet the skill factor really makes it enjoyable. Most of the significant bugs seems nonexistant but there is plenty of room for polish. Almost every part of the game could use another iteration pass. Animations, hitboxes, AI behavior, level design, etc all need some more attention. A few levels are almost completely pointless because you can just run straight through them with basically no danger. Don't expect Gauntlet style quality level design.
Overall I would say 4/5 for fun and its potential to scale up to something way more awesome pretty quick. Losing points for lack of polish in some areas.

Rating this game was tough. There are lots of great things about it, but I'm not sure if it is worth your time right now. Maybe in the future, it will get a boot kick.
BOID is a simplistic, yet still competitive RTS. It's simplicity allows the gameplay to be super fast paced, and allows even small decisions to make huge impacts in the game. It's chellenging, as there is no one path to victory. Pretty much every unit has some strength or weakness. You can use these to your advantage, or to your opponent's disadvantage; your choice.
Pros:
-Simple enough for anyone to pick up and play in a few short minutes.
-Diverse enough to allow complicated stategies for more experienced RTS players.
-Beautiful art.
-Custom map creator.
-New content every here and there.
Cons:
-Small, and very inactive community. It is near impossible to find someone to play with.
-Doesn't teach the player anything more than basic controls.
-Kinda glitchy (Especially map creator).
-Low redeeming value, unless you find friends to play with and experiment with strategies.
A usually short, but potentially long game with exceptional replay value.

This was one of the most amazing games that I have ever played, and I would definitely reccomend it to anyone who is a fan of this genre. **Note: I have seen some other reviews mentioning a save glitch that deletes their progress, and I too experienced this glitch; I will put my solution to this problem below the rest of the review so you do not have to lose hours of gameplay as I did.
*The game has wonderful pacing, with a slow acceleration, to where it never really feels slow, or boring
*The story is quite charming, and told in a way which makes it ever better: I doubt I will ever forget the plight of the Child of Light
*The world is absolutely beautiful, with a hand-painted aesthetic, and wonderful characters
*The soundtrack is enchanting, and complements the story immensely, not to mention being more than good enough to stand alone
*So much more that cannot be put into words
The only problem I have with this game is that it requires Uplay to run, and I probably lost a good 8+ hours to a save glitch (solution below). But overall, the game itself is fantastic, and I give it a 10/10.
**To solve the save glitch problem (which seems to be caused by Uplay failing to save your progress to the cloud, and then when it next starts up, and does its routine save synchronization, prioritizing the cloud over your local files, thus deleting the progress it failed to save), I ended up going into Uplay's settings (the gear in the upper right hand corner), and under General, I unchecked 'Enable cloud save synchronization...', and as well, under Network, I checked 'Always start Uplay in offline mode.' Then, as an extra fail-safe, I used task manager to end all of Uplay's processes (GameLauncher, Uplay.exe, and WebCore) after starting the game each time, effectively eliminating all chance of Uplay accessing the cloud, and deleting my local files. Additionally, I always waited for the auto-save symbol to completely fade before exiting the game, and always exited directly to Windows. These last two may be unnecessary, but I had already lost hours to the glitch, so I was taking no chances. This worked very well for me, and I hope it works for others.

I have only completed 2 other visual novels, one very short(less than 10 minutes reading) and one a more classic comedy ecchi visual novel. So take that in consideration when reading my review :)
- If you like visual novels and a LOT of reading (depending on which first route, one clear can take 6-8 hours maybe)
- If you don't mind a visual novel which has different stylearts. One styleart for backgrounds, one for for people in the scenes and one for "epic scenes".
- If you don´t mind something soviet related (not that there is any propaganda or anything, the soviet pioneere camp aspect could have been shifted with nearly any other kind of normal summercamp)
- If you don't mind quite a challenge to get all the endings (or don't mind using a guide to get some of the hard once)
- The game is without any doubt so well made, damn beautiful backgrounds! so many details, so many hidden things, but mostly the technical part is awesome! They have made it quite easy to skip text while you don't have to be afraid of missing any new text, new scenes (unless you set it in options to skip all) this makes so much easier to get all the endings without getting tired. Also so many saveslots, you can scroll back if you want to reread something or had pick the wrong choice, and there is a lovely gallery for collection of pictures, background and music for you to collect ingame.
- The story seems very like a classic harem cliché story but luckily it isn't! it is much more than that :) Much unknowness to explore(you have to clear all the endings to be able to understand the story)! And I did like the two endings which you might call the true endings (??? ending and haram ending. Those two wrap it all up!)
- Even though there is some ecchi/hentai in it, if you patch the game. The ecchi/hentai part doesn't overrule or ruin the story, it only adds a smaller aspect to the story.
- SO MANY CHOICES! So many endings!!!!! I can´t praise this highly enough!
- Very lovely music :3
- Lots of hidden of somewhat metatext to other endings, so pay attention! you might slip some quite good details. :P
-  d´uh, it is free!!
- some of the "epic scens" are quite badly drawn, I personally don't mind the different style from the normal scenes, but a few of them weren´t good at all!
- One does not simply get all the endings unless using very much time or help from guides (I myself got tired of keep trying to get some endings which I could not figure out, but others might find it good, a challenge indeed! :) )
- Some characters especielly Electronik, Olga Dmitrievna and Zhenya wasn't that well developed and I would have loved an ending for these characters! :D
- For me I could feel which of the characters the developers liked the most, so some characters weren´t that developed even some of the main girls :/
- yeah.... the main character, which you play, can sometimes be quite annoying as hell! and I understand why some people hate him and say that he is bland and such. But the main character just suffers from twillight syndrome, Bella who is a character without really any character at all so it is easier for anyone(mostly twillight fangirls) to put themselves in her place. Quite luckily the main character in this game is not as bland as her! still a lot of character, thoughts and such (some might be unlogical and annoying. :P ) He is a whiner, get over it! make him happy, that is your purpose of playing this game :P get him out of his misery
- Maybe I just have seen too many animes
but they gave me the tools to already almost correctly guess the plot from the very beginning
- Even though there is a lot to the story, it stills have a problem like all other dating visual novels.. The girls falls in love with main character with nearly no reason for doing so! Some are understandable, some aren't
This visual novel is the best one I have tried so far :) very interesting, I really loved to get to know the whole story and know every secret in the game. On the other hand it wasn't perfect at all! but good enough for me to keep on playing and enjoying it!! ^^

in an unique eerie way. It`s like you are wandering through the nightmares of your child self. Thus the
, if not scary when you are older than 5, is quite intense an sucks you in this world whit its bizarre creatures.
and the bad feeling of being followed, hunted or somehow in danger accompany you all the time. You learn about this world and your own story step by step, just by observing it and its countless details. There is no spoken or written narration at all. These things are the big plus of this game. The game
, which isn`t a bad thing for this game and what it wants to achieve. But in it`s mechanical core Little Nightmares is just a simple platformer/puzzle game.
At the same time the puzzles are my main point of critique. Often you just solve them by
and in addition under time pressure because you are hunted by something. Too many times you don`t have a chance to solve the puzzle the first time you encounter them, but also have only a few seconds to observe the scene and thus may die several times until you get it. Recently replayed The Banner Saga in order to have everything fresh in my mind when starting #2, and I have to say that I appreciated it nearly as much the second time through as I did the first. The plot wasn't as emotionally stunning since I knew what was going to happen, but the beautiful animations and music still helped draw out feelings for the characters. Overall the gameplay, graphics, and music combine to create a world so immersively desperate you can't help but be drawn in.
The gameplay is a mix of three systems: a choose your own adventure style story where your choices can definitely impact the future story and other characters, a caravan management system where you try to balance your need for food, fighters, and heroes, and (the majority of the gameplay) a turn based tactical/strategy RPG that contains serious quirks that set it apart from other SRPGs. You use one currency to both level up heroes and purchase new items for them to use as well as buy supplies for your caravan, and the choices you make can effect your caravan management and tactical fighting, so all of the systems twine nicely together. That said, the caravan management feels like the biggest miss of the three--very small seeming decisions can impact your caravan much more than how you spend your resources.
Several reviews are critical of the tactical fighting aspect and while they bring up some valid points overall I found the fighting to be enjoyable throughout all of two playthroughs. The main criticism I've seen is that the enemy types lack variety which leads to similar strategies working consistently. Overall I agree and wish that there were more different enemies or terrains to force you to mixup your tactics more. That said I found the fights overall engaging throughout, and found the normal difficulty appropriately hard--not a cakewalk by any means but also not impossible.
I hope that the future releases help expand the tactical options in fights and build the caravan management into a more robust system that feels more impactful on gameplay. I definitely recommend this game to any strategy rpg fans, fans of norse folklore, or fans of good storytelling games. I definitely felt that the amount of time and enjoyment I've got for the money I spent at full price to be well worth it. I'm off to try the second game.

The intro game starts off with the BOSS of saints row going after Cyrus the leader of stag. You'll kill him but you won't be able to stop him from launching a nuke at washington. As the crew makes it to the White Crib, an alien invasion hits the boss and captures everyone. Then they are proceeded to be put into a simulator where the game begins and all hell breaks loose.
The gameplay is not just like any other third person shooter in the series but since the game takes place in a simulation all hell breaks loose. You will not only run around in this openworld sandbox game but you'll gain superhuman abilities to fight the aliens. There are so many new variety of weapons to choose from. Aside from that there are scattered quests and objectives you can do to level up yourself. You can do alot of customization on your character and steal and ride cars but lets face it. Cars are useless when you have power.
The game didn't revolutionize anything in the openworld sandbox genre nor did it level the game's graphic by updating the engine. Cars are useless in the beginning and some of the quests sets could be done better. The outrageous badly written story that is funny, really well picked music, and the hilarious jokes involved in this game makes up for it. The game is downright fun and the weapons are fun as well. With the sale and all dlcs this is a must have title if you want to kill some time with shennenigans

At first, I damn near hated this game.  That's because I spent the first few hours thinking that permadeath was a thing in this game, and the game did absolutely nothing to tell me otherwise.  In an early battle, a certain character can die and be dead forever.  In fact, I've since learned that that character dies at that point in the story regardless.  However, as the game didn't explain this well, I assumed that, like Fire Emblem, all of my characters were mortal and, thus, anyone who fell in battle was not coming back.  This led to a lot of frustrated reloads when a battle didn't go perfectly and a character went down.
Of course, I then learned that that was not the case, and that characters were merely knocked out if they fell in battle.  This completely changed the game for me, as it went from incredibly frustrating to a lot of fun when I wasn't constantly concerned about my oft-used characters being dead forever.
With that knowledge, combat is quite enjoyable.  I wouldn't say it's incredibly strategic, and I think the abilities of a lot of characters aren't nearly as useful as simple attacks 90% of the time with only a few exceptions, but it is fun.  The only downside is that it's quite easy to game.  Since character strength is based on health and you and the enemy team take turns using a character, it's typically more convenient to take an enemy down to one or two strength and leave them alive rather than kill them outright, as a weak enemy who can only deal out a few hit points will then waste a valuable enemy turn that could have gone to a stronger foe.  The game becomes somewhat easy most of the time utilizing such a strategy.  You also need to focus on leveling up all of your characters, and so getting enemies down to one health and then letting your lower-level characters pick them off seems to be the smartest way to go about it.
There's also not much variety in the combat.  You basically fight the same four enemy types with varying strength and armor over and over again throughout the game, with a fifth thrown in for a couple of battles, along with several against enemies with the same class types as your own squad.
The story in the game is solid.  I liked the characters and the overall plot is interesting, although as the first of a trilogy you obviously can't expect it all to be wrapped up here.  This game sets the stage for the two acts to follow, and does a fairly good job of it.  I thought the ending was a little too abrubt.  It just kind of ends a minute after the final battle.  I didn't expect a full resolution, obviously, but a bit more meat after that fight would have been nice.
The main downside to the game is that character deaths can often feel arbitrary.  You never really know when a dialogue choice will mean the permanent death of a character, and that's more than a little annoying.  Nor, as others have said, do you know when you can pick just one dialogue choice most of the time.  This leads to some frustration, and it's all on the game's design.  I get the realism angle, as sometimes in life choices have unintended consequences, but it all feels so arbitrary here, and I certainly think it could have been handled better.
All in all, though, I would definitely recommend the game.  The visuals are fantastic, the combat is enjoyable, and the story is solid.  It's not a perfect game by any means (and I've read that the second game addresses a lot of the problems), but it's worth a play through if you like this style of turn-based RPG.

My first MMORPG since runescape way back when and I gotta say I've never been more addicted and intregued by a game (that isn't monster hunter). At first the experiance was overwhelming: so much information and stats and whatnot, with a HUGE world and a bare bones tutorial, it was pretty disorrientating. However, following the main quests set by the black spirit, and the plethora of in game video tutorials and the help wiki, I was able to grasp the basics after a few hours.
I then set out online to research as much as I could: my chosen class, gear, skills, money, mechanics, pvp. It was then where the game really pulled me in. BDO is one huge oyster, to be played and enjoyed at your pace, in your own way. 100 hours in and I can vouch for the immersion this game boasts.
There's simply too much to describe for a game priced less than 10 quid.
Now for the "pay-to-win aspects" of the game. Not really.
There is a sort of hidden monthly subscription you can buy that makes the game a whole lot less frustraiting and has significant benfits such as more inventory weight (a huge issue you will come across), getting more money from market place sales, experiance boosts and a few other asthetic bonuses. There's also many other items you can buy that make certian aspects of the game more conveinient, most significantly pets which auto pick up loot and have special effects.
All the above things can be bought with in game money, including the "subscription" item, IF those items are on sale. Which brings me to the aspect of selling pearl store items (thing you actually pay for). You are limited to the amount of pearl store items you can sell, and the return on these items is nowhere near enough to make selling them viable. So injecting a whole bunch of money into the game will yeild no real advantage over any other non-paying player, other than certain convieniances. Although that subscription item really is worth having imo.
Overall I'm very happy with this game and will be playing for 100s of hours in the future.

A fun JRPG with humor and charm.
Reminded me of Phantasy Star Online crossed with a Final Fantasy combat system. You can expect around 20+ hours of game play time.
- Self-aware writing. The game will take shots at itself, game tropes, and it's audience.
- Entertaining story with flanking bonuses for attack placement.
- Fluid graphics. 1080p @ 60fps. Art is very nice.
- Plan system makes gameplay more interesting. Basically you can "craft" dungeons from monster loot and upgrade them to change random pickups & add more powerful foes. Limited in-game "memory" will require some level of planning, but will require a second playthough for a completionist.
- Character appearance customizations. Some items are for vanity and for CPU modes, change stats and appearance.
- Arena content will provide some long-lasting gameplay.
- Some mechanics are not explained clearly or are not explained at the start. The game offers the Lily partner system, which allows non-active party members to tag in/out and provide assist attacks. However, there is no visible meter to gauge the progress of of character partner development. Other mechanics exist at the start but you "unlock" them as the story progresses. Great for NG+ gameplay, but a bit confusing for new players.
- Dungeons and monsters don't appear to have specific levels, so if you are used to "you must be between level X and Y to do this dungeon", then you'll probably want to spend more time grinding.
- I'm not one for gratuitous fan-service.
- Some boss mob fights devolve into spamming EXE/ultimate moves due to high HP regen.
- Combat movement controls can be a bit spotty. Have minor difficulty at times lining up attacks within attack space when there are several monsters in close proximity. Basically requires me to move around and re-adjust camera.
- Found out there can be some resolution issues for non-16:9 monitors, but can be alleviated with mods. In addition, the game will not operate with Nvidia Shadowplay by default due to the game mis-labelling it's fullscreen mode as "borderless window" instead of true fullscreen. You'll either need to enable desktop capture or use Steam streaming mode instead.

XCOM is a really fun game. I remember hearing about the older version, but never got around to trying it, so I came into XCOM pretty fresh. That survivor, the Argentinian Heavy, Jesus Pena, became my first Colonel, my first Psi, and an all-around badass.
Anyway, the game is a lot of fun. It rewards smarter, more cautious tactics, rather than rushing blindly forward, but it also rewards the calculated rush, as well. The skill in the game comes from learning when to abandon caution, and just go all-in.

When I looked at the store-page for Gunnheim, I assumed that it would be easy to figure out. I mean, this is a twin-stick shooter right? You're a huge viking with a big gun. You run through each level, shoot all the bad guys, and revel in the blood, guts, and glory. I was looking forward to a lot of dumb action, but it turns out that I got more than I bargained for. I hate using words like "promising" to describe Early Access titles, but there is some merit to this upcoming game.
Apparently there's a story that sets everything up, but I never pay attention to that nonsense. Let's just skip ahead to the basics; there are four areas, each area consists of five levels and a boss-fight. After completing the four areas you fight Odin. Each level tends to have a common goal: find the exit. It's up to you and maybe some friends to avoid traps, get past the demonic armies, and do whatever it takes to reach the next level. In many ways, shooting everything that moves isn't the key to surviving Gunnheim.
Often, when we play twin-stick shooters, they're designed around arenas. Going as far back as the days of Robotron and Smash TV, you would go into a room, enemies would fill the screen, and you had to destroy them all. It's a simple concept. However, arena shooters are also very compelling due to the on-screen chaos and the depth that comes from mastering the controls & weapons. Typically, these games are controlled with two sticks, one to move, and one to fire. Gunnheim uses the twin-stick method, but you have to press the right-trigger to fire.
Hold up a second, you have to press a button to fire? At first I thought this was an oversight by the developer, but it is in fact a very concious decision. Firing a gun in this game is something you have to think about. Unlike.. say..
, missing a shot probably isn't going to get you killed, but there are consequences . Whether these consequences are good or bad depends on the situation. Gunnheim is all about pacing, and most kills are actually a waste of time. Whenever you fire, the recoil pushes you backwards slightly. With some weapons the effect is much larger. If you're getting pushed back, you're not moving forward. With every shot you sacrifice a centimer of progress, and they can add up. So when you point your gun at an enemy, your first thought might actually be "Do I need to kill it?" The monsters in this game certainly aren't harmless, their numbers are high, and they'll pursue you to Ragnarok and back. But in most cases, you don't need to kill them.
Out-maneuvering adversity is one of the more important elements of this game. Every playable character has an invincible dash move. This takes time to recharge, but it's good for escaping bad situations, moving quickly, or even crossing pits. You can even use the gun's recoil to give your walking speed a little boost. Although there are numerous weapons, they have very limited ammo, and are random drops. You have to play with the mind-set that you won't get much in the way of assistance. Some levels even feature infinitely-spawning enemies to hammer this point home. You can kill a lot of creatures, but if you're not getting any closer to the exit, it's time to figure out a new strategy.
Going solo is fine in of itself, but this is game that deserves to be played with others. The level of difficulty scales with the number of players, and it can become more difficult than playing alone. Due to the larger number of enemies, you and your friends could become overwhelmed. This is one of those rare cases where having a second gun actually makes things more difficult, because you can't hope to eradicate everything. So again, the best strategy is to know when to shoot, and always focus on making it to the exit. If this means three players have to sacrifice themselves, just so the last person can escape, then that's exactly what it means. While players can be revived quickly and easily, they recover with pixel-health, and the monsters certainly aren't taking a breather. I ran into a situation where a hunter repeatedly shot my partner whenever I revived him. That jerk was camping his corpse! That's totally unfair! But seriously, there's a lot of decision-making that goes into every level of this game. You always have to consider what's best for the team, even if it means leaving them to die.
In terms of content, Gunnheim is currently on the lean side. As of this writing, there are four playable characters, all with their own weapons & special abilities. However, two of them have to be unlocked by completing the game on the normal and hardcore settings. The levels are very short, although there are a couple of truly rough ones that took me close to an hour. Interestingly enough, the levels are randomized for each area, so there's a possibility that more could be added. Another reason why multiplayer is preferable is because the game becomes more dynamic, depending on the number of players and what characters they use. One of the unlockables uses a sniper rifle, which grants them the best range in the game. It's up to the other players to keep an eye on the sniper and pick off nearby enemies. There are numerous other situations that can crop up, and the temporary weapon-drops can change how things play out as well. So while there isn't a lot of content, there's a good amount of replay-value.
Gunnheim is shaping up to be a very solid action game. Admittedly, I was surprised by the design-decisions it employs. Judgng by the art and talk about guns and gore, I expected a straight-up blastathon, not a game where I have to consider possibilities, and put an emphasis on not killing everything in sight. These unique qualities just might help it stand out in the crowd. So if you're looking for something different, consider keeping an eye out for this one.

What is there not to love about vikings, giant guns, and indiscriminate slaughter and gore? Gunnheim brings all that in oodles and then throws in a hand grenade of co-op action. Gunnheim takes cues from other games in this crowded genre, from Gauntlet, to FORCED. You play across many different levels and environments, using power ups, innate powers and firing non-stop at the hordes of angry enemies trying to chew your face off. After completing so many levels you are greeted by a big nasty boss who more then likely is going to stomp you into dust. While Gunnheim can be enjoyed by itself as a single-player game, it shines most when you take advantage of the up to 4 player Co-op. The game scales its difficulty and challenge based on the number of players, adding even more viking chaos and explosions. The game does have polish for an Early Access title, the graphics, controls, and music are all well done. However,  there is still plenty of work to be done here. Balancing, repeating content, and more gameplay elements are all things that need to be worked on before final release.  It's a fun game and very enjoyable with your friends, just the single-player mode needs a bit more work in my opinion. Gunnheim is an excellent top-down twin stick shooter.  I love these type of games and I haven't played a good one until Gunnheim came along, I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys games like this.
The gameplay is what you expect from a twin stick shooter, but the things that separate this game from other similar ones are what make it unique.  First off is the graphics, just as the dev's listed, it is not pixelated and that to me is very refreshing.  Yes pixels aren't bad, but can get tiring, with Gunnheim however the graphics are very charming, there is a lot of warmth when you play through the various levels.  The other thing is the setting of the game, I don't know why, but the idea of vikings using guns is hilarious and refreshing.  You would never think of a viking wielding a gun, but somehow the dev's made it work.
The temporary weapon drops add some flavor to the gameplay as you progress through the levels.  That way you're not using the same default gun throughout the whole game.  There are a variety of weapon drops such as plasma rifles, plasma cannons, cannons, buzzsaw shooters, grenade launchers, and the all mighty tactical nuke.  And yes all of these drops are pretty strong, but they don't last forever, there is limited use to them so that you don't blaze through the game with ease.
Overall the game is very playable.  It is a solid top-down twin stick shooter.  Do know that is is still in early access, there are only two playable characters so far and a handful of levels, but the dev's are continually adding and improving the game.  As of now you can beat the game from 45 min - 1 hour, but really though this game is so fun you're gonna keep playing more :D
The dev's are very interactive with the players in the forums.  They are open to all suggestions and feedback.  I have never met any dev's as nice as these :)
So I am positive that the amount of gameplay hours will definitely increase.
I do hope this review helps, I know it is lengthy, but this game deserves it.

I really loved this game.  The art and sound design are amazing.  The whole game is styled like a children's storybook and it works really well.  But not only is it beautiful (seriously this is one of the best looking games I've ever played), it is really well made.  The level design is amazing and the battle system is really good.  I actually dismissed the battle system at first, thinking it was just super simplistic turn based game play, but there is actually a lot of depth and complexity.  Being able to manipulate the turn order was really important, very fun and required a lot of skill.
I do have a few little quibbles.  First of all, the rhymes.  While it is a cute idea, I found a distressing number of the rhymes to be kind of weak.  Thankfully most of the game isn't voice acted (there is a narrator occasionally, but that's it), so you can sort of ignore this.
I also didn't like the fact that you can only use two characters at once during combat.  You can get eight playable characters (nine with downloadable content) with a really diverse set of skills and limiting us to only using two at once is sort of frustrating and basically meant I never used most of the characters except occasionally in boss fights.  This is especially perplexing as there can be three enemies on the field at once.
That being said, this is still an amazing game.  Although obviously it is not a game for everyone.  Are you a gamer that needs everything grim and dark and shooty?  This is not the game for you.  But if you can get in touch with your inner child (or inner fairy princess) then you should really get this game.

Not only are your options limited (there is iron, steel, silver, and tenebrium ore) but what you can make from those options is highly limited.  Certain items which should go together don't. The only use blacksmithing has is to improve the damage of weapons or defense points for armor.  The amount this goes up is neglible.
The NPCs are even worse than what could be found in games such as Neverwinter (yes, that old one which I really felt immersed in) and their reactions to characters are extremely limited to text dialogue.  I never felt immersed in the world of Divinity Original Sin.
As for their claim that you can react and destroy any items in some kind of special "physics engine," the items are limited too.  I got so tired of seeing the same textures and models of crates and barrels and buildings that every place felt the same.  They say there are puzzles to figure out, but even these are usually only solvable if you happen to chance across an item from another quest. My favorite moment was about halfway through a game, out matched by an enemy ship. Captain Picard was the last surviving crew member, trying to power up the warp drive. The sensors go out, leaving me blind to all movement on the ship. Suddenly the Intruder alert starts going off, so I make my way to the door control room to reinforce the doors. Crawl is unlike many co-op/multiplayer games I have played in the past.
I have been setting up weekly gaming nights for the last few years, and sadly, there aren't many multiplayer games that stay installed on my PC. Most dwindle and become obsolete after a few sessions. But not Crawl.
The game is very simple and approachable. Few buttons are used, and there is really no tutorial needed.
At the very beginning, you choose a deity and watch your pixelated characters drift into madness as you take control and kill your 1 - 3 friends before they murder you. If you survive the slaughter you continue deeper into the dungeon seeking loot, gold, and weapons.
But if one of your unhinged friends murder you at the outset, you now take the form or a floating spirit that is unable to physically attack the living friend. But it does not keep you from harming them in other ways. You are able to accumulate orbs that appear on the screen and possess things in the environment in an attempt to harm and eventually kill the living. Collect enough orbs and you can spawn a small, weak blob that you can possess and attack with. Or, just spawn multiple blobs and watch the chaos from the side lines hoping for the best.
Eventually, the hero will enter a room with inverted pentagrams chiseled into the floor, there you can summon a stronger monster that corresponds with your chosen deity.
As you and your friends proceed deeper into the dungeon, back-stabbing and killing each other all of the way, you gain stronger weapons and monsters. Becoming more efficient, eventually choosing to enter a boss room and face off against your undead friends who possess a pixelated horror that can be quite challenging. Succeed, and you are crowned the winner of Crawl. But lose, and allow your friends to try the boss fight.
The soundtrack fits the game perfectly. It works with the graphic scheme and will keep your heart rate elevated as you play.
The graphics are nostalgic and just plain fun. But if AAA games with next gen graphics are more your speed, you probably won't enjoy this one. It is pretty old-school.
The combat is tight and responsive. Attacks, evades, and movement all act exactly as you would expect with Keyboards, controllers. I have tested Playstation, XBox 1, and USB SNES controllers and it was a blast with all of them.
There really isn't much of a story. Your characters go insane in a monster infested dungeon, they kill all of their companions, and attempt to best the horrors waiting deep inside.

Always wait until a game is on sale.  This should be a universal rule on Steam.  I broke that rule.  I got impatient and bought it for about $20.  Less than one week later it's now on sale for about $10, and for what I paid I could have gotten the Game of the Century Edition.  I was a fool, but lesson learned.
Saints Row IV takes the Grand Theft Auto formula and feeds it pure mescaline.  Within a few hours I was running around like the Flash and leaping tall buildings in a single bound.  While the game cannot hold a candle to the half billion dollar production values of titles like GTA IV or V, it makes up for that with excellent character customization, completely over the top insanity, and a focus on freedom and fun.
The only thing I find a little off is how the superpowers you acquire in the game render the use of vehicles pretty much useless.  Why steal a car when you can sprint, jump, and glide to your destination even faster?  It seems like all too quickly I felt like Neo from the Matrix, and even Neo had to work his way up to being the One.
But damn does being The One make you feel like a badass.  I was clearing entire legions of crazy aliens with my bare hands.  The game makes you feel powerful, unstoppable even.  It's not even fair how crazy strong you are allowed to be.  Cheat codes in lesser games don't give you the kind of power this game gives you by default.
Yes, I would absolutley recommend this game.  Even though I own a copy of GTA V, the game that this one tends to get compared to, I keep coming back to Saints Row IV.  Get it, but wait for a sale first, unless you are impatient like me.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown, is a great, strategic, fun, time consuming  and at times, frustrating game.

If steam allowed neutral reviews I would probably use that rating.
- The combat is some of the best in any MMORPG or even RPG that I have ever played. It's like if you mixed a regular MMO with street fighter. It's really cool.
- Graphics are very good for an MMO, except I experience some grainy textures and changing settings like anti-aliasing in the game and in my control panel doesn't seem to help.
- The convenience items are very necessary for this game in my opinion. If you don't have the monthly value pack the game turns into a chore for the majority of the time and pets are essential. You are constantly carrying too much weight and there's a button that conveniently shows up on your screen that takes you right to the cash shop where you can purchase a larger weight limit. This button should also let the player know the fastest way to expand it via in-game methods as well. Just seems a bit like a cash grab.
- The pay to win comparisons are definitely valid. Many people will purchase cash shop items like outfits and they will sell them on the in-game marketplace, which they will then use to get silver and purchase weapons and armor. So not only are there essential things you need to make the game enjoyable, but many people have a big advantage when they use real world money to get in-game currency and items.
- There isn't much group content like dungeons and stuff for you to enjoy with friends.
- There is a horrible grind. Everything is grinding in this game. I don't mind grinding, but it gets to the point where you are just running around one shotting everything for days on end. Literally just running in a 50-yard loop. There are no mechanics for bosses to figure out with your friends or anything like that.
- I like how you can apply costumes to different types of armor. You and your friend can have the same piece of armor, but it will look completely different. At the same time, the default armor design is really bad unless you buy outfits. The outfits are pretty expensive as well.
- The PVP is really cool, but unfortunately, you'll just get completely destroyed by someone two levels above you. Skills and gear will matter if you happen to match up with someone the same level, but if they are just a bit above you then you are done for. I understand that you should reward the player that invests time, but it's a little much IMO.
- The game has a lot of RNG involved.
- The classes are designed well. There should be something for almost everyone, except for people who usually play healers in MMOs. You won't find that here since there aren't really any dungeons and stuff.
- There is absolutely no direct trading.
- You can gain money when AFK. You can fish and perform other similar actions. I find this a bit strange. I don't really have an opinion on it though...
- There is this progression toward what they call "awakening" at the back end of the level cap. You get a nice new weapon and updates for your skill tree. Some of the classes are completely changed during awakening and it's not for the best. You play one style for 56 levels and then all of a sudden it changes completely... Some ranged characters will become melee characters etc..

FIRST IMPRESSION:
So I have never played this game before. I bought it on sale for 5.99 and I figured that chances are the price will only go up, and that I have heared that the game is rather fun.
The game is fun. I have only scratched the surface, but so far I am enjoying it enough. However, the most important part that I want to write about is that the game is very overwelming at first. At the time of writing I am about 5.5 hours into the game. So far I am not really sure how to use my abilities, and what they do exactly. The information is there, I just have not looked it up within the game yet. The problem is, is that I have never had to look up just the basics of my skills when I first recieved them before. Usually I would get a general idea and if I needed more info, I would just read the text. How it is now for me is I am not really sure what skills I have and don't. Much of this could be solved by spending a few minutes reading everything and going through my skill screen. But in all of the games I have played before, I have not really had to do this. This could be either a UI problem, too much going on on the screen (i.e. text, video, and other flashing notifications), or my own lack of attention. Personally, I believe it is a little of all three.
My next problem is that the game is a little rough around the edges. Starting the game, the UI is jumbled with far too much information, there is a notification bar in the top center of the screen that says literally whatever is happeneing in the world. A guild is attacking another guild. Some guild accomplished this or that. Someone bought something on the marketplace. Someone listed something on the marketplace. What happens is that while you are playing, the top center of your screen is constantly blocked by these notifications. They have nothing to do with what you are doing, and it just makes the game very cluttered. You can turn these off in the options, but it should be turned off at the start imo.
Another small problem is the grammar in the game. There are many little mistakes that I have noticed that slightly irritated me. These are very small problems, but noticable if you skim the text like I do. Also, the voice acting is very mediocre imo.
With all of these problems, I will still reccommend the game however. I have already played almost an hour per dollar and I can easily see myself playing much more, especially if I figure out my skills. Though my computer is a little weak, the game is still very pretty, and the characters are the best I have seen in any game. Ever. Not just MMO's.

My most vivid memory of playing XCOM will always be of my 2nd tier sniper from my Ironman campaign. I believe his name was Steve, I just recruited him and sent him to back up my main units on a crisis mission. The city was on fire and xeno monsters we eating civilians at the port. Trying to save more people, I over extended my main assault and drew way too many aliens for him to defeat. I pushed Steve out of cover in front of my assault to take the damage instead, didn't like the way he looked. But somehow, Steve, after using up all of his assault rifle ammo and then taking out his side arm, helped kill the alien squad bearing down on them. It was after that mission that he became a sniper and earned his nickname 'Hawkeye'.
Couple missions later, was wearing some hand-me down exo suite, tricked it out to a forest green color. My squad was moving in on a downed alien abductor ship my interceptors had shot down. The main unit was moving through the ship corridors in door to door combat finishing off the crew.  I had 'Hawkeye' Steve grapple up to the roof of the ship sniping aliens from a height advantage.  He had just moved to the ledge of an opening towards the middle of the ship when it happened. A giant plasma shot from an unseen enemy took him down. He was too far away from my medic to revive him, sent him to try anyway. Knew he could only last little bit longer so had my Heavies launch their rockets at the qaud-legged alien tank that had taken the shot to cover the medic, the explosion would mean I would get less resources  from the mission, but if I could save 'Hawkeye' it would be worth it...He bled out just as the medic got to him.
I moved on with the campaign, trained a new second sniper to complement the team...but will always remember Steve 'Hawkeye's' sacrifice for humanity. I don't know of another game that made me scream and curse at my tv like this one did, ever action counts, every order means weather or not a squad member dies, if the aliens come that much closer to taking over Earth. And if you play like I did and don't just reload from a old save point, it makes you live with those choices and makes them all the more memorable. An un-folding story of how you saved/didn't save the earth from the @#$*#$@! aliens, and the choices you had to make.

Haha, see, I'm a poet. I shouldn't be writing stupid reviews with my poetic style. I should write children's fairy-tales. If Ubisoft can do it with Child of Light, why can't I? I can rhyme better than Black Mother Goose. Also known as Big Mama G. It's a thing, really. What else do you think black children get read to them before bed?
Their rights.
I mean, Child of Light is a pretty good game. Beautiful, fun to play, and is pretty artsy if you consider that Ubisoft is French. I mean, since when does France know a thing about art? Their idea of art is a black and white movie about a red balloon. Psh. But me, I'm just a manifestation of art and poetry. You know?
Child of Light is Ubisoft's attempt to make a game with a soul for once. And man, they did a pretty good job. For once. It's available on pretty much every major platform. And to be completely honest, I'd recommend playing on any other besides this one. Uplay is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥. Fantastic game, but Uplay is annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥
Aside from that, Child of Light is a magical experience.
This game has NO climbing in it. You can fly, instead.
A sort of turn-based RPG featuring a time-based system, very similar to Grandia, Child of Light is trying really hard to be a fairy-tale. It's got the princess, it's got the magic, it's got the evil queen, and it has midgets with beards. The whole shebang.
Little princess Aurora goes through a magical portal to Austria, where the game apparently takes place. The magical land of Austria. A land of fantasy and wonder. Too bad Austria is only a fictional world.
In Austria, she learns that an evil queen has stolen all the light of the world. There is only darkness now. Light is the good guy. Darkness is the bad guy.
Because white is good and black is bad.
Because white means purity and goodness, and black means evil and unemployment. And gang violence.
You'll fly through the fantasy world of Austria, fighting the creatures of darkness. The world is flat and 2-D, and layered with beautiful hand-drawn environments. It's an incredibly pretty game. Those Frenchmen might not be able to win wars, but damn. They're really good at drawing.
The combat system is actually pretty complex. There's a sort of time meter that small icons representing characters will move along. They move at different speeds depending on the character's stats, and all race to hit an action point. At that point, they can choose what move to use or what action to take. However, as they move along the action meter to charge up for that action, getting attacked will interrupt their move and send them back on the time meter.
You can only have two characters out at a time, but swapping them doesn't count as an action. If you swap out your magic user for your healer, they start at the point the other character left at. However, that does then open up weaker characters like supporters to attacks.
It's basically a game of juggling, trying to interrupt your enemies and swap out allies at the right moments to control the flow of battle. Not as easy as it sounds, as certain enemies can counter interruption and other moves. You'll also have to be wary of physical/magical attacks, and different elemental attacks. And especially not as easy as it sounds because I ♥♥♥♥ing suck at juggling.
Controlling the flow of battle is the most important aspect of the game. And lucky for you, there's a slightly more direct way to manipulate it. You have a little firefly companion that can do little but shine light. But that light can slow down enemies, stun them before you run into them, and open special chests and such on the map. And during combat he can be used to influence the flow of battle quite a bit. Slowing down enemies just enough to interrupt them, or using his light to heal allies before they die. Normally he's controlled by player one, but if you're playing on Wii U he can be used by a second player with a Wii Remote Super Mario Galaxy style. A great way to get Grandma in on the action.
While the combat system itself is smooth and flows great, other areas of the battle system aren't so smooth.
Namely, the equipment system. You'll equip your characters with different colored gems called "Oculi". Why they called them Oculi, I think it was just to make something rhyme somewhere that they couldn't find a good rhyme to.
Oculi have different properties, and bestow all sorts of powers and stat boosts depending on what it is and how it's equipped. They can be fused to craft stronger ones, or special ones. Or strong special ones.
A great concept, however the execution was sloppy and clunky. Whenever I got new gems I'd loathe going to equip them. It was a long process. An ordeal.
The gems you have equipped are not present in your crafting menu. Meaning to make use of gems, you need to unequip everything from everyone, craft gems, and then reequip everything to everyone. It's just annoying and frustrating, to the point where I'd avoid crafting gems for as long as I could. Which is sad, because the system itself is actually pretty cool.
The Oculi system is but a burnt croissant on the face of France, however. It's the only real drawback in an otherwise beautiful game.
The story can be pretty simplistic, but it's supposed to be a fairy-tale. And its dialogue is incredibly corny, because everything is forced to rhyme... but again, it's supposed to be a fairy-tale. They were purposeful design choices. To make the game cheesy. You know how much the French love their cheese. It's not really that bad... but it's kinda cringey at times. Depending on your lactose tolerance, it may or may not be that bad of an issue.
But aside from being cheesy and having an♥♥♥♥♥equipment system, it's a fantastic game and a great addition to the Wii U's lacking RPG library. Not only is it fun with solid mechanics, but it's stylized beautifully. The art style and music really deliver a memorable experience.
The style is great, and they put so much effort into giving the game a heart and soul. Which begs the question, why can't Ubisoft do this more often?
Not every game has to be a AAA franchise entry with guns and climbing and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥stealth mechanics. White people that can climb has been done so many times, you know?
I mean, the princess in this game is white too. But she FLIES.
That's a whole different genre.
If big budget game companies could learn that not everything is a AAA game that needs to be ♥♥♥♥♥d out into a franchise, maybe we could see more games like this made.

I've finished the game yesterday. It's a good game, but it's overrated.
Pros:
- Interesting, turn based combat system.
- Controlling two independent characters at once (would love to try this with multi).
- Classless character system.
- Mod system.
- Soundtrack.
Okays:
- Graphics.
- Amount of content.
Well, I think there's a lot of content, but not everything seems to be well thought out. I dislike the Diablo-esque loot system, where bosses or chests drop too much of random loot. Old BlackIsle games didn't do stuff like this :/
- Dialogues.
Lots of work went into them, but they seem to be unpolished sometimes. Sometimes they're quite clichee.
- Plot. Beginning was good. The rest.. okay. The execution wasn't always good - sometimes too light-hearted, and not that consistent atmoshpere.
Cons:
- Too big adventage for elemental users.
- Too big focus on the combat, not on the plot development. The fights are challenging on normal difficulty, but once you have to repeat 5 fights 3 times each to advance the plot a little, it becomes tiresome. Especially since the combat is kind of repetetive. (played as a Knight and a Marksman)
- Pixel hunting puzzles.
- Lack of interface for crafting.
- The way mouse is raycasted over objects. Sometimes I would have to move my mouse to an exact spot to hit a monster, otherwise I would use Action Points trying to walk behind it before attacking.
In the end I think it is a well made game, but not a revolutionary one. The game lacks a little bit of polish here and there. It has some 'novel' concepts, which should be interesting to those who weren't exposed to them before.
But I don't think this game deserves 10/10. Maybe compared to nowdays RPG titles, yes. But compared to broader RPG experience, I'd say it's 7/10.

To put it shortly, Divinity: Original Sin has proved what all of us who experienced Baldur's Gate knew already: CRPGs are still damn good games, and the design style hasn't aged much.
This game, much like Icewind Dale before it, also proves that CRPGs don't need engaging stories to be good games. And I am not even slighting the story of the game; it seems rather cliche, but I haven't progressed that far in the main plot. I am actually omitting any opinion of the game's story from this review, because this game stands on its gameplay alone, much like Quake, or Dota 2.
Icewind Dale was a similar example, and the primary reason it is so engaging without needing to care about narrative elements is good encounter design. If you have a series of encounters that are varied and present options to the observant often, the result is a really fun tactical combat experience with progressing characters. The mechanics surrounding the chemistry and physics of the game's various elements and spells often produce unexpected and highly amusing results, including burning zombies that explode every time you hit them; zombies bleed ooze (poison liquid), which is flammable, and burning creatures instantly react with any liquids they stand in. Creating a smoke screen out of either vaporizing water or burning oil is also very useful if you want to force your opponents to come closer and waste time moving around. The spells will be familiar to those who have played D&D tie-in games, yet they are modified in theme to fit with the game's magic system, and many of them will interact with the environment much more dynamically.
The game's environmental effects engine is robust, and a sure sign of an intelligent decision early on in Divinity: Original Sin's design: it was designed to be a computer RPG from the ground up. Which is to say, the effects of all of the elements and physics in the game's environment would be impossible or at least incredibly infeasible to reproduce in a tabletop gaming environment. This means that the game was not designed with the same restrictions that applied to D&D's rules, which make up the framework of CRPG staples like Baldur's Gate, and even derivative mechanical systems like the one found in Planescape: Torment. Careful examination of almost all of the game's fine details show a structured traditional RPG rule system designed to be processed by software from the ground up, not calculated by hand on a tabletop. I don't know about you, but I personally greatly appreciate this. They could have been lazy and copy-pasted d20 rules into their game, but they didn't and it shows they care about pushing the envelope and not only reviving interest in the CRPG genre, but also innovating in it.
I can't say that much about balance and scaling, because I haven't gotten to the late game yet. However, it seems like at the very beginning, melee isn't too strong. Similarly to D&D, once key buff effects are available on-demand in your party (Haste, just like D&D again), your melee fighters become dramatically more threatening. Rogues seem to be effective using either a melee or a ranged strategy; backstabbing is brutally effective as long as you don't draw aggro, but a crossbow's "slow but powerful" characteristics make it ideal for a single killing shot from stealth. Having at least one ranged specialist in your party is a good idea. Strategically-placed barrels can very often be put to use against the enemy giving you the advantage at the beginning of the fight. Traps and specific enemies (zombies, explodoskeletons) can also be shot with normal or special arrows to cause them to backfire with devastating effect on the enemy. I do dare say that having a wide array of elemental magic available is far better than specializing in one school of it. Experienced players will be able to combo all of their various spells' side effects on the environment to devastating effect. Pyrokinetics and geomancy along with hydrosophism and aerotheurgy are the obvious combinations (ooze and oil are flammable, water and wetness conducts lightning), but there are other useful combinations of effects hidden away for you to discover. Witchcraft is the odd man out, offering spells that inflict physical effects like Bloodletting, and direct status effect spells like Blind. It is also unique for bearing the Ressurect spell and a powerful spell that shields an ally from all types of elemental damage.
All that aside, I do want to mention the quest design. When I said I wouldn't talk about the story, I was referring to the main plot of the game; other RPG quests are almost always completely unrelated and often completely independent in quality from the main quest. The quests are quite good for the most part, although those of us who are rusty to RPG quests that actually make you think might struggle a little at first. Divinity does not start off shy in this department, and throws you into an almost entirely pacifist quest tree to solve the murder of Councillor Jake of the town of Cyseal. Solutions in these quests will often necessitate alternate solutions when one is locked out, such as after a lost argument in the game's somewhat frustratingly chance-based disagreement resolution system. It's goddamned rock paper scissors, but you can hit spacebar to skip it. I'm not sure if it flips a coin for this result; preferably, a die roll based on the opposing characters' Charisma score or something, but I do not know. Even more fleshed out than the quests is the game's exploration factor. The game has so many strange encounters as the player travels through the game world that one might even begin to think they were procedurally generated somehow. Of course, the game encourages you to discover these places and encounters, throwing XP at you just for finding some place new.
That sums up my gameplay review of Divinity: Original Sin. I do believe that this game has ushered in a revival of the CRPG genre.

Divinity: Original Sin is a fantastic game.  I can't recommend it enough.  I grew up playing the older turn-based RPGs such as Torment and Baulder's Gate, as well as the Fallout series so this game was right up my alley.  Even if you've never played a turn-based RPG you owe it to yourself to check it out.
The graphics are really good for the genre and the spell effects are great.  The sound quality was also pretty good except the background characters' lines got annoying..."nobody has as many friends as the man with many cheeses" and "How did you find Hiberheim this time of year my dear.... cold, very cold"   will be forever etched into my memory as well as other lines too numerous to count.
The game is LONG.  I played around 100 hours, doing almost all of the side quests.  There is loot galore in addition to the ability to craft some very strong armors.  I didn't explore crafting into late into the game however adding element resistances to armor was extremely helpful in the endgame.  I also crafted some rings to boost Constitution on a couple of characters to make up for deficiencies.
This game was a joy to play and I am really looking forward to see what Larian comes up with next.
