There's nothing as great as blasting off a Fleshpound's head with a sawed-off shotgun.
As for its predecessor, I felt this game was dumbed down on its difficulty. I had a harder time surviving in
than I did in this game. So, overall it was a bit more fast-paced, and gives the player a friendlier experience with survival than it did before. For instance, I feel more terrified about facing the Patriarch in the earlier game. But, with this game, I go in guns blazing against a roided Patriarch, shouting "LEROY JENKINS!" That's the only part where the game fails - challenge.
This is somewhat worked around if you consider daily, and weekly challenges. They tend to change, and they can be done for dosh. Dosh that you get to unlock stuff in the Vault. It's not half-bad. But, there's some lack of challenge there, too. But, it's something more to do, so I won't complain about it too much. Sometimes, doing all the challenges will net you cool cosmetic items that you could use to outfit your character(s).
You also have a progression system - each skillset, or perk, starts off at level 0, until level 25. And you have about 10 perks. That's a LOT of gameplay you got there. And it's a good mix of them. From melee-specialized perks to long-range perks. With the Gunslinger perk, you feel like Clint Eastwood in Zombieland. Now that I think about it, that casting isn't a bad idea. And as you level up with the perks, the more skills you get to unlock and utilize during your rage-fuelled battle against the zeds. That's when you need to start upping your ante. Normal will be too easy for you... maybe you're so good that you want to start doing the waves in Hell on Earth difficulty... I'm a scrub, so I can't.
The game contains three modes - Solo, Co-op, and PvP. Solo is, of course, you going at it by yourself. Co-op can be done in ranked or unranked matches, public or private. PvP has human players going against player-controlled zeds. So, yes, in this mode, you can play as the zeds! Maybe even the Patriarch if you get lucky (or good enough)!
This game is heavily tilting towards NVIDIA users (yay for me!).
If you use a powerful enough NVIDIA GPU, then you get to use a special option called the NVIDIA FleX, with which you can turn on additional blood and gore effects. Every time you pop a zed's a$$, it will flow out this oozy, thick, disgusting fricking juice that is supposed to be blood. PRETTY COOL!
But, the game looks radical. They paid attention to even the tiniest details. The graffiti, the paintings around spooky places, the bloody smears across every wall, the abandoned sights, the apocalyptic atmosphere, the wrecked cars, the creepy laboratories, the fleshy appearances of each zed, the touchy-feely guns, the outfits of the characters - it's one of the best looking games made with
Now, let's re-release it on
, please. That's going to be surreal. Burning Paris is my most favourite map of the game, simply because of such details. It captures the grim atmosphere of the game perfectly.
You'll notice why I had to make a separate category for music. That's because there's amazing music in this game! And not just any battle music! They actually made the effort to get metal bands, and play for the game! And the soundtrack is goooooood!
Any metal fan would fall in love with it. If you don't like the vocals, you could always turn them off, and just drown in the instrumental versions. You really get into the game with it. It's not
without hardcore metal. Really. Take out the music, and it's just...
The music is what drives the game. The gameplay can get repetitive. It can get creepy as hell, it is a lot of fun with friends. It can feel like it's lacking something, it can make you feel like it's got potential to introduce something cool to us... like guest characters, and stuff. It's great that they do occasional events from time to time to bring back players, like the Summer, Halloween and Christmas updates.
Is it better than
? Yes. Those who feel it is the opposite, I believe that is your nostalgia talking.
What would be cool is if they released tiny campaigns for each character. That would be cool.
Buy the game? I say wait for the sale. Even when discounted, it's pretty expensive. So, technically, it's about dedicated interest. Buy it only if you're into blood, metal, and mindless gameplay.

TLDR: This game is great if you enjoy horde shooters. In this review i break down the perks, how i best see them, and also how bad people are at this game.
This game is great, but there are some key issues with it.
Now this is coming from someone who played a decent amount of Killing Floor 1 as well, and the games play vastly different. Whereas KF had a much more unforgiving curve, being out of position on Hell on Earth will result in a team wipe, KF2 is easier.
Full Disclaimer, I'm a Berserker main. Berserker is a class i fully acknowledge as fundamentally broken, but it's also the only class I can ever win a game on HoE with. All the things im about to state are also from playing the game on Long only (10 waves per match) as I feel Long was how the game was meant to be played.
Back on topic, then. There are 10 perks in this game, of which only about 5 or 6 are useful. From my experience, the most worthless perks are SWAT and Survivalist as they offer nothing new to any team. The other perks all have roles, but some overlap. Allow me to clarify; Sharpshooter and Gunslinger have near identical roles. This isn't shocking to me, but it is worth noting.
All the perks from Killing Floor return here, but are significantly changed. Berserker's are still the best class for solo play, but lack a solid weapon progression throughout the game. Medic's got both shafted and buffed. Healing darts are heatseaking now and they have more on perk weapons than just SMGs now. The downside to their change is that the armor buffs that made medic so amazing in Killing Floor 1 is gone, no more cheap armor and insane effectiveness.
The second biggest change is sharpshooter. This perk has been effectively split in half from Killing Floor. In KF they had the option of being a pistol-whipping, head-popping, slow-reloading crack shooter or using an EBR, Crossbow, or a massive f**king rifle. Now they're limited to just rifles for on-perk weapons, and are the best tank-busting class in this game. Their other half, the pistol side, became the Gunslinger perk. This perk is a hot mess no matter how you look at it. On one hand, they fixed the horrible aiming system for dual wielding in KF with the option to aim down an iron sight. But they fly through ammo very fast, and often one clip of whatever you're using cannot bring down a large zed.
The most convenient perk change has to be demolitionist, though. Sonic resistant rounds (making your projectiles immune to siren screams) brought this perk back into relevance. in KF they lacked this, and as such were almost always forgone when building a team because sirens come in packs on higher difficulties and they come often. Other than that change, this perk is still the inefficient trash mop and fleshpound destroyer it always was.
Onto firebug. If you play firebug, head this call. Do. Not. Shoot. At. The. Enemies.
Why? Because its extremely inefficient. I play on suicidal or Hell on Earth almost exlusively at this point, and about 90% of firebugs do not know how to play the perk well. For one, do not set a large zed on fire. let the other perks deal with them. Secondly, read your bloody options for specialization! The trash mop perk meant to save all the other classes ammo can be one of the best perks in the entire game if played properly. Forcing zeds through tight doorways and then being specced properly can mean the difference between 50 flamethrower ammo and 150.
I say this with no sarcasm at all, the most effecitve firebug specialization as of this review, December 20 2017, is as follows: Bring the Heat, Ground Fire, Napalm, Firestorm, and Pyromaniac. Learn how this synergizes, and you will be great.
Moving on from firebug, we have the good ol' support. Supports are nearly carbon copied from KF, with the only difference being the ammo pack they now carry. The only comments I have for this perk are the Boomstick is phenominal, the M4 is a meme, and the AA12 might be the best gun in the game.
Now to commandos. This perk went from being mediocre in KF to being good in KF2. On higher difficulties, this class is a supplimental trash mop for your zerker/firebug/demo-who-has-nothing-big-to-kill. It's main feature that makes it useful now, however, is that the call outs for cloaked zeds are shared, meaning everyone in a raidus sees stalkers too. This will save your team's♥♥♥♥♥ Other than that, its a mediocre class.
Now onto medic. This class changed maybe the most from KF. the darts now heatseak, your armor is average and your survivablitiy went way down. On the flipside, this is the most essential team perk in the game. A good medic will be nearly entirely left side specialized. The ability to not only heal team mates from a distance but also give them buffs like movement speed and more damage is superb on higher difficulties. The only thing left to say about this perk is that the medic assault rifle is the best supporting gun in the game, as it heals at a rate of 5 HP/s instead of the average 3.33 HP/s. This matters a ton on higher difficulties as a fleshpound's basic hit does upwards of 40 damage.
SWAT is a bad perk, i've never seen someone play it well.
Survivalist is supposedly a perk for late joiners, which is bad. Late joiners are, in my personal opinion, the worst thing about this game. Being able to join after wave 6 on a long match, only to increase the zed count and their HP, just so that when you die because no one gave you dosh for joining late, you can leave and screw the lobby. Joining an in-progress game should be cut off at halfway through the match, meaning on a short game no joining past wave 2. on a medium game, no joining once wave 4 starts. On a long match, no joining past wave 5. They made a perk just for those players, and that is why i despise it. Not just because it's a bad perk, because it's a bad perk, but also the principal of it.
Now to talk about my perk in detail. Berserker is, in my opinion anyway, the workhorse of the team. I dont say this to be cocky, but as an observer of mechanics. The berserker is the most cost efficient perk in the game, meaning it takes the least amount of dosh to get going and stay going. It is also, unless you have a swat, the tank of the team. Meaning it will engage larger zeds while the rest of your group peppers it with bullet holes.
There are a few nuances of this perk, however. For one, I am aweful at parrying. There are players out there who are great at it, and more power to them. The bone crusher parry is very strong, if used correctly. Onto the more subtle things then, your swing differs with how you move. if you are strafing, then your attacks will have a wider berth but do 75% damage. Zerker headshots are one of the most overpowered things in this game, at least to me. An Eviscerator used by a zerker with smash can 2 hit a scrake if both blades are headshots. 3 hit to 4 hit a fleshpound the same way, depending on the number of players.
Long story short here, this game is much easier than KF. Much, much easier. If you were looking for something harder, you're♥♥♥♥♥♥outta luck mate. This game is fantastic with friends, as i personally enjoy locking mine in rooms with raged scrakes or fleshpounds, but you also cannot kill team mates with welders anymore.

This game is serious fun if you can corral at least two other people into your place to play at the same time. Honestly? This game is MADE for playing with players of way different power levels. Casuals can have fun playing with monsters (obviously the coolest part of the game anyway) and the skilled players that lured them into this trap can have fun trying to survive as the player against some truly heinous odds.
The skill differential is going to come in handy when you get to the bosses - the bosses are seriously spammy, so anyone with a modicum of skill can do some SERIOUS damage fairly easily. That means that to win, even if you're overleveled, you had better be a friggin' bullet dodgin' bad♥♥♥♥♥ The bosses actually really take away from my enjoyment of the game - they are really hard to beat for a laid back player like myself! Fortunately, this game packs in so much style and gives such intensely fun moments in the "mundane" encounters that, even local only, it's worth the low price of admission. An incredible party game.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within are two excellent games. I say two, because they are, in effect, different games. XCOM:EU is much slower and rewards the safe option, while XCOM:EW rewards risk. Both are good in their own right, and which one you prefer depends on personal preference. So, on to the review:
THE GOOD:
-- You get attached to your soldiers
-- Great tactical and strategic gameplay
-- Very high-stakes combat
-- You can lose!
-- Ironman mode: one save the whole game. Highly recommended.
-- Complementary character classes
THE BAD:
-- You get attached to your soldiers
-- You can lose...
-- Can be very janky (E.g., reloading right after sprinting, hard to select the right soldier, etc)
-- Very RNG based, can be infuriating sometimes (Shotguns missing at close range, things like that)
As far as my personal experience with the game goes, it's a rollercoaster. Early game is hectic AF, trying to keep all the countries in the council. This lasts until the first major story mission, and from there you can (at least on normal) keep all the countries together. The odds of losing go down significantly after that, unless you lose a soldier late game, which is hell. Losing a Colonel near the end game ensures that you burn through your entire stock of rookies in short order, but if you recover from that, you've lived through the worst. Without the Enemy Within DLC, the maps do get repetitive quickly, but that doesn't necessarily have to be a bad thing. The story is a bit vague, which is something I did not like. The gameplay itself, though, is stellar. If you like turn based strategy, this is absolutely the game for you. Despite its flaws, I have to highly recommend XCOM: Enemy Unknown for any fan of the genre. And let's face it... I was mostly nitpicking anyway.

Child of Light is  beautiful game.
It's rare that I play a game and take time to stop and just look and listen to it, and think - "this is breathtaking". The visuals are lovely - I love Aurora's model in particular with the way her hair floats and how her dress moves. The soundtrack is equally beautiful - deceptively simple and yet incredibly moving. I could listen to it all day (and indeed I have for the last couple of days!).
The story itself is captivating, which I wasn't expecting. I genuinely wanted to continue to play, even when I'd gotten a little tired of the combat, as I desperately wanted to see what was going to happen next. I felt genuinely invested in Aurora's quest, which again is not something that I find often in a game.
I love that while the hero is a little girl, there is no mention or indication at all that this may somehow be a handicap or that she's fighting against the odds (of being female), that she needs to be saved, that she's not strong enough, that she's a timid doe, etc., or the equally annoying "ha, take that men, I can do it anyway because girl power!!1!". She just has her resolve, her courage, and her quest. As a female player this is incredibly refreshing, and I would encourage anyone with young daughters to get this game for them.
In terms of mechanics: I really like that you can give the mouse to someone else to play as Igniculus the Firefly and so play with two people at the same machine. I've not seen that before and it's a nice touch.
For me, the combat is the only thing that let the game down a bit for me in that it gets a bit samey after a while. Having said that, that's my own fault because I attacked everything I came across - had I wanted to avoid fighting, that's VERY easy to do.
I did feel that perhaps the very end of the game was a little rushed in events, but overall I can heartily recommend the game as something to experience.
Rarely do I think "This game was worth the money" - this is one of those rare times. Buy. Enjoy!
p.s. I didn't have any problems with UPlay. This might be because I already had it installed?

First and foremost, let me start off by saying that there will be spoilers throughout this review. If you’re even remotely interested in keeping the story for when you run through Episode 1 yourself, I’d suggest waiting to read this. If you’ve watched season three of the HBO T.V. series or read “A Feast For Crows”, you’re probably OK reading through this as there will not be many surprises.
The last three to four years have produced quite a few shoddy games based in the world of A Song of Ice and Fire. The abysmal RTS, and the better-but-not-great attempt at an RPG. It’s also pretty widely known that I’ve been a gigantic fan of George RR Martin since middle school, that being over ten years ago now. I’ve read and reread that entirety of the book series quite a few times, and have dabbled in the various communities that have sprung up to discuss the legitimacy of various children, hierarchy of families, and the events of Westeros. With that being said, I’m usually a giant stickler that a game stay true to the lore, or spirit of writing, that comes across in dialogue and plot. Telltale games did an absolutely phenomenal job at erasing the damage that the previous games had inflicted upon me.
A bit of a background on the political landscape that the game takes place in. Eddard Stark has been murdered at the hands of Joffery Baratheon. The North has risen under the banner of his son, Rob Stark. The rest of the realm, save Dorne, is in turmoil at the hands of the various men who have attempted to claim that they are the One True King of Westeros. The game begins with you playing the role of a young squire in service to House Forrester. Specifically, you are the squire of Gregor Forrester, the lord of the lands and titles of House Forrester. You are camped out at The Twins, the home of House Frey, and the downfall of Rob Stark, King of the North.
The Red Wedding is just about to take place, and with it, the fall of The King in the North.
Game-play & Mechanics
At first, I wasn’t thrilled with the game-play. The game is more of a visual story than a real attempt at wandering around Westeros, leveling up a character, or anything you expect in a typical adventure style game. This was my first foray into a story-based Telltale game, however, and from everything I’ve read about their other titles, this seems to be fairly commonplace. The longer I played, the more I came to like the system. The quick time events were fairly clever, if not a bit confusing at first, and lead to a couple of deaths before I truly figured them out. Several times throughout the story there were invisible walls that kept you from exploring other areas of the game. I first noticed this inside Fort Ironrath, the home of House Forrester, but on my second play-through noticed it more in the wooded areas and places you’d expect a bit more openness. While it was a bit annoying and killed the immersion a bit, Telltale did a good job of adding in other areas that were there solely to be explored, such as the tower in Fort Ironrath. It had no purpose other than to venture to the top, and watch your citizens go about their daily lives.
The ability to inspect most things in the game coupled with the deeper meaning that a lot of the objects held was a trait that I liked very much. A great example of this was procuring the Sentinel bracer as Ethan Forrester. This opened up new dialogue with your uncle, your mother, and the candidates for Sentinel, as well as your siblings. You could even have unique dialogue or description options just by looking at something prior to talking to someone. I’m not one to stave off excess description, and Telltale did a fine job supplying me with things to study and read.
Though the few shortcomings that I’ve noted here were not game-breaking or ridiculously unpleasant, ultimately at the end of the episode I would say that the mechanics and game-play were the one true weakness of the title. The quick time events weren’t repetitive, but you did find yourself wishing for more things to do. More interaction outside of the plot/story. For example, I would have loved to been able to, as a squire, help Rodrick or Gregor don their armor, or suit up for battle. Or, upon my return to Ironrath, to have a brief time where I could fight with the other squires in the courtyard during training. Even having the ability to fight a wooden practice dummy would have been engaging enough to dispel this complaint.
Dialogue & Voice Acting
The voices in this game were a bit surprising to me. It’s not very often you get to hear the voices of a very prominently placed TV show like “Game of Thrones” make their way into a video game, or, I should say, a video game you want to play. I could poke a stick at the other titles stemming from A Song of Ice and Fire, but it’d be a bit redundant. The voice acting was pleasant, well manicured, and did a very nice job making the story both alluring and compelling. I did not have any real complaints about any portion of the acting bit of the first episode.
Story & Plot
Upon receiving a review copy of Telltale’s apparent successful foray into Martins mind, I was extremely worried. The story was the most important piece to such a grand undertaking, and George Martin left plenty of pitfalls and snares along the way to destroy even the most solid of attempts at creating parallel dialogues and sub-plots within the Game of Thrones. My first instinct proved to be false, however, because worry was not needed. The way that Telltale managed to fashion a seemingly unmentioned house, portion of the North, and still remain realistic and true to George RR Martins characters still has me astounded. Throughout my two times through the story, I found no major plot holes, and was even impressed with the timing in which they had the events of House Forrester unfold. Telltale did an excellent job of staying true to the characters set forth by Martin, particularly Ramsay Snow and Cersei Lannister. Ethan Forrester was also a welcome addition to a story line that had a hidden dagger in the dark. True to his style, the ending twist had me up and out of my seat before I knew what I was doing, something that had not happened since I had read “A Storm of Swords”. All-in-all, this is a story that, so far, I can genuinely say belongs in the world of A Song of Ice and Fire.
Graphics
Though the least important, in my opinion, criteria for measuring the depth of a game, Telltale’s A Game of Thrones Episode one did not fall short. The quick time events had great animations, with nothing too jittery or glitchy. The limited amount of landscape you were able to see had quite a bit of detail, particularly playing as Ethan Forrester in the courtyard of Ironrath, and playing as the young squire Gared during his journey North as he is hiding from Ramsay Snow. Though not the games strongest point, I would venture to say that a lot of thought and talent went into the seemingly hand painted environments and impressive looking quick time events.
In Conclusion
It’s not very often that, as gamers, we are given the opportunity to buy a story and watch as it unfolds around us. Here lately it seems we are bombarded with launch day DLC, or essentially paying money to beta test developers games. With Telltale’s A Game of Thrones, we are given more than that. We are given the ability to play an interactive story with incredible lore that has, in my mind, stayed true to the spirit of George RR Martins works. Right now, the game is retailing for just $30 on the Steam store. While this review only covers the very first episode, there are a confirmed six planned in all, and by purchasing Telltale’s latest work, you receive access to all the episodes as they launch. If you enjoy the world of A Song of Ice and Fire, and can enjoy an Episodic point and click adventure, this title is well worth the money.

Fun simplistic RTS with 5-10 minute rounds. It's fast-paced and games can be quite tense.
The AI has 4 difficulty levels and is reasonably challenging. Class system, while being simple, provides enough variety for a lot of different strategies, and strategies that will work on some maps won't work on others - sometimes simply because there won't be "bases" that can turn units into a type that your strategy depends on. So game constantly encourages player to think of new ways of utilizing available units. And there is easy and flexible map editor.
Now a few words about multiplayer. Boid is clearly built with it in mind, it's really fun. As of now, there is 1v1 mode (and developers talk about implementing 2v2, 4 players FFA and perhaps something else - but I'm not sure if this is among official plans or just a possibility). Bad news about multiplayer is that it can take quite some time to find an opponent online. Good news is that you can play against AI while the game is looking for an opponent for you.
Developer actually listens to the community and not a small number of  frequently requested features and improvments has been implemented because of this.
I'd recommend Boid to people who aren't very good at RTSes but want some fast strategic/tactical fun - as I'm one of that bunch and game plays well :) Also Boid looks like a good entry point to real-time strategizing.

Despite what other reviews had said, I actually found the battle sytsem thus far to be above average. I've had to employ several different strategies thus far to fit the battle situation. I really want this game to get the credit it deserves.  Many people will compare it to far cry, and I agree with the comparison, but the movement system is industry-leading in my opinion.  The Following DLC really feels like a continuation and enhancement to the game in the best way possible.  Whether the story realy fits, I can't decide, but it has a giant new map, new mechanics and skills, and tons to do.  The dense cities of the original game are replaced with open farmland.  The environment is far more dangerous.  I have yet to decide if the added difficulty is a pro or con.  I began the DLC with a max-level character and a full inventory of weapons and I still find the game challenging; more so than running through the old map areas.  Trying to level the new skill trees along with the original skills could be a daunting task, but I have yet to try that.  The vehicle adds a whole new element to the game and seems to fit really well with the challenges presented by a more open map, not just transport but cover and weaponary as well.  Gun play was also added as a major rathar than minor element.  There are new guns and lots more ammo to be had.  The extra fire power seems to make dungeon areas more approachable, but in the open landscape, if you have to shoot, you'd butter run.  I'd recommend this game to anyone whether they like zombie games or not.

I decided to wait a while to write a review on this game as I needed to at least "beat the game" once (current play time is just over 60 hours).  Divinity: Original Sin is an extremely punishing game to those who think you can brute force down the enemies.  You need to follow the story line and appreciate the game in its entirety to be able to succeed.  While the previous statements may have been negative, the game is 100% worth every penny and I would recommend it to any of my friends.  I have had the most personal fun playing co-op mode with one of my best friends (Escape -> Assign Characters is too hidden!) and it makes the replayability so much more considering you can always try new heroes and/or mercs.
With all the positives there are some things that don't make a lot of sense, Crafting and Blacksmithing come to mind.  Have no idea why Crafting is in the game after 60 hours or how to use it.  Blacksmithing is a free repair... which means it's just tedious to use and item durability doesn't serve a purpose then.  The first time you play thru the game make sure you save often and try and balance your team/abilities/read an initial play guide.  If not, you are going to have a very bad time and get to about level 7 or 8 and hit a brick wall that can honestly be impassable.
My recommendation is grab a friend, spend some long nights/weekends together and play one of the best action based RPGs I've played in a very long time.  Enjoy your travels together!

I've been dreaming about this game, thinking about it while I'm at work, researching like crazy about the spells and the leveling system. This is the game I've been looking for.
Now I am a huge, HUGE fan of the Dragon Age franchise, especially DA:O. But Dragon Age is cake compared to this game. I didn't realize how much help you get from other games when playing through them. Tons of attribute points. Plenty of skills. Mana. It's all silly.
No hand holding here. Tough fights. Expect to die. A lot. You can basically do whatever you want in terms of characters, but you definitely definitely have ot plan ahead. If you don't, you will be wasting attribute points, ability points and talent points you can't get back. (or can you?)
There is risk in every decision you make. But the world is so expansive and there is so much going on that you find yourself exploring more and more and pushing your limits.
The drop-in CO-OP is outstanding. I can join my friend's game and start as his secondary main character, we split the companions up and we have our own little group. It's amazing.
The only real complaints I have are that a) no handholding means that its a very minimal tutorial, which means certain mechanics like leveling up and acquiring skills you have to look up yourself, and b) the looting button doesn't show things you can interact with, only real loot on the ground.
Get it. So much fun.

Let me preface this with:  One semi-spoiler follows:
First, if you're a fan of "Classic RPGs" such as the Ultima series (the developers even mention the Ultima VII homage) and Baldur's Gate series (they also mention the classic D&D feel to the game) then this game is hands-down the game for you.
It's ever-so-slightly buggy being a kickstarter game that's early out of the gates (and by slightly, I mean I've had two crashes in 20+ hours of gameplay, and there's incredibly minor glitches, such as items that should be stackable not stacking correctly) but these bugs do absolutely nothing to deter you from playing the game.
So that's pretty much everything "bad" I can say about the game.  Now the good:
Not having played the first two of the Divinity series, I was able to come into this game and feel "almost" right-at-home immediately.  You don't need to have familiarized yourself with the prior games to pick this one up at all.  It's definitely it's own stand-alone title with apparently some references to the previous games in the series.
However, the "almost" comes in here:  Since the Ultima series (20+ years ago) I've lost my expectation (and enjoyment) of playing an RPG based on "common sense" decision making.  When RPGs first came out, they were about making logical decisions to determine what to do next.  Since Ultima and Baldur's Gate, games have been dumbed down so much that they have become a process of playing against the game mechanics, not actually immersing yourself in the game.  For example, Skyrim, Fallout 3/New Vegas, and agregious of all, World of Warcraft, have become games where you click on a dialogue, you read it (or don't) then you walk to the next waypoint marked on your map, read the journal entry that tells you precisely what to do, do it, and return to the guy that gave you the "quest" to turn it in.  The very word "quest" has lost its meaning in RPGs today.
That is not this game... You have to unlearn EVERYTHING you've learned for the past 20 years, and for players younger than their 30's, this game will be a completely new experience for you.  Here's the spoilers:
As an example, when you come into the story (I refuse to call this a "game"), your first mission is to solve a murder.  (This should sound familiar to the Ultima 7 fans).  You start by fighting your way into the town, and finding that it's overrun by orcs, and undead, while some nefarious sole is using a type of dark magic (the "source") to have murdered someone.  An overburdened (and pretty much dickish) head of the "Legion" of the town has his hands full, and can't be bothered with this murder that (most likely) was committed by the man's wife.
With that, you have to start putting together the clues.  You don't have waypoints to follow, you only have vague suggestions.  "Perhaps you should start by looking at the crime scene."  So you go to the scene to find a bloody mess, and, not much else.  When you return to the Commander to inform him, he suggests that you "take a look at the body."  No waypoints, no checkmarks as to "where the body is."  You have to use COMMON SENSE.  Dude's been dead for awhile, where would the body be?  You make your way to the grave yard (all of this based on your own ability to think, not by any NPC telling you "HEY!  GO TO THE GRAVE YARD!  IT'S AT COORDINATES X,Y!), and you find the grave.  Need to dig up the grave to find the body?  Probably going to need a shovel for that... Find a shovel.  Dig up the grave, and damn, no body.  A sheep's corpse is in there.  Report back to the Commander.  "Well," he suggests, "Obviously the only one that can answer the question of WHY there's not a BODY in the GRAVE is the mortician, right?  Then shouldn't YOU be talking to HIM?"  But where's the mortician?  Where would a mortician live in the real world?  Near the gravesite, perhaps?  And so goes the game.  Don't be quick to condemn people based on circumstantial evidence, either.  How would you handle this if it was a real investigation?  Would you break into people's houses, grab evidence, then run back to the judge?  No!  You'd question witnesses, even the suspects themselves.  This game does not hand-hold you through a series of check points.  It's your job to figure out what you would do in a real world scenario, and play it through actual thought processes, not a series of waypoints.  And the writers and developers have done a PHENOMINAL job of making sure everything MAKES SENSE.
As another example/spoiler, if you come across a guy that tells you that his brother's grave is "right at my feet", don't LOOK for a gravesite to click on.  Don't look for a mound of dirt to click.  Pull out your shovel, and start digging where he stands.  That's how the game mechanics here work.
The game does it's best to guide you (for instance, if you're not ready to step through a gate into an area where creatures are many levels above you, the guards will SUGGEST you don't, but they won't stop you).   But you're free to do as you will, and play the game as it suits you.  Everything you do has consequences, whether good or bad.  Sure, you could go in and steal a shop-keeper blind, kill him for the experience, and then kill every guard that comes after you (assuming you can) but then who are you going to buy stuff from later?  How many people are going to hate you for those actions and not have any desire to help you as a result?
You cannot go into this game trying to beat the "mechanics" of it.  You just can't, and won't.  It's a true ROLE PLAYING game.  And done so beautifully that after having played thousands of hours in nearly every triple-A title that has come out, this is the one game that I believe deserves PC Magazine's "Game of the Year" title.
This is not a game.  It's an experience, and it's on par with the Ultima and Baldur's Gate series, but oh-so-much-more.  Its co-op system makes me think they designed it specifically for the older generation to get their spouses involved (it really is an incredible game for spouses to play together).
Then there's the battle systems.  "Turn based" battle is an immediate turn-off for many gamers, since everything has gone to hack and slash, or "Final Fantasy" style turn base.  This hearkens back to the days of Baldur's Gate with its turn-based system, but takes it many steps further.  Much more like a table-top game, the terrain, what you're carrying, your position, and
impacts the battle field.  Is it raining?  Probably not a good idea to try and use "burning" as your main attack.  But hey, everything's wet, so maybe lightning is good?  Lots of water on the ground?  How about you freeze it under their feet to slip them up?  Not raining, but you're geared for lightning and ice?  Maybe MAKE it rain, and hope you can get everyone good and soaked before firing off the ice?  Perhaps try to duck behind a plateau and snipe at the enemy's heads that peek over, while they shoot into the ground?  EVERYTHING comes into play.
I wish I had enough characters left to explain the way that tactics in the battle play out, but I can only say, in summary:
If 100+ game hours of a game that REQUIRES you to forget everything you have learned about playing games in the past 20 years, and truly playing an incredibly well thought-out, in depth, immersive RPG that hearkens back to the days of Ultima and Baldur's Gate that
sounds like your kind of game, you will kick yourself in the teeth if you pass this one up.

This game's tag line "No game is the same" is really true. Think of this as minecraft + tf2. In this game, you are working to protect your cube(s) while simutaneously trying to destroy the other team's cube(s). The game starts out with a build phase, in which you use your selected blocks to fortify your base and make it as hard as possible for the other team to get in and destroy your cubes. In this phase, there is a force field protecting you from spying or going into the other base. Then, the force field drops and you battle. Matches in this game are typically long (30+ minutes) so don't play this if you know you need to go somewhere else within an hour. That does bring up a very major con about this game, you can't quit. Literally, in game, there is no quit button, you can only use task manager. I can get why this is, because the match suddenly becoming a 3v6 isn't good, but there must be a better way to handle this. As for the battle, it is great. Currently there are 6 classes to choose from. Each class has it's own weapons, skills, and special blocks.
All of these classes, though seemingly very different, work together in magnificent ways. Though I dread when the meta sets in and every base is the same, this game is excellent in its current state.
Overall rating: 9/10

XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within are two excellent games. I say two, because they are, in effect, different games. XCOM:EU is much slower and rewards the safe option, while XCOM:EW rewards risk. Both are good in their own right, and which one you prefer depends on personal preference. So, on to the review:
THE GOOD:
-- You get attached to your soldiers
-- Great tactical and strategic gameplay
-- Very high-stakes combat
-- You can lose!
-- Ironman mode: one save the whole game. Highly recommended.
-- Complementary character classes
THE BAD:
-- You get attached to your soldiers
-- You can lose...
-- Can be very janky (E.g., reloading right after sprinting, hard to select the right soldier, etc)
-- Very RNG based, can be infuriating sometimes (Shotguns missing at close range, things like that)
As far as my personal experience with the game goes, it's a rollercoaster. Early game is hectic AF, trying to keep all the countries in the council. This lasts until the first major story mission, and from there you can (at least on normal) keep all the countries together. The odds of losing go down significantly after that, unless you lose a soldier late game, which is hell. Losing a Colonel near the end game ensures that you burn through your entire stock of rookies in short order, but if you recover from that, you've lived through the worst. Without the Enemy Within DLC, the maps do get repetitive quickly, but that doesn't necessarily have to be a bad thing. The story is a bit vague, which is something I did not like. The gameplay itself, though, is stellar. If you like turn based strategy, this is absolutely the game for you. Despite its flaws, I have to highly recommend XCOM: Enemy Unknown for any fan of the genre. And let's face it... I was mostly nitpicking anyway.

Polychromatic is, in essence, a spiritual successor to Geometry Wars. The basic concept of the game is the same, a endless SHMUP shooter consisting of several waves of various types of enemies with the clear all bombs and simplified graphics. The change from vectric wireframe to minimalism is a nice distinction factor and the change in how the enemies behave gives it enough distinction from its inspiration.
But with that said is there really a reason to buy the game? I'm of a mixed opinion.
On the positive side is the core gameplay. It takes from a highly successful SHMUP formula and makes its own unique game with great visuals and unique sound effects. Controls are fluid and smooth, and the variety of enemy units makes the endless waves pretty enjoyable.
On the negative side though, there is almost no variety in game type. You have three game types. First is endless waves, which gives you a stock of lives and bombs (and dashes that give you momentary invulnerability), there's timed which gives you 2 minutes and adds more time on each wave completion, and there's "one life to live" in which if you duy you're done. There's no other game option beyond that. Given the formula it's replay value is rather in the core game, but some structured gameplay variation would be nice.
Next is the music. It feels... jarring. I wouldn't say it's bad really, but it's definitley a very distinctly different from the sound effects and visuals of the game. Feels like (I think I described it as) weird electronic lounge music that gets hyper all of the sudden.
Finally is the price, where I'm not sure given my first issue how I feel. Ten dollars is alot to ask for, especially when its inspiration is $4 on steam, and gameplay wise the only thing differentiating it is the enemy behaviors and graphics.
So do I recommend the game? With hesitation, but yes. If Steam had something akin to a five star rating I'd give it a 2.5. It's a solid game on its own, but the pricepoint and lack of gameplay options hurt it. Still I can't say I don't recommend it. If you can pick it up on sale I'd say it's worth some time spent as it's a great formula. Just a little disappointed that there wasn't more to it.

Polychromatic is a colourful, twin-stick arena shooter from Brushfire Games. You, a small blue shape, must fight off waves of other shapes in order to get as many points as you possibly can. Polychromatic is very much about trying to get progressively better scores to not only beat your previous personal best but also in order to get higher on the leaderboard which creates a real sense of competitiveness even though you’re playing by yourself.
Polychromatic is very simple in its appearance, relying on the vibrant colours of the different shapes to make it interesting. While this does work relatively well for the game as it makes all the shapes really stand out, I was very much left with a sense of blandness due to the grey background of the game arena. One thing I did really like about the presentation was the fact that information about your current game is displayed in the middle of the arena, rather than on any UI elements around the screen.
Polychromatic is split into three different game modes; Endless mode, Timed mode and One-Life mode. The major things that stay the same across the game modes is that you always have access to three blast power-ups and three dash power-ups (more can be earned by beating waves) and each consecutive wave is progressively longer and harder to beat.
Endless mode consists of you beating as many waves of shapes as you can before you run out of lives. In Endless mode you start with three spare lives though more can be earned by beating waves of shapes. As far as I’m aware there is no ‘wave cap’ so in theory you could play forever but since the game’s difficulty does ramp up a fair bit I don’t see that being at all possible.
Timed mode gives you infinite lives but only two minutes on the clock to beat as many waves as you can. Each time you beat a wave ten seconds is added on to the clock. It’s worth remembering that respawning takes around two seconds so while you may have infinite lives it’s in your best interests to keep yourself going as long as possible.
One-life mode is identical to Endless mode but instead of starting with three lives and getting more every few waves you only have one life so you better hope you’re good at dodging!
There’s not much to say about gameplay other than what I’ve covered in my description of game modes. As you whizz around what appears to be a petri-dish of shapes you fire tiny circles at said shapes in order to eradicate them! As well as these tiny circles you also have the two power-ups I mentioned earlier at your disposal. The blast power-up sends out a ring of the little circles to eradicate shapes all around you, of course these circles spread out the further away from you they get so it’s best to use it when there’s a high concentration of enemies very close to you. The dash power-up sends you shooting around the little arena at a faster than usual speed while also making you a lean, mean shape-squishing machine, i.e. any shapes you touch while the dash power-up is active will be destroyed.
The sound effects are very good in Polychromatic and fit with the game nicely. The soundtrack is also good but I felt like it didn’t really fit with the game. With a game like this I’d expect quite lively music, something along the lines of electro or dubstep to really get you into the game for the more frantic, later waves. However, the music we’re presented with, while very nice, has a more relaxing feel to it and just felt out of place to me.
Polychromatic is a fun little twin-stick shooter, with a simple aesthetic, good gameplay and a real sense of competitiveness due to the leaderboards. The only thing holding this game is its price tag but chances are you’ll think it’s worth it if you like this kind of game, if not then hold off until a sale.

Child of Light is an extremely gorgeous piece of work. From its method of storytelling to its stunning visuals and appropriately airy and pleasant orchestral soundtrack, everything about this game's presentation ties together like a fine piece of poetry. Sure, the writing is a little clumsy at times, and they reeeeally stretch the language to hit the nail on the head for some of those rhymes (see what I did there?), but the heart is there and that's why Child of Light shines as brightly as it does. It just has a ton of heart and love in it and its creators' care for the project shines through and is ultimately infectious.
Child of Light's RPG elements are heavily inspired by Game Arts' Grandia series. Combat plays out with all characters assigned a spot on a timeline at the bottom of the screen. When a character or enemy hits a specific point on the timeline, they are then allowed to act. If a character or enemy is successfully attacked in the moments before their action is carried out, their attack is interrupted and they are pushed back on the timeline to hopefully try again. Combat mostly boils down to who can control the timeline better with their attacks or employing dirty tricks like slow down spells or status effects that inhitibt a character's movement on the timeline. All of the game's random battles have this strategic element, and boss fights even more so, which makes encounters not feel so mashy as RPGs can tend to be.
Combat is enhanced further by the way you customize your characters. Level ups grant skill points that you can spend on skill trees to grow your characters toward the stats and moves you want the most, though there's never any need to maximize any one part of a skill tree if you want your characters to do a little bit of everything. The Oculi system helps customization further by allowing you to imbue your characters with elemental attacks, defenses, and abilities to alter their or their enemy's stats on the timeline. These aren't the deepest systems ever, but they add enough depth to keep the character progression important.
So yeah, Child of Light is pretty awesome. Its only flaws are that it can be a tad too easy (I HIGHLY recommend throwing the difficulty up to Expert as soon as you have the ability to) and a character or two don't quite get their chances to shine in the story before the game wraps up. Other than that, fans of JRPGs will be incredibly happy with what Child of Light has to offer with its engrossing story, beautiful world, and solid RPG mechanics.

The Banner Saga has breathtaking artistic landscapes to see as your caravan travels accross them encountering situations in which you have to decide as a leader of the caravan what is the best course of action. The results of which are never entirely clear and some can have absolutely dire consequences you won't see coming and won't be able to stop (think "Red Wedding"). The soundtrack is beautiful and suits the theme of the game, journey and struggle. Decisions you make can also affect the warriors who join your plight and you're unlikely to see them all.
The combat system is interesting. It won't be to everyone's taste but I quite enjoyed the alternating team based combat. Varl's are like giants and by nature they can take and give more damage and can be used strategically to block paths. Humans are smaller and can get around better but whilst weaker, they do have strengths and abilities to help in combat. Damage is equal to your health and reduced by your enemies armor. The combat revolves around making decisions on whether you hurt an opponent immediately so that their attacks are weaker or their armour, so your next attacks are stronger. It is strategically wise to weaken opponents and keep them alive (which seems counter-intuitive) because it means more weak enemies take turns, avoiding the hard hitters.
You play the game from multiple perspectives in the early chapters. I played and completed the game on Hard and the combat is imbalanced in this mode. The enemies will have higher stats than your humans and varl; combat against them can be grueling, especially in parts of the game where you controlling the human caravan. Losses do not result in a game over but they can make the game even harder and you feel punished for it as morale drops and you enter battle with less willpower.
Playing on hard, the fights are tough and the journey difficult. The game feels grueling and travelling with your caravan feels immersive because it hammers in the melancholy tone that the game attempts to set as your people flee from the marauding armies and devastation. The final battle was ridiculously challenging. Unlike the rest of the game where it is better to divide and conquer, your strategy needs to change and you need to focus on the boss. This battle took me multiple attempts to beat and I did not have a tank that everyone recommends bringing for this battle. Surprisingly, I never got frustrated with my continual losses because I always learnt something and took what I learnt into the next attempt as I changed things around. Some may find this frustrating though and give up on the game (or lower the difficulty - which you can do at any time). It does, however, diminish the end scenes (wish they were skippable), as you see it for the umpteenth time.
Some of the most epic and interesting moments in the game were when there was voice over narrating the story and epic scenes were happening in the background. Sadly these moments are too far and few in between and could do with more VO and animations.
The war events would be better if instead of 4 standard courses of action, each one played out more like a RPG novel and it gave you varying situations and options on what to do for those situations.
The level up system feels punishing at times. You can waste resources on a party member's stats only to lose them in a situation you could not see coming. The game offers a finite amount of battles throughout a playthrough and so your resources are limited and poor choices in how you distribute your renown can cost you in the end battle as you are forced to take 2 party members (out of a party of 6) and you'd hope you'd leveled them up and spent resources on both of them. Thankfully, there is a point in the end, where your party is reinforced and supplied with lots of renown and if you've mis-distributed those resources for the final battle, you can revert to that save and attempt to redistribute the renown better for the final fight.
The story is incomplete and is only the first part of 3 Banner Sagas. There are characters and things introduced in this story that are developed further and were clearly saved for the later parts. The first part of the Banner Saga is about the start of events that will lead to a more epic journey. In a way, it's like the "Fellowship of the Ring" to the "Lord of the Rings".

EDIT: I wrote the review below, and yet within 24 hours returned to the game. My experience was entirely different, and I came to love it. The thing is.... it's not a game about romance. Not really. And while I had a fictional-character-crush on Alisa and wanted a more satisfying ending, that's really not what this game is about. It's about mystery, about understanding who one is and choosing whether or not to chance. The girls are there, and you can indeed romance many of them.... but it's about the self-revelation one has by spending time with them. In dialectical terms, they are the antithesis to the thesis of your main character's status quo, and the exploration of these storylines produce the synthesis you end with. Romance can be a part of it, but in a way, it can also be extraneous because it's about a transformation of the self and the choice between living a flavorless, reclusive life and one of joy and abundance.   So far as I've yet seen, there's not so much a  trite "she made me a better man", as the contrast of a girl's character and the interactions you have giving the main character a new perspective if he chooses to look. From this vantage, he can change. Or, I suppose, not.

So, if you're in it for the romance, you might be let down. But there's something more interesting going on here, and I now feel I can recommend it for people who want something more.
Original review included below, as it may help illuminate my journey with this game to date.
[Oy. This game.
There's so much to love about this game. The backgrounds are jaw-droppingly gorgeous. The sense of place and time it conveys is stunning, and the presentation is bright and inviting. The music, as well, is lovely. In terms of basic aesthetics, there is so much to love here, and I would almost recommend it on that basis alone.
Culturally, I find it fascinating as well. The sense of nostalgia for one's youth  is universal. It takes place in the Soviet equivalent of the scout camps of my youth, so is relatable. From my cultural context, that it is bright and positive from the perspective of a kid in the former USSR is quite interesting.  Most of the game takes place in the early/mid 1980's. As a kid of roughly the same age in that timeframe  in the USA, it's fascinating to see memories of that time and place from the other side of the cold war. There was an awareness, before the fall of the Soviet Union, that they were not so different from us, as a people. This kinda was lost in the "We won, you lost" attitude after that fall of that system, but it's nice to see a representation..... fictional but based on the creators' memories.... of my Soviet counterparts.
Alas, the story... the story.
The characters are all basic anime tropes, except possibly, one. She has more going on than one can see on a surface level, but I didn't follow her path. The rest all fall into the usual categories. Super positive beautiful girl, impish younger girl, angry and abrasive girl with a heart of gold. They're all represented. It's to be expected, and I don't fault the creators for bringing out these types. After all, interesting stories can still be told with them. I followed the angry girl, as the prickly hotheaded type with a soft and vulnerable core always appeals to be. Truth be told, I had intended to follow them all except for the younger girl. But angry girl, Alisa, had to be first.
She delivered, to a great extent. There were those moments of vulnerability, the clumsy ways of trying to express affection.... all the things I find adorable. So what could go wrong?  Well, in the end, they just didn't sell it. There wasn't the payoff. Oh, sure, for those who just wanna get to the sex scene, that happens (although tastefully blacked out in this version). But the emotional arc never pays off, and the point of view character is infuriatingly passive aggressive. Almost to the last, he's unable to express any emotion. Indeed. he seems so annoyed by her that the last minute "oh, I guess I love you" rings false. There's no believable "She's annoying, but  there's something about her" moments building throughout her arc, so when they toss that in at the end, it just doesn't seem feasible. Furthermore, there was no investment in giving any reason for her attraction to our POV character. It just happened because, of course it has to. But no reason for the attraction on her part is given, nor hinted at. This sort of visual novel hinges on satisfying romantic arcs, and in Alisa's case, it's clumsy and doesn't work.
Of course, there are other arcs, and mysteries that go unexplained in the path I took. However, the way Alisa's story falls flat, and misses it's chances to sell the romance... well, I don't feel inclined to explore further. In a game like this, that is a failure.
There's a lot to recommend in this game, but overall? I just can't give this the thumbs up. It comes so close to being amazing, but that makes the fumbled story arc I followed all the more frustrating. Perhaps other paths are better and at any rate t's free, so if you have nothing better to do and little money, I guess give it a shot. Otherwise, look elsewhere.]

Let me start by saying this: The Banner Saga is not a bad game, but merely a decent one and I do not think it's worth the full asking price.
The Good:
+The soundtrack by Austin Wintory is amazingly atmospheric.
+The story, world and characters are quite good, especially since norse mythology is underused in general.
+The combat draws from other games like Heroes of Might and Magic and Fire Emblem.
+Great animations both during travel and while in combat.
The Bad:
-Sound effects repeat way too often and I'm pretty sure Varl, Humans and even Dredge have the same pained emotes.
-The story is not finished, which means that you more or less have to buy the next game to get a proper ending.
-A lot of characters repeat but with a few other details and just a swap of color.
-The map is confusing to read and it can be almost impossible to decipher where you're going and how much you should provision.
-Random events are scarce and too random, seriously just find a guide, especially for the ones where your characters die.
-Renown doesn't make any sense as a concept in the game. Slaying enemies, making good choices and reaching milestones grants renown points. These points can then be used to level up characters when they have enough kills, buy items and buy provisions. But how exactly does your renown pay for food? And why do I lose renown when my heroes level up? Adding further to this is the fact that the game is one long escape from the apocalypse, but due to how renown is gained, you have to fight in as many battles as possible to level up the most and buy more provisions.
-The combat UI is clunky.
-Furthermore, combat feels off in many ways. See your HP is also your damage, I quite like this mechanic, however this leads to situations where it's actually better to let enemies live rather than killing them. The reason is because the initiative system always switches sides until only the last enemy remains.
Bottom Line:
The Banner Saga is a decent game that can be fun at times, but lots of small nagging design flaws will be trying your patience throughout, if you must play it, buy it during a sale.

If you're interested in the first installment,
At least 50% of the gameplay is an unrealized Oregon Trail as randomized situations cause your clan to fight, argue, rejoice, or die off. Being nice to people in Banner Saga presents an equal chance of receiving resources and getting stabbed in the back. Read a game guide, attempt to roleplay, or flip a coin.
The nagging survival elements consist of managing food supply and morale. Food supply can be bought with Renown, your experience points, which takes away from the pool used to level up party members. This fight for balancing the health of your clan with the power of your party takes away from the possible enjoyment of combat and skill allocation.
Fighting with a party of developed skills is arguably much more fun than keeping your clan members alive. Unless you care about the weak consequences (the resulting dialogue is similar to a waving finger), you might as well not care about their health. On the other hand, Morale supports combat by increasing strength of actions, but I did not see this as a necessity.

Saints Row IV from Volition does what SR series has always delivered in the series - lot of laughs + fun. As if Saints Row: The Third (SR:TT or SR3) didn't ramp up the over-the-top nature of the series, SR4 takes it to another level on the absurdity, ridiculousness, insanity, humor, parodies, jokes, punchlines, crassness, wittiness + fun. SR4 tries to out-do it in numerous ways - and in many ways, SR4 succeeds in doing just exactly that.
After the crazy events from SR3, The Leader of The Saints has now become The President Of The United States. After this + putting Keith David (who plays himself!) in the Cabinet, an alien named Zinyak (who is fantastic + often hilarious, I might add) invades Earth + enslaves everybody into a Simulation World similar to The Matrix. To break free of this, The Saints are on a ship (which reminds me of the Normandy from Mass Effect series) and they try to fight the battle in both the Simulation + Real World to free themselves from this insanity. As if SR3 wasn't ridiculous enough, this here takes things here in SR4 to another level. With also tons of references to events, characters + whatnot from previous SR games - this game also is a Love Letter from Volition that written is directly to their fans that have stuck with them since its inception.
For SR4, you can forget what you know from SR3 about gameplay. This isn't as much of a GTA-style 3rd-person action game where you do most of your moving around the gameworld by driving vehicles - especially when you're in the simulation-world. While you can still do those things in the simulation world + in the "real world", most of the time (which'll be spent in the Simulation World) SR4 takes this to the Prototype series + super-hero side of things. Once you're in the simulation-world, you can run up walls, run around the game-world ultra-fast, knock cars over, jump wicked high - which is a lot of fun + a new way to run around a SR game-world. You can even switch the radio station of the game, while you're not even in a car!
For parodies, jokes, punchlines + anything humor-related - knowing your pop culture from music to video games certainly helps. The humor never ends, as it take stabs at Mass Effect series, BioWare games (Romance mechanics), 50's classic TV shows (such as Leave It To Beaver), video games (there are Mortal Kombat references, for starters), entering pop culture icons playing themselves (Roddy Piper + Keith David), breaking the 4th wall entirely, twerking + so many other things that I don't know where to begin here. If one joke doesn't hit you, it'll be too late b/c the next one will likely have already hit you, leaving you likely in hysterics.
The only thing SR4 really has going against it here is re-used assets. This feels more like a classic-style big-sized expansion-pack - which stands alone, in this case (since you don't need to own any game to run this here). The game-world from SR3 was reused + might feel overly familiar to players - even though it has been modified, re-tweaked, reworked, reskinned, revamped + remixed. Sure, there are some new areas - but most of the time, you'll be in the huge Simulation World.
When it's all said + done - after spending around 27 hours with SR4, this game has delivered lots of laughs, fun, insanity, wittiness, jokes, action, nonsense, fun & "I can't believe the game went there" moments. SR4 might not have the freshness that SR3 had with its actual game-world (since Steelport from SR3 was reused + remixed here for SR4) - but even that can't stop this game from being fun to play + a barrel of laughs. SR4 still manages to deliver so much fun, comedy, jokes + the new super-powers direction - that it's impossible to not enjoy what is here. So many games take themselves so seriously these days, but SR series always seems to be that breath of fresh air gaming needs every time that another one comes around. Not many game series are as over-the-top, funny + as ridiculous as Saints Row - yet Volition manages to keep delivering that every time out, knocking it right out of the park. If that isn't enough of the icing on the cake, here's the cherry on top - fans who have loved the previous SR game, this game is a Love Letter from Volition that is most definitely for you.
Final Grade = B.

TLDR: Good for those who want a fresh take on the Diablo formula. Supporting the developers is worthwhile. Not a game you should play for story and choice, though the lore is fun. Good gameplay, good design, old game engine.
Good:
- Active developers who live up to their promises. Steadily updated throughout early access with meaningful content, and continue developing both DLC and new free quests and areas, as well as balance patches.
- Mod support and a small but dedicated modding scene. I've stopped playing for now but I'm excited to revisit it with mods in the future.
- Interesting and overlapping progression and character development systems.
- Characters aren't shoehorned into a few particular builds to be competitive. If you think of a character, there's usually a way to make it work. Aside from not getting enough physique, its hard to 'ruin' a character.
- Interesting and varied items
- Convenient item management with plenty of space, sorting, component merging etc.
- Good worldbuilding, plenty of text for lore nerds
Your Mileage May Vary:
- The world and all dungeons are handcrafted instead of randomized. Enemy spawns are random outside of bosses, and passages are randomly blocked or unblocked. Some random quests. Some people might swear by the random areas in Diablo and PoE.
- Often sacrifices conveniences such as quest markers, instead you need to read descriptions and familiarize yourself with the world. I like this and consider it part of the worldbuilding, but it might frustrate some.
- The lore is good but the story is formulaic. On the other hand, is that really why you are playing a Diablo style game?
- There are some elements of choice, but the differences aren't drastic and this mechanic really isn't utilized after the first act and a half.
- That Wall Where Your Numbers Are Not High Enough To Pass exists, but is usually encountered in New Game Plus Plus. It's fun enough to just move on to a new character.
Bad:
- The engine is old and doesn't always run as smoothly as you would expect for a 2016 game.
- Audio is repetitive and usually uninteresting. Put on a good podcast while you play.
- Major anticlimax after beating the final boss.

While not highly original, Polychromatic does a good job at what it is, a twin stick shooter.
Polychromatic works like most twin stick shooters where one analog stick controls movement and the other controls the aim of your weapon. You can also collect two different power ups which includes releasing a burst that kills all of the nearby enemies and a speed burst that makes you temporarily invulnerable.
Polychromatic has three different modes. One mode has you try to score as many points as you can with a given set of lives (earning more based on points scored). Another mode gives you a certain amount of time where you try to score as many points as possible. Finally there is a mode where you get only one life and try to score as many points as you can before you die.
While the artwork looks simplistic I actually liked it quite a bit. With a simple graphics style the game runs really well even when there are a bunch of enemies and bullets on the screen at the same time. I also liked that all of the enemies have distinctive shapes and colors which makes it easy to determine what special abilities each enemy has.
The only real problem with Polychromatic is that it is not that original. If you don't like twin stick shooters I don't think Polychromatic will change your mind. If you like twin stick shooters though I think you can get quite a bit of play time out of Polychromatic.
Note: I received a free review copy from the developer.

If you’d prefer a video version of this review, I made one that outlines similar points:

Polychromatic instilled an old feeling in me that I used to get, but it was a very specific set of events that led me to that feeling.
I’ll explain what I mean in a bit, but first; Polychromatic is a top down endless twin-stick shooter, that is designed to be played casually.. You have to survive for as long as possible while also destroying as many of the other shapes as you can.
The game does a good job of making each different enemy shape behave in different ways, and I noticed, in particular, things like group AI and AI in general were done very well; I know that stuff like that can be difficult to get right, but the enemies move in a way that is challenging to avoid but still completely predictable and that should be commended.
It’s also just a generally well polished game, and that might be because the mechanics are simple; and maybe they’re too simple. Initially, when I played the endless mode for the first time, I felt like, while the gameplay was good, there was little incentive for me to keep playing. It felt kind of bare-bones.
That was before I saw the leaderboard, and this is what I mean by instilling an old feeling in me; since I have a promotional copy of this game (that is, one that comes out before the official release date) the global leaderboards were quite empty. I instantly got tunnel vision; I had to get the highest score in the world before this game released. So I tried again… and again.. and again.. and suddenly was having so much fun. In the end I failed; I gave up once I reached fourth place, but the main point is that this is where the game really shines. The gameplay is designed perfectly for leaderboard competition.
The problem is, what are the chances that you, the viewer, are going to experience this? The way I see it, there will either need be so few people playing the game that you have a realistic chance of reaching the number one spot globally, or there will need to be so many people playing the game that there is enough competition in your friends list to make it worthwhile.
Because, I’m gonna go ahead and say that it’s unlikely you’ll get much from this game from a purely isolated experience. Sure the gameplay is solid, but after a few attempts it becomes the same thing over and over. Yeah you can try and get better every time, but to what end? The game is infinite, even the timed mode is still infinite it’s just how far you can get within a certain time.
So I can only recommend this game if you are of the small subset of people who not only enjoy competition on leaderboards, but are in a position that that’s going to be fun for you. And then, you need decide if that’s worth $10. For me, I think the experience I had, and still am having since I’m gonna keep trying, is worth that price. But I have a feeling that’s only going to last until release day.
It’s a difficult one, but I feel I’ve given you the information you need to make an informed decision about this. Officially I will be recommending it, but be aware of what my feelings are behind that recommendation.

This is a great MMO and it is worth the current $10 price tag.  But it has a massive amount of issues and I will go over those in a bit.
Pros:
This game has open combat similar to Tera.  Its extremely fast paced and extremly fun when it comes to killing monsters and looting them.
This game is extremely beatuiful.  Its graphics are breath taking and the detail put into the game is stunning.
The amount of things you can do in this game are nearly endless.  You don't have to choose what professions you want to get into as you can do anything at any point and when you gain contribution points you can buy houses and purchase workers and have those workers gather supplies and make items for you.  The game expands on a regular basis and they patch this game often.
Daily log in bonuses insure that you get rare items and a constant income just for logging in.  They also do events that can earn you a fairly decent amount of silver coin as well which means that if you play your rewarded and the system they have in place works quite well.
There is no trading from player to player when it comes to items found in game and by doing that they have managed to create the most stable market that I have ever seen in any MMO.  Because there is no trading people can't undercut on the market which means that each item you find will have a value to it so in turn your able to make an income doing just about anything in the game.
Cons:
Hidden Information: Set bonuses from items don't show up on your character statistics chart, any hidden bonuses that you get from your regular weapon transfered to your awakened weapon also do not show.  This game has a huge amount of hidden information that is both frustraiting and pointless.  If information is added into the game it should be accessable and it clearly isn't.  It wouldn't be hard at all to make your character screen display more information in an easy format that says yes you have these set bonuses active and this is what it gives you and yes you get this much from your normal weapon to your awakened power.
Pay to Convenience: Without a quick travel option or flying mounts you will find yourself spending 30 plus minutes riding a horse from town to town just to transfer items.  To avoid this you have to pay real money to transport items without going to each town, buying a 30 day value pack will also increase the amount of bag spaces your warehouses get as well as how much space you yourself get when it comes to bag space and weight.  Playing without this isnt easy while being a new player and you will find yourself giving up because you cant carry anything or do anything without spending a lot of time going from town to town.
Gear upgrading:  This game has the most toxic and frustraiting system when it comes to gear improvment out of any game i have ever encountered.  You will be given black weapon stones or armor stones and you have to apply that to gear in order to improve it.  Once you hit a certain level you will begin to fail upgrades and as you fail upgrades the maximun durability of your item decreases.  To improve that maximun durability you have to go purchase or find the exact item your trying to upgrade and consume those 2 items into one another.  Gone are the days of finding a really good piece and equipting it.  With this game you may have to find 20 or more of the same piece of gear to get it to a decent +15.  This means that a green Grunil piece of gear will probably be far better than end game boss armor until you are able to afford 20 30 million armor pieces.  The upgrading system makes no sense and will have you confused as to how a 300k costing piece of gear is far more supirior than a 30million costing piece of boss gear seeing the 300k is both cheaper and easier to upgrade as well as obtain.  To me the gear system makes little sense and its frustraiting expensive process.
Quest progress:  You wlil get quests from your black spirit and as you follow that questline you will get inventory expandors which is a great concept the problem is that you will end up getting quests that will put you in the middle of an area and you will lose the black spirit quest due to the quest hiding inside of another quest in a given area and its impossible to see where it is or how to track it so you will end up losing where you were going or how to get back to that point.  In short you followed the quest out there it managed to hide itself inside of another quest giver you log off because your tired you get back on and realize your quest log is full so you delete some to get your daily quest and go do that and then end up losing your quest progress not being able to remember where it was or how to go back and get it.
Knowledge tracking:  The knowledge system is a good system but the format its currently in is horrible.  Its extremely hard to navigate to the knowledge your looking for to the point where you have to click navigate to it and trust me you will end up getting lost and confused.  Making that navigation easier may help some users.
It has some huge problems and these problems prevent me from enjoying the game on several seperate occations.  But that doesn't make this game a horrible game.  This game holds a lot of potental and its worth the current price tag.  I have gotten quite a bit of play time out of it and it has been extremely fun.
