little about it:
- it's only 1vs1 player
- a strategy game where in order to win you have to be faster than your opponent in conquering strategic points on the map and also be able to hold them.
- you do not controll the way your units spawn, the more spawning points you controll, the more units you produce, thus is essential to controll at least the same amount of spawning points as your opponent to be able to stay in the game.
- each "basic unit" (is actually a good unit, but average on all stats) can be transformed to different units if you controll certain points on the map. Each unit has its own advantages and drawbacks, some are faster but weaker, some are slower but stronger, some are weaker but have range, some heal, etc.
- at first it feels a little strange(slower mouse movement - but you can adjust it in options menu), game allows you to zoom out(you are able to see the entire map) but this zooming is used just for observing, you'll have to zoom back in to be able to controll your units. After playing some games, I got used to it and it seems natural now.
Pros:
- simple, very easy to learn but harder to master
- can be played "casual" as games can be really fast(minutes) so you don't need hours to play a game.
- low price
Cons:
- Almost no players to play against for now(still early access) so you'll be mostly stuck playing against bots(the hard difficulty is pretty challenging).. or you can always play against friends if you have them(I'm lonely)
- you can play only ~5 maps vs bots, while online there are more options ~20
- only 1v1. Maybe in the future it would bring a nice twist to be able to play it with more players.

FTL is a space-faring roguelike where you are the captain of a starship. You control your crew members which vary in race and abilities, as well as the systems of your ship. The ultimate goal is to reach the Federation base to deliver vital intel to defeat the Rebel fleet. You encounter the rebels, allies and pirates across your journey. Will you accomplish your mission?
Since the update that the developers gave this game, there are three difficulties to choose from Easy, Normal, or Hard. There are several different ships to choose from, as well as different system layouts for each ship. Even if you choose the same ship and layout, every playthough will be significantly different. Encounters in space, as well as the map layout in each sector are randomized every time. The currency in the game "scrap" which is used to upgrade your ship and purchase from stores is also random from the rewards.
If you like a challenge, this game can really deliver. Hard mode lowers your scrap rewards, forcing you to make hard choices as a captain. It's a battle for survival in a harsh galaxy. Being able to pause the game (bound to space by default) is your main defense. It gives you time to issue commands to your crew as well as change system power or target specific systems in the enemy ship.
Try unbinding pause if you really want something that's going to test your ability.

Everlasting Summer frequently switches it's genre from mystery, to fantasy, to slice of life with almost no regard for the reader's sanity. That being said, it did so surprisingly well. The premise of another time and another world is so overused in modern video games, books, and movies; whoop-de-doo, another protagonist find him/herself stuck in another world and is trying to get home. The difference between these stories and Everlasting Summer's is that, you forget that it's a fantasy, you forget this isn't real. Characters felt well-thought out and I found myself impressed and surprised at the amazing storytelling, but enough generalizations.
Pros:
+The length: I consider myself a fast reader and I put 40+ hours into the game. If you're looking for something good to occupy your time with, this is it.
+Well-rounded characters: the archetypes felt a little overdone, but well done all the same
+The background art: beautifully done. I don't believe I have seen such detail in almost any other visual novel I've come across, let alone a free one.
+The Premise: alright most people don't go deep into it, but hear me out. It was believable; obviously it's fantasy, but how many times have you fallen asleep or zoned out for a minute and had no idea where you were? I actually did enjoy the smooth, quick transition to the main story.
+The Varied Endings: I won't tell any spoilers, but daaaaaaaaaang, I was not expecting some of those. Every piece of the story feels like a separate novel and that's what makes it work. The difference is, little incongruencies kept popping up that made you scratch your head and want to know what the heck was going on. But the mastery was the fact that it all came together in the end. Beautifully done.
Cons:
- The length: If you're looking for full completion on all routes or all achievements quickly, don't even look at this.
-The Main Character: there were times when I was left wondering what Semyon was possibly thinking and others when he was seemingly the most intelligent person in the camp. Just a little nitpicky with the consistencies.
-The Choices: I love when you are able to "choose your own adventure." It really helps immerse the player in what's going on in the story, but some of the choices were a little ridiculous while some just seemed like they were thrown together for a last minute draft. Not a big deal, just a tad strange.
Overall: 9/10
Everlasting Summer is an amazing story with real characters and a fantastic mix of plot lines. The writers did an amazing job of pulling the reader in and making them feel the characters. I almost feel guilty for not paying for it and you SHOULD feel guilty if you don't get it.

The best 11$ you could spend on a game. A game with a very simple premise: throw dodgeballs at other people (or bots). There are many varied levels for all styles of play and many different game modes. Don't like the default game modes? Make your own! The game creator is easy to use and you can make some pretty "interesting" game modes (super fast players with massive super-bouncy-laser balls). Not much to talk about in terms of graphics, they're minimalist, and in this case it works very well. Also worth mentioning that I don't think i've ever run into a single bug. For 11$, this game is jam-packed with features that make it worth easily 25$, maybe 30$. My only complaint is with regards to the items system and bot behaviour. If you're unaware, you get items at certain time intervals and you can combine 5 basic items to make an advanced item, and 5 advanced items to make cosmetic items. The basic items are gears, springs, bolts, nuts, and screws. I have 0 gears and about 15 of each other item, so i'm not sure if i'm just really unlucky or if the item drops need rebalancing but either way it's pretty frustrating. Bots can be pretty cheap too at times by catching balls from behind their backs or having perfect aim and perfect compensation for movement from the other side of the arena, even on medium difficulty. Despite that though, the game is a ridiculous amount of fun and is constantly being updated. There's some other features i've left out (like being able to add your own music) but I think i've explained enough why this is worth a buy. I definitely recommend picking this up for $10.99! And if you have some friends, pick up four copies for $27.99 (a massive deal if you ask me).

Divinity Original Sin was a disappointment to me at best, and I cannot understand how it achieved game of the year 2014 and 9/10 on various reviews. Here's why (TL;DR at the bottom):
DOS promised to be a Baulders Gate experience and really was not. As others have said, lore was lacking as was the story. I found the plot ot be unengaging and difficult to follow because I was reading and reading and reading, might as well have been the original Guild Wars.  Much of the dialogue could have been condensed to clear and concise conversations, but instead was full of bloat and questions that did not always make sense. I will admit that I have become accustom to cut scenes which may be part of my problem.
DOS also promised an "open world" I don't know what that may mean to you, but to me it means that you can complete tasks in any order that you desire, sure you may be encouraged to go to certain areas and not others based on the difficulty of the enemy, but don't break the game because I didn't find some piece of parchment stuffed into a stump that I didn't even know existed.  They could take a cue from Skyrim and make sure that something or someone will tell you that it even exists if it will break the game. As far as I have seen, DOS is quite linear because if you don't play it the way that it was inteded then you will not progress what little plot there is.
With regard to combat difficulty, I found it near impossible to have a favorable outcome in some encounters simply because in many areas all the enemies are immune to the same thing e.g. water, poison, fire, electricity; particularly early on I note this. I noted that enemies often felt overpowered compared to my characters even after re-gearing.  I also found combat to be clunky as I would run characters up to the enemy after my cursor had reset from the action that I chose for some reason, which was extremely frustrating even in the tactical view.
In terms of leveling, I was somewhat sad about how Larian doled out experience points and the split system of attributes and abilities drove me a bit crazy because I was never sure when I would get what. I was unimpressed with how slow it felt to level up after the first 2-3 levels.
I wanted to like this game more than I do. Don't get me wrong, I still might play this when the mood strikes, just don't expect baulder's gate. If you really want to check this game out, wait for a Steam Sale.

TLDR: Good for those who want a fresh take on the Diablo formula. Supporting the developers is worthwhile. Not a game you should play for story and choice, though the lore is fun. Good gameplay, good design, old game engine.
Good:
- Active developers who live up to their promises. Steadily updated throughout early access with meaningful content, and continue developing both DLC and new free quests and areas, as well as balance patches.
- Mod support and a small but dedicated modding scene. I've stopped playing for now but I'm excited to revisit it with mods in the future.
- Interesting and overlapping progression and character development systems.
- Characters aren't shoehorned into a few particular builds to be competitive. If you think of a character, there's usually a way to make it work. Aside from not getting enough physique, its hard to 'ruin' a character.
- Interesting and varied items
- Convenient item management with plenty of space, sorting, component merging etc.
- Good worldbuilding, plenty of text for lore nerds
Your Mileage May Vary:
- The world and all dungeons are handcrafted instead of randomized. Enemy spawns are random outside of bosses, and passages are randomly blocked or unblocked. Some random quests. Some people might swear by the random areas in Diablo and PoE.
- Often sacrifices conveniences such as quest markers, instead you need to read descriptions and familiarize yourself with the world. I like this and consider it part of the worldbuilding, but it might frustrate some.
- The lore is good but the story is formulaic. On the other hand, is that really why you are playing a Diablo style game?
- There are some elements of choice, but the differences aren't drastic and this mechanic really isn't utilized after the first act and a half.
- That Wall Where Your Numbers Are Not High Enough To Pass exists, but is usually encountered in New Game Plus Plus. It's fun enough to just move on to a new character.
Bad:
- The engine is old and doesn't always run as smoothly as you would expect for a 2016 game.
- Audio is repetitive and usually uninteresting. Put on a good podcast while you play.
- Major anticlimax after beating the final boss.

I remember reading about this game years ago in some gaming magazine and thinking, wow, that could be the next Diablo 2. I literally have not heard about this game since, and only stumbled into this game searching deep into my discovery queue. This game should be plastered all over the front page. This has got to be one of the most underrated action RPG games ever.
- Polished, smooth gameplay. It's just fun hack and slash gameplay.
- Very interesting and well designed itemization (gear/upgrades/stat variety/build options)
- A clever skill system borrowed from Titan Quest that provides deep customization (dual class etc.)
- A vast gear/weapon socketing system, also strongly reminiscent of Titan Quest (tons of options)
- Interesting features like faction reputation and the rewards that come from reaching certain stages.
- Super useful re-spec feature allowing you try out all sorts of ideas
- Lots of game options. Particularly stuff like the UI scaling feature! Easily scale ALL the UI to your preference, making things easier to read or see.
- Extremely good controller support. Can't stress this enough!
- Honestly I don't know.
- Bought the game immediately after seeing it on Steam I was honestly offended that I had not known it was released. I immediately recognized the polish of the gameplay which only got me more excited.
I decided to start with a 2-Handed Melee Shaman build and did so until around level 33 (24 hours in, in my case). I started to feel like my spec was getting a bit stale, so I decided to try out the re-spec system. To my surprise, the cost of unlearning your talents/skills was a really small amount, and I then proceeded to try out all sorts of different spec/class ideas, eventually deciding on a mix of Shaman/Nightblade.
Since then I've been enjoying a completely fresh build with all new mechanics even more than my original build. In another 30 levels, if I feel I'm bored, I'll just try out something else!
Buy this game, especially if you love action RPGs like Diablo 2 and are looking for a fix. 10/10

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a great RPG. It has likeable characters and a very nice visual style. I had wanted to try the Hyperdimension series for years and took this oppritunity to finally do so.
The only flaws I find with the game are its linear approach to story telling and the grinding. The grinding wouldn't be that bad if the dungeons weren't all copy-paste. Sometimes you need to grind 10 levels just to defeat the next boss-- something that is insanely frustrating when the majority of enemies don't give sufficient EXP. You'll end up farming specific monsters which give the most EXP with the least risk or waste to your inventory. In my personal case, I farmed the ♥♥♥♥ out of a whale for around 30 levels. Now I'm farming a stronger whale enemy who gives me 50000+ EXP in a zone which all the other monsters give an average of 500 EXP.
The music is pretty lame. The tracks aren't bad themselves but they often loop the same 1-2 songs throughout the majority of the game.
Voice acting is tight in both English and Japanese versions. Nep Nep's an obnoxious♥♥♥♥♥♥ Due to the nature of the game's humor and the particular charm of certain voices, I'm playing in English. There are many refrences to other games. From Final Fantasy and Tekken to Metal Gear and Zelda. Although the deeper you get into the game, the frequency of these jokes lessen. If you don't know games well enough, a lot of jokes will go over your head. I don't think I missed any personally, but it's so naturally woven into the tongue and cheek banter of the characters, you'd better be on point or some refrences may go completely unnoticed.
Gameplay is really fun, but can become a tad boring due to the grinding. The game's story progression is a bit predictable and repetitive too. You're almost always going to face double bosses. Lose to a boss, grind for 10 levels, beat the boss, SURPRISE THERE'S ANOTHER BOSS AFTERWARDS-- only it's not a surpise because it happens every chapter, multiple times.
I love the customization of characters, buying new clothes, etc. Although there are no extra outfits for Compa and IF, which is very annoying and doesn't make any sense. While IF is an optional character in your party, Compa has been essential to my team due to her healing abilities. It'd be nice to see her have more than just accesory changes. Neptune's outfits suck, too.
Overall I've enjoyed the game a lot more than I expected to, regardless of my critisms. I have fallen in love with the charm, as well as the artistic style of Hyperdimension and will continue to buy and play these games. I'm even interested in checking out its anime soon.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a really charming, cool and grindy game. It's not for everyone but the people who'd like it, will really like it and that's regardless of its shortcomings.
I love Hyperdimension.

-The Ninja feels too weak for being a short range class, special is an escape (or quick return)
-The Soldier is OP, a rocket launcher that can easily destroy brick and an assault rifle that is as long ranged as the sniper. Special is powerful and can be used to get at enemies behind cover.

-The Engineer is good, just remember he is defense only.
-The Scientist is OP, having access to healing blocks, ammo blocks, high damage lingering grenades, and reusable toxic traps. A bunkered scientist does not die or let anyone get close.
-The Robot is a weaker Soldier with more health for less power and his special targets himself for bombardment rather then an enemy.
The creation factor in this game is good, but can lead to games lasting as long as an hour should both teams choose to bunker down. Quite a bit of balancing is needed before I can recommend paying for this game

Divinity: Original Sin is a mixed bag. There are plenty of positive reviews out there. I personally enjoyed the game enough to beat it, but I will be focusing on the negative.  The main reason for this is there are many mechanics in the game that are frustrating as a player and I think people should at least be aware of these issues. And if RPGs already aren't your cup of tea, these issues are probably enough to make it unenjoyable.
Divinity: Original Sin goes out of its way to be misleading, time wasting, and obtuse. If you're someone who enjoys not looking at a wiki when playing a game, you'll be hard pressed to do that with this game. I'll begin with a list of scenarios that have happened to me and then go into more depth. This may come across as nitpicky, but the more you play the game the more you realize scenarios like this are fairly common.
In one particular boss fight, I struggled for 2 minutes trying to align my mouse perfectly so I could actually hit the boss. The hitbox of enemies doesn't match the actual sprite, sometimes it is much smaller. This is a problem when the screen gets cluttered and you have multiple people wailing away at a boss. Sprites also move in an "idle" animation while the game is waiting for you to make your moves, causing the tiny hit box to move around while you're trying to click. If you click at the wrong moment (very easy to do), well you just moved your character, perhaps took a reaction attack from the opponent, moved through poison or fire, and now you can perform fewer actions as you move back to your original spot to try again. Eventually, I figured out the hitbox was essentially a 2x2 grid (almost down to the pixel) centered on the persons head, but it required so much precision I got so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off trying to stab this boss, I just simply reloaded the game and waited for them to move out of the bush before starting combat. You can rotate the camera or press "b" to do a top down mode, but sometimes this doesn't help either (though top down works ~99% of the time, but it took about 60 hours and a friend to find out this particular camera angle usually works).
I decided to do a temple of trials for a particular quest line. Halfway through I realized the opponents in the temple are too strong for me to deal with at my current level. But there's a certain set of switch puzzles that took an infuriating amount of time. The game leads you to believe that if you try enough pots, barrels, and boxes the switches will open- but no, you can only use activate two of the switches with those. You need a very precise weight to trigger all the switches. That's okay, if I hadn't tried about 100 pots/barrels/boxes before looking at a Wiki to realize the game was just screwing with me at this point. Now you usually can leave areas without any real penalties, but my party contracted rot- which is essentially incurable by normal means and requires a rare item and ticks down your health by 1 health per turn until its cured (to a minimum of 1 health). Now you can use a rare item later in the dungeon, but considering I had to  reenter the temple and reaquire rot to finish the quest later, I decided not to. But this required me to run around the game for 5 hours until I found the relatively rare item to cure the condition (and it only happened because my friend happened to tell me where two were that I missed). In the meantime I had to heal my party about every minute so the rot didn't chunk my health.
There's a perception stat that helps you see hidden things, along with making you have a higher crit percent. If only it actually helped you be more perceptive against enemies.  I was derping around a cave and sort of knew some enemies were coming up, so I casted increased sight. Shame it didn't matter, the invisible enemies lurking in the bushes don't trigger until you trigger an enemy in broad sight further up no matter how perceptive your character is. They also can't be hit until they move once. So if you took the main route and kept your party close, you're now horribly flanked regardless of what statistical and personal decisions you made. Your only option is to reload the game and keep your party further back and then agro with a ranged weapon. Why not reward the player for actually planning instead of running semi-scripted battles and reward reloading the game because now you know how its scripted? It feels like most of the challenge from ordinary fights is from these scripted events given where I'm at in the game, and not the actual fight itself.
Other major complaints:
1. Nearly every fight in the first map involves fire and/or poison. Contracting one of these twice is enough to kill a party member early without healing, and if they come into contact with each other they explode.  The end result is you spend a disprorptionate amount of time running away to remove poison/fire early in the game. There aren't any real countermeasures available early, at least not ones you can afford/waste skill points on. It's nice in small doses, but it seems like the later in the game it gets the more prone my screen is getting coated with hazards from magic spells. If I had a rain spell I could just clear it, but I don't (party choices- too late to turn back, and I can't find a skill book).
2. Vendor randomness severely limits your spell and equipment choices. You don't learn spells/skills like a typical RPG where you level up and learn them- you need skill books. Which would be fine, except vendor loadouts change when you level, and if something isn't there, it isn't there. There are some presets or high probability skill books that are almost always there, but the rarer stuff is hard to get. Later in the game there's more vendors which helps alleviate this problem, but you can go through the game and not know a spell even exists until a boss smashes you with it. Some people would argue this increases the replayability of the game, but if I don't read a wiki I don't even know what I'm missing. There's also not an awful lot of choice in the early game, because what you have often comes down to what drops/spawns in dungeons.  Isn't this typically when characters start to differentiate? Leveling didn't feel particularly rewarding as a result.
3, The AI is extremely hit or miss. If you reload a game and play a fight, sooner or later the enemies do really derpy things. An example is my friend ignited an oil barrel which caused a plume of smoke around the boss. The boss sat still and burned to death because it couldn't see outside the cloud and the skeletons refused to cross the fire. A boss just sits there while eating projetiles and spells because it can't see? Another fight later has a boss that can summon a quasi-AOE fire spell that can do like 300 damage. Turns out the best way to beat him is to reload until the boss sits around♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥its turns on other stuff and just pray to your deity he doesn't ever use it. I can't help but feel something is being lost when that's the extent of the AI and how I'm using the save/load system.
4. I feel like for being a fairly open game, it goes out of its way to force me down a certain path, Which would be fine, but having to wander around until you find monsters that are about your level and just reloading/running away when you don't feels ham fisted. Enemy level spikes don't feel natural, and often I'm unsure where to go becaues its possible to have 10+ concurent quests fairly easily. The game really doesn't prime the player enough by having difficult but barely possible fights to let them know it might be a bad idea to keep wandering down this road.
I could go on, but I'm running out of space. Suffice to say there's a lot of flaws in this game, and it tends to compound as the game goes on. There's so many simple improvements that could have been made.

Child of Light is a great game, full of rich story, cute characters and absolutely stunning graphics. Aurora is an adorable protagonist, and the way she discovers her merry band of travellers feels very natural. I cannot stress enough how beautiful the art is - if you love being inspired by the way a game marries art and functionality, then you'll enjoy Child of Light just as much as I did. The combat is similar to a lot of like-minded games, but not in a bad way - the plethora of different abilities your characters can use and upgrade is fun to explore.
(As an aside, I've seen a lot of people complain about the UPlay platform but so far I haven't had a single problem - not to say that people reading this review shouldn't pay attention to the issues others have had with it, as it could very well depend on the computer running it.)
All in all, I don't think I have a bad thing to say about the game! Anything I could say would be nit-picking.
My recommendation? If you like pretty games and a cute story, go play it!

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a great RPG. It has likeable characters and a very nice visual style. I had wanted to try the Hyperdimension series for years and took this oppritunity to finally do so.
The only flaws I find with the game are its linear approach to story telling and the grinding. The grinding wouldn't be that bad if the dungeons weren't all copy-paste. Sometimes you need to grind 10 levels just to defeat the next boss-- something that is insanely frustrating when the majority of enemies don't give sufficient EXP. You'll end up farming specific monsters which give the most EXP with the least risk or waste to your inventory. In my personal case, I farmed the ♥♥♥♥ out of a whale for around 30 levels. Now I'm farming a stronger whale enemy who gives me 50000+ EXP in a zone which all the other monsters give an average of 500 EXP.
The music is pretty lame. The tracks aren't bad themselves but they often loop the same 1-2 songs throughout the majority of the game.
Voice acting is tight in both English and Japanese versions. Nep Nep's an obnoxious♥♥♥♥♥♥ Due to the nature of the game's humor and the particular charm of certain voices, I'm playing in English. There are many refrences to other games. From Final Fantasy and Tekken to Metal Gear and Zelda. Although the deeper you get into the game, the frequency of these jokes lessen. If you don't know games well enough, a lot of jokes will go over your head. I don't think I missed any personally, but it's so naturally woven into the tongue and cheek banter of the characters, you'd better be on point or some refrences may go completely unnoticed.
Gameplay is really fun, but can become a tad boring due to the grinding. The game's story progression is a bit predictable and repetitive too. You're almost always going to face double bosses. Lose to a boss, grind for 10 levels, beat the boss, SURPRISE THERE'S ANOTHER BOSS AFTERWARDS-- only it's not a surpise because it happens every chapter, multiple times.
I love the customization of characters, buying new clothes, etc. Although there are no extra outfits for Compa and IF, which is very annoying and doesn't make any sense. While IF is an optional character in your party, Compa has been essential to my team due to her healing abilities. It'd be nice to see her have more than just accesory changes. Neptune's outfits suck, too.
Overall I've enjoyed the game a lot more than I expected to, regardless of my critisms. I have fallen in love with the charm, as well as the artistic style of Hyperdimension and will continue to buy and play these games. I'm even interested in checking out its anime soon.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a really charming, cool and grindy game. It's not for everyone but the people who'd like it, will really like it and that's regardless of its shortcomings.

Saints Row IV... What a letdown. Granted, it was still fun, but man... everything about it was just disappointing. SR3 was better in regards to almost everything. Yes, the fact that you've got superpowers is entertaining... for about ten minutes. Then you realize that they aren't really too helpful as one would let on. In fact, they become a chore to try and use effectively over your guns.
Because of these superpowers, a lot of core gameplay mechanics I liked from 3 begin to vanish, one of them (and a rather big one to me) being cars. I remember back in the days of SR3 when I'd invite a buddy to play co-op, and then spend a brief moment showing off my favorite cars that I've aquired through hours of gameplay. In SR4, why would you want a car when you can literally sprint faster than the fastest type of car in the game?
The plot is fine, but that's just it. It's not great, or even good. It's just... fine. Solid, yes, but meaningful? I personally don't think so. All of what happens takes place in a virtual reality, one that has a very, VERY annoying visual effect that pixelates random objects around you (whether that be a building, a car... what have you) and then re-focuses them back to how they're supposed to be. The worst part is that the only way to turn it off is through cheats. Through cheats! Really?!
Enough about that horrid visual effect. What's really bothersome is that since all of what happens happens in a virtual reality, I constantly had the feeling that what I was doing was meaningless. I invisioned SR4 to take place in Washington DC. I wanted the giant Saints Flow monster to rip the Washington Memorial apart, and then, after his demise, perhaps see it being put back together again. But no. Instead, I got a virtual reality Steelport, with only one type of enemy (aliens) as opposed to four (the cops and the three gangs) in the last title.
This game might've been more fun had it not launched under a Saints Row title. Because of the success from the last title though... I just can't recommend it. Look at it more as a DLC for Saints Row 3, as it was meant to be. That said, wait for it to go on sale, and you might not be as disappointed as I was.

Perhaps ironically, I was spurred to write this by the announcement of XCOM 2. Which has to say something, that I've regularly played this game since it was released.
XCOM: EU is a wonderful turn-based squad-level strategy game. Both the strategic and tactical levels are solidly developed (tactical probably moreso, honestly) to deliver a tight game where deaths feel like they have weight and you're almost always pushing against a force that feels just a little overwhelming.
The Good:
-Solid, functional interface giving you almost all the data you need (better LOS projection pls).
-Squad-building is enjoyable and creates interesting teams that excel in different environments.
-Characterization is fun and tight--there's a lot of personality in the randomly-given nicknames and short audio clips.
-Especially early and mid game feel tightly tuned to be difficult, but manageable.
The Bad:
-The endgame kinda drags, and if you drag it out intentionally, you will end up dramatically outclassing the alien menace. (compare to Xenonauts, where the invasion escalates over time to eventually become almost totally unmanageable)
-Tech tree isn't super interesting--little reason to take one approach over another.
The Different:
-Cut out almost all of the micromanagement of the original (I like this, though Xenonauts hit on a middle ground that also worked very well)
-Expansion is great and adds a lot to the game--would definitely recommend buying it alongside.

Though the story line of the campaign just sort of dropped off at the end, the main quest line was very good.
There are plenty of sidequests to keep you busy for a long time, but for replayability it won't be of much value. Once you level up all your stats (not terribly difficult to do) there would be no point in starting over from ground zero.
Combat mechanics and animations are fluid and the panorama view of the open world is beautiful.
The only dislike I have for the game is the inability to level up specific weapons. You are constantly on the hunt for new, higher level weapons, and while this added to the desperate feeling of the game at lower levels, it became an annoyance at higher levels when I just wanted to keep the weapons I had fallen in love with.
Overall, 9.5 out of 10. Great game.

I've played a lot of hours of a lot of MMO's. From WoW (Where I will admit I was a Wrath baby), to RIFT, Tera, ArcheAge (Rip

Stands the test of time.

Block N Load is something new and fresh to the game market. With it's catchy music, unique art style and competitive multiplayer, this game brings a lot of fun and friends to your PC. Each character you choose has a totally different fighting style and Silhouette, they each have a role to play on this team based multiplayer. Pick the wrong character setup and you may not do to well so choose wisely.
You are a 5 man team facing another 5 man team with your own side of the map. Once the match begins you have a few minuites to prep your base by setting up traps, reinforcing things or building anything you can think of that may help win the game. During this time you cannot see or go to the other teams base, once the timer hits zero each team is free to attack. You may still build after the timer but you will have non friendlys attacking you at any time. The way to win is to attack they enemies cube, a small square genereator looking cube. Depending on the map chosen in the beginning by voting, you may have up to 3 cubes to destroy.  Once one of the two teams destroys all of the cubes it is game over where you can look at your stats before heading back to start a new mach.
I fell in love with Block N Load. It's refreshing to see something new on the market with a great community including friends from all over the world. Everyone is there to help you because they need you in order to win. The devs are very good at responding to any questions, concearns or just to chat occasionally. I find myself not wanting to stop playing even when I need to. Every game I find myself on the edge of my seat as I get into fast paced battles with other players seeing who can outsmart our destroy the other.  Each play is different and the game can change and flip at any moment, you will find yourself stuck fighting and defending untill one team breaks through enemy lines taking you and your cube down or vise versa. That is what makes me love this game, that is why I reccomend this game. No other game can you laugh, fight, and sometimes cry all in one match.

- Incredible for use as a drinking game (local multiplayer). The game lends itself to unparalleled social/competitive (local multiplayer) gameplay thanks to the (often fast-paced, and frantic) 1v3 chaotic brawling.
- Narration, sound effects, and music are sensational, giving a strong sense of nostalgia. The narration is kooky as hell, and damn it works well.
- Game art feels spot-on. Pixelated graphics aren't everyone's cup of tea, though this game makes it work extremely well.
- Put together perfectly. Every aspect of the game feels as though it was developed with all the other parts of the game in mind. Very polished.
Cons (or lack thereof):
- The game does not (yet) have online multiplayer, however the developers have been very clear in stating that this is one of their primary focuses for addition to the game, moving forward.
Summary:
Do yourself a favour and grab this game. You won't regret it. Get a handful of mates together, and dive in, head first. It takes more than a great game to have me write a Steam review, and this game makes no exception to that rule.

Not sure why this game got so much love. It's Oregon Trail, with grid-based combat. That's not a bad thing, but it's not amazing either.
Takes just over 7 hours for a playthrough. I have no idea how anyone takes 12+ hours as some other reviews put it. It's not like this is some open world game where you can make choices to extend the gameplay. I can only assume people went afk during fights? /shrug
And, that 7 hours is padded by lots of stretches of time watching your caravan enter a town or waypoint, ever so glacially, while you twiddle your fingers.
There are, presumably, randomly generated events that occur while you're traveling the countryside, but they pop very rarely, so it's mostly just you watching your caravan glacially walk between point A and point B. Definitely should have drastically increased the encounter rate.
As for the reviews that claim there are deep effects from your choices in those events? Hogswash. Utter baloney.
And, balancing your supplies, rest, etc? No, not really. Morale is completely unimportant. Had the worst morale for pretty much the entire game. No food at all for about 1/3 of the game. Was completely unimportant.
Combat isn't terribly strategic, and the last "boss" battle is extreamly easy if you just focus on the boss and ignore the minions. That said, you can up  the difficulty. But, as there's  not a ton of strategy to be had, upping the difficulty doesn't really do much for the game.
As for the story. This won a BAFTA. I have no idea how. There's a hint of an epic story in the background, but what you're actually given in the game amounts to very little, with a big jump in the story in the midpoint, making you wonder what the point even was of 1/2 of the 2 sides of the story.
In conclusion, the game would  have been drastically improved if it didn't have so much "dead" time while playing, just watching your caravan walk across the screen. More events. Drastically shorten the pointless 1-3 minutes of just watching your caravan enter a town, etc. A playthrough is 7 hours, but you're only going to spend half that actually playing, rather than just watching your screen, twiddling your thumbs. Not sure what could be done to combat without just starting over, but it's incredibly basic. Perhaps more mobility to spice things up for the enemy?
Oh, and it'd be remiss not to mention the game is only $4.99 on iOS and Android, both of which can be streamed to a TV. $20 on consoles and PC seems a stretch, especially since this is a 3 episode game, and most definitely not a AAA game ($60 for complete game would be AAA pricing).

FTL is a space-faring roguelike where you are the captain of a starship. You control your crew members which vary in race and abilities, as well as the systems of your ship. The ultimate goal is to reach the Federation base to deliver vital intel to defeat the Rebel fleet. You encounter the rebels, allies and pirates across your journey. Will you accomplish your mission?
Since the update that the developers gave this game, there are three difficulties to choose from Easy, Normal, or Hard. There are several different ships to choose from, as well as different system layouts for each ship. Even if you choose the same ship and layout, every playthough will be significantly different. Encounters in space, as well as the map layout in each sector are randomized every time. The currency in the game "scrap" which is used to upgrade your ship and purchase from stores is also random from the rewards.
If you like a challenge, this game can really deliver. Hard mode lowers your scrap rewards, forcing you to make hard choices as a captain. It's a battle for survival in a harsh galaxy. Being able to pause the game (bound to space by default) is your main defense. It gives you time to issue commands to your crew as well as change system power or target specific systems in the enemy ship.
Try unbinding pause if you really want something that's going to test your ability.

The Banner Saga is a great game that really took me by suprise initally.  Visually the game is absolutely gorgeous.  It's probably the first thing you noticed about this game in trailers, screenshots, or when booting up the game.  Everything is hand drawn and animated like some sort of classic Disney film, except that this Disney film is filled with bloody Norse battles during the Ragnarok.  This game's visual design is not only unique and exciting, but really helps bring the game world to life.  This game will also age extremely well visually.
The actual game part of this game is split in two.  First up is a turn based, grid based RPG tactics type game.  It's not a complex game, despite featuring stats for characters and unqiue classes.  At the end of the day it's about proper positioning and class abilities.  The game uses a unique health and armour system, which is great, and has a satisfying amount of classes to bring depth to the table.  It's got depth to it and it doesn't overstay it's welcome, making it a fun system all around.
The other half of this game is the text based RPG story.  While half this game is about defending a caravan from bandits, armies and other undesirables, the other half of this game is leading your caravan and making the tough choices.  When I say leading I don't mean you pick where your caravan goes; all that is set.  What you determine is how to manage resources, clansmen and fighters, and moral decisions.  It's pretty fun and well written to boot.
The final component of this game is it's story, which is fantastic.  This game is meant to be the first part in a saga, and it's absolutely awesome in it's writing and atmosphere.  I don't want to spoil much, but here is the premise:  You are a caravan leader attemping to guide your people to safety through the apocalype in a norse mythology inspired world.  Along the way you discover more about the world and get sucked into the fate of it.  I know the concept of a 'good; story is pretty subjective, but I feel that I can say that the banner saga has an objectively good story.  It is well written, does not over use twists or shocks, and has a strong world background.  It uses multiple themes to express the varied elements of the story.
Overall, the great visuals, gameplay and story of this game come together to convey a wonderful and engaing world that is worth visiting. Best part is that this is still a relatively cheap game that is well worth the price. Be sure to pick up it's sequel as well to continue the Saga if you like it!

This is a solid team shooter with a lot going on. The original KF was a fairly decent game, but for me, it had a lot of negatives. Perk progression was VERY grindy. The game wasn't very fluid. Graphics were okay but not fantastic. Gameplay modes were very limited (but I did enjoy the story/objective based modes). Whilst KF2 tackled most of the issues I had with the original early into it's release, the game has continued to develop and become a better and better title. KF2 is a game that I think I will keep coming back to for a long time, and I think you should too!
The game plays smooth and feels more fluid than the original. The graphics are greatly improved. The devs have now added daily, weekly and seasonal challenges to keep things fresh. Whilst the original KF only had the Patriarch as a boss, KF2 had 2 bosses on launch and has since added another two - I definitely think that this is a massive step in the right direction and it would be great to see even more bosses over time. I know it's a small thing, but the user interface of this game is also massively better and more user friendly than the original. The game has also added a skin/loot system where you can get crate drops by playing, tickets to trade for items in seasonal games, items for completing weekly or seasonal challenges or you can just buy loot through the market place for cash. I know that some people don't like skins in games, but it's entirely optional and I think it's a great system, especially considering just how much free loot/skins you can get for free!
Levelling each perk is still a grind, especially at later levels, but on the whole the process is much easier and it's still massively better than the system for the original. I would actually like there to be more story/objective modes added. I think that in a game which relies and focusses so much on teamwork, it would be a shame not to have some storylines added like they had in the first game... I wouldn't mind returning to the steampunk fairground either, even if it was just a re-skin of the original story mode in the first game.
All in all this is a very good team shooter which is a massive improvement on the original KF game. The devs are continually adding new content and are continually improving the game. If you are a fan of crazy, fun and slightly weird shooters, you're doing yourself a disservice if you aren't playing this game right now.

Positive points :
Unique gameplay - First, I don't know any other dodgeball game, and second it differs a lot from your usual fps as you don't have any weapon but should instead pick up balls to throw at your ennemies. Those balls taking time to move allow for dodging or catching the ball thrown at you, catching it will also eliminate the thrower. Also, the movement system is original too, as being a robot on wheels allows you taking ramps to make big jumps and such (you also have a classic jump key in addition) and you will keep moving until you use brakes, giving you the opportunity to look around for targets while moving in a straight line for example. Add to that some powerups (such as Jetpacks or Bigger Balls) among others, and you've got a game like no other with lot of possibilities.
Skill-based gameplay - Balls being affected by gravity and taking time to move around, you have to predict where your opponent is going to hit him. Add to this the possibility of still touching after a single bounce to hit enemies hidden and such, it opens for quite some possibilities. However, your opponent is not powerless as outside of dodging the shot, he can catch it (which eliminates you instead), or even deflect it by throwing a ball at it or use an held ball as a shield. But that's not all as you have a lot of possible trick shots (i.e. 'Dunk', a shot from above, or harder, an 'Helicopter', done by doing a 360 while in air just before throwing the ball)
Simple and fun gameplay - It doesn't take much time to learn how to play the game as it can be resumed to throwing balls at enemies/target and avoiding balls thrown at you. Even though you'll still be far from mastering various things (aim, trick shots, etc...), you can start playing multiplayer once you've got the basics (controls and such) without feeling too bad compared to more experienced players. With the endless possibilities with ramps, trickshots, powerups, etc..., and the variety in maps and game modes (see below), you will have a lot of fun and won't get bored easily.
Great variety of maps - Quite a lot of maps (16 atm) and still growing (atleast 3 are being worked on as i'm writing this), from simple maps to complex ones. Each one is unique, with different layouts and allowing for different playing styles. It goes from simple square maps to multi-floor maps with lots of ramps, or even a level with quarter pipes and skatepark-like ramps.
Great variety of game modes - Again, you've got a lot of choice there, ranging from the classic Deathmatch or Elimination modes to Hoops, a basketball-like mode, or Super Ball, where you have to survive as much as you can while holding a golden ball, Score Battles where you win score through trick shots. Some are simple, other are complex or better fit for experienced players, but overall the variety will keep you busy. Also, all of those games can be played either in teams or FFA (although some aren't really fit for FFA).
Decent amount of singleplayer content - You've got the main solo mode with Arcade, where you try to survive through rounds and bosses, while trying to score as much points as you can (to buy various upgrades) aswell as several challenges with various objectives (those can be survival, scoring, etc...), with all of those modes (both Arcade & Challenges) having their own leaderboads for you to compete with other players and showing you're the best. You can also play some normal matches with bots, which while not perfect are still quite well done (also those bots can be used to fill multiplayer games).
Good soundtrack - The soundtrack fits perfectly the game. Although, maybe a bit small but not enough to feel too repetitive, it is really good with none of the tracks sounding like another one, and them enhancing the game's ambiance. And if you're not fan of it, or would just prefer playing to your own playlist, you can even replace with a Spotify playlist
Unique ambiance - The 'disco' part of the game with the lights and music is also quite unique in its kind. Graphics, lightings and soundtrack all works well together in making the game feel like no other.
Robot customization - There is a great number of options to customize your robot as you want, from changing its color (only for FFA) to setting the face it will make on victory or defeat. Add to this a great variety of craftable cosmetics (you will obtain craft components through playing), ranging from hats to ball and ball trails and even replacing your robot's body. Of course, all of those are tradeable and even sellable on the market.
LAN Multiplayer & Split Screen - You can play on LAN multiplayer, working the same as Online Multiplayer, or Split Screen up to 4 Players with your friends (if you have 4 gamepads). The simple gameplay allows for everyone being able to play properly and have some fun. Add to this the unique ambiance and it will make a great LAN party (especially with some good speakers for everyone to enjoy).
Great developper - The dev is a single guy (Erik Asmussen) who keeps improving his game, even two years after its release. There's usually an update atleast every 2 months, adding either new maps, gamemodes, cosmetics or other additions/improvements. Additionally, he is very open and active on the Steam Forums, sharing infos on the next updates (and asking for the community's opinions), answering questions, etc...
Negative points :
Small community - As good as the community is, it is quite small, and there might not be that much player outside of active hours.
Lack of a competitive scene - The skill-based gameplay would fit pretty well for competitions, but as a consequence of the small community, there's not enough people to develop a structured competitive scene.
Conclusion :
It's an excellent indie game, with a unique gameplay and ambiance which will bring you a lot of fun. However, as a lot of other multiplayer indie games, it suffers from not being known enough and not having a big enough userbase.

For a game that prides itself on roleplay, it's practically nonexistent. The storyline isn't exactly compelling, either. You play a couple of frail, overhyped losers sent to solve a murder and then left to find your own way without any guidance. Exploration consists of wandering around aimlessly, clicking through dialogue trees in order to gain precious XP, stealing ridiculously valuable items that people just leave lying around, venturing into the wilderness to die a horrible death, and quicksaving and reloading ad nauseum whenever anything goes wrong, because if something goes wrong you die.
The game is deliberately and sadistically obtuse, giving you lots of options at character creation without telling you that most of them are worse than useless. Every ability point, skill point, and talent is somehow simultaneously precious and yet meaningless because you can find items lying around that give you big boosts to your various stats. Why create a thief type character when you can just pour all your valuable points into skills that give you abilities like Teleportation that are simultaneously overpowered and yet necessary and then wear a random pair of gloves that'll make you a better pickpocket and sneakthief than an unequipped rogue who relies on their own abilities? You can't really feel special when all your advantages come from stuff that you picked up out of some random innkeeper's basement. The game manages to boast a vast array of random magical gear Diablo-style without any of it feeling special or interesting.
Folks who like the game tend to talk about the old-school difficulty like it's a selling point. That's fair enough, if that's your thing. I love Dark Souls, which is also infamous for its difficulty and merciless learning curve, so I can appreciate that even if it's not my thing (I couldn't get into games like Jagged Alliance 2, either, which Original Sin reminds me a lot of in terms of difficulty). Personally, I like more meaningful roleplaying in my RPGs, especially when the give-and-take between the heroes is supposed to be one of the big highlights of the game.

So after re visting and spending a few more hours in the game as a Ocultist/rogue. i have found some of my original issues false but still found issues with my own Personal taste that made this game good but not interesting enough to continue.

So I just got the season pass to get The Folllowing and the other new DLC today. I loved the original game, me and my boyfriend are currently in a two person game.This is a normal difficulty game.  Currently we're still in the slums (back tracking for sidequests) We discovered first off, you run a TON faster, it's almost like you have a natural speed boost, just without the stamina boost to match. We've also discovered that if you're in different outfits your character moves slightly different when standing still. The Ninja has a tigher, smaller posture, like you're ready to bolt off the nearest building and end up 3 blocks away. The Urban Explorer makes you look angrier, darker and well... angry just fits his tone to the character.  (Yes, we're the kind of nerds to notice the random crap like this xD)
Also, GRAPHICS, HOLY CRAP GRAPHICS! It's smoother, cleaner, prettier, the weather system REALLY shows. you can see individual rain drops hitting the ground/buildings/assorted random objects, the wind is cleaner, very realistic, the wind rustling through the trees matches beautifully.  The runners have an upgraded programming that makes them more intelligent (to a degree in terms of where they can climb) and... they seem faster and more aggressive. Alright... tried night mode, and whoever is in charge really needs to evict the new neighbors... They're quiet rude. It's changed a bit, the night stalkers are faster, meaner, deal more damage, come in larger numbers, summon larger hoards of volatiles and have gotten uglier. Not to mention, they're much harder to kill... I got stupidly lucky and managed to kill one from the back with 2 shots from the Golden Double Barrel but that seemed to have been a fluke and it took 10 shots for the next one. You either find the sweet spot, or you run out of ammo trying to find it. Make sure you're stocked up on night vision boosters, not being able to see now can be a death sentence when before it was just a minor annoyance to accidentally fall off a building.
The merchants now have pictures of every item they have for sale, so if you're looking at buying a katana you can see what it looks like. The new guns, we've so far found a golden double barrel shotgun (2550 damage) that will happily take out small groups of zombies, only downside is it only has 2 shots per load, so it's a slower weapon but the damage and destruction it causes are so worth it. Just as a side note on the shotgun... When you get this weapon, find a group of like 20+ zombies and just start shooting into the crowd, the reload is so fast if you're far enough away (about 20 or so meters) none of them can get you and you turn the entire street into jelly. The gun my boyfriend got is the Advanced Military Rifle (274 damage) which is replacing his Camo Military Rifle (137 damage) he can't stop raving about the damage increase and how it seems more accurate from the hip while moving. The Golden German Pistol (331 damage) similar accuracy and handling to the original German pistol but with more damage and a bit more accurate. Reload is similar to the regular German Pistol. The Engraved Semi-Auto Shotgun (2550 damage) rapid fire compared to the Golden (8 shots vs. 2 for Golden) not as good as the Golden Double Barrel it seems as there's a definite accuracy difference between the Golden and Engraved, Engraved having a slower reload time. But overall the shotgun has had some MAJOR improvements and will definitely be used more than it was in the original game where you could be 2 meters away and still miss the zombie... The Advanced Police Rifle (368 damage) basically the sniper rifle for Dying Light (at least so far without testing the crossbow yet) watched my boyfriend pull off a ~75m headshot on a zombie. Two shots to kill a runner, the handling when sniping "is sweet" (his words haha) but if you've got something up in your face it's just like the old police rifle but with more damage, awkward and misses some times. So far, if you find a gold colored weapon, it'll most likely just become your new best friend.
(Note: None of these weapons have been upgraded or adjusted in anyway via weapon upgrades)

This game is truly amazing.  It has everything I have wanted in an MMO for a long while.  You have instanced player housing and can visit other players homes.  You actually get buffs from the furniture and rewarded based on interior design.  You can craft furniture, or when hunting animals or crafting you have a chance to get a wolf head to mount on the wall or a set of cookware for the walls, a plate of food for the table, etc.  You can build a boat and sail into the ocean for some fishing with friends.  You can invest contribution which is basically a persistent level between alts that allows you to earn money passively/make advanced items.  With contribution you can buy homes for workers that you send into the world to get materials and earn you money.
There are quite a few differenty character classes for both males and females(they are genderlocked though), so a lot of variety there.  The combat is very action oriented but more like Dynasty warriors. That being said, that in an mmo is unheard of and amazing.
Lastly, after a small amount of time investment, you can afk earn money, so even if you don't play alot, if you have time to periodically touch the game, repair equipment, feed workers, and play the black spirit adventure board game; then you'll have tons of money and materials to work with for life skills or to support buying new equipment.

One of the best open world zombie games to come out in forever, or maybe ever? Sorry DayZ. Take Dead Island with a hint of Mirror's Edge and you end up with Dying Light. The graphics are beautiful, the gameplay is solid, and the story is better than most games today but still not the greatest. Techland put a lot of work into this game to make it very enjoyable, even after the disappointment from Dead Island. There's nothing better than running around, chopping limbs off of zombies and smashing bandits heads open. As for the night time game play, let's just say playing in a dark room with headphones on may not be the best idea. However, night time is scary as hell and it's a great experience. The base game was well worth it, and I was glad that I ended up buying it and beating it.
As for The Following, I can already tell this DLC is going to be so worth it. The first 10 minutes of The Following is great. You start in the new map immediately and you can see the scenery from where you start. Open fields with 50+ zombies standing around, mountains in the distance..awesome. The driving mechanics are solid, and I can't wait to customize my buggy. That's all I can say for The Following as I need to finish it to complete the review for it.
Dying Light is worth the $$ if you can afford it, and want a true zombie experience. This is probably the only game in the past 10 years that can get zombies right, and I'm not counting Resident Evil.

I went into this optimistically, and holy hell was I surprised to have my expectations blown out of the water!
Pros:
- Unique premise for a game.
- Challenging AI (if playing solo). It's possible to pick the pace of the game by including 1-3 AI players on top of the hero you control.
- Incredible for use as a drinking game (local multiplayer). The game lends itself to unparalleled social/competitive (local multiplayer) gameplay thanks to the (often fast-paced, and frantic) 1v3 chaotic brawling.
- Narration, sound effects, and music are sensational, giving a strong sense of nostalgia. The narration is kooky as hell, and damn it works well.
- Game art feels spot-on. Pixelated graphics aren't everyone's cup of tea, though this game makes it work extremely well.
- Put together perfectly. Every aspect of the game feels as though it was developed with all the other parts of the game in mind. Very polished.
Cons (or lack thereof):
- The game does not (yet) have online multiplayer, however the developers have been very clear in stating that this is one of their primary focuses for addition to the game, moving forward.
Summary:
Do yourself a favour and grab this game. You won't regret it. Get a handful of mates together, and dive in, head first. It takes more than a great game to have me write a Steam review, and this game makes no exception to that rule.

I beat this game on my Xbox 360 years ago, I got it on my PC because it's still a great game to play.
• Great comedy
• Character customization
• Good o' South Park humor
• Great plot and side quest to do
• Collectible Chinpokomon
• Thousands of weapons and equipment
• Princess Kenny
• A big open world to explore at your own pace
• This was before Ubisoft required you to use Uplay.
I do have a few things to say about this game, though of how great it is, it does suffer from some things that any RPG would consider essential.
• The New Game+ doesn't add anything new.
• There is no gear over level 14.
• Like I said before, it has a big open world to explore. However, once you beat the game, some areas get locked due to story related events. Meaning if you missed a Chinpokomon or some gear in some areas, it's no longer accessible.
• With that being said, there are some things you can miss in the game, resulting you to lose a chance at some Achievements and will either have to get them on the next run or start over. Such as Chinpokomon and Friends, which can be annoying if you're trying to get the Achievement for it, considering there are 120 friends.
• This is nitpicky, but there is a glitch unlocks an Achievement that I didn't even do the requirements for, which was a bit weird.
Overall though, this is a great game to play just for the South Park humor and gameplay. In terms of replayability, there isn't much.

Wow, okay this will be my first legit review for any game ever. please keep in mind that these sort of games are my favourite kind to play, so althoug imperfect, i may be a little biassed towards it.I was very cautious when considering whether to buy this game or not. The Steam reviews have not been so good so I really fought with myself for two days before crumbling under the pressure and buying it. I mean what's the worst that can happen? I paid $6. After playing for a little bit over the span of two days, i have quickly realised that this game has consumed over thirty hours of my life. I realised that Steam reviews can't always be trusted, considering that this game has less than perfect reviews, but I do know this type of game isn't for everybody. Everybody has their tastes, and I STRONGLY suggest you at least give this game a try. You get a free two hours afterall. I will warn you though, you may easily waste two hours creating a character so i suggest you use a base character and go straight into the game to really get a feel for it. I'll also say that you should NOT go into this game expecting an RPG game. it is NOT an RPG. I would consider this game closer to a Sandbox MMO, due to the fact that you'll find yourself not really roleplaying all that much like you would in games like Skyrim or Runescape even. You can be a fisherman in this game or a trader, but you'll feel the same way doing both of those activities, although they are so diverse. so now that we have that out of the way, I will say that this is one of the best Sandbox games that I have played in ages.
First impressions: I will admit that I still have no idea what Im doing in this game and there are all sorts of items and little things that buff your items that I have no experience with. Google hasn't been able to really help me always, but so far 99% of the players in the game are more than happy to assist me. I have barely explored the world, so there will be all sorts of features probably left out of this review, but after thirty hours, i feel that a review is appopriate.
Pros:
-Epic combat
-Beautiful graphics
-A dozen of skills to spend hours training
-Massive open world
-Decent servers (mostly)
-Autorun feature (no quick teleport so this feature is a godsend)
-An interesting Node system that allows you to own properties (I haven't fully explored this feature so please Google it if you're interested in learning more)
-A marketplace that allows players to trade universally with each other
-Guilds/ Clans allow you to interact with other players and become a part of the community
Cons:
-you need to pay real money to really make your character look any different
-The game can stutter at times
-servers are sometimes unstable during the day
-Sometimes the chat can become a toxic mess (can disable)
-The UI can get a little spammy (can disable)
-Sometimes it really feels like there's too much to do and might become overwhelmed
-Once you get to a higher level, killing enemies becomes very very easy
-Can't do individual trading with other players
All in all there really is no need to ever pay more money than what you paid in the original price. most things that can be bought with real money can be aquired from a few days of grinding. This game is not perfect, but it has been such an enjoyable experience for me. The best advice i can give anybody considering buying this game is to not expect an rpg like WoW or Runescape, but instead expect an openworld Sandbox style MMO. Another thing to keep in mind is to not take this game too seriously. I have seen countless people complain over "the grind" in the game istelf. yes there does involve a bit of grinding, but if you play this game somewhat casually to have a fun time and waste some time, then the grind feels much more enjoyable. For people who have played Runescape (Specifically Classic), the grind in that is much worse than the grind in this so it shouldn't be a problem for those people. Players will definitely need to invest some time in this game to get far, but so far after thirty hours, it has not once felt like a chore to me. I STRONGLY recommend that anybody buy this game and give it a try for $6, but i do believe that once this game is no longer on sale, The price is still very much worth it. The game normally is $10.99. Even investing a mere twenty hours into this game means you've gotten your money's worth, and I know that for me, I can easily put 100 more hours into this game. After casually playing for thirty hours, I have ONLY discovered 8% of the world. This game truly has so much content in it. Im so pleased that this game has been brought to Steam because before that, I had never heard of it. i would love to see this community grow bigger in the future. I strongly advise you to at least give this game a try. You may be strongly pleased, and if not, that's perfectly okay too! This review definitely isn't very well thought out or written, but after over a day of constant enjoyment, I figured that I had to write a review for this game, because I strongly believe that this game is of higher quality than what the overall rating for this game displays. After 100 hours i might realise there's a fatal error in this game, and if there is, I'll be sure to update the review. For the time being I know there are many many people on the fence whether to buy this game or not, and i hope I helped a few people make a final decision.
*Update* Sorry for any confusion when I list this game as a "Sandbox MMO" I know it's sort of vague, but I believe that calling this game an RPG is a little misleading because you'll find that you don't really do any real roleplaying in this game. There is a roleplay chat, but people just use it to casually discuss certain things about the game. People with a good imagination can easily roleplay in this game, however. ie. Fisherman,trader, lumberjack, cook, ect. I'll try to find a better thing to call this game. A fantasy Sandbox MMO? It definitely has Rolep-laying potential, but I don't think many people see it as an RPG. The reason I define it more as a "Sandbox game" is because you can run around for hours doing nothing of any importance and you can have fun. I love wandering around without an reason similarly to how i would in minecraft. All in all everybody might have a different genre to consider this game, but I do apologise if I caused any confusion by considering it simply a "sandbox MMO"

What I would pay to have a couple of friends that I could play this game with on the couch.
The game is so good, that even playing solo (when it's obviously intended as a multiplayer game) is sooo charming.
It's a free-for-all but slightly asymmetric game that allows the players to essentially choose their own dungeon crawl, by controlling pretty much every meaningful piece of the game other than dungeon generation.
You start just like any other arcade game of the like, 2-4 players (if solo, with CPUs) choose their name and deity. Start by being the hero while the others are the enemies in the dungeon rooms. They act as spirits that can possess the enemies and begin attacking you. Once dead they move on to possess something else to ruin your day.
I was clueless and turned the CPU up on Normal because I thought they were on my team. WRONG. Once your time as the hero has been ended, you take the place of your killer and become the spirit now trying to kill the new hero!
Once the chapters end, you get to use your points to upgrade your enemies to what I'm sure becomes a chaotic end. Eventually boss battles come into play, but who gets to fight it?!
Again, this game is totally playable alone, but you will be VERY aware that you're missing out on a lot of fun by playing with others.

There is a lot of meat to this game. It offers you a great deal of customization regarding your character, and multiple activities when exploring the world. You are not limited to killing monsters as you move forward, you get the opportunity to explore side-areas, save various NPCs that will meet you back in town and fill the cities, earn points to deepen your customization, and probably somet stuff I forgot about.
The game runs well, plays well, and is offered at a very attractive price. The difficulty is great and I enjoy the ability to use the "Veteran" mode right from the beginning to make it more challenging. It lasts long enough that you won't feel like you were sold an unfinished product.
My one complaint so far? Visually, the game could be better. I'm not talking about the quality of the graphics, but rather the art design. The characters, the monsters and the environment "blend" with each others a little too much. When your screen is filled with multiple monsters and spell effects, the result is not always attractive. With that said, this is my one problem with the game.
Overall, for the price it's sold at and how much fun it has to offer, I recommend it for fans of the genre. If you're not a fan of Hack'n'Slash games, I don't think this is the game that will convert you. If you like the genre already, this will give you something to sink your teeths into.

Perhaps ironically, I was spurred to write this by the announcement of XCOM 2. Which has to say something, that I've regularly played this game since it was released.
XCOM: EU is a wonderful turn-based squad-level strategy game. Both the strategic and tactical levels are solidly developed (tactical probably moreso, honestly) to deliver a tight game where deaths feel like they have weight and you're almost always pushing against a force that feels just a little overwhelming.
The Good:
-Solid, functional interface giving you almost all the data you need (better LOS projection pls).
-Squad-building is enjoyable and creates interesting teams that excel in different environments.
-Characterization is fun and tight--there's a lot of personality in the randomly-given nicknames and short audio clips.
-Especially early and mid game feel tightly tuned to be difficult, but manageable.
The Bad:
-The endgame kinda drags, and if you drag it out intentionally, you will end up dramatically outclassing the alien menace. (compare to Xenonauts, where the invasion escalates over time to eventually become almost totally unmanageable)
-Tech tree isn't super interesting--little reason to take one approach over another.
The Different:
-Cut out almost all of the micromanagement of the original (I like this, though Xenonauts hit on a middle ground that also worked very well)
-Expansion is great and adds a lot to the game--would definitely recommend buying it alongside.

The early access bit:
TL;DR - It's an excellent game, well worth the price of admission. Everything seems to work, and work well.
This is a very simple to learn RTS, with good level design (thus far), a pretty good base mechanic, and a brilliant art style (literally and figuratively, the lighting is a bit intense).
The basic premise is that you control a constantly-spawning highly mutable lifeform, and by taking and holding various points around the map you gain access to different sets of abilities for your units. Basic units spawn at a constant rate, and the biggest challenge lies in determining what to turn them into and where to attack. Resource management boils essentially down to "how long do I wait before expanding", which is a simple enough thing to measure.
The good stuff:
As I've said, the art design is excellent. Seriously, everything is pretty clear in its function at a glance and the game looks gorgeous.
It's got a really intuitive interface. Even novice RTS players should be able to pick this up and figure out just about everything extremely easily.
Speedy matches aren't something I'm used to in any RTS. It's nice to be able to knock out a quick game or two instead of an hours-long slog sometimes.
It's quickly engaging, and the additional features that are supposed to make that even better.
The downsides:
If you're looking for something with a lot of depth, look elsewhere. There aren't lots of resources to juggle, there's no campaign, it is exactly what it appears to be.
It's really heavy into micromanaging units for a sizeable portion of each game. Towards the end it can get a bit more macro, but misplacing half a dozen guys (not tough to do) can have pretty dire consequences early on.
Momentum is massively important. This isn't a negative thing necessarily, but it becomes pretty clear pretty quickly who has the advantage in a battle. It's possible to come back if you're behind, but there's an obvious tipping point.
You can't control units while you're zoomed out. That's a bit of an odd design decision and I'm sure there's a reason for it, but it's a little bit frustrating.
All in all this is extremely well done, and for the price you seriously can't beat it for entertainment value.

- The Game of thrones's spirit isn't quite transcripted. Here, they emphasize the serie's flaws: Many useless, slow scenes compensated by one intense scene, and they are greedy on those. I really wanted to like this game but in terms of gameplay is really frustrating:
* The combat is absurd: each team plays one unit every turn (chess style). Health and damage are the same stat. So the weaker the unit, the less damage it makes.
* This two combined forces you into just weaken the enemies without killing them until the very end of the battle. If you kill the weak guys, the strong guys will act instead, so you are giving the enemy an advantage. Sorry but this doesn't make any sense and its really frustrating that the game forces you to use this exploit.
* Archers do not have enough range. If you can shoot them, they can come an hit you in the next turn unless there is someone in between.
* Once you move you cannot move again even if you have enough points. If you special ability is out of range, but you still had movement points: sorry buddy, wait until next turn.
* Trying to have a balanced party of guys at similar levels is a bad strategy. Just keep 6 strong ones because battles keep getting harder and harder and you cannot keep up and you don't have enough supplies to heal the weak guys.
* If you didn't focus on levelling up your main party, the last battle will be impossible. I had to lower the difficulty after hours of frustration.
* Some people in you party will leave. So after you bothered to try to level up this guy, and wasted a lot of supplies to try to win battle with this one, he/she leaves and you never see him again.
* Is not clear where are you going every time, or how long it takes. Trying to balance morale/rations/rest is frustrating because you have no clue how many rations you need until the next stop.
* The story is unfinished.
I wouldn't mind the lack of proper gameplay if the game was more cinematic. I think It should have more voice acting, or more animated cutscenes for to have a strong art/story selling point.
