This game has a lot of promise. For each thing it does right, though, it finds a way to make that same thing also a drawback. I really wanted to like this game, and I gave it a lot more playtime than I give most of the other games I get on Steam, but I still can't bring myself to recommend it unless these problems are resolved.
The character customization options are really great, and you can make a wide variety of different characters. However, the abilities that are available in each discipline are randomized, so there's a chance (and it happened to me) that you just can't get the skill you want. Additionally, you only get to fully customize half of your party; the other half comes pre-built, and while you do get to choose which specific people join your party, this is still unnecessarily limiting. In a game so focused on customization, why not allow you to customize all four party members?
I also really like the tactical combat. Positioning and controlling the terrain and using status effects to your advantage are all really well done. However, every meaningful battle has some kind of gimmick that, if you are unprepared for (and you will be, on your first playthrough), will probably wreck you before you even understand what just happened. I get that it's not holding your hand, and that's fine, but it just doesn't work very well in this game.
Compare to Dark Souls, which has a similar mechanic. You are going to be matched up against enemies who do things you aren't prepared for, and you're going to die for it. In Dark Souls, that's built into the game design, and you can learn from your mistakes and try again. In Divinity: Original Sin, that's game over. Load a previous save. In Dark Souls, if you die, it's your own fault. In Divinity, if you die, it might have been your fault, or it might have been the RNG. In one game, this mechanic is a driving force of fun, and in the other, it's a driving force of needless frustration. This failure pushes the difficulty curve in Divinity to be a complete trainwreck. Areas you've done before are trivial, and in new areas you better be trigger-happy on the quicksave button, because you never know when something new is going to pop up to ruin your day.
Divinity: Original Sin is built to be a challenging game with unforgiving combat. It is both of those, but it does it at the expense of fun, rather than for the enhancement of it. With just a few tweaks, I think it could be vastly improved. I really like the idea of this game, and have enjoyed some moments of it immensely, but when looking back at my whole experience, I feel like I was cheated out of what this game could have been.

Ok, so it finally ended. Season 1, anyway. Took about a year for 10 hours of story. It's about as slowly paced as a work of fiction could possibly be.
So, my final verdict is that it's pretty bad. It's about on par with Bone as Telltale's weakest game. The plot is slow and meandering, and even in the finale most of it goes nowhere. A lot of scenes only exist to cram in characters from the show. Telltale obviously doesn't do much in the way of changing the story of their games based on your decisions, but at least previous games would make some small adjustments. Here your choices seem to be entirely meaningless, as you usually get the same dialogue responses and events always loop back to a single path. It becomes a less interesting version of a TV show.
There are three main plotlines, one in the North with two warring houses, one at the Wall because Jon Snow is popular, and one in King's Landing because Tyrion is popular. The plots for the Wall and King's Landing don't affect the main story or do anything interesting. They basically rehash the character arcs of Jon Snow and Sansa, so it's nothing you haven't seen before.
The potentially interesting thread is the fight for House Forrester. I say "potentially," because it veers hard left into inanity pretty quickly. Since Telltale needs everything to loop back to the same circumstances to save budget on animation and voice acting, your choices can never be more than window dressing. If you recruit an army, they need to disappear before they can fight. Your character is either a cripple who can't fight, or a great fighter who is conveniently crippled moments before a big fight. This cheapness really lets the air out of any potential rising action.
The story also inexplicably misses what makes Game of Thrones popular, as well as any basic mechanics of storytelling. At the end of each episode, your progress needs to be reset so that the next episode can always start from a single unified point. This treadmill effect stalls out any character development or plot development. The story is always: House Forrester is weak and House Whitehill is strong. The villains are all cartoonish and stupid. Each main character is a one note caricature of popular characters from the books/show, without the depth.
Without character development, you're left with the plot alone. Because of the small budget and lack of resources, the Forresters always lose. Whatever you do is deleted to start the next episode. People claim that this mirrors the source material, but that horribly misses the point of the source material. It isn't that the heroes always lose, it's that the heroes *can* lose. They shouldn't have plot armor, but if they fail, it should be for their own missteps and flaws. Ned loses not because he's a Stark, but because he did dumb heroic things in a world that doesn't coddle heroes. If anyone can read the books or watch the show and think that anyone can die at any time, they simply haven't been paying attention. The writers for this game haven't been paying attention.

Going into this game, I had no idea what to expect. The few videos I had seen showed little of what the game was about. I decided to go ahead and take the plunge, and I didn't regret it in the slightest. This game had me immersed in the world within the first ten minutes, and I quickly became very attached to the characters. Without spoiling it, there are some interesting twists, and the story was exciting and engaging.
Gameplay: 9/10
The gameplay itself is like a cross between Oregon Trail and Xcom. If you don't know what those are i encourage you to look them up. The main game is focused around your caravan, and you will manage supplies and people, as well as make important decisions from here. And let me tell you, the decision making is AMAZING. I could rant for a long time about it, but in short, unlike most games the choices you make actually matter. The combat is turn based, with your chosen characters carrying out their attacks and then giving the enemy a chance to counter. It's challenging but not too difficult, and if you're going into the game for the story aspect alone you can lower the difficulty. The only negative to the gameplay is that there are limited ways to gain supplies, it'd be nice if there was a way to send your people out to gather. Overall though, the gameplay is solid and fun.
Story: 10/10
The story is absolutely awesome. It keeps you entertained and wanting more. You get attached to each character, which makes you want to try as hard as you can to keep them alive. Because they CAN die. All of them. You've been warned.
Audio: 7/10
The music in this game is great. It fits the world perfectly, and the right tracks play at all the right times. The sound effects are solid, but rather simplistic. It'd be great to see more voice acting in the game, since the little voice acting they had was superb.
Graphics: 10/10
Though at first I was a little put off by the animation style, it quickly became one of the most endearing aspects of the game. Each character is hand drawn and their appearance almost always fits their personality.
Overall: 9/10
This game is memorable and fun, and I will definitely be replaying it many times. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a good story, or a game to just sit down and enjoy.

So figured I would chime in with my experience so far with Black Desert, Currently as you can tell only at about 18 Hours in so I would consider this still very early impressions, Just to give some background I come from mainly playing EvE online played it for years, Plus Rift and Guild Wars for a few hundred hours each. So I will give my experience and how BDO can realate to these other MMOs.
First Off I wouldn't consider BDO a very good MMO so far there hasn't been anything to draw me into getting into a guild or clan or anything, You don't hear about the thousand player battles like EvE you don't have the need to join up with enough people to be able to defend a wormhole, or mine enough to support building ships. Unlike Rift guild wars or other MMOs you also don't really feel the need to join up to go on raids, dungeons etc. (hell so far I couldn't even tell ya anything other than world bosses which meh). BUT! What it is so far is a very good single player game with a bunch of lunatics running around to liven the place up, not to say you can't do the normal MMO stuff just to say 18 hours in I don't really feel the need so until then it's a good if grindy single player game.
Second be warned unless you come from something hideously complex like EvE you will probably hit a pretty decent brick wall, The life skills and random crap you can do from hiring workers to run your shops to trading and everything else could get down right confusing very fast, But thats where you have to take your time at first read guides and just try try again. It is not for the faint of heart or short of patience, The combat is also just about as complex but we will get to that in a second.
Third the combat is fantastic if you like any games that play in the vein of action games such as arkham knight, bayonetta and others, while not quite as score oriented the combat would feel just at home, It's all about combos and, in some classes dodging, I choose musa and I find myself not relying on armor or defense so much as just getting out of the way and hitting hard.
I guess thats about it really There is A lot to this game if you don't have much patience I wouldn't bother but if you have the time and patience and don't mind the grind you will fall in love, Plus good lord it's cheap I even splurged on explorers pack and I'm perfectly happy with the 18 hours I got for $23, So if the Idea intrigues you I would tell you all day just go for it, It will probably be $5 well spent.
And Just cause TL;DR Grindy Single Player action Game with MMO Elements you can ignore and very nice combat and some nice complexity. Reccomend any day.
Also quick addendum the story as far as i can tell sucks and or doesn't actually exsist. So yea don't expect that, the black spirit is kinda entertaining sometimes though.

EDIT: I still largely stick to what I've said below and found that it hasn't really changed. That said, this game went on a pretty good sale during the winter and I'd wholeheartedly encourage other people to get it when it does go on sale.
Despite the fanservice and what not, this game is actually quite good. Simple mechanics, very high damage, plentiful resources, and a colorful, varied cast gives the game a very fast and exciting pace. While it's lacking a bit in the tutorial department, there's plenty of resources on the mizuumi wiki, youtube, and the training room for even a novice like me to sink my teeth in. After seeing it but never really playing it in my local arcade, I decided to give it a shot.
So why the negative review?
Simple answer: It's not worth the current asking price of 30 USD. It feels more like a 15 dollar purchase or less.
This game costs as much as Blazblue Chronophantasma right now and offers very little content for the casual player with a fraction of Blazblue's competitive playerbase.
There's 2 story/arcade campaigns, a score attack, traditional netplay, VS, and training room. That's it. No challenge mode, no unlockable super characters, nothing. The AI in this game is ok but you're not gonna get much longevity out of it. That leaves you with network mode which is about what you'd expect for a poverty anime fighter. This isn't Blazblue where you can find a dozen matches on discord in 5 min. or so; it's gonna take some time.
While Nitropluz Blasterz's strong points lie in it's accessibility, there's honestly not enough depth in the combat to justify such a whopping asking price. There's nothing fancy here, it's very much by the numbers. You get a "blast" which is essentially a burst+super mode. The combo system goes from light, medium, heavy, into progressively stronger supers with little varation aside from assists and blast cancel. There's not much innovation which makes this very much feel like a simpler Mahvel: Anime Edition. Sure, you get a guard break move and a dedicated defense button but those feel like quality of life additions rather than meaningful contributions.
If the price ever falls or you actually recognize a majority of the cast, feel free to buy it as it's quite fun at the end of the day. Just not 30 dollars worth of fun.

Having played the original on the Playstation 3, and then playing this I find it hard to believe I actually played through the entire original.  The original PS3 version you played generally for the cutscene interactions because they were amusing and fun.  The battles were a chore and slow paced and annoying.  This version which is running more or less off the Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory engine is so much more enjoyable and fun in every area.
First, the good:
No need for a Playstation Vita.  I almost got a vita just to play these games.  Saved a few bucks right there.
Graphics look nice.  They aren't mind blowing, but the cartoonish look works excellent for this series.
Cutscene interaction are generally fun to read.  Some moments you will roll your eyes and say "Well, it's Japanese, they're weird", but the banter can be amusing.
The battle system is quick and fun, not slow and tedious like the original PS3 version.  The use of combos and abilities is satisfying and the animated fighting sequences are fun to see and not so overly long.

BAD STUFF
You get overwhelmed with all these 'plans' left and right.  I do like the plan system but it can get tedious if you are a completionist and you have to grind dungeons for materials.  The fact you generally have to look up on a guide online to know where some things are is a bit annoying.  Unless you have an amazing photographic memory, you will be doing this.  Would be nice if there was a better in-game way to let you know where certain things are.  Dungeon info and Monster info isn't always enough.

Some of the text once in a great while is cut off in the text box.  It doesn't happen too often, so it isn't a huge strike against the game, but it is there.  Hopefully it will be fixed in a patch down the road.
As much as i love the various costumes for the characters, it would be nice to actually preview the costume before buying it in the game.  I have always found that really odd in this series that they don't let you preview the stuff.  I hope at least in RE:3 when it comes out they change that.  I don't expect it, but it would be a nice surprise.
Overall this game is fun.  It's not an overly serious JRPG.  If you like cute anime girls punching, kicking and slashing various weird monster models you will love it!  It's also quite long.  You do get your money's worth.  I'm 50 or so hours in and i'm not done yet, but i did alot of 'plan' grinding, so it might go a bit faster if you do a bit less of that.

Ingredients:

- Butter
Instructions:
- Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper.
- Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.

Quite possibly my favourite licensed game of all time.
Stick of Truth holds up as both a fantastic homage to South Park's 20-year tradition of gross-out humour and biting satire and a competent, surprisingly deep turn-based RPG.
World-building is as excellent as one would expect: a script written by Stone and Parker is standard South Park fare, replete with a full cast of characters. Simply exploring the town and speaking to each NPC is fun enough, and the unqiue side-quests given by each character are usually hilarious. The story is as one would expect: plenty of gross-out comedy that at times even surpasses the show. The main plot does not outstay its welcome, and is bolstered by some high-quality side-quests being integrated into the story.
The RPG side of things is perhaps less stand-out in terms of quality, though that is no bad thing. When first jumping into the game I expected RPG-lite mechanics there mostly to allow the plot to progress and the jokes to land. In fact, there is a surprising amount of depth in both weaponry, abilities and fight mechanics. The game never lets you get too reliant on  one tactic or item through some good enemy variation. The only criticism here is difficulty: before playing I had been warned about the game's ease, and most were right. I cannot remember dying, which does not speak to my ability as much as it does the game's forgiving design. RPG vets might want to start on 'Hardcore' difficulty. To be sure, this is a game for the fans: RPG enthusiasts who do not consider themselves as such can comfortably skip this one.
It is rare that I actively want to replay a game after the credits roll, much less straight away. With Stick of Truth, I jumped straight back in, trying a new class and abilities, and trying to find anything I missed first time around. The quality of the script and game-world is absolutely excellent, backed by a rock-solid set of RPG mechanics throughout. For even the most casual fan of the show and up, this is an excellent experience, recommended at full price or anything less.

You may wonder to yourself, "Why should I buy a First Person Shooter that's this old?" Well, let me answer you with the reasons SWBFII tends to be the only FPS game I will play with my friends on a regular basis. Let me start with the single player. As much as FPS games are not the best for their story, SWBFII takes it away with the story of the 501st throughout the Star Wars universe with objectives that can tend to be more than just "Take this point" or "Kill this person" as you would see in any other FPS. From the tutorial until the last mission in game, the story objectives will either frustrate you (*Cough* Order 66 *cough*) or make you beg for more. Then there's galactic conquest, which is outside the campaign itself. This lets you control the republic, CIS, rebel alliance or empire and go through different planets, taking them over to fuel your empire while you research upgrades and troops to use. Next, the troops you choose. Every class has the same equivalent on the opposing team EXCEPT for the special troops (Dark Trooper, Clone Commander, Imp Officer, Wookiee, Bothan, Jet Trooper, Magnaguard and the rolling droids, don't remember what they're called). Each side has a heavy-weapons guy, a medic/engineer, a soldier and a sniper as well as two specials which I listed. Next, multiplayer, it's much more organized and less of a cluster than CoD. Melee is non-existent and it's rather equal in terms of game-play... not in terms of skill. The modes are much more organized between CTF-1 (one flag both sides fight to capture), CTF-2 (Classic Capture the Flag), Regular (until reinforcements run out), assault (First to get certain score wins) and so on. Next thing I like are the heroes, If you have them enabled in multiplayer, you can easily destroy a team... if not focused... which always happens. Otherwise, great first-person shooter. That if you choose can be third-person as well. A buy well worth the money.

Now before you go judging this game by its vector style graphics and shouting the forbidden word (Minecraft) take a look at what the game is trying to offer. This game is nothing like minecraft, sure it has the cube like style and ability to build but it is done in a unique way. You start off on one side of a symmetrical map, your primary objective is to build defences around your various "cores", after the pre-round timer has reached zero the wall in-between you and your foes will disappear, allowing you to attack them and them to attack you. This is where the games first person shooter / MOBA style combat is introduced, fighting off against the opposing team in an aim to destroy their base and simultaneously defend your own. This game is tonnes of fun and best played with a couple of friends. Although it is not without its downsides, for example how repetitive the gameplay can get or the limited range of classes available, but that being said this is in early access and you should not let these factors deter you from playing it. We can only hope that the developers continue this great work with the players in mind and listen to what we have to say.

So, a free visual novel. Is it worth your time? It certainly isn't everyone's cup o' tea but it is worth a shot purely for that £0 price tag.
Firstly, the best part of this visual novel: the story. The story itself isn't all that bad. It's about a guy who was on his way across town on a bus who suddenly finds himself, completely inexplicably, in a completely different area, in the middle of nowhere in a different season. How? Why? Who cares? Let's play some everlasting summer, bro. References aside, the main character cares, a lot. Semyon spends a lot of time looking for answers as to where he is and how the hell he ended up there. Eventually he realises that he can get zero relevant answers by looking for them and decides he will partake in the activites of this soviet pioneer camp and perhaps the answers will come to him.
Secondly, the worst part of this visual novel: the artwork. At times the artwork is completely reasonable and you might even think this could have easily worked in a game you would have paid for. At others it is absolutely terrible. One image in particular comes to mind when Semyon is at a table talking to a girl and the scene is just a picture of this girl as she talks to you. I'm pretty sure there were several points during that conversation where her eyes were pointing in different directions. No, she did not have a lazy eye, it was just bad artwork. During the better times, on one route in particular the artwork was pretty damn striking, even if they did reuse some of the backgrounds. Overall, don't play this novel if you expect good artwork.
The music was pretty good in this game and created a decent atmospheric feel. Not much else to say about it.
The characters were ok in this visual novel. They weren't terribly well fleshed out but you can manage to get emotionally attached to them in their routes on all bar one route where all logic is thrown out the window. Not in a bad way, in a completely unexpected, nonsensical, ♥♥♥♥-the-standard-story sort of way. That route exists and when you find it don't play it while half asleep.
Overall, this is a very good visual novel for the free price tag but in terms of normal visual novel standards, it isn't all that great.

Child of Light is a hybrid of side-scrolling adventure and turn-based action (i.e like Final Fantasy VII). It is a charming game that instantly pulled me in with its beautiful artwork-styled graphics and emotional, heartfelt sound track.
Story: Child of Light starts with a young girl named Aurora who is from 1895 Austria. One day, she disappears from her loving father's grasp and is transported to a dream-like world known as Lemuria. As you progress through the game, many events unfold regarding Aurora's father the Duke and you will see why Aurora is part of this new and strange world. The story is beautifully tragic, told with rhymes that work well for the most part and the ending is fairly sad.
Graphics: The graphics of this game just pop off the screen. Rarely, have I been blown away and completely immersed by a game's visuals that are as breathtaking as Child of Light's which looks like it leaped off the canvas of an artist! The way the game is presented works will to complement the game's fairytale story.
Gameplay: It bends the traditional conventions of an RPG by mixing side-scrolling adventure and turn-based action. Even though it may be strange to many fans of games such as Final Fantasy at first, you will come to get used to the mechanics and I believe that you will enjoy it much more. Battles happen when Aurora touches a creature and this is when the game switches to turn-based. I like that Child of Light takes inspiration from newer RPGs in that it is more action-packed with the interrupt mechanic (where spells or action of someone can be halted if they are hit first) and that Igniculus, the firefly plays a major role during combat. You can use the left-trigger on consoles to lighten up the firefly which causes enemies to be slowed OR to heal allies in a fight. It is an innovative system that is a lot of fun and keeps you on your toes.
Overall, Child of Light is one of my favourite RPGs (along with Final Fantasy VII and IX) and all the elements mesh together well to create a unique experience that is very memorable.
I'd give the game a 9/10.

Baldur's Gate with a splash of XCOM. Linear and not particularly repeatable, but a good co-op diversion with a dedicated partner.
No cover drawn from its XCOM heritage, but tactical combat control and lockdowns are the order of the day. Scoundrels, Men at Arms, and Expert Marksmen are effectively 'mages in armor', with broad spell variety saved for dedicated INT casters, who will have a few skill trees due to less attribute dependence. Spend some time studying the character generation and level up systems, as understanding how tightly you will need to specialize is vital - the game is parsimonious with stat improvements. The tactical combat will pull no punches though the AI can sometimes be baited into foolish mistakes of positioning. Get friendly with your quicksave key, and put a grin on - the combat can be brutal, and a winning contest can go south quickly when new enemy abilities make their first appearance. D:OS won't warn you about what's coming.
For mages doing damage, elemental combinations are the order of the day, and being able to apply all of the earth(poison)/fire and water/air(electricity) pairings is useful, but specialize in one pairing. Countering these works as you might imagine - water dries up when heated, fire goes out when rained upon. Be able to counter them all, amongst your group. Poison can be burned off (explosively!). Ice will melt, faster with help. Witchcraft is the INT caster version of Man-at-Arms, with fewer controls, but more ranged debuffs and pet summons - an armored decapitator appearing behind enemy lines is nothing to sneer at. (Nor are the various elementals and animals from the elemental skills, for that matter, but one summon per caster at a time.)
The writing is adequate, but not stellar. The first who-dun-it wasn't particularly inspiring, and oftentimes progression has been a matter of "what level are
enemies?" rather than a cohesive sense of direction and progress. The quest journal is next-to-useless for many quests, providing little or no information to follow up. Use markers liberally, and don't be ashamed to augment the game's lacking journalling with some of your own. If you're doing every quest, expect to either miss a few things or need a walkthrough/guide from time to time.
The rock-paper-scissors mechanic for the 'persuasion minigame' is by turns novel and tiresome. It's cute the first couple of times you see it, and it's a new way to 'randomize' a mechanic that no one seems to get right (persuasion) but it misses the mark in not having an "autoplay". Frankly, I don't want to play RPS against the computer, or my partner, and if the point is to provide some uncertainty to 'speech checks', that's fine - but I don't care for the minigame much. Fortunately, it's been relatively rare thus far...
Character control is relatively straightforward - two players control four characters between them, in any combination. The host controls who gets to run which, allowing one player to AFK while the other plays a combat or to allow a tactical novice to mind only a single character in combat, etc. Wife and I split our characters into two teams of two, and it works out well - I run the NPC warrior Madora (man-at-arms) and shadow cleric (witchcraft/some water/man-at-arms), she handles the mage duties (one in all colleges for access, specializing earth/fire for stronger effects) and the sneaky rogue Wolgraff we recruited.
Combat is turn based and is the real meat of the game, with players asked to deploy skills and weapons to defeat foes in a number of varied battlefield conditions. Often, a different approach or tactical plan is the difference between victory and reloading, and fights have been challenging often.
All around, an enjoyable game, but remember those roots - the game doesn't pretend to be a more modern RPG, no matter the pretty graphics, so study up on how the level system works. It doesn't pretend to have autopilot combat, either. Bring your tactical thinking to the table.
...and get ready to read, because this is a long, slow march, not a sprint.
Edit:
Bugs, however, abound. Often, we notice desync issues when the host reloads the game and player #2's characters appear to have no stats (base scores all reset to 5) and not be wearing their gear, etc. We've not experienced any corruption from these episodes, but save often to avoid screams of hair-rending frustration when player 2 says "My character is bugged. Again." I'm amazed this wasn't caught and corrected, given how prevalent it's been for us!
We've seen a couple of minor oddities (one bug involved a repeatedly-exploding poison gas trap that killed a boss in a single round because the poison would detonate, leave a fire puddle, the gas would refill the area, detonate... The boss standing in the cloud never took a combat turn - the explosion cycle took himn from 100% to 0% in one round of chained, buggy explosions (not that I'm complaining).
Learn how to temper armor and weapons, learn how to make basic equipment (Madora makes a decent smith) and you can take advantage of movement speed penalty reductions on heavy armor and enhanced basic damage on weapons (for free). Don't play 'hard mode' if you don't have to!
If you're into RPGs this one's worth a look, but don't expect all the rough corners to be filed down or a 100% bug-free experience, because they're not and it's not.

So figured I would chime in with my experience so far with Black Desert, Currently as you can tell only at about 18 Hours in so I would consider this still very early impressions, Just to give some background I come from mainly playing EvE online played it for years, Plus Rift and Guild Wars for a few hundred hours each. So I will give my experience and how BDO can realate to these other MMOs.
First Off I wouldn't consider BDO a very good MMO so far there hasn't been anything to draw me into getting into a guild or clan or anything, You don't hear about the thousand player battles like EvE you don't have the need to join up with enough people to be able to defend a wormhole, or mine enough to support building ships. Unlike Rift guild wars or other MMOs you also don't really feel the need to join up to go on raids, dungeons etc. (hell so far I couldn't even tell ya anything other than world bosses which meh). BUT! What it is so far is a very good single player game with a bunch of lunatics running around to liven the place up, not to say you can't do the normal MMO stuff just to say 18 hours in I don't really feel the need so until then it's a good if grindy single player game.
Second be warned unless you come from something hideously complex like EvE you will probably hit a pretty decent brick wall, The life skills and random crap you can do from hiring workers to run your shops to trading and everything else could get down right confusing very fast, But thats where you have to take your time at first read guides and just try try again. It is not for the faint of heart or short of patience, The combat is also just about as complex but we will get to that in a second.
Third the combat is fantastic if you like any games that play in the vein of action games such as arkham knight, bayonetta and others, while not quite as score oriented the combat would feel just at home, It's all about combos and, in some classes dodging, I choose musa and I find myself not relying on armor or defense so much as just getting out of the way and hitting hard.
I guess thats about it really There is A lot to this game if you don't have much patience I wouldn't bother but if you have the time and patience and don't mind the grind you will fall in love, Plus good lord it's cheap I even splurged on explorers pack and I'm perfectly happy with the 18 hours I got for $23, So if the Idea intrigues you I would tell you all day just go for it, It will probably be $5 well spent.
And Just cause TL;DR Grindy Single Player action Game with MMO Elements you can ignore and very nice combat and some nice complexity. Reccomend any day.
Also quick addendum the story as far as i can tell sucks and or doesn't actually exsist. So yea don't expect that, the black spirit is kinda entertaining sometimes though.

This is a turn based JRPG-style game that is becoming more rare these days. The artwork is fantastic, and the music is hypnotising. Artwork is an understatement for this game.
Combat is very fluid. There is a "timeline" at the bottom of the screen that keeps track of your characters and the enemies. You move through the timeline based on your speed stat, and any buffs/debuffs you have going. When you reach the end you hit the casting portion of the timeline. This is when you choose your action. you then move through this part of the timeline and complete the action at the end. Some actions are longer to complete than others. If you or an enemy takes damage while in the casting portion, before pulling the attack off, you are "inturrupted" and lose your turn basically. It's a great aspect that requires more strategy then "pick big spell make big boom."
Overall it's a very enjoyable game, and New Game+ makes every game batter.

I think I'll jot down a few thoughts here, now that I'm nearly finished with my first run through the game.  Approaching 100 hours in, bearing in mind that I've left the game idling a lot and I restarted after mucking around for ~20 hours, it has probably taken me fewer than 70 hours to get to almost-done... but either way, I'd say this all reflects pretty well on the game since there have only been a handfulI've wanted to play that much of these last several years.  I'm easily distracted (particularly when it comes to video games longer than 10-20 hours) and I often start games and leave them unfinished, but Divinity: Original Sin is one I don't want to STOP playing.  I want to play through it again, even, next time with more co-op.
Anyway, you're probably not looking at my review to find out that this is a classic turn-based and party-based CRPG with loads of new game polish (super lush graphics) and all the freedom one might hope for from a game like this.  At this point I would say the game is preceded by its reputation, and while I have yet to play Dragonfall or Grimrock 2, I'd say this is pretty clearly the real best RPG of 2014 (my personal disappointments with Dark Souls 2, which is actually a pretty great game, notwithstanding (and I don't care about Dragon Age)).  There's little to no handholding, but by virtue of well-considered design it's friendly to players like myself, who may not have cut their teeth on all the classics like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, or the earlier Divine Divinity games.  Once I had a feel for how to get around and do things on my own, I just wanted to explore every corner of this game.  The turn-based combat is so much more enjoyable to me than the frantic clicking of similarly isometric action RPGs for the PC as Diablo, Torchlight, and Path of Exile.  I enjoy those games, but you see, X-Com has always been one of my absolute favorites, so the combination of freedom and thoughtful combat really hits the spot.  Elemental hazards factor in constantly, making every decision in battle interesting.
Larian may just be coming into their own despite having had a following for some time now, and Original Sin deserves to be more than just a diamond in the rough.  It deserves to be King Diamond, the Original Sin...ger of Mercyful Fate.  *long, gross fart sound*  (Oh, yeah, all the achievements are named after songs by Dio, Black Sabbath, etc.  Apparently those Larian dudes love their heavy metal.)
Seriously, though — heck of a game.
It is a great tactical game with some annoying chances of missing when odds should be high... besides that love this game to death.

My Cons-

-The Create a Character feature allows you to customize your character whenever you want with a plethora of Fugly faces for you to choose.
-Certain parts of the map your characters can clearly see the enemy hiding behind a tiny cover, but just because its a cover the enemy gains the 20% evasion.
-I don't understand why merchants want to buy alien corpses but not weapons/armors/items; I'm pretty sure people would like weapons/armors/items during an alien invasion.
-The maps get repetitive.  You see a lot of the same designs over and over as well.
-Unless you have Ghost Armor or items to go into stealth for surveying surrounding, its next to impossible to ambush/flank the enemies without them reacting to you.
-OverWatch tends to lead to overkilling the first enemy, allow other enemies to come in later.
-Ending♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off; It pulled the Mass Effect 3 ending.  I hated that ending.

Have you ever spent months cultivating a rare plant only for it to spontanously combust into flames one evening while watering the little fella? Have you ever finally worked up the courage to ask that cutie you've been crushing on all year only to have a giant mantis rip off the lunch room ceiling and devour her head-first?
Have you ever been to Flint, Michigan?
If so then this is the game for you, where you watch as you fruitlessly surge ever onwards towards your goal, despite no matter how prepared you actually are. You will form bonds with your tiny pixelated crew members as you care for their well being and watch them risk life and limb to save their other comrades and the ship- all in a futile effort to prolong the inevitable. And it is only when your last remaining crew member dies, gasping for breath while trying to fix the O2 pump as missiles and gatling-laser fire spank across the ruined hull of your once beautiful ship will you realize that this game is a deceptively sinister mistress. Spiraling you ever onwards to a eventual loss and sense of remorse and guilt while you ponder off what went wrong with the image of your frozen crew members listing aimlessly through the void of space to give you solace.
Also has an amazing soundtrack to listen to as you and everyone you have grown attatched to in the last 35 minutes dies a horrible death.
10/10

I'm sure you get the picture by now.  An absolutely amazing game that would be better with online multiplayer.  Going into a bit more detail though, I get enough joy out of this game simply by contemplating the intricately designed mechanics.  Everything in the game is simple to comprehend, yet expertly arranged in order to complement everything else.  For example, just look at the ectoplasm system.  Every time the human breaks scenery, it creates ectoplasm for the ghosts.  Therefore the human wouldn't want to break scenery, except that ghosts can pick up unbroken scenery and throw it at him.  To keep the ghosts in check, scenery doesn't yield ectoplasm when broken by a ghost. Where to start..
BDO is overwhelming in the best way. I've never played an MMO with such possibilities for a character. It's got all the standard bells and whistles of a MMO: main quests, side quests, areas to explore, mobs, guilds, mounts, pets. It has NPC interaction and relationship building with NPCs, which effects a lot of things. It has "knowledge" - as you explore the world, talk to NPCs, participate in combat or life skills it gives you more knowledge and makes things easier. Life skills are incredible; one life skill alone can take up 100% of your game time if you so choose.
For example - I train, level, and breed horses. My goal is to get a pair or two of Level 30 Tier 8 horses. Ambitious. The process is delightfully complicated and grindy at times but is extremely fun for me. This is almost all I do on BDO, ever.
The combat is amazing. I'm not terribly impressed with the skill system but it's fine. The world is enormous and varied, you will never get bored of exploring. You can make great money by fishing AFK (and some other AFK activities) without any skill or dedication, and you can make extremely good money fishing with more dedication. Learn how to craft a fishing boat and hunt down a whale. Trust me, that takes a lot of time. But so fun! Or focus completely on combat and level to 52/53, join a guild for some wars, or go for PvP.
A negative for me though is that this game is a huge drain on system resources. My PC is laggy on ultra low settings but my PC kinda sucks. The graphics are insane, the game is so beautiful even on my ultra low settings.
Like I said before, it can be very overwhelming at times. There is just so much to do and learn. Take your time, have fun. It's gonna be the best money you ever spent on an MMO. Guarantee it. (It's a one-time fee! No monthly fees!)

7/10 - stellar effort, great anime sprites, some disappointing arena's stop it being higher.
7/10 - Great soundtrack, good voicing(Japanese voicing as a warning), some annoying character noises but overall solid.
10/10 - I bloody loved the gameplay, the transition from a straight up story mode beat 'em up to a VN was such a great idea. The fighting mechanics were great as well! Which surprised me!
10/10 - Going out on a limb here and saying that this story, whilst being nothing spectacular, is a 10/10 because for a fighting game, its genuinely had a lot of love and attention. Not to mention a whole host of familiar anime characters thrown in the mix.
8/10 - Honestly, its a very good fighter, albeit not on SFIV's level but certainly better than most other top notch fighters. Add to that a cast of highly likeable anime characters and you've got yourself a hit. Personally the idea of doing Saber's "EXCALIBUR!" attack sold the game to me alone.
First of all, if you don't like anime, there's probably other fighters you should check out. Street Fighter IV is perhaps the best fighter ever made, I'd check that out. That being said, if you don't dislike anime and like fighters, this is actually pretty good. It's got surprising depth for what could have been a simple anime cash in.
The difficulty curve is steep, just hitting combo's can be tough and the final boss ramps up the difficulty tenfold. That being said its not impossible. It didn't take me long before I had Saber rip the boss a new one. The playable characters are all taken from the popular back catalogue that the company has, including FATE: Stay/Night, Psycho-Pass, Sonico, Demonbane, Arcane Heart and many more. So once you finish the main "story" you are treated to a new 2 hours or so VN including a lot of these characters set in the Demonbane series universe. This is a great addition and shows the devs know their demographic!
The graphics are great just to see people like Saber or Akane(psychopass) on steam. However they let themselves down slightly with some poor arena's to play in. Looking at your waifu and fighting with amazingly animated and importantly, WELL FRAMED characters is brilliant. Their "ultimate" attacks are treated with an anime CG which is beautiful. However the backgrounds are a bit limp and generic, whats more there are only 10 separate ones. Its a shame the same love for the heroines was not given to the background, as otherwise the stellar animation and graphics would be given a 10/10. If you can ignore or like the limited arena's, the graphics are great. As I said, importantly there are a lot of frames, which for a fighter can lead to very good multiplayer play!
The sound was great without excelling. Good voicing which you'd expect really, but in Japanese if that bothers you, all text obviously in native language. The music was amazing, I loved it. Sometimes characters getting hit caused odd noises on certain characters which detracted somewhat from the sounds score. But overall, I'd probably buy the soundtrack, its very good!
Quick unrelated positive note for the devs, as an achievement hunter, all the achievements are through "offline" play. I can not thank the devs enough for this design choice, it means the game will always be 100%'able even long after the servers get killed or the community dies. On that note, I managed to find full lobies every search so far as of the 19th of December 2016.
Overall I'd buy this game. Its better than Street Fighter V and most other current fighter alternatives, whilst giving anime fans a chunk of amazing characters to love and enjoy!

As most of the other reviews tell you, the artistic style and presentation of the game are fantastic.   The music is amazing and the consequences of choices are real.  You make the best choices you can, but there will be good decisions that go wrong, of that you can be sure.   I actually felt dread having to make some of these decisions.
The combat is turn-based, which I really like.   It has been pointed out in other reviews that there is one main strategy in combat.  Maim.  Since the amount of damage a unit can do is dependent on their health (it's strength actually, I think), weakening the unit's health will make sure they can do very little damage.  The combat is in the style of chess or Go, where each player can make one move then its the other player's turn.  So if you kill the weakened unit, the enemy's initiative order moves up, leaving them with stronger average units, but the same number of turns.  This can be a little frustrating.  Definitely not enough to keep me from recommending the game though.  There are a few different general unit types, and you can customize them as they level up, so the combat never felt boring, just illogical sometimes.
The map is huge, but unfortunately, where you go on the map is a decision made for you by the backbone of the story.  You can spend a lot of time reading about the different places on the map and even more time wishing you had a bit more freedom in your movement to go to those places.   It's a testament to the developers that the world pulled me in so much, but I do wish there were more choices in the movement of the caravan.
Also, if it's your 50th time fighting Bellower, it's ok to turn the difficulty down.

I tend to have a habit of buying random cutesy anime games, even if they are decent at best. So I bought this, expecting to play it in spite of people... but I ended up really liking it.
Like, really, really liking it. I expected this to be a decent (if even that) JRPG but after a few hours I was hooked with the ridiculously likable characters, non-sensical story, and simple-yet-interesting mechanics.
---------------------------------------
This being on PC, the PC port stuff comes first:
It's not that good. It's not good at all really, but it does run at 60FPS, goes up to 1080p, and has borderless window as an option. No real graphics options. It's still quite obvious that it's a port of a Vita game, but the game still looks really nice, in my opinion.
Do be aware that there are no button prompts in-game for keyboard controls. It always displays with Xbox buttons. I prefer playing the game with the 360 controller. If you play with the keyboard, note that if you can get past the fact that there are no help prompts, and that the controls are kind of awkward, the game is still very much playable.
---------------------------------------
Now, onto gameplay:
The battle system is a turn-based tactical RPG. You have your characters on one side, the enemies on the other. You move up to them and punch them. When attacking you can select between Rush attacks (quickly fills your EXE Gauge), Power attacks (deals heavy damage), and Break attacks (significantly lowers the enemy's Guard Points, so your Power attacks do more damage, can also inflict Guard Break). There are also SP moves, which are akin to abilities and spells, and EXE Drives, which are your special moves that use up your EXE Gauge's charges. Another handy feature is that all the CPU characters (The goddess characters) can use HDD. This transforms your character and dramatically raises all of the stats, for the cost of 20% of your max SP.
Oh, the enemies you fight? They're the usual slimes, dragons, flowers, flying whales, dating sims, tetris blocks, and otakus you see in normal RPG's.
There are also plenty of things to do on the world map, such as unlocking plans which you use for the Remake System, a mechanic that is kind-of like crafting (you trade in materials for a boatload of things), and Disc Development, which are kind-of like accessories, giving you many different buffs depending on the discs you used. There are also many... interesting NPC's which spawn over the course of the game, giving you... insightful comments or just stuff in general.
---------------------------------------
Now... story:
The game puts you in control of Neptune, or as we all know her, Nep-Nep. After a massive fall down from the heavens she finds herself with amnesia. She hears a voice from a so called Histoire, telling her to collect all of the Key Fragments to release her. This leads her on a non-sensical (mostly because of Neptune herself) journey all over Gamindustri. During the game you meet loads of interesting characters, all being completely different from the next. Personally, the characters were my favorite. To mention a few: There's Vert, the mega gamer, MAGES., the Steins;Gate reference  incarnate character, Noire the tsundere... the list goes on. Honestly, the characters themselves can make a purchase worth it, even if you aren't too into cute JRPG's.
The game also has a pretty crazy end-game if you get all of the DLC's. If you love difficult bosses and a boatload of things to do, you'll definitely love it. Not even close to finished and still having tons of fun.
---------------------------------------
However, as many amazing things this game has... it has many flaws (which I've heard the sequels improve on).
The first being random difficulty spikes. I don't mean the kind that will make you die a few times... I mean the few that will nearly make you slam your hand into your monitor. The most prominent being as early as chapter 2 (experienced people will know who I am talking about). Then there are also dungeons which are ridiculously easy... followed by one dungeon who happened to have an enemy that could go "viral" and destroy you. Happy times!
Re-using dungeon layouts. A lot. With this I mean that you will through-out the story see dungeons that you have already been in, but they have different enemies and harvest points. Optional dungeons follow the same trend, unfortunately. I personally didn't see this as a major thing, but I know some people out there could be irritated by this.
Text formatting going off-screen. Yeah that might sound weird, but basically, there are times when the text goes out of the text boxes so you can't see all of it. It happens in dialogue and on descriptions, and it's quite a shame (especially if you have Japanese voices on).
---------------------------------------
TL;DR Section
Pros:
+ Amusing nonsensical story*
+ Loads of references
+ Amazing cast of characters
+ Simple yet addicting battle system
+ Great end-game full of content
Cons:
- Crazy difficulty spikes
- Repetitive dungeon design
- Sloppy text-formatting
- Generally a bad PC port + no keyboard prompts, awkward controls
All-in-all, I would highly recommend this game. Incredible fun, full of laughs and "tense" moments. But do be wary of the few quirks that comes with the PC port, and game in general.
*I find the nonsensical story as a positive things because I find that breaking the 4th wall is hilarious,  which this game does /A LOT/.

Silly as frick. The story isn't as consistently, jaw-droppingly inspired in its absurd escalations as SR3, but the game plays way better. As a counterpoint to GTA 5, which was the deathknell of the open-world crime game by way of being mired in its conventions and weirdly vicious approach to everything, SR4 is the deathknell by way of showing the absolute limits of what you can do with the formula. What I mean is, within the first hour you get superpowers that let you jump really high, run really fast, and basically fly. Combined, all three of these make stealing in a car, driving around and committing crimes seem antiquated and ridiculous. It's faster and more satisfying to super-run through cars, super jump across rooftops, and fly.
It is hard to talk about what happens in the game without giving away huge spoilers, but let's just say that its entire tone is a very knowing sense of the word "badical." It takes itself very seriously, even when the things it is taking seriously are how totally badass it was that you just climbed a really tall tower and got to the top, or how a confrontation with the alien overlord starts with you, the President of the United States, jumping out of the huge 8-barrel POTUS-branded AA cannon that is stationed on the White House lawn, and running at the crashed alien scout you just shot down, jumping at the front window and shooting it out with a pistol and immediately engaging in a Rowdy Roddy Piper/Keith David "They Live"-esque brawl with said overlord.
Anyone who takes it seriously and makes a character that looks remotely realistic is absolutely playing the game completely wrong and seems to have missed the pitch slider on the voices. The game is basically Your Fricking Ridiculous Power Fantasy: The Game, and is designed around both exceeding your wildest expectations while also subverting them. If there is one thing that the game is willing to critique, it is itself; its existence, your desire to play it, and the video game industry as a whole. It's never condescending when it does this, and comes across as the wet fever dream of a designer at the end of their life, transcribed via dying breaths, and developed as a celebratory eulogy to everything that once was. Its comments are made with a light touch, even when the game itself is so intent on destroying the world and starting over.

This visual novel is, and I say this with the utmost confidence, one of the most interesting and engrossing visual novels which I have played to date. As a visual novel with high quality looking assets, I wanted to enjoy it but I couldn't.
The story plot from as far as I have played, didn't stir any interest from me (besides its beautiful assets ofc).
The protagonist is just a guy who feels sorry for himself and thinks too much, heaps of inner dialogue that jump from one topic to the next not really serving any purpose besides telling the reader what we already know from a paragraph or so in; he feels sorry for himself. Instead of assuming we know that by now, this concept gets dragged on for such a long time making -me- feel sorry for myself as he goes on and on about his boring lifestory.
I think what makes it really hard for me to continue playing is my lack of interest in the protagonist as a character I will have to put up with the whole visual novel through. While I understand his sentiments and probably the purpose of him being so lifeless before he gets to the actual camp and 'lives it up' or something like that, I still don't get it and I don't agree with the execution.
Another thing that bothered me was the blurr effects in the beginning when he looks around his room. I don't quite understand the purpose of that and it just annoyed me. Is he still sleepy or something? Why can't he talk about that instead of how ordinary and uninteresting his life is? At least that would serve an actual purpose.
Like I said, I haven't played much and I wanted to give it a chance but it is what it is.
It may be considered as a 'visual novel loved by many' in the description but I'm sorry, count me out. It just isn't for me.
Soviet Games, I hope you continue making more visual novels to come with your beautiful assets and put more thought into the writing delivery/ cut out the unnecessary bits because the length of a story doesn't equal quality.

Grim Dawn may be a little harder to get into than most hack n' slashes, but it's crafted with an old-school gaming approach coupled with newer solutions found in the latest games.
Rich, dark atmosphere has a surprising amount of depth and choices that impact gameplay. While the storyline isn't that involving (saving the world from invading monster factions and learning why), seeing how the people in-game are affected definitely is. Under all this there's plenty of cleverly hidden lore and hard-to-find secret areas.
Pros:
+Good twist on typical skill tress, where you select two classes and find synergy between them, and decide how deeply you invest into a class
+Devotion is a system of common abilities that can back up the weakness of your character. For example, if you lack survivability, you can go for a number of defensive procs. The shrines for these devotion points are found throughout the world, which encourages exploration
+Very cool bosses, tough dungeons, good enemy variety
+An interesting faction system to make the grind matter a little more
+Powerful legendary items that are rarer than in most ARPGs, making them more prestigious
+After 200 hours, there's still so much to do
Cons
- Netplay experience may vary
- Often doesn't feel rewarding enough. You'll have a very hard time finding legendaries for your build, may have to trade
- Feels grindy. It takes a lot of time to slog through all the difficulties to get to Ultimate, and farming infamy for the enemy factions can be very tedious
With hundreds of build combinations, an expansive world, and the ability to play with friends, Grim Dawn breathes new life into the old-school hack n' slash games. It may feel too grindy at times, but the combat is crisp and satisfying at all times.

TL;DR Decent Titan Quest mod that can be recommended ONLY to die-hard fans of TQ and Diablo. However, if you are new to the genre or looking for a complete story, you should look elsewhere.
* Quite addictive loot oriented ARPG. Twin brother of Titan Quest, sister of Torchlight, cousin of Diablo, 1st cousing once removed of Incredible Adv. of Van Helsing, teenage grandkid of Path of Exile
* Good, not great, but good music
* Stable. Had only 1 crash over the span of 60+ hours.
* Potions and currency picked up automatically
* A lot of inventory room, which reduces runs to the shop. Although Torchlight-like pet would be better.
* Some of the lore is very dark, grim and written well.
* Couple references to movies and books
* Unfinished story that probably will be complete with the upcoming DLC
* Gets repetitive, but it is inevitable with most ARPG. Only two types of quests: kill or find something by killing
* A single cutscene and no noticeable transitions or stories between Acts
* Confusing UI elements and some gameplay mechanics
* Mostly boring loot, that does not add much beside higher stats before the end-game.
* No quest pointers on the map unless you are close to the destination
* Can not add map markers to return to places you were not able to fully explore
* Gets quite easy (on Veteran) after a few hours and you have to finish the game several times to unlock next difficulties
* For the most part, uninspiring locations feel the same and have similar layout
* Unable to fully respec, meaning that you can sink 50 points (~17 levels, which is 1/3 by the end of 1st playthrough) into a class that you might not even use.

This is a very interesting game. It takes MOBA style objectives in order to win, FPS style shooting, Minecraft style building all bundled together into one game. When first entering a game you have 5 mins to build with blocks. The goal of the game is to Protect your "cores" while attacking the enemy's. Within these 5 minutes you have to build fortifactions, and maybe a setup to build into No man's land. When this time is up the barrier that blocks you disappears and you attack. Every character is uniquely designed weapons wise. The medic has a gun that arcs balls, a robot with a chaingun, a soldier with a m60, a hunter with a sniper (scopeless), a ninja with shurikans, and an engineer with a shotgun. While these characters are interesting I do have to admit certain guns are directly more powerful than others. The sniper rifle can be used in CQB and is generally better than the Medic's "bubble gun". In certain times it can even trump the shotgun that can only be used in close quarters. While the chaingun does do fast damage. With that said maybe these classes aren't right for me since I use cogwheel the robot tank mostly. With all that said, this game plays well and is a lot of fun.  However I came along with some issues.
Number 1: The game can be VERY slow. As in the two teams just defend and no  one tries to make a move. I've been in many hour + games.
While this is mostly the player's fault, it can be resolved with a timer ticking down or some sort of penalty.
Number 2: If you get stuck with a new player, you lost.
The game has a video explaining what to do, and it doesn't explain well. A hands on tutorial would be best to fix this
Number 3: If one person leaves, you are at a serious disadvantage and have a way greater chance at losing the game.
Like issue number 1, this is more player's error, but can be fixed with a severe penalty. Leaving a game because you died once is no reason to make your team lose.
Numbner 3.5: There are as many AFKers as people that leave too.
Once again, have a penalty for AFKing, or make it easy to report these players
Number 4: This game is no way worth the price it's being asked. It's a fun game, but not a $30 fun game.

Divinty: Original Sin is a phenomenal RPG, and I'm sure many other people will tell you that. You've probably also heard about it's similarity to Baldur's Gate, which I happily agree with. However, like Baldur's Gate, there are several parts of the game that are, to say the least, a bit rough around the edges. For example, me and my friend were walking on the beach, and we came across an active minefield, seemingly completely at random. So, for about 40 minutes, we tried to get through it without dieing, which failed. I'm sure you can understand my problem with random, unexplained, undetectable mines that kill me instantly. This is was my ONLY complaint, as literally every other individual atom the game was extremely high quality till that point. This happened only about 2 hours in. Now comes my second problem. We ran around, snuck into houses, broke doors, and bought tons of stuff thinking it would help us progress. We did the story quest up until a certain point, but then were unable to prgress due to enemies of far higher level than we were at the time. So, I did the unthinkable, and looked it up on the wiki. The problem, as was soon revealed to my aggravated self, was that in hour 1, my friend had said no to a question, which cut us off of a 10,000 XP questline, which would have allowed us to level up to the point we could fight the enemies we were being crushed by. I loaded my earliest save with a few quiet mumbles about how much I wanted to stab people, and realized that the literal first thing we did in the town we spent 7 hours in made it so that, no matter what we did, we could not progress. I will still reccomend this game, beacuse of every other thing about it being amazing.

As much as I wanted to like this game, it does fall short and hits its head on the side of the table.
Where to start, even? Graphics! I'm not sure why there is a zoom option. It only makes the sprites, which are fixed in resolution, shoddy looking and blurred. The GUI is terribad, really really god awful. Many times, sprites and their HP/SHIELD icons overlap, and you cannot tell who has how much health. Also, I felt that, during marching scenes and the bridge-battle, too many sprites were reused, which created a cheap Habbo Hotel feel to the whole scene. God is in the details, developers!
Bugs here and there. Made one of the archer characters completely unusable, as her ability to create an arrow trap locks up the game, and all you can do is to kill the process and start again from the last save point. While on this, the developers are struggling with bringing the game to Linux as a platform to the point that they have decided to drop support in the sequel. Speaks volumes if you ask me. Performance was bad, and memory leaks forced me to kill the game after 40 minutes of gameplay, in the middle of combat, and restart it just to avoid an inevitable spiral to 1 FPS land.
I didn't like the resource management in the game. Most of your resources come from the Giants fighting plenty good fights. Then, those resources are spent on food for the villagers, so that your teeny-tiny people do not starve to death. Maybe I should have just let them starve to death and spend the Renown on upgrading my units? I'm not sure there are consequences to letting your villagers die, really, as the whole game seems to lack consequences to decisions, besides in what shape and form you start your battle and whether someone dies instantly/disappears or not. Most choices felt completely bipolar and without much effect on the world or even our own situation. Sometimes you get ♥♥♥♥ed over, but that's about it.
Story-wise, I like what they did with the characters. The Norse-myth inspired world they painted does bring warmth to my Norse-mythology tinkering heart. The MAP alone is worth an article on lore and love that pours through it. However, what you get for your money is half a game, a prequel to the end of the world. As it turns out, the developers really liked the basic plot device of Game of Thrones, and the Northern barbarians/obsidian people are being pushed into your people by the possibly terrible, unknown force.
All in all, the game feels like a great concept done in mediocre fashion.

Put Star Ocean, Final Fantasy and Phantasy Star Portable together with crazy cute flavouring and you probably have Hyperdimension Neptunia Re:Birth1.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re:Birth1 is an all-girl casted (spare a few NPCs) turn based RPG that doesn't take itself too seriously, with easy to learn but hard to master combat system. Felistella has taken the best of Hyperdimension Neptunia, Hyperdimension Neptunia mk2 and Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory, ripped apart the first of the three and rebuilt it, bringing us the definitive Hyperdimension Neptunia experience.
The story is presented using 3D animations in the visual novel style, has decent pacing and the humour has quite a few laughs (but some groans, too). You'll move the story along primarily through dungeons and events activated in one of the game's four cities. Dungeons are explored in 3D third person, with treasure to find, resources to harvest and of course, lots of monsters to fight. While exploring a dungeon, monsters are encounted by making contact with them. You can get a pre-emptive attack on these monsters by performing a Symbol Attack, in which you swing your weapon at their hit box in the dungeon to initiate a battle. Should you fail to do so, monsters have a chance to launch a Surprise Attack. Otherwise who gets the first move is determined by the characters' agility stat vs the monsters'. Once defeated, monsters respawn after about a minute for you to fight again if you so desire, though they are easy to avoid should you not as they have relatively short leashes.
One thing to note about the combat is that it has some really steep difficulty spikes. All monsters are not created equal, and while the last fight may have gone smooth as butter, the next one may be tough as nails. Certain monsters can become infected with a virus that will recover all damage they have sustained, and provide healthy boost to their stats. A single viral monster can potentially wipe out your party without either careful planning, or a quick escape! The toughest monsters in each dungeon, fortunately will not actively chase you if you don't want to fight them. Seemingly sure of their superiority and unconcerned with your insignificance, 'Risky Monsters' will ignore your existence unless you actively engage them.
Outside of the combat system, the game has fully fleshed out shops with new weapons and armour regularly added. But besides that, the player has the ability to add items to the store through the Remake system. The Remake system is this game's version of crafting, which, as you'd expect allows you to craft items of all varieties including, but not limited to consumables, weapons, armour and costumes. But you can also use the Remake system to, with the right materials, alter the game's difficulty (easier or harder), manipulate which items drop in which dungeons, or even create new dungeons and quests altogether, should you have obtained the required Plan(s) to do so. Some of the harder side dungeons, which are difficult well beyond that of the story dungeons as well as the DLC Colusseum, can add quite a bit of longevity to a playthrough, and into New Game+.
At its end, as far as JRPG PC ports go, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 sets the standard. After a little buggy release, the game runs smoothly on PC hardware new and old, supporting a wide variety of resolutions up to 1080p (but not 1200p for my monitor, the dastards!). However, it has a fixed graphics quality setting that looks okay but is about par for the course with what a PS3 or VITA would be capable of. My solitary complaint about the port is that the game does not seem to run in true fullscreen. My screen still goes into sleep mode while the game is running if I have walked away for a few minutes. This might seem like an upside to some, but for me it's a minor annoyance.

is a traditional Japanese role playing game combined with a visual novel. The game caters to a niche audience and makes no effort to accommodate newcomers or uninitiated. The storyline borders on the acceptable limits of both the narrative meta and the digital millennium copyright act. The gameplay is demandingly taxing on the player’s patience. Furthermore, the presentation is borderline insanity and will ultimately make or break the experience.
is a game that only pleases a very narrow audience through a collection of either off-putting or appealing elements.
The game’s storyline demands an extreme measure of patience from the player and a great deal of tolerance for overused references and clichés.
is set in Gameindustria; an analogous universe that represents the four sided console war of the seventh generation. Each nation or faction is governed by a goddess, or avatar, that represents the faction’s home console. The player takes control of Neptune, an amnesiac avatar who represents Sega, who in turn has to travel the world and gather allies and fight enemies in the respective lands referencing Sony, Microsoft and Nintendo.
Each nation is headed by a respective goddess with each their own distinct appearance and personality. The ensemble cast is rounded out by characters representing popular franchises and companies such as Tekken and Monster Hunter. The plot has Neptune search the lands for her purpose in life and reason behind the constant attacks on everyone’s nations by a mysterious adversary. The majority of the plot is told through scrolling text accompanied with expressive portraits. The sheer extent of time that is spent reading is jarring. A large portion of the narrative is dedicated to characters’ development, usually manifesting in a three-way discussion on the merits of substantial bosoms or the palatability of dairy products. The discussions are rife with references to videogame history, internet memes and porn chichés which all add up to a staggering number of times that the player will end up rolling their eyes and sighing in mild annoyance. The overall experience is not helped by the characters instance on breaking the fourth wall and actually berating themselves for talking too much, only to resume the cacophony of clichéd locution.
In all, the plot wafer thin in depth, richly spread with stale tropes and references.

Gameplay revolves around a battle system and exploration with some novel ideals, but ultimately grows stale and monotonous. When not trapped in an incessant lecture on the benefits of fruits from the nightshade family the game plays like a traditional Japanese role playing game. The player explores dungeons with different enemies and treasures to fulfil quests and craft new items. The crafting system allows the player not only to make new weapons and armour, but also reduce the difficulty to increase the amount of power generated when using attacks or the amount of experience points awarded after a fight.
A general battle will be turn based, with each character being a given a slot in a sequential order governed by the character’s statistics. The player must the position the character adjacent to the enemy and select from the available attacks. Attacks come in three varieties and are either geared toward the generation of EXE power, dealing raw damage or the deterioration of the enemy’s defence gauge. When a certain amount of EXE power is earned additional attacks may be used or the special abilities may be unleashed to generally annihilate the enemy in a grandiose and gratuitous manner befitting of a mainstream Japanese cartoon. While the system is fully customisable and offers some level of depth, it quickly degenerates into an automated sequence where EXE building will be followed by guard breaking and ultimately unleashing the aforementioned special attacks to quickly end the fight. However, while there is a system in place with elemental attacks and a physical versus magic attack split, it hardly ever has any effect on the battle’s procedure; eliminating any all need for proper tactics.
Furthermore, the game’s difficulty tends to spike to unreasonable levels and demands a degree of mandatory grinding for experience before allowing the player to pass to the next chapter of the story. Naturally, grinding comes into play when using the craft system as it demands items only dropped by certain enemies. These enemies only drop the items by chance, so repetition sets in fast when the same enemy is slain over and over in an attempt to acquire a particular item.
stagnates fast under its almost archaically traditional combat system and barely acceptable random drop mechanics while exploring monotonous and linear dungeons.
The overall presentation is where game finds its initial appeal, however, upon further inspection will be the most prominent factor for playing or dropping the game. While the game is bright and colourful, both in setting and characters, the game is terribly guilty of reusing its assets to a criminal extent. It is not uncommon to find the exact same enemy in the final stage as one you found in the introduction stage. Only the name will make any difference.
The dungeons themselves fall victim to the recycling of assets as well. The game contains exactly one warehouse map, and it is reused five times, each time filled with the same or palette swapped enemies.
The main characters themselves in the meantime suffer from stale animations. Characters seem to float over the ground rather than walking on it. Jumping might as well have been teleportation because it violates roughly eight of the twelve rules of animation. When attacking, there is either a blinding flurry with no weight to it, or a brutal swing that looked cool, but did not do any significant damage.
During the story scenes the characters interact through portraits with various expressions. Particular focus is placed on character’s chest area. Considering the lack of assets in the aforementioned region on some of the characters in addition to the rather revealing attire, it might not be the best game to have installed on a hard drive if the player’s country of residence has a legal grey area in regards to the depiction of underage looking characters.
The visuals are accompanied by music and voice acting that breach any and all limits that can be endured by a living soul. The music is catchy and appropriately a blend of techno, rock and chiptune. However, the cuts are extremely short, so the same few notes play ad infinitum until insanity ensues. The voice acting is beyond comprehension. Most characters have voices that are so high pitched they can shatter glass. The fact that most of the delivery consists of screaming and yelling only aggravates the situation. Considering that all the of game’s text is voiced will quickly lead to the realisation that in addition to a JRPG, this game also contains an audio book where the entire novel is screamed at you. Luckily the game features an English voice track that is considerable more subdued and less obnoxious in addition to not dubbing half the dialog in lieu of some much needed silence.
In all,
is a very special game with a number of features that appeal to a very small audience. However, for everyone else, this game suffers from stale gameplay, agonising voice acting, grating music, substandard animation and modelling, a bizarre story and dubious character development. Yet, if all of the aforementioned complaints are exactly the elements you are looking for in a game, then I would recommend it. Anyone else will want to take note of it, and rather look for a more conventional game.
